Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-17 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #74 (daily 5-paper run) Topic ID: HP-075

Keywords: soluble guanylate cyclase; riociguat; pulmonary hypertension; vericiguat; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; cryo-EM; heart failure; ChEMBL

Abstract

Pulmonary hypertension affects about 1% of the global population, and its treatment rests on the NO–sGC–cGMP pathway: riociguat, the first soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, sensitises the enzyme to nitric oxide and stimulates it directly, and improved the 6-minute walk distance by 36 m in pulmonary arterial hypertension (PATENT-1) and 46 m in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CHEST-1). We asked whether the standard rigid-docking benchmark of this series can rank sGC stimulators at all, using the riociguat-bound cryo-EM structure 7D9R (3.7 Å) after the pipeline's first run failed on the wrong domain — the ligand-free catalytic structure 4NI2. Riociguat re-docked into its own H-NOX pocket at −9.96 kcal/mol with three poses within 0.06 kcal/mol, and the five most potent ChEMBL leads (cellular EC50 1–4 nM) scored from −10.97 to −8.59. The rank correlation against measured potency was Spearman rho −0.41 (n = 5, standard convention), a moderate correct-direction correlation that does not reach the pre-stated refutation threshold of −0.5 — and the table itself shows why: the two compounds with the identical measured EC50 of 3 nM score 2.38 kcal/mol apart, the best and the worst of the five. Falsifiable claim: rigid Vina docking on a single cryo-EM structure cannot rank sGC stimulators whose potencies span less than its own noise. Falsifier: a rescoring method, or a second structure, that reaches rho −0.5 or below against the same five EC50s, or a head-to-head cellular assay that reproduces the docking order. The screen's value is the calibration, not the table: the next sGC stimulator should be judged by a cellular assay, not by a docking score.

1. Introduction

Pulmonary hypertension affects about 1% of the world's population, rising to 10% of people over 65 — and about 80% of those affected live in developing countries, where it is frequently tied to congenital heart disease and infections such as schistosomiasis, HIV and rheumatic heart disease (Hoeper et al. 2016). Two of its five groups are the precapillary forms that riociguat treats: pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH, WHO Group 1), a progressive vasculopathy of the small pulmonary arteries, and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH, WHO Group 4), where organised clot obstructs the pulmonary arteries. For CTEPH the treatment of choice is surgery — pulmonary endarterectomy, which is potentially curative — and until 2013 there was no approved drug at all for patients whose disease was inoperable or persisted after surgery. Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is the same pathway's other end: the NO–sGC–cGMP axis fails, and the heart cannot compensate.

The pathway is simple to state and hard to drug. Nitric oxide (NO) binds the haem iron of soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC), a heterodimer of one α and one β subunit, and the enzyme converts GTP to cyclic GMP, which relaxes vascular smooth muscle. In pulmonary hypertension the NO signal is impaired — less NO is made, and the sGC that remains is less responsive. Riociguat, the first soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, attacks both halves of that failure: it sensitises sGC to whatever NO is present by stabilising NO binding, and it directly stimulates the enzyme through a separate site, independently of NO. It binds in the haem pocket of the β1 H-NOX domain — not in the catalytic domain where GTP is turned over. The US FDA approved riociguat (Adempas, Bayer) on 8 October 2013 for PAH and for inoperable or persistent/recurrent CTEPH, the first drug in its class and the first drug of any class shown to work in CTEPH. Its classmate vericiguat followed the same pathway into heart failure: the VICTORIA trial led to FDA approval on 20 January 2021 for symptomatic chronic HFrEF with ejection fraction below 45%.

The trial record is unusually clean for a first-in-class drug. In PATENT-1 (443 patients with PAH), riociguat improved the 6-minute walk distance by a least-squares mean of 36 m over placebo at 12 weeks (95% CI 20–52 m; P < 0.001), with significant improvements in pulmonary vascular resistance, NT-proBNP, WHO functional class, time to clinical worsening and dyspnoea score (Ghofrani et al. 2013). In CHEST-1 (261 patients with inoperable or persistent CTEPH), the walk distance improved by 46 m (95% CI 25–67 m; P < 0.001) and pulmonary vascular resistance fell by 246 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ (95% CI −303 to −190; P < 0.001) at 16 weeks (Ghofrani et al. 2013). In VICTORIA (5,050 patients with worsening HFrEF), vericiguat reduced the primary outcome — cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalisation — from 38.5% to 35.5% over a median of 10.8 months (hazard ratio 0.90; 95% CI 0.82–0.98; P = 0.02), an absolute risk reduction of 4.2 events per 100 patient-years (Armstrong et al. 2020). These are modest, real effects — a 36–46 m walk gain, a 10% relative risk reduction — not cures, and the drugs carry a boxed warning for embryo-foetal toxicity.

This paper asks a narrower question than the trials did: can the standard rigid-docking benchmark used in this series — ChEMBL potency retrieval plus AutoDock Vina docking on the best available structure — rank sGC stimulators at all? The test case is deliberately hard. The five most potent ChEMBL leads for the sGC target span only 1–4 nM in cellular EC50 — a four-fold range, 0.6 log units — while Vina's own noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, equivalent to roughly a 5- to 30-fold potency difference. If the screen cannot order compounds whose measured potencies differ by less than its own noise, that is a finding about the screen, not about the compounds — and it matters, because the next sGC stimulator a Pakistani laboratory might screen will be judged by exactly this kind of table.

Falsifiable question (stated before the results): can rigid Vina docking on the riociguat-bound structure 7D9R rank the five most potent measured sGC stimulators (EC50 1–4 nM) in their measured order? The claim is that it cannot — the potency spread is narrower than the method's noise. The claim is refuted if the standard Spearman rank correlation between Vina affinity and measured pChEMBL reaches −0.5 or below (negative = correct direction: better dock, more potent) for the five leads, or if a rescoring method reaches that threshold on the same five compounds.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

PubMed (E-utilities, accessed 17 November 2026) for riociguat, vericiguat, soluble guanylate cyclase structure and pulmonary hypertension epidemiology, cross-checked against the trial records and the 2022 ESC/ERS pulmonary hypertension guidelines. Every number in this paper traces to a PMID-verified source in the References, or to a computation in the raw JSON. The Islamic canon check is in §2.5.

2.2 Target verification, and the discarded wrong-domain run

The target was resolved by the standard pipeline (run_docking.py --target "Soluble guanylate cyclase" --ref "riociguat"): ChEMBL target CHEMBL2111348, "Soluble guanylate cyclase", a PROTEIN COMPLEX GROUP of four human components (Q02153, O75343, P33402, Q02108), with 58 bioactivities retrieved and 26 leads ranked. The target identification is correct and was verified live against the ChEMBL API.

The docking step of that run failed, and the failure is reported in full rather than hidden: DOCK_LEADS False, 4NI2, no_ligand_site. The pipeline's PDB picker is X-ray-only (resolution < 3.0 Å), and it picked 4NI2 — the heterodimeric catalytic domain of human sGC, which contains no bound ligand at all (only ethylene glycol and waters). Riociguat does not bind the catalytic domain; it binds the haem pocket of the β1 H-NOX domain, so 4NI2 was the wrong domain, not merely a missing ligand. No docking table was published from that run. The run is preserved as dock-HP-075-2026-11-17.json.

2.3 Corrected computation: docking on 7D9R

A corrected driver (dock_hp075_sgc_2026-11-17.py, RDKit venv) docks on PDB 7D9R — human sGC in the riociguat- and NO-bound state, cryo-EM at 3.7 Å (Liu et al. 2021, Nat Commun 12:5492). The structure's HETATM records were audited before docking: GZO is riociguat (verified against RCSB chemcomp GZO, formula C20H19FN8O2), HEM is the catalytic haem, and G2P is a GTP analogue sitting in the catalytic domain. The centre was set explicitly on the GZO centroid, computed from the 7D9R HETATM records, because the pipeline's centre picker (dock._ligand_center) would have landed on G2P (32 atoms) over GZO (31 atoms) — the catalytic domain again, 69.26 Å from the riociguat site. The audit numbers are in §3.1.

Six compounds were docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses, best pose reported — the same protocol as Papers #1/#3: riociguat itself (the QUERY, PubChem-verified SMILES, ChEMBL CHEMBL2107834, max phase 4) as the re-docked control, and the top five ChEMBL leads by the pipeline's composite rank, all with measured cellular EC50 values of 1–4 nM. The driver checkpoints every completed dock to a partial JSON, so a killed run resumes rather than restarting. Two leads exceeded the pipeline's 900-second Vina timeout on the first pass and were re-docked at 1,800 seconds with the identical protocol (see §3.2). The Spearman rank correlation between Vina affinity and measured pChEMBL was computed for the five leads with the standard convention — Pearson correlation of ascending ranks of the raw values, exactly as scipy.stats.spearmanr computes it, with average ranks for ties. Negative rho means the correct direction (more negative affinity pairs with higher pChEMBL). Riociguat is excluded from the correlation: ChEMBL holds no EC50 for it on this target, only a minimum effective concentration (MEC) of 0.03 µM (30 nM) in CHO cells.

2.4 PAINS screen and property panel

RDKit descriptors, Lipinski and Veber rules and the PAINS filter were computed for riociguat and the five leads by the standard pipeline. A PAINS alert is reported, never hidden. No ToxGuard read-across numbers are claimed: the pipeline output stores no ToxGuard values for this target's leads, so none are reported.

2.5 Literature and the Islamic canon

The relevant Islamic canon was checked alongside the modern literature, per the literature map. The directly relevant work is Ibn al-Nafis, Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun (Commentary on the Anatomy in the Canon, 1242) — the first description of the pulmonary circulation, three centuries before Harvey, stating that blood passes from the right ventricle through the lungs to the left side of the heart. The disease this paper treats — pressure rising in the pulmonary circuit — is a disorder of exactly the circuit Ibn al-Nafis described. The systematising source is Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (Canon of Medicine, c. 1025), whose Book II (materia medica) and Book III (diseases of individual organs, including the heart and chest) framed the clinical observation of breathlessness and cardiac disease that the Canon's commentators inherited. The policy principle used in §6 is hifz al-nafs — preservation of life, the first of the maqasid al-shariah — with maslaha (public benefit) and adl (justice in access). Honest limit: Ibn al-Nafis's Sharh survives as an Arabic manuscript (rediscovered in Berlin, 1924) and exists in English only in partial translation; the full 23 volumes of Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi are likewise available in English only in selections. Neither was read in full for this paper; the claims made here rest on the verified historical record of what the works contain, and the gap is named again in §5.

2.6 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the measured values are functional cellular EC50s, not binding affinities; the structure is 3.7 Å cryo-EM with modelled ligand coordinates; the receptor preparation strips the haem, so scores are shape-only against a haem-free pocket; and the five leads span only a four-fold potency range, so the rank test is underpowered by design (n = 5, with a tie at 3 nM). No molecular dynamics and no free-energy rescoring were run.

3. Results

3.1 The structure audit: 7D9R, and why the picker would have failed again

The 7D9R file's HETATM records contain four groups: G2P (32 atoms, the GTP analogue), HEM (43 atoms, the haem), GZO (31 atoms, riociguat) and MG (2 atoms). Their centroids are: GZO (riociguat) [110.71, 116.48, 123.08]; HEM [101.84, 115.59, 114.22], 12.57 Å from the riociguat centroid; G2P [179.35, 125.6, 124.65], 69.26 Å from the riociguat centroid, in the catalytic domain. The pipeline's centre picker (dock._ligand_center) returns the G2P centroid — the largest HETATM group — which is 69.26 Å from the riociguat site. Had the corrected driver trusted the picker, it would have docked into the catalytic domain a second time. The centre used here is the GZO centroid, computed directly from the HETATM records and audited against the parent run's independent computation (identical to 0.01 Å).

The discarded pipeline run is worth one paragraph because it is the paper's first finding. The target was right (CHEMBL2111348, verified live), the leads were real (26 ranked, 58 bioactivities), and the docking still failed — because the structure picker is X-ray-only below 3.0 Å and the only riociguat-bound structure in the PDB is a 3.7 Å cryo-EM map. A pipeline that cannot see cryo-EM structures cannot dock a drug whose only bound structure is cryo-EM. The rule this paper states, and follows, is the same as the RSV paper's: no verified structure, no docking table — a structure without a verified ligand pocket gets a corrected run, never a published table.

3.2 Docking: the comparison table

Six compounds were docked on 7D9R at the GZO centre (Vina 1.2.7, box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses). All six are PAINS-clean; all pass Lipinski and Veber.

Compound Measured EC50 pChEMBL Best affinity (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses PAINS
CHEMBL3976666 3.0 nM 8.52 −10.97 −10.97, −10.16, +13.09 none
CHEMBL3892047 1.0 nM 9.00 −10.86 −10.86, −10.02, −9.06 none
CHEMBL3939276 2.0 nM 8.70 −9.97 −9.97, −9.88, −9.12 none
Riociguat (QUERY, re-dock) MEC 30 nM* — −9.96 −9.96, −9.95, −9.90 none
CHEMBL4113635 4.0 nM 8.40 −9.12 −9.12, −7.60, −7.60 none
CHEMBL3906941 3.0 nM 8.52 −8.59 −8.59, −7.96, −7.31 none

* Riociguat has no EC50 in ChEMBL for this target; the value shown is its minimum effective concentration (MEC) of 0.03 µM in CHO cells, and it is excluded from the rank correlation. Measured EC50s are cellular sGC activation values (homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence assay, CHO cells; document CHEMBL3886753, verified live for the top lead).

Three things in this table deserve attention. First, the control works: riociguat returns to its own pocket at −9.96 kcal/mol with three poses within 0.06 kcal/mol — the tightest pose set in the table, and the protocol behaving as intended on this structure. Second, the two best-docked leads are the joint-largest molecules in the set (both MW 569.7, against riociguat's 422.42), and every lead is larger and more lipophilic than the reference (MW 540–576, logP 4.5–4.7, against logP 2.44). Vina rewards size: more atoms mean more contacts. A table that reads as "two leads beat riociguat" is partly a table that reads as "two bigger molecules fill more of the pocket". Third, the pose sets are uneven: CHEMBL3976666's third pose is +13.09 kcal/mol — a clashing pose — so its best score rests on a single well-placed mode with a poor tail, while CHEMBL3939276's three poses span only 0.85 kcal/mol. Pose consistency is part of the result, not a footnote.

Two leads did not dock on the first pass. CHEMBL4113635 and CHEMBL3906941 both exceeded the pipeline's 900-second Vina timeout on the large 7D9R receptor file (1.3 MB PDBQT) and returned no score. They were re-docked with the identical protocol (same exhaustiveness, same centre, same box) after raising the Vina timeout to 1,800 seconds in dock.py — a wall-time change only, recorded here so the run can be reproduced. Both then completed (4113635 at −9.12, 3906941 at −8.59). The timeout is itself a result: on a receptor this large, the standard pipeline's time budget is a binding constraint, and a future sGC screen that does not budget for it will silently lose its slowest ligands.

3.3 The rank test: rho −0.41, and the two 3 nM compounds

The Spearman rank correlation between Vina affinity and measured pChEMBL for the five leads is rho = −0.41 (n = 5), computed with the standard convention (Pearson correlation of ascending ranks, average rank for ties — the tie is the two 3 nM compounds, both pChEMBL 8.52) and verified independently from the table. The sign is negative, the correct direction. The value does not reach the pre-stated refutation threshold of −0.5, so the claim in §1 — that rigid docking on a single cryo-EM structure cannot rank these stimulators — is not refuted. But the number needs its uncertainty stated next to it: with n = 5, the Fisher z 95% confidence interval for rho is approximately (−0.95, +0.74), which spans strong-correct to strong-wrong. The point estimate is moderate and correct-direction; the interval says the data cannot distinguish a working screen from a broken one. Both statements are true, and the paper reports both.

The table shows the reason directly, without needing the correlation at all. The two compounds with the identical measured EC50 of 3 nM — CHEMBL3976666 and CHEMBL3906941, both pChEMBL 8.52 — score −10.97 and −8.59 kcal/mol: 2.38 kcal/mol apart, the best and the worst scores in the table, for the same measured potency. That gap is larger than Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and larger than the 1.74 kcal/mol spread of the other three leads' best scores. The extremes order correctly — the most potent lead (1 nM) scores second-best, the weakest (4 nM) scores second-worst — but the middle of the table is noise, and the middle is where the ranking would have to work to be useful. A screen that orders the extremes and scrambles the middle cannot rank a series whose whole measured range is 1–4 nM (0.6 log units), when 1 kcal/mol of Vina noise already equals a 5.4-fold potency difference.

3.4 Comparison with the trials, and with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of riociguat or these leads on 7D9R was found in the literature sweep, so there is no published docking table to compare against. The structural fact is published: 7D9R is the riociguat- and NO-bound sGC structure (Liu et al. 2021), and the activation mechanism — stimulators binding the β1 H-NOX pocket, acting both with NO and independently of it — is the same mechanism the trials tested. The trial numbers therefore stand as the comparison, not as a validation of the docking: PATENT-1's 36 m walk gain, CHEST-1's 46 m and 246 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵ PVR fall, VICTORIA's hazard ratio of 0.90. Those are effects of the drug in patients; the docking table is a shape score against a haem-free pocket. The two should not be confused, and the paper does not confuse them: nothing in §3.2 predicts a walk distance or a hazard ratio.

The property panel adds one caution to any follow-up. The five leads are all larger and more lipophilic than riociguat (MW 540–576 vs 422; logP 4.5–4.7 vs 2.44), with TPSA 75–84 against riociguat's 138. If a laboratory took the docking table at face value, it would prioritise the two biggest, most lipophilic compounds — the ones most likely to carry solubility and off-target liabilities — over the proven drug. That is the practical cost of an uncalibrated screen, and it is why §4.5 sends the leads to a cellular assay before any animal work.

4. Discussion

4.1 The mechanism, and what docking can and cannot test

The NO–sGC–cGMP pathway gives this paper a mechanism with a test for each link, and docking tests exactly one of them. Link one: NO binds the haem iron of the β1 H-NOX domain and activates sGC ~200-fold; the test is the 7D9R structure itself, which shows riociguat bound in the H-NOX pocket 12.57 Å from the haem, with NO present (Liu et al. 2021). Link two: a stimulator must fit that pocket while the haem is in its reduced, NO-bound state; the test is the re-dock — riociguat returned to its own pocket at −9.96 kcal/mol with three poses within 0.06 kcal/mol, which is the protocol working as intended on this structure. Link three: the pocket must discriminate between analogues that differ 1- to 4-fold in cellular potency; the test is the rank correlation in §3.3, and it is the only link docking can fail. Link four: a better cellular EC50 must mean a better drug in a patient; docking tests nothing here — that link belongs to the trials, which is why §3.4 puts the docking result next to PATENT-1, CHEST-1 and VICTORIA rather than in place of them.

The haem caveat cuts both ways and must be stated plainly. The receptor preparation keeps ATOM records only, so the haem — the very cofactor the stimulator's binding depends on — is stripped before scoring. Every score in §3.1 is therefore a shape-only score against a haem-free pocket, the exact analogue of the metal-stripping caveat in this series' metallo-β-lactamase papers, where inhibitors whose binding is metal chelation were scored on shape alone. A stimulator that gains affinity from haem contact will be systematically under-scored, and a compound that merely fills the pocket will be over-scored. The re-dock controls for this only partially: riociguat scores well despite the missing haem, which shows the pocket's shape alone carries signal — but it does not show that the shape signal ranks analogues correctly.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

The table contains something that looks like a win — two leads score better than the reference drug (−10.97 and −10.86 against riociguat's −9.96) — and it must not be read as one. First, both are bigger molecules, and Vina rewards size; the score gap between the best lead and riociguat (1.01 kcal/mol) is inside the method's noise and is the size a 150 Da difference buys. Second, the best-docked lead's pose set includes a +13.09 kcal/mol third pose, a clash that says the pocket accommodates the molecule in one mode and rejects it in another. Third, and decisively, the two 3 nM compounds bracket the table: the same measured potency gives the best and the worst score. A method that cannot distinguish two compounds of identical potency cannot be said to have found a better compound when it scores one of them above the reference. The moderate rho of −0.41 is consistent with this reading — the extremes order correctly, the middle is noise — and its confidence interval, (−0.95, +0.74), is consistent with almost anything. The honest summary is: the screen is not random, and it is not usable for ranking. Both halves matter. A laboratory that screens the next sGC series with this protocol and picks the top scorer will pick partly on size and partly on luck, and the paper's proposed validation (§4.5) is designed so that the cellular assay, not the docking table, does the picking.

4.3 Association only

Docking scores are an association, not a causal claim: no randomised experiment, natural experiment or instrumental variable is involved, and no causal identification is claimed. The validated control in this paper is the re-docked reference drug, not a causal design. A lead that scores well has a shape compatible with the H-NOX pocket; whether it stimulates sGC in a cell is a separate, empirical question that only the cellular assay answers.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. A flexible-side-chain or MM-GBSA rescoring of the same six compounds on 7D9R reaches rho ≤ −0.5 against the same five measured EC50s. Falsifier: the rescoring run itself; rho above −0.5 refutes it, and the screen stays unusable for ranking.
  2. Docking the same compounds on a second sGC structure (6JT0, unliganded, 4.0 Å; or 6JT2, NO-activated, 3.8 Å) reproduces the 7D9R order. Falsifier: a different order on the second structure — which would show the ranking is structure-dependent, not compound-dependent.
  3. The five leads' cellular EC50s, re-measured in a single head-to-head HTRF assay in CHO cells, preserve the 1–4 nM order in ChEMBL. Falsifier: a different order in one assay run — which would show the ChEMBL spread is assay noise, and no docking method could have ranked it.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain riociguat and the five leads commercially (all are ChEMBL-recorded compounds; riociguat is an approved drug) and confirm identity and purity by LC-MS. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): head-to-head HTRF cellular sGC activation assay in CHO cells, the assay context of the recorded EC50s, all six compounds in the same run, with and without 50% human serum as in the original assay — the single experiment that tests both the potency spread and the docking order. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): flexible docking / MM-GBSA rescoring of the same six compounds on 7D9R, compared against the assay order. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): report all results, including the negatives — a screen that cannot rank is a result. Total cost is one cell assay and six compounds, not a screening campaign.

5. Limitations

  1. One structure, rigid receptor, 3.7 Å cryo-EM. A single riociguat-bound structure, no side-chain flexibility, no MD, no rescoring; the ligand coordinates are modelled, not X-ray. The rho reported here is a property of this protocol on this structure, not of docking in general.
  2. Haem stripped. The receptor preparation removes the haem 12.57 Å from the riociguat centroid; scores are shape-only against a haem-free pocket, and any haem-contact affinity is invisible to the screen.
  3. Functional EC50s, not binding affinities. The measured values are cellular sGC activation EC50s in CHO cells; the rank correlation compares docking against function, and function includes permeability, serum binding and cellular context that docking cannot see.
  4. Almost no potency spread to rank. The five leads span 1–4 nM (0.6 log units) with a tie at 3 nM; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol (≈ 5- to 30-fold). The rank test is underpowered by design — n = 5, and the smallest detectable effect is larger than the spread being ranked. A null result here is expected, not surprising.
  5. One document series. The five leads are close analogues from a single ChEMBL document series (CHEMBL3886753) with near-identical property profiles (MW 540–576, logP 4.5–4.7); the assay homogeneity helps comparability but the chemical diversity is narrow, and the result may not generalise to other sGC chemotypes.
  6. No Pakistan data. No verified Pakistan registry or prevalence figure for PAH or CTEPH was found; the policy section (§6) therefore recommends building the registry before committing to a listing decision, rather than assuming a patient number.
  7. Islamic canon gaps. Ibn al-Nafis's Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun was not read in full: it survives as an Arabic manuscript with only partial English translation. Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi was not read in full: the 23 volumes exist in English only in selections. The canon claims in this paper rest on the verified historical record of these works' contents, not on a full reading.

6. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP), with the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination. Decision: whether to list riociguat on the National Essential Medicines List and negotiate its price for the public sector. Exact change: DRAP should list riociguat for inoperable or persistent/recurrent CTEPH first — the indication where no other oral drug exists and surgery is unavailable to most patients — and negotiate a tiered price with the manufacturer before extending the listing to PAH, where cheaper alternatives (endothelin-receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors) already exist. The listing should be conditional on a Pakistan pulmonary-hypertension registry: if, after two years, the registry counts fewer than 200 treated CTEPH patients nationwide, the listing reverts to named-patient import only, and the funds return to the PAH programme. If the evidence changes, reverse this: if a local registry shows a large, diagnosable CTEPH population, or if a generic riociguat enters at under 20% of the originator price, extend the listing to PAH without waiting for the two-year review.

The principle is hifz al-nafs — preservation of life, the first of the maqasid al-shariah — applied through maslaha (public benefit: spend where no alternative exists) and adl (justice in access: a drug that only the rich can buy does not serve the population it was approved for). The same principle that Ibn al-Nafis served by describing the pulmonary circuit — knowledge of the body in the service of preserving it — is the principle behind making the drug that treats that circuit reachable. The evidence for the recommendation is thin in one place and the paper says so: there is no Pakistan patient count, which is why the recommendation is "list narrowly and count", not "list broadly and hope". The trial that would settle the value question in Pakistan is a registry, not another docking run.

7. Conclusion

Riociguat re-docks into its own H-NOX pocket on 7D9R at −9.96 kcal/mol, and the structure audit shows the previous pipeline failure was a wrong-domain pick, not a property of the target. The five leads rank with Spearman rho −0.41 (n = 5), below the pre-stated −0.5 bar for a usable screen, and two compounds with the same 3 nM EC50 sit 2.38 kcal/mol apart — the best and worst scores in the table. The honest conclusion is the calibration, not the table: a screen whose noise exceeds the potency spread it is asked to rank cannot rank, and the next sGC stimulator should be judged by a head-to-head cellular assay, not by a docking score. The clinical case for the class is already made by the trials — a 36–46 m walk gain in pulmonary hypertension, a 10% relative risk reduction in worsening heart failure — and the policy question in Pakistan is access and counting, not more computation.

Presatovir Scores −6.15 kcal/mol on Prefusion RSV F (5KWW), but Rigid Docking Cannot Rank RSV Fusion Inhibitors

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) caused an estimated 33.0 million lower-respiratory episodes and 101,400 deaths in children under five in 2019, with more than 97 percent of deaths in low- and middle-income countries, and no small-molecule antiviral is approved.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-17 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #73 (daily 5-paper run) Topic ID: HP-072

Keywords: RSV; fusion protein; presatovir; rilematovir; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; prefusion F; antiviral; ChEMBL

Abstract

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) caused an estimated 33.0 million lower-respiratory episodes and 101,400 deaths in children under five in 2019, with more than 97 percent of deaths in low- and middle-income countries, and no small-molecule antiviral is approved. Presatovir, an RSV fusion inhibitor, cut viral load in a human challenge study but failed its Phase 2b trial in haematopoietic-cell transplant recipients, with no viral-load or clinical benefit and treatment-emergent fusion-protein substitutions in 21 percent of treated patients with lower-respiratory infection. We asked whether standard rigid docking can rank RSV fusion inhibitors at all. A first automated run docked onto the wrong structure — a 51-residue fragment (29QJ) — and was discarded in full. The corrected benchmark docks presatovir, the co-crystallised inhibitor rilematovir, and five ChEMBL leads with measured potency onto the prefusion F structure 5KWW (2.5 angstrom), at the verified rilematovir-pocket centre. Presatovir scores −6.15 kcal/mol and rilematovir −5.36, but the ranking against measured potency is essentially random (Spearman rho +0.1, n = 5): the most potent measured compound (EC50 0.47 nM) scores −4.94, while presatovir's own ChEMBL record scores best at −6.53, and the same molecule docked twice from two SMILES encodings differs by 0.38 kcal/mol. Rigid Vina docking on a single prefusion structure cannot rank RSV fusion inhibitors, and no lead can be claimed better than presatovir from this screen. The falsifier is a rescoring method, or a second prefusion structure, that reaches rho of −0.5 or below against the same five measured potencies, or a cell assay that reproduces the docking order.

1. Introduction

RSV is the leading viral cause of severe lower-respiratory infection in infants, and a major cause in immunocompromised adults and the elderly. Li et al. estimated that globally in 2019 there were 33.0 million RSV-associated acute lower respiratory infection episodes (uncertainty range 25.4–44.6 million), 3.6 million hospital admissions, and 101,400 RSV-attributable deaths in children aged 0–60 months, with more than 95 percent of episodes and more than 97 percent of deaths in low-income and middle-income countries (Li et al. 2022, PMID 35598608). In adults aged 60 years and older in high-income countries, the 2019 burden was approximately 5.2 million cases, 470,000 hospitalisations and 33,000 in-hospital deaths (Savic et al. 2023, PMID 36369772). In Pakistan, RSV circulates year-round and is tracked in national sentinel surveillance of respiratory viruses (2022–2025; PMID 41600791). There is no approved small-molecule antiviral for RSV.

The fusion (F) protein is the obvious target. RSV F is a class I fusion protein that drives viral entry by refolding from a metastable prefusion conformation to a stable postfusion six-helix bundle; locking the prefusion state blocks entry. The prefusion structure was solved by McLellan et al. in 2013 (PMID 23618766), and the same pocket now has a co-crystallised inhibitor: JNJ-53718678 (rilematovir) bound to prefusion F (5KWW, 2.5 angstrom; Roymans et al. 2017, PMID 28761099). Presatovir (GS-5806) is the most clinically tested fusion inhibitor in the class. It reduced viral load and symptoms in a human challenge study (DeVincenzo et al. 2014, PMID 25140957), then failed in the patients who needed it most: in haematopoietic-cell transplant (HCT) recipients with RSV lower-respiratory infection, presatovir did not reduce viral load or improve any clinical outcome (Marty et al. 2020, PMID 31915807), and in HCT recipients with upper-respiratory infection it did not meet its prespecified endpoint either (Chemaly et al. 2020, PMID 31793991). Resistance emerged during treatment in a fifth of the lower-respiratory patients (Porter et al. 2020, PMID 32071058). Meanwhile the class itself is not dead: ziresovir met its primary endpoint in a Phase 3 trial in hospitalised infants (NEJM 2024, PMID 39321361), and prevention has moved to long-acting monoclonals — nirsevimab (74.5 percent efficacy in MELODY; Hammitt et al. 2022, PMID 35235726) and clesrovimab, licensed by the FDA in June 2025 (MMWR 2025).

Falsifiable question (stated before the results): can the standard rigid-docking benchmark of this series — ChEMBL potency retrieval plus AutoDock Vina docking on the best available structure, with a validated control — rank RSV fusion inhibitors by their measured potency? The claim is that it cannot, on a single prefusion structure, and the paper's own calibration (Spearman rho against measured pChEMBL, with a re-docked co-crystallised control) is the test. The claim is refuted if a rescoring method, or a second prefusion structure, reaches rho of −0.5 or below against the same five measured potencies, or if a cell assay reproduces the docking order.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

PubMed (E-utilities, accessed 17 November 2026) for presatovir (18 hits), rilematovir/JNJ-53718678, ziresovir, nirsevimab and clesrovimab, cross-checked against the burden estimates of Li et al. (2022) and Savic et al. (2023) and the trial records on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02254421, NCT02254408, NCT03379675). Every number in this paper traces to a PMID-verified source in the References, or to a computation in the raw JSON. The Islamic canon check is in §2.5. No presatovir in-vitro EC50 is quoted anywhere in this paper: no PMID-verified source for it was retrieved, and the paper does not invent one.

2.2 Target verification, and the discarded wrong-structure run

RSV F was resolved by accession, not by text search: UniProt P03420, Fusion glycoprotein F0, Human respiratory syncytial virus A (strain A2), 574 amino acids, 92 PDB cross-references. ChEMBL holds exactly one target with component accession P03420: CHEMBL3856166, "Fusion glycoprotein F0", SINGLE PROTEIN, with 67 bioactivities (verified live 17 November 2026). The text-search trap is named, not fallen into: a ChEMBL pref_name search for "respiratory syncytial virus fusion" returns CHEMBL2074 — human maltase-glucoamylase — first, the same trap that produced discarded runs earlier in this series (maltase substituted for PfPI4K, GyrB, DHFR and PTP1B). This run's target resolution was correct; its structure pick was not.

The standard pipeline run (run_docking.py --target "Respiratory syncytial virus fusion protein" --ref presatovir) resolved the target correctly (P03420 → CHEMBL3856166, 52 bioactivities retrieved, 26 leads ranked) and then docked onto the wrong structure. Its PDB auto-pick takes the best-resolution X-ray structure under 3.0 angstrom with a drug-like HETATM centre, and chose 29QJ (1.32 angstrom): "RSV fusion protein N-terminal heptad repeat domain in complex with double-stapled peptide 4/4G" — a 51-residue fragment (residues 159–209) bound to a stapled peptide (MK8, 76 atoms). Its "ligand centre" (6.04, 12.10, 85.20) is the centroid of that stapled peptide on the fragment, not the presatovir pocket: presatovir binds a pocket in the prefusion trimer, at the interface of the protomers, which a 51-residue fragment does not contain. The run's docking scores (presatovir −6.55, CHEMBL3410450 −6.04, and three more) are discarded in full and preserved as dock-HP-072-2026-11-17-WRONG-STRUCTURE.json. Its leads list — real RSV F actives from CHEMBL3856166 — was verified correct by accession and reused. The rule this paper states, and follows, is: no verified structure, no docking table — a structure without a verified ligand pocket gets a corrected run, never a published table.

2.3 Corrected computation (5KWW, verified centre)

A corrected driver (dock_hp072_rsv_f_2026-11-17.py, RDKit venv) docked on PDB 5KWW, "Crystal Structure of Inhibitor JNJ-53718678 In Complex with Prefusion RSV F Glycoprotein", 2.50 angstrom, prefusion trimer (Roymans et al. 2017). The co-crystallised ligand is 6YA — JNJ-53718678 (rilematovir), formula C21H20ClF3N4O3S, MW 500.9, an exact match to PubChem CID 118892432. Centre audit: dock._ligand_center on the 5KWW PDB file returns (20.60, 18.96, 19.21), the centroid of 6YA (33 atoms); the other HETATM groups are NAG (glycan, excluded by the picker), NHE (buffer, 13 atoms, smaller than 6YA) and SO4/HOH (junk). The centre was verified against a hand-computed 6YA centroid (20.60, 18.96, 19.21) and matches to within 0.01 angstrom — the centre is audited, not hand-rolled. Docking used the same Vina 1.2.7 protocol as Papers #1/#3: box 22.5 angstrom, exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses, best pose reported. Seven compounds were docked: presatovir (reference, PubChem CID 58029842, SMILES verified live), rilematovir (positive control — the co-crystallised ligand, re-docked into its own pocket), and the top five ChEMBL leads from the discarded run, all with measured EC50 values. A Spearman rank correlation between Vina affinity and measured pChEMBL was computed for the five leads (hand-rolled ranks; no scipy assumed); negative rho is the correct direction (better dock, more potent). All outputs are in dock-HP-072-2026-11-17.json.

2.4 Honesty limits

No RMSD was computed for the re-docked rilematovir, so pose recovery against the crystal pose is not claimed — only the score and the tight pose spread are reported. The five pChEMBL values mix two assay contexts (RSV A2 infection of HepG2 cells, and the D486N mutant F protein in Hep2 cells), which weakens the calibration; the assay context is stated per compound in Table 3.1. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the whole docked set spans only 2.28 kcal/mol, so most gaps in the table are inside the noise. No molecular dynamics or free-energy rescoring was run. No lab data were generated.

2.5 Literature and the Islamic canon

The classical canon was checked alongside the modern literature, as the programme requires. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) describes respiratory illness and fevers in detail, Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900) records fever and respiratory remedies, and Ibn al-Nafis's Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun (1242) first described the pulmonary circulation — the anatomical context of a respiratory virus. All three predate the identification of RSV (1956) by centuries, so none names the virus or the fusion protein, and no Canon-listed plant was docked or screened in this run; the paper claims no traditional-medicine finding. The honest limit, named here: the full 23-volume Kitab al-Hawi exists in English only in selections, and most classical Arabic medical manuscripts remain undigitised; the sweep covers the named canonical works, not every book ever written.

3. Results

3.1 The wrong-structure run, and what it would have published

Had the structure audit been skipped, the pipeline would have published a benchmark of presatovir at −6.55 kcal/mol and four ChEMBL leads at −6.04 to −3.96, all docked onto a 51-residue fragment at the centroid of a stapled peptide. The run completed with "PIPELINE OK: True". Only the structure line — 29QJ where a prefusion trimer should have been — betrayed it. This is the same failure family as the maltase runs, one step later in the pipeline: the target was right, the structure was wrong, and the output looked complete. The defence is the same in both cases: verify by accession, and verify the structure against the bound ligand.

3.2 Docking on prefusion F (5KWW): the comparison table

Compound Vina best (kcal/mol) Poses Measured potency Assay context PAINS
CHEMBL3410450 (= presatovir, ChEMBL record) −6.53 −6.53, −6.44, −6.29 EC50 1,193 nM (pChEMBL 5.92) F D486N mutant, Hep2 none
Presatovir (QUERY, PubChem CID 58029842) −6.15 −6.15, −6.09, −5.80 — (same molecule as above) — none
CHEMBL4747540 −4.94 −4.94, −4.89, −4.47 EC50 0.47 nM (pChEMBL 9.33) RSV A2, HepG2 none
CHEMBL4779491 −4.59 −4.59, −4.43, −4.27 EC50 2.1 nM (pChEMBL 8.68) RSV A2, HepG2 none
CHEMBL4640616 −4.55 −4.55, −4.54, −4.52 EC50 2.0 nM (pChEMBL 8.70) RSV A2, HepG2 none
CHEMBL4647328 −4.25 −4.25, −4.06, −4.06 EC50 440 nM (pChEMBL 6.36) F D486N mutant, Hep2 none
Rilematovir (CONTROL, co-crystallised ligand) −5.36 −5.36, −5.36, −5.31 nanomolar (Roymans 2017) — none

All seven compounds are PAINS-clean and drug-like (MW 491–537, logP 1.72–3.85, 0–1 Lipinski violations each). Presatovir: MW 532.07, logP 2.97, 2 donors / 7 acceptors, TPSA 125.93 angstrom², 5 rotatable bonds, 1 Lipinski violation. Rilematovir: MW 500.93, logP 3.85, 0 donors / 4 acceptors, TPSA 78.89 angstrom², 7 rotatable bonds, 1 Lipinski violation. ToxGuard read-across for presatovir is weak (maximum neighbour similarity 0.271) and is not quoted as safety evidence.

Three things in this table deserve attention. First, the duplicate: presatovir docked twice — once as the PubChem query, once as its ChEMBL record CHEMBL3410450 (pref_name PRESATOVIR, synonyms GS-5806; verified live) — scores −6.15 and −6.53, a 0.38 kcal/mol gap between identical molecules, because the two SMILES encodings differ in stereochemistry specification and RDKit generates different starting conformers. That gap is the run's noise floor, and every gap between distinct compounds in the table is of the same order or smaller. Second, the control: rilematovir re-docked into its own pocket scores only −5.36 — weaker than presatovir, weaker than its own ChEMBL twin — with three poses within 0.05 kcal/mol of each other. A proven nanomolar inhibitor, in its own crystal pocket, does not top this table. Third, the ranking is inverted against measurement: the most potent measured compound (CHEMBL4747540, 0.47 nM) scores −4.94, fifth of seven, while the weakest measured (presatovir's own record, 1,193 nM against the D486N mutant) scores best. Spearman rho between Vina affinity and measured pChEMBL is +0.1 (n = 5) — no correlation.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of presatovir on 5KWW was found in the literature sweep, so there is no published docking table to compare against. The structural fact is published: 5KWW is the JNJ-53718678 complex (Roymans et al. 2017), and 6EAD is the F140I inhibitor-escape-variant structure (2.8 angstrom), which confirms that the F140 region is part of the inhibitor pocket. Absolute Vina scores are protocol- and structure-dependent and cannot be compared across studies; only the within-protocol ranking in Table 3.1 is interpretable, and that ranking is the paper's negative result.

3.4 The clinical record, and why it matters more than the table

Presatovir's clinical history is the reason the docking result is a negative finding rather than a lead. In the human challenge study it worked: viral load 250.7 vs 757.7 log10 PFUe·h/mL (P < .001), mucus 6.9 vs 15.1 g (P = .03). In HCT recipients it did not. The Phase 2b lower-respiratory trial (NCT02254421, 60 patients, 31 presatovir / 29 placebo) found a viral-load difference of −0.02 log10 copies/mL (95% CI −0.62 to 0.57; P = .94), median supplemental-oxygen-free days 26 vs 28 (P = .84), incident respiratory failure 10.3 vs 10.7 percent (P = .98), and all-cause mortality 0 vs 7.1 percent (P = .19). The Phase 2 upper-respiratory trial (NCT02254408, 189 patients) found a viral-load difference of −0.33 log10 (95% CI −0.64 to −0.02; P = .040) against a prespecified alpha of 0.01 — not significant — and progression to lower-respiratory complications 11.2 vs 19.5 percent (odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.22–1.18; P = .11); a post-hoc lymphopenia subgroup did show fewer complications (13.3 vs 64.3 percent, P = .008), which is hypothesis-generating, not evidence. Resistance-associated substitutions emerged in 6 of 29 presatovir-treated lower-respiratory patients (20.7 percent) and 10 of 89 upper-respiratory patients (11.2 percent), against none on placebo; V127A was already present at baseline in 8 subjects. The drug was well tolerated in both trials — the failure was efficacy, not safety. The class, meanwhile, has a positive Phase 3: ziresovir in hospitalised infants (n = 244) improved the Wang bronchiolitis score by 0.8 points (95% CI −1.3 to −0.3; P = .002) and cut viral load by 0.6 log10 at day 5, though resistance-associated mutations appeared in 15 participants (9 percent). The target is druggable; presatovir, in HCT recipients, was not the drug.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: the screen's failure is the finding

This paper set out to rank RSV fusion inhibitors and found that its own screen cannot rank them. The value of the run is the calibration, not the table. A docking protocol that gives its co-crystallised control −5.36, its reference drug −6.15, and the most potent measured compound −4.94 — with a duplicate-molecule noise floor of 0.38 kcal/mol and a Spearman rho of +0.1 — has no ranking power on this target. The honest conclusion is that the five ChEMBL leads, however potent in cells, cannot be ordered by this screen, and none can be claimed better than presatovir from these scores. The sub-nanomolar leads (CHEMBL4747540 at 0.47 nM, CHEMBL4640616 at 2.0 nM, CHEMBL4779491 at 2.1 nM) remain what they were before docking: measured cell potencies with no structural ranking attached.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Presatovir's −6.15 is not a win. It is 0.38 kcal/mol behind its own duplicate record, and only 0.79 kcal/mol ahead of the control — barely twice the duplicate noise floor — and it sits in a table whose control — a proven nanomolar inhibitor in its own pocket — scores worse. The three poses of presatovir span 0.35 kcal/mol and the three poses of rilematovir span 0.05, so the poses are converged; the problem is the scoring function on this pocket, not the sampling. The pocket was crystallised around rilematovir, so any pocket-shape effect should favour the control, not presatovir — and still the control scores lower. The most likely reading is that rigid docking on a single prefusion structure, with no side-chain flexibility and no rescoring, cannot separate compounds whose measured potencies span 0.47 nM to 1,193 nM when the assay contexts differ (wild-type A2 infection vs the D486N mutant) and the binding site is a shallow, hydrophobic, inter-protomer groove.

4.3 Association only

This is a retrospective docking benchmark, not a causal experiment. It shows that Vina scores on 5KWW do not track measured RSV F potency for these five compounds, that presatovir's clinical failure is consistent with a weak and resistance-prone inhibitor, and that the pipeline's structure picker can silently dock onto a fragment. It does not show that any lead is inactive, that presatovir is inactive in any other population, or that another docking method would fail the same way. The causal identification is validated-control re-docking (rilematovir into its own pocket); beyond that, the paper is association only.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. A flexible-side-chain or MM-GBSA rescoring of the same seven compounds on 5KWW reaches rho ≤ −0.5 against the same five measured potencies. Falsifier: the rescoring run itself; rho above −0.5 refutes it, and the screen stays unusable for ranking.
  2. Docking the same compounds on a second prefusion structure (5EA3, JNJ-2408068 complex, 2.75 angstrom; or 6VKC, JNJ-36811054 complex, 2.6 angstrom) reproduces the 5KWW order. Falsifier: a different order on the second structure — which would show the ranking is structure-dependent, not compound-dependent.
  3. CHEMBL4747540 (0.47 nM) inhibits RSV A2 in a cell assay at sub-nanomolar EC50, while presatovir does not beat it. Falsifier: a head-to-head A2 HepG2 assay; if presatovir matches or beats it, the ChEMBL potency gap is an assay artefact.
  4. Presatovir's D486N weakness is the resistance mechanism that matters clinically. Falsifier: a D486N virus that presatovir still inhibits at wild-type potency in the same assay — which would point the resistance story at the other emergent substitutions instead.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain presatovir, rilematovir and the three sub-nanomolar leads commercially and confirm identity and purity by LC-MS. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): head-to-head RSV A2 infection assay in HepG2 cells (the assay context of the three sub-nanomolar measurements), EC50 for all five compounds in the same run, with a D486N-mutant counter-screen in parallel — the single experiment that tests both the potency gap and the resistance hypothesis. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): flexible docking / MM-GBSA rescoring of the same five compounds on 5KWW and 5EA3, compared against the assay order. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): report all results, including the negatives — a screen that cannot rank is a result. Total cost is one cell assay and five compounds, not a screening campaign.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only, and a negative calibration. No compound in this paper was tested in a cell; the headline is that the screen cannot rank, not that any lead works.
  2. Single structure, rigid receptor. One prefusion structure (5KWW), no side-chain flexibility, no MD, no rescoring; the rho of +0.1 is a property of this protocol on this structure, not of docking in general.
  3. Mixed assay contexts. The five pChEMBL values mix RSV A2 HepG2 infection with the D486N mutant in Hep2 cells; the calibration is weaker for it, and the presatovir record (1,193 nM) is a mutant measurement, not a wild-type one.
  4. No RMSD for the control. Rilematovir was re-docked into its own pocket but pose recovery was not measured, so the control validates the score scale, not the pose.
  5. No presatovir EC50 quoted. No PMID-verified in-vitro EC50 for presatovir was retrieved; the paper uses the challenge-study and trial numbers instead, and does not invent the missing value.
  6. No lab data, no clinical recommendation. Nothing here changes treatment; the prevention standard remains the monoclonals, and the treatment gap remains open.
  7. Islamic canon gaps (named, per the programme's rule). The Canon and Kitab al-Hawi were checked through named works, not read in full; the full 23-volume Hawi exists in English only in selections, and most classical Arabic medical manuscripts remain undigitised.

6. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP), the National Institute of Health Islamabad, and the Federal Directorate of Immunization — and, for the method rule, every public funder of computational drug discovery in Pakistan. Three exact changes, each with its falsifier:

  1. Do not fund a presatovir-analogue programme on docking scores alone; require the head-to-head cell assay first. The five leads in Table 3.1 cost one assay to order, and this paper shows the docking order is random (rho +0.1). A programme that picks its lead from this table would pick presatovir's own record — the weakest measured compound — and call it the winner. Reverse this only if a rescoring method reaches rho ≤ −0.5 on this same set, in which case the docking order becomes usable evidence again.
  2. Prioritise prevention procurement over a new small-molecule programme. With 101,400 under-five deaths a year, more than 97 percent in countries like Pakistan, and two long-acting monoclonals now licensed (nirsevimab 74.5 percent efficacy; clesrovimab licensed June 2025), the fastest mortality reduction is a prevention programme, not a fusion-inhibitor discovery programme — especially when the only positive Phase 3 in the class (ziresovir, infants) still showed resistance in 9 percent. Reverse this if a fusion inhibitor posts a positive Phase 3 in infants with a resistance rate below that 9 percent, or if monoclonal supply or price makes prevention unreachable in Pakistan.
  3. Require accession-verified targets and structure audits in every publicly funded computational screen. Any screening proposal must state the UniProt accession, the ChEMBL target ID it resolved to, and the PDB ID with the bound ligand its centre was verified against; any run that falls back to text search or to a resolution-sorted structure pick must declare it. This paper's discarded fragment run is the evidence: without that rule, public money can fund a complete benchmark docked onto a 51-residue fragment. Reverse this only if the auto-picker is shown to return the correct structure first for a blinded set of viral accessions. Islamic principle behind the recommendations: preservation of life (hifz al-nafs, Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat) — RSV kills more than a hundred thousand young children a year, so a screening method that mis-ranks antivirals is a failure to protect life, not a technical footnote; and stewardship (khilafah, Qur'an 2:30) — public research funds are a trust, and a steward does not spend a trust on a benchmark of the wrong structure. Where the Islamic sources and the modern evidence point the same way, this paper says so; they do here.

7. Conclusion

Presatovir scores −6.15 kcal/mol on the prefusion RSV F structure 5KWW, at a centre verified against the co-crystallised inhibitor rilematovir — and the number means almost nothing, because the same screen gives the co-crystallised control −5.36 and the most potent measured compound −4.94, with a rank correlation of 0.1 against measured potency. The clinical record agrees with the negative reading: presatovir failed its Phase 2b trials in transplant recipients, with resistance emerging in a fifth of the lower-respiratory patients, while the class's one positive Phase 3 (ziresovir) and the licensed monoclonals carry the field forward. The memorable number is 0.1: the correlation between docking and measurement for RSV fusion inhibitors on this structure. The next step is one cell assay, not more docking.

Rigid Docking Cannot Rank the GRL0617 Series on SARS-CoV-2 PLpro: the 2.67 µM Reference Scores Best and the 42 µM Compound Beats Both Leads

SARS-CoV-2 papain-like protease (PLpro) cleaves the viral polyprotein and strips ubiquitin and ISG15 from host proteins, suppressing type-I interferon — a second viral protease with no approved inhibitor, unlike the main protease (Mpro), which has nirmatrelvir.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-17 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #72 (daily 5-paper run) Topic ID: HP-073

Keywords: SARS-CoV-2; papain-like protease; PLpro; GRL0617; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; BL2 loop; antiviral drug discovery

Abstract

SARS-CoV-2 papain-like protease (PLpro) cleaves the viral polyprotein and strips ubiquitin and ISG15 from host proteins, suppressing type-I interferon — a second viral protease with no approved inhibitor, unlike the main protease (Mpro), which has nirmatrelvir. GRL0617, a non-covalent PLpro inhibitor first described against SARS-CoV in 2008, remains the best-validated PLpro chemotype: it inhibits SARS-CoV-2 PLpro at 2.05 micromolar (median of 21 ChEMBL records) and blocks viral replication in cells and in mouse models, and its optimised analogues reach 0.11–0.67 micromolar. We benchmarked rigid AutoDock Vina docking on the GRL0617-bound structure 7JRN (2.48 angstrom) against five compounds from a single FRET assay (Ma et al. 2021): GRL0617 (2.67 micromolar in this assay) plus four analogues spanning 0.11–42 micromolar. The re-dock control worked — GRL0617 scored −9.90 kcal/mol in its own pocket — but the ranking failed: Spearman rho = +0.15 (n = 5). The weakest compound (42 micromolar) scored third-best (−9.14), beating both named leads Jun9-72-2 (−7.74) and Jun9-84-3 (−8.21), while the most potent analogue (0.11 micromolar) scored second (−9.74). All five compounds are PAINS-clean, so the failure is not assay artefacts but the method: the analogues' advantage is an ionic hydrogen bond to Asp164 and closure of the flexible BL2 loop, which rigid docking cannot score. Falsifiable claim: rigid Vina docking into 7JRN cannot rank PLpro inhibitors, and any PLpro claim resting on it alone is untested. The falsifier is a head-to-head test — run induced-fit docking or MM-GBSA on the same five compounds in the same pocket: if it recovers rho below −0.5 where rigid Vina gives +0.15, the failure is the rigidity and the claim stands; if it also fails, the pocket itself defeats scoring-based ranking.

1. Introduction

COVID-19 has caused nearly 780 million confirmed cases and more than 7.1 million reported deaths worldwide (WHO COVID-19 fact sheet, accessed November 2026), including about 1.58 million confirmed cases and 30,656 deaths in Pakistan (National Institute of Health, Pakistan, 2023). The virus still circulates, and the antiviral cupboard holds exactly one oral drug class: nirmatrelvir, which inhibits the main protease (Mpro, nsp5). The second viral protease has been left behind.

Papain-like protease (PLpro) is the nsp3 protease domain (replicase polyprotein 1ab residues 1564–1878; nsp3 residues 746–1060; EC 3.4.19.12; UniProt P0DTD1). It cuts the three N-terminal junctions of the replicase polyprotein, and it is also a deubiquitinase and deISGylase: it strips ubiquitin and ISG15 from host proteins, which shuts down type-I interferon signalling and lets the virus spread while the innate immune response is blind (Shin et al. 2020). A PLpro inhibitor is therefore two drugs in one — an antiviral and an immune-restoring agent — and that is why PLpro, not Mpro, is the underexploited target. It has no approved drug and no drug in late-stage trials.

GRL0617 is the reference compound for this target. Discovered against SARS-CoV PLpro in 2008 (IC50 0.6 µM; Ratia et al. 2008), it was repurposed for SARS-CoV-2, where it inhibits PLpro at 2.05 µM (median of 21 ChEMBL IC50 records, range 0.6–7.0 µM; 2.05 ± 0.12 µM in the Ma et al. 2021 FRET assay) and shows antiviral activity in Vero E6 cells (EC50 23.64 µM) and in Caco-2-hACE2 cells (19.96 µM). Structure-based optimisation from the GRL0617-bound structure produced the Jun9 series, with Jun9-75-4 (0.62 µM), Jun9-72-2 (0.67 µM) and Jun9-84-3 (0.67 µM) roughly threefold more potent than GRL0617 and threefold more active antivirally (EC50 6.6–8.3 µM; Ma et al. 2021). A 2025 invalidation study confirmed the field's central fact: most reported PLpro inhibitors act unspecifically (thiol-reactive or redox-active), and "GRL0617 and its derivatives remain the best-validated compounds with demonstrated antiviral activity in cells and in mouse models" (Kuzikov et al. 2025).

The companion paper in this series (HP-037) benchmarked the same rigid-docking method on Mpro and got the first positive rank correlation in the series (Spearman ρ = +0.48, n = 5): the most potent nirmatrelvir analogue scored best. This paper asks whether the same method works on the second protease, using the same protocol, the same reference-drug logic, and a cleaner test — five compounds from one assay, one paper, spanning 372-fold in potency.

Falsifiable question (stated before the results): can rigid AutoDock Vina docking into the GRL0617-bound PLpro structure 7JRN rank five GRL0617-series inhibitors in the order of their measured IC50 values? The claim is that it cannot, because the analogues' potency gain comes from an ionic interaction and a loop closure that a rigid receptor cannot represent. The claim is refuted if the docking scores rank the compounds in measured order (ρ ≤ −0.5), and confirmed in its strongest form if the ranking is inverted (ρ ≥ +0.5).

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

PubMed (E-utilities, accessed 17 November 2026) for GRL0617 + PLpro (65 hits), cross-checked against the ChEMBL bioactivity record and the full text of Ma et al. 2021 (PMC8265724) and Shin et al. 2020 (PMC7116779). Every number in this paper traces to a PMID-verified source in the References, or to a computation in the raw JSON. The Islamic canon check is in §2.7. The analysis plan — target, structure, docking set, and the Spearman test — was fixed before any docking score was seen; nothing in the Results is post-hoc except the mechanistic reading of the failure, which is labelled as such.

2.2 Target verification, and the discarded wrong-target run

PLpro was resolved by accession, not by text search: UniProt P0DTD1 (Replicase polyprotein 1ab, SARS-CoV-2, 7,096 aa); the PLpro (nsp3) domain is pp1ab residues 1564–1878, catalytic Cys111 (pp1ab Cys1674) and His272 (pp1ab His1835). The only ChEMBL target carrying component accession P0DTD1 as a single protein is CHEMBL4523582 (Replicase polyprotein 1ab). That target also holds Mpro activities, so PLpro potencies were filtered by assay description (contains "papain" or "PLpro"): 699 PLpro IC50 activities from 561 distinct molecules (ChEMBL, accessed 17 November 2026).

The standard pipeline run (run_docking.py --target "SARS-CoV-2 papain-like protease" --ref GRL0617) failed exactly as the series has seen before: its ChEMBL text search returned CHEMBL2074 (human maltase-glucoamylase) first, resolved UniProt to P0DTC1 (replicase polyprotein 1a), and docked 26 maltase ligands into 8AZC (the NSP3 macrodomain) with every dock failing. That run is discarded in full and preserved as dock-HP-073-2026-11-17-WRONG-TARGET.json. It is the paper's first finding, again: a text-search fallback manufactures a complete, plausible-looking, entirely wrong result, and only the accession check catches it.

2.3 Structure and centre audit

PDB 7JRN: wild-type SARS-CoV-2 PLpro in complex with GRL0617, 2.48 Å, X-ray (Ma et al. 2021, PMID 34341772). The docking centre is the co-crystallised GRL0617 centroid computed by the pipeline's own dock._ligand_center — never hand-rolled — and audited in the driver: the pick is residue TTT (GRL0617), chain A, 23 heavy atoms (C20H20N2O), centroid [9.82, −11.83, 32.76]. The second TTT copy (chain J, the symmetry-related copy) was not averaged in, because the picker groups by full residue identity. The catalytic Cys111 sits in the pocket; GRL0617 binds the BL2 groove adjacent to it, not the catalytic site itself.

2.4 Docking protocol

AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exhaustiveness 8, box 22.5 Å, best of three poses reported, same centre and box for all five compounds. Docking set (all from Ma et al. 2021, one FRET assay, document CHEMBL5107976): GRL0617 (CHEMBL549695; IC50 2,670 nM in this assay; paper value 2.05 ± 0.12 µM) as the reference and re-dock control; CHEMBL5079592 (113 nM, the most potent compound in the series); Jun9-72-2 (CHEMBL5173886; 670 nM); Jun9-84-3 (CHEMBL5182315; 670 nM); CHEMBL5200289 (42,000 nM, the weakest in the set). The two Jun9 names were verified PubChem → InChIKey → ChEMBL → activity; the other two analogues are tabled by ChEMBL ID only, because the paper's text does not name them and no name is invented. Rank correlation: Spearman ρ between best Vina score and measured pIC50 (pIC50 = −log10(IC50 in M)), ties by average ranks; negative ρ is the correct direction (better dock, more potent). Causal identification, named explicitly: validated-control re-docking (GRL0617 into its own crystal structure) — the only causal claim is about the method's ranking ability, and it rests on that control; everything else in this paper is association.

2.5 PAINS screen and ToxGuard

RDKit PAINS filter for every compound; RDKit descriptors (Lipinski/Veber); ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (k = 15) reported with its maximum neighbour similarity, so the reader can see how weak the coverage is.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking ≠ activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the receptor is rigid and the BL2 loop is frozen in its GRL0617-bound closed conformation; no MD or free-energy refinement was run; no experiment was performed. The measured IC50s are single-assay values from one paper (n = 5 compounds), and two of them tie at 670 nM.

2.7 Literature and the Islamic canon

The classical canon was checked alongside the modern literature, as the programme requires. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (c. 1025) classifies epidemic fevers (humma) and Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi (c. 900, 23 volumes) and On Smallpox and Measles (c. 910) record the clinical distinction of eruptive fevers — all centuries before the viral aetiology of COVID-19, so none names PLpro, and no Canon-listed remedy was docked or screened in this run; the paper claims no traditional-medicine finding. The honest limit, named here: the full 23-volume Hawi exists in English only in selections, and most classical Arabic medical manuscripts remain undigitised; the sweep covers the named canonical works, not every book ever written.

3. Results

3.1 The ChEMBL landscape for PLpro

ChEMBL holds 699 PLpro IC50 activities (561 molecules) against the polyprotein target — a target that is, on paper, well covered. The most potent records in the database are 1–3 nM, from two 2024 ACS Medicinal Chemistry Letters patent-disclosure papers (PMID 39140061, 39563803); those values are single rounded records and were not used in the docking set, because a rank test needs one assay, not the smallest numbers in the database. The usable benchmark is the Ma et al. 2021 series: 57 compounds in one FRET assay, IC50s from 113 nM to 56 µM.

3.2 The discarded run, in one paragraph

The standard pipeline resolved the target to human maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074), UniProt P0DTC1, and docked 26 maltase ligands into the NSP3 macrodomain (8AZC), all failing. It completed with "PIPELINE OK: True". Only the target line betrayed it. This is the sixth time in this series the maltase substitution has had to be caught by hand (after GyrB, DHFR, PTP1B, Mpro, PfPI4K); the rule stands: no accession match, no benchmark.

3.3 Docking: the comparison table

CHEMBL5079592 (most potent) 113 −9.74 −9.74, −9.25, −8.79
CHEMBL5200289 (weakest in set) 42,000 −9.14 −9.14, −8.71, −8.00
