2026-11-16 Health Draft ready

Dapagliflozin Re-Docks at −11.00 kcal/mol on Its Own Cryo-EM Structure — but the Screen Ranks the Most Potent Lead Last

Dapagliflozin blocks the kidney's sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) and has transformed diabetic kidney disease and heart failure, but finding a better SGLT2 inhibitor still relies on screens that must first prove they can rank the drugs we already have.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-16 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #68 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: SGLT2; dapagliflozin; empagliflozin; diabetic kidney disease; cryo-EM; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; polyol pathway

Abstract

Dapagliflozin blocks the kidney's sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) and has transformed diabetic kidney disease and heart failure, but finding a better SGLT2 inhibitor still relies on screens that must first prove they can rank the drugs we already have. We asked whether a standard automated docking pipeline ranks SGLT2 inhibitors by their measured potency. The pipeline (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → Vina 1.2.7) found no X-ray structure for SGLT2 and skipped docking entirely, so we docked dapagliflozin, four ChEMBL leads and empagliflozin on 8HEZ, the 2.8 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human SGLT2 bound to dapagliflozin itself, with the grid centre verified as the bound dapagliflozin's centroid. Dapagliflozin re-docks at −11.00 kcal/mol; its duplicate ChEMBL record scores −11.61, a 0.61 kcal/mol gap between identical molecules that sets the run's noise floor. The lead CHEMBL3703792 leads at −12.34, empagliflozin scores −12.03, and the LeadForge star lead CHEMBL5288495 scores −11.48 — but the docking rank against the measured potencies is exactly inverted (Spearman rho −1.0, n = 4): the most potent lead (IC50 0.308 nM) scores worst (−9.76) and the least potent (0.551 nM) scores best. The measured band is only 1.8-fold wide, so the inversion is a property of a band too narrow to rank, not a real anti-correlation — and empagliflozin, six times less potent than dapagliflozin (3.1 versus 0.49 nM), still out-scores it by 1.03 kcal/mol. The screen cannot rank SGLT2 inhibitors within this potency band, and the star lead is indistinguishable from dapagliflozin itself (0.48 kcal/mol behind its duplicate record, inside the 0.61 noise floor). The falsifiable next step is a glucose-uptake assay: if the measured IC50 rank does not match the docking rank, docking is not a ranking tool for this target. And the polyol-escape caveat from Paper #3 stands: an SGLT2-only inhibitor, however potent, does not address the sorbitol pathway that damages retina, kidney and nerve.

1. Introduction

SGLT2 reabsorbs most of the glucose filtered by the kidney, and blocking it spills glucose into the urine, lowers blood glucose, and — through mechanisms that go beyond glucose lowering — protects the kidney and the heart. In Pakistan, where 34.5 million adults live with diabetes at the highest age-standardised prevalence in the world (IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th edition, 2025), that protection matters: diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of kidney failure, and the SGLT2 inhibitors are the first drug class in decades to change its course. Dapagliflozin's evidence is the strongest in the class. In DAPA-CKD (4,304 patients with CKD, with or without diabetes), it cut the primary composite — a sustained 50% fall in eGFR, end-stage kidney disease, or death from renal or cardiovascular causes — from 14.5% to 9.2% over a median 2.4 years (hazard ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.51–0.72; number needed to treat 19), with the kidney composite at HR 0.56 and death at HR 0.69 (Heerspink et al., N Engl J Med 2020;383:1436–1446, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2024816). In DAPA-HF (4,744 patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction), it cut worsening heart failure or cardiovascular death from 21.2% to 16.3% (HR 0.74, 0.65–0.85) (McMurray et al., N Engl J Med 2019;381:1995–2008, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1911303). The benefit is independent of diabetes status in both trials.

The structural basis arrived only recently. There is no X-ray structure of human SGLT2; the structures are cryo-EM. Niu et al. resolved the human SGLT2–MAP17 complex bound to empagliflozin at 2.95 angstrom (7VSI, Nature 2022;601:280–284) and showed empagliflozin occupying both the sugar-binding site and the external vestibule, locking the transporter in an outward-open conformation. Hiraizumi et al. then resolved the complex with five inhibitors, including dapagliflozin (8HEZ, 2.8 angstrom, Nat Struct Mol Biol 2024;31:159–169), and showed the four synthetic inhibitors binding the outward-facing conformation while phlorizin binds inward-facing. That history creates a precise, testable problem for docking. A pipeline that only accepts X-ray structures finds no structure at all for SGLT2 and skips docking — the correct behaviour for its own rules, and a failure of the rules. And a screen that docks on the cryo-EM structure must first prove it can rank dapagliflozin against empagliflozin and against leads whose measured potencies span less than two-fold.

This paper is SGLT2-only by design (topic HP-006), and it carries the polyol-escape caveat stated in Paper #3 of this series. Blocking SGLT2 lowers blood glucose, but glucose that enters insulin-independent tissues — retina, kidney, nerve — still feeds the polyol pathway: aldose reductase reduces it to sorbitol, consuming NADPH and depleting the glutathione those cells need against oxidative stress, while sorbitol itself cannot cross membranes and draws water in. Paper #3's rationale for a dual aldose-reductase + SGLT2 inhibitor was exactly this escape: an SGLT2-only drug, however potent, does not address polyol-mediated damage. The screen below ranks SGLT2 fit; it says nothing about the polyol pathway, and the paper does not pretend otherwise.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised Vina protocol on the dapagliflozin-bound cryo-EM structure (8HEZ), the docking rank of the SGLT2 inhibitors will track their measured potencies, and the LeadForge star lead CHEMBL5288495 (IC50 0.35 nM) will out-score dapagliflozin. Falsified if the rank correlation is below 0.5, or if the star lead does not out-score dapagliflozin by more than the duplicate-molecule noise floor.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-16 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-15, which contained no SGLT2 item). Key sources: Heerspink et al. 2020 (doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2024816) for DAPA-CKD; McMurray et al. 2019 (doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1911303) for DAPA-HF; Niu et al. 2022 (Nature 601:280–284) for 7VSI; Hiraizumi et al. 2024 (Nat Struct Mol Biol 31:159–169, doi:10.1038/s41594-023-01134-0) for 8HEZ; Michel et al. 2015 (Naunyn Schmiedebergs Arch Pharmacol 388:801–816, doi:10.1007/s00210-015-1134-1) for empagliflozin's IC50 of 3.1 nM and its selectivity; and the IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th edition (2025), for the Pakistan diabetes burden. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Computation

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2" and reference drug dapagliflozin (run_docking.py, RDKit venv). UniProtKB resolved SGLT2 to P31639 (human SLC5A2, 672 amino acids), ChEMBL to target CHEMBL3884 (Sodium/glucose cotransporter 2, single protein, human), which returned 22 bioactivities; the similarity screen kept 22 and the ranking produced 23 leads. The pipeline's structure picker found no experimental structure meeting its criteria (X-ray only, under 3.0 angstrom) and docking was SKIPPED — error no_pdb_found — which the task protocol requires the paper to state honestly rather than to work around silently. The pipeline output is hidden_files/dock-HP-006-2026-11-16.json.

Because no X-ray structure exists, a control docking was run on 8HEZ, the 2.8 angstrom cryo-EM structure of the human SGLT2–MAP17 complex bound to dapagliflozin (hidden_files/dock_hp006_8hez.py, same Vina defaults: AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, one box of 22.5 angstrom, exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported). The centre [66.86, 66.86, 76.15] is from D._ligand_center and was verified by computing the HETATM group centroids directly from the PDB file: it is exactly the centroid of the bound dapagliflozin (ligand code LE6, chain A, residue 802, 28 atoms). The other HETATM groups are water molecules, a sodium ion (centroid [76.29, 61.39, 69.96]) and an N-acetylglucosamine (NAG, chain A, residue 801, centroid [60.43, 63.11, 114.25]) — the glycosylation site, far from the inhibitor pocket, and not the centre. Six compounds were docked: the query plus the top four leads, and empagliflozin (SMILES fetched live from PubChem PUG REST by name) as an approved-drug comparison. The query (dapagliflozin, MW 408.88, logP 1.84, TPSA 99.38, zero Lipinski violations, PAINS-clean, highest Tox21 read-across 0.076) carries no ChEMBL activity value in the pipeline output; its ChEMBL record CHEMBL429910 carries IC50 0.49 nM, and other ChEMBL assays for the same target report EC50 1.1 nM and IC50 6.7 nM — the paper quotes the stored value and names the spread. The leads' potencies are the ChEMBL bioactivity values for target CHEMBL3884, quoted as stored (IC50 values; the pipeline output does not record assay conditions, and the paper does not invent them).

2.3 PAINS and safety panel

RDKit PAINS filter and the ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) were applied to every compound, exactly as in Papers #1/#3 and the 2026-11-15 run.

2.4 Analysis plan (stated before results)

The analysis plan was fixed before docking: (i) report the 8HEZ docking table with measured SGLT2 potencies from the ChEMBL record and the literature; (ii) treat CHEMBL429910, the ChEMBL record of dapagliflozin itself, as a duplicate-reproducibility check against the query, exactly as Paper #64 did for olaparib; (iii) compute Spearman rank correlation of docking score against measured potency; (iv) declare the screen unable to rank within the band if the correlation is below 0.5 or the duplicate gap exceeds the gaps between distinct compounds. No post-hoc re-ranking was performed; any exploratory observation is labelled as such.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. The structure is cryo-EM at 2.8 angstrom, not X-ray, and the docking is rigid: SGLT2 is a transporter that cycles through outward-open, occluded and inward-open states, and a single rigid conformation cannot model that cycle or the sodium-coupled transport step. No compound was assayed. The polyol pathway, the paper's stated caveat, is not modelled here. No cure claims are made.

3. Results

3.1 The pipeline found no structure — docking was skipped

The pipeline's structure picker accepts X-ray structures under 3.0 angstrom only. Human SGLT2 has no X-ray structure; its experimental structures are cryo-EM (7VSI at 2.95 angstrom, 8HEZ at 2.8 angstrom). The pipeline therefore returned no_pdb_found and skipped docking. That is the correct behaviour under its own rules, and it is also a failure of the rules: a pipeline that cannot use cryo-EM structures cannot dock the target that defines the class, and a user who did not read the log would receive a lead ranking with no docking at all. The docking below is the manual control that the pipeline's rules excluded.

3.2 Docking on the dapagliflozin-bound cryo-EM structure (8HEZ, 2.8 angstrom)

Compound Measured SGLT2 potency Vina on 8HEZ (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL3703792 IC50 0.551 nM (ChEMBL) −12.34 (−12.34, −9.34, −8.78) clean
Empagliflozin IC50 3.1 nM (literature) −12.03 (−12.03, −9.74, −9.38) clean
CHEMBL429910 (= dapagliflozin) IC50 0.49 nM (ChEMBL) −11.61 (−11.61, −10.07, −8.40) clean
CHEMBL5288495 (star lead) IC50 0.35 nM (ChEMBL) −11.48 (−11.48, −9.45, −8.46) clean
Dapagliflozin (QUERY) IC50 0.49 nM (ChEMBL record); other assays EC50 1.1 nM, IC50 6.7 nM −11.00 (−11.00, −10.09, −8.42) clean
CHEMBL3703868 IC50 0.308 nM (ChEMBL) −9.76 (−9.76, −8.81, −8.49) clean

Scores in kcal/mol, best of three poses (all poses in parentheses). All six compounds are PAINS-clean, carry zero Lipinski violations each (MW 408–461, logP 1.13–3.28), and show no decisive Tox21 signal (highest single read-across 0.362 for the star lead, 0.076 for dapagliflozin). Pose spreads are 1.27–3.56 kcal/mol — wider than the converged 6L88 control in Paper #67, tighter than the unconverged 4PF3 run, and moderate enough that the best-pose numbers are usable but not precise.

Three findings matter. First, the duplicate check: dapagliflozin docked twice — once as the query, once as its ChEMBL record CHEMBL429910 — scores −11.00 and −11.61, a 0.61 kcal/mol gap between identical molecules. That is the run's noise floor, and it is larger than the 0.37 gap Paper #64 found for the olaparib duplicate. Any gap smaller than 0.61 between two compounds in this table is indistinguishable from re-docking the same molecule.

Second, the rank is exactly inverted against the measured potencies. The four ChEMBL leads' measured order is CHEMBL3703868 (0.308 nM) > CHEMBL5288495 (0.35) > CHEMBL429910 (0.49) > CHEMBL3703792 (0.551); the docking order is the precise reverse, Spearman rho −1.0 (n = 4). The most potent lead scores worst (−9.76) and the least potent scores best (−12.34), a 2.58 kcal/mol gap across a 1.8-fold potency band. The paper reports the −1.0 and declines to treat it as a real anti-correlation: a 1.8-fold band is narrower than any assay can resolve, and the inversion is what noise looks like when the signal is smaller than the noise. The honest statement is that the screen cannot rank within this band — not that it ranks backwards.

Third, the approved-drug comparison fails the same way Paper #67's did. Empagliflozin (IC50 3.1 nM) is about six times less potent than dapagliflozin (0.49 nM by the stored ChEMBL value), yet it out-scores dapagliflozin by 1.03 kcal/mol (−12.03 versus −11.00). And the star lead CHEMBL5288495 (IC50 0.35 nM) scores −11.48 — 0.48 kcal/mol behind dapagliflozin's duplicate record, inside the 0.61 noise floor, and 0.86 behind the leader. The star lead is indistinguishable from dapagliflozin itself by this screen. The hypothesis is falsified on both counts: the rank correlation is −1.0, not above 0.5, and the star lead does not out-score dapagliflozin by more than the duplicate noise floor.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina docking score for dapagliflozin on 8HEZ was found to compare against, and the paper does not invent one. The reference point is the structural literature: Niu et al. 2022 showed empagliflozin occupying both the sugar-binding site and the external vestibule of the outward-open transporter (7VSI), and Hiraizumi et al. 2024 showed the four synthetic inhibitors, including dapagliflozin, binding the outward-facing conformation (8HEZ). Our re-dock places dapagliflozin at −11.00 kcal/mol in its own co-crystal pocket with poses of −11.00, −10.09 and −8.42, consistent with re-docking into its own cryo-EM structure. The earlier LeadForge figure for the star lead (−7.03 kcal/mol against dapagliflozin's −4.84) is NOT reproduced here: it came from a different structure and protocol whose grid centre was never verified after the centre-pick bug, and the two numbers are not comparable. The honest comparator is the clinical one: dapagliflozin's kidney and heart-failure benefits (DAPA-CKD HR 0.61; DAPA-HF HR 0.74) and its selectivity (about 1,200-fold over SGLT1; empagliflozin over 2,500-fold) are properties of the drugs in patients and in cells, and no docking score on 8HEZ predicts them.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say that dapagliflozin re-docks in its own pocket at −11.00 kcal/mol, that the duplicate-molecule noise floor is 0.61 kcal/mol, and that the lead CHEMBL3703792 tops the table at −12.34 — a candidate worth the glucose-uptake assay, not a verdict. It can say that the pipeline's X-ray-only rule excludes the only structures that exist for this target, and that a cryo-EM structure at 2.8 angstrom docks fine once the centre is verified against the bound ligand. It cannot rank SGLT2 inhibitors within a 1.8-fold potency band: the rank is inverted, the star lead is indistinguishable from dapagliflozin, and the weaker approved drug out-scores the stronger one. It cannot say anything about the polyol pathway, which is the paper's stated caveat and the reason Paper #3 proposed a dual inhibitor.

4.2 The cryo-EM lesson

The pipeline's structure picker is the finding, not a footnote. It accepts X-ray structures under 3.0 angstrom and nothing else, so for SGLT2 — a target whose structures are all cryo-EM — it silently returns no docking and a lead ranking built on similarity and ADMET alone. Paper #65 found the same pattern for GLP-1R, where the picker chose a 1.80 angstrom extracellular-domain crystal over the 3.1 angstrom cryo-EM structure of the full receptor with the drug bound, and the drug re-docked 3.14 kcal/mol stronger on the cryo-EM structure. The lesson generalises: the picker's resolution filter is a proxy for quality, and for membrane proteins — transporters, GPCRs — the best structure is often the cryo-EM one the filter excludes. The fix is to let the picker accept cryo-EM structures and to verify the centre against the bound ligand, as this paper did; the fix is stated here as a pipeline change, not implemented in this run.

4.3 The polyol-escape caveat, restated

An SGLT2-only inhibitor lowers blood glucose by spilling it into the urine, but the glucose that reaches insulin-independent tissues still enters the polyol pathway, where aldose reductase reduces it to sorbitol at the cost of NADPH, depleting glutathione and drawing water into cells that cannot export sorbitol. That is the damage mechanism in retina, kidney and nerve, and it is not addressed by a better SGLT2 score. Paper #3's dual aldose-reductase + SGLT2 rationale stands: the next screen in this series should dock against both targets and require a lead to score on both, or the programme should say plainly that it is optimising glucose lowering and kidney protection, not the polyol damage. This paper optimises the former and states the limit.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Potency hypothesis. In a glucose-uptake assay in SGLT2-expressing cells, the measured IC50 rank of the docked set reproduces the 8HEZ docking rank. Falsified if the rank correlation is below 0.5 — in which case docking is not a ranking tool for this target, and the programme should screen by uptake assay directly.
  2. Selectivity hypothesis. The best lead CHEMBL3703792 is at least 1,000-fold selective for SGLT2 over SGLT1 in the same assay, matching dapagliflozin's profile. Falsified if selectivity is below 100-fold — in which case the lead risks the gastrointestinal effects of SGLT1 blockade, whatever its SGLT2 score.
  3. Polyol hypothesis. In a diabetic rat model, the best lead plus an aldose-reductase inhibitor reduces retinal sorbitol more than the lead alone, at the same glucose lowering. Falsified if the combination adds nothing — in which case Paper #3's dual rationale does not hold in vivo, and the SGLT2-only path is sufficient for that endpoint.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): glucose-uptake (AMG) assay in SGLT2- and SGLT1-expressing cells for the docked set plus dapagliflozin and empagliflozin as controls; report IC50 with 95% CI and the SGLT2/SGLT1 selectivity ratio. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): aldose-reductase inhibition assay for the best lead, to test the dual-inhibition rationale directly. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): urinary glucose excretion and kidney sorbitol in a diabetic rat model for the best lead versus dapagliflozin, with and without an aldose-reductase inhibitor. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): hERG and CYP inhibition screen for the lead. Success criterion: the lead matches dapagliflozin's glucose lowering with at least 1,000-fold SGLT2 selectivity — not merely a better docking score.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this paper. Vina noise (±1–2 kcal/mol) is larger than several of the gaps reported, and the duplicate-molecule gap (0.61 kcal/mol) is the measured noise floor for this run.
  2. A single rigid cryo-EM conformation: SGLT2 cycles through outward-open, occluded and inward-open states, and rigid docking cannot model that cycle or the sodium-coupled transport step; no MD or free-energy refinement was run.
  3. The measured potency band is 1.8-fold wide (0.308–0.551 nM), narrower than any assay can resolve; the −1.0 rank correlation is a property of that band, not evidence of anti-correlation.
  4. Measured potencies mix ChEMBL bioactivities and literature IC50 values from different assays; dapagliflozin itself is reported as 0.49 nM (stored ChEMBL IC50), 1.1 nM (EC50) and 6.7 nM (IC50) in different assays.
  5. The polyol pathway is stated as a caveat, not modelled; no aldose-reductase docking or assay is in this paper.
  6. The Islamic canon sweep covers the available digitised canon relevant to the question (Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, c. 1025; Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi, c. 900); the full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections, and many classical Arabic manuscripts remain undigitised — the sweep names this gap rather than claiming completeness.
  7. No Pakistan-specific data on SGLT2 inhibitor prices, availability, or kidney-monitoring capacity are reported here; the burden numbers are national diabetes estimates (IDF Diabetes Atlas 2025).

6. Conclusion

Dapagliflozin re-docks at −11.00 kcal/mol in its own cryo-EM pocket (8HEZ), but the screen cannot rank SGLT2 inhibitors: the docking rank against measured potency is exactly inverted (rho −1.0, n = 4) across a 1.8-fold band too narrow to rank, the star lead CHEMBL5288495 (−11.48) is indistinguishable from dapagliflozin itself (0.48 kcal/mol behind its duplicate record, inside the 0.61 noise floor), and empagliflozin — six times less potent — out-scores dapagliflozin by 1.03 kcal/mol. The pipeline's X-ray-only rule skipped docking entirely for this target, because the only SGLT2 structures are cryo-EM; the manual control on 8HEZ, with its centre verified against the bound dapagliflozin, is what produced the numbers. And the polyol-escape caveat from Paper #3 stands: an SGLT2-only inhibitor, however potent, does not address the sorbitol pathway that damages retina, kidney and nerve.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) and the provincial health departments, with the Pakistan Society of Nephrology and the Pakistan Endocrine Society as clinical advisers. Decision: whether to add an SGLT2 inhibitor to the public formulary for diabetic kidney disease and heart failure, and at what price. Recommendation: add dapagliflozin (or a generic equivalent when available) to the formulary for patients with diabetic kidney disease or heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, on the DAPA-CKD and DAPA-HF evidence — the kidney composite fell by 39% and the heart-failure composite by 26%, with benefits independent of diabetes status — and pair the listing with urine albumin-to-creatinine testing in diabetes clinics, since the indication cannot be applied where albuminuria is never measured. Falsifier / reversal: if the negotiated price exceeds the per-patient cost of the current standard pathway without a measured kidney- or heart-failure-outcome gain, or if albuminuria testing coverage cannot be demonstrated in the prescribing facilities, reverse the formulary recommendation and keep the drug in the private market only. The principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life) with maslaha (public benefit) as the weighing rule, in the tradition of Ibn Sina's Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025): a health system preserves life by buying the drug whose benefit is proven in the patients who need it, and by building the testing that finds those patients — treatment and diagnosis together, not one without the other.

Olaparib Re-Docks at −11.24 kcal/mol on PARP1, but Rigid Docking Ranks Rucaparib Last and Cannot Reproduce the PARP-Trapping Order

PARP inhibitors kill BRCA-deficient cancers by synthetic lethality, but their cytotoxicity tracks PARP trapping — the stabilisation of PARP1 on DNA — more closely than catalytic inhibition, and trapping potency varies enormously between approved drugs (talazoparib ≫ niraparib > olaparib = rucaparib ≫ veliparib) while c…

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-16 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #64 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: PARP1; olaparib; synthetic lethality; BRCA; PARP trapping; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; saruparib

Abstract

PARP inhibitors kill BRCA-deficient cancers by synthetic lethality, but their cytotoxicity tracks PARP trapping — the stabilisation of PARP1 on DNA — more closely than catalytic inhibition, and trapping potency varies enormously between approved drugs (talazoparib ≫ niraparib > olaparib = rucaparib ≫ veliparib) while catalytic IC50 values cluster in the low-nanomolar range. We asked whether a standard rigid-docking screen can see trapping. Using the LeadForge protocol (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → Vina 1.2.7), we docked five ChEMBL PARP1 leads and olaparib on 6NRH, the 1.50 angstrom PARP1 catalytic-domain structure, then docked the five approved inhibitors plus the PARP1-selective saruparib on the same structure and grid. Olaparib re-docks at −11.24 kcal/mol; the best ChEMBL lead, CHEMBL4845834, scores −11.85, and every docked compound is PAINS-clean. Two controls expose the screen's limits. First, the pipeline docked olaparib twice — once as the PubChem query and once as its ChEMBL record — and the same molecule scored −11.24 and −10.87, a 0.37 kcal/mol reproducibility gap that sets this run's noise floor. Second, the docking rank inverts the measured potency rank of the four ChEMBL compounds (Spearman rho −0.6), and against the published trapping order the rank correlation is only 0.43: rucaparib, a mid-tier trapper equal to olaparib, docks worst at −7.87, below veliparib, the weakest trapper. Rigid docking ranks catalytic-site fit; it cannot see trapping, and on PARP1 it cannot even rank catalytic potency within a sub-nanomolar band. The falsifiable next step is a paired enzymatic-plus-trapping assay of the same set: if the trapping order predicts cell killing and the docking order does not, screening programmes must stop ranking PARP inhibitors by docking alone.

1. Introduction

Breast cancer is the single most common cancer among Pakistani women: GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates 30,682 new cases and 15,552 deaths in Pakistan in that year, 16.5% of all cancers diagnosed in the country, with most women still diagnosed at advanced stages (John et al., Discover Public Health 2026;23:1750, doi:10.1186/s12982-026-02844-8). A substantial share of these tumours are driven by defects in homologous recombination (HR) repair, most famously germline mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2. In 2005, two groups independently showed that inhibiting poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) kills BRCA-deficient cells while sparing HR-proficient ones — synthetic lethality, the first targeted-therapy concept built on a DNA-repair defect (Bryant et al., Nature 2005;434:913–917, doi:10.1038/nature03443; Farmer et al., Nature 2005;434:917–921, doi:10.1038/nature03445). Olaparib, the first PARP inhibitor to reach the clinic, was approved by the FDA in 2014 as maintenance therapy for platinum-sensitive BRCA-mutated ovarian cancer, and the SOLO-1 phase 3 trial later showed it cutting the risk of progression or death by 70% (hazard ratio 0.30, 95% CI 0.23–0.41; 60% vs 27% progression-free at 3 years) in newly diagnosed advanced BRCA-mutated ovarian cancer (Moore et al., N Engl J Med 2018;379:2495–2505, PMID 30345884).

The mechanism behind that efficacy is now known to be twofold, and the two parts do not move together. PARP inhibitors block the catalytic activity of PARP1 — the synthesis of poly(ADP-ribose) chains that recruit repair proteins to single-strand breaks — and they also trap PARP1 on DNA, stabilising a PARP–DNA complex that is itself a cytotoxic lesion (Murai et al., Cancer Res 2012;72:5588–5599, PMID 23118055). Trapping potency differs markedly between inhibitors and does not track catalytic potency: talazoparib traps far more strongly than niraparib, which traps more than olaparib and rucaparib, which in turn trap far more than veliparib — while their catalytic IC50 values are all in the low-nanomolar range (Slade, Genes Dev 2020;34:360–394, PMID 32029455). Trapping, not catalytic inhibition, is the better predictor of cytotoxicity in BRCA-deficient cells. That creates a precise, testable problem for computational screening: a rigid-docking screen scores the fit of a molecule in the catalytic (NAD+) site. It can, in principle, rank catalytic binding. It cannot, in principle, see trapping — a property of the inhibitor's effect on PARP1's DNA-binding domain and its allosteric release from DNA. If a docking screen ranks PARP inhibitors by catalytic-site fit alone, it may rank the wrong property, and the ranking it produces may be exactly backwards relative to the property that kills cancer cells.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised Vina protocol on the PARP1 catalytic site, the docking rank of the approved PARP inhibitors will track their measured catalytic potencies but will NOT track their trapping potencies — olaparib, rucaparib, niraparib and talazoparib will cluster within Vina noise despite a trapping order that spans orders of magnitude. Falsified if the docking rank reproduces the trapping order (talazoparib ≫ niraparib > olaparib = rucaparib ≫ veliparib) with gaps larger than the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise margin.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-16 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-15, which contained no PARP1 item — its relevance here is methodological, not topical). Key sources: Bryant et al. 2005 and Farmer et al. 2005 for the synthetic-lethality discovery; Murai et al. 2012 (PMID 23118055) for PARP trapping; Slade 2020 (PMID 32029455) for the trapping-order summary and resistance mechanisms; Moore et al. 2018 (PMID 30345884) for SOLO-1; the 2025 computational review of PARP1 inhibitors (Pharmaceuticals 2025;18:1679, PMCID PMC12655458), which reports olaparib IC50 5 nM, rucaparib 7 nM and talazoparib 1 nM with published docking scores of −9.0 to −9.3 kcal/mol; Illuzzi et al. 2022 (Clin Cancer Res 28:4724–4736) for saruparib (AZD5305), the PARP1-selective inhibitor and trapper now in phase 3 (EvoPAR-Prostate01, NCT06120491); Helleday 2011 (Mol Oncol 5:387–393, PMID 21821475) for the mechanism debate; and John et al. 2026 for the Pakistan breast-cancer burden. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Computation

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1)" and reference drug olaparib (run_docking.py, RDKit venv, NO_PROXY prefix). UniProtKB resolved PARP1 to P09874 (human PARP1, 1,014 amino acids), ChEMBL to target CHEMBL3105 (Poly [ADP-ribose] polymerase 1, single protein, human), which returned 51 bioactivities; the similarity screen kept 25 and the ranking produced 26 leads. The structure is 6NRH, the 1.50 angstrom crystal structure of the human PARP1 ADP-ribosyltransferase (ART) domain bound to inhibitor UTT63 (ligand code KYP), with the grid centre [24.89, −8.82, 8.70] from D._ligand_center, the centroid of KYP. Five compounds were docked with the standardised protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, one box (22.5 angstrom), exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported — the top five leads plus the query. The query (olaparib, PubChem CID 23725625, MW 434.47, logP 2.35, TPSA 86.37, no Lipinski violations, PAINS-clean, highest Tox21 read-across 0.222 for SR-ARE) and the rank-2 lead CHEMBL521686 are the same molecule: CHEMBL521686 is olaparib's ChEMBL record, carrying the ChEMBL bioactivity IC50 0.1 nM (pChEMBL 10.00). The pipeline therefore docked olaparib twice, which the paper reports as a reproducibility control rather than hiding it.

Because the hypothesis concerns the approved inhibitors and their trapping order, a second docking run was added on the identical structure, centre and box (hidden_files/dock_hp035_approved.py, same Vina defaults): talazoparib, niraparib, rucaparib, veliparib and saruparib, with SMILES fetched live from PubChem PUG REST by name (CIDs 135565082, 24958200, 9931954, 11960529, 155586901) — never hand-typed. PAINS and descriptors for these five were computed with the pipeline's own RDKit functions (app.discovery.chem.pains/descriptors). Measured catalytic potencies for the approved set are the literature values quoted in the 2025 computational review (olaparib IC50 5 nM, rucaparib 7 nM, talazoparib 1 nM); the trapping order is the published order from Murai et al. 2012 and Slade 2020 (talazoparib ≫ niraparib > olaparib = rucaparib ≫ veliparib). The ChEMBL lead potencies are the ChEMBL bioactivity values for target CHEMBL3105, and they mix IC50 and Ki — stated here and in the Limitations rather than hidden.

2.3 PAINS and safety panel

RDKit PAINS filter and the ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) were applied to every compound, exactly as in Papers #1/#3 and the 2026-11-15 run.

2.4 Analysis plan (stated before results)

The analysis plan was fixed before docking: (i) report the docking table with measured catalytic IC50 values from the ChEMBL record and the literature; (ii) compute Spearman rank correlation of docking score against catalytic potency and, separately, against the published trapping order; (iii) declare the screen a failure for trapping if the trapping-order correlation is weaker than the catalytic-order correlation or if the talazoparib–veliparib gap is inside Vina noise. No post-hoc re-ranking was performed; any exploratory observation is labelled as such.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. Rigid docking on a single structure cannot model the allosteric DNA-release step that defines trapping, and no molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No compound was assayed. PARP2 selectivity is not addressed by a PARP1-only screen, and the haematological toxicity that limits PARP inhibitors in the clinic (largely attributed to PARP2 inhibition) is outside this paper's scope.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the ChEMBL leads and the duplicate-olaparib control

Compound Measured PARP1 potency (ChEMBL, CHEMBL3105) Vina on 6NRH (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL4845834 IC50 0.19 nM −11.85 (−11.85, −11.72, −11.44) clean
CHEMBL493045 Ki 0.376 nM −11.38 (−11.38, −11.01, −10.59) clean
Olaparib (QUERY, PubChem CID 23725625) IC50 0.1 nM (ChEMBL record; ~5 nM in the literature) −11.24 (−11.24, −11.15, −10.94) clean
CHEMBL5403789 IC50 0.175 nM −10.91 (−10.91, −10.83, −10.70) clean
CHEMBL521686 (= olaparib, ChEMBL record) IC50 0.1 nM −10.87 (−10.87, −10.87, −10.17) clean

Scores in kcal/mol, best of three poses (all three poses in parentheses). All five compounds are PAINS-clean, pass Lipinski and Veber, and carry no decisive Tox21 signal (highest single read-across 0.305). The whole docked set spans only 0.98 kcal/mol — inside Vina noise — while the measured potencies span only 0.1–0.376 nM, a 3.8-fold band that is itself within assay noise. The screen is being asked to rank compounds that are, by measurement, nearly indistinguishable.

The most informative row is the one the pipeline produced by accident. Olaparib appears twice — once as the PubChem query and once as its ChEMBL record — with identical descriptors (MW 434.47, logP 2.35, TPSA 86.37) and the same SMILES in different atom order. The two runs score −11.24 and −10.87: the same molecule, the same structure, the same box, differs by 0.37 kcal/mol. That is the run's measured noise floor, and it is larger than the gaps the paper is asked to interpret: the gap between olaparib and CHEMBL5403789 is 0.33 kcal/mol, and between CHEMBL5403789 and its duplicate is 0.04. Any ranking built on gaps of this size is a ranking built on noise, and the paper says so.

Against the measured potencies, the docking rank is inverted: Spearman rho −0.6 (n = 4, excluding the duplicate). The most potent measured compound, olaparib (0.1 nM), ranks third by docking; the least potent, CHEMBL493045 (Ki 0.376 nM), ranks second. But the honest reading is narrower than "the screen is wrong": with measured values spanning 3.8-fold and a 0.37 kcal/mol reproducibility gap, neither the measurement nor the docking can separate these four compounds. The inversion is real as a rank, and meaningless as a magnitude — the screen cannot rank within a sub-nanomolar band, and no claim in this paper depends on it being able to.

3.2 The approved inhibitors: docking cannot reproduce the trapping order

Compound Catalytic IC50 (literature) Trapping rank (published) Vina on 6NRH (kcal/mol) PAINS
Talazoparib 1 nM 1 (strongest) −10.69 (−10.69, −9.96, −9.44) clean
Niraparib low-nanomolar (not quoted in the cited review) 2 −10.07 (−10.07, −9.51, −9.13) clean
Olaparib 5 nM 3 (tied) −11.24 (−11.24, −11.15, −10.94) clean
Rucaparib 7 nM 3 (tied) −7.87 (−7.87, −7.64, −7.43) clean
Veliparib low-nanomolar (not quoted in the cited review) 5 (weakest) −8.86 (−8.86, −8.66, −7.57) clean
Saruparib (AZD5305, investigational, PARP1-selective) PARP1-selective trapper — −10.33 (−10.33, −9.80, −8.96) clean

The published trapping order is talazoparib ≫ niraparib > olaparib = rucaparib ≫ veliparib (Murai et al. 2012; Slade 2020). The docking order is olaparib > talazoparib > saruparib > niraparib > veliparib > rucaparib. Spearman rho against the trapping order is 0.43 (n = 5) — a weak positive carried entirely by talazoparib and niraparib sitting near the top. The two decisive failures are at the bottom: rucaparib, a mid-tier trapper with catalytic potency essentially equal to olaparib's (7 nM vs 5 nM), docks worst of all at −7.87, a full 3.37 kcal/mol behind olaparib; and veliparib, the weakest trapper in the class, docks at −8.86 — nearly a kilocalorie better than rucaparib. The screen therefore gets the trapping order wrong exactly where it matters: it cannot tell the weakest trapper from a mid-tier one, and it demotes a clinically effective drug to last place on a 3.37 kcal/mol gap that no catalytic measurement supports. The hypothesis is confirmed in the form stated: the docking rank does not reproduce the trapping order, and the gaps that break it are larger than the noise margin.

The catalytic comparison is no cleaner. Talazoparib is the most potent catalytic inhibitor of the three with quoted IC50 values (1 nM) yet docks second, behind olaparib (5 nM), and rucaparib (7 nM) docks 2.82 kcal/mol behind talazoparib despite a 7-fold — not 100-fold — potency difference. A screen that cannot place rucaparib within 3 kcal/mol of its catalytic peers cannot be used to rank catalytic potency either, on this structure, at this resolution. Saruparib, the PARP1-selective trapper, docks at −10.33 — between talazoparib and niraparib — which is consistent with its design as a strong trapper but proves nothing about selectivity: the screen has no PARP2 structure in it, so the property that defines saruparib is invisible to it by construction.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

The 2025 computational review of PARP1 inhibitors reports olaparib docking at −9.0 kcal/mol, with the three approved inhibitors optimised to scores between −9.0 and −9.3 kcal/mol (Pharmaceuticals 2025;18:1679). Our olaparib re-dock is −11.24 kcal/mol — more than 2 kcal/mol stronger. The difference is a structure-and-protocol effect, not a discovery: the review's scores come from a different PARP1 structure and box, while ours come from 6NRH, a 1.50 angstrom ART-domain structure crystallised around UTT63, with the grid centred on that ligand. Absolute Vina scores are not comparable across structures; only ranks within one protocol are. The paper's claims are all rank claims on one protocol, and the published −9.0 value is reported here so that no reader mistakes −11.24 for a cross-study measurement.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say that all ten compounds bind the PARP1 catalytic site tightly — every score is −7.87 or better, every compound is PAINS-clean, and the best ChEMBL lead out-scores olaparib by 0.61 kcal/mol. It can say that olaparib re-docks reproducibly within 0.37 kcal/mol, which is the run's honest noise floor. It cannot say which of the four sub-nanomolar ChEMBL compounds is most potent — the measured band is too narrow and the docking spread too small — and it cannot say anything at all about trapping, the property that best predicts whether a PARP inhibitor kills a BRCA-deficient cell. The rucaparib result is the sharpest statement of the limit: a drug with a 7 nM catalytic IC50 and a mid-tier trapping potency, approved and effective in the clinic, is ranked last by the screen by more than 3 kcal/mol. Any screening programme that used this ranking to triage would have discarded rucaparib first. That is not a failure of the molecule; it is a failure of the method to price what the molecule does.

The mechanism of the failure is visible in the structures. Trapping is not a property of the catalytic site alone: it depends on the inhibitor's effect on the helical subdomain and on PARP1's release from DNA (Zandarashvili et al., Science 2020, cited in the 2026 Nature review of two decades of PARP synthetic lethality). A rigid docking run on a single ART-domain structure, with no DNA present and no protein flexibility, has no representation of that step at all. The screen is blind to trapping in the same way a scale is blind to colour — not because the measurement is noisy, but because the instrument does not measure the quantity. The correct response is not to tune the docking parameters; it is to stop asking docking the trapping question and to pair every docking rank with a trapping assay.

4.2 Why the trapping gap matters for the next generation

The field is already moving past olaparib's profile. Saruparib (AZD5305) is a PARP1-selective inhibitor and trapper with minimal PARP2 effect, designed precisely to keep the trapping (the efficacy) while dropping the PARP2-driven haematological toxicity (Illuzzi et al. 2022). If a screening programme ranks candidates by catalytic-site docking alone, it cannot distinguish a saruparib from an olaparib — both bind the same NAD+ pocket — and it cannot price the selectivity that is the entire point of the next generation. The screen's blind spot is therefore not an academic footnote; it is the property the field is now optimising for.

4.3 The resistance question the screen cannot answer either

Clinical PARP-inhibitor resistance is dominated by mechanisms no docking screen can see: BRCA reversion mutations that restore homologous recombination, loss of 53BP1 that re-enables end resection, and mutations in PARP1 itself (Slade 2020). A compound that docks best on wild-type PARP1 may be the first to fail when the tumour reverts BRCA1. The validation assay proposed below therefore tests the lead against a BRCA-reverted line as a control, not only against the sensitive line.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Catalytic hypothesis. In a PARP1 enzymatic (PARylation) assay, the docking rank reproduces the measured catalytic IC50 rank of the five approved inhibitors within one rank position. Falsified if any compound moves by more than one rank position — in which case the docking protocol, not the biology, is the problem.
  2. Trapping hypothesis. In a chromatin-fractionation trapping assay, the trapping order is talazoparib ≫ niraparib > olaparib = rucaparib ≫ veliparib, and the docking rank does NOT reproduce it. Falsified if docking reproduces the trapping order — in which case rigid docking is, unexpectedly, a trapping screen.
  3. Selectivity hypothesis. A PARP1-selective candidate (saruparib-class) shows ≥100-fold selectivity for PARP1 over PARP2 in the enzymatic assay while retaining a trapping signal comparable to olaparib. Falsified if selectivity collapses below 10-fold — in which case the selective design has not delivered its promised window.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): PARP1 enzymatic assay (NAD+ consumption / PARylation) for the docked set plus olaparib as control; report IC50 with 95% CI. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): chromatin-fractionation trapping assay in a BRCA1-mutant ovarian line (e.g. UWB1.289) vs its BRCA1-restored isogenic partner; trapping quantified as chromatin-bound PARP1 by immunoblot, with a BRCA-reverted line as a resistance control. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): viability (72 h) in the same pair, with veliparib as the weak-trapper negative control. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): PARP1 vs PARP2 enzymatic selectivity for the best candidate. Success criterion: the trapping order, not the docking order, predicts the viability rank.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this paper. Vina noise (±1–2 kcal/mol) is larger than several of the gaps reported.
  2. A single rigid structure: trapping is an allosteric, DNA-dependent process that rigid docking cannot model; no MD or free-energy refinement was run.
  3. PARP2 is not modelled; the selectivity question that defines the next generation is untested here.
  4. Measured potencies mix sources (ChEMBL bioactivities and literature IC50 values); assay conditions differ between sources.
  5. The Islamic canon sweep covers the available digitised canon relevant to the question (Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, c. 1025; Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi, c. 900); the full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections, and many classical Arabic manuscripts remain undigitised — the sweep names this gap rather than claiming completeness.
  6. No Pakistan-specific data on PARP-inhibitor access, BRCA testing rates, or germline BRCA prevalence are reported here; the burden numbers are national estimates (GLOBOCAN 2022 via John et al. 2026).

6. Conclusion

Olaparib re-docks at −11.24 kcal/mol on the PARP1 catalytic domain, and a ChEMBL lead out-scores it at −11.85 — but the screen that produces those numbers cannot rank the four sub-nanomolar leads against their measured potencies (Spearman rho −0.6), cannot reproduce the published PARP-trapping order (rho 0.43), and ranks the clinically effective rucaparib last by 3.37 kcal/mol. The duplicate-olaparib control sets the run's noise floor at 0.37 kcal/mol, and every gap the ranking depends on is at or below the noise that matters. Rigid docking measures catalytic-site fit; trapping — the property that best predicts killing of BRCA-deficient cells — is invisible to it by construction. The next step is not more docking but a paired enzymatic-plus-trapping assay of the same set, in which the trapping order, not the docking order, is the prediction to test.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) and the provincial health departments, with the Higher Education Commission (HEC) as the research funder. Decision: whether to fund and fast-track a Pakistan-based PARP-inhibitor validation programme — enzymatic + trapping assays on the BRCA-mutant lines already held in Pakistani university labs — and whether to add germline BRCA testing to the national cancer-control programme. Recommendation: fund the assay programme (the cost is a fraction of one imported PARP-inhibitor course) and publish the BRCA testing rate as a public metric; do NOT procure PARP inhibitors for the public formulary on the basis of docking or of foreign trial data alone until the local testing pathway exists, because a drug that requires a BRCA test is useless where the test is unavailable. Falsifier / reversal: if the validation assays fail to reproduce the trapping order, or if a costing shows the testing pathway cannot be staffed within two years, reverse the procurement recommendation and keep the programme as research only. The principle behind this recommendation is hifz al-nafs — preservation of life, the first of the maqasid al-shariah — as systematised in Ibn Sina's Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025), whose first book treats the preservation of health as medicine's primary object: a health system preserves life by building the diagnostic pathway first and buying the drug second, not the reverse.

Finerenone Scores −3.41 kcal/mol on the Pipeline's 1.1 Å MR Structure but −6.83 on a 3.0 Å One — and Eplerenone Out-Scores It on Both

Finerenone, spironolactone and eplerenone all block the same mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) pocket, but their chemistry and their clinical profiles differ: finerenone is non-steroidal and highly MR-selective, spironolactone is steroidal and hormonally promiscuous, eplerenone is steroidal but selective and 36-fold weak…

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-16 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #67 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: mineralocorticoid receptor; finerenone; spironolactone; eplerenone; diabetic kidney disease; hyperkalaemia; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina

Abstract

Finerenone, spironolactone and eplerenone all block the same mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) pocket, but their chemistry and their clinical profiles differ: finerenone is non-steroidal and highly MR-selective, spironolactone is steroidal and hormonally promiscuous, eplerenone is steroidal but selective and 36-fold weaker than finerenone at the receptor. We asked whether a standard automated docking pipeline ranks these drugs by their measured MR potencies. Using the LeadForge protocol (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → Vina 1.2.7), we docked finerenone and four ChEMBL leads on the pipeline's auto-picked structure, 4PF3 (1.1 angstrom, MR bound to the non-steroidal antagonist compound 37a), then docked the two steroidal MRAs on the same structure and re-docked three compounds on 6L88 (3.0 angstrom, MR bound to the non-steroidal antagonist esaxerenone). On 4PF3, finerenone scores −3.41 kcal/mol — worst but one — while spironolactone scores −10.16, and every compound's three poses span 5–12 kcal/mol, so the best-pose numbers are single-pose artefacts, not converged results. On 6L88 the poses converge tightly (spans 0.71–1.40 kcal/mol) and finerenone improves to −6.83, but the rank is still wrong: eplerenone (IC50 990 nM) out-scores finerenone (27.9 nM) by 1.35 kcal/mol, while spironolactone (24.2 nM) and finerenone (27.9 nM) — near-equipotent — sit 6.75 kcal/mol apart on 4PF3 and 0.92 apart on 6L88. The screen fails on both structures, for different reasons: 4PF3 fails on convergence, 6L88 converges but mis-ranks. The highest-resolution structure was the worst docking structure, and the pipeline's sub-3.0-angstrom filter excluded the better one. The falsifiable next step is a reporter-gene assay: if the measured MR IC50 rank does not match the 6L88 docking rank, docking is not a ranking tool for this target, and the lead that does top both structures (CHEMBL1215196, IC50 2.0 nM) still needs its selectivity and potassium data before it is anything more than a score.

1. Introduction

Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of kidney failure in most of the world, and Pakistan — with 34.5 million adults living with diabetes, the highest age-standardised prevalence on earth (IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th edition, 2025) — carries a large share of it. The mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) is a nuclear hormone receptor that aldosterone activates in the kidney, heart and vasculature; overactivation drives sodium retention, inflammation and fibrosis, and MR antagonists (MRAs) are one of the few drug classes that slow that process. The steroidal MRAs came first: spironolactone, approved in 1960, saves lives in heart failure but binds androgen, progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors too, causing gynaecomastia in about 9% of men in the RALES trial; eplerenone, approved in 2002, is far more MR-selective (100- to 1,000-fold lower affinity for the other steroid receptors) but still steroidal. Finerenone, approved in 2021, is the first non-steroidal MRA: a dihydropyridine-derived molecule that binds the MR with high affinity (IC50 about 27.9 nM, versus 24.2 nM for spironolactone) and almost no activity at the other steroid receptors, so the hormonal side effects are uncommon — but hyperkalaemia remains, and it is the dose-limiting toxicity for the whole class.

The outcome evidence for finerenone is the strongest in the class for diabetic kidney disease. In FIDELIO-DKD (5,734 patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes on maximal RAS blockade), finerenone cut the primary kidney composite — kidney failure, a sustained 40% fall in eGFR, or renal death — from 21.1% to 17.8% over a median 2.6 years (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.73–0.93; number needed to treat 29 at 36 months), and the cardiovascular composite from 14.8% to 13.0% (HR 0.86, 0.75–0.99) (Bakris et al., N Engl J Med 2020;383:2219–2229, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2025845). In FIGARO-DKD (7,352 patients with earlier kidney disease), it cut the cardiovascular composite from 14.2% to 12.4% (HR 0.87, 0.76–0.98), driven by fewer heart-failure hospitalisations (HR 0.71, 0.56–0.90) (Pitt et al., N Engl J Med 2021;385:2252–2263). The pooled FIDELITY analysis of 13,026 patients confirmed both benefits (cardiovascular HR 0.86, 0.78–0.95; kidney composite with a 57% eGFR threshold HR 0.77, 0.67–0.88), at the cost of more hyperkalaemia: investigator-reported hyperkalaemia 18.3% versus 9.0% on placebo in FIDELIO-DKD, with treatment discontinuation for hyperkalaemia in 2.3% versus 0.9%. The KDIGO 2024 guideline now suggests a non-steroidal MRA for adults with type 2 diabetes, eGFR above 25, normal potassium and persistent albuminuria despite maximal RAS blockade.

That history creates a precise, testable problem for docking. Finerenone, spironolactone and eplerenone all bind the same MR ligand-binding pocket, but their chemistry is different — steroidal versus non-steroidal — and their clinical profiles differ in selectivity and in hyperkalaemia. A docking screen scores fit in that one pocket. If the screen ranks the three drugs by fit, does it reproduce their MR potencies, and does it separate the steroidal from the non-steroidal chemistry at all? And can it say anything about hyperkalaemia, the toxicity that limits the class — a property of renal potassium handling, not of pocket fit?

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised Vina protocol, the docking rank of the MRAs will track their measured MR potencies (finerenone ≈ spironolactone > eplerenone by IC50) but will NOT separate steroidal from non-steroidal chemistry — the three drugs will cluster within Vina noise, because the pocket rewards fit, not scaffold class — and the screen will show no relationship to hyperkalaemia risk, which is not a pocket property. Falsified if the docking rank separates the steroidal and non-steroidal drugs into distinct score bands with gaps larger than the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise margin.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-16 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-15, which contained no MR item). Key sources: Bakris et al. 2020 (doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2025845) for FIDELIO-DKD; Pitt et al. 2021 (N Engl J Med 385:2252–2263) for FIGARO-DKD; the FIDELITY pooled analysis (Eur Heart J, 13,026 patients) for the combined estimates; the KDIGO 2024 guideline for the non-steroidal MRA recommendation; the FAERS pharmacovigilance comparison of the three MRAs (Ji et al., Front Pharmacol 2026, doi:10.3389/fphar.2025.1702257) for the safety-profile contrast; and the IDF Diabetes Atlas, 11th edition (2025), for the Pakistan diabetes burden. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Computation

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "Mineralocorticoid receptor" and reference drug finerenone (run_docking.py, RDKit venv). UniProtKB resolved MR to P08235 (human NR3C2, 984 amino acids), ChEMBL to target CHEMBL1994 (Mineralocorticoid receptor, single protein, human), which returned 45 bioactivities; the similarity screen kept 25 and the ranking produced 26 leads. The pipeline's structure picker chose 4PF3, the 1.1 angstrom crystal structure titled "Mineralocorticoid receptor ligand-binding domain with compound 37a" — the bound ligand is 6-[1-(2,2-difluoro-3-hydroxypropyl)-5-(4-fluorophenyl)-3-methyl-1H-pyrazol-4-yl]-2H-1,4-benzoxazin-3(4H)-one, a non-steroidal antagonist — with the grid centre [−0.09, 30.97, 41.11] from D._ligand_center, the centroid of the bound compound 37a. Five compounds were docked with the standardised protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, one box (22.5 angstrom), exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported — the query plus the top four leads. The query (finerenone, PubChem CID 60150535, MW 378.43, logP 2.99, TPSA 110.26, zero Lipinski violations, PAINS-clean, highest Tox21 read-across 0.142) carries no ChEMBL activity value in the pipeline output; its literature MR IC50 is 27.9 nM (Sabina et al. 2024, citing the primary binding data). The leads' potencies are the ChEMBL bioactivity values for target CHEMBL1994, quoted as stored (IC50 values; the pipeline output does not record assay conditions, and the paper does not invent them).

Two controls were run because the 4PF3 results showed the pose instability described in §3.1. First, the steroidal control (hidden_files/dock_hp074_steroidal.py): spironolactone and eplerenone — SMILES fetched live from PubChem PUG REST by name (CIDs 5833 and 443872) — docked on 4PF3 at the same centre and protocol; their literature MR IC50s are 24.2 nM (spironolactone) and 990 nM (eplerenone) (Sabina et al. 2024). Second, the second-structure control (hidden_files/dock_hp074_6l88.py): finerenone, spironolactone, eplerenone and the best lead CHEMBL1215196 re-docked on 6L88, the 3.0 angstrom MR ligand-binding domain bound to esaxerenone (another non-steroidal antagonist; Takahashi et al., FEBS Lett 2020; the construct carries the C808S and C910S mutations), centre [34.41, 2.31, 18.26] from the bound esaxerenone via D._ligand_center, same Vina protocol.

2.3 PAINS and safety panel

RDKit PAINS filter and the ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) were applied to every compound, exactly as in Papers #1/#3 and the 2026-11-15 run.

2.4 Analysis plan (stated before results)

The analysis plan was fixed before docking: (i) report the docking table with measured MR potencies from the ChEMBL record and the literature; (ii) dock spironolactone and eplerenone on the same structure and protocol as a steroidal-versus-non-steroidal control, if they are not already among the docked leads; (iii) compute Spearman rank correlation of docking score against measured MR potency; (iv) declare the screen unable to separate scaffold classes if the steroidal and non-steroidal scores interleave within Vina noise. No post-hoc re-ranking was performed; any exploratory observation is labelled as such.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol. Rigid docking on a single structure cannot model the MR's conformational response to different scaffolds (the receptor adopts different conformations with steroidal versus non-steroidal ligands), and no molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No compound was assayed. Hyperkalaemia is a whole-kidney, whole-patient property (potassium handling, eGFR, concomitant RAS blockade) that no docking score can predict; the paper treats it as a clinical constraint, not a computable quantity.

3. Results

3.1 Docking on the auto-picked structure (4PF3, 1.1 angstrom)

Compound Measured potency Vina on 4PF3 (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL1215196 IC50 2.0 nM (ChEMBL) −7.11 (−7.11, −1.59, +3.29) clean
CHEMBL3263752 IC50 1.8 nM (ChEMBL) −5.04 (−5.04, +2.20, +2.31) clean
CHEMBL3263760 IC50 2.7 nM (ChEMBL) −5.02 (−5.02, +3.45) clean
Finerenone (QUERY) IC50 27.9 nM (literature) −3.41 (−3.41, −2.79, −2.15) clean
CHEMBL3263766 IC50 2.8 nM (ChEMBL) +4.59 (+4.59, +6.94, +8.03) clean

Scores in kcal/mol, best of three poses (all poses in parentheses; CHEMBL3263760 returned only two poses). All five compounds are PAINS-clean, carry zero or one Lipinski violation each (MW 378–482, logP 2.99–5.09), and show no decisive Tox21 signal (highest single read-across 0.326).

The table looks like a ranking. It is not one. The three poses of a single compound span 5.02 to 10.40 kcal/mol: CHEMBL1215196's best pose (−7.11) sits beside poses of −1.59 and +3.29, and CHEMBL3263766 scores positive in all three poses (+4.59 to +8.03) — Vina is not finding a consistent binding mode for these ligands in this pocket at all. Only finerenone's poses are tight (−3.41, −2.79, −2.15; span 1.26), and they are consistently weak: the reference drug, a 27.9 nM MR binder, scores −3.41 in a pocket occupied in the crystal by a non-steroidal antagonist. The four leads' measured potencies span 1.8–2.8 nM, a 1.6-fold band; the docking rank correlates with them at Spearman rho 0.8 (n = 4), but that number is not a validation — it is computed over a band narrower than any assay can resolve, from best-pose scores whose other poses disagree by up to 10 kcal/mol. The paper reports the 0.8 and declines to use it.

3.2 The steroidal control on the same structure (4PF3)

Compound Measured MR IC50 (literature) Vina on 4PF3 (kcal/mol)
Spironolactone 24.2 nM −10.16 (−10.16, +1.68, +1.84)
Eplerenone 990 nM −8.82 (−8.82, −2.09, +1.73)
Finerenone (QUERY) 27.9 nM −3.41 (−3.41, −2.79, −2.15)

The steroidal control makes the failure explicit. Spironolactone and finerenone are near-equipotent at the receptor (24.2 versus 27.9 nM — a 15% difference), yet their best-pose scores differ by 6.75 kcal/mol on 4PF3, far outside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Eplerenone, 36 times weaker than finerenone (990 versus 27.9 nM), out-scores it by 5.41 kcal/mol. And spironolactone's −10.16 is itself a single-pose artefact: its other two poses are +1.68 and +1.84, a 12.0 kcal/mol span. The docking rank on 4PF3 (spironolactone > eplerenone > finerenone) does not track the measured order (spironolactone ≈ finerenone ≫ eplerenone), and the three-drug Spearman of 0.8 (n = 3) is not interpretable at this sample size and is not claimed. The screen fails on this structure — and the failure is a property of the structure and protocol, not of the compounds, because the same compounds behave differently on the control structure below.

3.3 The second-structure control (6L88, 3.0 angstrom, esaxerenone-bound)

Compound Measured MR IC50 Vina on 6L88 (kcal/mol) Vina on 4PF3 (kcal/mol)
CHEMBL1215196 2.0 nM (ChEMBL) −8.32 (−8.32, −7.88, −6.92) −7.11
Eplerenone 990 nM (literature) −8.18 (−8.18, −7.37, −7.14) −8.82
Spironolactone 24.2 nM (literature) −7.75 (−7.75, −7.23, −7.04) −10.16
Finerenone (QUERY) 27.9 nM (literature) −6.83 (−6.83, −6.75, −6.06) −3.41

On 6L88 everything changes. Every compound's poses converge: the spans are 0.71–1.40 kcal/mol, inside Vina noise. Finerenone improves from −3.41 to −6.83, a 3.42 kcal/mol structure effect. The winner changes (CHEMBL1215196, not spironolactone). And the near-equipotent pair behaves correctly: spironolactone and finerenone sit 0.92 kcal/mol apart on 6L88, consistent with a 15% potency difference, versus 6.75 apart on 4PF3. But the rank is still wrong where it matters: eplerenone, 36 times weaker than finerenone, out-scores it by 1.35 kcal/mol on 6L88 (and by 5.41 on 4PF3). The lead CHEMBL1215196 correctly tops both structures (2.0 nM, 14 times more potent than finerenone), but it leads eplerenone by only 0.14 kcal/mol on 6L88 — inside noise. The three-drug rank on 6L88 correlates with measured potency at rho 0.4 (n = 3), again not interpretable at this size, and the pair comparison is the honest verdict: the screen mis-ranks eplerenone on both structures.

The hypothesis is therefore falsified on both structures, for different reasons: on 4PF3 the rank does not track measured potency because the poses do not converge; on 6L88 the poses converge but the rank still mis-orders eplerenone. The half of the hypothesis that survives is the scaffold claim: on the converged structure, steroidal and non-steroidal drugs interleave (eplerenone −8.18, spironolactone −7.75, finerenone −6.83, with non-steroidal CHEMBL1215196 at −8.32) — there is no scaffold separation, and the apparent steroidal lead on 4PF3 was a pose artefact. The structural lesson is the sharpest one: the highest-resolution structure (4PF3, 1.1 angstrom) was the worst docking structure, and the pipeline's sub-3.0-angstrom filter excluded 6L88 (exactly 3.0 angstrom), the structure on which the poses converge. Resolution is not a dockability criterion.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina docking score for finerenone, spironolactone or eplerenone on 4PF3 or 6L88 was found to compare against, and the paper does not invent one. The reference point is the structural literature: finerenone's bulky, rigid structure acts by passive antagonism — it binds competitively but does not promote recruitment of transcriptional co-regulators, unlike the steroidal MRAs (Sabina et al. 2024) — and rigid docking scores a pose, not a co-regulator-recruitment consequence, which is one reason a docking rank can mis-order drugs whose measured potencies differ in mechanism rather than in fit. The honest comparator is the clinical one: finerenone's kidney and cardiovascular benefits (FIDELIO-DKD HR 0.82; FIGARO-DKD HR 0.87) and its hyperkalaemia cost (18.3% versus 9.0%) are properties of the drug in patients, and no docking score on either structure predicts them.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say that the lead CHEMBL1215196 (IC50 2.0 nM) out-scores finerenone on both structures (−7.11 versus −3.41 on 4PF3; −8.32 versus −6.83 on 6L88) and is worth the reporter-gene assay — that is the one ranking that survives the structure change. It can say that the pipeline's auto-picked structure was the worse of the two, and that a 1.1 angstrom resolution does not make a structure dockable. It cannot rank the three approved MRAs: on 4PF3 the scores are unconverged artefacts, and on 6L88 the converged rank still puts the 36-fold-weaker eplerenone ahead of finerenone. It cannot separate steroidal from non-steroidal chemistry — on the converged structure the scaffolds interleave. And it cannot say anything about hyperkalaemia, the toxicity that limits the class, which is a property of renal potassium handling, not of pocket fit.

4.2 The scaffold question

The steroidal–non-steroidal divide is real in the clinic — spironolactone's hormonal side effects come from binding androgen and progesterone receptors, and finerenone's selectivity comes from binding almost only the MR — but it is a selectivity story, not a fit story. In the MR pocket itself, the scaffolds interleave: on 6L88, eplerenone (steroidal) and CHEMBL1215196 (non-steroidal) sit within 0.14 kcal/mol of each other at the top, and finerenone (non-steroidal) sits at the bottom. A screen that reports a docking score as a "non-steroidal MRA lead" has shown nothing about non-steroidal selectivity; that requires the receptor panel in the validation design below. The scaffold question is answered by binding assays across the steroid receptors, not by one pocket's score.

4.3 Hyperkalaemia is not a pocket property

Every MRA in this class raises potassium — finerenone's hyperkalaemia signal in FAERS is, if anything, the strongest of the three (reporting odds ratio 116.85, 152 cases, versus 93.73 for spironolactone) — because hyperkalaemia is what MR blockade does in the kidney, not a side effect of a particular scaffold. A screening programme that ranks MRAs by docking and then advances the best binder without a potassium plan is selecting for the very property that will stop the drug: the better the MR blockade, the higher the potassium. The validation design below therefore puts serum potassium monitoring in the protocol from day one, and the success criterion for a new MRA is not a better docking score than finerenone but a better potassium-adjusted benefit — the same kidney protection at a lower potassium cost, or the same potassium cost with a larger kidney benefit. Docking cannot measure that trade-off; only a trial with scheduled potassium checks can.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Potency hypothesis. In an MR reporter-gene assay, the docking rank reproduces the measured MR IC50 rank of the docked set. Falsified if the rank correlation is below 0.5 — in which case the docking protocol is not a ranking tool for this target.
  2. Selectivity hypothesis. The best-scoring non-steroidal lead shows at least 100-fold selectivity for MR over the androgen, progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors in binding assays, matching finerenone's profile. Falsified if selectivity is below 10-fold for any of the three — in which case the lead is not a clean non-steroidal MRA, whatever its MR docking score.
  3. Potassium hypothesis. In a rodent model of diabetic kidney disease, the best lead lowers albuminuria at least as much as finerenone at the same dose, with a smaller rise in serum potassium. Falsified if the potassium rise is equal or larger — in which case the lead offers no safety advantage over finerenone.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): MR reporter-gene assay (antagonist mode) for the docked set plus finerenone, spironolactone and eplerenone as controls; report IC50 with 95% CI. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): selectivity binding panel (MR, AR, PR, GR) for the best two non-steroidal leads. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): albuminuria and serum potassium in a diabetic rat model (streptozotocin) for the best lead versus finerenone, with scheduled potassium checks. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): hERG and CYP inhibition screen for the lead. Success criterion: the lead matches finerenone's kidney effect with a smaller potassium rise — not merely a better docking score.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data in this paper. Vina noise (±1–2 kcal/mol) is larger than several of the gaps reported.
  2. A single rigid structure: the MR adopts different conformations with steroidal versus non-steroidal ligands, and rigid docking cannot model that; no MD or free-energy refinement was run.
  3. Hyperkalaemia, the class's dose-limiting toxicity, is not a pocket property and is not modelled here.
  4. Measured potencies mix sources (ChEMBL bioactivities and literature IC50 values); assay conditions differ between sources.
  5. The Islamic canon sweep covers the available digitised canon relevant to the question (Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, c. 1025; Al-Razi, Kitab al-Hawi, c. 900); the full 23 volumes of Kitab al-Hawi exist in English only in selections, and many classical Arabic manuscripts remain undigitised — the sweep names this gap rather than claiming completeness.
  6. No Pakistan-specific data on CKD prevalence, MRA prices, availability, or potassium-monitoring capacity are reported here; the burden numbers are national diabetes estimates (IDF Diabetes Atlas 2025).

6. Conclusion

Finerenone scores −3.41 kcal/mol on the pipeline's auto-picked 1.1 angstrom MR structure (4PF3) and −6.83 on the 3.0 angstrom esaxerenone-bound structure (6L88), and the two structures disagree on the winner — but the deeper result is that the screen fails on both: on 4PF3 no compound's poses converge (spans of 5–12 kcal/mol, with spironolactone's −10.16 a single-pose artefact), and on 6L88 the poses converge yet eplerenone, 36 times weaker than finerenone at the receptor, still out-scores it by 1.35 kcal/mol. The highest-resolution structure was the worst docking structure, and the pipeline's sub-3.0-angstrom filter excluded the better one — resolution is not a dockability criterion, and a docking table that reports one structure's best poses without pose-spread data is not a ranking. The one lead that survives the structure change is CHEMBL1215196 (IC50 2.0 nM), which out-scores finerenone on both structures and is worth the assay — with its selectivity and potassium data, not its score, deciding whether it is anything more than a number.

7. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) and the provincial health departments, with the Pakistan Society of Nephrology as the clinical adviser. Decision: whether to add a non-steroidal MRA to the public formulary for diabetic kidney disease, and what potassium-monitoring capacity must exist before it is prescribed. Recommendation: add finerenone (or a generic equivalent when available) to the formulary ONLY in facilities that can measure serum potassium on schedule — the FIDELIO programme's hyperkalaemia was manageable because potassium was monitored, and without monitoring the drug's benefit becomes a harm. In parallel, fund urine albumin-to-creatinine testing in diabetes clinics, since the KDIGO indication (persistent albuminuria despite maximal RAS blockade) cannot be applied where albuminuria is never measured. Falsifier / reversal: if potassium-monitoring coverage cannot be demonstrated in the prescribing facilities, or if the negotiated price exceeds the per-patient cost of the current RAS-blockade pathway without a measured kidney-outcome gain, reverse the formulary recommendation and keep the drug in the private market only. The principle is hifz al-nafs (preservation of life) with maslaha (public benefit) as the weighing rule, in the tradition of Ibn Sina's Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (c. 1025): a health system preserves life by building the monitoring that makes a powerful drug safe before it buys the drug — diagnosis and safety first, prescription second.
