Nintedanib Tops a PknB Docking Rank That Matches Measured Potency Exactly: Two Approved Cancer Kinase Inhibitors and the Mitoxantrone Caveat

PknB is an essential serine/threonine kinase of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and no PknB inhibitor has reached the clinic: the best published inhibitors are nanomolar in vitro and only micromolar against whole cells.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-15 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #62 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: PknB; Mycobacterium tuberculosis; nintedanib; sunitinib; mitoxantrone; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; kinase inhibitor repurposing

Abstract

PknB is an essential serine/threonine kinase of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and no PknB inhibitor has reached the clinic: the best published inhibitors are nanomolar in vitro and only micromolar against whole cells. We docked five compounds with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on 3ORK, the 1.60 angstrom structure of the PknB kinase domain (L33D mutant) with an ATP-gamma-S analogue in the ATP site: nintedanib, two matched-pair aminopyrimidine/pyrazole inhibitors from the same series, sunitinib, and mitoxantrone, the literature PknB inhibitor. The docking rank matches the measured potency rank exactly (Spearman rho 1.0, n = 4): nintedanib, Kd 3.6 nM, docks at minus 9.70 kcal/mol; the matched pair, Ki 13 and 17 nM, at minus 8.66 and minus 8.30; sunitinib, Kd 87 nM, at minus 8.24. Mitoxantrone, which has no attached PknB potency number and is excluded from the correlation, docks worst at minus 7.19 and carries a PAINS alert with the maximum Tox21 read-across for the DNA-damage assays SR-ATAD5 and SR-p53. Two approved cancer kinase inhibitors top a tuberculosis kinase ranking, and the literature inhibitor is the weakest and the most toxic — a clean repurposing signal and a warning in the same table. The falsifiable next step is a single-assay PknB kinase comparison of the four ranked compounds with a whole-cell assay on Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv: if nintedanib again measures most potent on the enzyme but fails on whole cells, the gap is confirmed as permeability, not potency.

1. Introduction

Tuberculosis killed more people than any other single infectious disease in 2024, and about 390,000 multidrug-resistant/rifampicin-resistant cases were estimated for that year (WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025). The pipeline of new tuberculosis drugs is thin, and repurposing approved kinase inhibitors is one of the few routes that can move fast, because the safety data already exist. PknB is the most attractive kinase target in Mycobacterium tuberculosis: it is essential for survival, it regulates cell growth, cell shape and cell division through substrates including GarA, GlmU and EmbR, and it phosphorylates the proteasome alpha-subunit PrcA. Its sibling kinases PknA and PknB are essential, while PknG drives virulence and persistence — which is why multitarget PknA/B/G inhibition is the current design goal, and why a 2026 study reported structural insights into multitargeting the Pkn kinases (Pollaniemi et al., Microbiol Spectr 2026;14:e0004926).

The history of PknB inhibitor discovery is a cautionary tale. A screen of more than 50,000 compounds found ATP-competitive inhibitors that were nanomolar in vitro but only micromolar against whole cells, and none prevented mycobacterial growth at submicromolar concentrations (Lougheed et al., Tuberculosis 2011;91:277–286, PMID 21482481). Mitoxantrone was identified in 2006 as a PknB inhibitor capable of preventing mycobacterial growth (Wehenkel et al., FEBS Lett 2006;580:3018–3022, PMID 16674948), with a co-crystal structure (2FUM) — but mitoxantrone is a DNA intercalator with well-known cardiotoxicity, and no potency number was ever attached to its PknB inhibition in that paper. The question this paper tests is whether a standard rigid-docking screen can rank PknB inhibitors at all, and whether the approved cancer kinase inhibitors nintedanib and sunitinib — both in the ChEMBL bioactivity record for PknB — are worth carrying forward.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol on the 3ORK ATP site, docking rank will track the measured PknB potency rank (nintedanib first, sunitinib last), and mitoxantrone will score worst, because it is the literature inhibitor with the weakest evidence. Falsified if the docking rank disagrees with the measured rank on any pair, or if mitoxantrone scores within Vina noise of the best compound.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-15 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-14, which screened 722 candidates and selected 8 — none on PknB, so the digest's relevance here is methodological). Key sources: Lombana et al. 2010 (Structure 18:1667–1677) for the 3ORK structure; Wehenkel et al. 2006 (FEBS Lett 580:3018–3022, PMID 16674948, doi:10.1016/j.febslet.2006.04.046) for mitoxantrone as a PknB inhibitor and structure 2FUM; Lougheed et al. 2011 (Tuberculosis 91:277–286, PMID 21482481, PMCID PMC3158675) for the 50,000-compound screen; Pollaniemi et al. 2026 (Microbiol Spectr 14:e0004926, PMID 42446239) for the multitarget Pkn-kinase structural work; the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 for the 2024 MDR/RR-TB case estimate; and the 2025 SSRN in-silico PknB screen (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5954835) for the recent computational context. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Computation

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "Mycobacterium tuberculosis serine/threonine protein kinase B (PknB)" and reference drug mitoxantrone (run_docking.py, RDKit venv, NO_PROXY prefix). Unlike the KRAS and VIM-2 topics, this run was clean: UniProt P9WI81 (PknB, gene pknB, M. tuberculosis H37Rv, 626 amino acids) resolved to ChEMBL target CHEMBL1908385 (Serine/threonine-protein kinase PknB), which returned 57 bioactivities and 26 leads. The structure is 3ORK, 1.60 angstrom — the PknB kinase domain L33D mutant (crystal form 2) with the ATP-gamma-S analogue AGS in the ATP site (Lombana et al. 2010) — with the centre [13.05, 14.71, 12.04] from D._ligand_center, the centroid of the AGS analogue. The L33D mutation must be stated: every score in this paper is on the mutant kinase domain, not the wild type.

Five compounds were docked with the standardised protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, one box (22.5 angstrom), exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported. The four measured compounds: nintedanib (CHEMBL502835; approved 2014), CHEMBL4177445, CHEMBL4172982 and sunitinib (CHEMBL535; approved 2006). Their measured potencies are the ChEMBL bioactivity values for target CHEMBL1908385: nintedanib Kd 3.6 nM; CHEMBL4177445 Ki 13 nM; CHEMBL4172982 Ki 17 nM; sunitinib Kd 87 nM. The two ChEMBL identifiers are a matched pair from one aminopyrimidine/pyrazole series — both MW 390.86, logP 2.79, TPSA 126.65, a 5-cyclopropyl-pyrazol-3-ylamino pyrimidine core, differing only in the sulfonamide phenyl substitution (meta vs para). Mitoxantrone (the query compound, PubChem-verified) carries no measured PknB potency number — Wehenkel et al. 2006 report it qualitatively as a PknB inhibitor that prevents mycobacterial growth — so it is excluded from the rank correlation and reported qualitatively.

2.3 PAINS and safety panel

RDKit PAINS filter and the ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) were applied to every compound. Four of the five are PAINS-clean; mitoxantrone carries a PAINS alert and fails Veber (TPSA 163.18, 12 rotatable bonds, 8 hydrogen-bond donors). Its Tox21 panel is in "measured" mode (maximum similarity 1.0 — the compound is in the Tox21 set) with the maximum values 1.0 for SR-ATAD5 and SR-p53, the two DNA-damage assays. Nintedanib and sunitinib show no decisive Tox21 signal (highest single values 0.239 for sunitinib NR-AhR and 0.084 for nintedanib SR-ARE).

2.4 Rank correlation

Spearman rank correlation was computed between the Vina scores and the measured PknB potencies for the four measured compounds (n = 4). The correlation mixes Kd and Ki values — two nintedanib/sunitinib Kd values against two matched-pair Ki values — which is stated here and in the Limitations rather than hidden. A correlation on four points is reported as a descriptive check, not as a validated ranking — the paper's real tests are the matched pair and the mitoxantrone negative control.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the gap between the first and last measured compounds (1.46 kcal/mol) is inside that noise, so the correlation is a rank match, not a magnitude match. The structure is the L33D mutant. The measured potencies mix Kd and Ki from the ChEMBL record, and the two matched-pair Ki values come from the same series while the two Kd values do not. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No compound was assayed, and no whole-cell data are reported here.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured PknB potency Vina on 3ORK (kcal/mol) PAINS
Nintedanib (CHEMBL502835) Kd 3.6 nM −9.70 (−9.70, −8.89, −8.72) clean
CHEMBL4177445 Ki 13 nM −8.66 (−8.66, −8.12, −7.77) clean
CHEMBL4172982 Ki 17 nM −8.30 (−8.30, −8.27, −8.16) clean
Sunitinib (CHEMBL535) Kd 87 nM −8.24 (−8.24, −7.94, −7.94) clean
Mitoxantrone (query) no PknB potency number −7.19 (−7.19, −7.14, −6.92) alert

Scores in kcal/mol, best of three poses (all three poses in parentheses). Measured potencies are ChEMBL bioactivity values for target CHEMBL1908385. Mitoxantrone is excluded from the rank correlation.

The ranking is exact. Nintedanib is first by 1.04 kcal/mol over the matched pair, and the matched pair is ordered correctly (13 nM before 17 nM, by 0.36 kcal/mol), and sunitinib is last among the measured compounds by 0.06 kcal/mol behind CHEMBL4172982 — a gap that is nothing, and which the paper does not pretend is a difference. Mitoxantrone, the literature inhibitor, docks worst at −7.19, a full 2.51 kcal/mol behind nintedanib.

3.2 Rank correlation: perfect, and carried by the extremes

Against the measured potencies, Spearman rho is 1.0 (n = 4). The value is carried by nintedanib sitting first and sunitinib sitting last in both rankings; the middle pair is ordered correctly but separated by only 0.36 kcal/mol in docking against a 1.3-fold measured gap. A correlation of 1.0 on four points, with the bottom two separated by nothing, is not a validated ranking — it is a screen that got the order right and cannot separate the bottom two. The honest reading is the same as in Paper #60 (KRAS G12D): the extremes are reliable, the middle is not.

3.3 The matched pair: the screen's sharpest test

CHEMBL4177445 and CHEMBL4172982 are the same molecule except for the sulfonamide phenyl substitution — meta in one, para in the other — with identical molecular weight (390.86), logP (2.79) and TPSA (126.65), and measured Ki values of 13 and 17 nM. Docking separates them by 0.36 kcal/mol, in the right direction. That is a real discrimination, but it is a small one: 0.36 kcal/mol is well inside Vina noise, and the 1.3-fold measured gap is itself within assay noise. The pair shows the screen can order a matched pair correctly; it does not show the screen can measure the gap. A screening programme that used the 0.36 kcal/mol difference to choose between them would be choosing on noise.

3.4 Mitoxantrone: the literature inhibitor that should not be the lead

Mitoxantrone is the only compound in this set with published evidence of preventing mycobacterial growth (Wehenkel et al. 2006), and it is the weakest by docking (−7.19), the only one with a PAINS alert, the only one that fails Veber, and the only one with maximum Tox21 values on the DNA-damage assays (SR-ATAD5 1.0, SR-p53 1.0 — measured, not read-across). The Tox21 values are consistent with its mechanism: mitoxantrone is a DNA intercalator, and its cardiotoxicity is well documented in its clinical use. The paper's conclusion is not that mitoxantrone does not inhibit PknB — Wehenkel et al. showed that it does, and structure 2FUM shows it in the ATP site. The conclusion is that it is a poor drug candidate for tuberculosis, and that a screen which ranks it last is ranking it correctly on the property that matters for a lead: it should not be the starting point.

3.5 ADMET and safety panel

Nintedanib (MW 539.64, logP 3.62, one Lipinski violation by molecular weight) and sunitinib (MW 398.48, logP 3.33, no violations) are both approved drugs with established human safety profiles — that is the point of repurposing them. The matched pair passes Lipinski and Veber outright. No decisive Tox21 signal appears for any of the four measured compounds. The safety story that matters is the one in Section 3.4: the literature inhibitor is the toxic one, and the approved drugs are the clean ones.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say that nintedanib is the best PknB binder in this set, by both measurement and docking, and that sunitinib is the weakest of the measured four, by both. It can say that the matched pair is ordered correctly. It cannot say that CHEMBL4172982 is worse than sunitinib — the 0.06 kcal/mol gap is nothing, and the measured gap (17 vs 87 nM, 5-fold) is real but invisible to the screen at this resolution. And it cannot say anything about mitoxantrone's potency, because there is no measured number to compare against; it can only say that mitoxantrone is the worst by docking and the most toxic by every other measure, which is a reason to stop, not a reason to test it first.

4.2 Why this is the clean win of the day

Papers #60 and #61 in this run are both docking failures — a rank inversion on KRAS G12D and a total blindness on VIM-2. This paper is the control that shows the same protocol can work: same Vina version, same box, same exhaustiveness, same PAINS and Tox21 panels, and the ranking comes out exact. The difference is the target, not the method: PknB's ATP site is a well-formed kinase pocket with a hydrophobic back pocket and a hinge, the kind of site rigid docking was built for, while VIM-2's zinc site and KRAS's switch-II pocket are the kinds it was not. The lesson is not that docking works or that it does not — it is that it works on some targets and fails on others, and the only way to know which is to run the control: a set of compounds with known potencies, ranked before the screen is trusted.

4.3 The repurposing question

Nintedanib and sunitinib are approved cancer drugs with known human pharmacokinetics. Nintedanib's Kd of 3.6 nM on PknB is the strongest measured value in this set, and its docking score of −9.70 is the best by more than a kilocalorie. The next step is not more docking — it is the enzyme assay and the whole-cell assay, because the 2011 screen's lesson is that nanomolar in vitro potency does not survive the mycobacterial cell wall. If nintedanib measures nanomolar on the enzyme and micromolar on whole cells, the project becomes a permeability problem, and the matched pair — smaller (MW 390.86) and more polar (TPSA 126.65) — is the more promising starting point for optimisation. If nintedanib fails on the enzyme, the docking rank is a false positive and the paper's conclusion is revised.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Enzyme hypothesis. In a single-assay PknB kinase comparison, nintedanib again measures most potent (IC50 below 10 nM) and sunitinib least potent (above 50 nM), with the matched pair between them. Falsified if any compound measures more than 5-fold from its ChEMBL value — in which case the ChEMBL record, not the screen, is the problem.
  2. Whole-cell hypothesis. Nintedanib's MIC against M. tuberculosis H37Rv is above 10 µM despite nanomolar enzyme potency, reproducing the 2011 pattern. Falsified if the MIC is below 1 µM — in which case nintedanib is a genuine repurposing candidate and the permeability problem does not apply to it.
  3. Mitoxantrone hypothesis. Mitoxantrone's PknB IC50, when measured, is above 1 µM — the weakest in the set, matching its docking rank. Falsified if it measures below 100 nM — in which case the docking rank is wrong and the literature inhibitor deserves a second look.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain nintedanib, sunitinib, the matched pair and mitoxantrone; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): PknB kinase assay (recombinant PknB, ATP-competitive format), all five compounds on the same plates, in triplicate — the single-assay comparison this paper could not make, and the direct test of hypothesis 1 and 3. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): MIC assay on M. tuberculosis H37Rv for the four measured compounds, plus cytotoxicity on a human cell line — the direct test of hypothesis 2 and the safety gate for any repurposing claim. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if any compound shows an MIC below 1 µM with a selectivity index above 10, dock its analogues and synthesise the best two; if all four are above 10 µM on whole cells, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per IC50 and per MIC determination is the minimum for a defensible potency claim; the nintedanib-versus-sunitinib comparison needs the same, because a false "nintedanib is best" call on a rank match is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. The structure is the L33D mutant kinase domain (3ORK); wild-type PknB may score differently, and the paper does not claim the ranking transfers to the wild type.
  3. The measured potencies mix Kd (nintedanib, sunitinib) and Ki (matched pair) from the ChEMBL record; the correlation treats them as one ranking, which is a stated approximation.
  4. Spearman rho is computed on four points; it is a descriptive check, not a validated ranking, and the bottom two compounds are separated by 0.06 kcal/mol — nothing.
  5. Mitoxantrone carries no measured PknB potency number and is excluded from the correlation; its docking rank is a hypothesis, not a result.
  6. No molecular dynamics, flexible-side-chain docking, or free-energy refinement was run.
  7. The 2011 screen's whole-cell data are quoted from the literature, not reproduced here; the permeability gap is a hypothesis, not a measurement in this paper.
  8. Nintedanib and sunitinib are approved for cancer, not for tuberculosis; repurposing requires the whole-cell and safety data in Section 4.5, and no clinical claim is made.
  9. No Pakistan-specific TB burden or PknB prevalence numbers are cited beyond the global MDR-TB count; the paper's relevance to Pakistan is the tuberculosis burden and the repurposing logic — approved drugs are the fastest route a resource-limited setting has.

6. Conclusion

On 3ORK, nintedanib docks at −9.70 kcal/mol against a measured Kd of 3.6 nM, the matched pair at −8.66 and −8.30 against Ki values of 13 and 17 nM, and sunitinib at −8.24 against a Kd of 87 nM — a docking rank that matches the measured rank exactly (Spearman rho 1.0, n = 4), while mitoxantrone, the literature PknB inhibitor, docks worst at −7.19 with a PAINS alert and maximum Tox21 values on the DNA-damage assays. Two approved cancer kinase inhibitors top a tuberculosis kinase ranking, and the literature inhibitor is the weakest and the most toxic. The next step is the single-assay kinase and whole-cell comparison in Section 4.5 — and, as a standing rule, the control that makes this paper trustworthy is the one Papers #60 and #61 lacked a clean result from: a set of compounds with known potencies, ranked before the screen is trusted.

Cilomilast Out-Scores Roflumilast on PDE4D Despite a 171-Fold Potency Gap, and Crisaborole Cannot Be Docked at All: Rigid Docking Misses the Contact Points That Define PDE4 Inhibition

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-15 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #63 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: PDE4; PDE4D; roflumilast; apremilast; cilomilast; crisaborole; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; psoriasis; atopic dermatitis

Abstract

Phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) is the target of four approved drugs — roflumilast, apremilast, crisaborole and difamilast — and a 2025 structural study proposed a simple rule for their potency: roflumilast preserves all three active-site contact points (metal-ion site, conserved glutamine, water network), apremilast two, crisaborole one, and the measured IC50s follow the rule (0.7 nM, 0.14 µM, 0.24 µM). We docked the three dockable drugs with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on 3G4L, the 2.5 angstrom human PDE4D structure co-crystallised with roflumilast. Cilomilast, the weakest of the three docked by 171-fold, scores best at minus 9.62 kcal/mol; roflumilast scores minus 9.14 and apremilast minus 8.93. The 171-fold potency gap between roflumilast and cilomilast is 0.48 kcal/mol in the wrong direction, and the rank correlation against measured potency is 0.5 (n = 3). Crisaborole, the third drug in the comparison set, cannot be docked at all: it is a benzoxaborole, and Vina rejects boron — the second boronate this run has failed to dock, after taniborbactam on VIM-2. The screen cannot see the contact points that define PDE4 potency, and it cannot see the boronate that defines the class's newest chemistry. The falsifiable next step is a single-assay PDE4D IC50 comparison of the four drugs with a metal-aware rescoring of the same poses: if the measured 200-fold range reproduces while every rescoring still ties them, the failure is confirmed as a scoring-function limit, not a pose-sampling error.

1. Introduction

Phosphodiesterase 4 hydrolyses cyclic AMP, and its inhibition raises intracellular cAMP and suppresses inflammatory cytokine production in immune and non-immune cells. The PDE4 family has four genes (PDE4A–D) and more than twenty isoforms; PDE4B drives the anti-inflammatory effect while PDE4D inhibition is associated with emesis, which is why PDE4B-selective design is the field's stated goal — the two differ at only a few active-site residues (Met583 in PDE4B vs Met639 in PDE4D; Leu674 vs Gln730). Four PDE4 inhibitors are approved: roflumilast (severe COPD, and topically for psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis and atopic dermatitis), apremilast (oral, psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis), crisaborole (topical, atopic dermatitis) and difamilast (topical, atopic dermatitis, Japan). Their potencies span more than three orders of magnitude, and a 2025 study in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology (Wang et al. 2025;145(6):1471–1488.e1, PMID 39608668) explained why: roflumilast most closely mimics the way cAMP binds, preserving all three major contact points in PDE4 — the metal-ion site, the conserved glutamine, and the water-molecule/hydrogen-bond network — apremilast preserves two, and crisaborole one, and the IC50s follow the rule (roflumilast 0.7 nM, apremilast 0.14 µM, crisaborole 0.24 µM). The same study's structural analysis, simplified for clinicians in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology (Issa et al. 2025;18(7):18–21), states the rule as "3-2-1": three contact points, two, one — and potency in the same order.

The question this paper tests is whether a standard rigid-docking screen can see the rule. If the screen's scores track the contact points, it should rank roflumilast first by a wide margin; if they do not, the screen is blind to the interaction that matters most in this target, and the 3-2-1 rule is invisible to the method most screening programmes actually use. A second question is forced by the chemistry: crisaborole is a benzoxaborole — it contains boron — and the VIM-2 paper in this same run (Paper #61) showed that Vina rejects boron outright. If crisaborole cannot be docked either, the protocol cannot rank the full approved set, and any ranking it produces is a ranking of a subset presented as a whole.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol on the roflumilast co-crystal structure, docking rank will track the measured PDE4 ranking (roflumilast first, apremilast last among the docked three), with roflumilast separated from cilomilast by more than Vina noise. Falsified if cilomilast scores within noise of, or better than, roflumilast, in which case rigid docking is confirmed blind to the contact points that define PDE4 potency.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-15 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-14, which screened 722 candidates and selected 8 — none on PDE4, so the digest's relevance here is methodological). Key sources: Wang et al. 2025 (J Invest Dermatol 145:1471–1488.e1, PMID 39608668, doi:10.1016/j.jid.2024.10.597) for the three-drug comparison set and the 3-2-1 rule; Issa et al. 2025 (J Clin Aesthet Dermatol 18(7):18–21) for the clinical simplification of the same rule; Hatzelmann & Schudt 2001 (J Pharmacol Exp Ther 297:267–279, PMID 11259554) for roflumilast 0.8 nM and cilomilast 120 nM in the same assay; Schafer et al. 2010 (Br J Pharmacol 159:842–855, PMID 20050849, PMCID PMC2829210) for apremilast 74 nM; Card et al. for the subtype-resolved values (roflumilast PDE4B 8.4 nM / PDE4D 6.8 nM; cilomilast PDE4B 25 nM / PDE4D 11 nM), as summarised in the 2025 Molecules review (Molecules 2025;30:692, PMID 39942796, PMCID PMC11820465); Hiyama et al. 2023 (J Pharmacol Exp Ther 386:45–55, PMID 37041087) for difamilast; and the 2026 MDPI review of PDE4 (Int J Mol Sci 2026;27:79) for the PDE4B/PDE4D emesis distinction. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Pipeline failure and correction

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "Phosphodiesterase 4" and reference drug apremilast (run_docking.py, RDKit venv, NO_PROXY prefix). It failed, and its numbers are DISCARDED (kept in hidden_files/dock-HP-077-2026-11-15.json for audit only). UniProt resolved to Q86H13 — the Dictyostelium discoideum phosphodiesterase — and the ChEMBL fallback picked CHEMBL2074 maltase-glucoamylase, the same wrong-target failure as the KRAS paper in this run (Paper #60). The 55 "ligands" are alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, not PDE4 ligands, and docking returned nothing (no_pdb_found). The pipeline's failure modes are systematic: a query that resolves to a non-human orthologue, and a ChEMBL fallback that picks the first text-search candidate regardless of relevance.

The correction (documented fallback, HP-027 precedent; script health-papers-agent/dock_pde4_3g4l_correction.py) uses structure 3G4L — the human PDE4D catalytic domain in complex with roflumilast, 2.5 angstrom — with the centre from D._ligand_center, the centroid of the co-crystallised roflumilast. The centre [21.53, −4.02, 30.58] was audited: the active-site zinc sits 8.17 angstrom from the centre and the magnesium 9.14 angstrom; the other metals in the file (36–55 angstrom away) belong to the other chains in the asymmetric unit and are not part of this pocket.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; one box (22.5 angstrom) and exhaustiveness 8 for every compound; best of three poses reported. Three compounds on 3G4L: roflumilast (re-dock control on its own structure; PubChem CID 449193, formula C17H14Cl2F2N2O3), apremilast (CID 11561674, C22H24N2O7S) and cilomilast (CID 151170, C20H25NO4). All three SMILES were fetched from PubChem by name and verified by molecular-formula match. Crisaborole was NOT docked (boron — see Section 2.4) and is carried as the measured reference only.

Measured potencies are the Wang et al. 2025 comparison set for the three dermatologic drugs (roflumilast 0.7 nM; apremilast 0.14 µM; crisaborole 0.24 µM) and Hatzelmann & Schudt 2001 for cilomilast (120 nM, human PDE4). The ranges are stated because they matter: apremilast measures 74 nM in Schafer 2010 and 0.14 µM in Wang 2025; crisaborole 0.24 µM in the Wang abstract and 0.75 µM in the same paper's text and in the JCAD review; cilomilast 11 nM (Card, PDE4D) to 120 nM (Hatzelmann). No choice of value within any of these ranges changes the ranking — roflumilast is first by at least 100-fold under every reported value — which is why the paper can use the Wang headline values for the correlation without the result depending on them. A metal-aware caveat applies to every score here: PDE4D's active site holds Zn(II) and Mg(II), and Vina treats them as static point charges and cannot price the metal-water network that the 3-2-1 rule says drives potency.

2.4 The boronate gap

Crisaborole is a benzoxaborole (C14H10BNO3). Vina's PDBQT parser rejects the boron atom type, so it cannot be docked by this protocol — the same failure the VIM-2 paper in this run documented for taniborbactam, and the same failure mode: the most modern chemistry in the class is invisible to the screen. The paper reports crisaborole's measured value (0.24 µM, Wang 2025) as the reference and does not pretend a docking score exists for it.

2.5 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every compound. All three docked compounds are PAINS-clean. Roflumilast carries one Lipinski violation (logP 5.03); apremilast and cilomilast pass Lipinski and Veber outright.

2.6 Rank correlation

Spearman rank correlation was computed between the Vina scores and the measured PDE4 IC50 values for the three docked compounds (n = 3). A correlation on three points is reported as a descriptive check, not as a validated ranking — the paper's real tests are the roflumilast/cilomilast pair and the crisaborole gap.

2.7 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the entire docking span in this study (0.69 kcal/mol) is inside that noise. Vina cannot price the metal-water network or the conserved-glutamine contact that the 3-2-1 rule says drives potency. Roflumilast's score is a re-dock on its own co-crystal structure (3G4L). The measured IC50s mix assays (Wang 2025 for the dermatologic three, Hatzelmann 2001 for cilomilast) and the structure is PDE4D while the headline values are for PDE4 generally — the paper does not claim a single-assay, single-isoform comparison. No molecular dynamics, flexible-side-chain docking, or free-energy refinement was run. No compound was assayed. The 2.5 angstrom resolution of 3G4L is modest; a sharper PDE4D structure (1XOM, 1.55 angstrom, with cilomilast) exists and was not used, because the re-dock control required the roflumilast structure.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured PDE4 IC50 Vina on 3G4L (kcal/mol) PAINS
Roflumilast (reference) 0.7 nM −9.14 (−9.14, −9.02) clean
Apremilast 0.14 µM −8.93 (−8.93, −8.92, −8.70) clean
Cilomilast 120 nM −9.62 (−9.62, −9.35, −9.22) clean
Crisaborole (measured reference, not docked) 0.24 µM — (boron; Vina rejects atom type B) clean

Scores in kcal/mol, best of three poses (all three poses in parentheses). Measured IC50s: roflumilast, apremilast and crisaborole from Wang et al. 2025; cilomilast from Hatzelmann & Schudt 2001. "—" means not docked.

Cilomilast scores best at −9.62, ahead of roflumilast by 0.48 kcal/mol — and roflumilast is 171-fold more potent by measurement. The most potent drug in the set does not rank first; the weakest of the three docked does. The docking span across all three compounds is 0.69 kcal/mol, against a 200-fold measured range (0.7 nM to 0.14 µM). The screen is not noisy on this question. It is flat.

3.2 Rank correlation: weak, and carried by the last place

Against the measured PDE4 IC50s, Spearman rho is 0.5 (n = 3). The value is carried entirely by apremilast sitting last in both rankings; the top two are inverted. A correlation of 0.5 on three points, with the 171-fold gap inverted, is not a validated ranking — it is a screen that gets the last place right and the first place wrong, which is the worst kind of failure for a screening programme, because the first place is where the lead is chosen.

3.3 The 3-2-1 rule is invisible to the scorer

The Wang paper's rule is a contact-point count: roflumilast preserves all three (metal-ion site, conserved glutamine, water network), apremilast two, crisaborole one, and the IC50s follow the count. The docking scores do not follow the count, because Vina's scoring function has no term for the metal-water network and treats the conserved glutamine contact as one hydrogen bond among many. Cilomilast, which also binds the metal site and the conserved glutamine, scores best — the scorer rewards the contacts it can see and cannot price the ones it cannot, so the compound with the most visible contacts wins regardless of its measured potency. The paper's conclusion is not that the 3-2-1 rule is wrong — the measured IC50s support it — but that a rigid-docking screen cannot test it, because the scorer does not contain the physics the rule is made of.

3.4 The boronate gap, second demonstration

Crisaborole cannot be docked by this protocol, for the same reason taniborbactam could not be docked on VIM-2 in Paper #61: Vina rejects boron. Two papers in one day, two different targets, the same failure — and in both cases the undockable compound is the newest chemistry in its class (a benzoxaborole for PDE4, a boronate for the MBLs). A screening programme built on Vina therefore cannot rank the full approved set of PDE4 inhibitors, and cannot rank the most important MBL chemotype. That is a tooling limit, stated twice, so that no future run silently drops the boronates and reports a ranking of everything else as if it were complete.

3.5 ADMET and safety panel

All three docked compounds are PAINS-clean. The safety story that matters is the PDE4B/PDE4D distinction: PDE4D inhibition is associated with emesis, which is why the field pursues PDE4B-selective inhibitors, and why difamilast (PDE4B IC50 0.74 nM in the 2023 JPET profile, 6.6-fold selective over PDE4D) is the current direction for topical use. The Tox21 kNN read-across panel was not run for the three docked compounds (they are approved drugs with established human safety profiles, and the panel adds nothing to a repurposing question that is already answered by the label).

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say that apremilast is the weakest of the three docked compounds, by both measurement and docking. It cannot say that cilomilast is better than roflumilast — the measurement says the opposite by 171-fold, and the 0.48 kcal/mol docking gap is inside noise and in the wrong direction. It cannot say anything about crisaborole, because there is no docking score to compare. A paper that reported "cilomilast is the best PDE4 inhibitor in this set" on the basis of these scores would be reporting the screen's blindness as a finding. The honest conclusion is narrower and more useful: rigid docking with a static-metal model has no discriminating power for PDE4 inhibitors across a 200-fold potency range, and any ranking it produces on this target should be discarded.

4.2 The day's pattern

Four of the five papers in this run are docking failures, and the fifth is the control that shows the same protocol can work. On KRAS G12D the ranking was roughly right but the middle was wrong (rho 0.65); on VIM-2 the screen was silent (0.07 kcal/mol span, rho 0.15); on PDE4D the top two are inverted (rho 0.5); on BTK the ranking was inverted against measured potency (rho −0.625). Only PknB came out exact (rho 1.0). The pattern is not that docking fails — it is that docking fails on four targets out of five, and the one success is the target whose pocket is a well-formed kinase ATP site, the kind of site rigid docking was built for. The lesson for any screening programme is the control: a set of compounds with known potencies, ranked before the screen is trusted, and a boronate in the set, because the boronate is the compound that shows whether the tool can even see the class.

4.3 Testable hypotheses

  1. Metal-aware hypothesis. Re-scoring the same three docked poses with a metal-aware protocol (zinc/magnesium coordination restraints, or a metal-specific scoring term) restores the measured ranking (roflumilast first, separated from cilomilast by more than 1 kcal/mol). Falsified if the metal-aware scores still rank cilomilast first — in which case the failure is in pose sampling, not scoring.
  2. Sharper-structure hypothesis. Re-docking the three compounds on 1XOM (PDE4D with cilomilast, 1.55 angstrom) restores the measured ranking. Falsified if cilomilast still scores best — in which case the 2.5 angstrom resolution of 3G4L is not the problem.
  3. Boronate hypothesis. A boron-capable docking protocol docks crisaborole on 3G4L with a score worse than apremilast's −8.93, matching its measured position as the weakest of the four (0.24 µM). Falsified if crisaborole scores better than roflumilast — in which case the boronate's potency, like the thiol's on VIM-2, is invisible to docking.

4.4 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain roflumilast, apremilast, cilomilast and crisaborole; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): PDE4D enzyme assay, all four compounds on the same plates, in triplicate — the single-assay, single-isoform comparison this paper could not make, and the direct test of the 200-fold range. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): metal-aware re-scoring of the docked poses for hypothesis 1, plus the 1XOM re-dock for hypothesis 2. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if the metal-aware rescoring restores the ranking, apply it to a small library of PDE4 inhibitors and synthesise the best two; if it does not, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per IC50 determination is the minimum for a defensible potency claim; the roflumilast-versus-cilomilast comparison needs the same, because a false "cilomilast is best" call on a 171-fold gap is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. Vina cannot price the metal-water network or the conserved-glutamine contact that the 3-2-1 rule says drives potency; the 0.69 kcal/mol span is the finding, not a defect to be averaged away.
  3. Roflumilast's score is a re-dock on its own co-crystal structure (3G4L); apremilast and cilomilast are cross-docked into a pocket shaped for roflumilast.
  4. The measured IC50s mix assays (Wang 2025 for the dermatologic three, Hatzelmann 2001 for cilomilast) and the structure is PDE4D while the headline values are for PDE4 generally; the ranges are stated, and no choice of value within any range changes the ranking.
  5. Spearman rho is computed on three points; it is a descriptive check, not a validated ranking.
  6. Crisaborole was not docked (boron); its IC50 is quoted from Wang et al. 2025, a different assay from Hatzelmann 2001, so the 343-fold gap to roflumilast is cross-assay.
  7. No molecular dynamics, metal-aware docking, or free-energy refinement was run — the methods that could actually price the metal-water network.
  8. The 3G4L structure is 2.5 angstrom resolution; the sharper 1XOM structure (1.55 angstrom, with cilomilast) was not used, and the paper does not claim the ranking would be the same on it.
  9. The PDE4B/PDE4D selectivity discussion is from the literature, not from any computation in this paper; no selectivity numbers were calculated.
  10. No Pakistan-specific PDE4 or dermatology burden data are cited; the paper's relevance to Pakistan is the methodological warning for local screening programmes and the repurposing logic — approved drugs are the fastest route a resource-limited setting has.

6. Conclusion

On 3G4L, cilomilast docks at −9.62 kcal/mol against a measured IC50 of 120 nM, roflumilast at −9.14 against 0.7 nM, and apremilast at −8.93 against 0.14 µM — a 171-fold potency gap rendered as 0.48 kcal/mol in the wrong direction, and a 200-fold measured range compressed into a 0.69 kcal/mol docking span — while crisaborole, the third drug in the comparison set, cannot be docked at all because Vina rejects boron. The screen cannot see the contact points that define PDE4 potency, and it cannot see the boronate that defines the class's newest chemistry. The next step is the single-assay PDE4D comparison in Section 4.4, with metal-aware rescoring of the same poses — and, as a standing rule, no docking screen on a metalloenzyme is trusted until it has passed the stereoisomer control and the boronate control: four stereoisomers with known potencies, and a boronate in the set, because the boronate is the compound that shows whether the tool can even see the class.

MRTX1133 Re-Docks at −12.71 kcal/mol on the KRAS G12D Switch-II Pocket and Sotorasib Scores Worst: A Corrected Docking Benchmark After a Wrong-Target Pipeline Run

KRAS G12D is the commonest KRAS allele, driving about 42% of KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancers, and it has no approved inhibitor: the covalent KRAS G12C drugs cannot work because G12D has no cysteine to bind.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-15 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #60 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: KRAS G12D; MRTX1133; sotorasib; switch-II pocket; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; pancreatic cancer

Abstract

KRAS G12D is the commonest KRAS allele, driving about 42% of KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancers, and it has no approved inhibitor: the covalent KRAS G12C drugs cannot work because G12D has no cysteine to bind. MRTX1133 is the first non-covalent, selective KRAS G12D inhibitor, with a pERK IC50 of 2 nM in AGS cells, but the standard pipeline run for this paper resolved the target to the wrong enzyme and docked it into the wrong pocket, so both numbers from that run are discarded here and the correction is documented in full. We docked MRTX1133, three analogues from the same discovery paper, and the G12C inhibitor sotorasib as a negative control with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on 7RPZ, the 1.3 angstrom KRAS G12D structure co-crystallised with MRTX1133 in the switch-II pocket. MRTX1133 re-docked at minus 12.71 kcal/mol; the analogues scored minus 11.62, minus 11.13 and minus 9.34 against measured pERK IC50s of 24, 530 and 24 nM; sotorasib scored worst at minus 7.74, as a G12C drug should on G12D. Rank correlation against measured potency is moderate (Spearman rho 0.65, n = 4), but two compounds with identical measured potency differ by 2.28 kcal/mol in docking, and the re-dock sits 2.52 kcal/mol clear of its own second pose. The screen ranks the series roughly right and cannot resolve equal potencies. The falsifiable next step is a single-assay pERK comparison of the four Wang-series compounds in one KRAS G12D cell line: if compounds 25 and 36 again measure identically while docking differs by more than 2 kcal/mol, the gap is confirmed as a scoring artefact, not a potency signal.

1. Introduction

KRAS is the most frequently mutated oncogene in human cancer, and G12D is its commonest allele — about 33% of all KRAS-mutant tumours, and about 42% of KRAS mutations in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), where roughly 93% of tumours carry a KRAS mutation. PDAC is among the most lethal common cancers, with a five-year survival rate in single digits, and KRAS G12D has been called undruggable for decades: the protein binds GDP/GTP with picomolar affinity, leaving no obvious pocket, and unlike G12C it offers no reactive cysteine for a covalent warhead. The G12C inhibitors sotorasib and adagrasib proved that the induced switch-II pocket could be drugged, but they depend on Cys12 and are inactive against G12D. MRTX1133, reported by Wang et al. in 2022, was the first non-covalent, potent and selective KRAS G12D inhibitor: an estimated KD of about 0.0002 nM against KRAS G12D, an AlphaLISA IC50 of 5 nM, a pERK IC50 of 2 nM and a 2D-viability IC50 of 6 nM in AGS cells, with more than 500-fold selectivity over wild-type KRAS (MKN1 viability IC50 above 3,000 nM), and 94% growth inhibition with tumour regressions in a Panc 04.03 xenograft at 30 mg/kg twice daily. Its phase 1/2 trial (NCT05737706) was later terminated before phase 2, and a 2026 study reported antimetastatic effects in a liver-metastatic PDAC model (Sci Rep 2026;16:4144). The follow-up candidates now include the covalent G12D inhibitor RMC-9805 and the PROTAC ASP3082, but no KRAS G12D drug is approved.

The question this paper tests is whether a standard rigid-docking screen can rank a congeneric KRAS G12D series — the same scaffold, the same pocket, potencies spanning 2 to 530 nM — and whether it can recognise a negative control. The test is strict because the series comes from one paper with one assay, so the measured ranking is as clean as published data gets. A second, methodological question is also answered here: the standard pipeline run for this topic failed twice (Section 2.2), and the correction is part of the paper, not hidden in a supplement.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol on the MRTX1133 co-crystal structure, docking rank will track the measured pERK ranking (MRTX1133 first, compound 15 last), and sotorasib will score worst, because it has no covalent anchor and no measurable G12D activity. Falsified if two compounds with identical measured potency differ by more than Vina noise, or if sotorasib scores within noise of the actives.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-15 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-14, which screened 722 candidates and selected 8 — none on KRAS, so the digest's relevance here is methodological). Key sources: Wang et al. 2022 (J Med Chem 65:3123–3133, PMID 34889605) for the MRTX1133 discovery, all measured potencies, and structures 7RPZ/7RT1/7RT2/7RT5; the 2025 Cancers review of KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer (Cancers 2025;17:2453, doi:10.3390/cancers17152453) for the clinical context and the NCT05737706 status; the 2024 Clin Cancer Res review of MRTX1133 (Clin Cancer Res 2024;30:655–662, doi:10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-23-2098) for the PDAC mutation frequencies; and the 2026 Scientific Reports antimetastatic study (Sci Rep 2026;16:4144, PMID 41501279). Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Pipeline failure and correction

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "KRAS G12D" and reference drug MRTX1133 (run_docking.py, RDKit venv, NO_PROXY prefix). It failed in two independent ways, and both numbers from that run are DISCARDED (kept in hidden_files/dock-HP-069-2026-11-15.json for audit only).

First, the target resolution: UniProt returned the TrEMBL entry A0ABF7PHA5 for the KRAS G12D variant, which has no ChEMBL target mapping, so the pipeline's fallback picked the first text-search candidate — CHEMBL2074, maltase-glucoamylase. The four "leads" it retrieved are silylated iminosugars (alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, Ki 4–28 nM against maltase-glucoamylase), not KRAS ligands at all.

Second, the structure and centre: the pipeline picked 9S84 (KRAS G12D D38C, GDP-bound, 1.64 angstrom — the protein is correct) but _ligand_center fell back to the GDP centroid, because GDP is the only HETATM group with six or more atoms once cofactors are excluded. That is the nucleotide pocket, not the switch-II pocket where MRTX1133 binds. The MRTX1133 score of −9.13 on 9S84 is therefore meaningless, and the iminosugar scores (−6.13 to −7.69) are scores of the wrong molecules in the wrong pocket.

The correction (documented fallback, HP-027 precedent; script health-papers-agent/dock_kras_7rpz_correction.py) uses structure 7RPZ — KRAS G12D in complex with MRTX1133, 1.3 angstrom (Wang et al. 2022) — with the centre from D._ligand_center, the centroid of the co-crystallised MRTX1133 in the switch-II pocket. The centre [1.71, 4.93, −23.16] was audited: 9.55 angstrom from the Asp12 alpha carbon (the mutant residue's side chain points into the pocket) and 17.81 angstrom from the GDP centroid, confirming the box sits on the switch-II pocket and not on the nucleotide site.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; one box (22.5 angstrom) and exhaustiveness 8 for every compound; best of three poses reported. Five compounds on 7RPZ: MRTX1133 (reference drug; SMILES PubChem-verified by the pipeline run, formula C33H31F3N6O2, MW 600.65) and three analogues from Wang et al. 2022 — compound 25 (the eutomer of the 24/25 pair, co-crystal 7RT2), compound 36 (co-crystal 7RT5) and compound 15 (co-crystal 7RT1) — plus sotorasib (PubChem CID 137278711) as the negative control. The three analogues' SMILES were obtained from the RCSB chemical-component InChI for their co-crystal ligands (7NL, 7OE, 7L8) and verified by molecular-formula match (C31H32F2N6O2, C33H32F2N6O, C29H31FN6O2); a first attempt to extract SMILES from the deposited PDB coordinates produced wrong, saturated structures and was discarded. Measured potencies are all pERK AGS IC50s from Wang et al. 2022 (same assay, same paper): MRTX1133 2 nM; 25: 24 nM; 36: 24 nM; 15: 530 nM. Sotorasib carries no measured G12D potency and is excluded from the rank correlation.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every compound. All five are PAINS-clean. MRTX1133 carries one Lipinski violation (MW 600.65); compound 36 carries one (logP 5.05); the other three pass Lipinski and Veber outright.

2.5 Rank correlation

Spearman rank correlation was computed between the Vina scores and the measured pERK IC50 values for the four Wang-series compounds (n = 4). The two tied measured values (24 nM, twice) were assigned the average rank 2.5. A correlation on four points is reported as a descriptive check, not as a validated ranking — the paper's real tests are the 25/36 pair and the sotorasib negative control.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; gaps smaller than that are not differences. MRTX1133's score is a re-dock on its own co-crystal structure (7RPZ), so the pocket is shaped for it — that advantage is reported, not hidden. The measured IC50s are cellular pERK values from one paper, not biochemical KDs, and they conflate binding with cell permeability; the KD ranking (MRTX1133 ~0.0002 nM, compound 15 0.8 nM, compound 5B 3.5 µM) is quoted in the text but the correlation uses the single-assay pERK values. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No compound was assayed.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured pERK AGS IC50 Vina on 7RPZ (kcal/mol) PAINS
MRTX1133 (reference) 2 nM −12.71 (−12.71, −10.19, −10.03) clean
Compound 36 24 nM −11.62 (−11.62, −10.74, −9.89) clean
Compound 15 530 nM −11.13 (−11.13, −9.82, −9.13) clean
Compound 25 24 nM −9.34 (−9.34, −9.27, −9.00) clean
Sotorasib (negative control) no G12D activity −7.74 (−7.74, −7.63, −7.49) clean

Scores in kcal/mol, best of three poses (all three poses in parentheses). Measured IC50s are pERK AGS values from Wang et al. 2022.

MRTX1133 is first by 1.09 kcal/mol over compound 36, and sotorasib is last by 1.60 kcal/mol behind compound 25 — the negative control behaves as it should. The ranking is roughly right. But the middle of the table is wrong in a specific way: compounds 25 and 36 have identical measured potency (24 nM) yet differ by 2.28 kcal/mol in docking, more than Vina noise; and compound 15, the weakest measured (530 nM, 22-fold weaker than 25), docks better than 25 by 1.79 kcal/mol. The screen gets the ends right and the middle wrong.

3.2 Rank correlation: moderate, and carried by the extremes

Against the measured pERK IC50s, Spearman rho is 0.65 (n = 4). The value is carried by MRTX1133 sitting first and compound 15 sitting last in the measured ranking while docking puts 15 third; remove the two extremes and the remaining pair (25 vs 36) is ranked backwards by 2.28 kcal/mol. A correlation of 0.65 on four points, with the tied pair inverted, is not a validated ranking — it is a screen that works at the extremes and fails in the middle, which is where a real screening programme makes its decisions.

3.3 The re-dock advantage

MRTX1133's best pose (−12.71) sits 2.52 kcal/mol clear of its second pose (−10.19), while the other compounds' poses are tightly grouped (compound 25's three poses span only 0.34 kcal/mol). The 7RPZ pocket was crystallised around MRTX1133, and the scoring function rewards that fit heavily — the same pocket-shape effect reported for ponatinib on 3OXZ in Paper #58. The −12.71 value is therefore partly a pocket-shape effect, not a pure affinity signal, and the 1.09 kcal/mol gap to compound 36 is inside the range that effect can produce. A fair comparison would re-dock each compound into its own co-crystal structure (7RT1/7RT2/7RT5 exist for exactly this purpose); that cross-structure comparison was not run here, and the paper does not pretend the single-structure ranking is final.

3.4 The 25/36 pair: what docking misses

Compounds 25 and 36 differ in the naphthyl substituent: 36 carries the optimised 7-fluoro-8-ethynylnaphthyl group that fills a hydrophobic pocket near Val9, Thr58, Phe78, Met72, Tyr96 and Ile100 and engages the conserved water network, while 25 carries a naphthalen-2-ol. The paper that discovered them reports that the 8-ethynyl group bridges the lipophilic and polar regions of the switch-II pocket through a non-classical hydrogen bond to the conserved water. Rigid docking scores 36 better than 25 by 2.28 kcal/mol, which is the right direction for the wrong reason if the water network is the mechanism — Vina's scoring of water-mediated contacts is crude, and the paper cannot tell from these numbers whether the gap reflects the water interaction or a pose artefact. What it can say is that two compounds the assay cannot distinguish are distinguished by the screen by more than noise, so the screen is resolving something the assay does not — and that something is as likely to be error as signal.

3.5 ADMET and safety panel

All five compounds are PAINS-clean. The Tox21 kNN read-across panel was not run for the three analogues (they are not in the pipeline's lead set); the pipeline's panel for MRTX1133 flags nothing decisive (highest signals SR-ARE 0.20, NR-AhR 0.18). The safety story that matters for this target is clinical, not computational: MRTX1133's phase 1/2 trial was terminated before phase 2, with pharmacokinetic variability and suboptimal exposure reported as the reason — a reminder that a picomolar KD does not make a drug. The three analogues are research compounds with no approval and no human safety data.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say two things with confidence: MRTX1133 binds its own pocket better than its analogues do, in the same direction as its measured potency; and sotorasib, a G12C drug, scores worst on G12D, as it should. It cannot say that compound 36 is better than compound 25 — the assay says they are equal, and the 2.28 kcal/mol docking gap is an unvalidated claim. Nor can it say that compound 15 is nearly as good as compound 36 — the assay says it is 22-fold weaker, and docking puts them 0.49 kcal/mol apart, inside noise. The screen is a validated positive control with a failed middle: useful for confirming MRTX1133 and rejecting sotorasib, useless for ranking the analogues against each other.

4.2 The pipeline failure is the second finding

The standard pipeline run failed twice on this topic — wrong enzyme (maltase-glucoamylase) and wrong pocket (GDP site) — and both failures were silent: the run exited 0, printed "PIPELINE OK: True", and saved a JSON with confident-looking numbers. The failure modes are systematic, not one-off: a TrEMBL accession with no ChEMBL mapping falls back to the first text-search candidate, and a structure whose only ligand is a cofactor falls back to the cofactor centroid. Any pipeline that can fail this quietly needs a target-identity check (does the ChEMBL target name match the query?) and a pocket check (is the centre within 10 angstrom of a catalytic or known-ligand residue?) before any number is trusted. This paper is the control experiment that shows why.

4.3 Testable hypotheses

  1. Equal-potency hypothesis. In one pERK assay on AGS cells, compounds 25 and 36 again measure within 2-fold of each other while their Vina scores on 7RPZ differ by more than 2 kcal/mol. Falsified if 36 measures more than 5-fold more potent than 25 — in which case the docking gap is real and the assay, not the screen, missed it.
  2. Cross-structure hypothesis. Re-docking each compound into its own co-crystal structure (15 into 7RT1, 25 into 7RT2, 36 into 7RT5) restores the measured ranking (36 and 25 tied, 15 last). Falsified if the ranking is unchanged — in which case the single-structure result is not a pocket-shape artefact.
  3. Sotorasib hypothesis. Sotorasib shows no measurable pERK inhibition in AGS cells at 10 µM. Falsified if it inhibits pERK by more than 50% at that concentration — in which case the negative control is not negative and the G12C/G12D selectivity claim needs revisiting.

4.4 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain MRTX1133, compounds 25, 36 and 15, and sotorasib; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): pERK assay on AGS cells, all five compounds on the same plates, in triplicate — the single-assay comparison this paper could not make, and the direct test of hypothesis 1. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): cross-structure re-docking for hypothesis 2, plus a 2D-viability assay on AGS and on MKN1 (wild-type KRAS) for selectivity. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if any analogue measures within 2-fold of MRTX1133 on pERK, dock its analogues and synthesise the best two; if all three are more than 10-fold weaker, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per IC50 determination is the minimum for a defensible potency claim; the 25-versus-36 comparison needs the same, because a false "36 is better" call on a tied pair is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. MRTX1133's score is a re-dock on its own co-crystal structure (7RPZ); the three analogues are cross-docked into a pocket shaped for MRTX1133.
  3. The measured IC50s are cellular pERK values from one paper, conflating binding with permeability; the KD ranking is quoted but not used for the correlation.
  4. Spearman rho is computed on four points with a tie; it is a descriptive check, not a validated ranking.
  5. The pipeline run's numbers are discarded, not corrected in place; the corrected docking is a separate script and file, and the two must not be mixed.
  6. No molecular dynamics, flexible-side-chain docking, or free-energy refinement was run — the methods that could actually price the water network in the switch-II pocket.
  7. Sotorasib's negative-control status rests on the absence of reported G12D activity, not on a measured G12D IC50 in this paper.
  8. The phase 1/2 termination reason (pharmacokinetic variability, suboptimal exposure) is as reported in secondary sources; the primary trial record states the status, not the reason.
  9. No Pakistan-specific access or burden data are cited; the paper's relevance to Pakistan is methodological — a cheap, open-source triage step a university lab can run before any assay.

6. Conclusion

On 7RPZ, MRTX1133 re-docks at −12.71 kcal/mol, and three analogues from the same discovery paper score −11.62, −11.13 and −9.34 against measured pERK IC50s of 24, 530 and 24 nM, with sotorasib worst at −7.74 as a G12C drug should be on G12D. The ranking is roughly right (Spearman rho 0.65) but two compounds the assay cannot distinguish differ by 2.28 kcal/mol in docking, and the re-dock sits 2.52 kcal/mol clear of its own second pose. The screen validates MRTX1133 and the negative control and fails in the middle, where real screening decisions are made. The next step is the single-assay pERK comparison in Section 4.4, with all four Wang-series compounds and sotorasib on the same plates — and, as a standing rule, no pipeline docking number is trusted until the target name and the pocket have both been checked against the query.
