Ibrutinib Re-Docks at −10.86 kcal/mol on Its Own BTK Structure, but Four Sub-Nanomolar Covalent Inhibitors Score Worse: Rigid Docking Cannot Price the Cys481 Bond

Ibrutinib, the first covalent Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor, binds irreversibly to Cys481 in the ATP pocket, and the C481S mutation — cysteine replaced by serine — removes that bond and is the commonest cause of acquired resistance in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-15 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #59 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Bruton's tyrosine kinase; BTK; ibrutinib; C481S; covalent inhibitor; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Abstract

Ibrutinib, the first covalent Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor, binds irreversibly to Cys481 in the ATP pocket, and the C481S mutation — cysteine replaced by serine — removes that bond and is the commonest cause of acquired resistance in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). The question this paper tests is whether a standard rigid-docking screen can rank covalent BTK inhibitors at all, given that the scoring function cannot price a covalent bond. We docked ibrutinib and four ChEMBL BTK ligands with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on 5P9J, the 1.08 angstrom BTK kinase domain co-crystallised with ibrutinib itself. Ibrutinib re-docked at minus 10.86 kcal/mol. All four test compounds carry the same acrylamide warhead and are measured at 0.04 to 0.05 nM against BTK in ChEMBL — roughly ten times more potent than ibrutinib's 0.5 nM — yet they docked worse: minus 10.13, minus 9.47, minus 8.64 and minus 8.43 kcal/mol. Rank correlation between docking score and measured potency is inverted (Spearman rho minus 0.63, n = 5): the most potent compound measured docks worst. The screen validates the protocol (the reference drug re-docks well on its own structure) and fails as a ranking tool for covalent inhibitors in the same run. The falsifiable next step is a single-assay kinase comparison of the four compounds against wild-type and C481S BTK: if their C481S IC50s collapse like ibrutinib's while pirtobrutinib's holds, the warhead series is covalent-only and the docking inversion is confirmed as a scoring artefact, not a potency signal.

1. Introduction

Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) sits downstream of the B-cell receptor and is indispensable for B-cell development and signalling; it phosphorylates PLCG2 after receptor engagement, driving calcium mobilisation and protein kinase C activation (UniProt Q06187). Blocking it transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies. Ibrutinib, the first-in-class covalent BTK inhibitor, was approved by the US FDA in 2014 for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL), followed by the covalent inhibitors acalabrutinib (2019) and zanubrutinib (2023). All three bind irreversibly to Cys481 in the ATP pocket. Resistance follows the bond: the commonest acquired mechanism is mutation of that same cysteine, most often C481S, which removes the covalent anchor and renders the drug ineffective — ibrutinib's measured potency falls from 0.7 nM on wild-type BTK to more than 1,000 nM on C481S. The non-covalent inhibitor pirtobrutinib was designed around this failure: it binds reversibly, independent of Cys481, with measured IC50s of 1.1 nM on wild type and 16 nM on C481S, and in the BRUIN CLL-321 phase 3 trial it achieved an overall response rate of 62% and a median progression-free survival of 20 months in heavily pretreated patients, earning accelerated FDA approval in 2023 for patients who had received at least two prior lines including a covalent BTK inhibitor and a BCL-2 inhibitor. But resistance to pirtobrutinib is already appearing through second-site BTK mutations, and a 2026 preprint characterising 34 BTK variants at seven resistance sites found that the T316A substitution confers broad resistance to both covalent and non-covalent inhibitors, while variants at L528 disrupt catalytic activity and V416, A428, M437 and M477 largely retain sensitivity to covalent inhibitors.

The practical question for a drug-discovery screen is narrower than the clinical one: can a standard rigid-docking protocol rank covalent BTK inhibitors, or does the missing covalent term corrupt the ranking? This matters because docking is the cheap triage step every university lab runs before any assay, and a screen that systematically mis-ranks the most potent compounds will send the wrong molecules to the bench. The test compounds here are a hard case by design: four ChEMBL ligands with measured BTK IC50s of 0.04–0.05 nM, all carrying the acrylamide warhead that forms the Cys481 bond, docked against ibrutinib's own co-crystal structure under one standardised protocol.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, the four acrylamide-warhead BTK ligands will dock within Vina noise (±1–2 kcal/mol) of ibrutinib's re-dock score, and their docking rank will track their measured potency — ibrutinib first, the four sub-nanomolar compounds at least as good. Falsified if the most potent compound measured docks worst, in which case rigid docking is confirmed blind to the covalent contribution that makes these compounds potent.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-15 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-14, which screened 722 candidates and selected 8 — none on BTK, so the digest's relevance here is methodological). Key sources: Bender et al. 2017 for the 5P9J structure and the Y551-sequestration mechanism; Honigberg et al. 2010 for ibrutinib's original characterisation; the 2025 MDPI review of pirtobrutinib in CLL for the BRUIN CLL-321 results and the C481S potency table; the 2025 Leukemia & Lymphoma review (PMID 39972943) for resistance mechanisms after covalent BTK inhibition; and the 2026 Research Square preprint (doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-9390771/v1) for the 34-variant resistance map. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Pipeline and structure choice

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK)" and reference drug ibrutinib (run_docking.py, RDKit venv, NO_PROXY prefix). The pipeline resolved the target to UniProt Q06187 (human BTK, 659 amino acids) and ChEMBL target CHEMBL5251, retrieved 19 known ligands with measured BTK activity, verified ibrutinib in PubChem (CID 24821094, SMILES confirmed against the reference structure), screened 25 analogues by Morgan-fingerprint similarity, and ranked 20 leads by the standard composite score (similarity 40 + Lipinski 20 + Veber 10 + PAINS 10 + Tox21 read-across 20). The pipeline's automatic structure pick was 5P9J — the BTK kinase domain co-crystallised with ibrutinib at 1.08 angstrom (Bender et al. 2017) — which is the correct control for this question: the reference drug is docked back into its own pocket, so a good re-dock score validates the protocol rather than discovering a lead. The grid centre [19.81, 7.16, 3.62] is the centroid of the co-crystallised ibrutinib, computed by the pipeline's _ligand_center.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; one box (22.5 angstrom) and exhaustiveness 8 for every compound; best of three poses reported. Five compounds on 5P9J: ibrutinib (reference drug, PubChem CID 24821094) and four ChEMBL ligands — CHEMBL5749648, CHEMBL5858594, CHEMBL5824452 and CHEMBL5826570. All four test compounds are acrylamide-warhead indole-carboxamides: each SMILES contains the C=CC(=O)N acrylamide group that forms the covalent bond to Cys481, and an indole-2-carboxamide core. Their measured BTK IC50s are ChEMBL-reported values (0.049, 0.05, 0.05 and 0.04 nM respectively); ibrutinib's measured BTK IC50 of 0.5 nM is from Honigberg et al. 2010, and the 0.7 nM wild-type / >1,000 nM C481S pair is from the pirtobrutinib resistance literature.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every compound. All five are PAINS-clean. All five pass Lipinski and Veber outright (ibrutinib: MW 440.51, logP 4.22, TPSA 99.16; the four test compounds: MW 343.40–399.43, logP 2.25–4.30, TPSA 79.19–82.43).

2.5 Rank correlation

Spearman rank correlation was computed between the Vina scores and the measured BTK IC50 values for the five compounds (n = 5). The two tied measured values (0.05 nM, twice) were assigned the average rank 3.5. A correlation on five points is reported as a descriptive check, not as a validated ranking — the paper's real test is the direction of the ranking, not the size of rho.

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; gaps smaller than that are not differences. Vina scores only non-covalent complementarity and cannot price the covalent bond to Cys481 — that is the point of this paper, not a footnote to it. No molecular dynamics, covalent docking, or free-energy refinement was run. No compound was assayed, and none was docked on a C481S mutant structure, so nothing here speaks directly to mutant activity. The measured IC50s come from different assays in ChEMBL and are compared as reported, not re-measured on one plate.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured BTK IC50 Vina on 5P9J (kcal/mol) PAINS
Ibrutinib (reference) 0.5 nM −10.86 (−10.86, −9.38, −9.00) clean
CHEMBL5749648 0.049 nM −10.13 (−10.13, −9.56, −9.39) clean
CHEMBL5858594 0.05 nM −9.47 (−9.47, −9.18, −9.13) clean
CHEMBL5824452 0.05 nM −8.64 (−8.64, −8.47, −8.14) clean
CHEMBL5826570 0.04 nM −8.43 (−8.43, −8.19, −7.78) clean

Scores in kcal/mol, best of three poses (all three poses in parentheses). Measured IC50s are ChEMBL-reported BTK values for the four test compounds and Honigberg et al. 2010 for ibrutinib.

Ibrutinib re-docks at −10.86 on its own structure, 0.73 kcal/mol clear of the best test compound and 2.43 clear of the worst — the protocol works, and the reference drug is the winner by the screen's own metric. But every test compound is measured 10 to 17 times more potent than ibrutinib (0.04–0.05 nM versus 0.5 nM), and every one of them docks worse. The inversion is not a tie: the gap between ibrutinib and CHEMBL5826570 (2.43 kcal/mol) exceeds Vina noise, and it runs the wrong way.

3.2 Rank correlation: inverted

Against the measured BTK IC50s, Spearman rho is −0.63 (n = 5). The most potent compound measured (CHEMBL5826570, 0.04 nM) ranks last by docking; the least potent (ibrutinib, 0.5 nM) ranks first. Only CHEMBL5749648 holds the same rank (second) by both measures. A negative correlation on five points is not a precise estimate, but its sign is the finding: this screen ranks covalent BTK inhibitors backwards. The reason is visible in the chemistry — all four test compounds carry the acrylamide warhead, and the covalent bond it forms with Cys481 is worth binding energy that Vina never sees. The screen is scoring the non-covalent fit of molecules whose potency is dominated by a bond the scorer cannot model.

3.3 The re-dock control cuts both ways

Ibrutinib's −10.86 is a re-dock: the pocket in 5P9J was crystallised around ibrutinib, so the score partly reflects pocket-shape fit to that one ligand, not a pure affinity signal. The four test compounds are cross-docked into a pocket shaped for a different molecule, which disadvantages them further. Both effects push the same way — the reference drug looks better than it is, and the test compounds look worse — and the paper reports both rather than treating the re-dock as a neutral benchmark. A fair comparison would re-dock each compound into its own co-crystal structure, or use a structure crystallised around a non-covalent ligand; neither exists for these four compounds in the public record.

3.4 ADMET and safety panel

All five compounds pass Lipinski and Veber with zero violations. The Tox21 kNN read-across panel flags nothing decisive: the highest signals are NR-AhR 0.519 for CHEMBL5749648 and 0.455 for CHEMBL5858594, and SR-ARE 0.22 for ibrutinib — read-across scores, not measured toxicity. The safety story that matters for this target is not in the panel: ibrutinib's clinical liabilities (bleeding, atrial fibrillation, hypertension) and pirtobrutinib's cleaner selectivity profile are clinical facts, invisible to a ligand-based screen. The four test compounds are research compounds with no approval and no human safety data.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say one thing with confidence: the protocol reproduces ibrutinib's binding pose and score on its own structure, so the pipeline is working. It cannot say which covalent BTK inhibitor is most potent, because the ranking it produces is inverted against the measured record. Any paper that reported "CHEMBL5826570 is the weakest BTK ligand because it docks at −8.43" would be reporting the opposite of the measured fact — it is the most potent compound in the set. The failure is specific and diagnosable: the scorer prices non-covalent fit and ignores the covalent bond, and for this chemotype the bond is the potency.

4.2 The covalent-docking correction

The correct computational test for this chemotype is not a better rigid dock: it is covalent docking (which models the Cys481 bond explicitly) or a free-energy comparison that prices the bond formation, followed by a kinase assay on wild-type and C481S BTK. The assay is the decisive step, because it also answers the question the docking cannot ask: whether these four compounds are covalent-only (and therefore dead against C481S, like ibrutinib) or retain non-covalent affinity (and therefore worth testing as pirtobrutinib-style leads). Their non-covalent docking scores (−8.43 to −10.13) are in the range a non-covalent inhibitor would need, which is a weak but real hint that they may retain some C481S activity — a hint the paper states as a hypothesis, not a finding.

4.3 Why this matters beyond BTK

Covalent inhibitors are now a mainstream design strategy — KRAS G12C, EGFR, BTK — and every one of them is screened by the same rigid-docking pipelines that fail here. The BTK case is a clean demonstration because the warhead is identical across the test set and the measured potencies are extreme (0.04–0.05 nM), so the inversion cannot be dismissed as assay noise. Any screening programme that ranks covalent and non-covalent compounds on one Vina scale is mixing two different quantities: non-covalent fit for one class, and non-covalent fit minus the missing bond for the other. The fix is cheap: flag the warhead, dock covalent and non-covalent series separately, and never let a covalent compound's Vina score stand as its potency claim.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Covalent-only hypothesis. In one kinase assay on wild-type and C481S BTK, all four test compounds lose more than 100-fold potency on the mutant, like ibrutinib, while pirtobrutinib loses less than 15-fold. Falsified if any test compound holds within 15-fold on C481S — in which case its non-covalent affinity is real and it is a candidate non-covalent lead.
  2. Covalent-docking hypothesis. Re-scoring the same five compounds with a covalent docking protocol restores the measured ranking (CHEMBL5826570 first, ibrutinib last). Falsified if the covalent scores still rank ibrutinib first — in which case the inversion has another cause and the warhead explanation is wrong.
  3. Pocket-shape hypothesis. Cross-docking ibrutinib into a BTK structure crystallised around a non-covalent ligand drops its score by more than 1 kcal/mol from −10.86. Falsified if it stays within noise — in which case the re-dock advantage is smaller than this paper assumes.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain ibrutinib, pirtobrutinib and the four ChEMBL compounds; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): kinase assay (ADP-Glo or equivalent) on recombinant wild-type and C481S BTK, all six compounds on the same plates, in triplicate — the single-assay comparison this paper could not make, and the direct test of hypothesis 1. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): covalent docking of the same six compounds for hypothesis 2, plus a BTK-dependent cellular assay (TMD8 or MEC-1) for the best two. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if any test compound holds within 15-fold on C481S, dock its analogues and synthesise the best two; if all four collapse, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per IC50 determination is the minimum for a defensible potency claim; the wild-type-versus-mutant comparison needs the same, because a false "C481S-active" call on a covalent-only compound is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. Vina cannot price the covalent bond to Cys481; the ranking inversion is the finding, not a defect to be averaged away.
  3. Ibrutinib's score is a re-dock on its own co-crystal structure (5P9J); the four test compounds are cross-docked into a pocket shaped for ibrutinib.
  4. The measured IC50s come from different assays in ChEMBL and were not re-measured on one plate; the 0.04–0.05 nM values are at the edge of what biochemical assays resolve reliably.
  5. Spearman rho is computed on five points and is driven by the ibrutinib-versus-rest inversion; it is a descriptive check, not a validated ranking.
  6. No compound was docked on a C481S mutant structure, so nothing here speaks directly to mutant activity.
  7. No molecular dynamics, covalent docking, or free-energy refinement was run — the methods that could actually price the warhead.
  8. The Tox21 panel is kNN read-across, not measured toxicity; the real safety liabilities of BTK inhibitors are clinical and invisible to this screen.
  9. The four test compounds are research compounds with no approval and no human data; their ChEMBL IC50s are the only measured evidence for them.
  10. No Pakistan-specific access or burden data are cited; the paper's relevance to Pakistan is methodological — a cheap, open-source triage step a university lab can run before any assay.

6. Conclusion

On 5P9J, ibrutinib re-docks at −10.86 kcal/mol, and four acrylamide-warhead BTK ligands measured at 0.04–0.05 nM — ten times more potent than ibrutinib — dock worse, at −10.13 to −8.43, with the ranking inverted against the measured record (Spearman rho −0.63). The screen validates the protocol and fails as a ranking tool for covalent inhibitors in the same run, because Vina cannot price the Cys481 bond that makes these compounds potent. The next step is the single-assay kinase comparison in Section 4.5, with ibrutinib, pirtobrutinib and the four compounds on wild-type and C481S BTK on the same plates — and, as a standing rule for any covalent series, covalent and non-covalent compounds must never be ranked on one rigid-docking scale.

Sorbitol Dehydrogenase Inhibitors Show No Rank Correlation on Three Docking Centres — and SORD Inhibition Already Failed to Help Diabetic Nerves in Rats

Sorbitol dehydrogenase (SORD) catalyses the second step of the polyol pathway, oxidising sorbitol to fructose. Its inhibitors were developed as a treatment for diabetic neuropathy, on the logic that blocking fructose formation should help.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Faculty of Pharmacy, SMBBMU, Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 14 November 2026 Topic ID: HP-054

Abstract

Sorbitol dehydrogenase (SORD) catalyses the second step of the polyol pathway, oxidising sorbitol to fructose. Its inhibitors were developed as a treatment for diabetic neuropathy, on the logic that blocking fructose formation should help. We benchmarked rigid AutoDock Vina docking against measured human SORD inhibition data for five Pfizer piperazino-pyrimidine sorbitol dehydrogenase inhibitors (SDIs), including the reference compound CP-166572. Three human SORD structures exist in the Protein Data Bank. The pipeline picked 1PL8 — the highest-resolution structure — but 1PL8 is an NAD+ complex with no inhibitor, and its automatic centre fell on the NAD+ cofactor centroid, 11.62 Å from the catalytic Zn2+. We ran two corrected dockings: one centred on the catalytic Zn2+ of 1PL8, and one on 1PL6, the inhibitor-bound structure, whose co-crystallised ligand is CP-166572 itself. On the NAD+ centre the most potent measured inhibitor — CHEMBL90344, IC50 27 nM — scored worst (−6.61 kcal/mol), and the rank correlation against measured potency was Spearman ρ = −0.2 (n = 4). On the Zn2+ centre all five compounds fell inside a single 0.79 kcal/mol band and ρ = +0.2. On the correct, inhibitor-bound structure the correlation was ρ = +0.35, and the re-dock control failed outright: CP-166572, re-docked into its own crystal structure, scored weakest of the five (−6.20 kcal/mol). No centre ranks the compounds. The result is consistent with the published animal record: in streptozotocin-diabetic rats the SORD inhibitor WAY-135706 lowered fructose but corrected neither nerve conduction velocity nor endoneurial blood flow, while an aldose reductase inhibitor corrected both; and biallelic loss-of-function SORD mutations cause hereditary motor neuropathy in humans, meaning pharmacological SORD inhibition mimics a disease-causing state. SORD is a weak target for diabetic neuropathy, and rigid docking without a metal-aware model cannot rank its inhibitors.

Keywords: sorbitol dehydrogenase; SORD; polyol pathway; diabetic neuropathy; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; CP-166572; Pakistan

Introduction

Pakistan carries the world's highest national diabetes prevalence: one in four adults (26.7%; 30.8% age-adjusted) — 33 million people — lived with diabetes in 2021, with an estimated 400,000 diabetes deaths that year and 26.9% of cases undiagnosed (IDF Diabetes Atlas, 10th edition, 2021). Diabetic neuropathy is one of the most common complications, and it has no disease-modifying treatment. The polyol pathway is the classic biochemical explanation for it: under hyperglycaemia, aldose reductase (AR) reduces glucose to sorbitol, consuming NADPH, and sorbitol dehydrogenase (SORD) then oxidises sorbitol to fructose, consuming NAD+. Tissues that lack SORD — retina, kidney, Schwann cells — accumulate sorbitol, and the pathway has been blamed for osmotic and oxidative nerve injury.

Two earlier papers in this series covered the first step of the pathway: aldose reductase, where the inhibitor epalrestat is approved in Japan and where docking could at least separate strong from weak inhibitors. This paper covers the second step, SORD, which was proposed as an independent target: if sorbitol is the problem, blocking its conversion to fructose should not help — but the original hypothesis was the reverse, that fructose formation and the NADH/NAD+ shift drive injury, so blocking SORD should help. Pfizer developed a series of piperazino-pyrimidine SDIs in 1998–2002, culminating in orally active compounds that normalised sciatic-nerve fructose in diabetic rats. No SDI ever reached the clinic. This paper asks two questions: (1) can rigid docking rank known SORD inhibitors at all, and (2) does the published evidence support SORD as a target for diabetic neuropathy?

Methods

2.1 Target and compound selection

Human sorbitol dehydrogenase (UniProt Q00796) was resolved to ChEMBL target CHEMBL2275 (57 known ligands). The reference compound was CP-166572 (PubChem CID 132302; 2-hydroxymethyl-4-[4-(N,N-dimethylaminosulfonyl)-1-piperazino]pyrimidine; C11H19N5O3S), a Pfizer-series SDI. No ChEMBL SORD IC50 is recorded for CP-166572, so it serves as a structural reference only. The pipeline ranked 26 leads by measured potency and docked the top five. All five are PAINS-clean.

2.2 Structures and the centre problem

Three human SORD structures exist in the Protein Data Bank, all from Pauly et al. (Structure 2003;11(9):1071–1085; PMID 12962626): 1PL6 (2.00 Å, "Human SDH/NADH/inhibitor complex"), 1PL7 (2.20 Å, apo) and 1PL8 (1.90 Å, "human SDH/NAD+ complex"). The pipeline picked 1PL8 — the highest-resolution structure — but 1PL8 contains no inhibitor, only NAD+, Zn2+ and waters. Its automatic centre therefore fell on the NAD+ cofactor centroid, [97.83, 30.36, 26.67] — 11.62 Å from the catalytic Zn2+ of chain A, [94.58, 35.23, 36.71], with the nicotinamide ring sitting within 8 Å of the metal. The substrate pocket sits at the edge of a 22.5 Å box centred there.

The structurally correct choice is 1PL6. Its co-crystallised ligand, HETATM 572, is 4-[2-(hydroxymethyl)pyrimidin-4-yl]-N,N-dimethylpiperazine-1-sulfonamide, formula C11H19N5O3S — CP-166572 itself, bound in the substrate pocket 6.28 Å from the catalytic Zn2+ (chain-A 572 centroid [102.75, 37.00, 35.25]; Zn-A [96.63, 36.11, 36.32]). The pipeline chose by resolution and missed the inhibitor-bound structure. We therefore ran three dockings, all AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exhaustiveness 8, box 22.5 Å: (i) the pipeline's automatic run on 1PL8 centred on the NAD+ centroid; (ii) a corrected run on 1PL8 centred on the catalytic Zn2+; (iii) a corrected run on 1PL6 centred on the co-crystallised CP-166572 centroid — in which the CP-166572 dock is a re-dock control against its own crystal pose.

2.3 Limitations of the docking model, stated in advance

The receptor preparation drops HETATM records, so the catalytic Zn2+ is not present in the docked receptor in any of the three runs: no metal coordination is modelled, and scores reflect only the shape and electrostatics of the apo pocket — even on 1PL6, where the metal sits 6.28 Å from the ligand. This is the same limitation reported for the urease paper in this series ("dock weakly without Ni2+"). SORD is a zinc-dependent dehydrogenase; any inhibitor that coordinates the metal will be scored wrongly. Rigid docking carries a documented ±1–2 kcal/mol noise band, and the rank correlation below uses only four compounds with measured values.

2.4 Literature

Measured potencies and source documents were taken from ChEMBL (accessed 14 November 2026) and verified against the original papers. The Cameron et al. (1997) head-to-head rat study and the Cortese et al. (2020) human genetics study were read in full. Diabetes burden figures are from the IDF Diabetes Atlas, 10th edition (2021). Structure identities and ligand 572 were verified by direct parse of the 1PL6 PDB file (HETNAM/FORMUL records) and the RCSB entry records for 1PL6, 1PL7 and 1PL8.

Results

3.1 The compounds

The five docked compounds are all Pfizer piperazino-pyrimidines (Table 1). CHEMBL90344 (27 nM) is the stereochemically defined form of Mylari et al.'s enantiomeric SDI 6; CHEMBL91846 (173 nM) is the same scaffold with stereochemistry unspecified — a 6.4-fold measured difference between the two forms, equivalent to ~1.1 kcal/mol at 298 K, inside Vina's noise band. CHEMBL151268 (93 nM) and CHEMBL423753 (140 nM) are regioisomers from Chu-Moyer et al. (2002), differing only in methyl placement on the pyrimidine ring. Two of the four measured values were confirmed in a second assay at higher values (CHEMBL151268: 350 nM; CHEMBL423753: 480 nM); the lower value was used, which favours the docking comparison.

Compound Measured IC50 (nM) Source 1PL8 NAD+ centre 1PL8 Zn2+ centre 1PL6 inhibitor centre
CHEMBL90344 27 Mylari et al. 2001 −6.61 −6.48 −6.54
CHEMBL151268 93 Chu-Moyer et al. 2002 −8.22 −6.78 −6.95
CHEMBL423753 140 Chu-Moyer et al. 2002 −7.92 −7.04 −6.95
CHEMBL91846 173 Mylari et al. 2001 −6.95 −6.43 −6.37
CP-166572 (QUERY) not recorded Pfizer series −6.99 −6.25 −6.20

3.2 NAD+ centre (1PL8, pipeline auto-pick): the most potent inhibitor scores worst

On the pipeline's automatic (NAD+ cofactor) centre, CHEMBL151268 scored best (−8.22 kcal/mol) and CHEMBL90344 — the most potent measured inhibitor at 27 nM — scored worst (−6.61 kcal/mol). The rank correlation against measured potency was Spearman ρ = −0.2 (n = 4): negative. The best score is also the least trustworthy: CHEMBL151268's third pose on this centre was +38.31 kcal/mol, a clash artefact, showing that the NAD+ pocket produces unstable poses. Scores on this centre were systematically stronger (best −8.22) than on the Zn2+ centre (best −7.04), by ~1.2 kcal/mol — the cofactor site gives spuriously favourable scores for compounds that do not belong there.

3.3 Zn2+ centre (1PL8, corrected): all five compounds inside one noise band

On the corrected Zn2+ centre, the spread collapsed: all five compounds scored between −6.25 and −7.04 kcal/mol, a 0.79 kcal/mol range — less than half of Vina's noise band. The 27 nM compound ranked third (−6.48); the 140 nM regioisomer ranked first (−7.04); the reference CP-166572 ranked last (−6.25). Spearman ρ = +0.2 (n = 4). Correcting the centre moved the correlation from −0.2 to +0.2, i.e. from nothing to nothing. The two regioisomers (93 vs 140 nM measured) separated in the wrong direction: the weaker compound scored better (−7.04 vs −6.78).

3.4 Inhibitor centre (1PL6, corrected): the re-dock control fails

On the correct structure — 1PL6, with CP-166572 co-crystallised in the pocket — the five compounds again fell inside a single 0.75 kcal/mol band (−6.20 to −6.95 kcal/mol), and Spearman ρ = +0.35 (n = 4): still essentially zero. Poses were stable this time (CHEMBL151268's three poses: −6.95, −6.90, −6.87), so the failure is not pose instability. The decisive result is the re-dock control: CP-166572, re-docked into its own crystal structure, scored −6.20 kcal/mol — the weakest of the five compounds. A method that cannot recognise the native ligand as the best binder in its own pocket cannot be trusted to rank analogues. The two regioisomers tied at −6.95, which is acceptable (93 vs 140 nM is a 1.5-fold difference), but the 27 nM compound ranked third again (−6.54).

3.5 The target's own record

The docking failure is not the interesting finding; the target's record is. Cameron et al. (1997) ran the decisive head-to-head in streptozotocin-diabetic rats: the SORD inhibitor WAY-135706 (250 mg/kg/day) versus the aldose reductase inhibitor WAY-121509 (10 mg/kg/day). WAY-135706 did what an SORD inhibitor should do biochemically — it raised sorbitol further (1.6–8.2-fold) and lowered fructose — and it did nothing that mattered functionally: motor nerve conduction velocity (−20.2% deficit) and sensory conduction velocity (−13.9%) were uncorrected, and endoneurial blood flow (−48.6% deficit) was uncorrected. The AR inhibitor corrected both. The authors' conclusion was explicit: the first step of the polyol pathway matters far more than the second for diabetic neuropathy.

The genetics then made it worse. Cortese et al. (2020) showed that biallelic loss-of-function SORD mutations are the most frequent cause of recessive hereditary motor neuropathy: 45 affected individuals from 38 families, carrying (most commonly) c.757delG (p.Ala253GlnfsTer27), with complete loss of SORD protein and raised intracellular sorbitol. SORD loss in Drosophila caused synaptic degeneration and motor impairment. The treatment that worked in that model was not more SORD inhibition — it was aldose reductase inhibition, reducing sorbitol influx. Pharmacological SORD inhibition mimics a disease-causing state.

Against that, the SDI programme's best results were real but narrow: Mylari et al. (2001) reported an enantiomeric SDI at least ten times more potent than their weak starting lead, with potent inhibition of SDH in diabetic rat sciatic nerve; Chu-Moyer et al. (2002) reported compound 86, a selective SORD inhibitor with ED90 of 1–2 mg/kg/day in chronically diabetic rats, normalising sciatic-nerve fructose for ~17 h after a single oral 2 mg/kg dose. Fructose was normalised. Nerves were not helped — that was Cameron's result, published four years earlier.

Discussion

Three findings, in order of importance.

First, the target fails its own test. An inhibitor that corrects the biochemical marker (fructose) without correcting nerve function is not a neuropathy drug. Cameron et al. showed this in 1997, and the programme continued for five more years on the strength of fructose endpoints. The Cortese et al. genetics result then inverted the rationale entirely: SORD loss causes neuropathy. Any future SORD inhibitor programme would have to explain why partial pharmacological inhibition is safe when complete genetic loss is pathogenic — and why it should work when the animal data says the second polyol step does not drive the functional deficit.

Second, rigid docking cannot rank SORD inhibitors — on any centre, including the right one. On the NAD+ centre ρ = −0.2, on the Zn2+ centre ρ = +0.2, on the inhibitor-bound structure ρ = +0.35, and the most potent compound never ranks first. The re-dock control is the cleanest statement of the failure: the co-crystallised ligand scores worst in its own pocket. Two structural reasons compound the problem: the catalytic Zn2+ — the defining feature of the active site, 6.28 Å from the ligand — is absent from the docked receptor in every run, and the method is rigid. A metal-aware method (explicit Zn coordination, or a structure with the metal retained) is a precondition for any meaningful SORD docking, not a refinement.

Third, structure choice matters more than the compounds — and resolution-first picking gets it wrong. The pipeline picked 1PL8 because it is the highest-resolution structure (1.90 Å vs 2.00 Å), and 1PL8 is the one structure of the three with no inhibitor in it. Moving the box 11.62 Å, from the NAD+ centroid to the Zn2+, shifted every score by up to 1.4 kcal/mol and flipped the ranking — a larger effect than the 1.1 kcal/mol separating the two stereoisomer forms. Papers that dock into 1PL8 without stating their centre are not comparable with each other, and pipelines that pick structures by resolution alone will repeat this error. The NAD+ centre also produces spuriously strong scores and unstable poses (+38.31 kcal/mol), which a single "best score" table would hide.

For Pakistan, where one in four adults lives with diabetes, the practical implication is to direct limited drug-discovery effort at the first polyol step — aldose reductase, where epalrestat is already approved in Japan and where the animal evidence is positive — rather than the second. SORD remains interesting as a diagnostic and genetics target (the Cortese et al. finding makes SORD sequencing relevant for unexplained hereditary neuropathy), but not as an inhibition target for diabetic neuropathy.

Limitations

  1. No lab data. All results are computational; no SORD assay was run.
  2. No metal in the model. The catalytic Zn2+ was dropped during receptor preparation in all three runs; metal coordination is unmodelled, even on 1PL6.
  3. Rigid docking, ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The 6.4-fold measured difference between the two stereoisomer forms (1.1 kcal/mol) is below the method's resolution.
  4. Small n. The rank correlation uses four compounds with measured values; a single additional compound could change ρ substantially.
  5. No measured potency for the reference. CP-166572 has no ChEMBL SORD IC50; its role is structural only — though its co-crystal structure makes it the ideal re-dock control, which failed.
  6. Second-assay values. Two compounds have higher IC50s in a second assay (350 and 480 nM); using the lower values favoured the docking comparison and it still failed.
  7. No RMSD for the re-dock. The re-dock control is reported as a score only; the docked pose was not compared atom-by-atom with the crystal pose.

Conclusion

Rigid docking into human SORD cannot rank known piperazino-pyrimidine inhibitors: Spearman ρ was −0.2 on the pipeline's NAD+ centre, +0.2 on the corrected Zn2+ centre, and +0.35 on the inhibitor-bound structure 1PL6 — and the co-crystallised ligand CP-166572 re-docked worst in its own pocket (−6.20 kcal/mol). The deeper finding is that the target itself failed: SORD inhibition lowered fructose without helping diabetic nerves in rats, and human SORD loss causes hereditary neuropathy. The polyol pathway's second step should not be pursued as a diabetic-neuropathy target on the current evidence; the first step, aldose reductase, is where the evidence sits. Any future SORD docking must be metal-aware, must use the inhibitor-bound structure, and must state its centre.

Rigid Docking Gets the Extremes Right on SARS-CoV-2 Mpro: the 0.04 nM Analogue Scores Best and Nirmatrelvir Ties for Last

Nirmatrelvir, the active component of Paxlovid, is a covalent inhibitor of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro, nsp5). We benchmarked rigid AutoDock Vina docking against measured inhibition data for nirmatrelvir and four analogues (Ki 0.04–3.1 nM), docked into the nirmatrelvir-bound structure 7SI9 (2.0 Å).

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Faculty of Pharmacy, SMBBMU, Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 14 November 2026 Topic ID: HP-037

Abstract

Nirmatrelvir, the active component of Paxlovid, is a covalent inhibitor of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro, nsp5). We benchmarked rigid AutoDock Vina docking against measured inhibition data for nirmatrelvir and four analogues (Ki 0.04–3.1 nM), docked into the nirmatrelvir-bound structure 7SI9 (2.0 Å). This is the first positive rank correlation in this series: Spearman ρ = +0.48 (n = 5). The most potent analogue (Ki 0.04 nM) scored best (−8.79 kcal/mol), nirmatrelvir itself (Ki 3.1 nM, consensus of ten ChEMBL records) tied for last (−8.22 kcal/mol), and the re-dock control worked — nirmatrelvir re-docked into its own crystal structure with tight poses (−8.22, −8.21, −7.93 kcal/mol). But the method compresses the differences: the measured potencies span 77-fold (~2.6 kcal/mol) while the docking scores span only 0.57 kcal/mol, so the middle of the ranking is noise. Two pipeline lessons are recorded: the first automated run used the wrong ChEMBL target (maltase-glucoamylase) and the wrong structure (the NSP3 macrodomain), with every dock failing; and the pipeline's top activity record for nirmatrelvir (Ki 0.26 nM) is an outlier against ten records at 3.0–3.11 nM. Rigid docking can rank Mpro analogues at the extremes, but not in the middle — and it cannot score the covalent bond that does much of the work.

Keywords: SARS-CoV-2; main protease; Mpro; nirmatrelvir; Paxlovid; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; covalent inhibitor

Introduction

COVID-19 has caused ~1.58 million confirmed cases and 30,656 deaths in Pakistan (National Institute of Health data, 2023), and the virus continues to circulate. The main protease (Mpro, also called 3CLpro, nsp5) cleaves the viral polyprotein at eleven sites and is essential for replication; it has no close human homologue, which makes it a selective antiviral target. Nirmatrelvir (PF-07321332) is a peptidomimetic nitrile that binds covalently to the catalytic Cys145 as a thioimidate; co-dosed with ritonavir — a CYP3A4 inhibitor that raises nirmatrelvir's plasma exposure — it is Paxlovid, the first oral antiviral for COVID-19 (Owen et al., Science 2021). Ritonavir's role is pharmacokinetic, not antiviral: it fixes nirmatrelvir's metabolism, not its target binding.

This paper benchmarks rigid docking for nirmatrelvir and four close analogues from a 2024 optimisation study (Ghosh et al., Eur J Med Chem 2024), and asks whether docking can rank a congeneric series of covalent inhibitors. The honest difficulty is stated up front: Vina scores non-covalent complementarity only, while these compounds' potency includes a covalent bond to Cys145. The comparison is fair in one respect — all five share the same nitrile warhead, so potency differences should track non-covalent interactions — and unfair in another, since the covalent contribution is invisible to the method.

Methods

2.1 Target and compound selection

SARS-CoV-2 Mpro (nsp5, residues 3264–3569 of the replicase polyprotein 1ab, UniProt P0DTD1) was resolved to ChEMBL target CHEMBL4523582, which holds 6,220 IC50 activities. The reference compound was nirmatrelvir (PubChem CID 155903259; C23H32F3N5O4, MW 499.53). The pipeline ranked 26 leads; the docking set is nirmatrelvir plus four analogues. All five are PAINS-clean. One pipeline entry was deduplicated: CHEMBL4802135 is nirmatrelvir itself (verified pref_name), so it was excluded as a duplicate of the QUERY.

2.2 Structure: the first run used the wrong target and the wrong structure

The first automated run failed twice over. The ChEMBL text search returns an unfiltered list (the same irrelevant results for every query — maltase-glucoamylase first), and the pipeline picked CHEMBL2074 (human maltase-glucoamylase) as the target; its "Mpro leads" were α-glucosidase inhibitors. It then docked them into 8AZC — the SARS-CoV-2 NSP3 macrodomain in apo form (0.93 Å), not Mpro — and every dock failed ("pdb parse failed"). The run was discarded in full. The corrected run reached CHEMBL4523582 by querying the pipeline with the UniProt accession P0DTD1, and used 7SI9 (2.0 Å), the room-temperature Mpro structure in complex with nirmatrelvir (Kneller et al., Nat Commun 2022;13:2268; PMID 35477935). The docking centre was the co-crystallised nirmatrelvir adduct centroid (ligand 4WI, chain A, [−10.40, 39.82, −17.96]) — the active site, at Cys145. All docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exhaustiveness 8, box 22.5 Å.

2.3 Limitations of the docking model, stated in advance

Covalent inhibition is unmodelled. Nirmatrelvir and all four analogues carry the same nitrile warhead, which forms a covalent thioimidate with Cys145; Vina scores only the non-covalent pose. The crystal ligand 4WI is itself the covalent adduct (the imino form), so the re-dock is a shape check, not a binding-energy check. Rigid docking carries a documented ±1–2 kcal/mol noise band, and the docking spread here (0.57 kcal/mol) is inside it. The measured Ki values come from different assays: nirmatrelvir's consensus is 3.1 nM (ten ChEMBL records at 3.0–3.11 nM), but the pipeline's top record gave 0.26 nM and is treated as an outlier; CHEMBL5178656 has Ki records at both 0.44 nM and 7.0 nM, and an IC50 of 100 nM in its original 2022 paper. The rank correlation uses only five compounds.

2.4 Literature

Measured potencies were taken from ChEMBL (accessed 14 November 2026) and verified against the source documents. The 7SI9 structure, the nirmatrelvir mechanism and the ritonavir-boosting rationale are from the primary literature. Pakistan case figures are from National Institute of Health data (2023).

Results

3.1 The compounds

The five compounds are a congeneric series: nirmatrelvir plus four P1/P4 analogues from Ghosh et al. (2024) (Table 1). CHEMBL5574604 replaces the P1 γ-lactam with a six-membered δ-lactam (Ki 0.04 nM, a single assay record). CHEMBL5589941 replaces the P4 trifluoroacetyl group with trichloroacetyl (Ki 0.2 nM). CHEMBL5178656 replaces the P4 trifluoroacetyl with acetyl (Ki 0.44 nM in the 2024 paper; 7.0 nM in a second record; IC50 100 nM in its 2022 paper). CHEMBL5590149 is a further P1/P4 analogue (Ki 1.1 nM). Their measured potencies span 0.04–3.1 nM, a 77-fold range equivalent to ~2.6 kcal/mol at 298 K.

Compound Measured Ki (nM) Modification vs nirmatrelvir Vina score (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses
CHEMBL5574604 0.04 P1 δ-lactam −8.79 −8.79, −8.21, −7.70
CHEMBL5590149 1.1 P1/P4 analogue −8.52 −8.52, −7.80, −7.32
CHEMBL5178656 0.44 P4 acetyl −8.32 −8.32, −7.53, −7.30
Nirmatrelvir (QUERY) 3.1 — −8.22 −8.22, −8.21, −7.93
CHEMBL5589941 0.2 P4 trichloroacetyl −8.22 −8.22, −7.24, −7.17

3.2 The extremes are right; the middle is noise

The rank correlation was Spearman ρ = +0.48 (n = 5) — the first positive correlation in this series. The most potent analogue (0.04 nM) scored best (−8.79 kcal/mol), and the least potent, nirmatrelvir itself (3.1 nM), tied for last (−8.22 kcal/mol). But the ordering in between is wrong: the 1.1 nM compound ranked second (−8.52), ahead of the 0.44 nM (−8.32) and 0.2 nM (−8.22) compounds. And the whole docking spread is only 0.57 kcal/mol, against a 2.6 kcal/mol measured range: the method compresses the differences by a factor of four. The re-dock control worked — nirmatrelvir's three poses were tight (−8.22, −8.21, −7.93) — so the failure is not pose instability; it is that non-covalent scoring cannot resolve potency differences that depend partly on covalent-bond formation kinetics, which vary with the P1/P4 groups.

3.3 The discarded first run

The first run's failure is worth one paragraph because it is a pipeline failure, not a science failure. A text search that returns the same irrelevant list for every query will eventually pick the wrong target — here, maltase-glucoamylase for a viral protease — and a structure picker that trusts the target will then dock into whatever structure the wrong target suggests — here, the NSP3 macrodomain. Both errors were caught because the target name, the structure title and the dock failures were all checked by hand. Automated pipelines that do not check these will publish α-glucosidase inhibitors as Mpro inhibitors.

Discussion

Two findings, one encouraging and one limiting.

First, this is the best docking result in the series — and it is still weak. A positive ρ (+0.48) with the extremes correct and a working re-dock control shows that rigid docking into a high-resolution, ligand-bound structure (2.0 Å, the native ligand's own pocket) carries real signal for Mpro. The 0.04 nM δ-lactam analogue scoring best is a genuine prediction worth testing. But a 0.57 kcal/mol spread for a 2.6 kcal/mol measured range means the method cannot rank the middle of the series: the 0.2, 0.44 and 1.1 nM compounds are indistinguishable to it, and two of the five are misordered. For analogue prioritisation, docking can shortlist the best candidate and discard the worst, but it cannot order the rest.

Second, the covalent bond is the unmeasured variable. All five compounds share the nitrile warhead, so in principle the Ki differences should track non-covalent fit — but covalent inhibition also depends on the warhead's reactivity and the geometry of attack, which the P1/P4 groups influence and Vina cannot see. The δ-lactam analogue's 77-fold advantage over nirmatrelvir (0.04 vs 3.1 nM) is far larger than its 0.57 kcal/mol docking advantage, which suggests much of its gain is in the covalent step or in interactions the rigid model misses. A covalent docking method (or a QM/MM estimate of the thioimidate formation) is the correct next step for this series, not more Vina runs.

For Pakistan, the practical point is that nirmatrelvir remains the available drug (as Paxlovid, with ritonavir boosting), and analogues like the δ-lactam compound are preclinical leads, not alternatives a clinician can use. The value of this benchmark is for the next round of analogue design: dock to shortlist, assay to rank, and model the covalent step explicitly.

Limitations

  1. No lab data. All results are computational; no Mpro assay was run.
  2. Covalent bond unmodelled. Vina scores non-covalent complementarity only; the Cys145 thioimidate is invisible to it.
  3. Small n. The rank correlation uses five compounds from one congeneric series; a single additional compound could change ρ substantially.
  4. Assay heterogeneity. Ki values come from different papers and assays; CHEMBL5178656 has records at 0.44 nM, 7.0 nM and IC50 100 nM, and nirmatrelvir's pipeline record (0.26 nM) disagrees with ten records at 3.0–3.11 nM.
  5. Single-assay potencies. The 0.04 nM and 0.2 nM values each rest on one assay record.
  6. Rigid docking, ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The 0.57 kcal/mol docking spread is inside the noise band.
  7. No RMSD for the re-dock. The re-dock control is reported as a score with tight poses; the docked pose was not compared atom-by-atom with the crystal pose.

Conclusion

Rigid docking into the nirmatrelvir-bound Mpro structure 7SI9 gives the first positive rank correlation in this series (Spearman ρ = +0.48, n = 5): the 0.04 nM analogue scores best (−8.79 kcal/mol), nirmatrelvir ties for last (−8.22 kcal/mol), and the re-dock control works. But the method compresses a 77-fold measured potency range into a 0.57 kcal/mol score range and misorders the middle of the series, and it cannot score the covalent bond that defines these inhibitors. Docking can shortlist Mpro analogues at the extremes; ranking them needs assays and covalent modelling. The discarded first run — wrong target, wrong structure, all docks failed — is a reminder that automated pipelines need a human check on the target and the structure before any score is believed.

ATP-Competitive mTOR Inhibitors Are All Sub-Nanomolar but Docking Spreads Them Over 1.78 kcal/mol — and Ranks Them Backwards

The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a serine/threonine kinase that controls cell growth and is frequently deregulated in cancer. First-generation mTOR drugs (rapalogs such as everolimus) are allosteric: they bind the FRB domain via FKBP12 and block substrate recruitment.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Faculty of Pharmacy, SMBBMU, Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 14 November 2026 Topic ID: HP-058

Abstract

The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a serine/threonine kinase that controls cell growth and is frequently deregulated in cancer. First-generation mTOR drugs (rapalogs such as everolimus) are allosteric: they bind the FRB domain via FKBP12 and block substrate recruitment. Second-generation inhibitors compete directly with ATP in the kinase domain and inhibit both mTOR complexes. We benchmarked rigid AutoDock Vina docking against measured mTOR inhibition data for five ATP-competitive inhibitors (IC50 0.10–0.20 nM), docked into the Torin2-bound kinase-domain structure 4JSX (3.5 Å). The five compounds are essentially equipotent in the assay — a two-fold range, equivalent to ~0.4 kcal/mol — but docking spread them over 1.78 kcal/mol (−7.67 to −9.45 kcal/mol) and ranked them backwards (Spearman ρ = −0.4, n = 5): the 0.20 nM compound scored best (−9.45 kcal/mol) and the 0.13 nM compound scored worst (−7.67 kcal/mol). The negative control could not be scored at all: everolimus, a 958-Da macrolide with ~30 rotatable bonds, crashed the docking run (Vina non-zero exit after ~20 min of compute), so no ATP-site score was obtained. The method invents differences where the assay sees near-equality, and it cannot even run the reference drug. Two pipeline lessons are recorded: the automated PDB lookup hung on the structure search, and its <3.0 Å resolution filter can never select a kinase-domain structure for mTOR, because every structure better than 3.0 Å is an FRB-domain fragment. Docking scores should not prioritise analogues among sub-nanomolar mTOR inhibitors.

Keywords: mTOR; kinase inhibitor; everolimus; Torin2; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; ATP-competitive; cancer

Introduction

The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a phosphoinositide 3-kinase-related protein kinase (PIKK) that controls cell growth in response to nutrients and growth factors and is frequently deregulated in cancer. It operates in two complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, with different substrates and functions. The first drugs against it — sirolimus (rapamycin) and its analogues everolimus and temsirolimus — are allosteric: the drug binds FKBP12, and the drug–protein complex binds the FRB domain of mTOR, blocking substrate recruitment and restricting access to the active site (Yang et al., Nature 2013). They inhibit mTORC1 preferentially and incompletely, and they do not touch mTORC2. Resistance and feedback reactivation of AKT limited their efficacy, which drove the development of second-generation, ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitors that occupy the ATP pocket and inhibit both complexes (García-Echeverría et al., Bioorg Med Chem Lett 2010).

This paper benchmarks rigid docking for five ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors with measured IC50 values of 0.10–0.20 nM, and asks whether docking can rank compounds that the assay can barely distinguish. Everolimus serves as the negative control: it does not bind the ATP site at all, so a method that scores it alongside ATP-competitive inhibitors cannot discriminate binding modes.

Methods

2.1 Target and compound selection

Human mTOR (UniProt P42345) was resolved to ChEMBL target CHEMBL2842 (47 known ligands). The reference compound was everolimus (PubChem CID 6436034; C53H83NO14; MW 958.24), an allosteric rapalog. The pipeline ranked 26 leads and docked the top five. All five are ATP-competitive kinase inhibitors with sub-nanomolar measured IC50 values, and all are PAINS-clean. Everolimus ranked 14th of 26 in the pipeline and has no ChEMBL mTOR IC50 attached in this run; it is included as the mechanistic negative control.

2.2 Structure: why the pipeline could not pick it

The automated PDB lookup (find_pdb_for_uniprot) hung during this run — it iterates up to twelve candidate structure downloads through a flaky proxy — and was bypassed. Its design would have failed anyway: it accepts only structures better than 3.0 Å, and for mTOR every structure better than 3.0 Å is an FRB-domain fragment (for example 4DRI at 1.45 Å and 3FAP at 1.85 Å). The kinase-domain structures are all 3.3–3.5 Å. We therefore selected 4JSX manually: the mTORΔN–mLST8 complex with Torin2 bound (Yang et al., Nature 2013;497:217–223; PMID 23636326), 3.5 Å, residues 1376–2549. The docking centre was the co-crystallised Torin2 centroid (chain A, [49.98, −1.37, −47.78]) — the ATP-binding pocket itself. All docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exhaustiveness 8, box 22.5 Å. The active site is, as Yang et al. describe it, "highly recessed owing to the FRB domain and an inhibitory helix protruding from the catalytic cleft" — a confined pocket, which matters for interpreting the scores.

2.3 Limitations of the docking model, stated in advance

The structure is 3.5 Å resolution — the lowest-resolution structure used in this series — so side-chain positions in the pocket are uncertain. Receptor preparation drops HETATM records, so Mg2+ and the ATPγS present in the related structure 4JSP are absent from the docked receptor. Rigid docking carries a documented ±1–2 kcal/mol noise band. The measured potency range (0.10–0.20 nM, two-fold, ~0.4 kcal/mol) is far below that noise band, so no ranking can be resolved even in principle. Everolimus is very large (MW 958, ~30 rotatable bonds) and may be under-sampled at exhaustiveness 8. The rank correlation uses only five compounds.

2.4 Literature

Measured potencies and source documents were taken from ChEMBL (accessed 14 November 2026) and verified against the original papers. The 4JSX structure and the FRB-gatekeeper mechanism are from Yang et al. (2013). The allosteric/ATP-competitive distinction is from García-Echeverría et al. (2010).

Results

3.1 The compounds

The five inhibitors come from four independent series (Table 1): a triazine (CHEMBL1091714, Verheijen et al. 2010), a pyrimido-pyrimidine from a 2015 patent document (CHEMBL3693444), and two pyrazolopyrimidines (CHEMBL576090, Richard et al. 2009; CHEMBL606423, Curran et al. 2010), plus CHEMBL1801204, whose value is compiled in the García-Echeverría et al. (2010) review. All five share the morpholine/morpholine-like hinge-binding motif typical of PI3K/mTOR kinase inhibitors. Their measured IC50 values span only 0.10–0.20 nM. One value is assay-dependent: CHEMBL1801204 is recorded at 0.13 nM in the pipeline's record and at 0.8 nM in a second assay record; the lower value was used, which favours the docking comparison.

Table 1. ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors docked on 4JSX (Torin2-bound kinase domain, 3.5 Å).

Compound Measured IC50 (nM) Source Vina score (kcal/mol)
CHEMBL576090 0.20 Richard et al. 2009 −9.45
CHEMBL1091714 0.10 Verheijen et al. 2010 −9.32
CHEMBL606423 0.19 Curran et al. 2010 −9.06
CHEMBL3693444 0.15 Patent document, 2015 −7.94
CHEMBL1801204 0.13 García-Echeverría et al. 2010 −7.67
Everolimus (QUERY) allosteric, no ATP-site activity — docking failed (Vina error after ~20 min, no score)

3.2 The ranking is backwards — and the spread exceeds the signal

The five inhibitors scored between −7.67 and −9.45 kcal/mol: a 1.78 kcal/mol spread for compounds whose measured potencies differ by 0.4 kcal/mol. The rank correlation was Spearman ρ = −0.4 (n = 5): the least potent compound (CHEMBL576090, 0.20 nM) scored best (−9.45 kcal/mol), and the second most potent (CHEMBL1801204, 0.13 nM) scored worst (−7.67 kcal/mol). The method does not merely fail to resolve the ranking — it inverts it, and it manufactures a 1.78 kcal/mol spread where the assay reports near-equality. Three compounds cluster at −9.06 to −9.45 and two at −7.67 to −7.94, a 1.1 kcal/mol gap between the clusters that has no counterpart in the measured data.

3.3 The negative control could not be run

Everolimus was included as the mechanistic negative control: it binds the FRB domain via FKBP12 and does not occupy the ATP site, so it should score poorly there — the same logic as miltefosine in the trypanothione reductase paper in this series, which scored −4.54 kcal/mol against −7.75 to −8.56 for genuine inhibitors. No such comparison was possible here. The everolimus dock ran for ~20 min of Vina compute on the 4JSX receptor and then failed with a non-zero exit and no score; the run's JSON records the error. A 958-Da macrolide with ~30 rotatable bonds against a 342-kDa receptor is beyond what this setup can handle in reasonable time. The control is therefore reported as failed, not as a score — and the failure is itself informative: the pipeline that ranks small ATP-competitive inhibitors cannot even evaluate the reference drug it was asked about.

Discussion

Three findings, in order of importance.

First, the method invents differences where the assay sees near-equality. Five inhibitors spanning 0.10–0.20 nM — a 0.4 kcal/mol range — were spread over 1.78 kcal/mol by docking, and ranked backwards (ρ = −0.4). The two clusters (−9.06 to −9.45 vs −7.67 to −7.94) have no counterpart in the measured data. Any analogue-prioritisation scheme built on these scores would have synthesised the wrong compounds first. The honest interpretation is that, within a set of sub-nanomolar inhibitors, Vina scores carry no ranking information at all — the measured differences are four times smaller than the method's noise.

Second, the control failure matters as much as the ranking failure. Everolimus is the clinically relevant reference for this target — the drug actually given to patients — and the docking setup could not produce a number for it. A benchmark that cannot run its own reference compound is incomplete, and any pipeline that silently drops large flexible ligands will systematically exclude exactly the macrolide and natural-product-like chemotypes that mTOR drug discovery started from.

Third, the pipeline's automation failed twice on this target, in ways that generalise. The PDB lookup hung on the structure search (twelve candidate downloads through a flaky proxy), and its <3.0 Å resolution filter can never select a kinase-domain structure for mTOR, because every sub-3.0 Å structure is an FRB-domain fragment. A resolution-first heuristic is a domain-blind heuristic: for multi-domain targets it will confidently pick the wrong domain. Structure selection needs a ligand-site check (is an ATP-site ligand bound?) before a resolution check.

For the clinic, the implication is narrow but real: ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors are a genuine advance over rapalogs — they inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2, where everolimus is mTORC1-biased — but choosing among sub-nanomolar candidates requires assays, not docking scores. The compounds in Table 1 are all potent enough that the decision between them should turn on selectivity (mTOR vs PI3K), pharmacokinetics and toxicity, none of which a Vina score measures.

Limitations

  1. No lab data. All results are computational; no mTOR assay was run.
  2. Low resolution. 4JSX is 3.5 Å; side-chain positions in the pocket are uncertain.
  3. Cofactors removed. Mg2+ was dropped during receptor preparation; the docked pocket lacks it.
  4. Measured range below noise. The 0.10–0.20 nM range (~0.4 kcal/mol) is far inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise band; ranking was unresolvable in principle.
  5. Small n. The rank correlation uses five compounds from four different series; a single additional compound could change ρ substantially.
  6. Assay heterogeneity. The five IC50 values come from four different papers and one patent document, measured in different assays; cross-series comparison adds noise beyond the docking itself.
  7. Everolimus docking failed. The macrolide's ~30 rotatable bonds against the 342-kDa receptor ended in a Vina error after ~20 min; no ATP-site score was obtained, so the negative-control comparison is absent rather than negative.
  8. One assay discrepancy. CHEMBL1801204 has a second assay record at 0.8 nM; using the lower (0.13 nM) value favoured the docking comparison and it still failed.

Conclusion

Rigid docking into the mTOR kinase domain (4JSX, Torin2-bound, 3.5 Å) cannot rank five ATP-competitive inhibitors that the assay reports as essentially equipotent (IC50 0.10–0.20 nM): it spread them over 1.78 kcal/mol and ranked them backwards (Spearman ρ = −0.4), with the 0.20 nM compound scoring best and the 0.13 nM compound worst. The reference drug everolimus could not be docked at all — the run failed after ~20 min — so no negative-control comparison was possible. Within a sub-nanomolar series, docking scores carry no ranking information, and analogue prioritisation should rest on measured selectivity, pharmacokinetics and toxicity instead. Structure selection for multi-domain targets must check the ligand site before the resolution.

This is an AI-assisted draft, not a peer-reviewed publication; all claims require independent laboratory verification. No funding was received. The author declares no conflicts of interest.

Rigid Docking Separates Genuine Trypanothione Reductase Inhibitors from Miltefosine but Ranks the Series Backwards

Trypanothione reductase (TR) is the flavoenzyme that keeps the trypanothione redox system of Leishmania and Trypanosoma parasites reduced; humans have no equivalent enzyme, which makes it a selective antiparasitic target.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Faculty of Pharmacy, SMBBMU, Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 14 November 2026 Topic ID: HP-024

Abstract

Trypanothione reductase (TR) is the flavoenzyme that keeps the trypanothione redox system of Leishmania and Trypanosoma parasites reduced; humans have no equivalent enzyme, which makes it a selective antiparasitic target. Leishmania donovani TR has no deposited crystal structure, so we docked against the Leishmania infantum homologue (87.2% sequence identity), structure 4ADW, centred on the bound physiological substrate trypanothione. We benchmarked rigid AutoDock Vina docking against measured inhibition data for four β-carboline–quinazolinone TR inhibitors (Ki 0.8–9.2 µM), with miltefosine — the oral clinical drug for visceral leishmaniasis, which is not a TR inhibitor — as a negative control. Docking separated the classes cleanly: the four genuine inhibitors scored −7.75 to −8.56 kcal/mol, while miltefosine scored −4.54 kcal/mol, a gap of at least 3.21 kcal/mol. Within the inhibitor series, however, the ranking was inverted (Spearman ρ = −0.6, n = 4): the two weakest measured inhibitors (Ki 7.2 and 9.2 µM) scored best (−8.56 and −8.40 kcal/mol), and the most potent (Ki 800 nM) ranked third (−8.13 kcal/mol). All four inhibitors fell inside a 0.81 kcal/mol band — one noise band — while their measured potencies span 11.5-fold. Rigid docking can tell a TR inhibitor from a non-inhibitor, but it cannot rank this series. The result supports TR as a target — the first-line antimonials act through it — while warning that docking scores alone should not prioritise analogues for synthesis.

Keywords: trypanothione reductase; Leishmania donovani; Leishmania infantum; visceral leishmaniasis; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; miltefosine; β-carboline

Introduction

Visceral leishmaniasis (VL, kala-azar) is fatal in over 95% of cases if untreated, with an estimated 50,000–90,000 new cases worldwide each year, of which only 25–45% are reported to WHO. In Pakistan VL is endemic in the northern high-altitude areas — Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Jammu Kashmir, with Khyber Pakhtunkhwa also at risk — where Leishmania infantum is the most commonly reported causative species; most cases are children under six. Reported VL numbers are small (seven cases in 2014), while cutaneous leishmaniasis dominates the national burden (over 10,000 cases in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa alone in 2026). Treatment rests on a handful of drugs: pentavalent antimonials, amphotericin B, paromomycin, and miltefosine, the only oral agent. Resistance and toxicity limit all of them, and no vaccine exists.

Trypanothione reductase (TR, EC 1.8.1.12) is the parasite's analogue of human glutathione reductase: it reduces trypanothione, the spermidine–glutathione conjugate that replaces glutathione in trypanosomatids. The trypanothione system is unique to these parasites, and human glutathione reductase shares only ~40% sequence identity with TR and has different substrate specificity, so TR inhibition should be selective. The target is validated by the oldest drugs in the field: pentavalent antimonials are reduced to Sb(III) in the parasite, and Sb(III) binds the catalytic cysteines of TR (Baiocco et al., J Med Chem 2009). Miltefosine, by contrast, does not act on TR: its antileishmanial mechanism is attributed to interference with phospholipid metabolism and membrane function (Dorlo et al., J Antimicrob Chemother 2012). That contrast makes miltefosine an ideal negative control for a docking benchmark: a method that scores it alongside genuine TR inhibitors cannot discriminate; a method that separates it can.

This paper benchmarks rigid docking on four β-carboline–quinazolinone TR inhibitors reported by Chauhan et al. (MedChemComm 2015), the only measured TR inhibitor series with usable potency data in ChEMBL for L. donovani TR, and asks whether docking can rank them.

Methods

2.1 Target, structure and the homologue problem

Leishmania donovani trypanothione reductase (UniProt P39050, 491 amino acids) was resolved to ChEMBL target CHEMBL2176840, which holds only six known ligands. P39050 has no PDB cross-reference in UniProt: no L. donovani TR structure has been deposited. The closest experimental structure is the L. infantum enzyme (UniProt A4HSF7, also 491 amino acids), with 87.2% ungapped sequence identity to P39050; the two species belong to the same L. donovani complex, and L. infantum is the species most commonly reported in Pakistani VL. We used 4ADW (3.61 Å), the L. infantum TR structure with the physiological substrate trypanothione bound (Baiocco et al., ChemMedChem 2013;8:1175; PMID 23733388). The docking centre was the chain-A trypanothione centroid [21.56, 41.03, −18.76], i.e. the active site itself. All docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, exhaustiveness 8, box 22.5 Å.

2.2 Compounds

The four inhibitors are β-carboline–quinazolinone hybrids from Chauhan et al. (2015): CHEMBL3735035 (Ki 800 nM), CHEMBL3735110 (Ki 6.5 µM), CHEMBL3736154 (Ki 7.2 µM) and CHEMBL3735109 (Ki 9.2 µM), all measured against L. donovani TR and all PAINS-clean. The reference compound was miltefosine (PubChem CID 3599; C21H46NO4P; hexadecyl 2-(trimethylazaniumyl)ethyl phosphate), verified directly against PubChem after the pipeline's in-run query lookup failed. Miltefosine has no reported TR inhibitory activity and serves as the negative control.

2.3 Limitations of the docking model, stated in advance

The receptor is a homologue (87.2% identity), not the assay species, and at 3.61 Å resolution — the lowest-resolution structure used in this series. Receptor preparation drops HETATM records, so the FAD prosthetic group and NADPH — both present in the crystal structure and both shaping the active site — are absent from the docked receptor. Rigid docking carries a documented ±1–2 kcal/mol noise band. Miltefosine's hexadecyl tail has ~19 rotatable bonds and may be under-sampled at exhaustiveness 8. The rank correlation uses only four compounds.

2.4 Literature

Measured potencies were taken from ChEMBL (accessed 14 November 2026) and verified against the source document. The 4ADW structure, the antimony mechanism and the miltefosine mechanism were verified against the primary literature. Pakistan burden figures are from the WHO leishmaniasis fact sheet and a 2019 case report from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Results

3.1 The compounds

The four inhibitors share the β-carboline–quinazolinone scaffold and differ only in their quinazolinone N-substituent: CHEMBL3735035 carries an N-pentyl group (Ki 800 nM); CHEMBL3735110 an N-ethyl group (Ki 6.5 µM); CHEMBL3736154 an N-(4-chlorophenyl) group (Ki 7.2 µM); CHEMBL3735109 an N-(4-methoxybenzyl) group (Ki 9.2 µM). Their measured potencies span 11.5-fold, equivalent to ~1.4 kcal/mol at 298 K — inside Vina's noise band, which already limits what any ranking can show.

Table 1. β-Carboline–quinazolinone TR inhibitors and miltefosine docked on 4ADW (L. infantum TR, 3.61 Å), substrate-centred.

Compound Measured Ki Vina score (kcal/mol) Top-3 poses
CHEMBL3736154 7.2 µM −8.56 −8.56, −8.31, −8.06
CHEMBL3735109 9.2 µM −8.40 −8.40, −8.32, −7.72
CHEMBL3735035 800 nM −8.13 −8.13, −7.55, −7.16
CHEMBL3735110 6.5 µM −7.75 −7.75, −7.54, −7.22
Miltefosine (QUERY) no TR activity −4.54 −4.54, −4.47, −4.26

3.2 Docking separates inhibitors from the non-inhibitor

The class separation is unambiguous: every genuine TR inhibitor scored −7.75 kcal/mol or better, while miltefosine scored −4.54 kcal/mol — a gap of at least 3.21 kcal/mol, more than three times Vina's noise band. Miltefosine's poses were also uniformly weak (−4.54, −4.47, −4.26), so the result is not a single bad pose. The method can tell a TR inhibitor from a drug that works elsewhere. This is the first clean negative-control separation in this series.

3.3 Within the series, the ranking is inverted

Within the four inhibitors the ranking fails: Spearman ρ = −0.6 (n = 4). The two weakest measured inhibitors scored best — CHEMBL3736154 (7.2 µM) at −8.56 and CHEMBL3735109 (9.2 µM) at −8.40 — while the most potent, CHEMBL3735035 (800 nM), ranked third at −8.13. All four inhibitors sit inside a 0.81 kcal/mol band, less than half of Vina's noise band, so the inversion is a within-noise effect rather than a large error — but it is an inversion all the same, and it means docking scores cannot prioritise analogues in this series. The N-pentyl compound is 8–11-fold more potent than the others in the assay and unremarkable in the dock.

Discussion

Two findings, pulling in opposite directions.

First, the negative control works. Miltefosine's −4.54 kcal/mol against −7.75 to −8.56 for genuine inhibitors is the clearest discrimination this series has produced. It shows that rigid docking into the trypanothione pocket is not simply rewarding any large hydrophobic molecule: the pocket recognises the β-carboline–quinazolinone scaffold and rejects an alkylphosphocholine. For a screening pipeline, that is useful — docking can be used as a first-pass filter to discard compounds that do not belong in the pocket at all.

Second, within-series ranking fails, and the reasons are visible. The measured potency range (11.5-fold, ~1.4 kcal/mol) is inside the method's noise band, so even a perfect method would struggle — but the inversion is systematic, not random: both of the weakest compounds out-scored the strongest. Three contributors are identifiable: (i) the structure is a homologue at 3.61 Å, so side-chain positions in the pocket are uncertain; (ii) FAD and NADPH are missing from the docked receptor, removing the cofactor contacts that shape the pocket; and (iii) the series differs only in the quinazolinone N-substituent, a region the rigid model may score mainly by size — the two largest substituents (4-chlorophenyl, 4-methoxybenzyl) scored best, suggesting the model rewards bulk where the assay rewards the smaller N-pentyl group. Any of these alone could invert a within-noise ranking.

For Pakistan, the practical points are: TR remains a sound target — it is parasite-specific, and the antimonials that still anchor VL treatment act through it — and the L. infantum structure is the right homologue for Pakistani VL, since L. infantum is the species most commonly reported there. But analogue prioritisation for TR needs more than Vina scores: the Chauhan et al. series itself was reported with its own molecular docking in 2015, and the field should treat docking as a filter (inhibitor vs non-inhibitor) rather than a ranker within a congeneric series, until a metal/cofactor-aware, higher-resolution model is available.

Limitations

  1. No lab data. All results are computational; no TR assay was run.
  2. Homologue structure. Docking used L. infantum TR (87.2% identity), not the L. donovani enzyme the Ki values were measured against.
  3. Low resolution. 4ADW is 3.61 Å; side-chain positions in the pocket are uncertain.
  4. Cofactors removed. FAD and NADPH were dropped during receptor preparation; the docked pocket lacks them.
  5. Rigid docking, ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The measured 11.5-fold potency range (~1.4 kcal/mol) is inside the noise band.
  6. Small n. The rank correlation uses four compounds; a single additional compound could change ρ substantially.
  7. Miltefosine sampling. Its long flexible tail may be under-sampled at exhaustiveness 8, though its score is so weak that better sampling is unlikely to close a 3.21 kcal/mol gap.
  8. Single source series. All four inhibitors come from one 2015 paper; the benchmark does not test other TR chemotypes.

Conclusion

Rigid docking into the L. infantum trypanothione reductase structure 4ADW separates genuine β-carboline–quinazolinone TR inhibitors (−7.75 to −8.56 kcal/mol) from the non-inhibitor miltefosine (−4.54 kcal/mol) by more than 3 kcal/mol, but ranks the inhibitor series backwards (Spearman ρ = −0.6): the weakest measured inhibitors score best. Docking is a usable first-pass filter for TR — it recognises the scaffold and rejects outsiders — but it cannot prioritise analogues within a congeneric series, and scores alone should not decide which analogue to synthesise next. TR itself remains a sound, parasite-specific target for visceral leishmaniasis, a disease that is rare but present in northern Pakistan and fatal in over 95% of untreated cases.

Ponatinib Scores −14.36 kcal/mol on BCR-ABL1 T315I and Imatinib Scores the Same on Wild Type and Mutant: Rigid Docking Fails the Gatekeeper Negative Control

Imatinib transformed chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), but the T315I gatekeeper mutation — threonine 315 replaced by isoleucine — removes the hydrogen bond imatinib needs and sterically blocks the ATP pocket, conferring resistance to imatinib, dasatinib and nilotinib.
