Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-14 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #58 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: BCR-ABL1; T315I; ponatinib; imatinib; chronic myeloid leukemia; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; gatekeeper mutation

Abstract

Imatinib transformed chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), but the T315I gatekeeper mutation — threonine 315 replaced by isoleucine — removes the hydrogen bond imatinib needs and sterically blocks the ATP pocket, conferring resistance to imatinib, dasatinib and nilotinib. Ponatinib was designed around this mutation, and asciminib now offers a myristoyl-pocket alternative, but no docking screen has been tested against the gatekeeper as a negative control. We docked ponatinib, imatinib and three ChEMBL ABL1 ligands (a GNF-7-series type-II inhibitor and two DFG-out hybrid ureas) with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on three murine Abl1 kinase-domain structures: wild type 3KFA (1.22 angstrom) and 3OXZ (2.2 angstrom, ponatinib-bound), and the T315I mutant 3OY3 (1.95 angstrom, AP24589-bound). Ponatinib re-docked at minus 14.33 kcal/mol on its own wild-type structure and scored minus 14.36 on T315I — indistinguishable, matching its measured sub-nanomolar potency on both forms (0.37 nM wild type, 2.0 nM T315I). But imatinib scored minus 10.41 on wild type and minus 9.60 on T315I, a 0.81 gap inside Vina noise, although its measured potency collapses from 10.8 nM on wild type to essentially inactive on T315I. The three other ligands cluster at minus 9.29 to minus 9.92 on both structures, and the choice of wild-type structure alone moves ponatinib's score by 2.79 kcal/mol — more than the mutation does. Rank correlation against measured ABL1 IC50s is weak (Spearman rho 0.5 on wild type, 0.6 on T315I, n = 5). The screen validates ponatinib's pan-BCR-ABL profile and fails its negative control in the same run. The falsifiable next step is a single-assay kinase comparison of ponatinib, imatinib and the GNF-7-series compound on wild-type and T315I ABL1: if imatinib's T315I IC50 is more than 100-fold weaker while its docking score is unchanged, rigid docking is confirmed blind to gatekeeper resistance.

1. Introduction

Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is uncommon — about 35,380 new cases worldwide in 2021, roughly 15% of adult leukaemias — but it is the disease where targeted therapy advanced furthest, and where resistance has kept pace. The BCR::ABL1 fusion kinase drives the disease, and imatinib, approved in 2001, turned a fatal leukaemia into a chronic one. About a quarter of patients respond poorly to imatinib, and the commonest cause is a point mutation in the BCR::ABL1 kinase domain: more than 90 such mutations are reported, and each carries its own pattern of sensitivity to the available inhibitors.

The most treatment-resilient of them is T315I. Threonine 315 is the gatekeeper residue: it sits where inhibitors form a hydrogen bond that anchors them in the ATP pocket. Replacing threonine with isoleucine removes that hydrogen bond and puts a bulkier, hydrophobic side chain where the drug needs to sit. The result is resistance to imatinib and to the second-generation inhibitors dasatinib, nilotinib and bosutinib. T315I accounts for 4–19% of resistance mutations in published series, and in a 2025 prospective study from the Armed Forces Institute of Pathology in Pakistan (133 imatinib-resistant CML patients), kinase-domain mutations were found in 42.9% — but T315I in only 1 patient (0.8%), while the P-loop mutation E255K dominated at 33.8% and was the only mutation found in patients who had progressed to blast crisis. In that same cohort, only 2 patients were receiving ponatinib and 1 asciminib: the drugs that work against T315I are barely reaching the patients who need them in Pakistan.

Ponatinib was designed specifically for this mutation: a carbon–carbon triple bond (ethynyl linker) threads past the isoleucine side chain where other inhibitors clash. It inhibits native BCR-ABL at 0.37 nM and the T315I mutant at 2.0 nM in cell-free assays, and in the phase 2 PACE trial (449 heavily pretreated patients) 70% of the 64 patients with T315I achieved a major cytogenetic response and 56% a major molecular response. The price is vascular toxicity: arterial occlusive events reached 31% of chronic-phase patients at five years, and the label carries a boxed warning for arterial occlusion, venous thromboembolism, heart failure and hepatotoxicity. Asciminib, which binds the myristoyl pocket instead of the ATP site, is the newer alternative: at 200 mg twice daily in T315I chronic-phase CML, 48.9% of patients achieved a major molecular response at two years (68.4% of ponatinib-naive patients, 34.6% of ponatinib-pretreated).

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen on the T315I mutant structure will rank ponatinib above imatinib and above the other ABL1 ligands, in the same direction as the measured potencies — and, crucially, imatinib will score clearly worse on the mutant than on wild type, because that is what resistance means. The test is the negative control: a screen that cannot see imatinib's failure on T315I cannot be trusted to rank anything else on this target. The reference drug must itself dock, or the comparison is void.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-14 (web search; PubMed; the daily digest of 2026-11-14, which screened 722 candidates and selected 8, none on CML — the digest's relevance is methodological, not topical, for this paper). Key sources: Cortes et al. 2013 (PACE trial, NEJM) and Cortes et al. 2018 (final five-year PACE results, Blood) for ponatinib efficacy and vascular toxicity; O'Hare et al. 2009 for the ponatinib IC50 values; Zhou et al. 2011 for the 3OXZ and 3OY3 structures; Choi et al. 2010 for the GNF-7 type-II series; Dietrich et al. 2010 for the DFG-out hybrid ureas; Cortes et al. 2024 for asciminib in T315I; and the 2025 AFIP Pakistan cohort for the local mutation spectrum. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Pipeline, the mouse-target correction, and the structure choice

The standard LeadForge pipeline was run with target "BCR-ABL1 T315I" and reference drug ponatinib (run_docking.py, RDKit venv, NO_PROXY prefix). The pipeline retrieved 37 known ligands from ChEMBL target CHEMBL3099, verified ponatinib in PubChem (CID 24826799), screened 25 analogues by Morgan-fingerprint similarity, and ranked 26 leads by the standard composite score (similarity, Lipinski, Veber, PAINS, Tox21 read-across). Two corrections are recorded here rather than hidden.

First, the pipeline resolved the target to UniProt P00520 — murine Abl1 — and to ChEMBL CHEMBL3099, annotated Mus musculus. The human target is ABL1 (P00519). This is not a pipeline error to hide: the entire crystallographic literature for ABL1 T315I is built on the murine Abl1 kinase-domain construct (residues 229–511), because that is what crystallised. Both structures used here are murine constructs, and the gatekeeper numbering (Thr315) is identical. The measured potencies quoted in this paper are ChEMBL-reported ABL1 values under that murine target, and the paper says so wherever they appear.

Second, the pipeline's automatic structure pick (best resolution with a drug-like ligand) chose 3KFA, a wild-type Abl1 structure (1.22 angstrom, vinyl-purine inhibitor B91). A wild-type structure cannot test a gatekeeper-mutant question, so the T315I docking was re-run on 3OY3 — the T315I mutant kinase domain in complex with the ponatinib analogue AP24589, 1.95 angstrom (Zhou et al. 2011) — and ponatinib was re-docked on its own wild-type co-crystal structure 3OXZ (2.2 angstrom) as the protocol control, with imatinib cross-docked into the same 3OXZ pocket to complete the matched wild-type/mutant pair. The 3KFA scores are kept as a second wild-type control, which turns out to matter: the choice of wild-type structure moves ponatinib's score by 2.79 kcal/mol (Section 3.4).

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; one box (22.5 angstrom) and exhaustiveness 8 for every compound. Three structures, all murine Abl1 kinase domain (residues 229–511):

  • 3KFA, wild type, 1.22 angstrom, with the vinyl-purine dual Src-Abl inhibitor B91. Centre [16.72, −8.41, 15.16] — the centroid of B91 computed by the pipeline's _ligand_center.
  • 3OXZ, wild type, 2.2 angstrom, with ponatinib (0LI). Centre [15.33, −7.55, 16.58] — the centroid of co-crystallised ponatinib; the re-dock control.
  • 3OY3, T315I mutant, 1.95 angstrom, with the ponatinib analogue AP24589 (XY3). Centre [15.64, 7.23, 3.76] — the centroid of the chain-A AP24589, computed with _ligand_center; the Ile315 CA is 8.89 angstrom from the centre, confirming the box sits on the ATP site. The chain-B ligand copy was not used.

Best of three poses reported per compound. Five compounds on 3KFA and 3OY3: ponatinib (reference drug, PubChem CID 24826799), imatinib (CHEMBL941, approved 2001), CHEMBL459850 (a 3,4-dihydropyrimido[4,5-d]pyrimidin-2(1H)-one from the T315I-active type-II series of Choi et al. 2010, whose exemplar GNF-7 inhibited wild-type and T315I Bcr-Abl in biochemical and cellular assays and showed in-vivo efficacy in a T315I xenograft), and CHEMBL1213975 and CHEMBL1213976 (diaryl-urea DFG-out hybrids built from Gleevec/Nexavar/BIRB-796 fragments, Dietrich et al. 2010). Ponatinib was docked twice on 3OY3 in independent Vina runs (−14.36 and −14.29, delta 0.07); the −14.36 run is tabulated. One control was attempted and discarded: an AP24589 re-dock on 3OY3 was abandoned because PubChem has no AP24589 record under that name and the SMILES extracted from the deposited coordinates by RDKit's MolFromPDBBlock was mangled (the ethynyl linker and imidazole were lost); the −9.10 value it produced is not reported anywhere in this paper.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every compound. All five are PAINS-clean. Ponatinib carries one Lipinski violation (molecular weight 532.57); the other four pass Lipinski and Veber outright.

2.5 Rank correlation

Spearman rank correlation was computed between the Vina scores and the measured ABL1 IC50 values for the five compounds (n = 5). The measured values are wild-type ABL1 IC50s from ChEMBL, except ponatinib, for which the T315I value (2.0 nM) is also known. A correlation on five points is reported as a descriptive check, not as a validated ranking — the paper's real test is the imatinib negative control (Section 3.2).

2.6 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; any gap smaller than that is not a difference. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No compound was assayed. The structures are murine kinase domains, not human BCR-ABL1, and both mutant and wild-type structures are rigid snapshots in one (DFG-out) conformation.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Ponatinib is the clear winner on every structure: 1.62 kcal/mol clear of the next compound on 3KFA, and 4.55 clear on 3OY3. The other four compounds sit within 0.63 kcal/mol of each other on T315I (−9.29 to −9.81) and within 0.50 on 3KFA (−9.42 to −9.92) — one noise band, no ranking among them.

3.2 The negative control fails: imatinib scores the same on mutant and wild type

This is the result the paper was designed to test, and it fails. Imatinib scores −9.57 on wild type (3KFA) and −9.60 on T315I (3OY3): a difference of 0.03 kcal/mol, zero. On the matched pair — the same pocket family, 3OXZ wild type versus 3OY3 mutant — it scores −10.41 versus −9.60, a gap of 0.81, inside Vina noise. The measured record says the opposite: imatinib inhibits wild-type ABL1 at 10.8 nM and is essentially inactive against T315I, which is why T315I patients cannot be treated with it. Rigid docking with a fixed box finds a pose for imatinib in the mutant pocket and scores it as if nothing changed. The gatekeeper mechanism — a lost hydrogen bond plus a steric clash — is invisible to this protocol. Any ranking this screen produces on T315I is therefore unvalidated against the one compound whose behaviour on the mutant is known with certainty.

3.3 Rank correlation: weak, and driven by one compound

Against the measured wild-type ABL1 IC50s (ponatinib 0.37 nM, imatinib 10.8 nM, CHEMBL459850 243 nM, CHEMBL1213976 244 nM, CHEMBL1213975 572.4 nM), Spearman rho is 0.5 on the wild-type structure 3KFA and 0.6 on the mutant structure 3OY3 (n = 5). Both values are carried entirely by ponatinib sitting first; remove ponatinib and the remaining four compounds are ranked by Vina in an order that has no relationship to their measured potencies — imatinib, the second most potent compound measured (10.8 nM), ranks fourth of five by Vina on both structures, tied with compounds 20–50 times weaker. The two near-tied potencies (243 vs 244 nM) make the swap between CHEMBL459850 and CHEMBL1213976 meaningless, but the imatinib mis-ranking is not a tie artefact: it is a 20-fold potency error. A correlation of 0.5–0.6 on five points, with the negative control failed, is not a validated ranking.

3.4 The structure matters more than the mutation

Ponatinib scores −11.54 on wild type 3KFA but −14.33 on wild type 3OXZ: the same drug, the same wild-type protein, a 2.79 kcal/mol difference from the choice of structure alone — larger than any mutation effect in this study (ponatinib WT→T315I: 0.03; imatinib WT→T315I: 0.81). The reason is visible in the poses: on 3OXZ and 3OY3 the best pose (−14.33, −14.36) sits 3.5–3.9 kcal/mol clear of the second pose (−10.48, −10.81), while on 3KFA the poses are tightly grouped. The 3OXZ/3OY3 pocket was crystallised around ponatinib-class ligands in the DFG-out conformation, and the scoring function rewards that fit heavily. The −14.3 values are therefore partly a pocket-shape effect, not a pure affinity signal — and the measured record agrees that the direction is right but the magnitude is overstated: ponatinib is 5-fold less potent on T315I than on wild type (0.37 → 2.0 nM), while docking scores them identical. Any paper that reports a single-structure docking score as a potency claim is reporting the structure it picked as much as the molecule it docked.

3.5 ADMET and safety panel

All five compounds pass Lipinski and Veber (ponatinib with one violation, MW 532.57, logP 4.46, TPSA 65.77); all are PAINS-clean. The Tox21 read-across panel flags nothing decisive: ponatinib's highest signals are SR-MMP 0.917 and SR-ARE 0.881 (kNN read-across, not measured). The safety story that matters for this target is not in the panel: ponatinib's arterial occlusive events (31% of chronic-phase patients at five years in PACE) are a clinical toxicity, not a property any ligand-based screen predicts. The GNF-7-series compound and the two hybrid ureas are research compounds with no approval, no human safety data, and no measured T315I potency in the public record beyond the series-level claims in their source papers.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the screen can and cannot say

The screen can say one thing with confidence: ponatinib binds the T315I pocket at least as well as it binds the wild-type pocket, in the same direction as its measured profile. It cannot say that imatinib fails on T315I, which is the best-established fact in this field — and because it cannot say that, it cannot rank the three research compounds either. Their scores (−9.29 to −9.92) are noise, and the most interesting of them — CHEMBL459850, from a series published as T315I-active in cells and in a mouse xenograft — scores −9.78, indistinguishable from imatinib's −9.60. A paper that reported "CHEMBL459850 is a T315I lead because it docks at −9.78" would be reporting the same number that the known-inactive drug gets.

4.2 The gatekeeper mechanism docking cannot see

T315I defeats imatinib through two effects Vina cannot model in a rigid receptor: the loss of a hydrogen bond to the threonine hydroxyl, and a steric clash with the isoleucine side chain that forces the drug out of its preferred pose. A fixed box and a rigid side chain let the docking algorithm find an alternative pose that avoids the clash and then score it as if the clash did not exist. The correct computational test of gatekeeper resistance is not a single rigid dock: it is a free-energy comparison (e.g. MM-GBSA or alchemical free-energy perturbation) that prices the lost hydrogen bond and the clash, or a flexible-side-chain dock that lets Ile315 move. Neither was run here, and the paper does not pretend otherwise. The honest conclusion is that standard rigid docking is the wrong tool for gatekeeper mutations, and this paper is the control experiment that shows it.

4.3 Ponatinib's safety price, and the asciminib alternative

Even where docking validates ponatinib, the clinical question is not potency but price. Ponatinib works in T315I — 70% major cytogenetic response in the PACE T315I subgroup — but a third of chronic-phase patients develop arterial occlusive events by five years, and dose reductions (from 45 mg to 15 mg) are the standard mitigation. Asciminib attacks the same kinase from the myristoyl pocket, where the gatekeeper is irrelevant: at 200 mg twice daily, 48.9% of T315I patients achieved a major molecular response at two years, with a different toxicity profile (lipase elevation 18.8% grade ≥3, thrombocytopenia 14.6%). For a Pakistani patient, the practical question is access: in the AFIP cohort, 2 of 133 resistant patients were on ponatinib and 1 on asciminib. A docking paper cannot fix access, but it can stop pretending that a better docking score is the bottleneck — the bottleneck is the drug reaching the patient.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Negative-control hypothesis. In one kinase assay on wild-type and T315I ABL1, imatinib's IC50 weakens by more than 100-fold on the mutant while ponatinib's weakens by less than 10-fold. Falsified if imatinib's T315I IC50 is within 10-fold of its wild-type value — in which case the published resistance is an artefact, which no one expects.
  2. GNF-7-series hypothesis. CHEMBL459850 inhibits T315I ABL1 in a kinase assay at an IC50 within 10-fold of ponatinib's 2.0 nM. Falsified if it is more than 10-fold weaker — in which case its docking score (−9.78) is noise, as this paper suspects.
  3. Structure-choice hypothesis. Ponatinib's docking score on a third wild-type ABL1 structure (neither 3KFA nor 3OXZ) falls outside the −11.54 to −14.33 range. Falsified if it lands inside it — in which case the 2.79 kcal/mol pocket effect is specific to this pair, not a general property of structure choice.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain ponatinib, imatinib, CHEMBL459850 and asciminib (as the myristoyl-pocket control); confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): kinase assay (ADP-Glo or equivalent) on recombinant wild-type and T315I ABL1, all four compounds on the same plates, in triplicate — the single-assay comparison this paper could not make, and the direct test of hypothesis 1. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): Ba/F3 cellular assay on Bcr-Abl wild-type and T315I lines, plus a wild-type ABL1 counter-screen for selectivity. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if CHEMBL459850 is within 10-fold of ponatinib on T315I, dock its analogues and synthesise the best two; if it is not, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per IC50 determination is the minimum for a defensible potency claim; the imatinib wild-type-versus-mutant comparison needs the same, because a false "resistant" call on the control is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. All structures are murine Abl1 kinase domains, not human BCR-ABL1; the gatekeeper numbering is identical, but the construct is not the fusion protein.
  3. Rigid-receptor docking cannot model the hydrogen-bond loss and steric clash that define T315I resistance; the imatinib negative control fails, and the paper reports that failure rather than hiding it.
  4. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; four of the five compounds sit inside one noise band on both structures.
  5. The choice of wild-type structure moves ponatinib's score by 2.79 kcal/mol — more than the mutation does — so absolute scores are not comparable across structures.
  6. The re-dock control is ponatinib on its own structure (3OXZ); a competent protocol is expected to recover a good score there, so −14.33 validates the protocol, not a lead.
  7. Only ponatinib carries a measured T315I potency; the three research compounds carry only wild-type ABL1 IC50s, so the T315I rank correlation cannot be computed against T315I measurements.
  8. Spearman rho is computed on five points and is driven by ponatinib; it is a descriptive check, not a validated ranking.
  9. The AP24589 re-dock on 3OY3 was attempted and discarded (no PubChem record; PDB-derived SMILES unreliable); no co-crystallised-ligand re-dock exists for the mutant structure.
  10. No molecular dynamics, flexible-side-chain docking, or free-energy refinement was run — the methods that could actually price gatekeeper resistance.
  11. The Tox21 panel is kNN read-across, not measured toxicity; ponatinib's real safety liability (arterial occlusion) is clinical and invisible to this screen.

6. Conclusion

On the T315I mutant structure 3OY3, ponatinib scores −14.36 kcal/mol — the same as its −14.33 re-dock on its own wild-type structure 3OXZ — matching its measured sub-nanomolar potency on both forms and validating its pan-BCR-ABL profile. But imatinib scores −10.41 on wild type and −9.60 on T315I, a gap inside Vina noise, although its measured potency collapses from 10.8 nM to essentially inactive: rigid docking cannot see the gatekeeper resistance it was asked to detect. The three research compounds cluster at −9.29 to −9.92 on both structures, inside noise, and the choice of wild-type structure alone moves ponatinib's score by 2.79 kcal/mol. The screen is a validated positive control with a failed negative control — useful for confirming ponatinib, useless for ranking anything else on T315I. The next step is the single-assay kinase comparison in Section 4.5, with ponatinib, imatinib, the GNF-7-series compound and asciminib on wild-type and T315I ABL1 on the same plates.

Vina Ranks the Weakest Measured PBP2a Binder First: Zero Rank Correlation on Two MRSA Acyl-Enzyme Structures

MRSA caused more than 100,000 deaths attributable to antimicrobial resistance in 2019, and its resistance rests on a single protein, PBP2a, encoded by mecA, whose closed active site excludes most beta-lactams; ceftaroline overcomes this by binding an allosteric site 60 angstrom away, opening the active site for a secon…

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-13 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #53 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: MRSA; PBP2a; mecA; ceftaroline; ceftobiprole; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; rank correlation

Abstract

MRSA caused more than 100,000 deaths attributable to antimicrobial resistance in 2019, and its resistance rests on a single protein, PBP2a, encoded by mecA, whose closed active site excludes most beta-lactams; ceftaroline overcomes this by binding an allosteric site 60 angstrom away, opening the active site for a second molecule to acylate Ser403, and clinical N146K/E150K mutations disrupt that trigger. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can rank PBP2a binders at all. We docked four ChEMBL MecA actives with measured Kd/IC50 values, ceftaroline (prodrug and active form), ceftobiprole and the carbapenem analogue L-695,256 into two acyl-enzyme structures — 1MWS (2.00 A) and the ceftaroline co-crystal 3ZG0 chain B (2.60 A) — with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 under one protocol, centres audited to 0.0 A from the co-crystallised ligands. The rank test failed on both structures: the Vina order (CHEMBL4862632 first) is unrelated to the measured order (CHEMBL4847813, Kd 129 nM, first), Spearman rho = 0.0, and the second-best measured binder, CHEMBL4879273 (Kd 168 nM), docked worst on both structures. A second independent Vina run reproduced the same order, and one ChEMBL ligand turned out to be ceftobiprole itself, the same molecule scoring 1 kcal/mol apart under two SMILES representations. No "beats ceftaroline" claim can be made from this screen, and Vina's non-covalent scores cannot model the covalent acylation that is ceftaroline's mechanism. The falsifiable next step is a PBP2a acylation assay (k2/Ks) of the four ChEMBL ligands against ceftaroline in wild-type and N146K/E150K PBP2a: if the measured acylation order matches the ChEMBL record rather than the Vina order, docking alone must not be used to prioritise PBP2a leads on these structures.

1. Introduction

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was the single deadliest pathogen–drug combination in the 2019 Global Research on Antimicrobial Resistance estimates: more than 100,000 deaths directly attributable to MRSA in one year, within 1.27 million deaths attributable to bacterial antimicrobial resistance overall. South Asia carried one of the highest attributable burdens, at 22 deaths per 100,000 population. MRSA's resistance rests on one protein. The mecA gene encodes penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2a), a transpeptidase that takes over cell-wall cross-linking when the bacterium's native PBPs are inhibited, and it does so because its active site is closed: protective loops shield the catalytic Ser403, so most beta-lactams cannot reach it at therapeutic concentrations.

Ceftaroline, a fifth-generation cephalosporin, is the drug that solved the closed-site problem without opening it by force. A first ceftaroline molecule binds a non-covalent allosteric site about 60 A from the active site, triggering a conformational change that opens the active site; a second molecule then acylates Ser403 and inactivates the enzyme. That mechanism is also its vulnerability: the clinical resistance mutations N146K/E150K (double mutant) and N146K/E150K/H351N (triple mutant) sit in the allosteric domain and disrupt the trigger, so the active site never opens. Ceftobiprole, the other anti-MRSA cephalosporin, retains activity against most ceftaroline-nonsusceptible isolates — in a 2025 survey of 8,184 US MRSA isolates, ceftobiprole MIC50/90 was 1/2 mg/L with 99.3% susceptible, against ceftaroline MIC50/90 of 0.5/1 mg/L.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen of ChEMBL MecA actives against ceftaroline on acyl-PBP2a structures will rank compounds in the same order as their measured Kd/IC50 values. The test is the rank correlation, not the best score — and the reference drug must itself dock, or the comparison is void.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-13 (web search; PubMed via the daily digest of 2026-11-13, which screened 627 candidates and selected 8, none on PBP2a — the digest's relevance is methodological, not topical, for this paper). Key sources: Murray et al. 2022 for the MRSA burden; Lim and Strynadka 2002 for the PBP2a structure; Fishovitz et al. 2014 and Otero et al. 2013 for the allosteric mechanism and the resistance mutations; Sader et al. 2025 for current ceftaroline and ceftobiprole MIC distributions. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented).

Two disclosures belong in Methods, not in a footnote. First, the ChEMBL API was down on the whole of 2026-11-13: target search, target-by-accession and activity endpoints all returned HTTP 500, verified by direct calls, by a browser fetch and by a delegated browser task. The standard pipeline therefore retrieved zero ligands. The four ChEMBL MecA potencies in this paper come from a LeadForge retrieval of 2026-10-29, when ChEMBL was live (target CHEMBL6187, "MecA (Staphylococcus aureus)"), and the SMILES are copied verbatim from that retrieval; the docking itself was re-run today. Second, the first docking run of this paper was killed by the runtime (SIGTERM) at 14 of 16 docks with no JSON saved, because results were only written at the end. The script was patched to save incrementally after every dock and to resume from a partial file, and re-run detached. The re-run is the primary dataset reported here; the first run's 14 scores survive in its log and are used only as a reproducibility check (Section 3.2).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt Q53707 (MecA PBP2a, S. aureus, 668 aa); ChEMBL target CHEMBL6187 (retrieved 2026-10-29, not re-verified today because the API is down). Two structures, both acyl-enzyme complexes: 1MWS, nitrocefin acyl-PBP2a, 2.00 A X-ray, chain A only (the full file is two chains and makes Vina crawl on this VM; the chain-A-only receptor is the verified 2026-10-29 precedent), centre [28.55, 29.22, 87.49] — audited against the chain-A nitrocefin NC1 centroid computed from the deposited coordinates with the pipeline's own _ligand_center function: distance 0.0 A. The two-chain NC1 average is 8.15 A away and is an artefact (chain-B NC1 is 6 atoms, 63.87 A away); it is not the centre. 3ZG0 chain B, ceftaroline acyl-PBP2a, 2.60 A X-ray, centre [−35.99, 44.39, 66.82] — the chain-B AI8 (ceftaroline, bound form) centroid; chain A was excluded because it fails RDKit sanitisation (a 1.81 A Gly402 O…Ser403 N contact misread as a bond). Best of three poses reported per compound. The same box (22.5 A) and exhaustiveness (8) were used for every compound on both structures, including ceftaroline itself. Eight compounds: the four ChEMBL ligands, ceftaroline fosamil (the administered prodrug, PubChem CID 9852981) and active ceftaroline (CID 74316801), ceftobiprole (CID 135413542) and L-695,256 (CID 9890833).

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter (the pipeline's own filter, classes A–C) applied to every docked compound. All eight compounds are PAINS-clean on both structures.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity, and for PBP2a it is doubly not activity: ceftaroline's mechanism is covalent acylation of Ser403, and Vina's scores here are non-covalent pose scores in acyl-enzyme structures — they cannot model the acylation step, and they cannot model the allosteric trigger, which was discussed but not docked (a second-molecule allosteric model is beyond Vina's single-ligand protocol). Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds. Both structures are acyl-enzyme complexes, so the pocket conformation is the acylated one, not the apo one a screening ligand first encounters. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated. The four ChEMBL potencies mix Kd and IC50 values from heterogeneous assays (pChEMBL 5.72–6.89); they are not head-to-head measurements, and the rank test mixes assay types. The ChEMBL potencies could not be re-fetched today because the API is down; they rest on the 2026-10-29 retrieval alone.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound 1MWS chain A (kcal/mol) 3ZG0 chain B (kcal/mol) Measured potency PAINS
CHEMBL4862632 −9.69 (−9.69, −9.53, −9.34) −10.08 (−10.08, −10.05, −9.62) Kd 264 nM none
CHEMBL4847813 −9.38 (−9.38, −9.05, −9.00) −9.73 (−9.73, −9.61, −9.52) Kd 129 nM none
CHEMBL520642 −9.32 (−9.32, −8.61, −8.51) −9.58 (−9.58, −9.38, −9.33) IC50 1900 nM none
CHEMBL4879273 −7.30 (−7.30, −7.20, −7.05) −7.62 (−7.62, −7.57, −7.37) Kd 168 nM none
Ceftaroline (active) −8.84 (−8.84, −8.22, −8.06) −7.64 (−7.64, −7.22, −7.21) MRSA MIC90 1 mg/L none
Ceftaroline fosamil −8.26 (−8.26, −8.24, −7.99) −8.62 (−8.62, −7.88, −7.47) MRSA MIC90 1 mg/L none
Ceftobiprole −10.30 (−10.30, −9.22, −9.21) −8.86 (−8.86, −8.33, −7.83) MRSA MIC50/90 1/2 mg/L none
L-695,256 −9.62 (−9.62, −9.32, −9.22) −9.84 (−9.84, −9.71, −9.45) none attached none

All eight compounds are large and flexible by screening standards (MW 469–685, 5–11 rotatable bonds); ceftaroline fosamil is the largest (MW 684.7, 11 rotatable bonds, TPSA 223.24) and the most flexible, and it scores worst of the two ceftaroline forms on both structures. Ceftobiprole is the most structure-dependent compound in the set: −10.30 on 1MWS (the best score in the whole screen) but −8.86 on 3ZG0, a 1.44 kcal/mol spread — the "best" compound in this screen depends on which structure you pick.

The rank test the hypothesis posed: the measured order of the four ChEMBL ligands is CHEMBL4847813 (Kd 129 nM) > CHEMBL4879273 (Kd 168 nM) > CHEMBL4862632 (Kd 264 nM) > CHEMBL520642 (IC50 1900 nM). The Vina order on 1MWS is CHEMBL4862632 > CHEMBL4847813 > CHEMBL520642 > CHEMBL4879273, and on 3ZG0 it is exactly the same: CHEMBL4862632 > CHEMBL4847813 > CHEMBL520642 > CHEMBL4879273. Spearman rho = 0.0 on both structures (n = 4). The weakest measured binder docks first, the second-best measured binder docks last, and the middle two swap. The hypothesis is falsified on both structures.

3.2 Reproducibility: the killed first run agrees

The first run's 14 surviving scores (logged before the SIGTERM kill) reproduce the re-run's order. On 1MWS the first run gave CHEMBL4862632 −10.47, ceftobiprole −10.32, L-695,256 −9.63, CHEMBL4847813 −9.37, CHEMBL520642 −9.26, active ceftaroline −8.81, fosamil −8.26, CHEMBL4879273 −7.21 — the same order as the re-run except that the top two swap, within noise. The largest cross-run differences are CHEMBL4862632 on 1MWS (−10.47 to −9.69, 0.78 kcal/mol) and active ceftaroline on 3ZG0 (−8.78 to −7.64, 1.14 kcal/mol); all other differences are 0.09 kcal/mol or less. Every cross-run difference sits inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the rank conclusion — rho = 0.0, CHEMBL4879273 last — is identical in both runs. Two independent Vina runs, same failed rank test.

3.3 One ChEMBL ligand is ceftobiprole

CHEMBL520642 and ceftobiprole have identical connectivity: the same molecular formula (C20H22N8O6S2) and the same canonical SMILES once stereochemistry is stripped; CHEMBL520642 is the stereochemistry-specified ChEMBL record of ceftobiprole, and the PubChem ceftobiprole SMILES is the same scaffold without stereochemistry. The dock set therefore contains one molecule twice, under two representations — and the same molecule scores differently: −9.32 versus −10.30 on 1MWS, and −9.58 versus −8.86 on 3ZG0. The input representation alone moves the score by about 1 kcal/mol, which is the same size as the gaps between the ranked compounds. This is reported as a finding, not hidden: the ChEMBL IC50 of 1900 nM attached to CHEMBL520642 and the whole-cell MIC50/90 of 1/2 mg/L attached to ceftobiprole describe the same molecule in different assays, and they must not both enter the rank test. The rank test in Section 3.1 uses the four ChEMBL ligands only; ceftobiprole enters as the clinical comparator, not as a fifth ranked ligand.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these four ChEMBL compounds on 1MWS or 3ZG0 was found at drafting time, so there is no published docking comparison to make. The depositing studies for both structures are structure papers, not docking benchmarks. The absence of a published comparator is stated, not filled in.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The paper's question changed while running it. It started as "which ChEMBL MecA ligands beat ceftaroline?" and became "can this screen rank PBP2a binders at all?" The answer is no on both structures, twice. A screen that ranks the weakest measured binder first and the second-best measured binder last is not a screen with a weak signal — it is a screen with no signal for this target at this setting, and the honest report is the zero, not the best score.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

CHEMBL4862632's −10.08 on 3ZG0 is the best ChEMBL score in the screen, and it is also the score of the weakest measured binder (Kd 264 nM) — a "win" that is a loss by the measured record. Ceftobiprole's −10.30 on 1MWS looks like a lead until the same molecule, under its ChEMBL representation, scores −9.32 on the same structure, and until the same compound scores −8.86 on 3ZG0. Three numbers for what is effectively one comparison, spanning 1.44 kcal/mol. The gaps between the ranked ChEMBL ligands (0.31–2.39 kcal/mol on 1MWS) are the same size as the representation noise, so no ordering between them is defensible from these scores at all.

4.3 The PAINS problem does not apply here — the mechanism problem does

All compounds are PAINS-clean, so no artefact controls are needed on that front. The design constraint this experiment imposes is different: any validation must measure acylation, not binding. Ceftaroline's efficacy is a second-order acylation rate (k2/Ks) after an allosteric trigger, and a non-covalent pose score in an acyl-enzyme structure measures neither the trigger nor the acylation. A validation assay that only measures equilibrium binding would repeat the screen's error in a different format.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Rank hypothesis. In a PBP2a acylation assay, the k2/Ks order of the four ChEMBL ligands matches their ChEMBL record order (4847813 > 4879273 > 4862632 > 520642). Falsified if the measured order differs — in which case the ChEMBL record itself, not just the docking, fails to predict acylation, and the ligands need re-measurement before any prioritisation.
  2. Representation hypothesis. The same molecule docked from its stereochemistry-specified and unspecified SMILES scores within Vina's noise on both structures (difference ≤ 2 kcal/mol). Supported by this run (differences 0.72–0.98 kcal/mol); falsified if a third representation scores more than 2 kcal/mol away — in which case the input preparation, not the scoring function, dominates the result.
  3. Resistance hypothesis. At least one of the four ChEMBL ligands acylates N146K/E150K PBP2a at a rate within ten-fold of its wild-type rate, where ceftaroline's rate collapses. Falsified if all four lose acylation on the mutant as ceftaroline does — in which case none of them addresses the clinical resistance mechanism, and the allosteric site, not the active site, is the target that matters.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain or synthesise the four ChEMBL ligands; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR — with explicit confirmation that CHEMBL520642 and ceftobiprole are the same molecule, so only one of them is carried forward as a test compound. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): PBP2a acylation assay (nitrocefin competition or Bocillin-FL binding) in wild-type PBP2a, measuring k2/Ks for all four ligands plus ceftaroline and ceftobiprole on the same plates, in triplicate. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): repeat the acylation assay on N146K/E150K PBP2a (the clinical allosteric mutant); whole-cell MRSA MICs for the best two ligands in the same strains. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if a ligand acylates the mutant, dock it into the mutant structure and compare the pose with the wild-type pose; if none does, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per k2/Ks determination is the minimum for a defensible second-order rate; the mutant comparison needs the same, because a false "retains activity" call on the resistance mutant is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the gaps between the ranked ligands are the same size as the representation noise.
  3. The rank test is n = 4 and mixes Kd and IC50 values from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays.
  4. The four ChEMBL potencies could not be re-fetched today (ChEMBL API HTTP 500); they rest on the 2026-10-29 retrieval alone.
  5. Vina's non-covalent scores cannot model covalent acylation or the allosteric trigger; the allosteric site was not docked.
  6. Both structures are acyl-enzyme complexes; the pocket conformation is the acylated one, not the apo one.
  7. CHEMBL520642 and ceftobiprole are the same molecule, so the set contains seven distinct compounds, not eight.
  8. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run.
  9. No N146K/E150K mutant structure was docked, although the topic posed the resistance question; the wild-type result says nothing about the mutant.
  10. A single rigid structure per run cannot represent the PBP2a conformational ensemble.

6. Conclusion

Four ChEMBL MecA actives dock in no measured-potency order on either of two acyl-PBP2a structures (Spearman rho = 0.0 on both, n = 4), with the weakest measured binder first and the second-best measured binder last, and a second independent Vina run reproduces the same order. One ChEMBL ligand is ceftobiprole itself, and the same molecule scores about 1 kcal/mol apart under two SMILES representations. The screen is therefore a reproduced negative result with a missing mechanism, not a lead claim. The next step is the acylation assay in Section 4.5, with ceftaroline measured on the same plates.

Momelotinib Re-Docks Best on JAK2 (8BXH) With a PAINS Alert, and the Rank Correlation Flips Sign Between Kd and IC50

JAK2 inhibitors transformed myelofibrosis care: ruxolitinib first in 2011, then fedratinib, pacritinib and momelotinib, all ATP-competitive inhibitors of the same JH1 kinase domain, differing mainly in their selectivity and in which cytopenias they worsen or spare.

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-13 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #56 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: JAK2; ruxolitinib; momelotinib; myelofibrosis; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; rank correlation; PAINS

Abstract

JAK2 inhibitors transformed myelofibrosis care: ruxolitinib first in 2011, then fedratinib, pacritinib and momelotinib, all ATP-competitive inhibitors of the same JH1 kinase domain, differing mainly in their selectivity and in which cytopenias they worsen or spare. The question is whether a standard docking screen can rank them by their measured potency on the JAK2 structure. We docked six compounds into 8BXH, the JAK2 JH1 structure co-crystallised with momelotinib (1.3 angstrom), with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 under one protocol: the four myelofibrosis drugs, plus tofacitinib and baricitinib as cross-class comparators. Momelotinib re-docked best at minus 9.73 kcal/mol, ruxolitinib scored minus 8.73 and pacritinib worst at minus 7.67. The rank test depends on which potency measure is used: against the four drugs' IC50 values the Spearman rho is 0.2, against their Kd values it is minus 0.4, both on four compounds, so the screen has no defensible rank signal either way. Momelotinib also carries the screen's only PAINS alert, despite being an approved drug, and the most selective drug in the set, pacritinib at 26-fold over JAK1, docks worst — a property the single-target screen cannot measure at all. The falsifiable next step is a single-assay kinase comparison of all six compounds on JAK2, with JAK1 selectivity measured on the same plates: if the measured order matches the Kd record rather than the Vina order, docking alone must not be used to prioritise JAK2 inhibitors on this structure.

1. Introduction

Myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven in most patients by the JAK2 V617F mutation, which leaves the kinase constitutively active and the bone marrow progressively fibrotic. Four ATP-competitive JAK2 inhibitors are approved for it — ruxolitinib (2011), fedratinib (2019), pacritinib (2022) and momelotinib (2023) — and they are distinguished less by their JAK2 potency than by their selectivity and their haematologic cost: ruxolitinib worsens anaemia, pacritinib spares platelets, momelotinib improves anaemia through ACVR1 inhibition. Their JAK2 potencies were measured head-to-head in one study (Miao et al. 2024, Lance Ultra kinase assay, 1 mM ATP): by IC50, ruxolitinib 3.2 nM, fedratinib 10 nM, momelotinib 11 nM, pacritinib 14 nM; by Kd, ruxolitinib 0.8 nM, fedratinib 4.3 nM, pacritinib 6.6 nM, momelotinib 6.7 nM. The two measures give different orders — pacritinib and momelotinib swap — which is the first warning that any rank test on this set is assay-dependent. A second study (Celik et al. 2023, Blood abstract, 1 mM ATP) gives a different order again: IC50 ruxolitinib 4 nM, fedratinib 14 nM, momelotinib 51 nM, pacritinib 53 nM.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen on 8BXH will rank the four myelofibrosis drugs in the same order as their measured potencies. The test is the rank correlation, not the best score — and the reference drug must itself dock, or the comparison is void.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-13 (web search; PubMed via the daily digest of 2026-11-13, which screened 627 candidates and selected 8, none on JAK2 — the digest's relevance is methodological, not topical, for this paper). Key sources: Miao et al. 2024 for the head-to-head Kd and IC50 values and the 8BXH structure; Celik et al. 2023 for the second, assay-dependent potency set. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented). Miao et al. 2024 Table 1 is the primary potency source; Celik et al. 2023 is cited only to show that the potency order is assay-dependent, not as a second primary.

2.2 ChEMBL outage and the PubChem fallback

The ChEMBL API was down on the whole of 2026-11-13: target search, target-by-accession and activity endpoints all returned HTTP 500, verified by direct calls, by a browser fetch and by a delegated browser task. The standard pipeline therefore retrieved zero ligands. The compounds in this paper were taken from PubChem by CID, with measured potencies attached only where a verified literature value exists. No analogues were fetched for this paper: the four myelofibrosis drugs plus two cross-class comparators are the complete set the topic poses.

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt O60674 (JAK2, human). One structure: 8BXH, JAK2 JH1 kinase domain in complex with momelotinib, 1.3 A X-ray (Miao et al. 2024). Centre [−11.91, 15.38, 20.25] — the centroid of the co-crystallised momelotinib computed from the deposited coordinates with the pipeline's own _ligand_center function; the distance to the largest HETATM group centroid is 0.0 A, confirming the box sits on the ATP site. Best of three poses reported per compound. The same box (22.5 A) and exhaustiveness (8) were used for every compound, including ruxolitinib itself. Six compounds: ruxolitinib (PubChem CID 25126798, reference drug), fedratinib (CID 16722836), momelotinib (CID 25062766, re-dock control), pacritinib (CID 46216796), tofacitinib (CID 9926791) and baricitinib (CID 44205240). The pipeline's earlier ruxolitinib score on the same structure and centre (−8.71) is a reproducibility check, not a second dataset: this run re-docked it under the single protocol reported here.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter (the pipeline's own filter, classes A–C) applied to every docked compound. Five compounds are PAINS-clean. Momelotinib carries a PAINS alert — the only alert in the screen, and the only alert in any of the five papers of this day's run.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds; the gap between fedratinib and ruxolitinib here is 0.09 kcal/mol, which is no gap at all. The rank test is n = 4, so both Spearman values reported are descriptive statistics, not significant correlations — the finding is that the sign flips between the two potency measures, not that either number is powered. The four potencies come from one head-to-head study (Miao et al. 2024) but a second study (Celik et al. 2023) gives a different order, so the "measured order" itself is assay-dependent. Tofacitinib and baricitinib carry no head-to-head JAK2 value from Miao et al. 2024 Table 1, so they enter the screen as comparators, not as ranked compounds. A single rigid structure was docked; the JAK2 JH1 domain is known to move on inhibitor binding. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound 8BXH (kcal/mol) Measured potency PAINS
Momelotinib −9.73 (−9.73, −9.64, −9.53) JAK2 Kd 6.7 nM, IC50 11 nM alert
Fedratinib −8.82 (−8.82, −8.77, −8.50) JAK2 Kd 4.3 nM, IC50 10 nM none
Ruxolitinib (reference) −8.73 (−8.73, −8.57, −8.24) JAK2 Kd 0.8 nM, IC50 3.2 nM none
Baricitinib −8.64 (−8.64, −8.50, −8.01) No head-to-head JAK2 value from Miao 2024 Table 1 none
Tofacitinib −8.22 (−8.22, −8.00, −7.88) No head-to-head JAK2 value from Miao 2024 Table 1 none
Pacritinib −7.67 (−7.67, −7.39, −7.07) JAK2 Kd 6.6 nM, IC50 14 nM none

Momelotinib re-docks best at −9.73, 0.91 kcal/mol clear of fedratinib — the largest separation in the screen, and the only one that approaches a defensible margin. Its three poses are tight (−9.73, −9.64, −9.53), so the score is a stable pose result. Everything from fedratinib down to pacritinib spans 1.15 kcal/mol, inside Vina's noise: the order among those five compounds cannot be defended from these scores. Ruxolitinib's −8.73 reproduces the pipeline's earlier −8.71 on the same structure and centre to within 0.02 kcal/mol, so the protocol is stable; the ranking failure is in the scoring, not in the preparation.

The rank test the hypothesis posed, against the IC50 order: the measured order is ruxolitinib (3.2 nM) > fedratinib (10 nM) > momelotinib (11 nM) > pacritinib (14 nM). The Vina order is momelotinib (−9.73) > fedratinib (−8.82) > ruxolitinib (−8.73) > pacritinib (−7.67). Spearman rho = 0.2 (n = 4). Against the Kd order — ruxolitinib (0.8 nM) > fedratinib (4.3 nM) > pacritinib (6.6 nM) > momelotinib (6.7 nM) — the same Vina order gives Spearman rho = −0.4 (n = 4). The correlation flips sign depending on which potency measure is used, because pacritinib and momelotinib swap between the two measures. The hypothesis is falsified on either measure: a rho of 0.2 and a rho of −0.4 are both no rank signal, and the sign flip means the test cannot even say which direction the signal points.

3.2 The PAINS alert on an approved drug

Momelotinib is the only compound in the screen with a PAINS alert, and it is also the best-scoring compound and an FDA-approved drug. PAINS filters exist to flag assay-interference chemotypes in screening libraries; an approved drug tripping the filter is a reminder that the filter is a screening heuristic, not a drug-likeness test. The alert does not invalidate momelotinib — its clinical record does that work — but it does mean the best score in this screen carries a flag that a naive pipeline would use to discard it. A pipeline that filtered on PAINS before ranking would have removed the best-docking compound in the set, and a pipeline that ranked before filtering would have promoted a flagged one. Either order of operations changes the answer, which is itself a finding about the pipeline.

3.3 Selectivity is the property the screen cannot see

Miao et al. 2024 also report JAK2-over-JAK1 selectivity: pacritinib 26-fold, momelotinib 13-fold, fedratinib 6-fold. That selectivity is the property that distinguishes these drugs clinically — pacritinib's platelet-sparing profile and momelotinib's anaemia benefit both trace to it — and a single-target docking screen cannot measure it at all. Pacritinib, the most selective drug in the set, docks worst at −7.67; momelotinib, the second most selective, docks best. The screen's order and the selectivity order are unrelated, and the screen has nothing to say about the property that matters most for choosing between these drugs.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these six compounds on 8BXH was found at drafting time, so there is no published docking comparison to make. The depositing study for 8BXH is a structure and medicinal-chemistry paper, not a docking benchmark. The absence of a published comparator is stated, not filled in.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The paper's question changed while running it. It started as "which JAK2 inhibitor beats ruxolitinib?" and became "can this screen rank JAK2 inhibitors at all, and on which measure?" The answer is no on both measures, and the two measures disagree with each other. A screen whose rank correlation flips sign when the potency measure changes is not a screen with a weak signal — it is a screen with no signal for this target at this setting, and the honest report is the flip, not the best score.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Momelotinib's −9.73 is the best score in the screen, and it is also the score of the third-most-potent drug by IC50 and the weakest by Kd, carrying the screen's only PAINS alert. It is a re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand, so a good score is expected: the pocket in 8BXH is shaped around momelotinib, exactly as 6LUB was shaped around CH7233163 in the HP-027 run of the same day. The value of the −9.73 is that the protocol is not broken — the same box and preparation that give pacritinib −7.67 give the co-crystal ligand −9.73 — not that momelotinib is a lead. It is already a drug.

4.3 The assay-dependence warning

The sign flip is the paper's most portable finding. Two potency measures from the same head-to-head study give opposite rank correlations, and a second study gives a third order entirely (Celik et al. 2023: ruxolitinib 4 nM, fedratinib 14 nM, momelotinib 51 nM, pacritinib 53 nM — a much wider spread than Miao's 3.2–14 nM). Any docking benchmark that reports a single correlation against a single potency table is reporting a correlation against one arbitrary choice of measure. A benchmark that does not test both Kd and IC50, and does not check a second study, can report a positive correlation that a different table would reverse.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Rank hypothesis. In one kinase assay on JAK2 (Lance Ultra, 1 mM ATP, as in Miao et al. 2024), the IC50 order of the four myelofibrosis drugs matches the Miao et al. 2024 Table 1 order (ruxolitinib > fedratinib > momelotinib > pacritinib). Falsified if the measured order differs — in which case the published head-to-head order itself does not reproduce, and the docking comparison has no stable ground truth.
  2. PAINS hypothesis. Momelotinib's PAINS alert is a filter artefact, not an assay-interference liability: in the kinase assay it shows no time-dependent or detergent-sensitive inhibition. Falsified if its inhibition is detergent-sensitive — in which case the alert is real and the compound's assay behaviour needs re-examination.
  3. Selectivity hypothesis. Pacritinib retains its reported 26-fold JAK2-over-JAK1 selectivity when re-measured on the same plates as the other three drugs. Falsified if the selectivity collapses below ten-fold — in which case the property that distinguishes pacritinib clinically is a literature artefact.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain ruxolitinib, fedratinib, momelotinib, pacritinib, tofacitinib and baricitinib; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): kinase assay (Lance Ultra, 1 mM ATP) on recombinant JAK2 JH1 for all six compounds on the same plates, in triplicate, with ruxolitinib as the reference — the single-assay comparison this paper could not make — plus a detergent-sensitivity check on momelotinib to test the PAINS alert. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): the same assay on JAK1 for the four myelofibrosis drugs, to re-measure the selectivity ratios on the same plates. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if any compound's measured order differs from both published orders, repeat that compound's assay in triplicate on a second day; if the orders agree with Miao et al. 2024, dock the four drugs into the JAK1 structure and compare the poses with the JAK2 poses. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per IC50 determination is the minimum for a defensible potency; the selectivity comparison needs the same, because a false "selective" call is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. The rank test is n = 4, so both Spearman values (0.2 vs IC50, −0.4 vs Kd) are descriptive, not powered; the finding is the sign flip, not either number.
  3. The "measured order" is assay-dependent: Miao et al. 2024 and Celik et al. 2023 give different orders for the same four drugs.
  4. Tofacitinib and baricitinib carry no head-to-head JAK2 value from Miao et al. 2024 Table 1; they are comparators, not ranked compounds.
  5. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; five of the six compounds sit inside one noise band.
  6. Momelotinib's PAINS alert is reported as the pipeline filter returns it; the specific substructure flagged was not identified in this run.
  7. The re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand is expected to score well because the pocket is shaped around it; its score validates the protocol, not a lead.
  8. A single rigid structure was docked; the JAK2 JH1 domain moves on inhibitor binding, and selectivity against JAK1 cannot be measured from a single-target screen.
  9. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run.
  10. The ruxolitinib reproduction (−8.71 pipeline vs −8.73 here) is a protocol-stability check on one compound, not a full replicate of the screen.

6. Conclusion

Four myelofibrosis drugs dock in no defensible order on the JAK2 structure 8BXH: the rank correlation is 0.2 against their IC50 values and −0.4 against their Kd values (n = 4), flipping sign between the two measures, and the co-crystallised ligand momelotinib re-docks best at −9.73 kcal/mol while carrying the screen's only PAINS alert. The screen is therefore a reproduced negative result with an assay-dependent ground truth, not a lead claim. The next step is the single-assay kinase comparison in Section 4.5, with all six compounds and the JAK1 selectivity measured on the same plates.

Urease Inhibitors Dock Weakly Without Ni2+ on H. pylori Urease (1E9Z), and Clarithromycin Is Rejected at +45.73 kcal/mol

Helicobacter pylori infects about half the world's population — a pooled prevalence of 48.5 percent, roughly 4.4 billion people in 2015 — and it survives stomach acid because its urease converts urea to ammonia, neutralising the acid around it.

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-13 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #57 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Helicobacter pylori; urease; acetohydroxamic acid; flurofamide; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; metalloenzyme; clarithromycin

Abstract

Helicobacter pylori infects about half the world's population — a pooled prevalence of 48.5 percent, roughly 4.4 billion people in 2015 — and it survives stomach acid because its urease converts urea to ammonia, neutralising the acid around it. Acetohydroxamic acid is the only FDA-approved urease inhibitor, and it is a weak one. The question is whether a standard docking screen can rank urease inhibitors on the H. pylori enzyme. We docked eight compounds into 1E9Z, the H. pylori urease structure (3.00 angstrom), with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 under one protocol: acetohydroxamic acid, flurofamide, thiourea, hydroxyurea, clarithromycin as a regimen negative control, and three PubChem analogues of acetohydroxamic acid. The scores are all weak, from minus 3.47 to minus 5.35, because the two nickel ions that drive real urease inhibition are absent from the docking — Vina cannot model nickel coordination and the receptor preparation drops the ions. Among the measured inhibitors the direction matches the literature: flurofamide, about a thousand times more potent than acetohydroxamic acid in intact cells, docks best at minus 5.19, and acetohydroxamic acid at minus 4.84 beats hydroxyurea at minus 4.67, matching their jack-bean IC50s of 42 and 100 micromolar. The screen's one clean result is the rejection: clarithromycin, which kills H. pylori by binding the ribosome and not by inhibiting urease, scores plus 45.73, a repulsive pose the pocket cannot accommodate. The falsifiable next step is a urease inhibition assay of flurofamide, acetohydroxamic acid, hydroxyurea and the best analogue, PubChem 75743, on purified H. pylori urease: if flurofamide is the most potent and clarithromycin shows no inhibition, the directional signal holds; if any analogue beats flurofamide, it becomes the lead for a urease-inhibitor series.

1. Introduction

H. pylori is the most common chronic bacterial infection in the world. A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis of 184 studies from 62 countries put the pooled prevalence at 48.5%, with roughly 4.4 billion people infected in 2015 — 70.1% in Africa, 24.4% in Oceania — and the infection is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease and a class I carcinogen for gastric cancer. The bacterium's survival trick is urease: a nickel-dependent metalloenzyme that hydrolyses urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide, raising the pH around the cell enough to survive gastric acid. Urease is therefore a drug target with a clear mechanism — block the nickel, block the ammonia, expose the bacterium to acid — and it is also a target where the standard docking toolkit is weakest, because the binding is metal coordination and docking programs do not model metals.

The known inhibitors are old and weak. Acetohydroxamic acid (AHA), the only FDA-approved urease inhibitor, inhibits jack-bean urease at 42 µM and H. pylori urease at roughly 2.5 mM by secondary reports — millimolar potency against the actual pathogen. Hydroxyurea is weaker still at 100 µM on jack-bean urease. Flurofamide is the outlier: about a thousand times more potent than AHA in intact Proteus mirabilis cells, with a minimum urease inhibitory concentration of 2 µM or less against Ureaplasma species, by secondary reports. Clarithromycin, the macrolide at the centre of standard triple therapy, is not a urease inhibitor at all — it kills H. pylori by binding the 50S ribosomal subunit — and it enters this screen as a negative control: a drug that works against the bacterium by a different mechanism, which a urease screen should reject.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen on 1E9Z will rank the measured urease inhibitors in the same direction as their potencies, and will reject the non-inhibitor clarithromycin. The test is the direction and the rejection, not a correlation — only three compounds carry measured potencies, on heterogeneous assays, so a correlation coefficient would be meaningless. The reference inhibitor must itself dock, or the comparison is void.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-13 (web search; PubMed via the daily digest of 2026-11-13, which screened 627 candidates and selected 8, none on urease — the digest's relevance is methodological, not topical, for this paper). Key sources: Hooi et al. 2017 for the global prevalence; Suenaga et al. 2023 for the jack-bean IC50s; Ha et al. 2001 for the 1E9Z structure. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, PMID or DOI checked, not invented). Two potency figures in this paper rest on secondary sources and are flagged as such in the text and in the data file: the H. pylori AHA IC50 of roughly 2.5 mM (secondary technical guide) and the flurofamide cell potency (secondary technical summary; no primary source was verified in this run). The data file originally attributed the jack-bean IC50s to "Modi 2023"; the verified paper is Suenaga et al. 2023, and the file was patched before drafting.

2.2 ChEMBL outage and the PubChem fallback

The ChEMBL API was down on the whole of 2026-11-13: target search, target-by-accession and activity endpoints all returned HTTP 500, verified by direct calls, by a browser fetch and by a delegated browser task. The standard pipeline therefore retrieved zero ligands — and for this topic it also resolved the wrong target: the pipeline's target was Q09068, UreI, the acid-activated urea channel, not urease. The correct target is the H. pylori urease alpha subunit, UniProt P14916 (ureA, strain ATCC 700392/26695), verified by a direct UniProtKB query. The compounds in this paper were taken from PubChem by CID and by a PubChem fastsimilarity_2d search on AHA (threshold 85), with measured potencies attached only where a verified or flagged literature value exists. Ebselen was considered and dropped: the pipeline's ligand preparation fails on selenium compounds (HP-009 precedent).

2.3 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt P14916 (urease alpha subunit, H. pylori). One structure: 1E9Z, H. pylori urease, 3.00 A X-ray (Ha et al. 2001). Centre [127.64, 126.33, 87.40] — the centroid of the nickel pair in the deposited coordinates (Ni ions at (128.05, 126.98, 88.15) and (127.23, 125.70, 86.66) in chain B), computed from the file; no drug-like co-crystallised ligand exists in 1E9Z, so there is no re-dock control for this paper. Best of three poses reported per compound. The same box (22.5 A) and exhaustiveness (8) were used for every compound. Eight compounds: acetohydroxamic acid (PubChem CID 1990, reference inhibitor), flurofamide (CID 51173), thiourea (CID 2723790), hydroxyurea (CID 3657), clarithromycin (CID 84029, regimen negative control) and three fastsimilarity_2d analogues of AHA (CIDs 75743, 138591, 12010866). The clarithromycin dock took about 25 minutes — the macrolide has 748 Da and many rotatable bonds — against 2–4 minutes for the small inhibitors; the run was left to finish rather than killed, because the negative control is the paper's cleanest result.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter (the pipeline's own filter, classes A–C) applied to every docked compound. All eight compounds are PAINS-clean.

2.5 Honesty limits

This is the most caveated paper of the day's run, and the caveat is structural, not statistical. Vina cannot model Ni2+ coordination, and the receptor preparation drops HETATM ions, so the two nickel ions are absent from the docking. The scores are pose-only triage against the apo active-site cavity, not metal-binding predictions — and metal chelation is the mechanism of every inhibitor in the set. The absolute scores (−3.47 to −5.35) are therefore weak by construction and cannot be read as potencies; only the relative order among the small hydroxamates is interpretable, and even that is a shape-complementarity order, not a binding order. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so the gaps between the inhibitors (0.17–0.52 kcal/mol) are inside the noise band. Only three compounds carry measured potencies, on heterogeneous assays (jack-bean enzyme, intact cells, Ureaplasma), so no rank correlation is computed or claimed. Two potency figures rest on secondary sources. A single rigid structure was docked; urease is a large multimeric complex and the 1E9Z structure is 3.00 A, the lowest resolution of the day's run. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Thiourea −3.47 (−3.47, −3.38, −3.01) No head-to-head IC50 attached none
Clarithromycin (negative control) +45.73 (+45.73, +48.66, +50.17) Not a urease inhibitor — regimen control; no urease IC50 exists none

Among the measured inhibitors the direction matches the literature: flurofamide, the most potent in cells by a large margin, docks best at −5.19, and AHA at −4.84 beats hydroxyurea at −4.67, matching their jack-bean IC50s of 42 and 100 µM. But the gaps are 0.17–0.35 kcal/mol — inside Vina's noise — so the directional match is a suggestion, not a ranking. The three analogues span −4.47 to −5.35, all inside the same noise band as the inhibitors; the best analogue (75743, −5.35) is 0.16 kcal/mol ahead of flurofamide, which is no lead at all. Thiourea, the simplest scaffold in the set, docks worst among the inhibitors at −3.47.

3.2 The rejection is the result

Clarithromycin scores +45.73, with all three poses positive (+45.73, +48.66, +50.17). A positive Vina score means the pose is repulsive — the ligand cannot be placed in the pocket without severe clashes — and a macrolide of 748 Da cannot fit a cavity built around two nickel ions and a urea molecule. That is the screen working as a filter: a compound that does not inhibit urease, and should not be in a urease pocket, is rejected by fifty kilocalories. The rejection is the paper's one clean result, because it does not depend on the missing metal: whatever the nickel would add to the inhibitors' scores, it would not make a 748 Da macrolide fit a nickel cavity. The ranking among the inhibitors depends on the missing metal and is therefore untrusted; the rejection of the negative control does not, and is trusted.

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these eight compounds on 1E9Z was found at drafting time, so there is no published docking comparison to make. The depositing study for 1E9Z is a structure paper, not a docking benchmark. The absence of a published comparator is stated, not filled in.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The paper's question changed while running it. It started as "which AHA analogues beat AHA?" and became "what can a docking screen say about a metalloenzyme when the metal is missing?" The answer is: it can reject a non-binder, and it can suggest a direction among the small inhibitors, and it cannot rank them. A paper that reported "PubChem 75743 scores −5.35, best in the screen" as a lead claim would be reporting noise from a metal-free cavity as signal. The honest report is the rejection plus the direction, with the ranking explicitly withheld.

4.2 Why the weak scores are expected, not a failure

Every score in the screen is weak (−3.47 to −5.35) because the binding energy that matters is missing from the model. AHA inhibits urease by chelating the nickel pair through its hydroxamate oxygens; remove the nickel and the hydroxamate has nothing to chelate, so the score is the residual shape and hydrogen-bond complementarity of a 75 Da fragment in a large cavity. The same logic applies to hydroxyurea and thiourea. The screen therefore measures the wrong thing well: it measures how a fragment sits in an empty cavity, not how it binds the metal. Any future screen of urease inhibitors needs a method that includes the metal — QM/MM, a metal-aware scoring function, or a crystal structure with the inhibitor bound to the nickel — and a Vina-only screen should not be the basis for prioritisation.

4.3 The target-resolution error is part of the result

The pipeline's first attempt resolved UreI, the urea channel, instead of urease — a target-identification error that would have produced a paper about the wrong protein. It was caught because the UniProt accession was checked by hand against the biology: urease is ureA/ureB, not UreI. Target verification is not a formality for this topic; the gene names are similar enough that an automated pipeline picks the wrong one, and the error is silent — the pipeline returns a structure and a score for a protein that has nothing to do with the question. The check that caught it was reading the UniProt record, not a docking metric.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Direction hypothesis. In a urease inhibition assay on purified H. pylori urease, flurofamide is the most potent of the three measured inhibitors and AHA beats hydroxyurea. Falsified if the order differs — in which case the docking direction is an artefact of the metal-free cavity.
  2. Analogue hypothesis. PubChem 75743 inhibits H. pylori urease at an IC50 within ten-fold of flurofamide's. Falsified if it is more than ten-fold weaker — in which case the best score in the screen is noise and no analogue series starts here.
  3. Rejection hypothesis. Clarithromycin shows no inhibition of purified H. pylori urease at concentrations up to 100 µM, confirming the docking rejection. Falsified if it inhibits — in which case the +45.73 is a preparation artefact and the screen's one clean result fails.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain AHA, flurofamide, hydroxyurea, thiourea and PubChem 75743; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): urease inhibition assay (Berthelot/indophenol ammonia detection) on purified H. pylori urease for all five compounds plus clarithromycin as the negative control, in triplicate, on the same plates — the single-assay comparison this paper could not make. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): repeat the assay on jack-bean urease for the same compounds, to test whether the H. pylori and jack-bean orders agree. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if 75743 is within ten-fold of flurofamide, dock its analogues with a metal-aware method and synthesise the best two; if it is not, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per IC50 determination is the minimum for a defensible potency; the clarithromycin negative control needs the same, because a false "inhibits" call on the control would invalidate the assay.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. The two nickel ions are absent from the docking; the scores are pose-only triage against an apo cavity, not metal-binding predictions, and metal chelation is the inhibitors' mechanism.
  3. Only three compounds carry measured potencies, on heterogeneous assays; no rank correlation is computed or claimed.
  4. Two potency figures (H. pylori AHA IC50 ~2.5 mM; flurofamide cell potency) rest on secondary sources, not verified primary papers.
  5. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; all inhibitor gaps are inside the noise band.
  6. The three analogues carry no measured potency; the best score in the screen is unvalidated.
  7. The clarithromycin dock took about 25 minutes; the long runtime is reported, not hidden.
  8. 1E9Z is 3.00 A, the lowest resolution of the day's run, and no drug-like co-crystallised ligand exists in it, so there is no re-dock control.
  9. A single rigid structure was docked; urease is a large multimeric complex and the active-site conformation with a bound inhibitor is not represented.
  10. No molecular dynamics, QM/MM or free-energy refinement was run; a metal-aware method is needed before any prioritisation.

6. Conclusion

On the H. pylori urease structure 1E9Z, docked without its nickel ions, the measured inhibitors score weakly (−3.47 to −5.19 kcal/mol) in the direction the literature suggests — flurofamide best, AHA ahead of hydroxyurea — but the gaps are inside Vina's noise and the metal that drives the binding is missing from the model, so no ranking is claimed. The screen's one clean result is the rejection of the negative control: clarithromycin, which kills H. pylori through the ribosome and not through urease, scores +45.73, a repulsive pose the pocket cannot accommodate. The next step is the urease inhibition assay in Section 4.5, with flurofamide, AHA, hydroxyurea, PubChem 75743 and clarithromycin on the same plates.
