AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-12 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #47 (daily paper run)

Keywords: KRAS G12C; sotorasib; adagrasib; divarasib; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; covalent inhibitor; switch-II pocket; drug resistance; Y96D

Abstract

KRAS G12C was the first "undruggable" oncogene to fall: the covalent switch-II pocket inhibitors sotorasib and adagrasib are FDA-approved, and divarasib is in Phase I, yet acquired resistance — most often the Y96D switch-II pocket mutation — limits their benefit, and the field still ranks new candidates with non-covalent docking scores. We asked whether standardised AutoDock Vina docking on the verified KRAS G12C structure 6OIM (1.65 Å, KRAS G12C covalently bound to sotorasib) can rank five covalent inhibitors by measured potency. The LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P01116, ChEMBL, PubChem, RDKit ADMET and PAINS screen, Vina 1.2.7) failed twice at target resolution — once returning zero bioactivities, once resolving KRAS to the wrong target, maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074) — so the lead set was rebuilt by direct verified queries against the correct ChEMBL target CHEMBL2189121 (4,666 activities at pChEMBL ≥ 5) plus PubChem verification of the three clinical drugs. On 6OIM, with the grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised sotorasib, Vina scored sotorasib −8.14, divarasib −8.06, adagrasib −7.58, CHEMBL4855521 −6.03 and CHEMBL4856277 −5.51 kcal/mol. The two ChEMBL leads carry the strongest measured potencies in the set — IC50 0.51 and 0.56 nM on the exact crystallised construct (KRAS G12C/C51S/C80L/C118S) — yet score worst, 2.11–2.63 kcal/mol behind sotorasib, a margin above Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. As a control, sotorasib scored −7.22 on wild-type KRAS-GDP (9IAY), which has no cysteine-12 to bind: Vina cannot see the covalent selectivity that makes the drug work. The falsifiable next step is a covalent-aware re-scoring of the same five compounds plus a same-plate biochemical assay on the 6OIM construct: if covalent docking does not restore the measured order, non-covalent scoring should be retired as a ranking tool for this target class.

1. Introduction

KRAS is the most frequently mutated oncogene in human cancer, and its glycine-12-to-cysteine mutant (G12C) occurs in approximately 12–15% of non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC) and about 3% of colorectal cancers. For three decades KRAS was considered undruggable: the protein has no deep pocket in its active, GTP-bound state, and its affinity for GTP is picomolar. The breakthrough was the discovery of an inducible pocket in and around switch-II that exists only in the inactive, GDP-bound state, adjacent to the mutant cysteine-12. Covalent inhibitors that reach into that pocket and bond to Cys12 lock KRAS G12C in its inactive form. Two such drugs are now FDA-approved — sotorasib (Lumakras, accelerated approval 28 May 2021; CodeBreaK 100: objective response rate 37.1%, median overall survival 12.5 months in previously treated NSCLC) and adagrasib (Krazati, accelerated approval 12 December 2022; KRYSTAL-1: objective response rate 43%, median duration of response 8.5 months) — and a third, divarasib (GDC-6036), showed single-agent activity in its Phase I trial.

The benefit is real and time-limited. Acquired resistance is near-universal, and the on-target fraction clusters in the switch-II pocket itself: secondary mutations at R68, H95, Y96 and Q99. The Y96D substitution is the most frequently observed switch-II pocket mutation in post-progression cohorts (14% of patients in a 143-patient cohort carried a switch-II pocket mutation, Y96D the commonest), and in vitro Y96D/S confers resistance to both approved drugs, while G13D and R68M remain sensitive to adagrasib but not sotorasib, and Q99L is resistant to adagrasib but sensitive to sotorasib. The next generation of inhibitors must therefore be selected against this resistance landscape — and selection is exactly where the field's cheapest tool, docking, is least trustworthy. A 2026 benchmark (Pyrite, arXiv:2611.14511) showed that even expert chemists rank docking poses near chance, and a 2026 sequence-to-hits pipeline (ANTIOCH-VS, arXiv:2611.14287) shows how easily a screening campaign can now be launched from sequence alone — which makes the ranking step, not the generation step, the bottleneck. This paper tests that ranking step on the target where it matters most.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised non-covalent Vina protocol on the verified KRAS G12C structure 6OIM, docking scores rank covalent KRAS G12C inhibitors in the same order as their measured potencies. The test is the within-protocol ranking of five inhibitors whose measured potencies span 0.51 nM to 11 nM, including two leads measured on the exact crystallised construct.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-12 (web search; PubMed; RCSB; ChEMBL and PubChem APIs). The daily literature digest of 2026-11-12 screened 840 candidates and contributed the two methods papers framing this study (ANTIOCH-VS and Pyrite, above). Key sources: Lanman et al. 2020 for sotorasib (J Med Chem 63:52–65); Canon et al. 2019 for the 6OIM structure (Nature 575:217–223); Skoulidis et al. 2021 for CodeBreaK 100 (N Engl J Med 384:2371–2381); Hallin et al. 2020 for adagrasib (Cancer Discov 10:54–71); Sacher et al. 2023 for divarasib (N Engl J Med 389:710–721); a 2025 molecular-dynamics and biochemical study for divarasib's nucleotide-exchange potency and its Y96D sensitivity (Sci Rep 15:24843); Tanaka et al. 2021, Koga et al. 2021 and Awad et al. 2021 for acquired resistance; Whitley et al. 2026 (Nat Commun) for the structural mechanisms of switch-II pocket resistance; and Broker et al. 2025 for the 9IAY wild-type control structure (J Med Chem 68:15649–15668). Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 The pipeline run — and its two disclosed failures

The LeadForge pipeline was run twice on 2026-11-12 (UniProtKB P01116, human GTPase KRas, 189 residues; query compound sotorasib, verified in PubChem as CID 137278711, C30H30F2N6O3). Both runs failed at the same step, in two different ways, and both failures are disclosed because they determine what this paper can and cannot claim.

Failure 1 (first run): target resolution by UniProt accession returned the correct ChEMBL target (CHEMBL2189121) but the bioactivity query returned zero ligands. A direct re-query of the same endpoint minutes later returned HTTP 200 with 4,666 activities — the failure was transient ChEMBL unreliability, not absence.

Failure 2 (second run): the by-accession endpoint returned HTTP 500, so the pipeline fell back to ChEMBL text search for "KRAS", which returned maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074) as its first hit — the same wrong target that corrupted the 2026-11-11 dengue paper's automatic run. The pipeline then retrieved 55 maltase-glucoamylase inhibitors (iminosugars; Tanimoto similarity to sotorasib ≈ 0.1) and docked five of them on the automatically picked structure. Those scores (best −9.12 kcal/mol) are meaningless for KRAS and are discarded; they do not appear in the results. The lesson, repeated from the 2026-11-11 centre audit: an automatic target or structure pick must be verified before any score is trusted.

2.3 The corrected benchmark

The lead set was rebuilt by direct, verified queries. ChEMBL target CHEMBL2189121 was queried for activities with pChEMBL ≥ 5 (HTTP 200; 4,666 activities). Most top hits are G12D/G12V assays, which are the wrong allele for this structure, so the set was restricted to the G12C-construct assays: the three most potent leads measured on KRAS G12C/C51S/C80L/C118S — the exact engineered construct of the 6OIM crystal structure (C51S/C80L/C118S are the structure's engineered mutations). Two could be resolved to structures: CHEMBL4855521 (IC50 0.51 nM, pChEMBL 9.29; a deuterated quinazolinone acrylamide) and CHEMBL4856277 (IC50 0.56 nM, pChEMBL 9.25). The third, CHEMBL4852458 (IC50 0.51 nM, same assay), could not be resolved: the ChEMBL molecule endpoint returned HTTP 500 on three attempts, so no SMILES is available for it. It is reported as missing, not invented. The three clinical drugs were verified in PubChem by name and CID — sotorasib CID 137278711, adagrasib CID 138611145 (C32H35ClFN7O2, MW 604.1), divarasib CID 146624881 (C29H32ClF4N7O2, MW 622.1) — and their isomeric SMILES were used for docking.

Docking used the verified structure 6OIM (KRAS G12C covalently bound to sotorasib/AMG 510, 1.65 Å; Canon et al. 2019), not the pipeline's automatic pick. The automatic pick was 9IAY (0.95 Å, "structure of 10 in complex with GDP-KRAS", Broker et al. 2025): its SEQADV records show no G12C mutation — it is wild-type KRAS-GDP in complex with a non-covalent pan-KRAS inhibitor (ligand WYU). Docking a G12C-selective covalent inhibitor into a wild-type structure is not a G12C benchmark, so 9IAY was demoted to a control: sotorasib was docked there once (score −7.22 kcal/mol, from the pipeline run) to test whether Vina can detect the drug's covalent selectivity.

On 6OIM, the grid centre was set exactly on the co-crystallised sotorasib (residue MOV, chain A, 41 atoms): centroid [1.87, −8.26, −1.36], computed with the pipeline's audited dock._ligand_center, which excludes the GDP cofactor (centroid [−6.13, 3.59, 7.31]) and waters. The audited centre was recomputed inside the docking script and matched the used centre to 0.0024 Å. Protocol, identical for all five compounds: AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported.

2.4 ADMET and PAINS screen

RDKit descriptors (molecular weight, logP, hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors, TPSA, rotatable bonds, Lipinski violations) and the PAINS filter were computed for all five compounds with the pipeline's chemistry module — the same code that scored the query compound in the pipeline run.

2.5 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity, and for this target the gap is structural, not statistical: Vina is a non-covalent scorer, and all five compounds are covalent inhibitors whose potency depends on bond formation with Cys12, a term Vina cannot compute. A Vina score here measures only non-covalent shape complementarity to the switch-II pocket. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds. One rigid structure (GDP-bound, inactive) cannot represent the GTP-bound state, the switch-II ensemble, or the resistance mutants. The measured potencies in Table 1 come from different assay types (binding Ki, nucleotide exchange, cellular signalling, ChEMBL IC50), so cross-assay ranking is indicative, not exact — except for the two ChEMBL leads, which share one assay on the exact crystallised construct. No molecular dynamics, covalent docking, or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated.

3. Results

All five compounds are PAINS-clean. All five breach Lipinski's molecular-weight or logP limits at least once — expected for switch-II pocket binders, which need size and lipophilicity to fill the pocket — so the ADMET panel does not separate them; the docking rank is the whole story.

3.2 The ranking is inverted for the most potent binders

The hypothesis fails. The two strongest measured binders in the set — CHEMBL4855521 and CHEMBL4856277, both sub-nanomolar on the exact crystallised construct — score worst by Vina (−6.03 and −5.51 kcal/mol), 2.11 and 2.63 kcal/mol behind sotorasib. That margin exceeds Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the inversion cannot be dismissed as scoring noise. Both ChEMBL leads are larger (MW 641–653 vs 561 for sotorasib) and more lipophilic (logP 5.28–5.94), with only three rotatable bonds each: their potency likely comes from a precise, rigid fit plus the covalent bond — exactly the contributions a rigid-receptor, non-covalent scorer undervalues. Within the three clinical drugs, Vina cannot separate anything: sotorasib and divarasib differ by 0.08 kcal/mol (noise), and adagrasib trails sotorasib by 0.56 kcal/mol (also noise), although divarasib's measured nucleotide-exchange potency (2.4 nM) is roughly five-fold better than sotorasib's binding Ki (11 nM) and its cellular potency is an order of magnitude better. The sotorasib re-dock (−8.14) confirms the protocol reproduces the crystal pose's pocket well; the protocol is sound — the scoring function is the problem.

3.3 The wild-type control: Vina cannot see covalent selectivity

Sotorasib scored −7.22 kcal/mol on wild-type KRAS-GDP (9IAY), which has no cysteine-12 for it to bond to — only 0.92 kcal/mol worse than its score on the G12C structure it was designed for, inside Vina's noise. A scorer that cannot distinguish the drug's true target from a protein it cannot covalently bind cannot rank candidates for this target class. The same blind spot explains Section 3.2: Vina rewards non-covalent complementarity and is silent on the covalent step that dominates measured potency.

4. Discussion

4.1 What this means for LeadForge and for the field

Every LeadForge paper to date has used the same Vina protocol as a ranking tool, and for non-covalent targets (FLT3, PPARγ, AmpC, the dengue protease) its failures were matters of noise or wrong structures — correctable by auditing. KRAS G12C is the first target in this series where the failure is in the physics: the scoring function lacks the term that matters most. Two practical consequences follow. First, any LeadForge run on a covalent target must pair Vina with a covalent-aware scorer (covalent docking, or a two-term score: non-covalent complementarity plus a warhead-reactivity term) before any ranking is reported; a Vina-only ranking for a covalent series is not a result, it is a shape contest. Second, the ChEMBL lane needs the same audit discipline as the structure lane: the pipeline's automatic target resolution failed twice in one day (a transient zero, then a wrong-target fallback to maltase-glucoamylase), and the wrong-target run produced confident-looking scores for the wrong enzyme. The fix applied here — direct verification of the ChEMBL target ID against the UniProt accession, and an allele check on the assays — should be a pipeline gate, not a manual rescue.

4.2 The literature context: ranking is the bottleneck, not generation

Today's digest makes the point from both sides. ANTIOCH-VS (Hasdemir et al. 2026) shows a complete screening campaign can now start from a protein sequence alone — generation is solved and cheap. Pyrite (Srivastava et al. 2026) shows the other side: on a 1,500-pair benchmark, even expert chemists rank docking poses near chance, and only purpose-built agents beat that bar. This paper is the same finding from inside a real campaign: the poses are easy to generate and the scores are easy to compute, and the ranking they produce is wrong for the compounds that matter most. The field's next gain is not more poses; it is scoring that knows what kind of chemistry it is scoring.

4.3 Resistance sets the bar for the next lead

The two ChEMBL leads are potent against the wild-type-pocket construct, but potency against today's pocket is not the selection criterion — survival against tomorrow's pocket is. Divarasib's nucleotide-exchange IC50 rises from 2.4 nM on G12C to 229 nM on G12C/Y96D, a ~100-fold loss from a single switch-II mutation, and Y96D is the commonest clinical resistance substitution. Whitley et al. (2026) classify the resistance mechanisms as Type I (loss of inhibitor contacts) and Type II (stabilisation of pocket-occluding switch-II conformations), with Y96D exhibiting both. A next-generation lead therefore needs either a Y96-independent contact network or a mechanism outside the switch-II pocket (the RAS(ON) tricomplex inhibitors are the live example). Neither ChEMBL lead has published resistance data; that is the first experiment to run on them, before any potency claim is repeated.

4.4 The falsifiable test

Two experiments decide whether this paper's conclusion holds. (1) Covalent-aware re-scoring: re-score the same five compounds with a covalent docking protocol (covalent bond to Cys12 modelled explicitly) on the same 6OIM structure. Prediction: the covalent-aware order restores the measured order — CHEMBL4855521 and CHEMBL4856277 at or near the top, ahead of sotorasib — while the non-covalent order reported here does not reproduce. If covalent scoring also fails to restore the order, the problem is the pocket model itself, not the covalent term. (2) Same-plate biochemical assay: measure all five compounds in one nucleotide-exchange assay on the 6OIM construct (KRAS G12C/C51S/C80L/C118S), plus the G12C/Y96D double mutant. Prediction: the two ChEMBL leads remain sub-nanomolar on G12C and lose potency on Y96D by at least an order of magnitude; sotorasib's Ki of 11 nM reproduces within two-fold. If the ChEMBL leads do not reproduce as sub-nanomolar on a shared plate, their ChEMBL numbers are assay artefacts and this paper's inversion claim falls with them.

5. Limitations

(1) Five compounds, one structure, one rigid-receptor protocol — a benchmark, not a screen. (2) Measured potencies mix assay types (Ki, nucleotide exchange, cellular signalling, ChEMBL IC50); only the two ChEMBL leads share an assay, so the cross-assay ranking is indicative. (3) The ChEMBL leads are unnamed, uncharacterised compounds from a single assay series; their structures were verified in ChEMBL but their provenance (patent vs paper) was not traced, and one sibling lead (CHEMBL4852458) could not be resolved at all because the ChEMBL molecule endpoint returned HTTP 500 three times. (4) No re-dock RMSD was computed for sotorasib against its crystal pose, so the −8.14 re-dock score is a pocket-fit check, not a pose-accuracy claim. (5) No molecular dynamics, no covalent docking, no free-energy calculation, no experiment. (6) ChEMBL was intermittently unavailable during this run (HTTP 500 on two endpoints); a re-query on another day could return additional G12C-construct leads.

6. Conclusion

On the verified KRAS G12C structure 6OIM, standardised non-covalent Vina docking ranks the two most potent measured binders last: CHEMBL4855521 and CHEMBL4856277 (ChEMBL IC50 0.51 and 0.56 nM on the crystallised construct) score −6.03 and −5.51 kcal/mol, 2.11–2.63 kcal/mol behind sotorasib (−8.14), whose measured Ki is 11 nM. Sotorasib scores nearly as well on wild-type KRAS (−7.22), which it cannot covalently bind. The hypothesis is rejected: for covalent KRAS G12C inhibitors, non-covalent Vina scores do not rank compounds by measured potency, and they should not be used as a ranking tool for this target class without a covalent-aware term. The two ChEMBL leads are genuine sub-nanomolar leads on the construct — and the next experiment is not more docking, it is a covalent re-score and a same-plate assay including the Y96D resistance mutant.

The Weakest Measured Binder Docks Best on CDK6: A Centre-Audited Benchmark of Four ChEMBL Leads Against Palbociclib on 6OQO

Breast cancer was diagnosed in 2.43 million women and killed 693,660 in 2024, and palbociclib — a CDK4/6 inhibitor that extended median progression-free survival in the PALOMA-2 trial — is limited by neutropenia and by resistance, so a better CDK6 binder would matter.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-12 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #48 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: cyclin-dependent kinase 6; palbociclib; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; breast cancer; CDK4/6 inhibitor; ChEMBL; structure-based screening

Abstract

Breast cancer was diagnosed in 2.43 million women and killed 693,660 in 2024, and palbociclib — a CDK4/6 inhibitor that extended median progression-free survival in the PALOMA-2 trial — is limited by neutropenia and by resistance, so a better CDK6 binder would matter. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can rank CDK6 ligands at all when the reference drug itself is the benchmark. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB Q00534 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL2508, 25 bioactivities → PubChem → RDKit ADMET/PAINS → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) and docked four ChEMBL CDK6 actives plus palbociclib into the 1.98 Å CDK6 structure 6OQO, with the grid centre audited to 0.005 Å from the co-crystallised inhibitor CPD24. One lead out-scored palbociclib — CHEMBL3237704 −11.18 versus palbociclib −10.19 kcal/mol — but the margin (0.99 kcal/mol) sits inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the ranking does not track measured potency: the most potent measured binder (CHEMBL5280928, Ki 0.2 nM) ranks third by Vina while the weakest (CHEMBL3237704, IC50 1.1 nM) ranks first, Spearman ρ = −0.32 (n = 4, p = 0.68). Palbociclib itself docked reproducibly across four independent runs (−10.20 to −10.09 kcal/mol, range 0.11). The falsifiable next step is a CDK6 kinase inhibition assay of the four leads against palbociclib with a CDK4 counter-screen: if the measured order matches the ChEMBL record rather than the Vina order, docking alone must not be used to prioritise CDK6 leads on this structure.

1. Introduction

Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women worldwide: GLOBOCAN 2024 recorded 2,434,087 new cases and 693,660 deaths in 2024. In Pakistan, 30,700 new cases were recorded in 2022, and more recent estimates put the annual figure near 44,000. Hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative (HR+/HER2−) disease is the largest subtype, and CDK4/6 inhibitors transformed its treatment: in the PALOMA-2 trial (N = 666), palbociclib plus letrozole extended median progression-free survival versus letrozole alone (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.46–0.72), but neutropenia affected 80% of patients (grade ≥3 in 66%, febrile neutropenia 1.8%), and resistance eventually emerges. A CDK6 binder that beats palbociclib — or matches it with a cleaner profile — would be clinically valuable, and a standardised docking screen is the cheapest way to look for one. The falsifiable hypothesis of this paper is: a standardised Vina screen on the CDK6 structure 6OQO ranks ChEMBL CDK6 actives in the same order as their measured potencies, with palbociclib as the reference.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

The burden figures are from GLOBOCAN 2024 (WHO) and the Pakistan figures from Dawn (2022, 30,700 cases) and Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital citing WHO (October 2026, ~44,000 cases/year). The PALOMA-2 efficacy and toxicity figures are from Finn et al., New England Journal of Medicine 2016;375(20):1925–1936. Today's literature digest (research-team digest 2026-11-12, 840 candidates screened, 8 selected) contained no paper topical to this benchmark and is cited only as a methodological source. All database identifiers were verified live on 2026-11-12.

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, exactly as Papers #1 and #3: UniProtKB Q00534 (CDK6, 326 aa, Homo sapiens) → ChEMBL target CHEMBL2508 ("Cyclin-dependent kinase 6", SINGLE PROTEIN) → 25 bioactivities (top 25 by pChEMBL of 1,038) → PubChem verification of palbociclib (CID 5330286) → RDKit similarity/ADMET/PAINS → Vina docking of the top 5 leads (the reference query plus four ChEMBL leads) into PDB 6OQO (CDK6 kinase domain, chain A, 1.98 Å, co-crystallised inhibitor CPD24, PDB component N1J, 34 atoms). Grid centre [22.80, 37.61, −9.50] was audited against the N1J centroid computed independently from the PDB file (agreement 0.005 Å; waters excluded by the pipeline's ligand-centre routine). Box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported for every molecule, same protocol for reference and leads.

Correction history (disclosed, not hidden). The first docking run for this topic was invalid and is discarded: the pipeline's UniProt text search for "Cyclin-dependent kinase 6" returned P24941, which is CDK2, not CDK6 (verified live against rest.uniprot.org: P24941 = cyclin-dependent kinase 2; Q00534 = cyclin-dependent kinase 6). That run resolved ChEMBL CHEMBL301 (CDK2) and docked on 6Q4G, a CDK2 structure; its numbers are kept in dock-HP-034-2026-11-12.json for audit and are not used anywhere in this paper. The corrected run targets UniProt accession Q00534 directly and monkey-patches the ChEMBL target to CHEMBL2508, verified live on the ChEMBL website (target report card, 2026-11-12), because the ChEMBL target-by-accession API endpoint returned HTTP 500 pages and timeouts throughout 2026-11-12. The bioactivities are the verbatim ChEMBL API response for CHEMBL2508 saved to hidden_files/chembl-activities-CHEMBL2508-2026-11-12.json (top 25 by pChEMBL of 1,038; same endpoint and query the pipeline uses), because the live activity endpoint timed out on limit=50 queries and intermittently returned HTML error pages on limit=10 queries all day; only the record transport differs, not the data. Of the 25 records, 21 distinct molecules remained after SMILES deduplication, giving 22 leads including the palbociclib query.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every docked molecule. All five docked molecules are PAINS-clean. The sixth-ranked lead, CHEMBL3698657 (IC50 0.41 nM), was not docked (only the top 5 are docked) and carries a PAINS alert; it is reported here so the alert is not hidden, and it would need redox controls in any assay.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity: Vina scores carry ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, a single rigid structure (6OQO) cannot capture induced fit, and no experimental data, molecular dynamics, or free-energy refinement were run. A docking "win" smaller than ~1 kcal/mol is not a superiority claim. No clinical recommendation follows from this paper.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured potency (ChEMBL) Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL3237704 IC50 1.1 nM (pChEMBL 8.96) −11.18 −11.18, −9.94, −9.51 clean
CHEMBL5751717 IC50 0.2 nM (pChEMBL 9.70) −10.24 −10.24, −10.17, −10.16 clean
Palbociclib (query) reference drug −10.19 −10.19, −10.07, −9.83 clean
CHEMBL5280928 Ki 0.2 nM (pChEMBL 9.70) −9.98 −9.98, −9.60, −9.46 clean
CHEMBL5892046 IC50 0.6 nM (pChEMBL 9.22) −9.78 −9.78, −9.61, −9.11 clean

All five molecules docked successfully on 6OQO. One lead out-scores palbociclib: CHEMBL3237704 at −11.18 kcal/mol, 0.99 kcal/mol better than palbociclib's −10.19. That margin sits inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and is not a superiority claim. The remaining three leads dock worse than palbociclib by 0.05–0.41 kcal/mol — also inside noise, so no lead can be called worse than palbociclib either.

Palbociclib's own docking is highly reproducible: four independent CDK6 runs on 6OQO returned −10.20, −10.13, −10.09 and −10.19 kcal/mol (range 0.11, mean −10.15). The reference is stable; the screen's noise is in the ranking, not the reference.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these four ChEMBL leads on 6OQO was found in the literature sweep, so there is no published docking comparison to make. The palbociclib value (−10.19 kcal/mol) is a new reference point for this structure under this protocol.

3.3 The ranking does not track measured potency

The docking order is mildly inverted against measured potency. The most potent measured binders — CHEMBL5280928 (Ki 0.2 nM) and CHEMBL5751717 (IC50 0.2 nM), both pChEMBL 9.70 — rank third and second by Vina, while the weakest measured lead, CHEMBL3237704 (IC50 1.1 nM, pChEMBL 8.96), ranks first. Spearman ρ = −0.32 (n = 4, p = 0.68): no significant rank agreement. In plain terms, on this structure, Vina cannot tell a 0.2 nM CDK6 binder from a 1.1 nM one — the potency spread among the four leads is only 5.5-fold, far narrower than Vina's resolving power.

ADMET is unremarkable across the docked set: molecular weights 447–553, logP 2.25–4.67, zero Lipinski violations except CHEMBL5892046 (1 violation, MW 552.63). ToxGuard Tox21 read-across flags (NR-Aromatase, SR-ARE, SR-ATAD5 and others) appear on every molecule including palbociclib itself; these are similarity-screen flags, not toxicity findings, and are reported as such.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question this paper set out to answer — can a standardised screen find a better CDK6 binder than palbociclib? — has a two-part answer. Technically yes, one lead out-scores the reference; scientifically no, because the margin is inside noise and the ranking contradicts the measured potencies. The honest reframe is that a single-structure Vina screen on 6OQO is a triage tool for CDK6, not a ranking tool: it can confirm that a molecule fits the ATP pocket (all five did, with consistent poses), but it cannot order sub-nanomolar binders by potency.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, 0.99 kcal/mol is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — a re-dock could erase it. Second, CHEMBL3237704's pose spread (−11.18, −9.94, −9.51) is the widest in the set, so its best pose is less consistent than CHEMBL5751717's (−10.24, −10.17, −10.16). Third, CHEMBL3237704 is the weakest measured binder of the four: if Vina were ranking by true affinity, the 0.2 nM compounds should lead. The screen's top hit is its least potent measured lead.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No docked molecule carries a PAINS alert, so no redox-control redesign is needed for these four. The undocked sixth lead (CHEMBL3698657, IC50 0.41 nM) does carry a PAINS alert; if it is ever assayed, it needs detergent and redox controls (e.g. DTT/catalase) to expose aggregation or redox-cycling artefacts.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL3237704 is not a better CDK6 inhibitor than palbociclib. A CDK6 kinase inhibition assay (ADP-Glo or equivalent) will measure its IC50 within 2-fold of palbociclib's, not better — refuting the docking "win".
  2. The Vina order is noise. A CDK6 assay of all four leads will reproduce the ChEMBL potency order (0.2 nM compounds first), not the Vina order — if it reproduces the Vina order instead, the screen gains credibility it does not currently deserve.
  3. Selectivity is the real differentiator. A CDK4 counter-screen will show whether any lead is CDK6-selective; a CDK6-selective lead with equal potency would matter more than a 1 kcal/mol docking margin, because CDK4 inhibition drives part of palbociclib's neutropenia.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): CDK6 kinase inhibition assay (commercial CDK6/cyclin D1, ADP-Glo readout) for the four leads plus palbociclib, 10-point dose–response in triplicate, with staurosporine as a control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): CDK4/cyclin D1 counter-screen for selectivity. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): cellular anti-proliferation assay (MCF-7, ER+ breast cancer) for any lead that beats palbociclib in Stage 1, with a palbociclib comparator and a CDK6-knockdown control to confirm on-target effect.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only: no experimental data, no molecular dynamics, no free-energy refinement.
  2. Vina noise (±1–2 kcal/mol) exceeds every margin reported here; the 0.99 kcal/mol "win" is not significant.
  3. Single rigid structure (6OQO, 1.98 Å); induced fit and the cyclin-bound conformation are not modelled.
  4. The four leads span only a 5.5-fold potency range (0.2–1.1 nM), too narrow for a rank-correlation test to be powerful (n = 4, p = 0.68).
  5. The ChEMBL bioactivities were fetched via a saved verbatim API response because the live endpoint was unstable all day (see Methods 2.2); the data are real ChEMBL records, but the fetch was not the pipeline's live call.
  6. No CDK4 selectivity data were computed; selectivity is the clinically relevant question and remains untested.
  7. Literature limits: the Pakistan case figure (~44,000/year) is a hospital-cited estimate, not a registry count.

6. Conclusion

On the CDK6 structure 6OQO, one ChEMBL lead (CHEMBL3237704) out-scores palbociclib by 0.99 kcal/mol — inside Vina's noise — while the docking order fails to track measured potency (Spearman ρ = −0.32, n = 4), with the weakest measured binder docking best. Palbociclib's own score is highly reproducible (−10.20 to −10.09 kcal/mol across four runs). The screen confirms these molecules fit the CDK6 ATP pocket; it does not rank them. The next step is a CDK6 kinase assay with a CDK4 counter-screen, not more docking.

Four Sub-Nanomolar Androgen Receptor Ligands Dock in Exact Measured-Potency Order on 8E1A — While Enzalutamide Itself Fails to Dock

Prostate cancer accounted for about 7.5% of all new cancers worldwide in 2024, roughly 1.5 million cases, and enzalutamide — an androgen receptor (AR) antagonist that extended median overall survival from 13.6 to 18.4 months in the AFFIRM trial — eventually fails in most men with metastatic castration-resistant disease…

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-12 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #51 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: androgen receptor; enzalutamide; F876L; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; prostate cancer; castration-resistant; drug resistance

Abstract

Prostate cancer accounted for about 7.5% of all new cancers worldwide in 2024, roughly 1.5 million cases, and enzalutamide — an androgen receptor (AR) antagonist that extended median overall survival from 13.6 to 18.4 months in the AFFIRM trial — eventually fails in most men with metastatic castration-resistant disease, in part because the F876L ligand-binding-domain mutation converts the drug from antagonist to agonist. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can rank AR ligands at all when the reference drug itself is the hard case. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P10275 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL1871, 38 bioactivities → PubChem → RDKit ADMET/PAINS → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) and docked four ChEMBL AR actives plus enzalutamide into the 1.2 Å AR ligand-binding-domain structure 8E1A, with the grid centre audited to 0.005 Å from the co-crystallised ligand. The four leads docked in exact measured-potency order — CHEMBL391548 −9.88 kcal/mol (IC50 0.02 nM), CHEMBL3818706 −8.47 (EC50 0.032 nM), CHEMBL3819048 −8.07 (EC50 0.16 nM), CHEMBL3819648 −6.96 (EC50 0.20 nM), Spearman ρ = 1.0 — but enzalutamide itself failed to dock, scoring +0.71 kcal/mol across all three poses, and a re-dock at exhaustiveness 32 returned the same failure (+0.69 kcal/mol), ruling out search depth as the cause; a fifth lead produced no docking result at all. No "beats enzalutamide" claim can therefore be made from this screen, and no F876L-mutant structure was docked, so the resistance question the topic posed remains untested. The falsifiable next step is an AR transactivation assay of the four leads against enzalutamide in wild-type and F876L AR: if the measured antagonist order matches the ChEMBL record rather than the Vina order, docking alone must not be used to prioritise AR leads on this structure.

1. Introduction

Prostate cancer is the second most diagnosed cancer in men and the fifth leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. The 2024 GLOBOCAN estimates put prostate cancer at 7.5% of all new cancers — roughly 1.5 million cases in a year in which 20.6 million cancers were diagnosed. Localised disease is nearly always survivable, with a five-year survival rate close to 100%, but metastatic disease drops that figure to about 30%. The androgen receptor, a ligand-activated nuclear transcription factor, is the primary driver of prostate cancer growth and progression, and it remains the central therapeutic target even after the disease stops responding to androgen deprivation.

Enzalutamide was the drug that proved the receptor stays druggable in castration-resistant disease. In the AFFIRM trial — 1,199 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after chemotherapy, randomised 2:1 to enzalutamide 160 mg daily or placebo — median overall survival was 18.4 months on enzalutamide versus 13.6 months on placebo (hazard ratio for death 0.63, 95% CI 0.53–0.75), and the trial was stopped early at a planned interim analysis. Enzalutamide inhibits AR nuclear translocation, DNA binding and coactivator recruitment, three steps beyond simple ligand competition.

Resistance follows in most patients. The mechanisms are AR-dependent in the majority of cases: AR gene amplification, ligand-binding-domain point mutations, and splice variants such as AR-V7 that activate signalling without a ligand-binding domain at all. The best-characterised point mutation is F876L. In a reporter-based mutagenesis screen, F876L converted enzalutamide from an antagonist into an agonist, and ectopic expression of AR F876L rescued prostate cancer cells from enzalutamide growth inhibition; molecular dynamics suggested the substitution repositions helix 12, the coactivator-recruiting helix, so that the drug-bound receptor adopts an active conformation. The same mutation confers resistance to apalutamide (ARN-509). A compound that antagonises F876L AR — the screen that found F876L also found three such compounds — is therefore the precise therapeutic need, and a docking screen that cannot even place enzalutamide in the wild-type pocket cannot be trusted to find one.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen of ChEMBL androgen-receptor actives against enzalutamide on a high-resolution AR ligand-binding-domain structure will rank compounds in the same order as their measured potencies. The test is the rank correlation, not the best score — and the reference drug must itself dock, or the comparison is void.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-12 (web search; PubMed/bioRxiv via the daily digest of 2026-11-12, which screened 840 candidates and selected 8, none on the androgen receptor — the digest's relevance is methodological, not topical, for this paper). Key sources: Sung et al. 2026 for the 2024 global cancer burden; Scher et al. 2012 for the AFFIRM trial; Balbas et al. 2013 for the F876L mutation and its agonist conversion; Quistini et al. 2025 for AR resistance mechanisms. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt P10275 (human androgen receptor, AR, 920 aa); ChEMBL target CHEMBL1871 (verified: "Androgen receptor", SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens); 38 bioactivities retrieved, 25 leads after RDKit similarity screening and ranking, 26 including the reference query; the top 5 leads docked plus the reference query (enzalutamide, PubChem CID 15951529, verified live). Structure: PDB 8E1A, the human AR ligand-binding domain (residues 664–919), resolution 1.2 Å, deposited from a structure-based study of novel AR inhibitors. Grid centre [26.97, 2.59, 4.23] — audited against the co-crystallised ligand 3E0 (chain A, residue 1001) centroid computed from the deposited coordinates with the pipeline's own _ligand_center function: distance 0.005 Å, i.e. the grid is exactly on the ligand-binding pocket. Best of three poses reported per compound. The same grid, box (22.5 Å) and exhaustiveness (8) were used for every compound including enzalutamide.

Two pipeline faults are disclosed here, not hidden. First, the fifth lead, CHEMBL3818497 (EC50 0.20 nM, pChEMBL 9.70), produced no docking result: no affinity, no poses, and no error was logged by the docking run. It is reported as missing in the table, not silently dropped. Second, a live ChEMBL activity-endpoint lookup at drafting time (to cross-check the per-lead potencies against the ChEMBL API directly) returned HTTP 500 on both network variants — the known EBI flakiness also seen on 2026-11-11. The potencies in the table therefore come from the pipeline's own ChEMBL retrieval during the run, which succeeded, and were not independently re-fetched.

No F876L-mutant structure was docked. The topic as posed asked for docking against the AR ligand-binding domain including the F876L mutant; the pipeline's structure picker returned the wild-type structure 8E1A only, and no mutant structure was substituted. The resistance question is therefore untested in this paper and is carried forward as the first validation step.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter (the pipeline's own filter, classes A–C) applied to every docked compound. All four leads and enzalutamide are PAINS-clean. The ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel flagged several nuclear-receptor and stress-response assays for every compound including enzalutamide (Section 3.1); these are similarity-based flags, not measurements, and they are reported as a screen result, not as toxicity findings.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity, and for a nuclear receptor it is doubly not efficacy: a docking score cannot distinguish an antagonist from an agonist, which is the entire question this paper asks — F876L is precisely a mutation that changes what a bound ligand does, not whether it binds. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds; the 1.41 kcal/mol gap between the first and second leads sits inside that noise. A single rigid structure (8E1A, co-crystallised with the inhibitor 3E0) cannot represent the conformational ensemble of the ligand-binding domain, and the pocket conformation is the 3E0-bound one, not the enzalutamide-bound one — no enzalutamide-bound AR structure was used. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated. Measured potencies come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays (one IC50, three EC50, different assay conditions); pChEMBL values are not head-to-head measurements, and the rank test mixes assay types. No measured AR potency for enzalutamide itself was retrieved in this run, so the reference enters the rank test by docking score only — and it failed to dock.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Vina best (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Measured potency (CHEMBL1871) pChEMBL PAINS
CHEMBL391548 −9.88 −9.88, −9.63, −8.88 IC50 0.02 nM 10.70 none
CHEMBL3818706 −8.47 −8.47 EC50 0.03162 nM 10.50 none
CHEMBL3819048 −8.07 −8.07, −8.06, −6.48 EC50 0.1585 nM 9.80 none
CHEMBL3819648 −6.96 −6.96 EC50 0.1995 nM 9.70 none
CHEMBL3818497 no result — EC50 0.1995 nM 9.70 none
Enzalutamide (query) +0.71 +0.71, +2.56, +7.05 — (not retrieved) — none

All four leads are small (MW 263–337), lipophilic (logP 3.74–4.44), Lipinski-clean (0 violations), with 1 hydrogen-bond donor, 2 acceptors and 1–2 rotatable bonds. Enzalutamide is larger (MW 464.44, logP 3.99) with 3 rotatable bonds. The ToxGuard read-across panel flagged NR-AR, NR-AR-LBD, NR-AhR, NR-PPAR-gamma, SR-ARE and SR-MMP for all five compounds, with additional ER/ER-LBD, aromatase, HSE and p53 flags varying by compound; no compound was flagged clean, and no compound was singled out — the panel does not discriminate between the leads and the reference, so it contributes nothing to ranking and is reported only for completeness.

The rank test the hypothesis posed: the Vina order of the four leads (391548 > 3818706 > 3819048 > 3819648) is exactly the measured-potency order (pChEMBL 10.70 > 10.50 > 9.80 > 9.70), Spearman ρ = 1.0 (n = 4). That is a clean pass on four compounds — and it is also a result that must not be over-read, for three reasons. First, n = 4. Second, the potency values mix one IC50 with three EC50 measurements from different assays. Third, the gap between the first and second leads (1.41 kcal/mol) is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so the only ordering the data actually support is "391548 first, 3819648 last"; the middle two are within noise of each other.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these four ChEMBL compounds on 8E1A was found at drafting time, so there is no published docking comparison to make. The depositing study for 8E1A is a structure-based study of novel AR inhibitors, but its own docking scores for its compounds were not retrieved in this run and are not compared here. The absence of a published comparator is stated, not filled in.

3.3 The reference drug failed to dock

Enzalutamide scored +0.71 kcal/mol as its best pose, with the other two poses worse (+2.56, +7.05). A positive Vina score means no favourable binding pose was found in the box: the ligand was placed, but every placement clashed or failed to make productive contacts. Three explanations are possible, and this run tested the first. (a) Exhaustiveness: Vina's default exhaustiveness of 8 may be too low for a ligand of this size and flexibility, and the search may simply have missed the pocket. A re-dock at exhaustiveness 32 returned +0.69 kcal/mol (poses +0.69, +2.49, +7.04) — essentially identical to the exhaustiveness-8 result (+0.71, +2.56, +7.05). The failure is therefore not a search-depth artefact. (b) Pocket conformation: 8E1A is bound to 3E0, a smaller inhibitor (20 heavy atoms in the deposited ligand), and the pocket may be in a conformation that does not accommodate enzalutamide's thiohydantoin core without rearrangement. (c) Ligand preparation: the 3D conformer generated from the PubChem SMILES may be a poor starting point. The re-dock eliminates (a) and leaves (b) or (c) standing. Whichever explanation holds, the consequence is the same: the reference comparator is absent from this benchmark, and any claim of the form "lead X beats enzalutamide" would be comparing a number against a failure, not against a drug.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The paper's question changed while running it. It started as "which ChEMBL AR ligands beat enzalutamide?" and became "can this screen rank AR ligands at all?" The answer to the second question is a qualified yes on four compounds and a no on the reference: the rank correlation is perfect, but the comparator failed. A benchmark that ranks the test set correctly and cannot place its own reference is a screen with a hole in the middle, and the honest report is the hole, not just the correlation.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four compounds, mixed assay types, and a 1.41 kcal/mol top gap inside the noise margin. The Spearman ρ = 1.0 is a property of four points, not a validation of Vina on AR. The leads are also extremely potent by their ChEMBL records (0.02–0.20 nM) — sub-nanomolar across the board — which means the screen selected from the extreme tail of the activity distribution, where rank order is easiest to get right and least informative about the middle of the distribution where real prioritisation happens. None of the four is identified by name in this run (ChEMBL IDs only); their chemotypes, selectivity against other nuclear receptors, and agonist-versus-antagonist character are all unknown from this data.

4.3 The PAINS problem does not apply here — the reference problem does

All compounds are PAINS-clean, so no artefact controls are needed on that front. The design constraint this experiment imposes is different: any validation assay must include enzalutamide as a measured comparator in the same assay, on the same plate, because the docking comparison against it failed. A validation that compares the leads only against each other would repeat the screen's error — it would rank compounds without anchoring them to the drug they are supposed to improve on.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Rank hypothesis. In an AR transactivation assay, the antagonist potency order of the four leads matches their ChEMBL record order (391548 > 3818706 > 3819048 > 3819648). Falsified if the measured order differs — in which case the perfect Spearman correlation was a four-point coincidence.
  2. Reference hypothesis. Enzalutamide's failure to dock is a search-depth artefact: a re-dock at higher exhaustiveness recovers a favourable score (≤ −7 kcal/mol). Falsified — the exhaustiveness-32 re-dock returned +0.69 kcal/mol, essentially identical to the standard run. The remaining explanations are pocket conformation or ligand preparation, and the hypothesis is now: docking enzalutamide into an enzalutamide-accommodating AR conformation recovers a favourable score. Falsified if no standard protocol places it favourably — in which case Vina at this setting cannot be used for AR antagonist ranking at all.
  3. Resistance hypothesis. At least one of the four leads antagonises AR F876L in a transactivation assay where enzalutamide acts as an agonist. Falsified if all four behave as agonists or are inactive on F876L — in which case the leads are wild-type binders only, and the resistance question needs a different chemotype.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain or synthesise the four leads; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR; confirm enzalutamide as the in-assay reference. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): AR transactivation (reporter-gene) assay in wild-type AR and F876L AR, dose–response for all four leads plus enzalutamide on the same plates, with an AR antagonist control and a vehicle control; read out antagonist IC50 and any agonist activity (the F876L test). Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): counter-screen the best lead against glucocorticoid and progesterone receptors for selectivity, and repeat the top two leads in a second AR assay format (e.g. binding). Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if a lead antagonises F876L, dock it into an F876L model and compare the pose with the wild-type pose; if none does, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per dose–response curve, eight concentrations, is the minimum for a defensible IC50; the F876L agonism test needs the same, because a false "antagonist" call on the mutant is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the 1.41 kcal/mol gap between the top two leads cannot rank them.
  3. The rank test is n = 4 and mixes one IC50 with three EC50 values from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays.
  4. The reference drug enzalutamide failed to dock (+0.71 kcal/mol); no comparison against it is possible from this screen.
  5. The fifth lead, CHEMBL3818497, produced no docking result and no error; its absence is unexplained.
  6. No F876L-mutant structure was docked, although the topic posed the resistance question; the wild-type result says nothing about the mutant.
  7. A single rigid structure (8E1A, 3E0-bound) cannot represent the AR ligand-binding-domain ensemble; docking cannot distinguish antagonist from agonist.
  8. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run.
  9. A live ChEMBL cross-check at drafting time returned HTTP 500; potencies rest on the pipeline's in-run retrieval alone.
  10. The four leads are identified by ChEMBL ID only; chemotype, selectivity and agonist/antagonist character are unknown from this data.

6. Conclusion

Four sub-nanomolar ChEMBL androgen-receptor ligands dock in exact measured-potency order on the 1.2 Å structure 8E1A (Spearman ρ = 1.0, n = 4), with CHEMBL391548 first at −9.88 kcal/mol against a measured IC50 of 0.02 nM. The benchmark's reference drug, enzalutamide, failed to dock at all, and the F876L resistance question was not tested. The screen is therefore a rank-order signal on four compounds with a missing comparator, not a lead claim. The next step is the assay in Section 4.5, with enzalutamide measured on the same plates.

Vina Ranks Lisinopril Last on ACE: A Centre-Audited Benchmark of Enalaprilat and Two ChEMBL Leads Against Lisinopril on the C-Domain Structure 6H5W

Hypertension affected 1.4 billion people in 2024 and only about one in five had it controlled, yet the most prescribed drug class for it — ACE inhibitors — makes 5–15% of patients cough, because the same enzyme that converts angiotensin I also degrades bradykinin, and blocking it lets bradykinin accumulate in the airwa…

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-12 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #50 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: angiotensin-converting enzyme; lisinopril; enalaprilat; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; hypertension; ACE inhibitor cough; bradykinin

Abstract

Hypertension affected 1.4 billion people in 2024 and only about one in five had it controlled, yet the most prescribed drug class for it — ACE inhibitors — makes 5–15% of patients cough, because the same enzyme that converts angiotensin I also degrades bradykinin, and blocking it lets bradykinin accumulate in the airways. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can find a better ACE binder than lisinopril, and whether that question is even the right one for a cough-free drug. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P12821 → ChEMBL target CHEMBL1808, 45 bioactivities → PubChem → RDKit ADMET/PAINS → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) and docked four ChEMBL ACE actives plus lisinopril into the 1.37 Å ACE C-domain structure 6H5W, with the grid centre audited to 0.005 Å from the co-crystallised inhibitor omapatrilat. All four leads out-scored lisinopril — CHEMBL80779 −8.86, enalaprilat −8.15 and −8.05 (duplicate ChEMBL records of one molecule), lisinopril's own ChEMBL record −7.88, against the PubChem lisinopril query at −7.62 kcal/mol — but the ranking is inverted against measured potency: lisinopril itself, the most potent measured binder at IC50 0.1 nM, docks worst, Spearman ρ = −0.5 on the three distinct molecules. Two reproducibility controls held: lisinopril docked twice 0.26 kcal/mol apart and enalaprilat twice 0.10 apart. The cough question is not answered by binding at all: bradykinin is cleaved by both ACE domains while angiotensin I is mainly cleaved by the C-domain, so a cough-sparing inhibitor must be C-domain-selective, which a single-domain docking score cannot measure. The falsifiable next step is a two-domain (N versus C) inhibition assay of the leads against lisinopril: if a lead inhibits the C-domain while sparing the N-domain, it is a candidate for the cough question; if it inhibits both like lisinopril, it is not, whatever its docking score.

1. Introduction

The World Health Organization's Global Hypertension Report 2025 put the number of people living with hypertension at 1.4 billion in 2024, with only about one in five having the condition under control, and uncontrolled high blood pressure claiming more than 10 million lives a year. ACE inhibitors are a first-line treatment, and lisinopril is among the most prescribed of them. Their efficacy is not the problem. Their tolerability is: a persistent dry cough that affects roughly 5–15% of patients on ACE inhibitors (with some studies reporting up to 35%), more often in women than in men (12.6% versus 4.4% in one lisinopril study), typically beginning weeks to months after starting treatment and resolving only 1–4 weeks after stopping the drug. It is the most common reason physicians switch a patient from an ACE inhibitor to an angiotensin-receptor blocker.

The mechanism is inseparable from the drug's action. ACE — kininase II — has two jobs: it converts angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, and it degrades bradykinin, a vasodilator peptide. Inhibiting the enzyme therefore does two things at once: blood pressure falls, and bradykinin (with substance P, which ACE also degrades) accumulates in the airways, sensitising the cough reflex. The cough is not an allergy and not an off-target effect; it is the on-target consequence of blocking bradykinin breakdown. Any ACE inhibitor that blocks the enzyme will raise bradykinin to some degree, which is why the "cough-free ACE inhibitor" is a harder problem than "a stronger ACE binder".

The one opening is that ACE is not one active site but two. Somatic ACE is a single polypeptide with two homologous catalytic domains, N and C, each with a zinc-containing active site, sharing about 55–60% sequence identity but with different substrate specificities. The C-domain is mainly responsible for converting angiotensin I in vivo; bradykinin is hydrolysed by both domains about equally; and several substrates, including the tetrapeptide AcSDKP, are cleaved essentially only by the N-domain. A C-domain-selective inhibitor would therefore lower angiotensin II while leaving the N-domain free to keep degrading bradykinin — the published rationale for pursuing domain-selective inhibitors as drugs with an improved side-effect profile. That is the precise question a docking screen must be judged against: not "does it bind ACE better than lisinopril?" but "does it bind the C-domain selectively?"

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen of ChEMBL ACE actives against lisinopril on a high-resolution ACE C-domain structure will rank compounds in the same order as their measured potencies, and the top-ranked lead will be a candidate for C-domain-selective inhibition. The test is the rank correlation, not the best score — and selectivity must be tested in a two-domain assay, not inferred from a single-domain docking score.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-12 (web search; PubMed/bioRxiv via the daily digest of 2026-11-12, which screened 840 candidates and selected 8, none on ACE — the digest's relevance is methodological, not topical, for this paper). Key sources: the WHO Global Hypertension Report 2025 for the burden numbers; Yilmaz 2019 for ACE-inhibitor cough incidence and mechanism; Taddei and Bortolotto 2016 for the bradykinin mechanism; Ehlers, Abrie and Sturrock 2013 for C-domain-selective inhibition. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI checked, not invented).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt P12821 (human angiotensin-converting enzyme, ACE, 1,306 aa); ChEMBL target CHEMBL1808 (verified: "Angiotensin-converting enzyme", SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens); 45 bioactivities retrieved, 25 leads after RDKit similarity screening and ranking, 26 including the reference query; the top 5 leads docked plus the reference query (lisinopril, PubChem CID 5362119, verified live). Structure: PDB 6H5W, the human ACE C-domain in complex with omapatrilat, resolution 1.37 Å. Grid centre [−6.89, 3.74, 14.52] — audited against the co-crystallised ligand omapatrilat (residue FT8, chain A, residue 711) centroid computed from the deposited coordinates with the pipeline's own _ligand_center function: distance 0.005 Å, i.e. the grid is exactly on the C-domain active site, at the catalytic zinc. Best of three poses reported per compound. The same grid, box (22.5 Å) and exhaustiveness (8) were used for every compound including lisinopril.

Two bookkeeping facts about the lead set, disclosed here because they change how the table reads. First, the ChEMBL record CHEMBL1237 is lisinopril itself: its SMILES has the same connectivity as the PubChem query SMILES, with stereochemistry specified, and identical descriptors (MW 405.5, logP 1.24). It was therefore docked twice — once as a lead, once as the query — which makes it a reproducibility control, not a second molecule. Second, CHEMBL577 and CHEMBL39538 are duplicate ChEMBL records of one molecule, enalaprilat: their SMILES differ only in stereochemistry specification, their descriptors are identical (MW 348.4, logP 1.13), and their measured potencies are the same within rounding (IC50 1.2 versus 1.202 nM). The comparison table therefore contains five entries but three distinct molecules, and the rank test is computed on the three distinct molecules.

Only the C-domain was docked. No N-domain structure was used, so nothing in this paper measures domain selectivity; the C-domain-selective question is posed, not tested.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter (the pipeline's own filter, classes A–C) applied to every docked compound. All five entries are PAINS-clean. The ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel was clean for lisinopril (measured data, no active assays) and for both enalaprilat records; CHEMBL80779 carries a single read-across flag (NR-AhR). A read-across flag is a similarity-based screen result, not a toxicity measurement, and it is reported as such.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity, and a docking score on one domain cannot measure domain selectivity, which is the entire question this paper asks about cough. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds; the 1.24 kcal/mol gap between the best lead and lisinopril sits inside that noise. A single rigid structure (6H5W, omapatrilat-bound C-domain) cannot represent the conformational ensemble of either ACE domain, and omapatrilat is a dual ACE/neprilysin inhibitor, not lisinopril, so the pocket conformation is not the lisinopril-bound one. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated. Measured potencies come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays (IC50 values from different assay conditions); pChEMBL values are not head-to-head measurements. No measured ACE potency for the PubChem lisinopril query was retrieved in this run; the reference enters the rank test through its ChEMBL record (CHEMBL1237, IC50 0.1 nM).

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Vina best (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Measured potency (CHEMBL1808) pChEMBL PAINS
CHEMBL80779 −8.86 −8.86, −8.83, −8.65 IC50 1.096 nM 8.96 none
CHEMBL577 (enalaprilat, record A) −8.15 −8.15, −7.76, −7.69 IC50 1.2 nM 8.92 none
CHEMBL39538 (enalaprilat, record B) −8.05 −8.05, −8.02, −7.89 IC50 1.202 nM 8.92 none
CHEMBL1237 (lisinopril, ChEMBL record) −7.88 −7.88, −7.71, −7.50 IC50 0.1 nM 10.00 none
Lisinopril (query, PubChem) −7.62 −7.62, −7.23, −7.18 — (not retrieved) — none

All five entries are small (MW 348–406), Lipinski-clean (0 violations), with 3–4 hydrogen-bond donors and 4–5 acceptors. The reproducibility controls held: the two lisinopril dockings differ by 0.26 kcal/mol (−7.88 versus −7.62) and the two enalaprilat dockings by 0.10 kcal/mol (−8.15 versus −8.05), both well inside Vina's noise and consistent with the same molecule being placed twice. These are the tightest reproducibility controls in this paper series, and they make the ranking result harder to dismiss as setup error: the protocol is reproducible, and it reproducibly ranks the most potent binder last.

The rank test the hypothesis posed: on the three distinct molecules, the Vina order is CHEMBL80779 > enalaprilat > lisinopril, while the measured-potency order is lisinopril (0.1 nM) > CHEMBL80779 (1.096 nM) > enalaprilat (1.2 nM) — the Vina order is the exact reverse of the measured order for the top and bottom, Spearman ρ = −0.5 (n = 3). Every lead out-scores lisinopril (by 0.26–1.24 kcal/mol against the query), yet lisinopril is the most potent measured binder by a factor of eleven over the next compound. The "win" is therefore an artefact of the scoring function, not a lead: a screen that ranks a 0.1 nM binder below 1.2 nM binders cannot be used to prioritise ACE inhibitors on this structure.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these ChEMBL compounds on 6H5W was found at drafting time, so there is no published docking comparison to make. The depositing study for 6H5W is a structural study of the ACE C-domain with omapatrilat; its own docking or affinity data for these compounds were not retrieved in this run and are not compared here. The absence of a published comparator is stated, not filled in.

3.3 The cough question is not a binding question

The screen's headline — four leads out-score lisinopril — is irrelevant to the cough problem for two independent reasons. First, the ranking is inverted against measured potency (Section 3.1), so the scores do not identify better binders. Second, and more fundamentally, cough is caused by bradykinin accumulation, and bradykinin is hydrolysed by both ACE domains about equally. A compound that binds the C-domain more tightly than lisinopril but inhibits the N-domain equally will raise bradykinin exactly as lisinopril does. The only escape is domain selectivity: inhibit the C-domain (which makes the angiotensin II that raises blood pressure) while sparing the N-domain (which keeps clearing bradykinin). This screen docked on the C-domain only, so it cannot distinguish a C-selective inhibitor from a non-selective one — the property that matters is precisely the one that was not measured. The paper's topic as posed ("cough-free alternatives") therefore cannot be answered by this screen; it can only be answered by a two-domain assay, proposed in Section 4.5.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The paper started as a search for a better ACE binder and became a demonstration that "better binder" is the wrong target twice over: the screen cannot rank binders correctly on this structure, and binding is not the property that causes or prevents cough. The useful result is the negative one — Vina on 6H5W ranks lisinopril last while it is the most potent measured binder — plus the precise statement of what would count as progress, which is a domain-selectivity measurement, not a docking score.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three distinct molecules is the smallest rank test this series has run, and the 1.24 kcal/mol gap between the best lead and lisinopril is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The measured potencies span only one order of magnitude (0.1–1.2 nM), so the test asks the scoring function to resolve differences it cannot resolve. CHEMBL80779, the top scorer, is identified by ChEMBL ID only; its chemotype and identity were not established in this run. And all four leads are already potent ACE inhibitors by their ChEMBL records — this is a screen among known nanomolar binders, not a discovery screen.

4.3 The PAINS problem does not apply here

All compounds are PAINS-clean, so no artefact controls are needed on that front. The design constraint this experiment imposes is different: any validation must measure both ACE domains, because a single-domain result cannot speak to the cough question, and it must include lisinopril on the same plates, because the docking comparison against it is inverted.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Rank hypothesis. In a single-domain ACE inhibition assay, the potency order of the three distinct molecules matches their ChEMBL record order (lisinopril > CHEMBL80779 > enalaprilat), not the Vina order. Falsified if the measured order matches Vina — in which case the ChEMBL records, not the docking, are the problem.
  2. Selectivity hypothesis. CHEMBL80779 inhibits the ACE C-domain more potently than the N-domain (selectivity ratio ≥ 10), while lisinopril inhibits both about equally. Falsified if CHEMBL80779 is non-selective — in which case it is not a cough-sparing candidate, whatever its docking score.
  3. Cough hypothesis. A C-domain-selective inhibitor lowers blood pressure in vivo with less bradykinin accumulation than lisinopril at equi-effective doses. This is a later, animal-stage test; it is stated here so the assay in Section 4.5 is designed toward it, not as a claim this paper can test.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): obtain CHEMBL80779 and enalaprilat; confirm identity and purity by LC-MS and NMR; confirm lisinopril as the in-assay reference. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): in vitro ACE inhibition assays on recombinant N-domain and C-domain separately (fluorogenic substrate, e.g. Abz-based), dose–response for all three distinct molecules plus lisinopril on the same plates, with domain-selective controls (RXP407 for the N-domain, RXPA380 for the C-domain, from the literature) and a vehicle control; read out IC50 per domain and the C/N selectivity ratio. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): bradykinin-degradation assay in the same domain preparations, to test directly whether a C-selective lead spares bradykinin breakdown. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): if a lead is C-selective, dock it into an N-domain structure and compare the poses to identify the selectivity determinants; if none is selective, report the negative result and stop. Sample-size logic: three independent biological replicates per dose–response curve, eight concentrations, is the minimum for a defensible IC50 and selectivity ratio; the bradykinin assay needs the same, because a false "sparing" call is the error that matters.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data were generated, and no compound was assayed.
  2. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the 1.24 kcal/mol gap between the best lead and lisinopril cannot rank them.
  3. The rank test is n = 3 distinct molecules, with measured potencies spanning only one order of magnitude (0.1–1.2 nM).
  4. The lead set contains duplicate ChEMBL records (two of lisinopril, two of enalaprilat); the table has five entries but three distinct molecules.
  5. Only the C-domain was docked; domain selectivity — the property the cough question turns on — was not measured.
  6. A single rigid structure (6H5W, omapatrilat-bound C-domain) cannot represent the conformational ensemble of either ACE domain.
  7. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run.
  8. Measured potencies come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays; pChEMBL values are not head-to-head measurements.
  9. CHEMBL80779 is identified by ChEMBL ID only; its chemotype and identity were not established in this run.
  10. The cough mechanism (bradykinin accumulation) is literature-based; this paper measures no cough endpoint.

6. Conclusion

Four ChEMBL ACE actives out-score lisinopril on the 1.37 Å C-domain structure 6H5W, but the ranking is inverted against measured potency (Spearman ρ = −0.5, n = 3 distinct molecules): lisinopril, the most potent measured binder at IC50 0.1 nM, docks worst. The screen is reproducible — lisinopril and enalaprilat each docked twice within 0.26 kcal/mol — and reproducibly wrong about the ranking. Separately, the cough question cannot be answered by binding at all: bradykinin is cleared by both ACE domains, so only a C-domain-selective inhibitor can spare it, and this screen measured no selectivity. The next step is the two-domain assay in Section 4.5.
