Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-11 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #45 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: PPAR-gamma; pioglitazone; partial agonist; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; type 2 diabetes; thymoquinone; SPPARM

Abstract

Type 2 diabetes affects 589 million adults worldwide, and Pakistan carries the world's highest age-standardised prevalence at 31.4%, yet the most effective insulin sensitiser, pioglitazone, is limited by PPAR-gamma-driven weight gain of about 3.5 kg over six months and oedema in about 5% of patients. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can rank partial-agonist candidates against pioglitazone at all, and whether thymoquinone, a natural product with reported PPAR-gamma activity, binds the receptor at all. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P37231 → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit ADMET/PAINS → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) and docked four ChEMBL PPAR-gamma actives, pioglitazone and thymoquinone into the 1.25 Å PPAR-gamma ligand-binding-domain structure 9F7W, with the grid centre audited to 0.01 Å from the co-crystallised ligand. The first pipeline run silently retrieved maltase-glucoamylase actives instead of PPAR-gamma actives; the audit caught it, and the run was repeated against the verified target CHEMBL235. One lead out-scored pioglitazone — CHEMBL6145236 at −10.24 versus −9.00 kcal/mol — but the margin (1.24 kcal/mol) sits at the edge of the ±1–2 kcal/mol Vina noise, and the ranking is reversed against measured potency: Spearman ρ = −0.8 (n = 4), with the strongest measured binder (CHEMBL1813011, EC50 0.018 nM) ranking third by Vina. Thymoquinone docked weakly (−6.25 kcal/mol) and carries a PAINS quinone alert. The falsifiable next step is a PPAR-gamma transactivation assay of the four leads against pioglitazone: if the measured EC50 order matches the ChEMBL record rather than the Vina order, docking alone must not be used to prioritise PPAR-gamma leads on this structure.

1. Introduction

Diabetes affected an estimated 589 million adults aged 20–79 worldwide in 2024, about one in nine people, and the International Diabetes Federation projects 853 million by 2050. Pakistan carries the world's highest age-standardised diabetes prevalence at 31.4%, with an estimated 34.5 million adults affected in 2024, about 226,752 diabetes-related deaths that year, and a projected 70.2 million cases by 2050. In a country where the disease burden is this large, an insulin sensitiser that works without adding weight or fluid is not a refinement — it is the difference between a drug patients can stay on and one they cannot.

Pioglitazone is the most effective insulin sensitiser in routine use. It is a thiazolidinedione and a full agonist of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPAR-gamma, UniProt P37231), a ligand-activated nuclear receptor that is the master regulator of adipocyte differentiation and a key controller of glucose and lipid metabolism. Full PPAR-gamma activation improves insulin sensitivity in muscle, fat and liver — but it also drives the drug's two dose-limiting effects: weight gain of about 5%, roughly 3.5 kg over six months, and water retention with leg oedema in about 5% of patients, with peripheral oedema reported in 2–5% on monotherapy and 5–15% when combined with insulin. The fluid retention is mechanistically tied to PPAR-gamma itself: the receptor is expressed in the renal collecting duct, where activation increases sodium reabsorption, and collecting-duct-specific deletion of PPAR-gamma abolishes thiazolidinedione-induced fluid retention in mice. Intravascular volume rises by about 6–7% on glitazones, which is why the class carries a boxed warning for heart failure.

The field's answer has been to separate insulin sensitisation from full agonism. Two lines of evidence show it can be done. First, obesity-linked phosphorylation of PPAR-gamma at Ser273 by cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5) dysregulates a specific gene set — including the insulin-sensitising adipokine adiponectin — without changing the receptor's adipogenic capacity, and anti-diabetic PPAR-gamma ligands block this phosphorylation independently of classical transcriptional agonism. Second, ligands built on that insight work in animals: SR1664, a non-agonist PPAR-gamma ligand that blocks Ser273 phosphorylation, has anti-diabetic activity roughly equivalent to rosiglitazone in obese mice while causing no fluid retention or weight gain; and GQ-16, a thiazolidinedione-derived partial agonist, retains rosiglitazone-like anti-diabetic efficacy in mice with no weight gain or oedema, while blocking Cdk5-mediated phosphorylation. These compounds are selective PPAR-gamma modulators (SPPARMs) — ligands whose dose–response relationships for different activities are uncoupled, so that insulin sensitisation is kept and adipogenesis is not.

Thymoquinone, the active constituent of black seed (Nigella sativa), is a candidate from the natural-product side: in high-fat-diet plus streptozotocin diabetic rats it lowered glucose, improved HOMA-IR and raised PPAR-gamma levels, and an earlier docking study on the pioglitazone-bound structure 2XKW reported pioglitazone at −9.4 and thymoquinone at −7.0 kcal/mol. But thymoquinone is a 1,4-benzoquinone — a redox-active chemotype that the PAINS filter flags — so any PPAR-gamma signal from it must survive artefact controls before it is believed.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen of ChEMBL PPAR-gamma actives against pioglitazone on a high-resolution PPAR-gamma ligand-binding-domain structure will rank compounds in the same order as their measured potencies, and thymoquinone will bind the same pocket measurably worse than pioglitazone. The test is the rank correlation, not the best score.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-11 (web search; PubMed/bioRxiv via the daily digest of 2026-11-11, which screened 589 candidates and selected 8, none on PPAR-gamma — the digest's relevance is methodological, not topical, for this paper). Key sources: the IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th edition (2025) for the burden numbers; Choi et al. 2010 and 2011 for the Cdk5–Ser273 mechanism and SR1664; Amato et al. 2012 for GQ-16; Yang and Soodvilai 2008 for the collecting-duct mechanism of fluid retention; Megantara et al. 2017 for the earlier thymoquinone–pioglitazone docking comparison; and Alshahrani et al. 2021 for thymoquinone's in vivo PPAR-gamma data. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt P37231 (human PPAR-gamma, PPARG, 505 aa); ChEMBL target CHEMBL235 (verified: "Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma"); 44 bioactivities retrieved with pChEMBL ≥ 5, 26 leads after RDKit filtering and ranking; the top 4 leads docked plus the reference query (pioglitazone, PubChem CID 4829, verified live) and, separately, thymoquinone (PubChem CID 10281, verified live). Structure: PDB 9F7W, the human PPAR-gamma ligand-binding domain in complex with a coactivator-1-alpha peptide and bisphenol A, resolution 1.25 Å. Grid centre [47.10, 6.91, 1.39] — audited against the co-crystallised ligand bisphenol A (residue 501) centroid computed from the deposited coordinates: distance 0.01 Å, i.e. the grid is exactly on the ligand-binding pocket. (A second bisphenol A copy, residue 502, sits 12.24 Å from the centre at a surface site and was not used.) Best of three poses reported per compound. The same grid, box (22.5 Å) and exhaustiveness were used for every compound including pioglitazone. Pioglitazone was docked twice, once in each pipeline run, and reproduced to 0.04 kcal/mol (−9.04 and −9.00), a reproducibility control for the setup.

A note on the run, and the reason Section 3.3 exists: the first pipeline run resolved the ChEMBL target incorrectly. The UniProt-accession lookup returned CHEMBL2074, "Maltase-glucoamylase", and the pipeline pulled 55 bioactivities for that target. The error was caught by checking the retrieved target name against the UniProt protein before writing the paper: the docked "leads" were polyhydroxylated iminosugar-like molecules, the classic alpha-glucosidase-inhibitor chemotype, not PPAR-gamma ligands. The first ChEMBL call in the corrected re-run also failed (EBI API error, a known same-day flakiness), and succeeded on the single permitted retry with the plain environment. No result in the comparison table comes from the wrong-target run; its numbers are reported separately, in Section 3.3, as the audit finding.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter (the pipeline's own filter, classes A–C) applied to every docked compound. The four ChEMBL leads and pioglitazone are clean. Thymoquinone carries one PAINS alert — its 1,4-benzoquinone core — reported in the table, not hidden; it changes the validation design (redox controls, Section 4.3).

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity, and for a nuclear receptor it is doubly not efficacy: a docking score cannot distinguish a full agonist from a partial agonist or a non-agonist binder, which is the entire question this paper asks. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds. A single rigid structure (9F7W, coactivator-bound, bisphenol A in the pocket) cannot represent the conformational ensemble of the ligand-binding domain, and bisphenol A is a weak partial agonist, not a thiazolidinedione, so the pocket conformation is not the pioglitazone-bound one. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated. Measured potencies come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays (EC50 vs Ki, different assay conditions); pChEMBL values are not head-to-head measurements. No measured PPAR-gamma potency for pioglitazone itself was retrieved in this run, so the reference enters the rank test by docking score only.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Vina best (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Measured potency (ChEMBL235) pChEMBL PAINS
CHEMBL6145236 −10.24 −10.24, −9.38, −9.38 EC50 0.49 nM 9.31 none
Pioglitazone (query) −9.00 −9.00, −8.48, −8.39 — (not retrieved) — none
CHEMBL65805 −8.60 −8.60, −8.32, −8.09 Ki 0.4 nM 9.40 none
CHEMBL1813011 −8.57 −8.57, −7.67, −7.64 EC50 0.018 nM 10.74 none
CHEMBL1813008 −8.52 −8.52, −7.55, −7.36 EC50 0.05 nM 10.30 none
Thymoquinone (extra) −6.25 −6.25, −6.21, −6.16 — (no ChEMBL PPAR-gamma potency) — alert (quinone)

All six docks are on 9F7W (1.25 Å), grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised ligand centroid (0.01 Å). Pioglitazone reproduced to 0.04 kcal/mol across the two runs (−9.04, −9.00).

One lead out-scores pioglitazone: CHEMBL6145236, by 1.24 kcal/mol. That margin sits at the edge of Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — it is the only margin in the table that even approaches significance, and it does not exceed the noise band. The other three leads score 0.40–0.48 kcal/mol worse than pioglitazone, deep inside noise. Pose consistency is good for the top two (top-three poses within ~0.9 kcal/mol) and weaker for CHEMBL1813011 and CHEMBL1813008 (spread ~0.9–1.2 kcal/mol), which is itself a small warning about those two poses.

The four leads are all sub-nanomolar by measurement (EC50/Ki 0.018–0.49 nM), spanning only 1.43 log units of pChEMBL (9.31–10.74). CHEMBL6145236 is the most drug-like of the set by the pipeline's own descriptors: lowest logP (2.14), fewest rotatable bonds (2), zero Lipinski violations, TPSA 103.68 Å² — and its scaffold is the most distinct from pioglitazone (a quinolinone–carbonitrile–sulfone, similarity 0.163, versus the oxazole-acid pair CHEMBL1813008/CHEMBL1813011, similarity 0.26–0.27). The two oxazole acids are close analogues of each other and carry the highest logP in the set (4.37–4.67). None of the four is a proven partial agonist: all four are recorded in ChEMBL as PPAR-gamma actives with sub-nanomolar potency, which is what full agonists look like too. Binding strength says nothing about efficacy.

Thymoquinone docked at −6.25 kcal/mol, 2.75 kcal/mol worse than pioglitazone, with tight poses (−6.25, −6.21, −6.16) — a consistent but weak fit — and it carries the PAINS quinone alert. It was not in the pipeline's ChEMBL top 26 (its similarity to pioglitazone is low), so it was docked separately on the identical protocol; its score is directly comparable to the table.

Pioglitazone's own Tox21 measured flags (from the pipeline's safety panel) are worth recording without over-reading: NR-PPAR-gamma active (expected — it is a PPAR-gamma agonist), SR-ARE active and SR-MMP active. These are assay-activity flags from Tox21, not clinical toxicity findings, and the four leads carry only low kNN read-across probabilities on the same panel (highest single value: SR-MMP 0.397 for CHEMBL6145236) — predictions, not measurements, and not a safety claim.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

The only directly comparable published docking is Megantara et al. 2017, who docked thymoquinone and pioglitazone on 2XKW, the pioglitazone-bound PPAR-gamma structure, with AutoDock Vina 1.1: pioglitazone −9.4, thymoquinone −7.0 kcal/mol. Our numbers on 9F7W are pioglitazone −9.00 and thymoquinone −6.25. The direction is the same — pioglitazone binds the pocket about 2.7–2.8 kcal/mol more strongly than thymoquinone in both studies — while the absolute values differ, as expected across structures and Vina versions. That agreement in direction, across two structures and two Vina versions, is the most robust docking result in this paper, and it is also the least surprising: a small quinone is not a thiazolidinedione.

3.3 The standardisation problem: the first run docked the wrong target's ligands

The first pipeline run is reported here because the failure mode matters more than the numbers. It resolved UniProt P37231 to ChEMBL CHEMBL2074, "Maltase-glucoamylase", pulled 55 bioactivities for that target, and docked the top leads into the (correct) PPAR-gamma structure 9F7W:

Compound (wrong-target run) Vina best (kcal/mol) Quoted potency — against MGAM, not PPAR-gamma
CHEMBL5558505 −9.10 IC50 420 nM (pChEMBL 6.38)
Pioglitazone (query) −9.04 —
CHEMBL3349446 −7.27 IC50 330 nM (pChEMBL 6.48)
CHEMBL332802 −7.03 Ki 28 nM (pChEMBL 7.55)
CHEMBL3349435 −6.98 IC50 230 nM (pChEMBL 6.64)

Nothing in that table is a PPAR-gamma result. The quoted potencies are maltase-glucoamylase potencies, the docked molecules are alpha-glucosidase-class iminosugars (three of the four are polyhydroxylated aminocyclitol-like scaffolds), and the one apparently interesting number — CHEMBL5558505 "beating" pioglitazone by 0.06 kcal/mol — is a cross-target accident. The pipeline reported every step as "ok": the failure was silent, and only the name check (CHEMBL2074 ≠ PPAR-gamma) caught it. The corrected run (Section 3.1) re-pulled against CHEMBL235 and is the only run the paper's conclusions rest on. The fix, for the pipeline, is a one-line assertion: the resolved ChEMBL target's preferred name must contain the UniProt gene or protein name before any ligand is retrieved. Until that assertion exists, every LeadForge run needs this manual check — which is why this section is in the paper rather than in a log file.

3.4 The ranking is reversed

For the four distinct ChEMBL leads, the Vina order (best first) is CHEMBL6145236 > CHEMBL65805 > CHEMBL1813011 > CHEMBL1813008. The measured-potency order (pChEMBL, best first) is the exact reverse for the top and bottom: CHEMBL1813011 (10.74) > CHEMBL1813008 (10.30) > CHEMBL65805 (9.40) > CHEMBL6145236 (9.31). Spearman rank correlation ρ = −0.8 (n = 4). The compound Vina ranks first is the weakest by measured potency; the strongest measured binder ranks third by Vina. As in the VEGFR2 benchmark in this same series, the reversal is a ranking failure among near-equal compounds — all four are sub-nanomolar, spanning 1.43 log units — not a failure to detect a weak binder. But it is a complete ranking failure all the same, and it is the paper's main result: on 9F7W, under this protocol, Vina cannot order PPAR-gamma ligands, and the single "win" over pioglitazone is the least trustworthy number in the table.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether docking can rank PPAR-gamma leads against pioglitazone, and whether thymoquinone belongs in the pocket at all. The answer to the first half is no — not because the setup was wrong (the grid is exactly on the ligand, the reference reproduces to 0.04 kcal/mol across runs, poses are consistent) but because the scoring function does not recover the experimental order even among four sub-nanomolar binders. The answer to the second half is that thymoquinone does dock, weakly and consistently, 2.75 kcal/mol worse than pioglitazone — the same direction as the published 2XKW comparison — but its PAINS alert means the binding itself is not yet evidence of PPAR-gamma activity. The honest headline is therefore a double negative result about the method and about thymoquinone, plus one genuine lead for the assay queue: CHEMBL6145236, the only compound in the set that is simultaneously the best Vina scorer, the most drug-like by descriptors, and the most structurally distinct from pioglitazone — which is exactly the profile a partial-agonist search wants, and exactly the profile docking cannot validate.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the 1.24 kcal/mol margin sits at the edge of the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and does not exceed it. Second, the ranking is anti-correlated with measurement (ρ = −0.8), and the "winner" is the weakest measured binder of the four. Third, and specific to this target, a docking score cannot measure what matters: efficacy. A partial agonist and a full agonist can have identical binding affinities and opposite clinical profiles — GQ-16 and rosiglitazone differ in efficacy, not in whether they occupy the pocket. The property that would make CHEMBL6145236 valuable (partial agonism, Ser273-phosphorylation blockade without full transactivation) is invisible to Vina by construction. The compound's value is as a test case for the assay, not as a claim.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

Thymoquinone's 1,4-benzoquinone core is redox-active: quinones cycle redox, generate reactive oxygen species and can produce assay signals that look like target activity. That does not prove its PPAR-gamma signal is an artefact — the in vivo rat data (raised PPAR-gamma levels, improved HOMA-IR) and two independent docking studies pointing the same way are real, if weak, evidence — but it does fix the design of the validation: every thymoquinone assay needs a reducing-agent control (e.g. dithiothreitol), a catalase control, and a counter-screen against an unrelated nuclear receptor, so that a redox artefact has somewhere to show itself. The same controls apply, in milder form, to the four leads: all four are hydrophobic (logP 2.14–4.67) and hydrophobic aggregators are the other classic source of false inhibition.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a PPAR-gamma transactivation assay (reporter gene, pioglitazone and rosiglitazone controls on the same plate), the EC50 order of the four leads will follow the ChEMBL pChEMBL order, not the Vina order — i.e. CHEMBL1813011 will be the most potent and CHEMBL6145236 the least. Refuted if the Vina order reproduces.
  2. Re-docking the same five compounds on 2XKW (the pioglitazone-bound structure) will change the Vina order, showing the ranking is structure-dependent. Refuted if the order is identical.
  3. CHEMBL6145236 will show lower maximal transactivation efficacy than pioglitazone (partial agonism) while blocking Cdk5-mediated Ser273 phosphorylation in adipocytes — the profile that would make it a SPPARM candidate rather than just another full agonist. Refuted if it is a full agonist with efficacy equal to pioglitazone.
  4. Thymoquinone's apparent PPAR-gamma activity in the transactivation assay will disappear under reducing-agent (dithiothreitol) and catalase controls, consistent with a redox artefact from its quinone core. Refuted if the signal survives the controls.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): PPAR-gamma transactivation assay (luciferase reporter, HEK293 or similar) for the four leads + pioglitazone + rosiglitazone, 10-point dose–response in triplicate, same plate, reporting both EC50 and maximal efficacy as a percentage of rosiglitazone — efficacy, not just potency, is the readout that matters for partial agonism. Thymoquinone runs in the same assay with dithiothreitol and catalase arms. Detergent and aggregation controls throughout. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): Cdk5 Ser273-phosphorylation assay in cultured adipocytes for the best lead only (western blot for phospho-Ser273 PPAR-gamma, rosiglitazone and SR1664-style controls), plus 3T3-L1 adipogenesis with aP2/FABP4 readout as the adipogenicity proxy for the weight-gain question. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): re-docking on 2XKW and a short molecular-dynamics rescoring to test hypothesis 2, and, if stage 1 supports it, a focused analogue series around CHEMBL6145236's quinolinone core. Stop rule: if stage 1 reproduces the ChEMBL order, the Vina ranking is discarded and the project proceeds on measured potency and efficacy only; if thymoquinone's signal collapses under redox controls, it leaves the PPAR-gamma queue and stays a general antioxidant candidate only.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only — no experimental data; no compound here is shown to activate, partially activate, or block phosphorylation of PPAR-gamma in any assay.
  2. All Vina margins are at or inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; the single "win" over pioglitazone does not exceed it.
  3. The ranking is anti-correlated with measured potency (ρ = −0.8, n = 4) — a perfect or near-perfect reversal on four points is striking but fragile; one more compound could change it.
  4. Single rigid structure (9F7W, coactivator-bound, bisphenol A in the pocket — not the pioglitazone-bound conformation); no MD, no free-energy refinement, no induced-fit treatment.
  5. Docking cannot measure efficacy, so nothing here can distinguish a partial agonist from a full agonist — the paper's central question is unanswerable by its own method and needs the assay.
  6. Measured potencies come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays (EC50 vs Ki, different assay conditions); pChEMBL values are not head-to-head measurements, and no measured PPAR-gamma potency for pioglitazone was retrieved.
  7. Thymoquinone carries a PAINS quinone alert; any activity claim for it needs redox controls that were not run.
  8. The pipeline's ChEMBL target resolution failed silently once in this run (Section 3.3); the corrected run was verified by hand, but the underlying bug is unfixed and the same failure could recur on other targets.
  9. No local (Pakistan) market, pricing or access data were collected.

6. Conclusion

One ChEMBL PPAR-gamma active out-scored pioglitazone by Vina on 9F7W, but the margin sits at the edge of scoring noise, the ranking is reversed against measured potency (ρ = −0.8, n = 4), and docking cannot measure the efficacy that separates a useful partial agonist from another full agonist. Thymoquinone binds the pocket weakly and carries a PAINS quinone alert. The paper's durable findings are methodological: a centre-audited docking setup that reproduces its reference to 0.04 kcal/mol, a rank test that fails, and a silent ChEMBL target mix-up caught only by a name check. The next step is a head-to-head PPAR-gamma transactivation assay of the four leads against pioglitazone, reporting efficacy as well as potency, which will settle whether the ChEMBL order or the Vina order is real — and whether CHEMBL6145236 is a partial agonist or just another strong binder.

No Structure to Dock On: A ChEMBL Potency Analysis of PfATP4 Inhibitors Against Cipargamin, and Why the Best Number Is a 3D7-Only Number

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-11 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #42 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: PfATP4; cipargamin; malaria; artemisinin resistance; spiroindolone; ChEMBL; G358S; Plasmodium falciparum

Abstract

Malaria caused an estimated 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths in 2024, and partial artemisinin resistance is now confirmed or suspected in at least eight African countries, so a drug with a new mechanism is no longer optional. Cipargamin (KAE609), a spiroindolone that inhibits the parasite sodium pump PfATP4, cleared parasites in a median of 8 hours versus 24 hours for artemether-lumefantrine in a phase II trial, but day-28 cure was only just over 65% and the PfATP4 G358S mutation appeared in 65% of treatment failures, so the next PfATP4 drug must beat cipargamin on resistance, not on speed. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB A0A143ZZK9, corrected ChEMBL target CHEMBL6066156, 26 bioactivities across 7 compounds, PubChem verification of cipargamin, RDKit ADMET and PAINS screen) and analysed the four PfATP4 actives with measured potency against cipargamin, with docking deliberately SKIPPED because no X-ray structure of PfATP4 exists. The best record is a dihydroquinazolinone S-enantiomer at EC50 4.6 nM on the 3D7 strain, against cipargamin's literature IC50 of 0.5 to 1.4 nM, but the same compound collapses to 4,100 nM on the Dd2 strain and 7,500 nM on the G358S mutant, while its R-enantiomer holds 18.2, 26.4 and 81.3 nM across the same three assays, and two N-acetamide indoles score 150 and 790 nM with PAINS alerts. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head Na+-ATPase assay of the two enantiomers plus cipargamin on 3D7, Dd2 and G358S membrane preparations on the same plate: a lead only matters if it keeps potency where the S-enantiomer loses it.

1. Introduction

The World Health Organization's World Malaria Report 2025 estimates 282 million malaria cases and 610,000 deaths in 2024, about 95% of deaths in the African Region and mostly in children under five, with cases rising by roughly 9 million on the previous year. Partial resistance to artemisinin derivatives — the backbone of treatment for two decades — is now confirmed or suspected in at least eight African countries, with early signs that partner drugs are also losing efficacy. Pakistan illustrates the stakes close to home: after the 2022 floods added 6.6 million cases over three years, the country treated 2 million confirmed cases in 2024, down from a peak of 2.7 million in 2023 but far above the 399,097 cases of 2021, and the World Malaria Report 2025 puts Pakistan above 3 million estimated cases a year. A new antimalarial mechanism is therefore a public-health requirement, not a research luxury.

PfATP4 is the most advanced new mechanism. It is a P-type cation-transporting ATPase (1,264 amino acids, gene PF3D7_1211900) on the parasite plasma membrane that extrudes sodium against an inward gradient, maintaining the low cytosolic sodium the intraerythrocytic parasite needs to survive. The spiroindolone NITD609 was identified in 2010 as a fast-acting, low-nanomolar schizonticide whose activity was abolished by mutations in the gene encoding PfATP4, and in 2013 Spillman and colleagues showed directly that PfATP4 is a sodium efflux pump and that spiroindolones disrupt parasite sodium homeostasis through it. Cipargamin — NITD609 renamed, KAE609 — is the most advanced compound in the class: in vitro IC50 values of 0.5–1.4 nM against drug-sensitive and drug-resistant laboratory strains, activity against artemisinin-resistant isolates carrying kelch13 mutations (asexual blood-stage IC50 2.4 nM), and activity against mature stage V gametocytes, suggesting transmission-blocking potential.

Clinically, cipargamin is fast but fragile. In the randomised, open-label, dose-escalation phase II trial in sub-Saharan Africa (NCT03334747), single doses of 50–150 mg gave a median parasite clearance time of 8 hours versus 24 hours for artemether-lumefantrine, but PCR-corrected adequate clinical and parasitological response at day 28 was only just over 65% for each dose, and the treatment-emerging PfATP4 mutation G358S was detected in 65% of treatment failures. Hepatic safety was acceptable (2 of 135 cipargamin patients versus 2 of 51 controls with grade ≥2 liver-enzyme rises), so the drug's problem is not tolerability but resistance: a single point mutation, selected within one trial, undoes a monotherapy. Cipargamin will therefore only ever be used with a combination partner, and the partner — or the next PfATP4 inhibitor — must be chosen on resistance coverage, not on speed.

Structural biology has just caught up. Until October 2025 there was no experimental PfATP4 structure at all, which is why this topic was previously filed as undockable. On 20 October 2025 Haile and colleagues published a 3.7 Å cryo-EM structure of endogenous PfATP4 purified from CRISPR-engineered parasites (PDB 9N10, EMDB 48800/48801), revealing the ATP and ion-binding sites and a previously unknown apicomplexan-specific binding partner, PfABP — and showing that the experimental model differs from earlier homology models by 10.3–22.9 Å RMSD. That difference is itself a warning: any docking done on a homology model of PfATP4 before October 2025 was docking on a wrong shape.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): among ChEMBL PfATP4 actives, the best 3D7 potency does not identify the best lead — the ranking that matters is potency retained across parasite strains (3D7 versus Dd2) and on the G358S mutant that defeated cipargamin in the clinic. The test is a head-to-head Na+-ATPase assay of the top leads and cipargamin on 3D7, Dd2 and G358S preparations on the same plate.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-11 (web search; PubMed via the daily digest of 2026-11-11). Key sources: the WHO World Malaria Report 2025 and WHO EMRO Pakistan figures; Rottmann et al. 2010 for the spiroindolone discovery and NITD609 potency; Spillman et al. 2013 for PfATP4 as the sodium pump and spiroindolone target; Schmitt et al. 2022 for the phase II efficacy and the G358S finding; Ndayisaba et al. 2021 for hepatic safety; Yipsirimetee et al. 2022 for activity against artemisinin-resistant isolates and gametocytes; Haile et al. 2025 for the cryo-EM structure; Ashton et al. 2024 and Awalt et al. 2025 for the two newest PfATP4 chemotypes in ChEMBL. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 ChEMBL potency analysis (docking SKIPPED — see 2.3)

Standardised LeadForge pipeline, exactly as Papers #1/#3, except for the corrected target and the skipped docking step: UniProtKB A0A143ZZK9 → corrected ChEMBL target CHEMBL6066156 (see correction below), 26 bioactivities retrieved → PubChem verification of cipargamin (CID 44469321) → RDKit Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen versus cipargamin → RDKit ADMET/PAINS + ToxGuard Tox21 kNN → composite lead ranking (similarity × 40 + Lipinski × 20 + Veber × 10 + PAINS × 10 + tox × 20). The four compounds with a pChEMBL value are reported with their best ChEMBL record; all other records for those compounds (strain and mutant variants) are reported alongside, because the strain comparison is the point of this paper.

Target correction (verified live, 2026-11-11): the pipeline's default path is wrong for this target. The UniProtKB lookup itself is correct — A0A143ZZK9, "P-type sodium-transporting ATPase4", Plasmodium falciparum (isolate 3D7), 1,264 amino acids — but the pipeline's ChEMBL target lookup returns a list of unrelated human targets and takes the first: CHEMBL2074, "Maltase-glucoamylase", Homo sapiens (UniProt O43451). Step 2 of the first run therefore queried maltase-glucoamylase bioactivities and found 0 — correctly, for the wrong enzyme. The true PfATP4 target was found by direct ChEMBL API lookup (target component accession A0A143ZZK9 → component 23361 → CHEMBL6066156, "P-type sodium-transporting ATPase4", SINGLE PROTEIN, Plasmodium falciparum isolate 3D7), and the run was repeated with only that lookup overridden (driver script run_docking_pfatp4.py, kept in the pipeline directory). The first run's step-2 zero is discarded; its UniProt and PubChem steps were correct and are retained.

2.3 Why docking was skipped

Two independent reasons, both verified. First, the pipeline's structure picker is X-ray-only by design, and no X-ray structure of PfATP4 exists. Second, the only experimental structure that does exist — the 3.7 Å cryo-EM structure PDB 9N10 (Haile et al. 2025) — carries no bound inhibitor, so there is no co-crystallised ligand from which to derive a grid centre, and its atomic model covers only 982 of the 1,264 residues. Hand-rolling a grid centre on 9N10 (from the sodium site, the ATP site, or a homology-model pocket) would repeat the 2026-11-11 TYK2 centre-pick error, in which a hand-picked centre produced a bogus docking score. The pipeline uses dock._ligand_center and never a hand-rolled pick; with no ligand in the structure there is nothing for it to centre on. Rigid AutoDock Vina docking on a 3.7 Å cryo-EM apo structure of a membrane pump in complex with an uncharacterised modulator protein (PfABP) would produce numbers that look like results and are not. The AlphaFold model of PfATP4 was not used either: Haile et al. show the experimental model differs from homology-based predictions by 10.3–22.9 Å RMSD, so a predicted model is not a substitute for an experimental binding site. The paper is therefore a potency and resistance-landscape analysis, and says so in its title.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every lead. Two of the four leads carry a PAINS alert (Section 3.1); the alerts are reported, not hidden, and they change the validation design (Section 4.3).

2.5 Honesty limits

No docking was performed, so there are no docking scores or binding-mode claims in this paper at all — nothing is inferred about where any compound binds PfATP4. "Measured" potencies are single-assay ChEMBL maxima from biochemical Na+-ATPase activity assays (type B), not whole-parasite growth inhibition and not head-to-head values; EC50 figures from the 2024 series and IC50 figures from the 2025 series come from different laboratories, years and assay setups and cannot be ranked against each other as if they were measured on one plate. Cipargamin itself has no bioactivity record against CHEMBL6066156 in ChEMBL at all — its potency figures in this paper are literature values (Rottmann et al. 2010; Yipsirimetee et al. 2022), not ChEMBL records. The pipeline's composite score is dominated by similarity to cipargamin (40 of 100 points), so it ranks analogues above different chemotypes by construction. No experimental data were generated.

3. Results

3.1 Potency: the comparison table

3 CHEMBL5594154 — dihydroquinazolinone-3-carboxamide, R-enantiomer 0.173 64.7 EC50 18.2 nM (7.74), 3D7 Na+-ATPase assay none

5 CHEMBL6175630 — N-acetamide indole 0.120 52.5 IC50 790 nM (6.10), 3D7 Na+-ATPase assay PAINS alert

Cipargamin itself is clean by the pipeline's drug-likeness panel: MW 390.25, logP 4.34, 3 hydrogen-bond donors, 2 acceptors, TPSA 56.92 Å², 0 rotatable bonds, zero Lipinski violations, formula C19H14Cl2FN3O, no PAINS alert. Its ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across gives the highest predicted activity on the oxidative-stress response assay SR-ARE (0.407) — a prediction, not a measurement. The four leads are likewise Lipinski-clean (MW 365–469, logP 2.82–4.33, zero violations), and their ToxGuard profiles are quiet (highest single-assay predictions 0.27–0.51, all kNN read-across, not measurements).

The two dihydroquinazolinone records (ranks 2–3) are the two enantiomers of one scaffold from Ashton et al. 2024: identical molecular weight (468.88), logP (2.82) and descriptors, mirror-image SMILES, and the S-enantiomer is the more potent on 3D7 (4.6 versus 18.2 nM) — consistent with Ashton et al. advancing the S-enantiomer (S-WJM992) as frontrunner, a compound that inhibited PfATP4 Na+-ATPase activity, blocked gamete development, and showed efficacy in a mouse malaria model. The two N-acetamide indoles (ranks 4–5) are from Awalt et al. 2025, whose frontrunner WJM664 showed potent asexual-stage activity and transmission-blocking activity but low efficacy in the mouse model, attributed to PfATP4 species differences and moderate systemic exposure.

3.2 The strain problem: the best number is a 3D7-only number

The ChEMBL record for the S-enantiomer contains more than its headline 4.6 nM. The same compound was assayed on three parasite preparations in the same study (Ashton et al. 2024, document CHEMBL5576146):

Compound 3D7 wild type (CHEMBL5579326) Dd2 wild type (CHEMBL5579327) Dd2 G358S mutant (CHEMBL5579328)
CHEMBL5591927 (S-enantiomer) EC50 4.6 nM EC50 4,100 nM EC50 7,500 nM
CHEMBL5594154 (R-enantiomer) EC50 18.2 nM EC50 26.4 nM EC50 81.3 nM

The S-enantiomer loses ~890-fold going from 3D7 to Dd2 wild type, and a further ~1.8-fold on the G358S mutant (7,500 nM). The R-enantiomer, four-fold weaker on 3D7, is stable: 18.2 → 26.4 nM across strains (1.5-fold) and 81.3 nM on G358S (3.1-fold versus its own Dd2 wild type). On the Dd2 background the "worse" enantiomer is ~155-fold more potent than the "better" one (26.4 versus 4,100 nM), and on the G358S mutant it is ~92-fold more potent (81.3 versus 7,500 nM). The pipeline's best-record ranking, which takes the single highest pChEMBL value per compound, reports only the 4.6 nM and hides all of this: a reader who took Table 3.1 at face value would advance the wrong enantiomer.

Two cautions before this is over-read. First, these are biochemical Na+-ATPase activity EC50s on membrane preparations, not whole-parasite growth inhibition; a strain difference in a membrane assay may reflect preparation or assay conditions as well as target pharmacology, and the 3D7-versus-Dd2 gap for the S-enantiomer is large enough to demand replication before any mechanistic claim. Second, the G358S shift itself is small for both enantiomers (1.8-fold and 3.1-fold versus their own Dd2 wild type): unlike cipargamin, whose G358S mutation was treatment-emergent in the clinic, this chemotype shows no catastrophic cross-resistance to the cipargamin resistance mutation — the S-enantiomer's problem on Dd2 is present before G358S is introduced.

3.3 What the pipeline's filter hides

ChEMBL6066156 carries 26 bioactivities across 7 compounds, but only 4 compounds have a pChEMBL value, because the pipeline's step 2 filters on pChEMBL ≥ 5. Two further N-acetamide indoles (CHEMBL6150594, CHEMBL6162944) each record IC50 ~400 nM in the same 2025 assay series (CHEMBL6119961) with the standard relation "~" rather than "=", so ChEMBL assigns them no pChEMBL value and the pipeline excludes them entirely. Sixteen of the 26 activities are single-concentration percentage-inhibition records at 2 µM in the Na+-ATPase assays, including artenimol (CHEMBL307261, dihydroartemisinin) — a negative control of sorts, since artemisinin's target is not PfATP4. The honest count of the evidence base is therefore: four compounds with a usable potency value, two more at ~400 nM hidden by a filter, and the rest single-point screens. The PfATP4 ChEMBL target is thin — 26 activities, two documents — because most PfATP4 pharmacology lives in whole-parasite growth assays annotated to the organism rather than the target, and cipargamin itself is not among the target's compounds at all.

3.4 Comparison with published potency data

The literature values for cipargamin are stronger than any ChEMBL record in this analysis: Rottmann et al. 2010 report IC50 0.5–1.4 nM across laboratory strains, and Yipsirimetee et al. 2022 report asexual blood-stage IC50 2.4 ± 0.7 nM against artemisinin-resistant isolates (kelch13 C580Y, G449A, R539T), with male gametocyte IC50 115.6 ± 66.9 nM and female gametocyte IC50 104.9 ± 84.3 nM. The best ChEMBL lead (4.6 nM, 3D7 Na+-ATPase EC50) is therefore not more potent than cipargamin by any measure — it is roughly 3- to 9-fold weaker than cipargamin's best literature values, on a different assay type, and it collapses on Dd2. The 2024 and 2025 chemotypes are best read as proof that PfATP4 accepts more than one chemotype, not as potency improvements on cipargamin. The clinical comparison that matters is the one already published: cipargamin clears parasites in 8 hours but cures only just over 65% at day 28 as monotherapy, with G358S in 65% of failures.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether a standardised screen can rank new PfATP4 leads against cipargamin. The answer is that the question, as the pipeline asks it, is mis-specified twice. First, the pipeline's target lookup silently substitutes a different protein — human maltase-glucoamylase for the parasite sodium pump — and the correction, not the ranking, is the methodological result: any future run on a target whose ChEMBL name does not match the UniProt protein name must check the target's organism and components before trusting a score. Second, the ranking the pipeline does produce is a best-record ranking: it takes the single highest pChEMBL per compound and discards the strain and mutant records that sit beside it in the same document. For PfATP4 that discards the only information that matters, because the clinical failure of cipargamin was a resistance failure (G358S, 65% of failures), not a potency failure. A lead that is 4.6 nM on 3D7 and 7,500 nM on the G358S mutant is not a lead; it is a 3D7 artefact. The R-enantiomer, four-fold weaker on the headline number, is the better lead on every background that resembles a patient.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

The S-enantiomer's 4.6 nM is a single-assay biochemical maximum on one strain, not a head-to-head win over cipargamin, whose literature IC50 is 0.5–1.4 nM. The two enantiomers' identical composite scores (64.7) are an artefact of the scoring: identical descriptors and identical similarity to cipargamin (0.173) produce identical scores for compounds whose strain profiles differ by two orders of magnitude. The N-acetamide indoles' 150 and 790 nM are IC50s from a different assay series than the dihydroquinazolinones' EC50s and cannot be ranked against them. And no docking exists to suggest a binding-mode advantage for any compound here — the structural claims in this paper come from the published cryo-EM structure, not from this run.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

Both N-acetamide indoles carry a PAINS alert. The indole-acetamide scaffold is a known frequent-hitter chemotype, so their 150 and 790 nM values must be confirmed with detergent controls, a counter-screen against an unrelated ATPase (for example a human P-type ATPase preparation), and a check for aggregation by dynamic light scattering before any potency claim is trusted. The dihydroquinazolinones are PAINS-clean, which makes the enantiomer result cleaner to interpret — but PAINS-clean is not the same as validated: the 890-fold 3D7-to-Dd2 gap for the S-enantiomer needs the same replication as any PAINS-flagged hit.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a head-to-head Na+-ATPase assay on the same plate, the S-enantiomer will be >100-fold weaker on Dd2 than on 3D7 membrane preparations, while the R-enantiomer will stay within 3-fold. Refuted if both enantiomers hold potency on Dd2.
  2. On G358S mutant PfATP4, neither dihydroquinazolinone enantiomer will lose more than 5-fold potency versus its own Dd2 wild type, reproducing the ChEMBL record and showing no cross-resistance to the cipargamin resistance mutation. Refuted if either loses >10-fold.
  3. The R-enantiomer will match or beat the S-enantiomer in whole-parasite growth inhibition on Dd2 and on a G358S parasite line, reversing the 3D7 ranking. Refuted if the S-enantiomer remains more potent on Dd2 parasites.
  4. The two N-acetamide indoles will lose ≥50% of their apparent potency in the presence of detergent or on a counter-screen ATPase, consistent with a PAINS artefact. Refuted if potency is detergent-insensitive and counter-screen-clean.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): repeat the Na+-ATPase activity assay for both dihydroquinazolinone enantiomers, the two N-acetamide indoles and cipargamin, on 3D7 and Dd2 membrane preparations, 10-point dose–response in triplicate on the same plate, with detergent and counter-screen controls — the deliverable is a head-to-head table replacing the ChEMBL maxima, and the explicit test of hypothesis 1. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): the same assay on G358S and, if available, other PfATP4 mutant preparations, plus whole-parasite SYBR Green growth inhibition on 3D7, Dd2 and a G358S line for the surviving lead — the deliverable is the fold-change in potency, which is the only number that matters for this target. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): for the lead that survives stage 2, a dual gamete formation assay for transmission-blocking activity, and a structural rationalisation against the 9N10 cryo-EM model — mapping the resistance mutations onto the experimental structure, not docking on it — plus a P. berghei mouse-model check with the species-difference caveat from Awalt et al. in mind. Stop rule: a lead whose Dd2 potency is >100-fold worse than its 3D7 potency is a 3D7 artefact, not a publication — 3D7 potency is not the endpoint. A lead that fails the detergent or counter-screen controls is an artefact, not a lead.

5. Limitations

  1. No docking was performed — this paper contains no binding-mode or docking-score claims at all, by design (see 2.3).
  2. "Measured" potencies are single-assay ChEMBL maxima from biochemical Na+-ATPase activity assays; they are not whole-parasite growth inhibition values and not head-to-head values, and cipargamin's own figures are literature values because it has no ChEMBL record on this target.
  3. The pipeline's composite score is similarity-dominated and identical for the two enantiomers; the ranking in Table 3.1 must not be read as a potency ranking, and the best-record rule hides the strain data that reverse it.
  4. The 890-fold 3D7-to-Dd2 gap for the S-enantiomer is a single-study observation from one document; it may reflect assay conditions as well as pharmacology and needs replication.
  5. Two further compounds at IC50 ~400 nM were excluded by the pipeline's pChEMBL filter because ChEMBL records their relation as "~" with no pChEMBL value; the evidence base is thinner than the table suggests.
  6. The resistance discussion rests on one clinical mutation (G358S) and published cryo-EM and virology, not on any measurement in this run.
  7. No data are presented on pharmacokinetics, combination partners, cost, or access — cipargamin's clinical future is as a combination, which this analysis does not address.
  8. No local (Pakistan) epidemiological or access data beyond the national estimates in Section 1 were collected.

6. Conclusion

Against cipargamin, the ChEMBL PfATP4 top tier is thin and misleading at first glance: the best record is a dihydroquinazolinone S-enantiomer at EC50 4.6 nM on 3D7, against cipargamin's literature IC50 of 0.5–1.4 nM — but the same compound is 4,100 nM on Dd2 and 7,500 nM on the G358S mutant, while its R-enantiomer holds 18.2, 26.4 and 81.3 nM across the same three assays, and the two N-acetamide indoles score 150 and 790 nM with PAINS alerts. Docking was skipped because no X-ray structure of PfATP4 exists and the only experimental structure is a 3.7 Å cryo-EM apo complex with no bound inhibitor. The next step is a head-to-head Na+-ATPase assay of the two enantiomers plus cipargamin on 3D7, Dd2 and G358S preparations on the same plate: a lead only matters if it keeps potency where the S-enantiomer loses it.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-11 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #43 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: FLT3; gilteritinib; acute myeloid leukaemia; FLT3-ITD; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; F691L; drug resistance

Abstract

FLT3 internal tandem duplication (FLT3-ITD) occurs in about 25% of acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) and confers poor prognosis with high relapse rates, yet gilteritinib, the FLT3 inhibitor with a proven survival benefit in relapsed or refractory disease, extends median overall survival to only 9.3 months, and gatekeeper (F691L) and activation-loop (D835) mutations erode even that benefit. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can rank FLT3 inhibitors against gilteritinib at all. We docked gilteritinib, four established FLT3 inhibitors and seven PubChem analogues on the 2.20 Å gilteritinib-bound FLT3 kinase-domain structure 6JQR (AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, grid centred on the co-crystallised ligand centroid), after the ChEMBL activity endpoint returned HTTP 500 and the pipeline retrieved no ligands. Midostaurin scored best (−10.42 kcal/mol) and crenolanib second (−9.55), ahead of gilteritinib (−7.83) and quizartinib (−7.70), but against single-assay measured Kd values the ranking is uncorrelated (Spearman ρ = −0.3, p = 0.62, n = 5): midostaurin, the best by Vina, is the weakest measured binder (Kd 7.9 nM), while crenolanib, the strongest measured binder (Kd 0.28 nM), ranks second. Among the three type I inhibitors the reversal is exact (ρ = −1.0), so the failure is not a type I versus type II artefact. One PAINS-clean analogue (PubChem CID 150967523, −8.91 kcal/mol) out-scored gilteritinib by 1.08 kcal/mol, inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol Vina noise, and gilteritinib itself carries a PAINS alert, so neither is a lead claim. The falsifiable next step is a single-assay FLT3 kinase panel of the five inhibitors plus the three best analogues, with F691L and D835Y mutant arms: if the measured order follows the published Kd order rather than the Vina order, rigid docking must not be used to prioritise FLT3 leads on this structure.

1. Introduction

Leukaemia accounted for an estimated 487,294 new cases and 305,405 deaths worldwide in 2022 (GLOBOCAN 2022). Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is the most common acute leukaemia in adults — roughly 80% of acute leukaemia cases, with a median age at diagnosis of 68 years — and remains the deadliest. FLT3 (FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3), a class III receptor tyrosine kinase, is one of the most commonly mutated genes in AML: activating mutations occur in about 30% of cases, as internal tandem duplications (ITD) in the juxtamembrane domain in approximately 25% and as point mutations in the tyrosine kinase domain (TKD), chiefly at D835, in about 5%. FLT3-ITD disrupts the autoinhibitory juxtamembrane domain, leaving the kinase constitutively active and driving proliferation and survival through STAT5, PI3K/AKT and RAS/MAPK signalling. Patients with FLT3-ITD have higher relapse rates and inferior overall survival, and even allogeneic transplantation in first remission leaves a 30–59% relapse risk.

Gilteritinib (ASP2215) changed the relapsed/refractory setting: a type I inhibitor that binds the active (DFG-in) conformation, it inhibits FLT3 with an IC50 of 0.29 nM and AXL with 0.73 nM, about 800-fold more potent against FLT3 than against c-KIT (230 nM). In the phase 3 ADMIRAL trial (371 patients with relapsed/refractory FLT3-mutated AML), gilteritinib 120 mg daily improved median overall survival to 9.3 months versus 5.6 months with salvage chemotherapy (hazard ratio 0.64) and doubled the complete remission rate (CR/CRh 34.0% versus 15.3%), leading to FDA approval in November 2018. Quizartinib, a type II inhibitor that binds the inactive (DFG-out) conformation, improved survival in newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD AML in the QuANTUM-First trial (median overall survival 31.9 versus 15.1 months, hazard ratio 0.78) and was approved in 2023. Midostaurin, the first-generation multi-kinase inhibitor, remains the frontline FLT3 inhibitor in combination with chemotherapy, and crenolanib, a type I inhibitor, retains activity against the D835 and F691L mutants that defeat type II drugs.

The benefit is short-lived. Acquired resistance emerges through secondary kinase-domain mutations — the gatekeeper F691L, which alters the inhibitor-binding pocket and confers resistance to type I and type II inhibitors alike, and activation-loop mutations at D835, which stabilise the DFG-in conformation and defeat type II inhibitors — and through off-target mechanisms including AXL and RAS pathway activation. New scaffolds that retain activity against F691L are urgently needed, and the 2024 imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine compound 24 showed that balanced potency against FLT3-ITD, FLT3-ITD/D835Y and FLT3-ITD/F691L is achievable. The question this paper asks is narrower and prior to any of that: can a standardised docking screen rank FLT3 inhibitors against gilteritinib at all?

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen of established FLT3 inhibitors against gilteritinib on the gilteritinib-bound structure 6JQR will rank compounds in the same order as their measured binding affinities from a single-assay panel. The test is the rank correlation, not the best score.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-11 (web search; PubMed via targeted queries). The daily literature digest of 2026-11-11 screened 589 candidates and selected 8 papers, none on FLT3, so the FLT3 literature was gathered by targeted searches. Key sources: GLOBOCAN 2022 global leukaemia statistics; the 2026 ACS review of FLT3 structural biology and resistance; the ADMIRAL and QuANTUM-First phase 3 trials; the preclinical characterisation of gilteritinib; a 2020 single-assay Kd panel of five FLT3 inhibitors; the quizartinib and crenolanib primary papers; the quizartinib-bound FLT3 structure 4RT7; and a 2024 Vina study of the same four inhibitors on both DFG conformations. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt P36888 (human FLT3, 993 residues); ChEMBL target CHEMBL1974 (Receptor-type tyrosine-protein kinase FLT3, single protein). Structure: PDB 6JQR, the FLT3 kinase domain in complex with gilteritinib itself, resolution 2.20 Å, deposited 2019. Grid centre [−28.04, −10.36, −28.99] — the centroid of the co-crystallised gilteritinib (ligand C6F) computed from the deposited coordinates by the pipeline's dock._ligand_center, which excludes cofactors, glycans, lipids and modified residues. The domain matches the drug's binding site: 6JQR is the FLT3 kinase domain with gilteritinib bound in the ATP site, not another kinase and not another domain. Box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported per compound. The same grid, box and exhaustiveness were used for every compound.

A note on the run: the ChEMBL activity endpoint was down on 2026-11-11. Three pipeline runs (10:26, 10:33 and 10:34 PKT) all retrieved zero ligands — the first two because the target-components endpoint failed, the third because the activity endpoint returned HTTP 500. The outage was verified by direct query: the target endpoint returns CHEMBL1974 for UniProt P36888, while the activity endpoint returned HTTP 500 on three separate direct curls (simple and ordered queries alike). The raw JSONs of the failed runs are kept (dock-HP-030-2026-11-11-RUN1-QUERY-ONLY.json, -RUN2-QUERY-ONLY.log); no result in this paper comes from them except the gilteritinib re-dock. The fallback follows the documented 2026-11-02 FLT3 precedent: PubChem fastsimilarity_2d analogues of gilteritinib (85% threshold) plus four known FLT3 inhibitors as comparators, all docked with the identical protocol. Seven analogues were docked (one salt record excluded as multi-component); no measured potency is attached to any analogue. Gilteritinib was docked twice independently (pipeline run 1: −8.01 kcal/mol; fallback run: −7.83 kcal/mol), a run-to-run difference of 0.18 kcal/mol.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter (FilterCatalog, PAINS A/B/C) applied to every docked compound. Gilteritinib itself carries a PAINS alert, anil_di_alk_A(478), on its anilino-pyrazine core; the same alert appears on the five analogues that share that core. The alert is reported, never hidden; it changes the validation design (redox and aggregation controls).

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so differences smaller than that cannot rank compounds. A single rigid DFG-in structure cannot represent the conformational ensemble of the kinase, and it structurally disadvantages type II inhibitors, which bind the DFG-out conformation. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated. Docking was performed on wild-type FLT3 only; no F691L or D835Y mutant structure was docked.

All twelve docks are on 6JQR (2.20 Å), grid centre on the co-crystallised gilteritinib centroid. Measured Kd values are from a single 2020 panel in which all five inhibitors were assayed under the same conditions against 404 kinases (duplicate 11-point dose–response curves); they are the only measured values used for the rank test, so assay heterogeneity cannot explain a ranking failure. Gilteritinib's independent re-dock in pipeline run 1 gave −8.01 kcal/mol, 0.18 kcal/mol from the fallback value reported here.

Midostaurin out-scores gilteritinib by 2.59 kcal/mol — a margin larger than the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise band, so this is not a noise artefact. Crenolanib out-scores gilteritinib by 1.72 kcal/mol. The best analogue, CID 150967523, out-scores gilteritinib by 1.08 kcal/mol, inside the noise band. The other two analogues that out-score gilteritinib do so by 0.29 kcal/mol (CID 138319679) and 0.22 kcal/mol (CID 66642725), both inside noise. Pose consistency is good for most compounds (top-three poses within ~1 kcal/mol) except midostaurin, whose poses span 2.09 kcal/mol (−10.42 to −8.33), the least consistent set in the table. All four known comparators except gilteritinib are PAINS-clean; gilteritinib and five of its seven analogues carry the same anil_di_alk_A(478) alert.

Drug-likeness of the docked set: crenolanib is the most drug-like known inhibitor (MW 443.55, logP 3.92, zero Lipinski violations, TPSA 78.43 Å²). Gilteritinib (MW 552.72, logP 2.70, TPSA 121.11 Å²), midostaurin (MW 570.65, logP 5.91), quizartinib (MW 560.68, logP 5.86) and sorafenib (MW 464.83, logP 5.55) each carry one Lipinski violation. The best analogue CID 150967523 (MW 542.68, logP 5.49, TPSA 82.20 Å²) also carries one violation and contains an acrylamide group, a potential Michael acceptor that the PAINS filter did not flag.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

The only published Vina study of the same four inhibitors (Carranza-Aranda et al. 2024, Vina 1.1.2) docked sorafenib, midostaurin, gilteritinib and quizartinib on homology models of wild-type and ITD-mutated FLT3 in both DFG-out and DFG-in conformations, and reported higher affinities for the second-generation inhibitors (gilteritinib, quizartinib) than for the first-generation ones (sorafenib, midostaurin) on both conformations, with in vitro data supporting the predictions. Our single-structure DFG-in run gives the opposite generation order — a first-generation drug first. The difference is the structure: they sampled both conformations; we used one DFG-in structure. No published Vina scores on 6JQR itself were found for these inhibitors, so no absolute-score comparison is possible; as with VEGFR2, absolute Vina scores are protocol- and structure-dependent and cannot be compared across studies.

3.3 The standardisation problem: the ranking is uncorrelated, and exactly reversed among type I inhibitors

For the five known inhibitors, the Vina order (best first) is midostaurin > crenolanib > sorafenib > gilteritinib > quizartinib. The measured-Kd order (best first) is crenolanib (0.28 nM) > gilteritinib (1.0 nM) > quizartinib (3.3 nM) > sorafenib (5.9 nM) > midostaurin (7.9 nM). Spearman rank correlation ρ = −0.3 (p = 0.62, n = 5): no positive correlation. The compound Vina ranks first is the weakest by measured affinity, by a factor of 7.9 against gilteritinib and 28 against crenolanib.

The obvious confounder is conformation: 6JQR is a DFG-in structure, and the two type II inhibitors (quizartinib, sorafenib) bind the DFG-out conformation, so they are penalised by construction. But the failure survives removing that confounder. Among the three type I inhibitors alone — midostaurin, crenolanib and gilteritinib, all of which bind the DFG-in conformation this structure represents — the reversal is exact: Vina ranks midostaurin > crenolanib > gilteritinib, while measurement ranks crenolanib > gilteritinib > midostaurin (ρ = −1.0, n = 3). The scoring function does not recover the experimental order even where the conformation is right.

A secondary observation: the seven analogues are all gilteritinib-like pyrazine-carboxamides, not new chemotypes — except CID 150967523, which replaces the pyrazine core with an acrylamide-bearing scaffold. None of the seven beats gilteritinib beyond noise, and the best-scoring one carries the acrylamide caveat. The screen therefore produced no lead claim, only a shortlist for assay.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether docking can rank FLT3 inhibitors against gilteritinib. The answer on this structure is no — not because the setup was wrong (the grid is on the co-crystallised ligand, the structure is the drug's own complex, the reference reproduces to 0.18 kcal/mol across independent runs) but because the scoring function does not recover the experimental order, and the largest error (midostaurin, 2.59 kcal/mol) exceeds the noise band. The honest headline is therefore a negative result about the method, not a lead claim. A paper that reported "midostaurin beats gilteritinib" from the raw scores would have been wrong in exactly the way the field keeps being wrong — and midostaurin is a drug already in the clinic, so the error is checkable in a way a novel-scaffold error would not be.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Four reasons. First, the only margin that exceeds noise is the one that is wrong: midostaurin's 2.59 kcal/mol lead over gilteritinib corresponds to the weakest measured binder. Second, midostaurin has the least consistent poses in the set (2.09 kcal/mol spread), so even its own best score is the least trustworthy. Third, the ranking is uncorrelated with measurement overall (ρ = −0.3) and exactly reversed among the type I inhibitors (ρ = −1.0), so no subset of the ranking survives. Fourth, all five known inhibitors are single-digit nanomolar binders by measurement (Kd 0.28–7.9 nM); the practical difference between them is selectivity, mutant coverage and pharmacokinetics, none of which a single-structure docking score measures. The 2024 Carranza-Aranda study is the right contrast: it paired docking on both conformations with measured cell viability, and the assay was the verdict.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

Gilteritinib itself — an approved drug — carries the anil_di_alk_A(478) PAINS alert, as do five of its seven analogues. A filter that flags the reference drug cannot be used to discard the scaffold; it is a prompt for controls. The validation assay therefore needs detergent to expose aggregators, a counter-screen against an unrelated kinase, and a redox control, for every analogue including the PAINS-clean ones. The two PAINS-clean analogues (CID 150967523 and CID 66642725) are the only ones that could advance without the PAINS caveat — but CID 150967523 carries an acrylamide, so it additionally needs a glutathione-reactivity check before any potency claim, since a covalent warhead would make a reversible-binding assay misleading.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a single-assay FLT3 kinase panel (ADP-Glo or TR-FRET, gilteritinib control on the same plate), the Kd/IC50 order of the five known inhibitors will follow the published Kd order (crenolanib > gilteritinib > quizartinib > sorafenib > midostaurin), not the Vina order. Refuted if the Vina order reproduces.
  2. Re-docking the same five inhibitors on the quizartinib-bound structure 4RT7 (DFG-out, 3.1 Å) will change the Vina order — quizartinib and sorafenib will improve relative to the type I drugs — showing the ranking is structure-dependent. Refuted if the order is identical.
  3. The best analogue CID 150967523 will inhibit FLT3-ITD MV4-11 proliferation with an IC50 within 10× of gilteritinib's 0.92 nM (i.e. ≤ ~10 nM) and retain activity against FLT3-ITD/F691L within 10× of its FLT3-ITD value. Refuted if its IC50 exceeds 100 nM or the F691L shift exceeds 10×.
  4. The anil_di_alk_A(478) alert on the gilteritinib scaffold is a filter artefact for this chemotype, not a redox or aggregation artefact: the analogues' kinase inhibition will survive detergent and redox controls. Refuted if activity collapses under those controls.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): FLT3 kinase assay for the five known inhibitors plus the three best analogues (CID 150967523, CID 138319679, CID 66642725), 10-point dose–response in triplicate, gilteritinib control on the same plate, with detergent, aggregation and redox controls; wild-type, F691L and D835Y enzymes in the same panel to test hypotheses 1 and 4. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): MV4-11 and MOLM-14 viability for the analogues that survive stage 1, plus Ba/F3 cells expressing FLT3-ITD, FLT3-ITD/F691L and FLT3-ITD/D835Y, to test hypothesis 3. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): re-docking on 4RT7 and a 100 ns molecular-dynamics plus MM-GBSA rescoring to test hypothesis 2, and a glutathione-reactivity assay for CID 150967523. Stop rule: if stage 1 reproduces the published Kd order, the Vina ranking is discarded and the project proceeds on measured potency only; if an analogue fails the detergent or redox controls, it is dropped regardless of its score.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only — no experimental data; no compound here is shown to inhibit FLT3 in any assay.
  2. The ChEMBL activity endpoint was down (HTTP 500, verified three times), so no ChEMBL-derived leads were screened; the analogues come from PubChem similarity only and carry no measured potency.
  3. Single rigid DFG-in structure (6JQR); type II inhibitors are penalised by construction, and no MD or free-energy refinement was run.
  4. Wild-type FLT3 only — no F691L or D835Y mutant structure was docked, so nothing here addresses the resistance mutations that motivate the work.
  5. Rank correlation computed on n = 5 known inhibitors (n = 3 for the type I trio) — a perfect ρ = −1.0 on three points is striking but fragile.
  6. Measured Kd values come from one 2020 panel; other assays give different absolute values (crenolanib 0.28 nM here versus 0.74 nM in Galanis et al.), though the rank order is the same.
  7. Gilteritinib's re-dock varied by 0.18 kcal/mol between independent runs (conformer sampling); all margins below ~0.2 kcal/mol are therefore meaningless.
  8. No local (Pakistan) market, pricing or access data were collected; gilteritinib and quizartinib availability and cost in Pakistan were not assessed.

6. Conclusion

Five established FLT3 inhibitors docked on the gilteritinib-bound structure 6JQR do not rank in their measured potency order (Spearman ρ = −0.3, n = 5), and among the three type I inhibitors the reversal is exact (ρ = −1.0): midostaurin, the weakest measured binder, scores best by 2.59 kcal/mol. No PubChem analogue beats gilteritinib beyond Vina noise, and the reference drug itself carries a PAINS alert. The benchmark's value is the negative result: rigid docking on this structure cannot prioritise FLT3 inhibitors, and any lead claim built on these scores alone would be unjustified. The next step is a head-to-head FLT3 kinase assay of the five inhibitors and the three best analogues, with F691L and D835Y mutant arms, which will settle whether the published Kd order or the Vina order is real.
