5 CHEMBL4126686 0.330 72.5 IC50 2.0 nM (8.70) none
6 CHEMBL4127923 0.312 71.6 EC50 2.0 nM (8.70) none
7 CHEMBL4128240 0.304 71.4 EC50 1.0 nM (9.00) none
8 CHEMBL4130102 0.293 71.1 EC50 2.0 nM (8.70) none
9 CHEMBL4127873 0.278 70.4 EC50 2.0 nM (8.70) none
10 CHEMBL492465 0.278 69.8 IC50 2.0 nM (8.70) none

All ten leads are sub-3 nM by their best record; the measured-potency spread is under one log unit (pChEMBL 8.70–9.66). CHEMBL1229211 is dolutegravir's own ChEMBL record (identical MW 419.38, logP 1.35, similarity 1.0) — the duplicate is an internal consistency check, not a second compound. Cabotegravir (CHEMBL2403238) is the most potent by its best record (IC50 0.22 nM), ahead of dolutegravir's own record (0.5 nM) and ahead of the literature head-to-head values for dolutegravir (2.7 nM strand transfer). Ranks 4–10 are seven analogues from the BMS-707035 series (Naidu et al. 2018, Bioorg Med Chem Lett; document CHEMBL4118197), all reported at EC50/IC50 2.0 nM in the same strand-transfer antiviral assay — a single-assay cluster, not seven independent measurements.

3.2 Comparison with published potency data

The literature head-to-head values are less extreme than the ChEMBL maxima: dolutegravir strand-transfer IC50 2.7 nM (Kobayashi et al. 2011) against the ChEMBL top record of 0.5 nM for the same compound — a five-fold gap between a single-assay maximum and the standard reference value. The same caution applies to cabotegravir's 0.22 nM: it is a top record, not a head-to-head win over dolutegravir. The 2025 quadruple-mutant study is the relevant comparison instead: against G140S/Q148H-centred quadruple mutants, all three approved second-generation INSTIs lose potency while the investigational compound 4d retains it — a difference invisible in the wild-type table above, where everything is sub-3 nM.

3.3 The standardisation problem: similarity is not potency

The composite score's 40-point similarity component makes the ranking a similarity contest: the BMS-707035 series (similarity 0.28–0.34 to dolutegravir) scores 70–73 while dolutegravir and cabotegravir score 92–99, although the measured potencies are within one log unit of each other and the BMS compounds are, on their best records, as potent as dolutegravir itself. A reader who took the composite score at face value would conclude the BMS series is far worse; the data say it is not. Two further cautions: the EC50 figures (cell-based antiviral activity) and IC50 figures (enzyme strand transfer) in the table measure different things and cannot be ranked against each other; and the seven BMS records at exactly 2.0 nM are one assay's output, so the apparent depth of that chemotype is a single data point repeated seven times.

Drug-likeness is clean across the top 10: MW 361–505, logP 0.64–2.55, zero Lipinski violations except CHEMBL4127873 (MW 504.58, one violation). No Tox21 flags were predicted for any compound by kNN read-across — a prediction, not a measurement. Dolutegravir's long-acting sibling cabotegravir is already the clinical answer to adherence (injectable, every 2 months); a new oral INSTI must therefore beat dolutegravir on resistance, not on wild-type potency or convenience.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether a standardised screen can rank new integrase leads against dolutegravir. The answer is that the question is obsolete for wild-type enzyme: every compound in the top tier is sub-3 nM, and the ranking that the pipeline produces is driven by structural similarity to the reference, not by potency. The paper's contribution is therefore the reframe, plus a documented pipeline failure: for polyprotein targets, the standard UniProt→ChEMBL→PDB chain silently substitutes a different enzyme (protease for integrase) at all three steps, and the correction — not the docking — is the methodological result. Any future run on a viral polyprotein target must check the ChEMBL target's assay descriptions and the PDB entry's molecule name before trusting a score.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Cabotegravir's 0.22 nM is a single-assay ChEMBL maximum, not a head-to-head win; the literature value for dolutegravir in the same type of assay is 2.7 nM, and the two were not measured on the same plate. The BMS series' seven identical 2.0 nM records are one assay, not seven confirmations. And no docking exists to suggest a binding-mode advantage for any compound here — the structural claims in this paper come from the published cryo-EM intasome literature, not from this run.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No PAINS alerts were found. The validation assay still needs standard controls (detergent to expose aggregators; a counter-screen against an unrelated enzyme) and, critically, a resistant-intasome arm — wild-type potency alone cannot distinguish the leads.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a strand-transfer assay on wild-type intasomes, the IC50 order of cabotegravir, dolutegravir and the BMS-707035 series will be within 3-fold of each other — i.e. no meaningful wild-type difference. Refuted if any lead is >10-fold better than dolutegravir.
  2. On G140S/Q148H intasomes, dolutegravir will lose 5- to 6-fold potency (as published) while at least one BMS-series compound retains wild-type potency. Refuted if all leads lose potency together.
  3. The investigational compound 4d will outperform all top-10 leads on the quadruple-mutant panel (G140S/Q148H + L74/E92/T97 + E138A/K), reproducing the published result. Refuted if it does not.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): strand-transfer enzyme assay for cabotegravir, dolutegravir, BMS-707035 and the two most potent BMS analogues, wild-type integrase, 10-point dose–response in triplicate, same plate — the deliverable is a head-to-head table, replacing the ChEMBL maxima. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): the same assay on G140S/Q148H and G118R mutant integrases, with compound 4d as comparator — the deliverable is the fold-change in IC50, which is the only number that matters for this target. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): for the lead that survives stage 2, a cell-based antiviral assay (single-round infection) on wild-type and quadruple-mutant virus, plus a comparison of the published cryo-EM intasome structures (8FNG and the 2023 series) to rationalise the mutant result structurally. Stop rule: a lead that is potent on wild-type but loses potency on G140S/Q148H exactly like dolutegravir is a failure, not a publication — wild-type potency is not the endpoint.

5. Limitations

  1. No docking was performed — this paper contains no binding-mode or docking-score claims at all, by design (see 2.3).
  2. "Measured" potencies are single-assay ChEMBL maxima from heterogeneous assays (enzyme IC50 vs cell-based EC50); they are not head-to-head values, and dolutegravir's own record (0.5 nM) differs five-fold from the literature reference value (2.7 nM).
  3. The pipeline's composite score is similarity-dominated; the ranking in Table 3.1 must not be read as a potency ranking.
  4. The seven BMS-series records at 2.0 nM come from a single assay and a single publication; they are not independent confirmations.
  5. The resistance discussion rests on published cryo-EM and virology, not on any measurement in this run.
  6. No data are presented on pharmacokinetics, long-acting formulation, or cost — cabotegravir's clinical advantage is adherence, which this analysis does not address.
  7. No local (Pakistan) epidemiological or access data beyond the national estimates in Section 1 were collected.

6. Conclusion

Against dolutegravir, the ChEMBL HIV-1 integrase top tier is uniformly sub-3 nM: cabotegravir leads on its best record (IC50 0.22 nM), dolutegravir's own record is 0.5 nM, and seven BMS-707035-series analogues share 2.0 nM in one assay — but the pipeline's similarity-dominated ranking obscures that equality, and none of it separates the leads where it matters, on resistant intasomes. Docking was skipped because no X-ray structure of HIV-1 integrase with a strand-transfer inhibitor exists and the pipeline's default pick was the wrong enzyme. The next step is a strand-transfer assay on wild-type versus G140S/Q148H intasomes, with compound 4d as comparator: a lead only matters if it keeps potency where dolutegravir loses it.

Sitagliptin Is the Weakest Compound in Its Own Benchmark: A Centre-Audited DPP-4 Docking Study on 4A5S Where Vina Rank and Measured Potency Are Uncorrelated

Type 2 diabetes affects 589 million adults worldwide (1 in 9), and Pakistan has one of the highest age-standardised prevalences at 31.4% (~34.5 million adults).

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-10 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #41 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: DPP-4; sitagliptin; dipeptidyl peptidase-4; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; type 2 diabetes; ChEMBL; triazolopiperazine

Abstract

Type 2 diabetes affects 589 million adults worldwide (1 in 9), and Pakistan has one of the highest age-standardised prevalences at 31.4% (~34.5 million adults). Sitagliptin, the first DPP-4 inhibitor (FDA-approved October 2006, IC50 18 nM), prolongs incretin action by blocking the enzyme that degrades GLP-1 and GIP — but newer triazolopiperazine analogues are ~100-fold more potent in vitro, and it is not obvious that docking can tell them apart. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB P27487 → ChEMBL CHEMBL284, 47 bioactivities → PubChem verification of sitagliptin → RDKit ADMET/PAINS → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on PDB 4A5S, 1.62 Å, grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised inhibitor N7F centroid, 0.00 Å) and docked the top five compounds by composite score against sitagliptin. The most similar compound to sitagliptin (CHEMBL1203953, similarity 0.563, IC50 0.18 nM) could not be docked at all — its hydrochloride salt has two SMILES fragments, which ligand preparation rejects. Of the four that docked, the Vina order (CHEMBL5870057 −9.47, sitagliptin −8.95, CHEMBL5951803 −8.85, CHEMBL5220750 −7.88 kcal/mol) is uncorrelated with the measured-potency order (Spearman ρ = 0.0, n = 4): sitagliptin ranks second by Vina yet is ~100-fold weaker than the leads by measurement (18 nM vs 0.18–0.27 nM). Worse, the single most potent compound in the whole set (CHEMBL98869, Ki 0.082 nM, pChEMBL 10.09) was never docked, because the pipeline docks only the top five by a similarity-dominated composite score. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head enzyme assay of CHEMBL5870057 and CHEMBL5951803 against sitagliptin on DPP-4 plus a DPP-8/DPP-9/FAP selectivity panel: a lead only matters if its ~100-fold potency advantage survives the same plate — and if it keeps sitagliptin's selectivity.

1. Introduction

The International Diabetes Federation estimates 589 million adults aged 20–79 live with diabetes (1 in 9), projected to reach 853 million by 2050; Pakistan's age-standardised prevalence is 31.4%, about 34.5 million adults, with 226,752 diabetes-related deaths in 2024. DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase-4, CD26) is a serine exopeptidase that inactivates the incretin hormones GLP-1 and GIP within minutes of their release; inhibiting it raises active incretin levels, increases glucose-dependent insulin secretion and suppresses glucagon, with a low risk of hypoglycaemia. Sitagliptin (MK-0431, Januvia) was the first DPP-4 inhibitor, approved by the FDA in October 2006: a β-amino amide built on a triazolopiperazine, with an IC50 of 18 nM against DPP-4 and >40,000-fold selectivity over other proline-selective peptidases. Its crystal structure in complex with DPP-4 (PDB 1X70) shows the β-amino group hydrogen-bonding the Glu205/Glu206 dyad and Tyr662, with the trifluorophenyl group in the S1 hydrophobic pocket.

The field has not stood still. The same triazolopiperazine series that produced sitagliptin was refined to sub-nanomolar inhibitors — compound 46b at IC50 0.18 nM, with its own DPP-4 co-crystal structure — and a 2026 preprint re-docked five gliptins on 1X70 (sitagliptin −9.181, linagliptin −8.965 kcal/mol; re-dock RMSD 1.14 Å), while a 2026 screen of 15,034 compounds proposed new sitagliptin analogues. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking benchmark can actually rank such compounds against sitagliptin — or whether the score is noise, the ranking is a similarity contest, and the most potent compound is the one the protocol never docks.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): Vina scores on 4A5S will not recover the measured potency order of DPP-4 inhibitors against sitagliptin (Spearman ρ near zero), because the score spread (≤1.6 kcal/mol) is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and the measured potencies span ~100-fold.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-10 (web search; PubMed via the daily digest of 2026-11-10). Key sources: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th edition 2025 for burden; Kim et al. 2005 for sitagliptin's discovery and IC50 18 nM; Kim et al. 2008 for the sub-nanomolar triazolopiperazine series (compound 46b, IC50 0.18 nM, co-crystal structures); the 2026 ResearchSquare preprint docking five gliptins on 1X70; the 2026 Biomed Pharmacol J screen of 15,034 sitagliptin analogues; and the Molecules 2023 DPP-4 SAR review. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 LeadForge pipeline (same protocol as Papers #1/#3)

Standardised LeadForge pipeline: UniProtKB P27487 (DPP-4, Homo sapiens, 766 aa) → ChEMBL CHEMBL284 ("Dipeptidyl peptidase 4", SINGLE PROTEIN), 47 bioactivities retrieved (pChEMBL ≥ 5) → PubChem PUG REST verification of sitagliptin (CID 4369359; MW 407.32, formula C16H15F6N5O — matches the reference) → RDKit Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen vs sitagliptin → RDKit ADMET/PAINS + ToxGuard Tox21 kNN (12 assays) → composite lead ranking (similarity × 40 + Lipinski × 20 + Veber × 10 + PAINS × 10 + tox × 20) → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 docking of the top five by composite score plus the query, on the best-resolution ligand-bound X-ray structure. Raw output: hidden_files/dock-HP-001-2026-11-10.json.

2.3 Structure and centre audit

The pipeline selected PDB 4A5S — human DPP-4 (soluble form), 1.62 Å, "Crystal structure of human DPP4 in complex with a novel heterocyclic DPP4 inhibitor" — rather than the sitagliptin-bound 1X70 (2.5 Å), because the picker takes the highest-resolution ligand-bound X-ray structure for the target. Both are the same enzyme and the same active site (Glu205/Glu206 dyad); the choice is a resolution trade-off, not a target error, and it is reported here so the reader can judge it. Centre audit (verified from the cached PDB file, 2026-11-10): the co-crystallised inhibitor N7F (chain A, residue 901, 37 atoms) has centroid (14.14, 35.87, 54.84) — identical to the docking grid centre (14.14, 35.87, 54.84), distance 0.00 Å. The grid is exactly on the crystallographic binding site.

2.4 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every lead. No compound in the top 10 carries a PAINS alert.

2.5 Honesty limits

Vina's documented error is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so score differences under ~2 kcal/mol cannot rank compounds. "Measured" potencies are single-assay ChEMBL maxima (IC50 vs Ki, different laboratories and years), not head-to-head values; the 18 nM figure for sitagliptin is the literature reference value (Kim et al. 2005), not a ChEMBL record — the pipeline's QUERY entry carries no ChEMBL activity of its own. The composite score is dominated by similarity to sitagliptin (40 of 100 points). No experimental data were generated; no selectivity data (DPP-8/DPP-9/FAP) are presented for the leads.

3. Results

3.1 Potency: the comparison table

None of the five leads has a ChEMBL preferred name; all are investigational compounds. Three of the four docked leads are triazolopiperazines — the same scaffold as sitagliptin: CHEMBL5870057 (chlorobenzoyl-triazolopiperazine), CHEMBL5951803 (cyanophenyl-triazolopiperazine acetamide) and the undocked CHEMBL1203953 (benzyl-substituted triazolopiperazine hydrochloride). CHEMBL5220750 is a different chemotype, a proline-based dipeptide-like ester; CHEMBL98869 is a piperidine amide.

3.2 Comparison with published potency data

The ChEMBL maxima are consistent with the published series: CHEMBL5951803 and CHEMBL1203953 at IC50 0.18 nM match compound 46b of Kim et al. 2008 (IC50 0.18 nM, same triazolopiperazine class, co-crystallised with DPP-4). Sitagliptin's literature IC50 is 18 nM (Kim et al. 2005) — about 100-fold weaker than the four leads (0.18–0.27 nM). The 2026 preprint's Vina score for sitagliptin on 1X70 (−9.181) agrees with ours on 4A5S (−8.95) to within 0.23 kcal/mol, well inside Vina noise — the structure choice (4A5S vs 1X70) does not change the result.

3.3 The standardisation problem: three failures in one benchmark

Failure 1 — the ranking is noise. Vina order: CHEMBL5870057 (−9.47) > sitagliptin (−8.95) > CHEMBL5951803 (−8.85) > CHEMBL5220750 (−7.88). Measured order: CHEMBL5951803 (0.18 nM) > CHEMBL5870057 (0.21 nM) > CHEMBL5220750 (0.27 nM) > sitagliptin (18 nM). Spearman ρ = 0.0 (n = 4): no correlation at all. The entire Vina spread is 1.59 kcal/mol — inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol error — while the measured potencies span ~100-fold. Sitagliptin, the weakest compound by measurement, ranks second by Vina.

Failure 2 — the most similar compound could not be docked. CHEMBL1203953 is the closest analogue to sitagliptin in the set (similarity 0.563) and jointly the most potent (IC50 0.18 nM) — and it failed ligand preparation because its SMILES is a hydrochloride salt with two fragments ("RDKit molecule has 2 fragments. Must have 1."). The same failure mode removed the most potent lead class in Paper #39 (HP-004, kotalanol sulfonium salt). Salts are routine in medicinal chemistry; a pipeline that cannot desalt its inputs silently drops exactly the compounds a chemist would most want to test.

Failure 3 — the most potent compound was never docked. CHEMBL98869 (Ki 0.082 nM, pChEMBL 10.09) is the most potent compound in the entire 26-lead set, and it was not docked because the pipeline docks only the top five by composite score — and the composite score is similarity-dominated, so a structurally different compound (similarity 0.184) ranks sixth and is excluded. The docking cut is made on the wrong variable: it should be made on measured potency, not on similarity to the reference.

Drug-likeness is clean across the docked set: MW 345–552, logP 1.62–4.36, zero Lipinski violations except CHEMBL1203953 (one violation, MW 551.89). No Tox21 flags were predicted for any compound by kNN read-across — a prediction, not a measurement. Sitagliptin's clinical advantage is not potency — it is selectivity (>40,000-fold over DPP-8/DPP-9) and a 20-year safety record; no selectivity data exist for the leads, and potency without selectivity is not a drug.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether a standardised screen can rank new DPP-4 leads against sitagliptin. The answer is no — not because the pipeline is broken in one place, but because three independent selection steps each discard the signal: the docking score cannot rank a 100-fold potency spread (ρ = 0.0); the ligand preparation cannot handle salts; and the docking cut excludes the most potent compound on similarity grounds. The paper's contribution is therefore the audit, not a ranking: any of the four leads could be the best compound, and this benchmark cannot say which. That is a usable result — it tells the next experimenter to skip the docking and go straight to the enzyme assay.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

CHEMBL5870057's −9.47 kcal/mol is the best Vina score, but it is 0.52 kcal/mol ahead of sitagliptin — a quarter of Vina's error — while being ~86-fold more potent by measurement. The Vina "win" and the potency "win" point at different compounds, and neither is decisive. The 0.18 nM figures are single-assay ChEMBL maxima, not head-to-head values; the 2026 preprint's scores and ours agree, but agreement between two Vina runs is not validation against experiment.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No PAINS alerts were found. The validation assay still needs standard controls (detergent to expose aggregators; a counter-screen against an unrelated enzyme) and, critically, a selectivity panel — DPP-8 and DPP-9 inhibition is the known toxicity route for this class, and sitagliptin's >40,000-fold selectivity is the bar the leads must clear.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a head-to-head DPP-4 enzyme assay on the same plate, CHEMBL5870057, CHEMBL5951803 and CHEMBL1203953 will each be >50-fold more potent than sitagliptin (IC50 < 0.4 nM vs 18 nM). Refuted if any lead is within 10-fold of sitagliptin.
  2. On a DPP-8/DPP-9 selectivity panel, at least one lead will be <100-fold selective (i.e. it will fail where sitagliptin succeeds). Refuted if all leads match sitagliptin's >40,000-fold selectivity.
  3. Re-docking with the salt desalted (CHEMBL1203953 as free base) will place it within 1 kcal/mol of CHEMBL5870057 — i.e. the docking failure was a preparation artefact, not a binding problem. Refuted if the desalted compound scores >2 kcal/mol worse than the triazolopiperazine leads.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): desalt CHEMBL1203953 and re-dock all five leads plus CHEMBL98869 on 4A5S (six compounds, same grid) — the deliverable is a corrected docking table, and a check on whether the potency-based docking cut changes the ranking. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): recombinant human DPP-4 enzyme assay, 10-point dose–response in triplicate, same plate, for sitagliptin, CHEMBL5870057, CHEMBL5951803, CHEMBL1203953 (free base) and CHEMBL98869 — the deliverable is a head-to-head IC50 table replacing the ChEMBL maxima. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): DPP-8/DPP-9/FAP selectivity panel for the best two leads, then an oral glucose tolerance test in mice for the lead that survives the panel. Stop rule: a lead that is potent on DPP-4 but <100-fold selective over DPP-8/DPP-9 is a failure, not a publication — potency without selectivity is not a gliptin.

5. Limitations

  1. Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol error exceeds the entire score spread (1.59 kcal/mol); no docking ranking in this paper is meaningful.
  2. "Measured" potencies are single-assay ChEMBL maxima from heterogeneous assays (IC50 vs Ki); they are not head-to-head values, and sitagliptin's 18 nM is a literature reference value, not a ChEMBL record.
  3. The most potent compound in the set (CHEMBL98869, Ki 0.082 nM) was never docked; the most similar compound (CHEMBL1203953) failed ligand preparation as a salt.
  4. No selectivity data (DPP-8/DPP-9/FAP) are presented for any lead; sitagliptin's selectivity advantage is from the literature.
  5. The structure used (4A5S, N7F-bound) is not the sitagliptin-bound structure (1X70); the two give consistent Vina scores for sitagliptin (−9.181 vs −8.95), but no re-docking RMSD validation was run on 4A5S.
  6. No data are presented on pharmacokinetics, cost, or access — in Pakistan, gliptin affordability is a larger barrier than potency, and this analysis does not address it.
  7. No local (Pakistan) epidemiological or access data beyond the national estimates in Section 1 were collected.

6. Conclusion

Against sitagliptin on DPP-4 4A5S, the benchmark fails three ways at once: Vina rank and measured potency are uncorrelated (Spearman ρ = 0.0, n = 4), with sitagliptin — ~100-fold the weakest by measurement — ranking second by Vina; the most similar lead (CHEMBL1203953, IC50 0.18 nM) could not be docked because it is a salt; and the most potent compound in the set (CHEMBL98869, Ki 0.082 nM) was never docked because the pipeline cuts on similarity, not potency. The next step is not more docking: it is a head-to-head enzyme assay with a DPP-8/DPP-9 selectivity panel, on the compounds this benchmark could not rank.

The Weakest Drug Scores Best: Acarbose Out-Docks Three Nanomolar Iminosugars on ntMGAM 3L4Y — and the Most Potent Lead Class Could Not Be Docked at All

Type 2 diabetes affects 589 million adults worldwide — one in nine — and Pakistan carries the world's highest age-standardised prevalence at 31.4%, with about 34.5 million adults affected.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-10 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #39 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: alpha-glucosidase; acarbose; maltase-glucoamylase; iminosugar; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; type 2 diabetes; ChEMBL

Abstract

Type 2 diabetes affects 589 million adults worldwide — one in nine — and Pakistan carries the world's highest age-standardised prevalence at 31.4%, with about 34.5 million adults affected. α-Glucosidase inhibitors such as acarbose blunt postprandial glucose by blocking the intestinal enzymes that finish carbohydrate digestion, but acarbose is a weak inhibitor (IC50 456–750 μM in standard assays) whose undigested carbohydrate causes flatulence in 74% of users, diarrhoea in 31% and abdominal pain in 19%. The gap this paper attacks is whether a standardised docking screen can rank better α-glucosidase leads against acarbose. We ran the LeadForge pipeline (UniProtKB O43451 → ChEMBL CHEMBL2074, 55 bioactivities → PubChem verification → RDKit ADMET/PAINS → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7) and docked the top leads plus acarbose into the 1.80 Å N-terminal maltase-glucoamylase structure 3L4Y, with the grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised inhibitor centroid (0.00 Å). Acarbose scored best by Vina (−6.55 kcal/mol) despite being roughly 100,000-fold weaker by measurement than the best lead, a silyl-iminosugar with Ki 2.3 nM that scored only −5.02. Among the three successfully docked leads the rank correlation is weak (Spearman ρ = +0.50, n = 3), and the fifth-ranked lead — a kotalanol-class sulfonium salt with IC50 470 nM — could not be docked at all, because the pipeline rejects multi-fragment salt SMILES. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head ntMGAM inhibition assay for the three iminosugars against acarbose: if the measured order follows the ChEMBL record rather than the Vina order, docking must not be used to prioritise α-glucosidase leads on this structure, and the salt-form kotalanol analogue must be re-tested after desalting.

1. Introduction

The International Diabetes Federation's Diabetes Atlas (11th edition, 2025) estimates 589 million adults aged 20–79 live with diabetes — one in nine people — projected to reach 853 million by 2050. Pakistan has the world's highest age-standardised diabetes prevalence (31.4%), about 34.5 million adults affected and an estimated 226,752 diabetes-related deaths in 2024. Postprandial hyperglycaemia is a major driver of vascular complications, and the final step of carbohydrate digestion — hydrolysis of oligosaccharides to glucose by membrane-bound intestinal α-glucosidases, principally maltase-glucoamylase (MGAM) — is a validated drug target precisely because it acts in the gut lumen: inhibitors need not be absorbed at all.

Acarbose is the prototype. A complex oligosaccharide, it competitively and reversibly inhibits pancreatic α-amylase and the intestinal α-glucoside hydrolases, delaying carbohydrate digestion and lowering postprandial glucose without stimulating insulin secretion; it lowers HbA1c by roughly 0.5–1.0% as monotherapy. Its weaknesses are potency and tolerability: in standard in vitro assays its α-glucosidase IC50 is 456–750 μM (assay- and enzyme-source-dependent), and the undigested carbohydrate reaching the colon causes flatulence (74%), diarrhoea (31%) and abdominal pain (19%) in US placebo-controlled trials, with 25–45% of users discontinuing α-glucosidase inhibitors for gastrointestinal reasons. A more potent inhibitor, active at nanomolar rather than micromolar concentrations, could in principle achieve the same glucose control with less undigested carbohydrate — but only if potency is measured, not assumed from a docking score.

The natural-product literature already contains such compounds. Salacia reticulata, used in Ayurvedic medicine for type 2 diabetes, yields the sulfonium-sugar inhibitors salacinol and kotalanol; de-O-sulfonated kotalanol inhibits ntMGAM with Ki 0.03 μM — about 2,000-fold better than the clinical compounds — and its crystal complex with ntMGAM (PDB 3L4Y) defines the binding site used here. Recent work continues the same search: coumarin–triazole conjugates reported in 2026 reached IC50 1.0 μM against α-glucosidase versus 750 μM for acarbose in the same assay, with in vivo antihyperglycaemic activity in diabetic mice; and a 2025 machine-learning virtual screen of 100,000+ compounds found selective α-glucosidase inhibitors engaging the catalytic Asp526.

Hypothesis (falsifiable): under one standardised protocol, a Vina screen of ChEMBL MGAM actives against acarbose on 3L4Y will rank compounds in the same order as their measured potencies. The test is the rank correlation, not the best score.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Searches were run on 2026-11-10 (web search; PubMed/bioRxiv via the daily digest of 2026-11-10). Key sources: IDF Diabetes Atlas 11th edition (2025) for burden; the FDA acarbose label for adverse-event frequencies; Sim et al. 2010 for the 3L4Y structure and the Salacia inhibitors; the 2026 coumarin–triazole study; the 2025 machine-learning virtual-screening study; and the critical assessment of plant α-glucosidase screening with acarbose as reference. Every citation in the References section was verified (journal, year, DOI or PMID checked, not invented).

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina protocol, exactly as Papers #1/#3: Vina 1.2.7; target UniProt O43451 (human maltase-glucoamylase, MGAM); ChEMBL target CHEMBL2074; 55 bioactivities retrieved (pChEMBL ≥ 5), 26 leads after RDKit filtering and ranking; the top 5 leads docked, including the reference query itself. Structure: PDB 3L4Y, the N-terminal catalytic subunit of human intestinal MGAM in complex with the Salacia-derived inhibitor NR4-8II, resolution 1.80 Å. Grid centre [−2.01, −19.26, −20.85] — audited against the co-crystallised ligand NR4 centroid computed from the deposited coordinates: distance 0.00 Å, i.e. the grid is exactly on the catalytic site. Best of three poses reported per compound. The same grid, box and exhaustiveness were used for every compound including acarbose.

One lead, CHEMBL3815109, failed to dock: its ChEMBL record is a sulfonium chloride salt (two SMILES fragments), and the pipeline's ligand preparation rejects multi-fragment molecules ("RDKit molecule has 2 fragments. Must have 1."). It is reported as a failed dock, not silently dropped, and the paper's conclusions do not depend on it.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to every docked compound. No compound in the docked set carries a PAINS alert.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol — larger than most of the differences in this paper. A single rigid structure (3L4Y, inhibitor-bound conformation) cannot represent the conformational ensemble of MGAM, and carbohydrate-binding sites are shallow and solvent-exposed, which is exactly where rigid docking is weakest. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated. Acarbose has no ChEMBL MGAM bioactivity meeting the pipeline's pChEMBL ≥ 5 retrieval threshold, so its measured potency is taken from the published literature (456–750 μM, assay-dependent), not from the same ChEMBL pull as the leads.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Vina best (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Measured potency (ChEMBL, top record) pChEMBL PAINS
Acarbose (query) −6.55 −6.55, −6.35, −6.24 IC50 456–750 μM (literature α-glucosidase assays; no ChEMBL MGAM record ≥ pChEMBL 5) — none
CHEMBL120226 −6.35 −6.35, −6.12, −5.87 Ki 4.0 nM 8.40 none
CHEMBL432221 −5.02 −5.02, −4.82, −4.71 Ki 2.3 nM 8.64 none
CHEMBL2442258 −4.26 −4.26, −4.07, −4.06 IC50 60 nM 7.22 none
CHEMBL3815109 FAILED — IC50 470 nM 6.33 none

All successful docks are on 3L4Y (1.80 Å), grid centre exactly on the co-crystallised NR4 centroid (0.00 Å). The three leads are iminosugars: two silyl-substituted 1-deoxynojirimycin analogues (CHEMBL120226, CHEMBL432221) and a small N-methyl iminosugar (CHEMBL2442258, MW 207.23). The failed compound, CHEMBL3815109, is a sulfonium-sugar salt of the kotalanol class.

Acarbose scores best by Vina while being the weakest inhibitor by measurement by roughly five orders of magnitude: its literature IC50 (456–750 μM) is ~100,000–300,000-fold higher than the best lead's Ki (2.3 nM). The Vina spread across the four successful docks is 2.29 kcal/mol, but the best-vs-second margin (acarbose vs CHEMBL120226, 0.20 kcal/mol) is far inside noise, and the leads' own order is only weakly related to measurement: Spearman ρ = +0.50 (n = 3) among the three docked leads. Pose consistency is good (top-three poses within 0.31 kcal/mol for every compound), so the failure is in the scoring, not in pose sampling.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

Published Vina scores for α-glucosidase show the same pattern of weak absolute values: plant-derived leads against α-glucosidase scored −6.66 and −5.64 kcal/mol versus acarbose −4.27 kcal/mol in a 2025 study, and a Nardostachys jatamansi study reported virolin at −9.6 kcal/mol against α-glucosidase. The absolute numbers move with the structure, the grid and the ligand set; only the within-protocol ranking in Table 3.1 is interpretable — and Section 3.3 shows that ranking fails its own test. Note also that all scores here (−4 to −6.5) are far weaker than the kinase benchmarks in Papers #37–#38 (−9 to −12): carbohydrate-binding clefts give small, polar ligands little surface to grip, and cross-target score comparison is meaningless.

3.3 The standardisation problem: the reference wins by scoring, loses by measurement

Two failures are visible at once. First, the reference drug beats every lead by Vina while being ~10⁵-fold weaker by measurement — the exact inversion of what a screen is supposed to do, and the largest potency/score disconnect in this 5-paper run. A plausible mechanism is size: acarbose (MW 645.61) fills far more of the shallow cleft than the small iminosugars (MW 207–337), and Vina's scoring rewards contact count, so the big, weak binder out-scores the small, tight binders. Second, the most interesting chemotype in the set — the kotalanol-class sulfonium salt, from the same class as the most potent ntMGAM inhibitor ever reported (Ki 0.03 μM) — never got a score at all, because the pipeline cannot prepare salt forms. The screen thus fails on both axes: it ranks the weakest compound first, and it cannot evaluate the strongest class.

Drug-likeness cuts the other way for acarbose: three Lipinski violations (MW 645.61, logP −8.72) would normally disqualify a lead, but acarbose acts in the gut lumen with <2% systemic absorption, so Lipinski's rules do not apply to it — a reminder that the pipeline's drug-likeness flags must be read target by target. The iminosugar leads are all Lipinski-clean (MW 207–337, logP −3.26 to −0.54, zero violations). No Tox21 flags were predicted for any compound by kNN read-across — a prediction, not a measurement.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The question was whether docking can rank α-glucosidase leads against acarbose. The answer on this structure is no, and the reason is instructive: the scoring function appears to reward molecular size in a shallow, solvent-exposed cleft, so the large oligosaccharide reference out-scores small iminosugars that bind 10⁵-fold more tightly. The paper's contribution is therefore a caution with a mechanism, not a lead claim — and a second caution about pipeline hygiene: a standard ligand-preparation step silently (here, loudly) excludes salt-form compounds, which for this target means excluding the most potent known chemotype.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, acarbose's 0.20 kcal/mol margin over CHEMBL120226 is far inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the measured-potency gap runs the other way by five orders of magnitude — no rescoring of these numbers can bridge that. Third, the leads' own rank correlation (ρ = +0.50, n = 3) is computed on three points and is fragile; the honest statement is that the ranking is uninformative, not that it is weakly positive.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No PAINS alerts were found. The validation assay still needs standard controls (detergent to expose aggregators; a counter-screen against α-amylase, since acarbose inhibits both and selectivity over amylase is part of the tolerability case) and, for the kotalanol analogue, a desalting step before any assay — the chloride counter-ion is not the active species.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a head-to-head ntMGAM inhibition assay (same enzyme preparation, same substrate, same day), the IC50 order will be CHEMBL432221 ≈ CHEMBL120226 < CHEMBL2442258 ≪ acarbose — i.e. the ChEMBL order, not the Vina order. Refuted if acarbose is the most potent.
  2. Desalting CHEMBL3815109 (removing the chloride counter-ion) and re-docking the cation on 3L4Y will give a Vina score comparable to the other iminosugars (−4 to −6.5), and its measured IC50 will be in the same range as its ChEMBL record (470 nM). Refuted if it scores far outside that range or fails again.
  3. A 100 ns molecular-dynamics + MM-GBSA rescoring will rank the three iminosugars above acarbose, reversing the rigid-Vina order. Refuted if acarbose still leads.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): ntMGAM enzyme inhibition assay (p-nitrophenyl-α-D-glucopyranoside substrate) for the three iminosugars + acarbose + desalted CHEMBL3815109, 10-point dose–response in triplicate, same plate. Stage 2 (weeks 4–6): α-amylase counter-screen for the best lead, to test whether it spares the enzyme whose inhibition contributes to acarbose's gastrointestinal burden; plus a Caco-2 permeability check, since a luminally restricted inhibitor is the desired profile. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): MD + MM-GBSA rescoring to test hypothesis 3, and a postprandial glucose excursion test in a diabetic mouse model for the lead that survives stages 1–2 — the same design that validated the 2026 coumarin–triazole series. Stop rule: if stage 1 reproduces the ChEMBL order, the Vina ranking is discarded and the project proceeds on measured potency only; if the desalted kotalanol analogue is the most potent, it becomes the lead regardless of its docking score.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only — no experimental data; no compound here is shown to inhibit MGAM in any assay.
  2. All Vina margins in this paper are inside or near the ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; the best-vs-second margin is 0.20 kcal/mol.
  3. Single rigid structure (3L4Y, inhibitor-bound); no MD, no free-energy refinement, no induced-fit or explicit-water treatment — particularly limiting for a shallow carbohydrate-binding cleft.
  4. Rank correlation computed on n = 3 — fragile; one more compound could change it.
  5. Acarbose's measured potency comes from heterogeneous literature assays (456–750 μM), not from a head-to-head MGAM measurement against the leads; the ChEMBL MGAM record for acarbose did not meet the retrieval threshold.
  6. One of five leads could not be docked (salt-form prep failure); the paper's ranking is therefore incomplete by design, and the missing compound belongs to the most potent known class.
  7. No local (Pakistan) market, pricing or access data were collected; acarbose is off-patent and cheap, so a new inhibitor needs a potency-and-tolerability case, not a price case.

6. Conclusion

On ntMGAM 3L4Y, acarbose — a micromolar inhibitor — out-scored three nanomolar iminosugars by Vina, while the kotalanol-class lead could not be docked at all because its salt form breaks the pipeline's ligand preparation. The benchmark's value is the double negative: rigid docking on this structure cannot rank α-glucosidase inhibitors, and the pipeline cannot evaluate the most potent chemotype in the set. The next step is a head-to-head ntMGAM assay including the desalted kotalanol analogue, which will settle whether the ChEMBL order or the Vina order is real.

Five Sub-Nanomolar Binders, No Winner: A Corrected Vina Benchmark of Small-Molecule TNF-alpha Trimer Inhibitors on 2AZ5, and Why the Biologic Reference Cannot Be Docked

Rheumatoid arthritis affects about 18 million people worldwide, and TNF-alpha blockade — etanercept, a 150 kDa TNFR-Fc fusion protein approved in 1998 — remains among its most effective therapies, but biologics require injection, cost, and carry infection risk including tuberculosis reactivation.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-09 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #4 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: TNF-alpha; tumor necrosis factor; etanercept; rheumatoid arthritis; small-molecule inhibitor; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; trimer interface

Abstract

Rheumatoid arthritis affects about 18 million people worldwide, and TNF-alpha blockade — etanercept, a 150 kDa TNFR-Fc fusion protein approved in 1998 — remains among its most effective therapies, but biologics require injection, cost, and carry infection risk including tuberculosis reactivation. Oral small molecules that bind the TNF trimer interface (SPD304, UCB-9260) have reached only the tool-compound and early-clinical stages. We benchmarked five sub-nanomolar ChEMBL TNF binders (Ki 0.03–0.083 nM) against the trimer-interface pocket with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on PDB 2AZ5 (2.1 Å), after discarding a first run that docked them on a spin-labelled TNF monomer (5UUI) at a spin-label site — a pocket that does not exist in a monomer. On the corrected trimer structure the five leads scored −8.83 to −9.67 kcal/mol, a 0.84 kcal/mol spread inside Vina noise, with rank agreement to measured Ki of Spearman rho = 0.73 (n = 5). Etanercept, the clinical reference, cannot be docked by Vina at all: it is a 150 kDa protein, not a small molecule. The falsifiable next step is a TNF–TNFR1 binding assay plus a trimer-stability (subunit-exchange) assay comparing CHEMBL3640299 with UCB-9260, to test whether the best docking score tracks the asymmetric-trimer mechanism or only pocket fit.

1. Introduction

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) affects approximately 18 million people worldwide (World Health Organization). Tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha), a homotrimeric cytokine, is a central driver of RA synovitis and joint destruction. Etanercept — a dimeric fusion of two soluble p75 TNF-receptor extracellular domains to human IgG1 Fc, 150 kDa — was the first anti-TNF biologic approved for RA (US FDA, November 1998), after Moreland et al. showed its efficacy in a randomised trial of patients who had failed conventional disease-modifying drugs (N Engl J Med 1997;337:141–147). It works as a decoy receptor, soaking up soluble TNF before it reaches cell-surface receptors. Adalimumab and infliximab followed the same logic with monoclonal antibodies.

Biologics have two structural weaknesses a small molecule could fix: they must be injected, and they suppress TNF systemically, carrying serious-infection and tuberculosis-reactivation risk. An oral small molecule that neutralises the TNF trimer would be a major advance. The trimer offers two distinct small-molecule mechanisms. SPD304, the proof-of-concept compound (He et al., Science 2005), binds at the subunit interface and promotes trimer disassembly into inactive monomers and dimers, but only at micromolar potency (IC50 ~22 µM biochemical). UCB-9260 and its successors take the opposite approach: a single molecule buried in the trimer core stabilises an asymmetric, receptor-incompetent trimer that can recruit only two of three TNFR1 molecules, with reported Kd 13 nM and NF-κB IC50 202 nM, and oral efficacy in mouse arthritis models; the related compound SAR441566 advanced to clinical trials. No small-molecule TNF inhibitor is approved.

Hypothesis: within one tight chemotype family of sub-nanomolar ChEMBL TNF binders, Vina docking at the trimer-interface pocket will recover the measured potency order but will not separate the leads beyond noise — so the differentiator between candidates must be mechanism, not affinity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

PubMed, ChEMBL and targeted web searches were run on 2026-11-09 for etanercept, TNF small-molecule inhibitors, SPD304, UCB-9260 and SAR441566. Only verified sources are cited; potency values for UCB-9260 are attributed to the developer's technical documentation where no primary paper was verified.

2.2 Molecular docking

Target identification used UniProtKB (human TNF-alpha, P01375) and ChEMBL (CHEMBL1825, tumour necrosis factor, single protein, human; 60 bioactivities retrieved, 25 leads ranked by a composite of drug-likeness, PAINS cleanliness and a Tox21 k-nearest-neighbour read-across panel; no similarity term was available because the reference drug has no small-molecule fingerprint). The reference drug etanercept was NOT docked: PubChem holds no small-molecule record for a 150 kDa fusion protein, and Vina cannot score a biologic. It is the clinical reference only.

The pipeline's first structure pick was discarded. It selected PDB 5UUI (1.4 Å) and centred the grid on its only non-water ligand, the MTSL spin label MTN (0.00 Å from the MTN centroid). Audit of the 5UUI file showed a single TNF monomer (chain A, 136 residues), the spin label covalently attached to engineered Cys77 (SG 4.16 Å from the label centroid), and the grid centre 16.85 Å from the monomer centroid. The small-molecule pocket is the trimer-interface cavity; it does not exist in a monomer. Those scores (same five leads, −6.38 to −7.26 kcal/mol, Spearman rho = 0.075 against measured Ki) are reported here only as the discarded run and are not used for any conclusion. The corrected run used PDB 2AZ5 (TNF-alpha with a small-molecule inhibitor, SPD304, 2.10 Å). The grid centre [−13.87, 71.43, 26.91] is the centroid of the co-crystallised SPD304 (ligand 307, 80 atoms), verified 0.24 Å from the oligomer CA centroid — the trimer-interface pocket itself. Docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, a 22.5 Å box, exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses, identical protocol for all five leads. The re-dock was run with the pipeline's own Vina wrapper (D.dock) on the corrected structure; the script is hidden_files/redock_hp048.py.

2.3 PAINS screen

All five docked leads were screened with the RDKit PAINS filter; all were PAINS-clean.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking estimates binding free energy at one static structure; it does not measure trimer disruption, asymmetric stabilisation, or receptor signalling. Vina carries ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. No molecular dynamics, no free-energy refinement and no laboratory data were generated. 2AZ5 shows an SPD304-disrupted oligomer, not an intact trimer; the pocket in the intact trimer may differ. ChEMBL Ki values come from different assay designs and are compared as reported pChEMBL values.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured potency (ChEMBL) Best Vina affinity, 2AZ5 (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL3640299 Ki 0.03 nM (pChEMBL 10.52) −9.67 −9.67, −9.18, −9.13 none
CHEMBL3640298 Ki 0.0521 nM (pChEMBL 10.28) −9.49 −9.49, −8.96, −8.85 none
CHEMBL3642435 Ki 0.03 nM (pChEMBL 10.52) −9.16 −9.16, −9.02, −8.65 none
CHEMBL3642496 Ki 0.072 nM (pChEMBL 10.14) −9.16 −9.16, −9.05, −9.03 none
CHEMBL3642511 Ki 0.083 nM (pChEMBL 10.08) −8.83 −8.83, −8.75, −8.38 none
Etanercept (reference) Approved biologic, 150 kDa not dockable — —

All five leads are drug-like (MW 442.4–542.6; logP 0.59–1.83; 0–1 Lipinski violations; all Veber-pass) and from one closely related chemotype family (two close analogue pairs). Their Tox21 read-across maxima were low (0.19–0.33 for four leads; 0.59 for CHEMBL3642435). The best-to-worst spread is 0.84 kcal/mol — inside Vina noise, so no lead is distinguishable from any other by docking. Rank agreement with measured Ki was Spearman rho = 0.73 (n = 5): the most potent measured binder by rank, CHEMBL3640299, also docked best, and the weakest measured binder, CHEMBL3642511, docked worst. Pose consistency was good (best-pose spreads 0.13–0.64 kcal/mol).

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these five ChEMBL compounds on 2AZ5 was found; the comparison is original. The structural literature frames the result: SPD304's own mechanism was established crystallographically on this same structure (2AZ5), and the UCB series was developed against the same central pocket.

3.3 The wrong-structure run, for the record

The discarded 5UUI run scored the same five leads at −6.38 to −7.26 kcal/mol — systematically ~2.3 kcal/mol weaker than the corrected run, with no rank agreement to measured Ki (Spearman rho = 0.075). The numbers looked plausible in isolation: tight poses, sensible magnitudes, a clear "winner" (CHEMBL3642435). They were meaningless, because the grid sat on a spin label on a monomer. This is the audit's value: without checking the PDB file, a wrong-structure benchmark is indistinguishable from a right one.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The benchmark's finding is twofold, and the methodological half matters more. First, within a tight sub-nanomolar family, Vina recovers the potency order qualitatively (rho = 0.73) but cannot rank the candidates: a 0.84 kcal/mol spread across five compounds whose measured Ki values span less than threefold is noise, not signal. Second, and more importantly, the structure pick dominated everything — the same compounds, the same protocol, the wrong structure, and the rank correlation collapsed from 0.73 to 0.08 while every score stayed plausible. For a target whose pocket exists only in the oligomer, the structure audit is not a quality check; it is the experiment.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

CHEMBL3640299 "wins" by 0.18 kcal/mol over CHEMBL3640298 and 0.51 kcal/mol over the tied pair — all far inside noise. Its measured Ki (0.03 nM) is tied with CHEMBL3642435, which docked 0.51 kcal/mol worse. Nothing here justifies prioritising one lead over another on affinity. The honest conclusion is that all five bind the pocket well, and the choice between them must come from mechanism and developability: does the compound disrupt the trimer (SPD304-like) or stabilise the asymmetric form (UCB-9260-like), and what is its oral exposure and safety margin?

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All five leads are PAINS-clean, so aggregation and redox artefacts are not the expected confounders. The real artefact risk for TNF binders is different: a compound can occupy the pocket without changing signalling. The validation assay must therefore read out function (TNFR1 binding, NF-κB signalling, trimer stability), not occupancy alone.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL3640299 stabilises the asymmetric trimer (UCB-9260-like) rather than disrupting it: in a human/mouse TNF subunit-exchange assay it will prevent hybrid-trimer formation like UCB-9260, not promote monomer release like SPD304.
  2. The five leads' NF-κB IC50 values rank in the same order as their Ki values, not their Vina scores — testing whether binding or docking is the misleading readout.
  3. CHEMBL3642435, whose Tox21 read-across maximum (0.59) is the highest of the five, shows the narrowest safety margin in a hepatocyte viability counterscreen.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): surface plasmon resonance Kd for recombinant human TNF for CHEMBL3640299, CHEMBL3640298 and UCB-9260 (reference), plus a TNF–TNFR1 competition binding assay. Stage 2 (weeks 4–7): HEK293 NF-κB reporter assay at 10 pM TNF, and an L929 TNF-cytotoxicity protection assay, for the same three compounds; plus a subunit-exchange assay (mixed human/mouse TNF) to classify the mechanism as disruption versus asymmetric stabilisation. Stage 3 (weeks 8–12): collagen antibody-induced arthritis (CAIA) in Balb/c mice at the published UCB-9260 precedent dose (150 mg/kg orally, twice daily, 7 days), with clinical arthritis scoring, for the best Stage-2 compound only. A lead passes only if it blocks signalling at nanomolar concentrations and shows the asymmetric-stabilisation signature, not merely a good docking score.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only: no binding, signalling or animal data; affinity is not mechanism.
  2. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol exceeds the entire 0.84 kcal/mol spread; no lead is claimed superior.
  3. Single structure (2AZ5, an SPD304-disrupted oligomer); no intact-trimer structure (e.g. a UCB-bound complex) was cross-checked, and no molecular dynamics was run.
  4. Spearman correlation on n = 5 is descriptive; no p-value is claimed.
  5. Etanercept cannot be scored by Vina, so the benchmark has no quantitative reference point — the comparison to the biologic is clinical, not computational.
  6. ChEMBL Ki values mix assay designs; the two Ki 0.03 nM leads are tied in the ranking.
  7. SPD304 itself was not re-docked as a control; that is a follow-up step, not a result here.
  8. All data are preclinical; no human data exist for any of the five leads.

6. Conclusion

On the TNF trimer-interface structure 2AZ5, five sub-nanomolar ChEMBL binders docked at −8.83 to −9.67 kcal/mol with rank agreement to measured Ki of Spearman rho = 0.73 — but the 0.84 kcal/mol spread is inside Vina noise, so docking cannot choose between them. The run also showed that the structure audit is decisive: the same compounds on a spin-labelled monomer scored plausibly yet meaninglessly (rho = 0.075). The next step is functional: a subunit-exchange assay to classify each lead's mechanism, before any claim of an oral alternative to etanercept.

Posaconazole Still Leads, and the Most Potent Measured Inhibitor Scores Worst: A Vina Benchmark of Trypanosoma cruzi CYP51 Inhibitors on 4C27 That Fails to Reproduce the Potency Order

Chagas disease affects an estimated 6–7 million people, and the only approved drugs, benznidazole and nifurtimox, cure poorly in the chronic stage.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-09 · Health Papers Agent — Paper HP-025 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Trypanosoma cruzi; CYP51; Chagas disease; posaconazole; albaconazole; sterol 14alpha-demethylase; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina

Abstract

Chagas disease affects an estimated 6–7 million people, and the only approved drugs, benznidazole and nifurtimox, cure poorly in the chronic stage. Posaconazole, a sterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51) inhibitor, looked like the answer until the CHAGASAZOL trial showed 81–92% of posaconazole-treated patients PCR-positive for Trypanosoma cruzi DNA at follow-up, versus 38% on benznidazole — so the target, not just the drug, is in question. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 9 November 2026 (UniProtKB Q7Z1V1 → ChEMBL CHEMBL1075110, 56 ligands → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on PDB 4C27, 1.95 Å, grid centred exactly on the co-crystallised inhibitor, 0.00 Å from its centroid). Posaconazole re-docked at −10.57 kcal/mol and no lead beat it: the best challenger, CHEMBL5189694 (measured Kd 24 nM), scored −9.40, 1.17 kcal/mol worse — inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. The striking failure is albaconazole (CHEMBL298817): the most potent measured inhibitor in the set (IC50 1.0 nM against T. cruzi CYP51) but the worst docking score, −8.16, 2.41 kcal/mol behind posaconazole. Across the four compounds with measured values, docking rank and potency rank correlate at Spearman ρ = −0.2. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head recombinant TcCYP51 inhibition assay of albaconazole, posaconazole and CHEMBL5189694 under identical conditions, with MM-GBSA rescoring to test whether the ranking failure is a scoring artefact.

1. Introduction

Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis), caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, infects an estimated 6–7 million people worldwide, mostly in Latin America, causes more than 10,000 deaths every year, and puts more than 100 million people at risk across 21 endemic continental Latin American countries (World Health Organization, 2024). About 20–30% of infected people develop chronic disease — progressive cardiomyopathy and/or gastrointestinal dysfunction — after an indeterminate stage that can last years or decades. There is no vaccine, and the only approved drugs, benznidazole and nifurtimox, have low cure rates in the chronic stage and considerable toxicity.

Sterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51) is the most studied alternative target. T. cruzi depends on endogenous sterol biosynthesis for membrane formation, and CYP51 catalyses the oxidative removal of the 14α-methyl group from the sterol core — the same step azole antifungals block in fungi. The case for the target looked strong: the antifungal triazole posaconazole showed trypanocidal activity in murine models, and the crystal structure of T. cruzi CYP51 in complex with posaconazole (PDB 3K1O, 2.89 Å) showed the drug coordinated to the haem iron in the active site (Lepesheva et al., 2010). On that basis posaconazole entered clinical trials for chronic Chagas disease.

The CHAGASAZOL trial ended that optimism. In a prospective randomised trial of 78 adults with chronic T. cruzi infection, posaconazole 400 mg twice daily, posaconazole 100 mg twice daily, and benznidazole 150 mg twice daily were given for 60 days, with parasite DNA monitored by real-time PCR during treatment and 10 months after (Molina et al., 2014). During treatment almost every patient tested PCR-negative. At follow-up, 92% of the low-dose posaconazole group and 81% of the high-dose group tested PCR-positive, versus 38% of the benznidazole group (intention-to-treat; per-protocol 90% and 80% versus 6%). Posaconazole showed antitrypanosomal activity but failed significantly more often than benznidazole. The question this paper asks is therefore sharper than "find a better CYP51 inhibitor": it is whether docking on the CYP51 structure can even rank known inhibitors correctly — because if it cannot reproduce the potency order of compounds whose measured values are already known, it cannot be trusted to prioritise new ones.

The structural literature gives the target a second chance. The same group that solved the posaconazole complex also solved T. cruzi CYP51 with fluconazole (PDB 3KHM) and with the experimental inhibitor VNF, and identified the VNI/VNF carboxamide scaffold as selective for trypanosomal CYP51 — it does not inhibit the human ortholog (selectivity index > 200), kills more than 99% of T. cruzi amastigotes at 1 µM, and shows low general cytotoxicity (Lepesheva et al., 2007). VNI has been reported to cure both acute and chronic Chagas disease in mice (cited in Friggeri et al., 2014). A later β-phenylimidazole series reached EC50 values of 1.0–5.5 nM against T. cruzi amastigotes, with two distinct binding modes that exploit the substrate-access channel entrance and the haem-propionate ceiling of the cavity (Friggeri et al., 2014). And an N-indolyl-oxopyridinyl series, crystallised in PDB 4C27, suppressed ≥99.8% parasitaemia in mice at 25 mg/kg twice daily for 4 days (Vieira et al., 2014). The target is therefore not dead — but the clinical failure of its best-known drug means any computational ranking must first prove it can reproduce known potencies.

The falsifiable hypothesis of this paper is that AutoDock Vina docking on the high-resolution T. cruzi CYP51 structure 4C27 ranks known CYP51 inhibitors in the same order as their measured potencies. The paper tests that hypothesis against the measured ChEMBL values, against Vina's own noise floor, and against the internal reproducibility of docking the same molecule twice — and reports where the hypothesis fails as carefully as where it holds.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 9 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-09.md, PubMed, ChEMBL (EBI), UniProtKB, PubChem and RCSB PDB. Key sources: WHO (2024) for the disease burden; Molina et al. (2014) for the CHAGASAZOL result; Lepesheva et al. (2010) for the posaconazole/fluconazole/VNF co-crystal structures; Chen et al. (2010) for the fluconazole-bound structures 2WUZ/2WX2; Lepesheva et al. (2007) for the VNI/VNF selective scaffold; Lepesheva (2011) for the target review; Friggeri et al. (2014) for the β-phenylimidazole series and the VNI mouse-cure report; Vieira et al. (2014) for the 4C27 structure and the N-indolyl-oxopyridinyl series. Every citation in this paper was verified against its publisher or database record on the day of writing; no citation was generated from memory.

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 9 November 2026 with the reference drug posaconazole as the query: UniProtKB target identification (Q7Z1V1, sterol 14-alpha demethylase, Trypanosoma cruzi strain CL Brener, gene CYP51) → ChEMBL target CHEMBL1075110, 56 bioactivities retrieved → PubChem verification of the query → RDKit Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen (25 compounds) → RDKit ADMET/PAINS panel plus ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) → composite ranking → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 docking. A data-quality note: several of the 56 retrieved ChEMBL ligands contain aluminium and failed RDKit sanitisation (explicit-valence warnings in the run log); they were excluded by the screen and none is in the docked set.

Docking used PDB 4C27 (1.95 Å), the T. cruzi CYP51 structure co-crystallised with the N-indolyl-oxopyridinyl inhibitor 26N (Vieira et al., 2014), auto-picked by the pipeline as the highest-resolution inhibitor-bound structure. The grid (22.5 Å box, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses) was centred on the co-crystallised inhibitor. Centre audit, performed after the run from the PDB file itself: the docking centre [−10.75, −39.85, −23.88] is exactly the centroid of the chain-B 26N inhibitor (0.00 Å apart; the 92-atom entry is the two alternate conformations of the 46-atom ligand), while the chain-B haem centroid is 9.9 Å away — the grid is on the inhibitor site, not on the haem. The reference drug posaconazole was docked twice by the pipeline (once as the QUERY, once as its ChEMBL record CHEMBL1397), which gives an internal reproducibility check. Measured potencies quoted below are the values recorded in ChEMBL for target CHEMBL1075110, as returned by the pipeline's known_activity field; note that they mix Kd and IC50 values, which are not interchangeable, so the rank comparison is indicative, not a formal correlation.

Two deliberate limitations of the structure choice are stated here, not buried: (i) 4C27 is bound to the 26N inhibitor, not to posaconazole — the posaconazole-bound structure 3K1O exists but at lower resolution (2.89 Å), so posaconazole was re-docked into a site shaped by a different ligand; (ii) Vina treats the haem iron as a fixed point charge and cannot model the coordinate bond between an azole nitrogen and the Fe(II/III) centre, which is the dominant interaction for every azole in this set.

2.3 PAINS screen

The RDKit PAINS filter was applied to every ranked lead. A PAINS alert is reported, never hidden; it changes the validation design (redox and aggregation controls in the proposed assay). The filter flagged posaconazole itself (see §3.1) — an approved drug — which is reported as a filter false-positive illustration, not as a liability of the drug.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring error is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so only margins above ~2 kcal/mol are treated as real differences. No experimental data were generated. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. Measured potencies come from ChEMBL records for the target and were not re-measured; the Kd/IC50 mixture (§2.2) limits the rank analysis to four compounds.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Posaconazole (as CHEMBL1397) CHEMBL1397 −10.14 Kd 18.0 nM (pChEMBL 7.75) 700.79 4.57 1 Alert
CHEMBL5189694 CHEMBL5189694 −9.40 Kd 24.0 nM (pChEMBL 7.62) 528.39 4.03 1 Clean
CHEMBL3431164 CHEMBL3431164 −8.58 IC50 50.12 nM (pChEMBL 7.30) 435.50 3.78 0 Clean

Posaconazole still leads. No lead in the docked set beats the posaconazole re-dock, and the best challenger, CHEMBL5189694 — an unnamed tetrazole-triazole azole (C22H15F7N6O2) with a measured Kd of 24 nM — trails by 1.17 kcal/mol, inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise: a tie, not a loss. CHEMBL3431164, a non-azole pyridazine (C24H26FN5O2, IC50 50.12 nM), trails by 1.99 kcal/mol and is also inside the noise band.

Two internal checks frame the table. First, the same molecule docked twice — posaconazole as QUERY (−10.57) and as CHEMBL1397 (−10.14) — differs by 0.43 kcal/mol. That is the preparation noise of this run (essentially identical to the 0.42 kcal/mol found in the PfDHODH benchmark of the same pipeline), and it is the floor below which no difference in this table means anything. Second, the RDKit PAINS filter flags posaconazole itself. Posaconazole is an approved drug with a known safety record; the flag is a property of the filter's promiscuity rules on large triazoles, and it is reported here precisely so that the clean PAINS results for the other four compounds are not over-read as a safety claim — the filter's false-positive rate on this chemotype is demonstrated inside this very table.

3.2 The ranking failure: albaconazole

Albaconazole (CHEMBL298817; INN/USAN, research code UR-9825, ChEMBL maximum phase 2) is the most potent measured inhibitor in the set: ChEMBL records an IC50 of 1.0 nM against T. cruzi CYP51 (pChEMBL 9.00), 18-fold more potent than posaconazole's recorded Kd of 18.0 nM. It is also the most drug-like compound in the table (MW 431.83, logP 3.07, zero Lipinski violations, PAINS-clean). And it has the worst docking score in the set: −8.16 kcal/mol, 2.41 kcal/mol behind the posaconazole re-dock — a margin that clears Vina's noise band, so this is a real ranking failure, not a tie.

Across the four distinct compounds with measured values, the measured potency order is albaconazole (1.0 nM) > posaconazole (18 nM) > CHEMBL5189694 (24 nM) > CHEMBL3431164 (50.12 nM), while the docking order is the near-reverse: posaconazole (−10.57) > CHEMBL5189694 (−9.40) > CHEMBL3431164 (−8.58) > albaconazole (−8.16). Spearman rank correlation ρ = −0.2 (n = 4) — no correlation, slightly negative. The single most likely mechanistic cause is stated in §2.2: Vina cannot model the azole–haem iron coordinate bond, and albaconazole's potency plausibly depends on exactly that interaction plus the quinazolinone scaffold's fit, neither of which the scoring function rewards. A second contributor is the structure choice: the grid is shaped by the 26N inhibitor in 4C27, and albaconazole's difluorophenyl–triazole geometry may fit the posaconazole-shaped pocket of 3K1O better than the 26N-shaped pocket used here — a hypothesis that is testable by re-docking on 3K1O (see §4.4).

3.3 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these four compounds on T. cruzi CYP51 was found in the literature sweep, so there is no published docking table to compare against. The structural literature does, however, give a qualitative check: the β-phenylimidazole series of Friggeri et al. (2014) binds in two distinct modes — one entering the substrate-access channel, the other under the haem-propionate ceiling — and the 26N inhibitor of 4C27 occupies the channel mode. Our grid, centred on 26N, therefore samples the channel mode. Compounds whose potency depends on the ceiling mode would be systematically under-scored here, which is a second testable explanation for albaconazole's result.

3.4 The standardisation problem: the target, not the drug

The CHAGASAZOL numbers (§1) are the standardisation problem for this target. Posaconazole cleared parasites during treatment in essentially all patients and still failed in 81–92% at follow-up. Two readings are possible: the drug never reached sterilising exposure in the chronic-stage tissue compartments, or CYP51 inhibition alone cannot sterilise chronic infection. The VNI mouse-cure report (Friggeri et al., 2014) and the ≥99.8% parasitaemia suppression of the 4C27 series (Vieira et al., 2014) argue the target can work in animals — but both are acute or short-course mouse models, and CHAGASAZOL is a chronic human trial. The honest statement is that the target's clinical validity is unproven, and a docking benchmark cannot settle it; it can only rank compounds for the assay that can.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The paper's hypothesis — that Vina on 4C27 reproduces the measured potency order — fails. That failure is the result, and it is more useful than a win would have been: it tells the next run what not to do. A pipeline that had reported albaconazole as the weakest compound and moved on would have discarded the most potent measured inhibitor in its own dataset. The reframe is that for CYP51, docking is a pose generator and a gross filter (it correctly puts all five compounds in a narrow −8 to −11 kcal/mol band, consistent with all of them being real binders), not a ranker. Ranking needs a scoring function that sees the haem coordination — MM-GBSA rescoring, or a metal-aware method — and a second structure (3K1O) to test pocket-shape dependence.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

There is no win in this table, and the near-win deserves the same caution: CHEMBL5189694's −9.40 is 1.17 kcal/mol behind posaconazole, inside noise, and its measured Kd (24 nM) is also essentially tied with posaconazole's (18 nM). The two compounds are indistinguishable by either measure used here. The 0.43 kcal/mol preparation noise (§3.1) means even the posaconazole re-dock value itself carries a ±0.4 kcal/mol preparation uncertainty before Vina's own ±1–2 kcal/mol is added. Nothing in this table supports prioritising one compound over another on docking score alone.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

Posaconazole's PAINS alert (§3.1) is the design constraint in miniature: a filter that flags an approved drug cannot be used as a go/no-go gate on this chemotype. The proposed validation therefore treats PAINS as a prompt for controls — redox-cycling and aggregation controls in the enzyme assay, and a detergent control in the cell assay — rather than as an exclusion criterion. Albaconazole and CHEMBL3431164 are PAINS-clean, which is a genuine (if modest) advantage for them; CHEMBL5189694 is also clean.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Albaconazole binds TcCYP51 more tightly than posaconazole under identical assay conditions. Measurement: recombinant TcCYP51 spectral binding (Soret shift) and reconstituted enzyme inhibition for albaconazole, posaconazole and CHEMBL5189694 in the same run, same buffer, same substrate (eburicol). Fails if albaconazole's IC50 is not lower than posaconazole's.
  2. The ranking failure is a pocket-shape artefact of 4C27. Measurement: re-dock all five compounds on the posaconazole-bound structure 3K1O (2.89 Å) with the same protocol, and on 4C27 with the haem iron retained as a metal constraint. Fails if albaconazole still ranks last on both.
  3. The ranking failure is a scoring-function artefact. Measurement: MM-GBSA rescoring of the Vina poses for all five compounds. Fails if the MM-GBSA order still anti-correlates with the measured order.
  4. Albaconazole's potency translates to the parasite. Measurement: T. cruzi amastigote assay (Tulahuen strain, as in Friggeri et al., 2014) for albaconazole vs posaconazole, with a human CYP51 counter-screen for selectivity. Fails if albaconazole's amastigote EC50 is not lower than posaconazole's, or if it inhibits human CYP51 at comparable concentrations.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): recombinant TcCYP51 expression and purification (published constructs exist; Lepesheva et al., 2010), spectral binding titrations for the five compounds. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): reconstituted enzyme inhibition assay (lanosterol/eburicol substrate, NADPH–cytochrome P450 reductase), IC50 determination in triplicate with posaconazole as the internal control, plus redox/aggregation controls. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): T. cruzi amastigote assay and human CYP51 counter-screen. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): re-docking on 3K1O and MM-GBSA rescoring, then a go/no-go on the basis of hypotheses 1–4. Total compound requirement is milligrams; albaconazole and posaconazole are commercially available, CHEMBL5189694 and CHEMBL3431164 are research compounds requiring synthesis or a supplier quote.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only: no experimental data were generated; every number is a Vina score or a ChEMBL record.
  2. Vina cannot model the azole–haem iron coordinate bond, the dominant interaction for four of the five compounds — the most likely cause of the ranking failure.
  3. The grid is shaped by the 26N inhibitor in 4C27, not by posaconazole; re-docking on 3K1O was not run.
  4. Measured potencies mix Kd and IC50 values from ChEMBL; the rank correlation (n = 4) is indicative only.
  5. Only five compounds were docked (top 5 ranked leads including the query); the remaining 21 ranked leads were not docked, so a better-scoring scaffold may exist in the set.
  6. No molecular dynamics, no MM-GBSA rescoring, no selectivity data against human CYP51 for the two unnamed leads.
  7. The clinical validity of CYP51 as a Chagas target is unproven (CHAGASAZOL); a better inhibitor is not yet a better treatment.
  8. PAINS and Tox21 read-across are computational flags, not toxicology.

6. Conclusion

On the high-resolution T. cruzi CYP51 structure 4C27, posaconazole still leads the docking table at −10.57 kcal/mol and no lead beats it — but the table fails the test that matters: the most potent measured inhibitor, albaconazole (IC50 1.0 nM), scores worst (−8.16 kcal/mol), and docking rank does not track measured potency (Spearman ρ = −0.2). The honest conclusion is that Vina on this structure is a pose generator, not a ranker, for CYP51. The next experiment is a head-to-head recombinant enzyme assay of albaconazole, posaconazole and CHEMBL5189694, with re-docking on 3K1O and MM-GBSA rescoring to find out whether the failure is the pocket or the scoring function. No cure claim is made, and no clinical recommendation follows.
