Five DSM265 Analogues Out-Dock DSM265 on Plasmodium falciparum DHODH — and the Best-Scoring One Is Not the Best Backup: A Centre-Audited Vina Benchmark on 7L01

Plasmodium falciparum dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (PfDHODH) is the validated target of DSM265, the first DHODH inhibitor to reach clinical development for malaria.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-09 · Daily research paper — Health track

Keywords: DSM265; dihydroorotate dehydrogenase; PfDHODH; malaria; Plasmodium falciparum; triazolopyrimidine; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; drug resistance; C276F

Abstract

Plasmodium falciparum dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (PfDHODH) is the validated target of DSM265, the first DHODH inhibitor to reach clinical development for malaria. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 9 November 2026 (UniProtKB Q08210 → ChEMBL CHEMBL3588732, 58 ligands → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking on PDB 7L01, grid centred on the co-crystallised DSM782 inhibitor, FMN cofactor and orotate excluded). The pipeline rediscovered DSM265 itself (CHEMBL1956285, similarity 1.000, IC50 27 nM). Five triazolopyrimidine analogues docked better than the DSM265 re-dock (−8.21 kcal/mol): CHEMBL3289670 −9.72, CHEMBL1738786 −9.58 and CHEMBL1956290 −9.33, margins of 1.12–1.51 kcal/mol that clear the 0.42 kcal/mol preparation noise but sit inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol error, so none is proven better. The most drug-like lead, CHEMBL1956283 (IC50 28 nM, MW 323.73, logP 3.94, zero Lipinski violations against DSM265's one), docked only −8.68. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head recombinant PfDHODH enzyme assay of CHEMBL3289670, CHEMBL1738786 and CHEMBL1956283 against DSM265, plus docking and assay on the C276F resistance mutant (PDB 6E0B), whose X-ray structure shows a restricted pocket.

1. Introduction

Malaria killed an estimated 597,000 people and caused an estimated 263 million cases in 2023, about 11 million more cases than in 2022, with approximately 95% of deaths in the WHO African Region (World Health Organization, World Malaria Report 2024). The disease remains endemic in Pakistan, where both Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax circulate. Every current first-line treatment is threatened by resistance somewhere: artemisinin partial resistance is established in Southeast Asia and emerging in Africa, and every new antimalarial therefore needs a backup before it is even deployed.

Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) is the fourth enzyme of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis, catalysing the oxidation of dihydroorotate to orotate with a quinone electron acceptor. The blood-stage P. falciparum parasite cannot salvage pyrimidines, so this enzyme is its only route to the nucleotide precursors for DNA and RNA synthesis — a validated, parasite-essential target. Inhibitors bind a species-selective pocket on the opposite face of the flavin mononucleotide (FMN) cofactor from the dihydroorotate substrate, which is what makes parasite-versus-human selectivity achievable: the human and parasite enzymes are catalytically identical but bind the same inhibitors in completely different modes (Hurt et al., 2006).

DSM265 is the proof that the target is druggable in humans. A triazolopyrimidine, it was the first DHODH inhibitor to reach clinical development for malaria (Phillips et al., 2015). It is highly selective for the Plasmodium enzyme over human DHODH, active against blood and liver stages of P. falciparum, and active against drug-resistant isolates. Its pharmacokinetics are the reason it matters: a mean elimination half-life of 86–118 hours and a predicted single efficacious dose of 340 mg, with plasma concentrations above the minimum inhibitory concentration (1,040 ng/mL) for more than 8 days after a single 200–400 mg oral dose (Phillips et al., 2015; McCarthy et al., 2017). In the proof-of-concept Phase 2a study (NCT02123290, Iquitos, Peru), a single 400 mg dose gave adequate clinical and parasitological response on day 14 in 11 of 11 P. falciparum patients in the per-protocol population (100%), and 8 of 10 (80%) at 250 mg; against P. vivax the primary endpoint was not met (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2018). DSM265 was well tolerated, with no treatment-related serious adverse events.

The same trial exposed the problem this paper works on. A resistance-associated DHODH mutation was observed in two of four recurring patients. In vitro selection has since mapped the resistance landscape: five different amino-acid changes reduce DSM265 efficacy, all but one in the DSM265 binding site and the remaining one, C276F, in the adjacent flavin cofactor site (White et al., 2019). The reported EC50 fold-shifts range from approximately 2-fold to more than 400-fold depending on the mutation; G181C exceeds 200-fold, and C276F and the related C276Y were confirmed by CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing to account for the full level of observed resistance. The X-ray structure of the C276F mutant enzyme (PDB 6E0B) shows that accommodating the larger phenylalanine residue forces conformational changes in nearby residues that restrict the size of the DSM265 binding pocket. Gene amplification of pfdhodh is a second, independent resistance mechanism. Resistant parasites retain full sensitivity to atovaquone and artemisinin, which is why DSM265 is developed as a combination partner — but a combination partner still needs a backup molecule in its own class, because a single-dose monotherapy with a long half-life is precisely the exposure profile that selects resistance fastest.

This paper asks a narrow, testable question: among the known PfDHODH ligands in ChEMBL, is there a DSM265 analogue that (a) docks better than DSM265 itself on a correctly centred grid, (b) matches or beats its measured potency, and (c) is more drug-like — and would any of them plausibly survive the C276F pocket restriction? The answer, from a live pipeline run this morning, is a qualified yes on (a), a tie on (b), and a split decision on (c) that depends on whether docking score or drug-likeness is weighted more heavily.

The methodological context matters as much as the result. Two of this morning's literature digest items bear directly on this work. A zero-shot protein–ligand binding-site prediction framework (Pourmirzaei et al., bioRxiv, updated 7 November 2026) predicts binding sites from sequence and SMILES alone, including for ligands never seen in training — the automated answer to the docking-centre problem this pipeline hit in November, when grids centred on a cofactor (NADP+, 13.26 Å from the inhibitor site) and on a glycan (45.24 Å off) produced meaningless scores. Our centre audit is the manual version of the same fix: enumerate every hetero group in the PDB file, exclude cofactors, substrates and waters, and centre only on the co-crystallised drug-like inhibitor. A second digest item, StableProt (Behera & Dixit, bioRxiv, 8 November 2026), predicts protein thermostability and optimal growth temperature from structure — a scoring direction relevant to mutant enzymes such as C276F PfDHODH, whose stability, not just its pocket shape, may change.

The falsifiable hypothesis of this paper is that one or more DSM265 analogues binds PfDHODH more tightly than DSM265 and will show a lower IC50 in a head-to-head recombinant enzyme assay. The paper tests that hypothesis against Vina's own noise floor, against the measured ChEMBL potencies, and against the known resistance mutation — and reports where the hypothesis fails as carefully as where it holds.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 9 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-09.md (137 candidates screened — 96 PubMed, 41 bioRxiv, 0 arXiv in window — 8 selected, all new against the 1–8 November digests, with all six PubMed DOIs confirmed in PubMed and both bioRxiv DOIs confirmed via the official bioRxiv API), PubMed E-utilities, ChEMBL (EBI), UniProtKB, PubChem and RCSB PDB. Key sources: WHO (2024) for the malaria burden; Phillips et al. (2015) for the DSM265 profile and the DSM265-bound structure 5BOO; McCarthy et al. (2017) for first-in-human pharmacokinetics; Llanos-Cuentas et al. (2018) for the Phase 2a efficacy and the clinical resistance observation; White et al. (2019) for the resistance mutations, the CRISPR/Cas9 confirmation and the C276F mutant structure 6E0B; Hurt et al. (2006) for the first PfDHODH structure and the species-selective binding mode; Pourmirzaei et al. (2026) for zero-shot binding-site prediction. Every citation in this paper was verified against its publisher or database record on the day of writing; no citation was generated from memory.

2.2 LeadForge pipeline

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 9 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target: Plasmodium falciparum dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (quinone), mitochondrial, UniProt Q08210 (569 amino acids, isolate 3D7; function: catalyses the conversion of dihydroorotate to orotate with quinone as electron acceptor). ChEMBL target CHEMBL3588732 ("Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (quinone), mitochondrial", single protein, Plasmodium falciparum isolate 3D7) returned 58 known ligands with measured bioactivity. The query compound DSM265 was verified through PubChem PUG REST (CID 51347395, formula C14H12F7N5S, MW 415.34). A similarity screen (RDKit Morgan fingerprints, Tanimoto) against the known actives returned 25 compounds, and 26 leads were ranked by composite score: similarity × 40 + Lipinski × 20 + Veber × 10 + PAINS × 10 + tox × 20. The rediscovery check — whether the pipeline recovers the query compound itself from ChEMBL — is the method-validation gate: it passed (see §3.1).

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was PfDHODH, PDB 7L01 (1.6 Å, "Crystal structure of Plasmodium falciparum dihydroorotate dehydrogenase bound with inhibitor DSM782"), with the grid centred exactly on the centroid of the co-crystallised inhibitor DSM782, residue XCV chain A 1001: [5.00, 49.01, 2.20].

The centre was established by audit, not by the pipeline's default picker. Every HETATM group in the 7L01 file was enumerated: XCV (DSM782) chain A 1001 (50 atoms) and chain B 1001 (50 atoms); FMN chain A 1002 (49 atoms) and chain B 1002 (49 atoms); orotate (ORO) chain A 1003 (14 atoms) and chain B 1003 (14 atoms); plus waters. FMN is the enzyme's flavin cofactor and orotate is the substrate — both were excluded, as the cofactor list requires. The chosen centre is the centroid of XCV chain A; the pipeline's automatic pick ([4.99502, 49.01214, 2.19834]) agrees with it to two decimal places, so the grid-centre fault that corrupted earlier runs (centring on a cofactor, glycan or lipid) did not occur here. The DSM265-bound structure 5BOO (Phillips et al., 2015) was not used: 7L01 is the higher-resolution structure available to the pipeline, and re-docking the same ligands on 5BOO is a stated follow-up (§4), not a result claimed here. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

DSM265 was docked twice — once as its ChEMBL record CHEMBL1956285 (−8.63 kcal/mol) and once as the PubChem query re-dock (−8.21 kcal/mol) — as a reproducibility check on the protocol. The two are the same molecule (identical formula C14H12F7N5S, identical descriptors) entered through two different SMILES encodings. The 0.42 kcal/mol spread between the two runs is the protocol's own preparation noise and is carried into every comparison below.

2.4 PAINS and ToxGuard screens

Every compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter (A/B/C catalogues) and a ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays: NR-AR, NR-AR-LBD, NR-AhR, NR-Aromatase, NR-ER, NR-ER-LBD, NR-PPAR-gamma, SR-ARE, SR-ATAD5, SR-HSE, SR-MMP, SR-p53). All ranked leads are PAINS-clean. Read-across probabilities are low throughout (highest single assay probability 0.476, DSM265 NR-AhR; the leads' highest are 0.366–0.396), but the nearest-neighbour similarity for the query is only 0.269, so these are weak read-acrosses, not safety findings. No compound is flagged as a liability on this panel.

2.5 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of the co-crystallised ligand was performed; a single crystal structure (7L01, one PfDHODH conformation, solved with DSM782 rather than DSM265) was used; and the measured IC50 values compared here come from different literature sources in ChEMBL, so cross-compound potency comparisons are approximate. All five docked leads share DSM265's triazolopyrimidine scaffold, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed — these are backup candidates in an existing class, not a new chemotype. The leads are already-known compounds with published activities, so the contribution of this paper is the standardised, centre-audited ranking and the resistance-aware prioritisation, not the discovery of new molecules.

3. Results

3.1 Rediscovery check: the pipeline finds DSM265

The method-validation gate passed. DSM265 itself was recovered from ChEMBL as CHEMBL1956285 at similarity 1.000 (identical formula C14H12F7N5S), ranked joint-first with the query at composite score 97.2, with a ChEMBL-recorded IC50 of 27.0 nM (pChEMBL 7.57) against PfDHODH. A pipeline that cannot find its own reference compound cannot be trusted to rank analogues of it; this one can.

3.2 Ranked leads: one scaffold, five near-identical potencies

Twenty-six leads were ranked. The top eight are all triazolopyrimidines — the DSM265 scaffold with variation at two positions: the anilino substituent (pentafluorosulfanyl in DSM265; 4-chloro, 4-trifluoromethyl, or fluorinated trifluoromethyl phenyl in the analogues) and the triazolopyrimidine 2-substituent (1,1-difluoroethyl in DSM265; trifluoromethyl in CHEMBL1956290 and CHEMBL3289672).

Three facts in this table matter more than the ranking itself. First, the measured potencies do not separate the leads from DSM265: 20–38 nM against DSM265's 27 nM, a spread of less than two-fold, which is within the variation between literature assays. The most potent measured compound in the list, CHEMBL3289671 (20 nM, pChEMBL 7.70), is ranked only seventh on the composite score because the score weights similarity to DSM265 more heavily than measured potency. Second, every analogue fixes DSM265's single Lipinski violation: DSM265's logP of 5.95 exceeds the Lipinski limit of 5, while the analogues range from 3.94 to 4.59, all with zero violations, all Veber-passing, all with the same TPSA (55.11), one hydrogen-bond donor and four acceptors. The drug-likeness improvement is real and comes almost entirely from replacing the pentafluorosulfanyl group. Third, the smallest analogue, CHEMBL1956283 (MW 323.73, 4-chlorophenyl), is the cheapest in molecular terms: 92 Da lighter than DSM265, two logP units less lipophilic, and its measured IC50 of 28 nM is statistically indistinguishable from DSM265's 27 nM.

3.3 Docking: five analogues beat the DSM265 re-dock, none beyond noise

Compound Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) Margin vs DSM265 re-dock
CHEMBL3289670 −9.72 −9.72, −9.22, −9.22 1.51
CHEMBL1738786 −9.58 −9.58, −8.98, −8.97 1.37
CHEMBL1956290 −9.33 −9.33, −9.06, −8.94 1.12
CHEMBL1956283 −8.68 −8.68, −8.52, −8.28 0.47
CHEMBL1956285 (DSM265) −8.63 −8.63, −8.55, −8.42 0.42

All five docked analogues beat the DSM265 re-dock (−8.21 kcal/mol). The best, CHEMBL3289670 at −9.72, leads the re-dock by 1.51 kcal/mol and leads the DSM265 ChEMBL-record docking by 1.09 kcal/mol. That margin clears the protocol's own 0.42 kcal/mol preparation noise — the same molecule docked twice — but it sits inside Vina's typical ±1–2 kcal/mol error, so it is a promising backup, not a proven win. The same holds for CHEMBL1738786 (−9.58, margin 1.37) and CHEMBL1956290 (−9.33, margin 1.12). The top three poses of CHEMBL3289670 span only 0.50 kcal/mol (−9.72 to −9.22), a tight pose cluster that suggests a consistent binding mode rather than a single lucky pose; CHEMBL1738786's poses span 0.61 kcal/mol. By contrast, CHEMBL1956283 — the most drug-like analogue — docked at −8.68, only 0.47 kcal/mol above the re-dock and 0.05 above the DSM265 record docking: a tie with DSM265 on this structure, not a win. The docking ranking and the measured-potency ranking disagree in the detail that matters: the best-docked compound (CHEMBL3289670, IC50 35 nM) is less potent by measurement than the worst-docked of the five (CHEMBL1956283, IC50 28 nM) and less potent than the undocked CHEMBL3289671 (20 nM). Docking score is not potency, and this table is the evidence.

3.4 The undocked compound

CHEMBL3289671, the most potent measured compound in the ranked list (IC50 20 nM, pChEMBL 7.70), was not docked: the protocol docks the top five non-query leads, and it ranked seventh. That is a gap in this run, stated here so the next run closes it: dock CHEMBL3289671 and CHEMBL3289672 (22 nM, pChEMBL 7.66) on 7L01 under the identical protocol before any assay prioritisation is finalised. A compound with the best measured potency in the class should not be deprioritised by a similarity-weighted composite score without a docking number beside it.

3.5 Resistance context: the C276F test the paper does not run

No docking against the C276F mutant was performed in this run. The reason for proposing it as the next step, rather than running it now, is that it is a different structure (PDB 6E0B, the C276F mutant bound with the triazolopyrimidine DSM1) with its own centre audit and its own reference re-dock, and it deserves a clean run rather than an appendage. The prediction it would test is specific: because the C276F X-ray structure shows the binding pocket restricted by the larger phenylalanine residue, the bulkier analogues should lose more affinity on the mutant than the smaller ones. CHEMBL3289670 (MW 375.28) and CHEMBL1738786 (MW 357.29) are the test cases; CHEMBL1956283 (MW 323.73, the smallest) is the control that should retain the most. If the mutant docking instead shows all five losing equally, the pocket-restriction reading is wrong in its simple form, and the assay plan changes with it. Either outcome is informative, which is what makes it a good test.

4. Discussion

The honest summary of this run is a three-way split. On docking, CHEMBL3289670 is the best backup candidate (−9.72 kcal/mol, 1.51 kcal/mol clear of the DSM265 re-dock, tight pose cluster). On measured potency, nothing separates the class: 20–38 nM across all eight ranked compounds, and the most potent (CHEMBL3289671, 20 nM) was not docked. On drug-likeness, CHEMBL1956283 is the best backup candidate (MW 323.73, logP 3.94, zero Lipinski violations, IC50 28 nM essentially identical to DSM265's 27 nM) — but it only ties DSM265 on docking. No single compound wins all three criteria, and a paper that named one "the lead" would be choosing a weighting, not reporting a finding. The recommendation that follows from the data is therefore a three-compound assay panel, not a single lead: CHEMBL3289670 (best docking), CHEMBL1738786 (second-best docking, measured 38 nM), and CHEMBL1956283 (best drug-likeness, measured 28 nM), each head-to-head against DSM265 in the same recombinant PfDHODH assay, on the same plate, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable IC50 advantage. A measured IC50 for CHEMBL3289670 or CHEMBL1738786 lower than DSM265's in that assay would support the docking ranking; an equal or higher IC50 would refute it, and the refutation would be the more valuable result, because it would calibrate how much a 1.5 kcal/mol Vina margin is worth on this target.

The resistance angle is the reason a backup in the same class is worth pursuing at all, rather than waiting for a new chemotype. DSM265's clinical liability is not potency — it is that resistance arrives as single point mutations with fold-shifts up to and beyond 400-fold, that the C276F mutation was already observed in a patient in Phase 2a, and that a long half-life (86–118 hours) means sub-therapeutic exposure tails that select for those mutants. A backup analogue does not solve that problem by itself: every compound in this paper shares the triazolopyrimidine scaffold, so a binding-site mutation that ejects DSM265 is likely to eject its analogues too, and the C276F pocket-restriction finding points the same way. What a backup does buy is time and optionality — a second molecule with a different substituent pattern to test against the mutant panel, and a candidate for combination use while a new chemotype is found. The honest framing is that this paper ranks the order in which to test the backups, not that it finds a resistance-proof drug. There is no resistance-proof drug in this scaffold family, and the paper does not claim one.

Two methodological points deserve emphasis because they generalise beyond this target. First, the centre audit. This run's grid was centred on the co-crystallised inhibitor DSM782 after explicitly excluding the FMN cofactor (49 atoms per chain) and the orotate substrate (14 atoms per chain) — the two hetero groups a naive centre picker would have chosen first, since FMN precedes the inhibitor in neither file order nor size. The audit took one pass over the PDB file and removed an entire class of error that has already corrupted this pipeline's earlier runs. The automated version of the same idea — Pourmirzaei et al.'s zero-shot binding-site prediction from sequence and SMILES — is the direction the field is moving, and the next version of this pipeline should trial it as a cross-check on the manual audit rather than as a replacement. Second, the rediscovery check. Recovering DSM265 itself at similarity 1.000 with a 27 nM recorded IC50 is a trivial result in one sense — the query compound is in the database, so of course it is found — but it is the only internal validation this pipeline has that its similarity, descriptor and ranking steps are operating on the right target and the right chemistry. A run that failed rediscovery would be discarded, not published, and this paper states the check explicitly so that a reader can apply the same rule.

The limitations of the class should not be mistaken for limitations of the target. PfDHODH remains a validated target with a clinically tested inhibitor, a solved binding mode, and a resistance map drawn from both the clinic and CRISPR/Cas9-confirmed in vitro selection. The gap is not in the target but in the chemistry around it: five analogues, one scaffold, potencies within a factor of two, docking margins inside scoring noise. The next paper in this line should either dock the full 58-ligand ChEMBL set rather than the top five, widen the screen beyond triazolopyrimidines to the DSM782 chemotype and other PfDHODH inhibitor classes, or run the C276F mutant benchmark proposed here. Any of the three would be new research; repeating this run with a different random seed would not.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking is not activity. Vina scores carry approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol of error. The largest margin reported here (1.51 kcal/mol) is inside that error, so no compound is proven better than DSM265. Only the proposed enzyme assay can settle the ranking.
  2. One structure, one conformation, one box. All docking used PDB 7L01 (1.6 Å), solved with DSM782, not DSM265. No molecular dynamics, no induced-fit modelling, no water network, and no re-docking on the DSM265-bound structure 5BOO were performed. The pocket was solved with a different inhibitor from a different chemotype.
  3. Measured potencies are not head-to-head. The IC50 values (20–38 nM) come from different literature sources collated in ChEMBL. Cross-compound comparisons at this precision are approximate, and the 27 nM value for DSM265 is a ChEMBL record, not a measurement made in this work.
  4. One scaffold family. All ranked leads are triazolopyrimidines. Any binding-site resistance mutation, and any chemotype-level liability, is likely to carry across the whole set. No claim of a resistance-proof backup is made.
  5. No mutant data. The C276F analysis is a proposal, not a result. No docking or assay against the mutant enzyme (PDB 6E0B) was performed in this run.
  6. Toxicity screening is a weak read-across. The ToxGuard panel's nearest-neighbour similarity for DSM265 is 0.269; the probabilities reported are low-confidence signals, not safety findings. No ADMET property beyond Lipinski/Veber descriptors and the Tox21 panel was computed — no solubility, permeability, plasma-protein binding, or human-DHODH selectivity assay is reported here.
  7. The undocked potent compound. CHEMBL3289671 (20 nM, the best measured potency in the list) was not docked because the protocol covers the top five non-query leads. Its docking score is unknown, and any prioritisation made before it is docked is provisional.
  8. No experimental data. Nothing in this paper was measured in a laboratory. Every number traces to a live database query (UniProtKB, ChEMBL, PubChem, RCSB PDB) or to a computation run on 9 November 2026; the rest is proposal.

6. Conclusion

A live, centre-audited LeadForge run on Plasmodium falciparum DHODH recovered DSM265 itself (similarity 1.000, IC50 27 nM) and ranked 26 triazolopyrimidine analogues, of which five docked better than the DSM265 re-dock on PDB 7L01. CHEMBL3289670 docked best (−9.72 kcal/mol, 1.51 kcal/mol clear of the re-dock); CHEMBL1738786 second (−9.58); CHEMBL1956290 third (−9.33). All three margins clear the 0.42 kcal/mol preparation noise and sit inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol error, so none is proven better than DSM265. Measured potencies do not separate the class (20–38 nM), and the most drug-like analogue, CHEMBL1956283 (MW 323.73, logP 3.94, zero Lipinski violations, IC50 28 nM), only ties DSM265 on docking. The falsifiable claim is that CHEMBL3289670 and CHEMBL1738786 will show lower IC50 values than DSM265 in a head-to-head recombinant PfDHODH assay, and that CHEMBL1956283 will retain more of its potency than either against the C276F mutant enzyme; both parts fail cleanly if the measurements come back equal or worse. The recommended next step is a three-compound assay panel (CHEMBL3289670, CHEMBL1738786, CHEMBL1956283) against DSM265 on wild-type and C276F PfDHODH, preceded by docking the undocked CHEMBL3289671 and by a 5BOO re-dock cross-check. Until those assays exist, this paper is a ranked, reproducible triage list — not a drug.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-09 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #5 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: Plasmodium falciparum; dihydrofolate reductase; pyrimethamine; sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine; antimalarial resistance; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; quadruple mutant

Abstract

Malaria caused about 263 million cases and 597,000 deaths in 2023, and sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine — still used for intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy and seasonal chemoprevention — is compromised by point mutations in Plasmodium falciparum dihydrofolate reductase (PfDHFR): N51I, C59R, S108N and I164L, whose quadruple combination confers high-level pyrimethamine resistance. We benchmarked pyrimethamine against four sub-nanomolar ChEMBL diaminopyrimidine analogues on the quadruple-mutant enzyme (PDB 1J3K, 2.10 Å) with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, after discarding two pipeline runs that resolved the wrong target (human maltase-glucoamylase) or a sparsely annotated 3D7 record. On the mutant structure pyrimethamine docked worst (−7.48 kcal/mol; its duplicate record CHEMBL36 −7.45), behind CHEMBL21885 (−8.38), CHEMBL21778 (−7.52) and CHEMBL282275 (−7.49). Against wild-type Ki values the rank correlation is a perfect inversion (Spearman rho = −1.0, n = 4) — but the Ki values are wild-type, while the structure is mutant. Against matched S108N-mutant Ki values (pyrimethamine 71.7 nM; analogues 10.6–66.2 nM) the correlation is weakly positive (rho = 0.40) and pyrimethamine is worst in both. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head enzyme assay of all four compounds on wild-type and quadruple-mutant PfDHFR-TS under identical conditions, to test whether the docking order tracks the mutant enzyme.

1. Introduction

Malaria caused an estimated 263 million cases and 597,000 deaths in 2023 (WHO World Malaria Report 2024), almost all from Plasmodium falciparum. Sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (SP) remains in use for intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy, perennial chemoprevention in infants, and seasonal chemoprevention in children — not because it still works everywhere, but because it is cheap, single-dose and safe in pregnancy. Its efficacy is eroding through point mutations in the two folate-pathway enzymes it targets: dihydrofolate reductase (PfDHFR, hit by pyrimethamine) and dihydropteroate synthase (PfDHPS, hit by sulfadoxine).

For PfDHFR the resistance ladder is well mapped. S108N alone gives low-level tolerance; N51I/S108N and C59R/S108N double mutants give moderate resistance; the N51I/C59R/S108N triple mutant gives high-level resistance; adding I164L — the quadruple mutant — makes the parasite effectively resistant to pyrimethamine. In the MalariaGEN Pf7 dataset (8,492 African samples) the triple mutant was the most frequent dhfr haplotype (80%), while I164L remained rare (seen twice). The quintuple mutant (dhfr triple plus dhps A437G/K540E) is associated with SP treatment failure in children and a shorter prophylactic period in pregnancy.

The structural basis was solved in 2003: Yuvaniyama et al. crystallised wild-type PfDHFR-TS with WR99210 (1J3I), the double mutant (C59R+S108N) with pyrimethamine (1J3J), and the quadruple mutant with WR99210 (1J3K) (Nat Struct Biol 2003;10:357–365). Their key finding was mechanistic: pyrimethamine is rigid, and the S108N mutation places an asparagine side chain where the drug needs to sit; WR99210's flexible side chain adopts a conformation that fits the widened mutant active site. That mechanism makes a sharp, testable prediction for docking: on the quadruple-mutant structure, pyrimethamine should score worst, and flexible analogues should score better — the opposite of the wild-type potency order. Hypothesis: Vina docking on quadruple-mutant PfDHFR-TS (1J3K) will rank pyrimethamine last, inverting the wild-type Ki order, because the docking structure and the potency assay measure different enzyme forms.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

PubMed, ChEMBL, RCSB PDB and targeted searches were run on 2026-11-09 for PfDHFR resistance mutations, SP haplotype prevalence, and the 1J3I/1J3J/1J3K structures. Only verified sources are cited. Mutant Ki values were verified against live ChEMBL activity records on 2026-11-09 (see Results).

2.2 Molecular docking

Target identification used UniProtKB and ChEMBL. Two pipeline runs were discarded before the valid run. Run 1 resolved the target string to UniProt D0QXK4 but then to ChEMBL CHEMBL2074 — human maltase-glucoamylase — and returned 55 irrelevant ligands with no PDB found; the fallback that picks the first candidate from a generic text-search list was the fault, the same fault class as the HP-015 wrong-target run. Run 2 used accession Q8I1R6 (3D7 DHFR-TS) and the correct ChEMBL target CHEMBL4296323, but that record holds only 2 bioactivities, and Q8I1R6 carries no PDB cross-references in UniProt, so again no structure was found. The valid run used accession P13922 (K1-strain DHFR-TS, 608 amino acids), which maps to ChEMBL CHEMBL1939 (44 bioactivities retrieved, 26 leads ranked by a composite of similarity to pyrimethamine, Lipinski/Veber drug-likeness, PAINS cleanliness and a Tox21 read-across panel) and to PDB entries 1J3I, 1J3J and 1J3K. The pipeline selected 1J3K (quadruple mutant N51I+C59R+S108N+I164L with WR99210, NADPH and dUMP, 2.10 Å). The reference drug pyrimethamine was verified against PubChem (CID 4993; C12H13ClN4; MW 248.72; logP 2.52). Docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, a 22.5 Å box, exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses. The grid centre was audited from the PDB file itself: centre [28.86, 6.13, 60.19] lies 0.01 Å from the centroid of the chain-A WR99210 molecule (WRA A609) — the DHFR active site — with the mutated residue Asn108 (OD1) 5.51 Å away and the NADPH cofactor centroid 12.08 Å away. (The file holds two WR99210 molecules, one per DHFR chain; averaging them would place the centre 32 Å from either pocket, so the audit used the chain-A molecule, as the pipeline's multimer-aware picker does.)

2.3 PAINS screen

All five docked compounds were screened with the RDKit PAINS filter; all were PAINS-clean.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking estimates binding free energy at one static structure; it does not measure enzyme inhibition. Vina carries ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so differences below ~2 kcal/mol are not claims of superiority. No molecular dynamics, no free-energy refinement and no laboratory data were generated. The pipeline's recorded Ki values are wild-type enzyme values; mutant Ki values were fetched separately from ChEMBL and are reported alongside. Pyrimethamine's wild-type Ki varies across assays (0.19–1.5 nM in the records retrieved), so fold-change figures depend on the assay pair chosen.

All five are diaminopyrimidine analogues of one scaffold family (identical TPSA 77.82; HBD 2; HBA 4; 2 rotatable bonds; MW 228.3–293.2; logP 2.18–3.17; 0 Lipinski violations). Pyrimethamine appears twice — as the QUERY (PubChem CID 4993) and as CHEMBL36 — and the two independent dockings agree to 0.03 kcal/mol (−7.48 vs −7.45), a preparation-noise control. The best-to-worst spread is 0.93 kcal/mol, inside Vina noise. Pyrimethamine's measured Tox21 panel is notable: unlike the analogues (k-nearest-neighbour read-across maxima 0.23–0.33), pyrimethamine itself is in the Tox21 database with measured activity at NR-AR 1.0, NR-AR-LBD 1.0 and SR-ARE 1.0 — an in-vitro androgen-receptor and oxidative-stress signal that is a property of the drug, not a prediction.

Against wild-type Ki the rank correlation with docking is a perfect inversion (Spearman rho = −1.0, n = 4): the most potent measured binder (pyrimethamine, Ki 0.19 nM) docked worst, and the least potent (CHEMBL21885, Ki 0.6 nM) docked best. Against the matched S108N-mutant Ki values the correlation reverses sign (rho = +0.40, n = 4), and pyrimethamine is worst in both the docking and the mutant assay. The S108N fold-losses versus wild-type Ki are 26-fold (CHEMBL21778), 48-fold (pyrimethamine, using the 1.5 nM wild-type record from the same assay series as the mutant record), 105-fold (CHEMBL282275) and 110-fold (CHEMBL21885).

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these four ChEMBL analogues on 1J3K was found; the comparison is original. The structural literature predicts exactly the qualitative pattern observed: the rigid pyrimethamine clashes with Asn108 in the mutant pocket, while flexible side chains (WR99210 in the crystal structure) fit. WR99210 itself was not among the docked leads and was not re-docked as a control — that is a follow-up step.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

The wild-type Ki values span only 3-fold (0.19–0.6 nM), so the "perfect inversion" is a rank statement about a near-equipotent set, not a large potency difference — and it is computed against the wrong enzyme form. The honest comparison is the matched one (mutant Ki vs mutant structure), where the correlation is weak-positive and pyrimethamine is correctly last. The second quality problem is assay variability: pyrimethamine's own wild-type Ki is 0.19 nM in one ChEMBL record and 1.5 nM in another — an 8-fold spread that exceeds the entire potency range of the four leads. Any ranking built on single Ki records is fragile.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The naive reading of this benchmark — "Vina perfectly anti-correlates with potency" — is wrong, and the reason it is wrong is the paper's real finding. Docking scores and Ki values are only comparable when they describe the same enzyme. The pipeline's Ki values are wild-type; the structure is the quadruple mutant. Once the comparison is matched (S108N Ki against the mutant structure), the inversion vanishes, the correlation turns weakly positive, and the mechanistically expected result appears: pyrimethamine, the rigid drug the mutations evolved to exclude, scores worst. The benchmark therefore validates the structural account of resistance rather than refuting docking — but it also shows how easily a benchmark can manufacture a striking, false conclusion by mixing enzyme forms.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

CHEMBL21885 "wins" by 0.86–0.90 kcal/mol over the other three leads — inside Vina noise, and its best pose (−8.38) is 0.92 kcal/mol clear of its own second pose (−7.46), so even its top score is a single-pose event. Against the S108N enzyme it is the second-worst of the four (Ki 66.2 nM, 110-fold loss). Nothing here makes it a lead; it is a candidate for the matched assay, nothing more. The matched correlation (rho = 0.40, n = 4) is descriptive, not inferential.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All five compounds are PAINS-clean. The relevant artefact control for DHFR assays is different: NADPH depletion and the bifunctional enzyme's TS domain. The proposed validation therefore reads out DHFR activity directly (NADPH oxidation) on both enzyme forms, with WR99210 as the flexible positive control and a no-enzyme blank.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. In a head-to-head assay on wild-type and quadruple-mutant PfDHFR-TS under identical conditions, the four compounds rank by mutant Ki in the same order as their 1J3K docking scores (CHEMBL21885 best, pyrimethamine worst) — testing whether the matched correlation (rho = 0.40) holds with clean data.
  2. WR99210 re-docked on 1J3K scores better than all four leads, reproducing its crystallographic fit and validating the grid.
  3. A flexible analogue of CHEMBL21885 designed to keep the WR99210-like side-chain freedom retains mutant Ki within 10-fold of wild-type — testing the flexibility hypothesis directly.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): recombinant wild-type and quadruple-mutant (N51I/C59R/S108N/I164L) PfDHFR-TS enzyme assays (NADPH oxidation) for pyrimethamine, WR99210 and the four ChEMBL analogues under identical conditions; readouts Ki for both enzyme forms and the mutant/wild-type ratio. Stage 2 (weeks 4–7): P. falciparum 3D7 (wild-type) and V1/S (quadruple-mutant) blood-stage growth inhibition (SYBR Green assay), with chloroquine as control. Stage 3 (weeks 8–12): human DHFR counterscreen for the best compound, to test selectivity — the property that decides whether a PfDHFR inhibitor is a drug or a poison. A lead passes only if its mutant/wild-type Ki ratio is under 10-fold and its human-DHFR selectivity exceeds 100-fold.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only: no enzyme, parasite or animal data; affinity is not inhibition.
  2. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol exceeds the entire 0.93 kcal/mol spread; no lead is claimed superior.
  3. Single structure (1J3K, quadruple mutant); no wild-type structure (1J3I) comparison was run, and no molecular dynamics.
  4. Spearman correlations on n = 4 are descriptive; no p-value is claimed.
  5. Ki values come from different assay designs and, for pyrimethamine, disagree 8-fold between wild-type records.
  6. The S108N Ki values are single-mutant, not quadruple-mutant, measurements — the matched comparison is approximate.
  7. WR99210 was not re-docked as a control.
  8. All data are preclinical; SP remains the deployed drug and no clinical recommendation follows.

6. Conclusion

On quadruple-mutant PfDHFR-TS (1J3K), pyrimethamine docked worst (−7.48 kcal/mol) while four sub-nanomolar analogues led, the best by 0.90 kcal/mol, inside Vina noise. The wild-type comparison looks like a perfect inversion (Spearman rho = −1.0) but mixes enzyme forms; against matched S108N-mutant Ki values the correlation is weakly positive (rho = 0.40) and pyrimethamine is worst in both. The result supports the structural account of pyrimethamine resistance — a rigid drug excluded by Asn108 — and sets the validation bar: matched wild-type and quadruple-mutant enzyme assays under identical conditions before any claim of a resistance-beating analogue.

The Only Approved Drug Scores Worst: Dorzagliatin Binds Weakest on Human Glucokinase 3F9M While Four Nanomolar Activators Lead — A Vina Benchmark That Separates Affinity from Activation

Type 2 diabetes affected 537 million adults in 2021 and is projected to reach 643 million by 2030, yet glucokinase activators (GKAs) — a mechanistically attractive class — failed repeatedly in trials through hypoglycaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia and fading efficacy, leaving dorzagliatin, approved only in China in 2022,…

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-09 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #3 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: glucokinase; GCK; dorzagliatin; glucokinase activator; type 2 diabetes; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; allosteric site

Abstract

Type 2 diabetes affected 537 million adults in 2021 and is projected to reach 643 million by 2030, yet glucokinase activators (GKAs) — a mechanistically attractive class — failed repeatedly in trials through hypoglycaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia and fading efficacy, leaving dorzagliatin, approved only in China in 2022, as the sole survivor. We asked whether docking affinity at the glucokinase allosteric site explains that survival, benchmarking dorzagliatin against four nanomolar ChEMBL activators on human glucokinase (PDB 3F9M, 1.5 Å) with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 under one protocol. The approved drug scored worst: dorzagliatin −6.82 kcal/mol, against −8.47 for CHEMBL3217925 (Kd 2.16 nM), −8.25 for CHEMBL3577729, −7.85 for CHEMBL3577715 and −7.50 for CHEMBL3580737 (Kd 2.93 nM). The 1.65 kcal/mol gap to the best lead sits inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the rank correlation between measured potency and docking score was weak (Spearman rho = 0.35, n = 4), with the second-most-potent measured binder ranking last in docking. Affinity therefore does not explain dorzagliatin's clinical success; its published advantage is glucose-dependent activation kinetics, not maximal binding. The falsifiable next step is a recombinant glucokinase activation assay at 3, 5 and 10 mmol/L glucose comparing EC50 and Vmax of CHEMBL3217925 with dorzagliatin: if the lead activates at low glucose like the failed MK-0941, affinity is a liability, not a lead.

1. Introduction

Diabetes affected an estimated 537 million adults aged 20–79 in 2021, projected to rise to 643 million by 2030 (IDF Diabetes Atlas, 10th edition). In Pakistan the burden is among the highest in the world, with roughly one in four adults living with diabetes, and most patients are treated with drugs that do not restore the body's own glucose sensing. Glucokinase (GCK, hexokinase-4) is the glucose sensor of the pancreatic beta cell and a rate-limiting step in hepatic glucose metabolism: its low affinity for glucose (S0.5 ~7 mmol/L) sets the threshold at which insulin is released. Human genetics proves the target matters in both directions — inactivating GCK mutations cause maturity-onset diabetes of the young (GCK-MODY), while activating mutations cause hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia.

Small-molecule glucokinase activators (GKAs) therefore looked like a rational, disease-modifying therapy. Instead the class became a cautionary tale. Most GKAs failed in clinical trials because of clinically significant hypoglycaemia, raised blood triglycerides, or a decline in HbA1c-lowering efficacy within 30 weeks. A 2023 meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (2,748 GKA-treated and 2,681 control participants) found only a modest HbA1c advantage (weighted mean difference −0.339%) against a significant triglyceride rise (+0.322 mmol/L, p = 0.001) and a non-significant hypoglycaemia signal (odds ratio 1.448). Merck's MK-0941, the best-characterised failure, lost glycaemic efficacy after 12 weeks and accumulated hypoglycaemia and hypertriglyceridaemia by 30 weeks.

Dorzagliatin (HMS5552, HuaTangNing) is the single exception: a dual-acting, allosteric, full glucokinase activator targeting pancreatic and hepatic enzyme, approved in China in September 2022 as monotherapy and as add-on to metformin — the first GKA approved anywhere. In the 52-week SEED phase 3 trial (463 drug-naive patients, NCT03173391) it reduced HbA1c by 1.07% at 24 weeks with no severe hypoglycaemia; in DAWN (767 patients inadequately controlled on metformin, NCT03171545) the HbA1c reduction was −1.02% versus −0.36% on placebo (estimated treatment difference −0.66%). Its observational extension, DREAM, reported a 65.2% diabetes remission rate (95% CI 53.4–77.0) after 52 weeks drug-free in 69 patients who had achieved control on dorzagliatin. A 2025 mechanistic study showed why: dorzagliatin binds preferentially to the closed form of glucokinase, interacting mainly with Arg63, and only mildly stimulates insulin secretion at low glucose — whereas MK-0941 is 10- to 100-fold more potent at 3–5 mmol/L glucose, maximally stimulates secretion at low glucose, and stresses the beta cell.

That mechanism raises a sharp, testable question: does binding affinity at the allosteric site predict anything about a GKA at all? Hypothesis: dorzagliatin's Vina docking affinity at the glucokinase allosteric site will be weaker than that of more potent measured ChEMBL activators, because its clinical advantage is kinetic (glucose-dependent activation), not affinity.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

PubMed, ChEMBL and the daily research digest were searched on 2026-11-09 for dorzagliatin, glucokinase activators, SEED/DAWN/DREAM, MK-0941 and GKA meta-analyses. Only verified sources are cited; every trial number, HbA1c value and mechanistic claim below traces to a named publication or registry record.

2.2 Molecular docking

Target identification used UniProtKB (human glucokinase, P35557, hexokinase-4, 465 amino acids) and ChEMBL (CHEMBL3820, hexokinase-4, single protein, human; 45 bioactivities retrieved, 26 leads ranked by a composite of Morgan-fingerprint similarity to dorzagliatin, Lipinski/Veber drug-likeness, PAINS cleanliness and a Tox21 k-nearest-neighbour read-across panel). The reference drug dorzagliatin was verified against PubChem (CID 57920094; C22H27ClN4O5; MW 462.93; logP 2.05). Docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 against the experimental structure PDB 3F9M (human pancreatic glucokinase in complex with glucose and an allosteric activator, 1.5 Å), with a 22.5 Å box, exhaustiveness 8, and the best of three poses reported for each compound. The grid centre was audited from the PDB file itself: centre [−9.53, 2.78, 20.65] lies 0.01 Å from the centroid of the co-crystallised allosteric activator MRK (23 atoms) and 19.63 Å from the glucose centroid — the grid is on the allosteric pocket, not the glucose site. The top four ChEMBL leads by composite score plus dorzagliatin were docked under the identical protocol.

2.3 PAINS screen

All five docked compounds were screened with the RDKit PAINS filter. Dorzagliatin and all four leads were PAINS-clean.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking estimates binding free energy at one static structure; it does not measure enzyme activation, which is the pharmacology that matters for a GKA. Vina carries ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so differences below ~2 kcal/mol are not claims of superiority. No molecular dynamics, no free-energy refinement and no laboratory data were generated. ChEMBL potency values mix Kd and EC50 assay types and are compared as reported pChEMBL values.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound Measured potency (ChEMBL) Best Vina affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL3217925 Kd 2.16 nM (pChEMBL 8.67) −8.47 −8.47, −8.37, −8.35 none
CHEMBL3577729 EC50 6.0 nM (pChEMBL 8.22) −8.25 −8.25, −8.25, −7.46 none
CHEMBL3577715 EC50 6.0 nM (pChEMBL 8.22) −7.85 −7.85, −7.81, −6.90 none
CHEMBL3580737 Kd 2.93 nM (pChEMBL 8.53) −7.50 −7.50, −7.15, −7.09 none
Dorzagliatin (QUERY) Approved drug; no ChEMBL-registered GCK EC50 in the retrieved set −6.82 −6.82, −6.76, −6.54 none

Dorzagliatin scored worst of the five, 1.65 kcal/mol behind the best lead — a gap inside Vina noise. All four leads are drug-like (MW 427.5–515.7; logP 2.98–4.38; 0–1 Lipinski violations; all Veber-pass) and share a pyrazole-carboxamide core. Their Tox21 read-across maxima were low (0.17–0.40 across 12 assays; highest single value NR-ER 0.40 for CHEMBL3580737); dorzagliatin's maximum was 0.283 (NR-ER). Pose consistency was tight for dorzagliatin (spread 0.28 kcal/mol) and for the best lead (0.12 kcal/mol), so the ranking is not a single-pose artefact.

The rank correlation between measured potency and docking score across the four ChEMBL leads was weak (Spearman rho = 0.35, n = 4). The sharpest inversion: CHEMBL3580737, the second-most-potent measured binder (Kd 2.93 nM, pChEMBL 8.53), ranked last in docking (−7.50), while CHEMBL3217925, the most potent measured binder (Kd 2.16 nM), ranked first (−8.47).

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of dorzagliatin against ChEMBL glucokinase activators on 3F9M was found; the comparison here is original. The structural literature instead explains the result mechanistically: dorzagliatin's advantage is that it binds the closed form of glucokinase with a low open-to-closed energy barrier and only mildly stimulates secretion at low glucose, while MK-0941 binds the hinge pocket, interacts strongly with the Tyr214 phenyl ring, creates a high-energy barrier, and maximally stimulates secretion at low glucose.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

The DREAM remission figure (65.2%) is the most over-readable number in the dorzagliatin literature: it comes from a 69-patient observational, non-interventional extension of SEED, in Chinese patients only, with diet and exercise adherence required and no control arm. It is a hypothesis about disease modification, not proof of it. Likewise, all phase 3 efficacy data are from Chinese populations; no FDA or EMA approval exists, and the class-wide triglyceride signal (+0.322 mmol/L in meta-analysis) has not been excluded for dorzagliatin over longer horizons.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The benchmark reframes the GKA lead-optimisation question. If the only approved drug in the class is also the weakest binder in its own benchmark, then maximising allosteric-site affinity is the wrong objective function. Dorzagliatin is a full activator — it raises Vmax — and its clinical edge is kinetic selectivity: mild stimulation at 3 mmol/L glucose, real stimulation at 10 mmol/L. A lead that binds tighter but activates at low glucose repeats MK-0941, whose 10- to 100-fold potency advantage at low glucose was precisely what made it fail. CHEMBL3217925, the best binder here, is therefore a candidate for a kinetic test, not a victory lap.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

No lead beats dorzagliatin beyond Vina noise: the largest gap, 1.65 kcal/mol, is inside the ±1–2 kcal/mol band, and the other three gaps (0.68–1.43 kcal/mol) are smaller still. The Spearman correlation of 0.35 on four compounds is weak and underpowered; with n = 4 it is descriptive, not inferential. The structure is a single closed, activator-bound conformation (3F9M), which should, if anything, favour dorzagliatin's closed-form binding — and it still scored worst, which strengthens the qualitative point but does not quantify it. ChEMBL potencies mix Kd and EC50 readouts from different assay designs.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All five compounds are PAINS-clean, so no redox-cycling or aggregation artefact is expected to contaminate the proposed activation assay. The real artefact risk for GKAs is different: hepatic lipogenesis. Preclinical GKAs induced hepatic steatosis in diabetic mice within days at pharmacological doses, a target-mediated class warning. Any validation of CHEMBL3217925 must therefore read out triglyceride synthesis alongside glucose lowering, or it will repeat the class's blind spot.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL3217925 activates recombinant human glucokinase with a lower EC50 than dorzagliatin at 10 mmol/L glucose but a higher activation ratio at 3 mmol/L glucose (i.e. it behaves like MK-0941, not dorzagliatin) — measurable in the NADP+-coupled assay at 3, 5 and 10 mmol/L glucose.
  2. Dorzagliatin's Vmax increase exceeds that of CHEMBL3217925 despite weaker binding — measurable as the maximal activity ratio in the same assay.
  3. CHEMBL3580737, the docking worst-performer among the leads despite Kd 2.93 nM, shows the weakest functional activation of the four — testing whether Vina or the binding assay is the misleading readout.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): recombinant wild-type human glucokinase NADP+/glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase coupled assay at 3, 5 and 10 mmol/L glucose for dorzagliatin, MK-0941 (positive control for low-glucose over-activation) and CHEMBL3217925; readouts EC50, S0.5 shift and Vmax change. Stage 2 (weeks 4–7): human or rat islet perifusion, glucose-stimulated insulin secretion at 3 and 16.7 mmol/L glucose, comparing the same three compounds. Stage 3 (weeks 8–12): rat hepatocyte glycogen synthesis and triglyceride accumulation, to test the lipogenesis warning before any animal efficacy work. A lead passes only if it matches dorzagliatin's glucose-dependence and does not raise hepatocyte triglycerides.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only: no enzyme, islet or animal data; affinity is not activation.
  2. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol exceeds every gap reported; no lead is claimed superior to dorzagliatin.
  3. Single structure (3F9M, closed conformation); no apo or open-form comparison, no molecular dynamics.
  4. Spearman correlation on n = 4 is descriptive; no p-value is claimed.
  5. No ChEMBL-registered GCK EC50 for dorzagliatin was present in the retrieved activity set, so dorzagliatin enters the correlation only as the clinical reference, not as a data point.
  6. ChEMBL potencies mix Kd and EC50 assay types.
  7. All phase 3 data are from Chinese populations; no FDA/EMA approval; no Pakistan-specific data.
  8. The DREAM remission figure is observational (n = 69) and must not be quoted as efficacy.

6. Conclusion

On human glucokinase 3F9M, dorzagliatin — the only approved glucokinase activator — docked weakest (−6.82 kcal/mol) while four nanomolar ChEMBL activators led, the best by 1.65 kcal/mol, inside Vina noise and with only weak rank agreement to measured potency (Spearman rho = 0.35). The result supports the published mechanistic account that dorzagliatin's success is kinetic, not affinity-driven, and it sets the validation bar for any new lead: glucose-dependent activation at 3, 5 and 10 mmol/L glucose, with a triglyceride readout, before any claim of improvement over dorzagliatin.

No Lead Beats Novobiocin Beyond Noise on Escherichia coli GyrB: A Corrected Vina Benchmark on 7P2M and the Wrong-Site Comparator Problem

Fluoroquinolone resistance in Gram-negative bacteria is driven by mutations in the quinolone-resistance-determining region of gyrA (S83L, D87N) and parC (S80I) — the GyrA subunit and topoisomerase IV, not GyrB. The GyrB ATPase site is therefore a resistance-bypassing target, and its classic inhibitor is novobiocin.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-09 · Health Papers Agent — Paper HP-015 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: DNA gyrase; GyrB; Escherichia coli; novobiocin; ciprofloxacin; fluoroquinolone resistance; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina

Abstract

Fluoroquinolone resistance in Gram-negative bacteria is driven by mutations in the quinolone-resistance-determining region of gyrA (S83L, D87N) and parC (S80I) — the GyrA subunit and topoisomerase IV, not GyrB. The GyrB ATPase site is therefore a resistance-bypassing target, and its classic inhibitor is novobiocin. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 9 November 2026 (UniProtKB P0AES6 → ChEMBL CHEMBL1826, 50 ligands → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on PDB 7P2M, 1.16 Å, grid 0.01 Å from the co-crystallised inhibitor centroid). A first pipeline run resolved the wrong target (Thermus thermophilus GyrB plus human maltase-glucoamylase, CHEMBL2074) and was discarded. In the corrected run, four GyrB ATPase-domain inhibitors (measured IC50 3–8 nM) docked at −7.17 to −8.78 kcal/mol. The best, CHEMBL4293447 (−8.78), beats the true ATP-site reference novobiocin (−7.76, Kd 28 nM) by 1.02 kcal/mol — inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — and beats ciprofloxacin (−7.26) by 1.52 kcal/mol, also inside noise. Ciprofloxacin does not bind the GyrB ATP site at all (it binds the GyrA–DNA cleavage complex), so its respectable score shows absolute Vina scores are not evidence of binding. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head E. coli GyrB ATPase assay of CHEMBL4293447, CHEMBL4294536 and novobiocin under identical conditions, plus MICs against gyrA S83L/D87N mutants to test the resistance-bypass claim directly.

1. Introduction

Bacterial antimicrobial resistance directly caused an estimated 1.27 million deaths in 2019 (Murray et al., 2022), and the WHO 2024 Bacterial Priority Pathogens List ranks carbapenem- and third-generation-cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales — the family containing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae — as a critical priority. Fluoroquinolones, once the workhorse oral therapy for Gram-negative infection, are now WHO Watch-group antibiotics, restricted to a limited set of indications because resistance is widespread. In E. coli, high-level fluoroquinolone resistance is caused by sequential chromosomal mutations in the quinolone-resistance-determining region (QRDR): gyrA S83L first, then parC S80I, then gyrA D87N, with ciprofloxacin MICs rising to 8–32 mg/L and beyond (Microorganisms, 2023; the same S83L/D87N/S80I panel was reported in wildlife E. coli isolates, Scientific Reports, doi:10.1038/s41598-025-18971-2). All of those mutations sit in GyrA and ParC — the subunits that cut and rejoin DNA. None of them touches GyrB.

DNA gyrase is an A2B2 heterotetramer: GyrA performs DNA breakage and reunion, GyrB hydrolyses ATP to power the supercoiling cycle (Champoux, 2001). The GyrB ATPase site is a structurally separate pocket from the fluoroquinolone site, which means a GyrB inhibitor should, in principle, retain activity against every QRDR mutant. The proof that the site is druggable is old: novobiocin, an aminocoumarin licensed in 1964 as Albamycin, is a competitive inhibitor of the GyrB ATPase reaction, binding the N-terminal ATP pocket with nanomolar affinity (ChEMBL record CHEMBL36506; Kd 28 nM against E. coli GyrB). Its oral form was withdrawn for lack of efficacy, and it weakly inhibits human Hsp90 — but as a target-site proof it stands. The site has been re-validated recently: Cotman et al. (2023) developed benzothiazole GyrB ATP-pocket inhibitors with potent activity against Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, both WHO-priority pathogens, with no cross-resistance to novobiocin, and solved the E. coli GyrB24 co-crystal structure 7P2M (1.16 Å) with their inhibitor LMD43.

This paper asks a narrow, testable question: among the known E. coli GyrB ligands in ChEMBL, is there one that docks better than novobiocin on 7P2M, matches or beats its measured potency, and is more drug-like — and does the standard comparator, ciprofloxacin, even belong in the comparison? The falsifiable hypothesis is that at least one known GyrB inhibitor beats novobiocin beyond Vina's noise floor on a correctly centred grid. The paper tests that hypothesis against the measured ChEMBL potencies, against the noise floor, and against a deliberately included wrong-site control.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 9 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-09.md, PubMed, ChEMBL (EBI), UniProtKB, PubChem and RCSB PDB. Key sources: Murray et al. (2022) for the AMR mortality burden; WHO (2024) for the priority-pathogens list; Champoux (2001) for the gyrase mechanism; Microorganisms (2023) for the QRDR mutation panel and resistance rates; Cotman et al. (2023) for the 7P2M structure and the benzothiazole series; ChEMBL activity records for the measured potencies below. Every citation in this paper was verified against its publisher or database record on the day of writing; no citation was generated from memory.

2.2 Molecular docking — and a discarded first run

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 9 November 2026 with ciprofloxacin as the query: UniProtKB target identification → ChEMBL bioactivities → PubChem verification → RDKit Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen (25 compounds) → RDKit ADMET/PAINS panel plus ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays) → composite ranking → AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 docking (box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of 3 poses).

The first run was discarded, and the reason is documented here because it is a fault class, not a footnote. With the topic string "DNA gyrase (GyrB subunit)", the pipeline resolved UniProtKB Q5SHZ4 — DNA gyrase subunit B from Thermus thermophilus — and ChEMBL target CHEMBL2074. CHEMBL2074 was verified against the ChEMBL API to be human maltase-glucoamylase (MGAM, UniProt O43451), not a gyrase at all: its 55 "leads" were alpha-glucosidase inhibitors docked onto a thermophile GyrB structure (PDB 6ENH). That run's scores are meaningless and are not reported in this paper; its raw JSON is kept as hidden_files/dock-HP-015-WRONG-TARGET-2026-11-09.json for the audit trail. The corrected run used the precise target string "Escherichia coli DNA gyrase subunit B", which resolved UniProtKB P0AES6 (E. coli strain K12, DNA gyrase subunit B) and ChEMBL CHEMBL1826 (DNA gyrase subunit B, single protein, E. coli, 50 bioactivities). All results below are from the corrected run only. A data-quality note: several of the retrieved ChEMBL ligands contain aluminium and failed RDKit sanitisation (explicit-valence warnings in the run log); they were excluded by the screen and none is in the docked set.

Docking used PDB 7P2M (1.16 Å), E. coli GyrB24 in complex with the benzothiazole inhibitor LMD43/EBL2560 (Cotman et al., 2023), auto-picked as the highest-resolution inhibitor-bound structure. Centre audit, performed after the run from the PDB file itself: the docking centre [−18.60, −15.05, 6.55] is 0.01 Å from the centroid of the co-crystallised ligand N1N (LMD43); the only other hetero group, a phosphate ion, is 10.68 Å away — the grid is on the inhibitor's ATP pocket, not on a crystallisation artefact. Novobiocin, the true ATP-site reference, is not among the pipeline's top-5 ranked leads (its similarity to the ciprofloxacin query is low), so it was docked separately with the identical protocol (same structure, centre and box; PubChem CID 54675769) and is reported in the same table. Ciprofloxacin was docked by the pipeline as the QUERY; it is retained in the table as a wrong-site control, not as a comparator — it binds the GyrA–DNA cleavage complex, a different pocket on the same enzyme.

2.3 PAINS screen

The RDKit PAINS filter was applied to every ranked lead. All five docked compounds are PAINS-clean; a PAINS alert is reported, never hidden, and none occurred here. The Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) is reported in the pipeline JSON; no compound in the docked set raised a high-probability toxicity flag.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity. Vina's scoring error is ±1–2 kcal/mol, so only margins above ~2 kcal/mol are treated as real differences. No experimental data were generated. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. Measured potencies are ChEMBL records for the E. coli GyrB target and were not re-measured; the four leads' IC50s (3–8 nM) come from a single assay format (inhibition of E. coli GyrB residues 1–220) while novobiocin's values come from different assays (Kd, ATPase IC50, supercoiling IC50), so cross-assay comparisons are indicative only. Only five compounds were docked.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

CHEMBL4294536 CHEMBL4294536 −7.93 IC50 3.0 nM (pChEMBL 8.52) 542.59 4.73 1 Clean
CHEMBL4278317 CHEMBL4278317 −7.84 IC50 8.0 nM (pChEMBL 8.10) 554.60 4.92 1 Clean
Novobiocin (true ATP-site reference) CHEMBL36506 −7.76 Kd 28 nM; IC50 154 nM (ATPase) / 200 nM (supercoiling) 612.63 3.63 2 Clean
Ciprofloxacin (QUERY, wrong-site control) CHEMBL100 −7.26 No GyrB ATP-site activity (binds GyrA–DNA) 331.35 1.58 0 Clean
CHEMBL4281775 CHEMBL4281775 −7.17 IC50 6.0 nM (pChEMBL 8.22) 561.59 4.41 1 Clean

The best lead, CHEMBL4293447, beats novobiocin by 1.02 kcal/mol and beats ciprofloxacin by 1.52 kcal/mol. Both margins sit inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise: no lead beats either reference beyond noise. The measured potencies tell the same story of a tie: the four leads' IC50s span only 3–8 nM (a 2.7-fold range, within normal assay variation), and the most potent measured compound, CHEMBL4294536 (3.0 nM), ranks only second by docking, while the weakest measured, CHEMBL4278317 (8.0 nM), ranks third. Across the four leads, docking rank and potency rank correlate at Spearman ρ = 0.35 (n = 4, one tied pair) — weak, and with a 2.7-fold potency spread there is almost nothing for a ranker to reproduce. The four leads are one chemotype family: thiazole/pyridine-carboxamide GyrB ATPase-domain inhibitors from a single 2018 European Journal of Medicinal Chemistry series (assay on E. coli GyrB residues 1–220; e.g. CHEMBL4293447, activity record 18804670, assay CHEMBL4275017). The docked set therefore tests one scaffold four ways, not four scaffolds.

Two controls frame the table. First, ciprofloxacin's −7.26: a compound with no activity at this pocket scores within 1.5 kcal/mol of the best lead. Absolute Vina scores are not evidence of binding; only the margin against a same-site reference means anything, and here the margin against novobiocin is 1.02 kcal/mol — noise. Second, novobiocin's own profile: the reference is the worst compound in the table by drug-likeness (MW 612.63, 2 Lipinski violations, PSA 200.01, withdrawn) and yet the most potent by binding (Kd 28 nM). Every lead beats novobiocin on drug-likeness (MW 542–562, 1 violation) but none beats it on docking beyond noise. The trade the series offers is therefore developability, not potency.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina benchmark of these four compounds on E. coli GyrB was found in the literature sweep, so there is no published docking table to compare against. The structural context is the Cotman et al. (2023) series itself: their compound 27 achieved a 10-fold improved aqueous solubility, 10-fold improved inhibition of topoisomerase IV from A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa, 10-fold decreased inhibition of human topoisomerase IIα, and no cross-resistance to novobiocin relative to their starting compound 1. Our docked leads predate that optimisation (2018 series) and carry the liabilities Cotman et al. optimised away: MW >540, logP 4.4–4.9, one Lipinski violation each. The 7P2M structure is the optimised series' structure, not the 2018 series' — a mismatch worth stating: the grid is shaped by a benzothiazole (LMD43), while the docked leads are a different chemotype.

3.3 The standardisation problem: one scaffold, one assay format, one structure

Three standardisation gaps limit this paper. First, scaffold diversity: all four leads come from one 2018 series, so the benchmark cannot say whether the ATP pocket prefers this chemotype or merely tolerates it. Second, assay format: the leads' IC50s are all from the GyrB 1–220 ATPase-domain assay, while novobiocin's values span binding (Kd 28 nM), ATPase (154 nM) and supercoiling (200 nM) assays — the 5- to 7-fold gap between novobiocin's Kd and its IC50s is a reminder that the leads' 3–8 nM IC50s and novobiocin's 28 nM Kd are not directly comparable quantities. Third, the resistance-bypass claim that motivates the target has not been tested for these leads: no MIC data against gyrA QRDR mutants were in the retrieved records.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The paper's hypothesis — that a known GyrB inhibitor beats novobiocin beyond noise — fails on docking and is untestable on measured potency, because the measured potencies are tied. That is not a null result; it reframes the series. The 2018 compounds are already single-digit-nanomolar GyrB inhibitors; the problem they need to solve is not potency but the developability gap the Cotman series later closed (solubility, plasma free fraction, human topoisomerase IIα selectivity). A docking benchmark that rewards only the score will keep re-selecting the same potent-but-heavy scaffold. The useful ranking for this series is a multi-objective one: docking score, solubility, and human topoisomerase IIα selectivity — and the falsifiable claim is about MICs in QRDR mutants, not about a docking margin.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

CHEMBL4293447's −8.78 is the best score in the table and its 1.02 kcal/mol margin over novobiocin is the largest margin available — and it is still noise. The preparation noise measured in this pipeline family is ~0.43 kcal/mol (same molecule docked twice), and Vina's own error is ±1–2 kcal/mol; a 1.02 kcal/mol margin clears neither bar that matters. The ciprofloxacin control (§3.1) shows why the absolute value is not a fallback: −7.26 for a non-binder. Nothing in this table supports prioritising CHEMBL4293447 over novobiocin, or over the other three leads, on docking alone.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

No PAINS alerts occurred in the docked set, so there is no PAINS constraint on the proposed validation beyond the standard ones: aggregation and redox controls in the enzyme assay, and a detergent control in the cell assay. The more relevant artefact risk for this series is the opposite one — the compounds are large, lipophilic (logP 4.4–4.9) and poorly soluble, so apparent potency in a cell assay can be driven by aggregation or membrane partitioning. The validation design therefore includes a solubility measurement and a counter-screen against human topoisomerase IIα (the selectivity liability Cotman et al. optimised against) before any MIC claim.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL4293447 inhibits E. coli GyrB ATPase more potently than novobiocin under identical conditions. Measurement: ATPase assay (GyrB 1–220) for CHEMBL4293447, CHEMBL4294536 and novobiocin in the same run, same ATP concentration. Fails if CHEMBL4293447's IC50 is not lower than novobiocin's.
  2. The leads bypass fluoroquinolone resistance. Measurement: MICs of the four leads and ciprofloxacin against isogenic E. coli carrying gyrA S83L, gyrA S83L/D87N and parC S80I. Fails if the leads' MICs rise with the mutants the way ciprofloxacin's do.
  3. The docking margin is a pocket-shape artefact of 7P2M. Measurement: re-dock all six compounds on the novobiocin-bound E. coli GyrB structure 1AJ6 with the same protocol. Fails if CHEMBL4293447 still leads by the same margin.
  4. The series' liability is solubility, not potency. Measurement: kinetic solubility and human topoisomerase IIα inhibition for the four leads. Fails if solubility is high and human topoisomerase IIα is not inhibited — in which case the Cotman optimisation was unnecessary for this scaffold.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): E. coli GyrB (1–220) expression and ATPase assay set-up, novobiocin as the internal control, solubility measurement for the four leads. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): head-to-head ATPase IC50s in triplicate, plus human topoisomerase IIα counter-screen. Stage 3 (weeks 7–10): MICs against wild-type E. coli and the three QRDR-mutant isogenics, with ciprofloxacin as the control. Stage 4 (weeks 11–12): re-docking on 1AJ6 and a go/no-go on hypotheses 1–4. Compound requirement is milligrams; the four leads are research compounds requiring synthesis or a supplier quote, novobiocin and ciprofloxacin are commercially available.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only: no experimental data were generated; every number is a Vina score or a ChEMBL record.
  2. No lead beats novobiocin beyond Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise; the best margin is 1.02 kcal/mol.
  3. Ciprofloxacin is a wrong-site control, not a comparator; its score (−7.26) demonstrates that absolute Vina scores do not establish binding.
  4. All four leads are one chemotype from one 2018 series; scaffold diversity is zero.
  5. Measured potencies mix assay formats (GyrB 1–220 ATPase IC50s for the leads; Kd, ATPase and supercoiling IC50s for novobiocin); cross-assay comparisons are indicative only.
  6. The 7P2M grid is shaped by a benzothiazole (LMD43), not by the docked chemotype; re-docking on the novobiocin-bound 1AJ6 was not run.
  7. No MIC data against QRDR mutants were available; the resistance-bypass claim is untested for these leads.
  8. The first pipeline run resolved the wrong target (human maltase-glucoamylase) and was discarded; the corrected run is reported, but the fault shows the pipeline's target resolution needs a human check every time.
  9. No molecular dynamics, no MM-GBSA rescoring, no human topoisomerase IIα selectivity data for the leads.

6. Conclusion

On the high-resolution E. coli GyrB structure 7P2M, four known GyrB ATPase-domain inhibitors dock at −7.17 to −8.78 kcal/mol, and the best, CHEMBL4293447, beats the true ATP-site reference novobiocin (−7.76) by only 1.02 kcal/mol — inside Vina's noise. Their measured IC50s (3–8 nM) are essentially tied with each other, and the series' real gap is developability (MW >540, logP ~4.4–4.9), not potency. The honest conclusion is that this benchmark cannot prioritise among these compounds on docking, and that the next experiment is a head-to-head ATPase assay plus MICs against gyrA QRDR mutants — the measurement that would actually test the resistance-bypass claim. No cure claim is made, and no clinical recommendation follows.

Two Furoxan Analogues Out-Dock Praziquantel on Schistosoma TGR — But Praziquantel Does Not Target TGR: A Corrected Vina Benchmark on 8PDD

Schistosomiasis required preventive treatment for at least 253.7 million people in 2024, yet only 39.6% of them were reached, and control still rests on a single drug, praziquantel, which kills adult worms but not eggs or immature worms and does not prevent reinfection.
