Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-08 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #4 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: schistosomiasis; thioredoxin glutathione reductase; praziquantel; furoxan; oxadiazole 2-oxide; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; neglected tropical disease

Abstract

Schistosomiasis required preventive treatment for at least 253.7 million people in 2024, yet only 39.6% of them were reached, and control still rests on a single drug, praziquantel, which kills adult worms but not eggs or immature worms and does not prevent reinfection. Thioredoxin glutathione reductase (TGR) of Schistosoma mansoni is a selenocysteine flavoenzyme that is the parasite's sole route for both thioredoxin and glutathione reduction — a validated drug target with no human equivalent. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking) against the 1.25 Å SmTGR structure (PDB 8PDD), docking praziquantel plus five known TGR inhibitors (measured potencies 10–100 nM) with an identical AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol. Two furoxan (oxadiazole 2-oxide) analogues out-docked praziquantel: CHEMBL3322292 (IC50 83 nM) at −10.93 kcal/mol and CHEMBL3322287 (IC50 10 nM) at −10.27 kcal/mol, against praziquantel at −9.59 kcal/mol — but praziquantel does not act on TGR, so beating it on this site is a cross-docking control, not a therapeutic comparison, and the docking order inverts the measured potencies (the 83 nM compound docks better than the 10 nM compound by 0.66 kcal/mol). The grid centre was corrected during the run: the first attempt centred on the FAD cofactor, and re-docking at the redox-active cysteine site changed no ranking and shifted scores by at most 0.66 kcal/mol, showing the conclusion is robust to that error. The falsifiable next step is a TGR enzyme assay of the two furoxans head-to-head with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable potency advantage; a furoxan that inhibits TGR at its ChEMBL IC50 and kills schistosomula would refute the claim that docking order on this target is uninformative.

1. Introduction

Schistosomiasis is an acute and chronic parasitic disease caused by blood flukes of the genus Schistosoma. The World Health Organization records that at least 253.7 million people required preventive treatment in 2024, of whom more than 100.5 million were treated — only 39.6% coverage — and deaths are estimated at 14,353 per year, a figure WHO itself notes is likely underestimated. The disease is endemic in 78 countries, with 50 requiring preventive chemotherapy. Control rests almost entirely on one drug, praziquantel, donated by Merck for free distribution since 2007: a single dose is usually curative, with cure rates above 80–90% in many series, but it kills adult worms only — not eggs or immature worms — and it does not prevent reinfection, so people return to contaminated water and are infected again. A second drug with a different mechanism is the single most important unmet need in schistosomiasis control.

Thioredoxin glutathione reductase (TGR) is that mechanism's best-validated target. Schistosomes lack separate thioredoxin reductase and glutathione reductase enzymes: a single selenocysteine-containing flavoenzyme, TGR, performs both reductions, and it is essential for the parasite's redox balance. Humans have separate enzymes, so a selective TGR inhibitor has a built-in therapeutic window. TGR was validated as a drug target by Kuntz et al. (2007), who showed the enzyme is essential and that the gold drug auranofin inhibits it and kills schistosomes. The oxadiazole 2-oxide (furoxan) class is the most studied TGR inhibitor chemotype: furoxans inhibit SmTGR in the low-nanomolar range and kill the parasite, acting in part through nitric-oxide release and covalent modification of the redox-active cysteines.

The question this paper asks is deliberately narrow and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known TGR inhibitors on the true S. mansoni structure, and does the ranking track measured potency? The falsifiable hypothesis is that the docking order will disagree with measured TGR IC50 values, and that any margin under 2 kcal/mol is inside Vina's noise.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 8 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-08.md (no schistosomiasis item that day), the WHO schistosomiasis fact sheet, BMJ Best Practice, ChEMBL (EBI), RCSB PDB and UniProtKB. Key sources: the WHO fact sheet for burden and treatment coverage; Kuntz et al., PLoS Med 2007 for TGR validation; and the 8PDD structure paper (de Souza Neto et al., Sci Rep 2024) for the target structure. All ChEMBL potency values quoted were re-checked live against the ChEMBL API on 8 November 2026 for the target "Thioredoxin glutathione reductase" (CHEMBL6110, Schistosoma mansoni).

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target resolution was verified by hand: ChEMBL target CHEMBL6110 ("Thioredoxin glutathione reductase", SINGLE PROTEIN, Schistosoma mansoni) is correct; UniProt resolution was not the failure point here.

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure is PDB 8PDD, S. mansoni TGR at 1.25 Å resolution (de Souza Neto et al., Sci Rep 2024), the highest-resolution SmTGR structure available. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Six ligands were docked: praziquantel itself (QUERY, PubChem CID 4891) as a cross-docking negative control — praziquantel's mechanism is disruption of calcium homeostasis and tegument damage, not TGR inhibition — and the top five pipeline-ranked TGR inhibitors with measured potencies of 10–100 nM. Two of the five are furoxan (oxadiazole 2-oxide) analogues, identified from their ChEMBL structures.

Centre correction (fault, found and fixed during this run). The first docking run centred the grid on the FAD cofactor centroid, [7.30, −2.84, 57.31], because 8PDD holds no drug-like ligand and the pipeline's _ligand_center fallback picks the first HETATM group with six or more atoms when nothing survives its cofactor/glycan/lipid exclusions — and FAD is a cofactor that the exclusions did not catch in this structure. That first run's scores are kept for audit in the data file and are reported in Section 3.3, but they are not the result. The corrected centre is [8.28, −4.52, 51.60], the midpoint of the FAD isoalloxazine centroid [6.23, −4.20, 52.39] and the midpoint of the redox-active Cys154–Cys159 disulfide SG atoms [10.33, −4.84, 50.80] (Cys154 SG is 4.59 Å and Cys159 SG 3.22 Å from the FAD isoalloxazine — both distances verified in the PDB file). The same six ligands were re-docked at the corrected centre, and the corrected run is the result reported here.

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: praziquantel and all five leads were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 panel was run for each lead. Praziquantel's panel is measured data, not read-across: NR-ER 1.0. This is a Tox21 assay readout, not a clinical claim, and is reported here so it is not misread as a toxicity finding. The two furoxans' highest read-across probabilities were NR-ER 0.41 (CHEMBL3322292) and NR-AhR 0.17 (CHEMBL3322287); the remaining leads' highest read-across probabilities were 0.07–0.52. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements.

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of a co-crystallised ligand pose (RMSD) was performed — 8PDD has no co-crystallised inhibitor to re-dock; a single X-ray structure (8PDD, one TGR conformation) was used; the receptor was held rigid; the selenocysteine residue (Sec597 in SmTGR) is modelled as cysteine in the docking preparation, so any selenium-specific interaction is invisible to this protocol; the leads are already-known TGR inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed. Praziquantel's docking score on TGR says nothing about praziquantel as a drug, because praziquantel does not act on TGR. Schistosome killing was not measured for any lead.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound SmTGR potency, ChEMBL Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) MW logP Lipinski violations PAINS Top tox
CHEMBL3322292 (furoxan analogue) IC50 83 nM −10.93 −10.93, −9.29, −9.16 469.5 0.83 0 clean NR-ER 0.413
CHEMBL3322287 (furoxan analogue) IC50 10 nM −10.27 −10.27, −9.68, −8.67 357.3 −1.01 0 clean NR-AhR 0.169
Praziquantel (reference, negative control) — −9.59 −9.59, −9.31, −8.22 312.4 2.53 0 clean NR-ER 1.0 (measured)
CHEMBL1535744 Potency 100 nM −7.74 −7.74, −7.19, −6.28 274.4 3.10 0 clean NR-ER 0.155
CHEMBL1456339 Potency 100 nM −7.33 −7.33, −7.11, −7.09 296.2 3.44 0 clean NR-AhR 0.094
CHEMBL1365586 Potency 100 nM −6.51 −6.51, −6.09, −6.01 306.5 3.04 0 clean NR-AhR 0.070

All docking on PDB 8PDD (S. mansoni TGR, 1.25 Å), corrected grid centre [8.28, −4.52, 51.60] (midpoint of FAD isoalloxazine and Cys154–Cys159 disulfide), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, Vina 1.2.7, 8 November 2026. Potencies are ChEMBL on-target values, re-checked live on 8 November 2026. Praziquantel does not target TGR; its score is a cross-docking control.

The headline, stated honestly: two furoxans out-dock praziquantel on TGR — and that comparison is meaningless as a drug comparison, because praziquantel does not act on TGR. The real comparison is between the leads themselves, and it fails: the 83 nM compound (CHEMBL3322292) docks better than the 10 nM compound (CHEMBL3322287) by 0.66 kcal/mol — the docking order inverts the measured potency order at the top of the table. The margins that matter are all inside noise: the two furoxans differ by 0.66 kcal/mol, and each beats praziquantel by 0.68 and 1.34 kcal/mol — the second inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, the first only just outside it. The three 100 nM compounds score −7.74 to −6.51 kcal/mol, a full 2.5–4.4 kcal/mol below the furoxans, so the screen does separate the potent from the weak — it just cannot order the potent ones. Pose consistency does not rescue the top ranking: CHEMBL3322292's second pose drops to −9.29, a 1.64 kcal/mol gap from its best pose, the largest pose spread in the set, so its best score is the least stable of the six.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for any of these leads on 8PDD was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for two furoxan TGR inhibitors, praziquantel as a cross-docking control, and three 100 nM inhibitors on the 1.25 Å SmTGR structure are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the centre audit trail and the correction. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: the two furoxans span measured TGR IC50 values of 10 and 83 nM, an 8-fold spread, and their docking order is inverted relative to it. Vina ranks poses, not IC50s, and on this site it ranks the top two backwards.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

The centre fault is the story of this paper's methods section, and its resolution is reassuring: the first run centred on the FAD cofactor [7.30, −2.84, 57.31] and gave CHEMBL3322292 −11.24, CHEMBL3322287 −10.16, praziquantel −9.31, CHEMBL1535744 −8.40 and CHEMBL1365586 −6.33 kcal/mol — the same ranking as the corrected run, with shifts of at most 0.66 kcal/mol. The FAD isoalloxazine sits adjacent to the redox cysteines (3.22–4.59 Å), so a grid centred on FAD still overlaps the redox site; the error was real but small, because the cofactor and the active site are neighbours in this enzyme. That is luck, not validation: in the aldose-reductase case that motivated this audit, the cofactor centre was 13.26 Å from the inhibitor site and the ranking inverted. The pipeline's _ligand_center fallback — first HETATM group with six or more atoms when nothing survives the exclusions — still silently picks a cofactor when a structure holds no drug-like ligand, and it did so here; the fix is a hard rule that a structure with no drug-like ligand gets no automatic centre at all, and a human picks the site. The second fault was the screen's design: praziquantel was chosen as the reference drug because it is the standard of care, but it is not a TGR inhibitor, so the paper's central comparison is a control, not a contest. The honest framing is that this paper benchmarks TGR inhibitors against each other, with praziquantel as the negative control that proves the site binds non-TGR drugs too.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a negative benchmark with a useful control — and a methods warning. There is no lead here: the two furoxans are already-known TGR inhibitors, their docking scores invert their measured potencies, and the drug they "beat" does not act on the target. The durable findings are the benchmark values for two furoxans and praziquantel on 8PDD (with full pose lists), the demonstration that Vina inverts an 8-fold potency difference at the top of this table, and the centre-correction audit: a cofactor-centred grid and a redox-site-centred grid gave the same ranking with shifts under 0.66 kcal/mol, because in TGR the cofactor and the active site are neighbours — a result that would not generalise to a target where they are apart. The more important finding is the reference-drug error: choosing the standard of care as the docking reference is only valid when the standard of care acts on the target, and here it does not.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the margins that matter are inside noise: the two furoxans differ by 0.66 kcal/mol, and the smaller furoxan–praziquantel margin is 0.68 kcal/mol, both inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the ranking must be checked against measured SmTGR IC50 values — the two leads span 10 and 83 nM, and a docking order that inverts that order is a measurement of the scoring function, not of the molecules. Third, the reference comparison is void: praziquantel does not inhibit TGR, so out-docking it proves only that the site accepts a non-TGR drug, which is expected for a large flavoprotein active site. A docking "win" against praziquantel on TGR is not a discovery; it is a benchmark value awaiting an assay.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All leads are PAINS-clean, which removes one artefact class from the validation design — but the furoxan chemotype is a known covalent/reactive class, and PAINS-clean does not rule out covalent or redox-mediated assay interference, which is precisely how furoxans are thought to act on TGR (nitric-oxide release, cysteine modification). The Tox21 flags are low (highest read-across 0.41–0.52) and must not be reported as toxicity. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either. The validation assay must include redox controls, a counter-screen against the human thioredoxin reductase, and a reversibility test, because a furoxan that inhibits by covalent modification needs a different evidentiary standard than a reversible binder. The larger safety question — selectivity over the human enzyme, which is the whole point of targeting TGR — is not addressed by PAINS at all and needs a dedicated human-enzyme counter-screen for any lead that advances.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-docking furoxan (CHEMBL3322292) inhibits recombinant SmTGR with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value (83 nM) under identical assay conditions; a measured IC50 worse than 10 nM for CHEMBL3322287 would confirm the noise interpretation, while the reverse would refute it.
  2. A Vina re-dock of a fragment from the 8PDD fragment screen into its crystallographic site reproduces the experimental pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).
  3. Both furoxans inhibit SmTGR reversibly and selectively over human thioredoxin reductase by at least 10-fold; failure of selectivity would end the chemotype regardless of potency.
  4. Docking the same six ligands on the earlier SmTGR structure 2X99 gives the same ranking as on 8PDD; a different ranking would show the result is structure-dependent, not molecule-dependent.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): SmTGR enzyme inhibition assay for both furoxans and praziquantel as a negative control, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and the rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): schistosomula viability assay for any compound that clears Stage 1 at its measured IC50, plus a human thioredoxin reductase counter-screen at 10× the SmTGR IC50, with a reversibility test (dialysis or dilution) to distinguish covalent from reversible inhibition. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): adult-worm assay for the best compound, with praziquantel as the positive control, and a first-pass mouse tolerability check before any efficacy claim. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. Any margin under 2 kcal/mol is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and cannot be interpreted as a real advantage — the furoxan–furoxan margin is 0.66 kcal/mol. 3. The docking order inverts the measured potency order for the top two leads. 4. Praziquantel does not act on TGR, so the headline comparison is a control, not a contest. 5. Only one TGR structure (8PDD, one conformation) was docked; the earlier 2X99 structure was not scored. 6. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking RMSD validation was performed. 7. A single rigid receptor was used; the TGR active site's flexibility is not modelled. 8. The selenocysteine residue is modelled as cysteine in the docking preparation, so selenium-specific interactions are invisible. 9. The first docking run used a cofactor-centred grid; the correction is documented, but the pipeline fault that caused it is not yet fixed in code. 10. Schistosome killing was not measured for any lead.

6. Conclusion

Two furoxan TGR inhibitors out-dock praziquantel on the S. mansoni TGR structure 8PDD — CHEMBL3322292 at −10.93 and CHEMBL3322287 at −10.27 kcal/mol against praziquantel at −9.59 — but praziquantel does not act on TGR, so that comparison is a control, and the docking order inverts the measured potencies (the 83 nM compound beats the 10 nM compound by 0.66 kcal/mol). The honest reading is that on this site, non-covalent docking cannot rank known TGR inhibitors against each other — and the next experiment is a head-to-head enzyme assay with a pre-registered 2 kcal/mol rule plus a human-enzyme counter-screen, not more docking against the wrong reference drug.

Three Diazabicyclooctanes "Beat" Avibactam by Docking and Lose by Less Than 1 kcal/mol of Noise: A Vina Benchmark of KPC-2 Inhibitors on 6TD0 — and the Boronate Blind Spot

Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC-2) is the most commonly encountered class A beta-lactamase variant worldwide, and it confers high-level resistance to most available antibiotics; ceftazidime-avibactam is the standard inhibitor combination against it, but omega-loop variants such as D179N already escape it.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-08 · Daily research paper — Health track (HP-012)

Keywords: KPC-2; carbapenemase; avibactam; nacubactam; relebactam; diazabicyclooctane; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; antimicrobial resistance; Klebsiella pneumoniae

Abstract

Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC-2) is the most commonly encountered class A beta-lactamase variant worldwide, and it confers high-level resistance to most available antibiotics; ceftazidime-avibactam is the standard inhibitor combination against it, but omega-loop variants such as D179N already escape it. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking): target KPC-2 (UniProt Q9F663, ChEMBL CHEMBL6132, 4 bioactivities retrieved), structure PDB 6TD0 at 0.99 angstrom, grid centred exactly on the co-crystallised vaborbactam (centroid [15.45, 8.23, 21.26]), and six ligands docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 under an identical protocol. Nacubactam scored −7.65 kcal/mol, a 2-sulfamoyl diazabicyclooctane −7.50 and relebactam −7.35, against avibactam at −6.73 (re-dock −7.15) and tazobactam at −6.42 — margins of 0.62–0.92 kcal/mol, all inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so no compound can be called better than avibactam on these scores. Two clinically important boronates, vaborbactam and taniborbactam, could not be docked at all: the pipeline writes boron as PDBQT atom type "B", which this Vina build rejects, and their covalent boron–Ser70 mechanism is outside non-covalent docking in any case. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head KPC-2 inhibition assay (nitrocefin hydrolysis, purified enzyme, same plate) of nacubactam and relebactam against avibactam, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable Ki advantage; a measured Ki for nacubactam tighter than avibactam's would refute the noise interpretation, and re-running the same benchmark on the D179N variant structure (PDB 8G2R) would test whether the ranking survives the resistance mutation.

1. Introduction

The antimicrobial resistance (AMR) literature of the last 48 hours is a catalogue of the problem this paper works on. R-pyocins used as an evolutionary trap restored aminoglycoside sensitivity in a pan-drug-resistant clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate (Estrada et al., bioRxiv, updated 7 November 2026); vanA-positive vancomycin-resistant enterococci are highly prevalent in clinical isolates from central Iran, with linked biofilm and virulence profiles (Mezher et al., 2026); a pan-genome random-forest analysis of 465 pork-associated Salmonella Derby genomes separates isolates by country and finds Chinese isolates carrying the most AMR determinants, 15.3 per isolate (Chen & Cui, 2026); and a new review traces how biofilm tolerance becomes heritable resistance — the phenotype layer that gene-presence screens miss (Guchhait et al., 2026). The field is moving from detecting resistance to reversing it, and the tools for the detection side are still being built: SCCmecExtractor, a lightweight toolkit that extracts staphylococcal cassette chromosome elements from whole genomes, was benchmarked on 7,297 genomes across 70 species this month (MacFadyen, 2026). Against that background, the beta-lactamase inhibitor — the molecule that protects the antibiotic rather than killing the bacterium — remains the most clinically proven resistance-reversal strategy in routine use.

KPC-2 is the target that justifies that claim. It is, in the words of a 2021 mechanistic study, "the most commonly encountered class A beta-lactamase variant worldwide, which confer high-level resistance to most available antibiotics" (Lizana et al., 2021). It hydrolyses penicillins, cephalosporins, monobactams and carbapenems. The inhibitor that changed its clinical management is avibactam, a diazabicyclooctane (DBO) that inhibits KPC-2 by reversible covalent acylation of the catalytic Ser70: acylation and deacylation both proceed through a tetrahedral intermediate, with activation barriers of 19.5 and 23.0 kcal/mol and an estimated inhibition constant of 3.3 × 10⁻³, reported as in good agreement with the experimental value (Lizana et al., 2021). Avibactam is given with ceftazidime, and it is the reference drug for this benchmark.

Three other DBOs matter for the comparison. Relebactam is an approved DBO inhibitor given with imipenem–cilastatin. Nacubactam (OP0595) is an investigational DBO in development with meropenem; it differs from avibactam by an aminoethoxy side chain that was designed to add direct antibacterial activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa through penicillin-binding-protein inhibition. A fourth DBO, a 2-sulfamoyl analogue with no preferred name in ChEMBL (CHEMBL5483057; PubChem CID 172433364), is a close structural cousin of avibactam. Tazobactam, a penam sulfone, is the negative control: a beta-lactamase inhibitor with no useful KPC-2 activity. And two cyclic boronates, vaborbactam (approved, with meropenem) and taniborbactam (investigational), are the inhibitors this pipeline cannot dock — a failure that is itself a result, reported below.

The falsifiable hypothesis of this paper is that one or more of these DBOs binds KPC-2 more favourably than avibactam by a margin large enough to predict a measurable potency advantage, and that the docking margin predicts the measured ranking. The paper then tests that hypothesis against Vina's own noise floor and against the covalent mechanism that non-covalent docking cannot see.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 8 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-08.md (465 candidates screened, 8 selected), PubMed E-utilities, ChEMBL (EBI), UniProtKB and RCSB PDB. Key sources: Lizana et al. (2021) for the KPC-2 burden statement and the avibactam acylation/deacylation mechanism; Estrada et al. (2026, bioRxiv) for R-pyocin resistance reversal; Mezher et al. (2026) for vanA VRE prevalence; Chen & Cui (2026) for the Salmonella Derby AMR landscape; Guchhait et al. (2026) for the biofilm tolerance-to-resistance review; MacFadyen (2026) for SCCmecExtractor; Mastropietro & Bajorath (2026) and Singh et al. (2026) for the current state of agentic and computational lead optimisation, the context in which this pipeline operates. No measured Ki or IC50 values for the ranked DBOs against KPC-2 are reported in this paper, because none were retrievable from ChEMBL for this target (see §2.4) — that absence is a finding, not an omission, and the proposed assay is designed to fill it.

2.2 LeadForge pipeline

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target: Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase KPC-2, UniProt Q9F663; ChEMBL CHEMBL6132 ("Carbapenem-hydrolyzing beta-lactamase KPC", single protein, Klebsiella pneumoniae). ChEMBL returned 4 bioactivities for this target, and the pipeline ranked five leads by composite score (similarity × 40 + Lipinski × 20 + Veber × 10 + PAINS × 10 + tox × 20): the avibactam query (99.8), its ChEMBL record CHEMBL1689063 (99.8), the 2-sulfamoyl DBO CHEMBL5483057 (75.9), nacubactam CHEMBL3989959 (74.6) and tazobactam CHEMBL404 (64.9). Three named clinical comparators — relebactam, vaborbactam and taniborbactam — were added by PubChem name lookup (CIDs 44129647, 56649692, 76902493) and docked at the same centre under the identical protocol.

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 angstrom cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was KPC-2, PDB 6TD0 (0.99 angstrom, "Crystal structure of vaborbactam bound to KPC-2"), with the grid centred exactly on the centroid of the co-crystallised vaborbactam, residue 4D6 chain A 301: [15.45, 8.23, 21.26]. The centre was verified against the PDB file: the two alternate-location conformers of vaborbactam have centroids [15.45, 8.22, 21.34] (altloc A) and [15.45, 8.24, 21.18] (altloc B), both within 0.08 angstrom of the grid centre, and the only other non-water hetero groups in the file are glycerol and sulfate, which the centre picker excludes — the grid-centre fault that has corrupted earlier runs (centring on a cofactor, glycan or lipid) did not occur here. The avibactam-bound wild-type structure 4ZBE (1.8 angstrom) was checked as the alternative and not used, because 6TD0 is the higher-resolution structure and its co-crystallised ligand is also a KPC-2 inhibitor. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Avibactam was docked twice — once by the pipeline (−6.73 kcal/mol) and once as an independent re-dock at the identical centre, box and exhaustiveness (−7.15 kcal/mol) — as a reproducibility check on the protocol. The 0.42 kcal/mol spread between the two runs is the protocol's own run-to-run variation and is carried into every comparison below.

2.4 The boronate failure

Vaborbactam and taniborbactam could not be docked. Ligand preparation (meeko) writes the boron atom as PDBQT atom type "B", and Vina 1.2.7 rejects it: "PDBQT parsing error: Atom type B is not a valid AutoDock type (atom types are case-sensitive)." Both compounds failed identically, at the same step, with no poses produced. Two consequences follow. First, the co-crystallised ligand of 6TD0 could not be re-docked, so no self-docking validation of the protocol against the crystal pose is available for this structure — the avibactam re-dock above is the only reproducibility check. Second, the two boronates are exactly the compounds whose mechanism Vina could not model even if the atom type were accepted: cyclic boronates inhibit KPC-2 by forming a covalent bond between boron and the Ser70 oxygen, a tetrahedral boronate adduct, and non-covalent docking has no term for it. Mapping boron onto carbon to force a score would produce a number that misrepresents the chemistry, so no such score is reported. The boronate gap is a limitation of this pipeline, stated here so that a later run with boron-capable docking (or a covalent-docking protocol) can close it.

2.5 PAINS and ToxGuard screens

Every compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter (A/B/C catalogues) and a ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays). All six docked compounds are PAINS-clean. Read-across probabilities are low throughout (highest single assay probability 0.148, avibactam NR-AR; nacubactam's highest is SR-ARE 0.105; relebactam's highest is NR-ER 0.081; tazobactam's highest is NR-AR 0.054), but the nearest-neighbour similarities are also low (maximum 0.22–0.34), so these are weak read-acrosses, not safety findings. The named boronates are likewise PAINS-clean, with vaborbactam's highest read-across SR-ARE 0.319 and taniborbactam's NR-AhR 0.154 — again weak read-acrosses, and both are approved or late-stage compounds, so the panel adds no liability signal.

2.6 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, covalent docking, or re-docking validation of the co-crystallised ligand was performed (the boronate failure, §2.4); a single crystal structure (6TD0, one KPC-2 conformation) was used; and, most importantly, every DBO in this benchmark inhibits KPC-2 by reversible covalent acylation of Ser70 — a mechanism Vina cannot model — so every score reported here is missing the dominant binding term, exactly as the NDM-1 paper's zinc and the CYP51 paper's haem coordination were missing from theirs. ChEMBL holds no pChEMBL values for KPC-2 (all 50 recorded activities for CHEMBL6132 lack pChEMBL, and the retrieved bioactivities are substrate-hydrolysis and MIC records, not inhibitor potencies), so no measured ranking exists to check the docking ranking against. The leads are already-known inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Vaborbactam (CID 56649692) cyclic boronate not docked — 297.14 0.45 0 pass clean SR-ARE 0.319
Taniborbactam (CID 76902493) cyclic boronate not docked — 389.26 0.32 0 pass clean NR-AhR 0.154

Tanimoto similarity (Morgan fingerprints) to avibactam: relebactam 0.612, 2-sulfamoyl-DBO 0.659, nacubactam 0.646, tazobactam 0.127, vaborbactam 0.099, taniborbactam 0.098.

3.2 The margins are noise

Against the pipeline's avibactam score (−6.73), nacubactam leads by 0.92 kcal/mol, the 2-sulfamoyl DBO by 0.77 and relebactam by 0.62. Against the avibactam re-dock (−7.15), the same margins shrink to 0.50, 0.35 and 0.20. Every margin is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the choice of which avibactam run to compare against moves the "win" by almost half. The ranking is also fragile at the level of individual poses: relebactam's second pose (−7.11) is already worse than nacubactam's best, and tazobactam's best pose (−6.42) is only 0.20–0.31 kcal/mol behind avibactam's — a molecule with no useful KPC-2 activity scores within noise of the reference drug. That is the control working as intended: it shows the protocol cannot separate an active DBO from an inactive penam sulfone on scores alone.

3.3 The boronate blind spot

The two compounds the pipeline could not dock are not marginal. Vaborbactam is the co-crystallised ligand of the very structure used here, and it is an approved KPC-2 inhibitor; taniborbactam is the broadest-spectrum boronate in development, active against both serine- and metallo-beta-lactamases. Their absence from the table is a property of the tooling, not of the molecules, and it biases the benchmark in a specific direction: the only inhibitors that survive the pipeline are the ones whose chemistry Vina can represent, which is exactly the set whose covalent mechanism Vina cannot score. A benchmark that cannot dock its own structure's ligand is a benchmark that should be read as a pose screen of DBOs, not as a ranking of KPC-2 inhibitors.

3.4 The resistance-variant angle

Structures of KPC-2 variants in complex with avibactam are already deposited: the D179N variant (PDB 8G2R, 1.28 angstrom) and the G89D mutant (PDB 8RWP, 1.19 angstrom), alongside the wild-type avibactam complex 4ZBE (1.8 angstrom). The D179N structure is the direct structural counterpart of the ceftazidime-avibactam escape route: the omega loop that positions the catalytic machinery. No docking was run on 8G2R in this paper; it is named here as the immediate follow-up, because a DBO that only beats avibactam on wild-type KPC-2 is of limited use if the ranking collapses on the variant that actually circulates under ceftazidime-avibactam pressure.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The honest reading of Table 3.1 is not "three DBOs beat avibactam" but "four DBOs and one inactive control all score within about 1.2 kcal/mol of each other on wild-type KPC-2, and the two boronates cannot be scored at all." That is a negative result about the method, and it is consistent with the three previous benchmarks in this series: flavonoids "beat" acarbose on alpha-amylase by ~1 kcal/mol of noise; five HER2 inhibitors docked within noise of lapatinib; five COX-2 inhibitors showed docking selectivity that did not track measured selectivity. The pattern is now four for four: on a single-structure, single-protocol Vina benchmark, the reference drug is never beaten by a margin the method can defend.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three separate reasons, each sufficient. First, the noise floor: Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol error is larger than every margin in the table, and the avibactam re-dock alone moves the reference by 0.42 kcal/mol. Second, the missing mechanism: avibactam, nacubactam, relebactam and the sulfamoyl DBO all inhibit KPC-2 by reversible covalent acylation through a tetrahedral intermediate (Lizana et al., 2021), and Vina scores only the non-covalent pose — the same missing term that made the CYP51 benchmark blind to haem coordination and the NDM-1 benchmark blind to zinc. A DBO with a better non-covalent pose can still be the worse covalent inhibitor, and the assay that matters measures the acylation rate, not the pose. Third, the missing comparator: the boronates, which include the approved vaborbactam and the broad-spectrum taniborbactam, are absent, so the table cannot even claim to rank the clinically relevant set.

4.3 What the DBOs do offer

The result is not that the DBOs are interchangeable. Nacubactam's aminoethoxy side chain gives it direct antibacterial activity that avibactam lacks, and its development rationale is the combination with meropenem, not a better KPC-2 Ki. Relebactam's value is its approved combination with imipenem–cilastatin and its activity against KPC-producing isolates in that combination. The sulfamoyl DBO is a reminder that the DBO scaffold tolerates substitution at the 2-position — the same position that carries avibactam's carboxamide — and that ChEMBL's KPC-2 record, thin as it is, already contains analogues worth assaying. The docking table does not rank these properties; it only says that pose energy will not be the property that separates them.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

H1 (noise): In a head-to-head KPC-2 inhibition assay (nitrocefin hydrolysis, purified recombinant KPC-2, same plate, n = 3), nacubactam and relebactam show no measurable Ki advantage over avibactam (pre-registered rule: a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts a Ki ratio within 2-fold). A measured Ki for nacubactam more than 2-fold tighter than avibactam's refutes H1 and would be the first evidence in this series that a sub-noise docking margin predicted a real advantage.

H2 (variant): The same four DBOs docked on the D179N variant structure (PDB 8G2R) at the avibactam centroid keep the wild-type ranking (nacubactam ≥ sulfamoyl-DBO ≥ relebactam ≥ avibactam). A re-ordering on 8G2R — in particular avibactam falling behind — would show the wild-type benchmark does not generalise to the resistance variant and would redirect the assay in H1 to the D179N enzyme.

H3 (boronate): With a boron-capable docking protocol (covalent docking or a Vina build that accepts boron), vaborbactam re-docked into 6TD0 reproduces the crystal pose within 2 angstrom RMSD and scores within 1 kcal/mol of the best DBO. Failure would show the boronate mechanism needs a different method entirely, not a patched atom type.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): nitrocefin-hydrolysis KPC-2 inhibition assay for nacubactam, relebactam, the 2-sulfamoyl DBO and avibactam, purified enzyme, same plate, n = 3, with the pre-registered 2-fold decision rule from H1; tazobactam as the negative control (expected: no measurable inhibition at the tested range). Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): if Stage 1 shows any genuine advantage, repeat on purified D179N KPC-2 (H2) and add a whole-cell assay against a KPC-2-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate with the partner beta-lactam (ceftazidime for avibactam, meropenem for nacubactam, imipenem for relebactam) to test whether an enzyme-level advantage survives the outer membrane and efflux. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): if Stage 1 shows none, the project stops at the benchmark and the paper stands as a negative result; the boronate arm (H3) is pursued only if a boron-capable protocol is available, otherwise it is recorded as a pipeline gap for a future run. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; avibactam, relebactam and tazobactam are approved drugs, nacubactam and the sulfamoyl DBO are research chemicals, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. Every "winning" margin (0.62–0.92 kcal/mol against the pipeline avibactam run; 0.20–0.50 against the re-dock) is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and cannot be interpreted as a real advantage. 3. Vina cannot model the reversible covalent acylation of Ser70 that defines DBO inhibition, so every score is missing the dominant binding term. 4. The two boronates (vaborbactam, taniborbactam) could not be docked at all — boron is not a valid atom type in this Vina build — so the benchmark cannot rank the clinically relevant inhibitor set and no self-docking validation against the crystal pose was possible. 5. A single crystal structure (6TD0, one KPC-2 conformation) was used; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or covalent docking was performed. 6. ChEMBL holds no pChEMBL values for KPC-2, so no measured ranking exists to check the docking ranking against; the four retrieved bioactivities are the entire ChEMBL ligand record for this target, which is thin for a target of this importance. 7. The D179N variant benchmark (H2) was not run. 8. The Tox21 read-across probabilities are similarity-based predictions with low nearest-neighbour similarity (0.22–0.34), not measurements. 9. The 2-sulfamoyl DBO has no preferred name in ChEMBL and is identified here by its ChEMBL ID and PubChem CID only.

6. Conclusion

Nacubactam, a 2-sulfamoyl diazabicyclooctane and relebactam dock to wild-type KPC-2 at −7.65, −7.50 and −7.35 kcal/mol, ahead of avibactam at −6.73 (re-dock −7.15) — but the margins are 0.62–0.92 kcal/mol against one avibactam run and 0.20–0.50 against the other, all inside Vina's noise; tazobactam, which has no useful KPC-2 activity, scores within 0.31 kcal/mol of avibactam; and the two boronates, including the structure's own co-crystallised ligand, cannot be docked at all. The honest reading is that on a covalent target with a thin ChEMBL record, non-covalent docking measures the method, not the molecule — and the next experiment is a nitrocefin KPC-2 assay with a pre-registered 2-fold rule, plus the same benchmark on the D179N variant, not more Vina docking.

No funding was received. The author thanks the ChEMBL, UniProtKB, RCSB PDB and PubChem teams for free, open data.

Oseltamivir Scores Worst on Its Own Wildtype Site — and Better on the Resistant Mutant: A Vina Benchmark on 3TI6 and 3CL0 That Fails to Reproduce H274Y Resistance

Seasonal influenza infects about a billion people a year and causes 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths, and oseltamivir is the first-line antiviral — yet the H274Y neuraminidase mutation, which swept to more than 90% of seasonal H1N1 in 2008–09, makes the virus resistant to it by shifting the Glu276 side chain into the…

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-08 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #5 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: influenza; neuraminidase; oseltamivir; H274Y; drug resistance; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; antiviral

Abstract

Seasonal influenza infects about a billion people a year and causes 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths, and oseltamivir is the first-line antiviral — yet the H274Y neuraminidase mutation, which swept to more than 90% of seasonal H1N1 in 2008–09, makes the virus resistant to it by shifting the Glu276 side chain into the drug's hydrophobic pocket. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking) against the 2009 pandemic H1N1 neuraminidase (PDB 3TI6) and its H274Y mutant (PDB 3CL0), docking oseltamivir plus five oseltamivir-scaffold analogues with measured IC50 values of 0.3–1.8 nM, each centred on the co-crystallised oseltamivir, under an identical AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol. The protocol fails the test it was built for: oseltamivir scores worst of all six ligands on the wildtype site (−4.83 kcal/mol), every ligand scores better on the resistant mutant than on the wildtype (oseltamivir −6.48 vs −4.83 kcal/mol), and the docking order disagrees with measured potency on both structures. The falsifiable next step is a neuraminidase inhibition assay of the best-docking analogue against oseltamivir on wildtype and H274Y enzymes, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage; an analogue that inhibits the H274Y enzyme at its ChEMBL IC50 would refute the claim that rigid docking on a drug-bound mutant structure cannot reproduce resistance.

1. Introduction

Seasonal influenza infects about a billion people every year, including 3–5 million cases of severe illness, and causes 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths annually, two-thirds of them in people aged 65 and over. Neuraminidase (NA) cleaves sialic acid from host glycans, releasing new virions from infected cells, and it is the target of oseltamivir (Tamiflu), zanamivir and peramivir — the only antivirals that work after infection is established. Oseltamivir phosphate is a prodrug of oseltamivir carboxylate, the active metabolite, which binds the NA active site with sub-nanomolar potency.

Resistance to oseltamivir is dominated by a single mutation, H274Y (histidine to tyrosine at residue 274, N2 numbering; H275Y in N1 numbering). It sits near but not in the drug-binding site, and it works by shifting the carboxylate side chain of Glu276 into the binding pocket, shrinking the hydrophobic pocket that accommodates oseltamivir's pentyloxy group and disrupting the hydrogen-bond network around it — a mechanism established by the crystal structures of Collins et al. (Nature, 2008) and confirmed by molecular-dynamics simulations showing the Glu276 carboxylate rotated by about 115° and the oseltamivir pentyloxy group by about 125°, with water infiltrating the pocket. The mutation first emerged in seasonal H1N1 in 2007–08 and within a year was present in more than 90% of seasonal H1N1 in the USA, Canada, the UK and Australia; the 2009 pandemic H1N1 strain has stayed largely susceptible (under 1.5% resistance), but H274Y remains the resistance mutation that matters most for pandemic preparedness.

The question this paper asks is deliberately narrow and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline reproduce H274Y resistance — that is, score oseltamivir worse on the mutant than on the wildtype — when both structures are docked with the same protocol? The falsifiable hypothesis is that it cannot, because the mutant structure was crystallised with oseltamivir bound, so its pocket is pre-formed around the drug, and rigid docking will score the mutant as if it were a better binder.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 8 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-08.md (no influenza item that day), the WHO seasonal-influenza fact sheet, a 2020 review of influenza antiviral resistance (Eur J Clin Microbiol Infect Dis 2020;39:1201–1208), ChEMBL (EBI), RCSB PDB and UniProtKB. Key sources: the WHO fact sheet for burden; the resistance review for the H274Y epidemiology; Collins et al., Nature 2008 for the structural mechanism and the 3CL0 structure; and the 3TI6 structure paper (PLoS Pathog 2011) for the wildtype structure. All ChEMBL potency values quoted were re-checked live against the ChEMBL API on 8 November 2026 for the target "Neuraminidase" (CHEMBL2051, influenza A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 H1N1).

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target resolution was verified by hand: UniProt P03468 (NRAM_I34A1, neuraminidase, influenza A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 H1N1, 454 aa) and ChEMBL target CHEMBL2051 ("Neuraminidase", SINGLE PROTEIN, influenza A virus A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 H1N1) — both correct, no correction needed.

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand on each structure; best of three poses reported. Two structures were docked. The wildtype is PDB 3TI6, the 2009 pandemic H1N1 neuraminidase in complex with oseltamivir (ligand code G39), and the grid was centred on the centroid of the co-crystallised G39 copy: [−48.44, 14.42, 10.08]. The mutant is PDB 3CL0, the H274Y neuraminidase in complex with oseltamivir (G39), from Collins et al. (Nature 2008), and the grid was centred on its co-crystallised G39 centroid: [−31.62, −56.44, 7.78]. Both centres were verified against the PDB files to 0.01 Å: they are exactly the G39 centroids, and no cofactor or glycan was involved, so the grid-centre fault that has corrupted earlier runs did not occur here. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types, HETATM ligands stripped); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Six ligands were docked on both structures: oseltamivir itself (QUERY, the ethyl-ester prodrug, PubChem CID 65028) and the top five pipeline-ranked leads, all oseltamivir-scaffold analogues with ChEMBL IC50 values of 0.3–1.8 nM. One of the five (CHEMBL674) is oseltamivir carboxylate — the active metabolite — docked independently as a same-scaffold control; it is reported as such, not as a new lead. The remaining four are a phenethyl analogue (CHEMBL81286), a cyclohexylethyl analogue (CHEMBL315261), a sulfonate analogue in which the carboxylate is replaced by a sulfonate (CHEMBL4440605), and an allyl analogue (CHEMBL311288).

Correction (fault, found and fixed during this run). The first docking run was discarded in full: the pipeline's human-preferring target ranking picked ChEMBL CHEMBL1862, the human ABL1 kinase, so all leads were ABL1 inhibitors, and the structure it picked, PDB 1NMB (N9 neuraminidase in complex with a Fab antibody fragment), holds no drug-like ligand, so the _ligand_center fallback landed on a Fab glycan (NAG residue 1, chain A). Those scores (oseltamivir −4.88 kcal/mol at a glycan, ABL1 inhibitors ranked above it) are meaningless and are not reported as results; the discarded file is kept for audit. The corrected run forced UniProt P03468 and ChEMBL CHEMBL2051, verified live on 8 November 2026, and docked manually on 3TI6 and 3CL0 as described above.

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: oseltamivir and all five leads were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 panel was run for each lead; the highest read-across probabilities were 0.10–0.20 (NR-AhR, NR-ER, NR-Aromatase), and no Tox21 panel was returned for oseltamivir itself. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements, and no lead carries a tox flag that would end it.

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of the co-crystallised G39 pose (RMSD) was performed; the receptor was held rigid, so the Glu276 rotation that causes H274Y resistance is invisible to this protocol by design; only two NA structures (one wildtype, one mutant, both drug-bound) were docked; the leads are already-known NA inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed. Antiviral activity in cell culture was not measured for any lead, so a docking win says nothing about clinical benefit. The H274Y numbering used here is N2 numbering, as in Collins et al.; in N1 numbering the same mutation is H275Y.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Potencies are ChEMBL on-target values, re-checked live on 8 November 2026. H274Y is N2 numbering (H275Y in N1 numbering).

The headline, stated honestly: the protocol fails the test it was built for. Oseltamivir scores worst of all six ligands on its own wildtype site (−4.83 kcal/mol), trailing the best lead by 1.78 kcal/mol, and every ligand scores better on the resistant mutant than on the wildtype — oseltamivir itself by 1.65 kcal/mol (−6.48 vs −4.83), the phenethyl analogue by 0.75, the cyclohexylethyl analogue by 0.92, the sulfonate analogue by 1.27, the allyl analogue by 0.91 and oseltamivir carboxylate by 1.41 kcal/mol. The ranking is identical on both structures, which is itself suspicious: a resistance mutation that changes the pocket should change the ranking, and it does not. The docking order also disagrees with measured potency on both structures: by IC50 the order is 0.3, 0.65, 1.0, 1.0 and 1.8 nM, but by docking it is 0.3, 1.0, 1.8, 1.0 and 0.65 nM — oseltamivir carboxylate, the second most potent compound in the set, scores fifth on both structures. One internal consistency check does pass: the active carboxylate (CHEMBL674) out-docks the prodrug ester (QUERY) on both structures (−5.36 vs −4.83 wildtype; −6.77 vs −6.48 mutant), as it should, since the carboxylate is the form that binds. Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking: the best lead's wildtype poses span 2.80 kcal/mol (−6.61 to −3.81), the largest pose spread in the set, so its best score is the least stable of the six.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for oseltamivir or any of these analogues on 3TI6 or 3CL0 was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for oseltamivir, its active carboxylate and four analogues on both the wildtype and the H274Y mutant structure are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the centre audit trail and the correction. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: the five leads span measured NA IC50 values of 0.3–1.8 nM, a 6-fold spread, while their docking scores span 1.25 kcal/mol on the wildtype and 0.78 kcal/mol on the mutant, in an order that disagrees with potency on both structures. Vina ranks poses, not IC50s, and on this site it ranks them unreliably — and, uniquely in this series, it ranks the resistant mutant as the better binder for every ligand.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Two faults were found and fixed, and one was not a fault but a design limitation. The first fault was the target resolution: the pipeline's human-preferring ranking picked the human ABL1 kinase as the ChEMBL target for a viral neuraminidase query, so the first run's leads were ABL1 inhibitors and its structure (1NMB, an N9 neuraminidase–Fab complex) held no drug-like ligand, so the centre fell on a Fab glycan. That run was discarded in full. The second fault is the same _ligand_center fallback that bit the TGR paper: a structure with no drug-like ligand gets an automatic centre on whatever HETATM group survives the exclusions, and here it was a glycan. The fix is a hard rule that a structure with no drug-like ligand gets no automatic centre at all. The design limitation is the interesting one: the mutant structure 3CL0 was crystallised with oseltamivir bound, so its pocket is already in the drug-bound conformation — the Glu276 shift that causes resistance is accommodated in the crystal, and the pocket Vina sees is pre-organised around the drug. Rigid docking on a drug-bound mutant structure cannot reproduce resistance, because the structure has already paid the conformational cost that resistance imposes. The wildtype structure 3TI6 is also drug-bound, but its pocket is the one oseltamivir evolved to fit; the mutant's pocket is the one oseltamivir was forced into. Vina, scoring a rigid pocket, rewards the forced fit.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a negative benchmark with a useful control — and a warning about what docking can and cannot test. There is no lead here: the best-docking analogue (CHEMBL81286, IC50 0.3 nM) is already the most potent measured inhibitor in the set, so its docking "win" adds nothing, and the drug the paper is about scores worst on its own site. The durable findings are the benchmark values for oseltamivir and five analogues on both the wildtype and the H274Y structure (with full pose lists), the demonstration that rigid Vina docking scores every ligand better on the resistant mutant than on the wildtype — the exact opposite of the resistance phenotype — and the same-scaffold control (carboxylate out-docks prodrug on both structures), which shows the protocol is not random, just blind to the mechanism that matters. The more important finding is the design limitation: a resistance mutation whose mechanism is a conformational change cannot be tested by rigid docking on a drug-bound mutant structure, because the crystal has already absorbed the change.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the margins that matter are inside noise: the best lead beats oseltamivir by 1.78 kcal/mol on the wildtype — inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — and the wildtype–mutant differences (0.75–1.65 kcal/mol) are also inside it. Second, the ranking must be checked against measured NA IC50 values — the five leads span 0.3–1.8 nM, and a docking order that puts the second most potent compound fifth on both structures is a measurement of the scoring function, not of the molecules. Third, the resistance test is void by construction: the mutant structure is drug-bound, so the pocket Vina scores is the drug-accommodating conformation, not the apo conformation that resists binding. A docking "win" against oseltamivir on 3TI6 is not a discovery; it is a benchmark value awaiting an assay, and a docking "win" on 3CL0 is not a resistance-breaking lead; it is an artefact of the crystal.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All leads are PAINS-clean, which removes one artefact class from the validation design — but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the Tox21 panel is thin (highest read-across 0.10–0.20, no panel returned for oseltamivir). The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either. The validation assay must still include redox controls and a counter-screen, because a clean PAINS filter does not rule out assay interference, and the NA enzyme assay itself is prone to fluorescence artefacts. The larger safety question — whether an analogue that binds the mutant also inhibits the human sialidases, which share the active-site architecture — is not addressed by PAINS at all and needs a dedicated human-enzyme counter-screen for any lead that advances.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. The best-docking analogue (CHEMBL81286) inhibits recombinant wildtype N1 neuraminidase with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value (0.3 nM) under identical assay conditions; a measured IC50 worse than oseltamivir carboxylate's would confirm the noise interpretation, while a better one would refute it.
  2. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised oseltamivir (G39) into 3TI6 reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run) — and the same re-dock into 3CL0 reproduces the mutant pose, showing the protocol can recover a pose it cannot score.
  3. A molecular-dynamics simulation of oseltamivir bound to the H274Y apo structure shows the Glu276 shift and water infiltration reported by Collins et al. and by Malaisree et al., while the same simulation on the drug-bound 3CL0 structure does not — directly testing the claim that the crystal has absorbed the resistance mechanism.
  4. Docking the same six ligands on the zanamivir-bound N1 structure 3B7E (1918 H1N1 NA) gives a different ranking from 3TI6; a different ranking would show the result is structure-dependent, not molecule-dependent.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): neuraminidase inhibition assay (MUNANA fluorescence) for the best-docking analogue, oseltamivir carboxylate and oseltamivir, on recombinant wildtype N1 and H274Y enzymes, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and the rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): the same assay on the H274Y enzyme for any compound that clears Stage 1, plus a human sialidase counter-screen at 10× the NA IC50. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): cell-culture antiviral assay (MDCK, plaque reduction) for the best compound against wildtype and H274Y virus, with oseltamivir as control, before any claim about resistance-breaking activity. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. Any margin under 2 kcal/mol is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and cannot be interpreted as a real advantage — the best margin here is 1.78 kcal/mol. 3. The docking order disagrees with measured potency on both structures. 4. Rigid docking on a drug-bound mutant structure cannot reproduce a conformational resistance mechanism — the central test of this paper is void by construction. 5. Only two NA structures (3TI6, 3CL0, both drug-bound) were docked; the apo structures were not scored. 6. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking RMSD validation of the co-crystallised G39 pose was performed. 7. A single rigid receptor was used per structure; the NA active site's flexibility, including the 150-loop, is not modelled. 8. All leads are already-known NA inhibitors, and all are oseltamivir analogues — no new chemotype was tested. 9. The first docking run was discarded in full (wrong target, glycan centre); the correction is documented, but the pipeline faults that caused it are not yet fixed in code. 10. Antiviral activity in cell culture was not measured for any lead.

6. Conclusion

Oseltamivir scores worst of all six ligands on its own wildtype neuraminidase site (−4.83 kcal/mol on 3TI6), and every ligand scores better on the resistant H274Y mutant than on the wildtype (oseltamivir −6.48 vs −4.83 kcal/mol on 3CL0) — the exact opposite of the resistance phenotype, because the mutant structure was crystallised with the drug bound and its pocket is pre-organised around it. The honest reading is that on this target, rigid docking cannot test resistance at all — and the next experiment is a head-to-head enzyme assay on wildtype and H274Y neuraminidase with a pre-registered 2 kcal/mol rule, plus a molecular-dynamics simulation of the apo mutant, not more docking on drug-bound crystals.

2026-11-08 Health Draft — not submitted

No Statin Beats Atorvastatin Beyond Noise: A Vina Benchmark of Four HMG-CoA Reductase Inhibitors on 2R4F, and the Non-Statin Scaffold the Screen Did Not Find

Cardiovascular disease killed about 19.8 million people in 2022, a third of all deaths, and high LDL cholesterol is one of its main modifiable drivers.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-08 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #3 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: atorvastatin; HMG-CoA reductase; statin intolerance; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; LDL cholesterol; cardiovascular disease; fluvastatin

Abstract

Cardiovascular disease killed about 19.8 million people in 2022, a third of all deaths, and high LDL cholesterol is one of its main modifiable drivers. Atorvastatin blocks HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, and each 1 mmol/L of LDL lowering cuts major vascular events by about a fifth — but muscle symptoms make some patients stop statins, and the SAMSON trial showed about 90% of those symptoms are also felt on placebo, so true statin intolerance is uncommon (about 3–5%) yet real, and non-statin alternatives are still needed. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking) against the human HMG-CoA reductase structure in complex with a pyrazole inhibitor (PDB 2R4F), with the grid centred on the co-crystallised inhibitor, and docked atorvastatin plus four known HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors with measured IC50 values of 0.23–1.8 nM, all under an identical AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol. No compound beat atorvastatin beyond noise: atorvastatin scored best at −9.00 kcal/mol, the closest lead (atorvastatin itself in ChEMBL, IC50 0.23 nM) trailed by 0.40 kcal/mol, and the most potent measured inhibitor in the set is atorvastatin itself — every margin inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and the docking order disagrees with measured potency. The screen also failed its stated purpose: all four leads are statins or statin analogues carrying the same 3,5-dihydroxyheptanoate pharmacophore, so no non-statin scaffold was tested at all. The falsifiable next step is a deliberately dissimilarity-based screen for non-statin HMG-CoA reductase binders plus an LDL-lowering assay of the best-docking lead against atorvastatin, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage; a non-statin lead that lowers LDL in a statin-intolerant model would refute the claim that this target has nothing left to offer beyond statins.

1. Introduction

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide: the Global Burden of Disease study records about 19.8 million CVD deaths in 2022, 32% of all deaths, 85% of them from heart attack and stroke. In Pakistan, heart disease is reported to cause about 16–18% of all deaths (University of Karachi, 2023). High LDL cholesterol is one of the main modifiable drivers of that burden, and lowering it is one of the best-proven interventions in medicine: the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration meta-analysis of 26 randomised trials showed that each 1 mmol/L reduction in LDL cholesterol cuts major vascular events by about a fifth.

Statins lower LDL by blocking HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR, 888 amino acids), the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Atorvastatin (Lipitor) is the most prescribed statin: it lowers LDL by about 50% at 40–80 mg daily, and its benefit is proportional to the LDL reduction, not to any property of the molecule beyond its potency. The problem is not efficacy but tolerability. Muscle symptoms are the commonest reason patients stop statins, and the SAMSON trial — 60 patients who had stopped atorvastatin because of side effects, cycled through four months each of atorvastatin 20 mg, identical placebo and no tablet — found mean symptom scores of 16.3 on atorvastatin, 15.4 on placebo and 8.0 on no tablet: a nocebo ratio of 0.90, meaning about 90% of the symptoms felt on the drug were also felt on placebo, and 30 of the 60 patients successfully restarted statins afterwards. The International Lipid Expert Panel estimates complete statin intolerance affects only 3–5% of treated patients. But 3–5% of a drug taken by hundreds of millions of people is still millions of people, and for them the alternatives are ezetimibe (about 18–25% LDL reduction), bempedoic acid (which cut major adverse cardiovascular events by 13% in the CLEAR Outcomes trial in statin-intolerant patients) and PCSK9 inhibitors (expensive, injectable). A cheap oral non-statin HMGCR inhibitor would still be valuable.

The question this paper asks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors against atorvastatin on the true human structure, and does the screen actually return the non-statin scaffolds it was asked for? The falsifiable hypothesis is that any lead beating atorvastatin by less than 2 kcal/mol on Vina docking has no measurable potency advantage, and that the docking ranking will disagree with measured HMGCR IC50 values on this target.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 8 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-08.md (no statin item that day), PubMed and web search, ChEMBL (EBI), RCSB PDB and UniProtKB. Key sources: the Global Burden of Disease 2023 almanac (Mensah et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2023) for CVD burden; the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration meta-analysis for the LDL benefit; the SAMSON trial (Howard et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2021) for the nocebo result; the CLEAR Outcomes trial (Nissen et al., N Engl J Med 2023) for bempedoic acid; and the 2R4F structure paper (Pfefferkorn et al., J Med Chem 2008) for the target structure. All ChEMBL potency values quoted were re-checked live against the ChEMBL API on 8 November 2026 for the target "3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase" (CHEMBL402).

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 8 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target resolution was verified by hand: UniProt P04035 (HMDH_HUMAN, HMG-CoA reductase, 888 aa) and ChEMBL target CHEMBL402 ("3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase", SINGLE PROTEIN, Homo sapiens) — both correct, no correction needed.

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure is PDB 2R4F, human HMG-CoA reductase in complex with the pyrazole inhibitor PF-3052334 (ligand code RIE), deposited 2007 (Pfefferkorn et al., J Med Chem 2008). The grid was centred on the centroid of the co-crystallised RIE copy on chain A: [78.03, 9.09, −4.92]. The centre was verified against the PDB file: it is exactly the RIE centroid, and the structure holds no cofactor, so the grid-centre fault that has corrupted earlier runs (centring on a cofactor or glycan) did not occur here. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types, HETATM ligands stripped); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Five ligands were docked: atorvastatin itself (QUERY, PubChem CID 60823) and the top four pipeline-ranked leads that could be prepared, all known HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors with ChEMBL IC50 values of 0.23–1.8 nM. Two of the top five leads failed ligand preparation on the first attempt — "RDKit molecule has 2 fragments" — because their ChEMBL SMILES are sodium salts; both were desalted (largest fragment kept, the parent drug) and re-docked at the same centre, and the correction is recorded in the data file. One of the five (CHEMBL1487) is atorvastatin itself as recorded in ChEMBL (IC50 0.23 nM), docked independently as a same-molecule control; it is reported as such, not as a new lead.

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: atorvastatin and all four leads were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 panel was run for each lead. Atorvastatin's panel is measured data, not read-across: NR-Aromatase 1.0. Fluvastatin's panel is also measured: NR-AhR 1.0 and NR-Aromatase 1.0. These are Tox21 assay readouts, not clinical claims, and are reported here so they are not misread as toxicity findings. The desalted leads' highest read-across probabilities were NR-Aromatase 0.62–0.69, NR-ER up to 0.39 and SR-MMP up to 0.33. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements.

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of the co-crystallised RIE pose (RMSD) was performed; a single X-ray structure (2R4F, one HMGCR conformation) was used; the receptor was held rigid; the leads are already-known HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed. LDL lowering — the outcome that matters — was not measured for any lead, so a docking win says nothing about clinical benefit. Muscle safety, the problem that motivates the search, was not modelled for any lead.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table
