Two Leads "Beat" Macozinone by Docking and Lose by 1.23 kcal/mol of Noise: A Vina Benchmark of DprE1 Inhibitors on 4P8N and the Covalent Binding Vina Cannot See

Tuberculosis made about 10.8 million people ill in 2023 and killed about 1.25 million, and the search for shorter, safer regimens continues.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-06 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #2 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: DprE1; macozinone; tuberculosis; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; covalent inhibitor; benzothiazinone; ChEMBL

Abstract

Tuberculosis made about 10.8 million people ill in 2023 and killed about 1.25 million, and the search for shorter, safer regimens continues. Macozinone (PBTZ169), a benzothiazinone in phase 2 trials, covalently inhibits the Mycobacterium tuberculosis enzyme DprE1, blocking arabinan synthesis and cell-wall biogenesis, but its covalent binding cannot be modelled by standard docking, so a docking benchmark against it risks measuring the method rather than the molecule. We ran the LeadForge pipeline live on 6 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina docking): target DprE1 (UniProt P9WJF1, strain ATCC 25618 / H37Rv, ChEMBL CHEMBL3804751, 58 bioactivities), structure PDB 4P8N at 1.79 Å, grid centred exactly on the co-crystallised non-covalent inhibitor R57 ([16.51, −20.97, 1.7]), and five ligands docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 under an identical protocol. Two known DprE1 actives "beat" macozinone on docking — CHEMBL4763381 at −12.05 kcal/mol and CHEMBL4752208 at −11.74 kcal/mol, against macozinone at −10.82 kcal/mol — margins of 1.23 and 0.92 kcal/mol, inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. But both leads are far weaker by measured potency: IC50 200 nM and 140 nM against macozinone's 10 nM, so the docking ranking is inverted against experiment, and a third "lead", CHEMBL3330226 at −10.96 kcal/mol, is macozinone itself entered twice, scoring −10.96 versus −10.82 as the query. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head DprE1 enzyme inhibition assay of CHEMBL4763381 against macozinone under identical conditions, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage; a measured potency advantage for the lead, or covalent docking showing macozinone binds Cys387 far more tightly than Vina suggests, would refute the claim that the docking win is only a measurement of Vina's limits.

1. Introduction

Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases: according to the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024, about 10.8 million people fell ill with TB in 2023 and about 1.25 million died. Standard treatment still takes months, and drug-resistant TB needs longer, more toxic regimens, so new drugs with new mechanisms are urgently needed. DprE1 (decaprenylphosphoryl-beta-D-ribose oxidase) is one of the most validated new TB targets: it catalyses a step in arabinan synthesis, and blocking it stops cell-wall biogenesis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Macozinone (MCZ, PBTZ169) is a benzothiazinone that covalently inhibits DprE1 and is in phase 2 trials (NCT03334734); its minimum inhibitory concentration is 0.3 ng/mL by resazurin microtiter assay. It is not alone: BTZ043, the first benzothiazinone, is in phase 2b combination trials (NCT05926466, with bedaquiline and delamanid), and other DprE1 candidates in trials include TBA-7371 (an azaindole) and quabodepistat (a carbostyril). Macozinone also has a known human liability: human prostaglandin reductases PTGR1 and PTGR2 dearomatize it to H2MCZ, which loses antimycobacterial activity.

The question this paper asks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known DprE1 actives against macozinone, and what does an apparent docking "win" mean when the reference drug is a covalent inhibitor and the structure used holds a non-covalent inhibitor? The falsifiable hypothesis is that any lead beating macozinone by less than 2 kcal/mol on Vina docking has no measurable potency advantage, and that the docking ranking will disagree with measured IC50 values on this target.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 6 November 2026: the daily literature digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/, PubMed and web search, ChEMBL (EBI) and RCSB PDB. Key sources: the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024 for the TB burden figures; the macozinone phase 2 trial record (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03334734) and the BTZ043 phase 2b combination trial record (NCT05926466); the 2025 Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy report of macozinone's MIC of 0.3 ng/mL by resazurin microtiter assay; and the 2026 Nature Communications paper showing that human PTGR1/PTGR2 dearomatize macozinone to inactive H2MCZ (DOI 10.1038/s44321-026-00526-1). The covalent mechanism of benzothiazinones — the nitroso moiety forming a semimercaptal with Cys387 of DprE1 — is the established mechanism for this class and is the reason standard non-covalent docking cannot represent macozinone's real binding mode.

2.2 Molecular docking

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 6 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target: M. tuberculosis DprE1, UniProt P9WJF1, strain ATCC 25618 / H37Rv; ChEMBL CHEMBL3804751, 58 bioactivities retrieved. Twenty-five compounds passed the Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen and 26 were ranked by composite score. The top five ranked leads were taken forward to docking. All five are known DprE1 actives with published ChEMBL potencies; none has a preferred name in ChEMBL.

Docking was performed with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was M. tuberculosis DprE1, PDB 4P8N (1.79 Å, "M. tuberculosis DprE1 in complex with the non-covalent inhibitor QN118", ligand code R57), with the grid centred exactly on the centroid of the co-crystallised ligand R57, chain A: [16.51, −20.97, 1.7]. The centre was verified against the PDB file to 0.01 Å. The FAD cofactor centroid is 12.75 Å away — the centre is not on the cofactor, so the grid-centre fault that has corrupted earlier runs (centring on a cofactor or glycan) did not occur here. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

One pipeline fault was caught before reporting, and is documented here because it is part of the result. The lead list contains macozinone itself: CHEMBL3330226 has the same molecular weight as macozinone (456.49), Tanimoto similarity 1.0 to the query, and an identical toxicity panel, and it scored −10.96 kcal/mol against macozinone-as-query at −10.82 kcal/mol — the same molecule, 0.14 kcal/mol apart. This is the duplicate-entry fault seen in earlier papers (Papers #1 and #3): the pipeline treats the reference drug as a new lead when it appears in ChEMBL under a different entry. CHEMBL3330226 is therefore not a lead; it is a duplicate-entry control, and it is reported as such.

2.3 PAINS screen

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: all five leads and macozinone were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probabilities were SR-MMP 0.498 for CHEMBL4763381, SR-ARE 0.363 for CHEMBL4752208, SR-MMP 0.732 for CHEMBL3330226 and for macozinone (identical panels, as expected for the same molecule), and SR-MMP 0.551 for CHEMBL4868912. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements — and macozinone itself carries the highest flag in the panel (SR-MMP 0.732), so a flag here does not distinguish a lead from the reference drug.

2.4 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or covalent docking was performed; a single crystal structure (4P8N, one DprE1 conformation, holding a non-covalent inhibitor) was used; and, most importantly, Vina cannot model covalent binding, so macozinone's real binding mode — a semimercaptal with Cys387 — is not represented in any score reported here. The leads are already-known DprE1 actives, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound DprE1 potency, ChEMBL Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) MW logP Lipinski violations PAINS Top tox read-across

CHEMBL4752208 IC50 140 nM −11.74 −11.74, −11.74, −10.96 493.55 3.90 0 clean SR-ARE 0.363
CHEMBL3330226 (= macozinone) IC50 10 nM −10.96 −10.96, −10.27, −9.74 456.49 4.29 0 clean SR-MMP 0.732
Macozinone (reference, query) IC50 10 nM −10.82 −10.82, −10.11, −9.91 456.49 4.29 0 clean SR-MMP 0.732
CHEMBL4868912 IC50 50 nM −10.23 −10.23, −10.10, −9.72 466.59 2.67 0 clean SR-MMP 0.551

All docking on PDB 4P8N (M. tuberculosis DprE1, 1.79 Å), grid centre [16.51, −20.97, 1.7] (R57 chain-A centroid), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, Vina 1.2.7, 6 November 2026. All five leads are known DprE1 actives with no preferred name in ChEMBL.

The headline, stated honestly: two genuine leads "beat" macozinone by 0.92–1.23 kcal/mol on docking — CHEMBL4763381 by 1.23 kcal/mol and CHEMBL4752208 by 0.92 kcal/mol — but both are 14–20 times weaker by measured IC50 (200 nM and 140 nM versus macozinone's 10 nM). The docking ranking is inverted against measured potency: the best-docking compound is the weakest by IC50, and the most potent compound (macozinone, 10 nM) sits third in the table. Both margins are also inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so neither would be interpretable as a real advantage even if the potency order agreed. Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking: CHEMBL4752208 holds its best score across two poses, yet is 14 times weaker than macozinone by IC50; CHEMBL4763381's best pose (−12.05) is 1.63 kcal/mol clear of its second pose (−10.42), so even its own score is unstable across poses. The duplicate control is the cleanest number in the table: macozinone entered twice scores −10.96 and −10.82 kcal/mol, 0.14 kcal/mol apart — the pipeline's conformer-sampling error on this target is small, which makes the inversion against IC50 harder to blame on sampling and easier to blame on the scoring function and the missing covalent term.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for macozinone or any of these leads on 4P8N was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for macozinone and four known DprE1 actives on 4P8N are now on record for others to reproduce, together with the duplicate-entry control. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: the five distinct molecules span IC50 10–200 nM, a 20-fold spread, while their docking scores span 1.82 kcal/mol in the wrong order — Vina ranks poses, not IC50s, and on this target it ranks them backwards.

3.3 The standardisation / quality problem

Two things that could silently corrupt this result did not, and one thing that no structure check can catch did. The grid centre was verified against the PDB file to 0.01 Å and sits 12.75 Å from the FAD cofactor, so the cofactor-centring fault is absent here. The duplicate-entry fault did occur: macozinone appears in the lead list as CHEMBL3330226, and without the identity check (same MW, Tanimoto 1.0, identical tox panel) it would have been reported as a third lead "beating" the reference by 0.14 kcal/mol. The deeper problem is structural, not procedural: the reference drug is a covalent inhibitor and the structure used (4P8N) holds a non-covalent inhibitor, so the binding mode Vina scores for macozinone is not the binding mode macozinone uses. No grid-centre fix can repair that; only a covalent docking method can.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a measurement of Vina's limits on this target. There is no lead here: the two compounds that "beat" macozinone on docking are 14–20 times weaker by measured IC50, the third "lead" is macozinone itself, and the remaining lead (CHEMBL4868912, IC50 50 nM) scores worse than the reference (−10.23 versus −10.82). The durable findings are the benchmark values for macozinone on 4P8N (−10.82 kcal/mol, with full pose lists), the duplicate-entry control (0.14 kcal/mol), and the demonstration that on a covalent-inhibitor target, non-covalent docking ranks known actives in the opposite order to their measured potency.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the margins (0.92 and 1.23 kcal/mol) are inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, the ranking is inverted against measured potency — the best-docking compound is the weakest by IC50, by a factor of 20. Third, the scored binding mode is the wrong one: macozinone's potency comes from a covalent semimercaptal with Cys387, which Vina cannot model at all, so the reference drug's score is missing the very interaction that makes it potent. A docking "win" against a covalent reference drug, on a structure holding a non-covalent inhibitor, is not a discovery; it is a measurement of what the method leaves out.

4.3 The PAINS problem is the experiment's design constraint, not a reason to stop

All leads are PAINS-clean, which removes one artefact class from the validation design — but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the Tox21 read-across flags (SR-MMP up to 0.732) are predictions from neighbours, not data. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either — least of all because the reference drug flags the same assay most strongly. The validation assay must still include redox controls and a counter-screen, because a clean PAINS filter does not rule out assay interference.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL4763381 inhibits recombinant DprE1 with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value (200 nM) under identical assay conditions, and is less potent than macozinone (10 nM) — the docking predicts no measurable advantage; a measured IC50 for CHEMBL4763381 better than macozinone's would refute the noise interpretation.
  2. Covalent docking of macozinone at Cys387 (for example with CovDock) gives a binding energy substantially more favourable than the non-covalent Vina score of −10.82 kcal/mol, consistent with the covalent contribution Vina omits.
  3. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand R57 (QN118) into 4P8N reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).
  4. Canonicalising the SMILES of all 26 ranked leads and re-running the pipeline removes the macozinone duplicate (CHEMBL3330226) and changes no other lead's rank — a pipeline fix to be verified, not assumed.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): recombinant DprE1 enzyme inhibition assay for CHEMBL4763381, CHEMBL4752208 and macozinone, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule and the rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable advantage. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): whole-cell M. tuberculosis H37Rv MIC assay (resazurin microtiter assay, the same method reported for macozinone's 0.3 ng/mL) for any compound that clears Stage 1, with macozinone as control. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): covalent docking of macozinone at Cys387 (CovDock or equivalent) and, if Stage 1 shows any genuine advantage, a PTGR1/PTGR2 liability check, since human dearomatization to H2MCZ is a known route by which macozinone-class compounds lose activity. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. Both "winning" margins (0.92 and 1.23 kcal/mol) are inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and cannot be interpreted as real advantages. 3. Vina cannot model covalent binding, so macozinone's semimercaptal with Cys387 is absent from every score reported here; the structure used (4P8N) holds a non-covalent inhibitor. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, covalent docking, or re-docking validation of R57 was performed. 5. A single crystal structure (4P8N, one DprE1 conformation) was used; induced-fit effects are not modelled. 6. All leads are already-known DprE1 actives; no new chemical matter is proposed. 7. The pipeline's lead deduplication failed silently and required manual correction — other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited. 8. The PTGR1/PTGR2 dearomatization liability was not modelled for any lead.

6. Conclusion

No DprE1 active in this set beats macozinone: the two leads that score better on Vina docking are 14–20 times weaker by measured IC50, the third "lead" is macozinone itself, and both margins sit inside Vina's noise. The honest reading is that on a covalent-inhibitor target, non-covalent docking ranks known actives backwards — and the next experiment is a head-to-head DprE1 IC50 assay with a pre-registered 2 kcal/mol rule, plus covalent docking of macozinone at Cys387, not more Vina docking.

No ALK Inhibitor in This Set Beats Alectinib Beyond Vina Noise: A Benchmark Docking of Known ALK Inhibitors on PDB 4Z55

Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) rearrangements drive about 3–7% of non-small cell lung cancers, and alectinib is the standard first-line inhibitor: in the ALEX phase III trial it gave median progression-free survival of 34.8 months versus 10.9 months for crizotinib.

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-06 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #1 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: ALK; alectinib; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; non-small cell lung cancer; tyrosine kinase inhibitor; G1202R; ChEMBL

Abstract

Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) rearrangements drive about 3–7% of non-small cell lung cancers, and alectinib is the standard first-line inhibitor: in the ALEX phase III trial it gave median progression-free survival of 34.8 months versus 10.9 months for crizotinib. Resistance still emerges, most often through the G1202R solvent-front mutation, and the search for better ALK inhibitors continues. We asked whether a standardised, automated docking pipeline could rank known ALK inhibitors against alectinib on the ALK catalytic domain. The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 6 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina): target UniProt Q9UM73, ChEMBL CHEMBL4247, 50 bioactivities retrieved, 25 compounds passed the similarity screen and 26 were ranked. Five ligands were docked with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on PDB 4Z55 (1.55 Å), grid centred exactly on the co-crystallised ligand 4LO centroid [−21.06, 9.75, −7.5], box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, three poses, best of three reported. Two leads scored above alectinib: CHEMBL3946496 at −10.16 kcal/mol (IC50 0.32 nM) and CHEMBL3929615 at −10.10 kcal/mol (IC50 0.3 nM), versus alectinib at −9.48 kcal/mol — margins of 0.62–0.68 kcal/mol, inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol scoring noise, so no lead beats alectinib beyond noise. The most potent compound by measured IC50, CHEMBL3892880 (0.168 nM), scored only −9.54 kcal/mol, 0.06 kcal/mol above alectinib — docking cannot separate these compounds. All five ligands were PAINS-clean. The falsifiable next step is a head-to-head ALK kinase inhibition assay of CHEMBL3946496 against alectinib under identical conditions, plus docking and assay on G1202R-mutant ALK: a measured potency advantage greater than 2-fold, or retained activity against G1202R, would confirm a real lead; a tie would refute the docking margin.

1. Introduction

ALK rearrangements occur in approximately 3–7% of non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC), defining a molecular subgroup in which ALK tyrosine kinase inhibition is the standard of care. Alectinib, a second-generation ALK inhibitor, displaced crizotinib as first-line therapy in the ALEX phase III trial (Peters et al., N Engl J Med 2017): first-line alectinib gave median progression-free survival (PFS) of 34.8 months versus 10.9 months for crizotinib. The clinical question is therefore not whether alectinib works, but whether a better ALK inhibitor exists — one that binds the ALK catalytic domain more tightly, or that retains activity when resistance mutations appear.

Resistance is the central limitation. The G1202R solvent-front mutation is the most frequent alectinib-resistance mutation, occurring in about 29% of alectinib-resistant cases. In the J-ALEX trial's circulating free DNA analysis, secondary ALK mutations were detected in 9 of 67 patients (13%), including L1196M and G1202R, and patients with detectable secondary mutations had median PFS of 15.2 months versus 34.1 months without them. Third-generation lorlatinib addresses some of this resistance: in the CROWN trial, 7-year PFS was 55% with lorlatinib versus 3% with crizotinib. The gap this paper attacks is narrower and methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline rank known ALK inhibitors against alectinib on the ALK catalytic domain, and how large is the pipeline's own error? The falsifiable hypothesis is that four known sub-nanomolar ALK inhibitors, docked under an identical protocol, will score within Vina's noise of alectinib — and that any apparent "win" smaller than 2 kcal/mol is not a discovery.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 6 November 2026: the daily literature digest, PubMed and web search (verified references below), ChEMBL (EBI) and RCSB PDB. Key sources: the ALEX phase III trial for the alectinib-versus-crizotinib PFS comparison; the J-ALEX circulating free DNA analysis for secondary-mutation frequency and its PFS association; the CROWN trial for lorlatinib's long-term PFS; and the RCSB entry for PDB 4Z55.

2.2 Compound selection (LeadForge pipeline)

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 6 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Target: anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), UniProt Q9UM73, Homo sapiens; ChEMBL CHEMBL4247 (single-protein, human), 50 bioactivities retrieved live. Alectinib was verified in PubChem (MW 482.63). Twenty-five compounds passed the Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen and 26 were ranked by composite score (similarity ×40 + Lipinski ×20 + Veber ×10 + PAINS ×10 + tox ×20). The top four ranked leads were taken forward to docking, together with alectinib as the reference. All four leads are known ALK inhibitors with published ChEMBL potencies and no preferred name in ChEMBL: CHEMBL3946496 (IC50 0.32 nM), CHEMBL3929615 (IC50 0.3 nM), CHEMBL3953815 (IC50 0.3 nM) and CHEMBL3892880 (IC50 0.168 nM). None is alectinib itself — no duplicate-entry fault occurred in this run, unlike the MEK1 paper of 5 November 2026, in which the reference drug entered twice under two SMILES orderings.

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking was performed 6 November 2026 with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was human ALK, PDB 4Z55 (1.55 Å, "ALK catalytic domain complexed with pyrazolopyrimidine derivative of LDK378 (ceritinib)"), with the grid centred exactly on the centroid of its co-crystallised ligand 4LO: [−21.06, 9.75, −7.5]. The centre was verified against the PDB file itself (0.0 Å offset from the 4LO centroid) — the correct target for the pipeline's automatic centre picker, which on other structures has landed 13–45 Å from the inhibitor site by centring on a cofactor or glycan. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

2.4 PAINS screen and toxicity read-across

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: all four leads and alectinib were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probabilities were SR-p53 0.145 for CHEMBL3946496, SR-p53 0.299 for CHEMBL3929615, SR-p53 0.291 for CHEMBL3953815, SR-ARE 0.314 for CHEMBL3892880, and NR-Aromatase 0.265 for alectinib. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements — and alectinib itself carries a comparable flag, so a flag here does not distinguish a lead from the approved reference drug.

2.5 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement or binding-free-energy calculation was performed; a single crystal structure (4Z55, one ALK conformation) was used; wild-type ALK only was docked — the G1202R resistance mutant, the most clinically relevant target, was not docked; and the four leads are already-known ALK inhibitors, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

All docking on PDB 4Z55 (human ALK catalytic domain, 1.55 Å), grid centre [−21.06, 9.75, −7.5] (4LO co-crystallised-ligand centroid, 0.0 Å offset), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, Vina 1.2.7, 6 November 2026. CHEMBL3946496: MW 448.57, logP 4.57, 0 Lipinski violations. CHEMBL3929615: MW 496.66, logP 4.90, 0 violations. CHEMBL3953815: MW 452.60, logP 5.15, 1 violation. CHEMBL3892880: MW 463.38, logP 4.60, 0 violations. Alectinib: MW 482.63, logP 4.77, 0 violations.

The headline is a non-result, stated plainly: two leads "beat" alectinib by 0.62–0.68 kcal/mol — CHEMBL3946496 by 0.68 and CHEMBL3929615 by 0.62 — but both margins sit inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, so no lead beats alectinib beyond noise. The remaining two leads are statistically tied with alectinib (CHEMBL3953815 by 0.07, CHEMBL3892880 by 0.06 kcal/mol). Pose consistency does not rescue the ranking: the two "winning" leads drop by 0.80–0.96 kcal/mol from their best pose to their second pose, while alectinib holds within 0.43 kcal/mol across all three poses. And the ranking is inverted against measured potency: the most potent compound by recorded IC50, CHEMBL3892880 (0.168 nM), scores only 0.06 kcal/mol above alectinib, while the two leads with the best docking scores (0.32 and 0.3 nM) are the least potent of the four by IC50. The total spread across all five molecules is 0.68 kcal/mol — smaller than the 1.75 kcal/mol self-difference the same pipeline measured for trametinib against itself on 5 November 2026. Docking cannot separate these compounds.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina score for alectinib or any of these leads on 4Z55 was found to benchmark against — which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for alectinib and four known ALK inhibitors on 4Z55 are now on record for others to reproduce, together with a grid centre verified to 0.0 Å against the co-crystallised ligand. The ordering is not comparable to published potency: all five molecules are sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar ALK inhibitors (IC50 0.168–1.9 nM, an 11-fold spread), while their docking scores span 0.68 kcal/mol in no consistent order — Vina ranks poses, not IC50s.

3.3 The resistance problem this paper does not solve

The clinically relevant question is not whether a compound beats alectinib on wild-type ALK, but whether it retains activity against G1202R — the solvent-front mutation present in about 29% of alectinib-resistant cases, and associated in the J-ALEX circulating free DNA analysis with median PFS of 15.2 months versus 34.1 months without detectable secondary mutations. This paper docked wild-type ALK only. A compound that ties alectinib on wild-type ALK but binds G1202R would be the real lead; a compound that beats alectinib by 0.68 kcal/mol on wild-type ALK and fails against G1202R would be clinically irrelevant. The mutant was not docked because no G1202R-mutant ALK structure was used in this run — that is the obvious next experiment, and it is stated as a limitation, not hidden.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a benchmark with a negative headline. There is no lead here that beats alectinib: the two apparent winners win by less than the scoring noise, the most potent compound by measured IC50 scores essentially tied with the reference, and the total spread across the set (0.68 kcal/mol) is smaller than the pipeline's own measured self-difference for a single molecule (1.75 kcal/mol, trametinib, 5 November 2026). The durable findings are the benchmark values for alectinib on 4Z55 (−9.48 kcal/mol, with full pose list) and the verified 0.0 Å grid centre — a clean run with no duplicate-entry fault and no centre error, which makes the negative result trustworthy rather than an artefact of a broken pipeline.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, both margins (0.62 and 0.68 kcal/mol) are inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. Second, pose consistency argues against the winners: their second poses fall by 0.80–0.96 kcal/mol, while alectinib's poses hold within 0.43 kcal/mol. Third, potency and docking score disagree within the lead set: the most potent compound by IC50 (CHEMBL3892880, 0.168 nM) is ranked fourth of five by docking score, and the least potent leads by IC50 (0.32 and 0.3 nM) rank first and second — the ranking is inverted against potency at both ends of the table.

4.3 The PAINS/tox picture is clean but thin

No PAINS alerts is good, but PAINS-clean is a low bar for kinase inhibitors, and the Tox21 read-across flags (SR-p53 up to 0.299, SR-ARE 0.314) are predictions from neighbours, not data. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either — least of all because the reference drug flags a comparable assay (NR-Aromatase 0.265).

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL3946496 inhibits recombinant wild-type ALK with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL value (0.32 nM) under identical assay conditions, and inhibits it more potently than alectinib (1.9 nM cell-free) — the docking predicts no measurable advantage; a >2-fold advantage would confirm a real lead, a tie would refute the docking margin.
  2. CHEMBL3946496 and CHEMBL3929615 retain measurable activity against G1202R-mutant ALK in the same assay, while alectinib loses potency — the clinically decisive test, not yet run.
  3. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand 4LO into 4Z55 reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): recombinant wild-type ALK kinase inhibition assay (ADP-Glo or equivalent) for CHEMBL3946496, CHEMBL3929615, CHEMBL3892880 and alectinib, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): the same assay on G1202R-mutant ALK for any compound that clears Stage 1 — this is the experiment that decides whether a lead matters clinically. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): ALK-positive NSCLC cell-line viability (e.g. H3122) for any compound that clears Stage 2, with alectinib as control and an ALK-negative line as selectivity check. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. Both apparent "wins" (0.62 and 0.68 kcal/mol) are inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and are not interpretable as advantages. 3. The pipeline's own measured self-difference for one molecule (1.75 kcal/mol, trametinib, 5 November 2026) exceeds every margin in this paper. 4. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of 4LO was performed. 5. A single crystal structure (4Z55, one ALK conformation) was used; the ATP-binding pocket is flexible and induced-fit effects are not modelled. 6. Wild-type ALK only was docked — the G1202R resistance mutant, the most clinically relevant target, was not docked or assayed. 7. All leads are already-known ALK inhibitors; no new chemical matter is proposed. 8. The four leads have no preferred name, approval or development phase in ChEMBL; their availability and identity would need verification before any assay.

6. Conclusion

No ALK inhibitor in this set beats alectinib beyond Vina's noise: the best lead, CHEMBL3946496, scores −10.16 kcal/mol against alectinib's −9.48, a 0.68 kcal/mol margin that is smaller than the scoring error and smaller than the pipeline's own measured self-difference. The durable findings are the benchmark values for alectinib on 4Z55 and a clean, verified-centre run with no duplicate-entry fault. The next experiment is a head-to-head ALK IC50 assay of CHEMBL3946496 against alectinib, with G1202R-mutant ALK as the decisive second test — not more docking.

Five Triazolium Trypanothione Reductase Inhibitors Dock at −6.3 to −7.8 kcal/mol on Leishmania infantum TR: A Vina Benchmark, a Species Surrogate, and Two Pipeline Faults Caught

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is endemic in Pakistan — an estimated 59,255 cases in 2023 — and its only proven treatment in the country is still pentavalent antimonials, given as painful daily injections for 20 to 28 days, often unavailable in public facilities.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-05 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #2 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: trypanothione reductase; cutaneous leishmaniasis; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; Leishmania infantum; antimonials; triazolium; ChEMBL

Abstract

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is endemic in Pakistan — an estimated 59,255 cases in 2023 — and its only proven treatment in the country is still pentavalent antimonials, given as painful daily injections for 20 to 28 days, often unavailable in public facilities. Antimonials act in part by inhibiting trypanothione reductase (TR), the parasite-specific redox enzyme absent from the human host, so direct small-molecule TR inhibitors are the rational oral alternative. No standardised Vina benchmark for TR inhibitors existed, and this paper reports why the first two attempts to produce one failed. The LeadForge pipeline run on Leishmania major TR first mis-assigned the ChEMBL target to human maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074) — the same fault found in an earlier LpxH run — and no L. major TR target exists in ChEMBL and no L. major TR crystal structure exists. We therefore used Leishmania infantum TR as the surrogate (UniProt A4HSF7, ChEMBL CHEMBL1944501, 46 bioactivities) and docked five desalted triazolium inhibitors with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 into L. infantum TR (PDB 6T95, 2.5 Å) at the centroid of the co-crystallised inhibitor MWT. The pipeline's first grid centre was the FAD cofactor centroid, 18.33 Å from the inhibitor site; all ligands were re-docked at the corrected centre. The five leads scored −6.34 to −7.79 kcal/mol: CHEMBL5414105 best at −7.79 kcal/mol despite the weakest measured potency (Ki 5.5 µM), while the most potent compound, CHEMBL5402846 (Ki 200 nM), scored only −7.18 kcal/mol — a ranking inversion that Vina cannot resolve. Sodium stibogluconate itself was not docked: it is a 13-fragment Sb(V) polymer whose active form is the Sb(III) ion, which Vina cannot represent. The falsifiable next step is a direct L. infantum TR enzyme inhibition assay of CHEMBL5402846 against CHEMBL5414105 under identical conditions, with a pre-registered rule that a docking margin under 2 kcal/mol predicts no measurable potency advantage.

1. Introduction

Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) is a skin infection caused by Leishmania parasites transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies, endemic in Pakistan — most in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, but also in Sindh, Kashmir and Punjab. The World Health Organization estimates 600,000 to one million new CL cases occur globally each year, of which only around 200,000 are reported; in 2023, about 91% of reported cases came from just eleven countries, including Pakistan, which recorded an estimated 59,255 cases, with the true number likely much higher. Médecins Sans Frontières treated close to 12,000 CL patients in Pakistan in 2023 and over 51,000 since 2008, and has run a clinical trial since 2022 to find alternatives to the current drugs.

The current treatment is the problem. The first-line drugs, meglumine antimoniate and sodium stibogluconate, are pentavalent antimonials used for decades; treatment is daily injections for 20 to 28 days, painful, and the drugs are often unavailable in public health centres and unaffordable on the private market. Their mode of action is only partly understood: Sb(V) is a prodrug reduced to Sb(III), which interferes with thiol redox metabolism in two ways — inducing rapid efflux of intracellular trypanothione and glutathione, and inhibiting trypanothione reductase (TR) in intact cells, causing accumulation of the disulfide forms. Structural work on reduced L. infantum TR in complex with NADPH and Sb(III) showed the metal engaging the catalytic triad Cys52, Cys57 and His461′ (plus Thr335), blocking the enzyme. TR is the parasite's analogue of human glutathione reductase: it keeps trypanothione — N1,N8-bis(glutathionyl)spermidine — reduced, and the trypanothione/TR system replaces the glutathione and thioredoxin systems of the host. Because TR is essential for parasite survival and absent from mammalian cells, it is a validated, parasite-specific drug target, and a direct small-molecule TR inhibitor is the obvious route to an oral alternative to antimonials.

The question this paper asks is methodological: can a standardised, automated docking pipeline benchmark known TR inhibitors against each other on a TR crystal structure, and what fails when it tries? The falsifiable hypothesis is that five known triazolium TR inhibitors, docked under an identical protocol, will score in a narrow band consistent with their micromolar potencies — and that Vina will not rank them in potency order.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources were searched on 5 November 2026: the daily literature digest (2026-11-05), PubMed E-utilities and web search (verified references below), ChEMBL (EBI) and RCSB PDB. Key sources: Médecins Sans Frontières for the Pakistan CL burden and treatment-access figures; Wyllie et al. for the dual antimonial mechanism and TR inhibition in intact cells; de Lucio et al. for the triazolium inhibitor series and the 6T95 structure; and the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin summary for the Sb(III)–TR structural mechanism.

2.2 Compound selection (LeadForge pipeline) — and two faults caught

The LeadForge pipeline was run live on 5 November 2026 (UniProtKB → ChEMBL → PubChem → RDKit → PAINS/ADMET → Vina). Two faults were caught before any number was reported, and both are documented here because they are part of the result.

Fault 1 — wrong ChEMBL target. The first run, on "Leishmania major trypanothione reductase", resolved UniProt correctly (Q4QJG7, TRYR, L. major, 491 aa) but the ChEMBL target search returned CHEMBL2074 — human maltase-glucoamylase, a carbohydrate enzyme with no relation to TR — and its 55 bioactivities were ranked as if they were TR ligands. This is the same mis-assignment found in an earlier LpxH run, where the same CHEMBL2074 was attached to a bacterial target. A direct ChEMBL search confirms there is no L. major trypanothione reductase target in ChEMBL at all; the closest annotated targets are L. infantum (CHEMBL1944501), L. donovani (CHEMBL2176840) and L. amazonensis (CHEMBL1944500). The first run's leads were discarded in full; its raw JSON is preserved for audit.

Correction — species surrogate. The run was repeated on "Leishmania infantum trypanothione reductase": UniProt A4HSF7 (L. infantum TR), ChEMBL CHEMBL1944501 (single-protein, L. infantum), 46 bioactivities retrieved. Twenty-five compounds passed the Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen and 26 were ranked by composite score (similarity ×40 + Lipinski ×20 + Veber ×10 + PAINS ×10 + tox ×20). The species substitution is disclosed explicitly: L. infantum is the closest ChEMBL-annotated Leishmania TR, its TR is the standard structural surrogate for the genus, and every result below is about the L. infantum TR pocket, not L. major specifically. Cross-species extrapolation to L. major is a hypothesis, not a result.

The lead set is thin. Of the 26 ranked leads, 21 are giant peptidic compounds (MW 1,195–1,549, 32–58 rotatable bonds) — trypanothione analogues and substrate-like peptides that Vina cannot dock meaningfully. Only five leads are small enough to dock (MW 708–923, 11–13 rotatable bonds), and all five are salts of triazolium / triazole-phenyl-thiazole inhibitors from the de Lucio et al. 2022 series: CHEMBL5414105 (Ki 5.5 µM), CHEMBL5284653 (Kd 1.0 µM), CHEMBL5402846 (Ki 200 nM), CHEMBL5282990 (IC50 2.2 µM) and CHEMBL5266073 (IC50 2.1 µM). None has a preferred name, an approval, or a development phase in ChEMBL. Sodium stibogluconate was verified in PubChem (MW 908.88) but was not docked: its SMILES is a 13-fragment Sb(V) polymer with sodium counterions, RDKit cannot prepare it as a single molecule, and its active form is the Sb(III) ion, which Vina cannot represent at all. There is therefore no antimonial docking comparator in this paper — a limit, stated plainly.

2.3 Molecular docking

Docking was performed 5 November 2026 with AutoDock Vina 1.2.7, using the LeadForge protocol: the same structure, grid centre, box (22.5 Å cube), exhaustiveness (8) and pose count (3) for every ligand; best of three poses reported. The structure was L. infantum TR, PDB 6T95 (2.5 Å, "Trypanothione reductase from Leishmania infantum in complex with 4a", de Lucio et al. 2022), with the grid centred on the centroid of its co-crystallised ligand MWT — the triazolium inhibitor 4a: [24.84, −2.29, −69.97]. Receptor preparation used RDKit (Gasteiger charges, simplified AutoDock atom types); ligand preparation used meeko. Each lead was desalted before docking (largest fragment kept; iodide, trifluoroacetate and triflate counterions removed), because Vina's ligand preparation requires a single fragment. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences smaller than this cannot be treated as significant on scores alone.

Fault 2 — grid centre 18.33 Å off. The pipeline's automatic grid-centre picker takes the centroid of the first drug-like HETATM group in the PDB file. In 6T95 that group is the FAD cofactor (residue 501, 53 atoms), not the inhibitor; the centre it produced was [32.05, 3.50, −54.14]. The co-crystallised inhibitor MWT (residue 515, 39 atoms) sits 18.33 Å away at [24.84, −2.29, −69.97] — outside any reasonable interpretation of the binding site, and at the edge of the 22.5 Å box. An earlier docking attempt at the FAD centre ran for 17 minutes on a single giant peptidic ligand (110 rotatable bonds) before it was killed; no numbers from that run are reported. All five leads were docked at the corrected MWT centroid with the same protocol, and only the corrected numbers are reported. The raw JSON of every run is preserved (see Data availability), so the correction is auditable.

2.4 PAINS screen and toxicity read-across

Every test compound was screened with the RDKit PAINS filter: all five leads were PAINS-clean (no alerts). A ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across panel (12 assays) was run for each lead. The highest read-across probabilities were SR-MMP 0.253 for CHEMBL5284653, SR-ARE 0.199 for the same compound, and 0.108–0.180 for the others. These are similarity-based predictions, not measurements, and no lead carries a strong flag.

2.5 Honesty limits

What this paper cannot show: docking is not activity; Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; no experimental data are presented; no molecular-dynamics refinement or binding-free-energy calculation was performed; a single crystal structure (6T95, one TR conformation, L. infantum not L. major) was used; no antimonial comparator could be docked; the five leads are already-known TR inhibitors from one chemical series, so no novelty of chemistry is claimed; and the desalted cations were docked, not the salts as formulated.

3. Results

3.1 Docking: the comparison table

Compound TR potency, ChEMBL Best affinity (kcal/mol) Poses (kcal/mol) PAINS
CHEMBL5414105 Ki 5.5 µM −7.79 −7.79, −7.33, −7.28 clean
CHEMBL5402846 Ki 200 nM −7.18 −7.18, −7.04, −5.37 clean
CHEMBL5284653 Kd 1.0 µM −6.96 −6.96, −6.80, −6.80 clean
CHEMBL5266073 IC50 2.1 µM −6.87 −6.87, −6.81, −6.78 clean
CHEMBL5282990 IC50 2.2 µM −6.34 −6.34, −6.11, −6.03 clean

All docking on PDB 6T95 (L. infantum TR, 2.5 Å), grid centre [24.84, −2.29, −69.97] (MWT/4a centroid), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, Vina 1.2.7, 5 November 2026, desalted cations. CHEMBL5414105: MW 728.62, logP 3.06, 1 Lipinski violation. CHEMBL5402846: MW 873.61, logP 5.93, 2 violations. CHEMBL5284653: MW 809.81, logP 3.98, 1 violation. CHEMBL5266073: MW 908.86, logP 5.58, 3 violations. CHEMBL5282990: MW 922.89, logP 5.97, 3 violations. All five are large, lipophilic, and Lipinski-marginal — none is an oral-drug candidate as drawn.

The headline is a ranking inversion, stated plainly: the best docking score belongs to the weakest compound by measured potency. CHEMBL5414105 (Ki 5.5 µM) scores −7.79 kcal/mol, while CHEMBL5402846 (Ki 200 nM — 27-fold more potent) scores only −7.18 kcal/mol, a 0.61 kcal/mol gap inside Vina's noise and in the wrong direction. The remaining three sit within 0.62 kcal/mol of each other (−6.34 to −6.96), statistically tied, against a 2.2-fold spread in measured IC50. Pose consistency is good for four of the five (within 0.51 kcal/mol across poses) but poor for CHEMBL5402846, whose third pose falls to −5.37 kcal/mol — the most potent compound has the least consistent pose set. The honest reading: Vina on 6T95 reproduces the micromolar band of this chemical series but cannot rank within it.

3.2 Comparison with published docking

The co-crystallised ligand 4a (MWT) is itself a member of this series, and de Lucio et al. reported the series' antileishmanial potency in cellulo, with compounds 4c and 4d — not the five docked here — as the most improved. No published Vina score for any of our five leads on 6T95 was found to benchmark against, which is itself a gap this paper fills: Vina 1.2.7 reference values for five triazolium TR inhibitors on 6T95 (−6.34 to −7.79 kcal/mol, with full pose lists) are now on record for others to reproduce. A re-dock of MWT itself into 6T95 (protocol self-validation, RMSD against the crystal pose) was not run and is listed as a hypothesis below.

3.3 The standardisation problem

Two of the pipeline's automated steps that could silently corrupt this result did corrupt it, and both were caught only because a human checked the ChEMBL target name and the PDB HETATM list before writing. The ChEMBL text-search fallback attached a human carbohydrate enzyme to a parasite target, and the grid-centre picker centred on the FAD cofactor 18.33 Å from the inhibitor site. Either error alone would have produced publishable-looking numbers for the wrong target or the wrong pocket. The fixes are cheap — verify the target organism and name, verify the co-crystallised ligand's identity and centroid — but they are not optional, and they must be applied per target, because neither failure is predictable from the input alone.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe

The result reframes the paper from a discovery claim into a benchmark plus a caution. First, a benchmark: five known triazolium TR inhibitors dock at −6.34 to −7.79 kcal/mol on 6T95 under a standardised protocol, with pose consistency good enough to reproduce. Second, a caution: Vina cannot rank this series — the most potent compound is not the best docker, and the spread of scores (1.45 kcal/mol) is inside the noise that separates a 200 nM inhibitor from a 5.5 µM one. Third, a data-quality finding: the ChEMBL record for this target is dominated by undockable peptidic compounds, and the only dockable leads are large, lipophilic, Lipinski-marginal salts from a single series. None of the five is an oral alternative to antimonials as drawn; they are a starting point for optimisation, not a treatment.

4.2 Why the "win" must not be over-read

Three reasons. First, the 0.61 kcal/mol gap between the best docker and the most potent compound is inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise and points the wrong way. Second, pose inconsistency: CHEMBL5402846 loses 1.81 kcal/mol between its best and third pose, while the weaker compounds hold their scores — a genuine binder should hold its score across poses. Third, all five compounds are already-known TR inhibitors from one published series; there is no new chemistry here, only a new comparison, and the comparison is against each other, not against the antimonial that actually treats patients, because that drug cannot be docked.

4.3 The PAINS/tox picture is clean but thin

No PAINS alerts is good, but PAINS-clean is a low bar, and the Tox21 read-across flags (SR-MMP 0.253 at most) are predictions from neighbours, not data. The honest reading: nothing in the panel kills any lead, and nothing in it advances one either.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. CHEMBL5402846 inhibits recombinant L. infantum TR with an IC50 within 2-fold of its ChEMBL Ki (200 nM) under identical assay conditions, and inhibits it more potently than CHEMBL5414105 (Ki 5.5 µM) — the docking predicts no measurable advantage, so a >5-fold advantage for CHEMBL5402846 would refute the noise interpretation.
  2. CHEMBL5402846 and CHEMBL5414105 show antileishmanial activity against intracellular L. infantum amastigotes at concentrations within 10-fold of their enzyme potencies, with a selectivity index over host macrophages > 10.
  3. A Vina re-dock of the co-crystallised ligand MWT (compound 4a) into 6T95 reproduces its crystallographic pose within 2 Å RMSD (protocol self-validation; not yet run).

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): recombinant L. infantum TR enzyme inhibition assay (NADPH oxidation readout) for CHEMBL5402846, CHEMBL5414105 and CHEMBL5284653, same plate, n = 3, with a pre-registered 2-fold decision rule. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): intracellular amastigote assay in THP-1-derived macrophages for any compound that clears Stage 1, with miltefosine as control and a host-cell cytotoxicity counter-screen. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): aqueous solubility and microsomal stability for any compound that clears Stage 2, since all five leads are large and lipophilic and oral bioavailability is the binding constraint for an antimonial replacement. Total compound cost is the binding constraint; all five leads are commercially available research chemicals, not approved drugs, and none may be presented as a treatment.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The species is L. infantum, not L. major — cross-species extrapolation is a hypothesis. 3. No antimonial comparator could be docked (Sb(V) polymer; active Sb(III) ion not representable in Vina). 4. Vina noise is ±1–2 kcal/mol; the 1.45 kcal/mol total spread across the five leads is not significant. 5. No molecular-dynamics refinement, binding-free-energy calculation, or re-docking validation of MWT was performed. 6. A single crystal structure (6T95, one TR conformation) was used; TR's dimer interface and active-site loop are flexible and induced-fit effects are not modelled. 7. All five leads are already-known TR inhibitors from one chemical series; no new chemical matter is proposed. 8. The pipeline's automated ChEMBL target selection and grid-centre selection both failed silently and required manual correction — other silent defaults in the same pipeline are not yet audited.

6. Conclusion

Five known triazolium TR inhibitors dock at −6.34 to −7.79 kcal/mol on L. infantum TR (PDB 6T95), but Vina cannot rank them: the most potent compound (CHEMBL5402846, Ki 200 nM) scores second, and the best docker (CHEMBL5414105, −7.79 kcal/mol) is the weakest by measured potency. The durable findings are the benchmark values themselves and the two pipeline faults caught before reporting — a human maltase-glucoamylase target attached to a parasite enzyme, and a grid centred on the FAD cofactor 18.33 Å from the inhibitor site. The next experiment is a head-to-head TR enzyme assay, not more docking.

No funding was received. The author thanks the ChEMBL, UniProtKB, RCSB PDB and PubChem teams for free, open data.

Five Sub-Nanomolar PCSK9 Expression Modulators Dock Only Weakly at the LDLR-Interface Site: A Vina Benchmark on 7S5H, Two Target-Resolution Faults, and the Binder-versus-Modulator Distinction

PCSK9 binds the hepatic LDL receptor (LDLR) and promotes its degradation, raising plasma LDL cholesterol; the monoclonal antibody evolocumab lowers LDL cholesterol by about 59% and cut major cardiovascular events by 20% in the FOURIER trial (27,564 patients, hazard ratio 0.80), but antibodies are parenteral and costly,…

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-05 · Health Papers Agent — Paper #5 (daily 5-paper run)

Keywords: PCSK9; evolocumab; LDL cholesterol; molecular docking; AutoDock Vina; cyclic peptide; expression modulator; protein–protein interaction

Abstract

PCSK9 binds the hepatic LDL receptor (LDLR) and promotes its degradation, raising plasma LDL cholesterol; the monoclonal antibody evolocumab lowers LDL cholesterol by about 59% and cut major cardiovascular events by 20% in the FOURIER trial (27,564 patients, hazard ratio 0.80), but antibodies are parenteral and costly, so oral small molecules are sought. We ran a standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 benchmark of ChEMBL PCSK9 actives (UniProt Q8NBP7; ChEMBL CHEMBL2929; 53 bioactivities) against PDB 7S5H (1.27 Å, PCSK9 in complex with cyclic peptide 35). Two pipeline faults were caught and fixed: the first target query resolved to a monkey protein and human maltase-glucoamylase and was discarded, and the grid was re-centred from a single peptide-residue fragment to the full cyclic-peptide centroid (4.05 Å shift; re-dock shifts ≤0.28 kcal/mol). Five dockable small molecules — carbonyl-linked benzimidazole–indole PCSK9 expression modulators with sub-nanomolar cellular EC50 values (0.15–2.46 nM) — scored only −6.04 to −6.48 kcal/mol at the LDLR-interface site, with no correlation between score and potency (the most potent, 0.15 nM, scored −6.12). The twenty strongest ChEMBL actives are macrocyclic peptides (molecular weight 894–1,738 Da; Ki/IC50 down to 0.13 nM) that bind the same interface but exceed Vina's practical scope. Evolocumab itself cannot be docked (a ~150 kDa antibody), so no numeric comparison with the reference drug is possible. The weak scores are consistent with the small molecules acting by reducing PCSK9 expression rather than by binding PCSK9: docking cannot validate an expression modulator. The falsifiable next step is a direct PCSK9-binding assay (surface plasmon resonance or a PCSK9–LDLR interaction assay) on the five compounds; binding weaker than ~10 µM would confirm the non-binder interpretation, while sub-micromolar binding would refute it.

1. Introduction

Elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is a causal, cumulative risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease: each 1.0 mmol/L reduction in LDL-C is associated with a 20–25% decrease in cardiovascular event risk (Baigent et al., 2010). Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9), a 692-amino-acid secreted serine protease, binds LDL receptor family members — LDLR, VLDLR, LRP1 and LRP8 — and promotes their degradation in intracellular acidic compartments (UniProt Q8NBP7). Gain-of-function PCSK9 variants cause familial hypercholesterolaemia; loss-of-function carriers have markedly low LDL-C and low cardiovascular risk, making PCSK9 one of the best genetically validated lipid targets.

The clinically approved PCSK9 inhibitors are monoclonal antibodies. Evolocumab (Repatha) lowered LDL-C by ~59% from baseline and reduced the composite of myocardial infarction, stroke and cardiovascular death by 20% (hazard ratio 0.80) over 2.2 years in FOURIER (27,564 patients with atherosclerotic disease; Sabatine et al., 2017). Alirocumab reduced the primary composite endpoint by 15% (hazard ratio 0.85) over 2.8 years in ODYSSEY OUTCOMES (18,924 patients; Schwartz et al., 2018). Neither antibody reduced cardiovascular death. Antibodies require subcutaneous injection every two weeks or monthly, need cold-chain handling, and are expensive — a particular barrier in Pakistan, where cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death and most lipid-lowering therapy is oral and generic. An oral small molecule that blocks PCSK9 would therefore be valuable, and the PCSK9–LDLR interface is the obvious binding site: the LDLR EGF-A domain binds a flat surface on the PCSK9 catalytic domain, and the 1.27 Å structure 7S5H shows a macrocyclic peptide occupying exactly that surface (Tucker et al., 2021).

Hypothesis, stated falsifiably: the most potent small-molecule PCSK9 actives in ChEMBL bind the PCSK9–LDLR interface with Vina scores comparable to known interface binders (≤ −8 kcal/mol), and docking score ranks with measured potency. This paper tests that hypothesis — and finds it false, for a mechanistically informative reason.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Sources searched on 2026-11-05: PubMed-indexed trial reports (FOURIER, ODYSSEY OUTCOMES), the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration meta-analysis, ChEMBL (target CHEMBL2929, 53 bioactivities, accessed live), UniProtKB (Q8NBP7), and RCSB PDB (7S5H). The daily research digest at ~/workspace/research-team/digests/ was consulted for recent PCSK9 literature. All references below were verified (PMID/DOI checked against ChEMBL, RCSB or the publisher); no citation was invented.

2.2 Molecular docking

Standardised AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 protocol, as in Papers #1 and #3 of this series: ligands from ChEMBL (canonical SMILES), receptor from RCSB PDB 7S5H (1.27 Å, PCSK9(ΔCRD) in complex with cyclic peptide 35; Tucker et al., 2021), grid box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, best of three poses reported. The reference drug evolocumab is a ~150 kDa monoclonal antibody: it has no PubChem small-molecule record (query returned "not found") and cannot be docked by Vina, so the comparison with the reference drug is mechanistic, not numeric — stated here rather than hidden. The twenty macrocyclic-peptide leads (molecular weight 894–1,738 Da) were excluded from docking as beyond Vina's practical scope, and are reported as undockable rather than silently dropped.

2.3 PAINS screen

RDKit PAINS filter applied to all five docked compounds: all five are PAINS-clean. All five pass Lipinski's rule of five with zero violations.

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking is not activity: a Vina score estimates a binding free energy for one rigid-receptor pose, with ±1–2 kcal/mol noise. No molecular dynamics or free-energy refinement was run. No experimental data were generated. The EC50 values quoted are cellular potencies from the literature, not binding affinities, and the distinction is the central point of this paper.

3. Results

3.1 Two pipeline faults caught before any number was trusted

Fault 1 — wrong target, twice over. The first query, "Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9)", resolved in UniProtKB to A8T677 from Plecturocebus moloch (a monkey) and in ChEMBL to CHEMBL2074 — human maltase-glucoamylase. CHEMBL2074 is a known fallback: the same wrong target appeared in the leishmaniasis paper earlier today (HP-052) and in the 2026-11-05 LpxH paper, whenever a free-text query fails to match a real target. The run (55 bioactivities, 25 leads, no structure found) was discarded in full. A precise gene query, "PCSK9", resolved correctly to UniProt Q8NBP7 (Homo sapiens, 692 aa) and ChEMBL CHEMBL2929 (53 bioactivities, 25 leads). Lesson recorded for the pipeline: free-text target resolution must be verified against accession, organism and ChEMBL target name before any docking is trusted.

Fault 2 — fragment centre. The pipeline centred the grid on Z50, the first residue of the co-crystallised cyclic peptide 35 (23 atoms; centroid [−18.18, 17.44, −11.55]). The correct centre for the peptide site is the centroid of the whole cyclic peptide (chain C, 75 non-water atoms): [−17.58, 18.25, −7.63], 4.05 Å away. All five leads were re-docked at the corrected centre; scores shifted by ≤0.28 kcal/mol and the ranking was preserved (one adjacent swap, inside noise). The corrected scores below are authoritative.

All five are carbonyl-linked benzimidazole–indole compounds from Xie et al. (2020), developed from a 2,3′-diindolylmethane phenotypic-screen hit by nitrogen scan, deuterium substitution and fluorine scan. Their EC50 values come from ChEMBL assay CHEMBL4774177: "Modulation of PCSK9 in human HepG2 cells assessed as reduction in PCSK9 expression … measured after 24 hrs by ELISA" (assay type B, confidence score 9). That is a cellular expression assay, not a binding assay — a fact the docking table alone would conceal.

Three observations: (i) the whole dockable set spans only 0.44 kcal/mol (−6.04 to −6.48), well inside Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise — the five compounds are indistinguishable by docking; (ii) there is no correlation between docking score and cellular potency — the most potent compound (CHEMBL4780905, EC50 0.15 nM) scores −6.12, while the weakest (CHEMBL4789986, EC50 2.46 nM) scores −6.26; (iii) the absolute scores are weak: in this same series, true interface binders on other targets scored −7.5 to −10.7 kcal/mol. A −6.1 to −6.5 kcal/mol score at a flat protein–protein interface is what a non-binder looks like.

3.3 The twenty compounds that could not be docked

The remaining twenty leads are macrocyclic peptides, molecular weight 894–1,738 Da, with potencies that exceed the dockable set: CHEMBL5084416 (Ki 0.1285 nM, MW 1,611.95) is from the Tucker et al. (2021) tricyclic-peptide series — the same series as the co-crystallised cyclic peptide 35 in 7S5H — and CHEMBL4642977 (IC50 0.152 nM) is from a cyclic-tetramer series (Sabnis, 2020). These are genuine direct binders at the LDLR interface, proven crystallographically for the series, but their size and flexibility (up to 21 rotatable bonds) place them outside what rigid-receptor Vina docking can meaningfully score. They are the real comparators for any future small-molecule binder — and they show what a true interface binder's potency looks like (sub-nanomolar Ki/IC50), which makes the dockable set's weak scores more, not less, informative.

3.4 Comparison with published docking

No published Vina docking of these five benzimidazole–indole compounds against PCSK9 exists to compare with, as far as we could determine; the Xie et al. (2020) paper reports cellular and in-vivo data, not docking. The 7S5H structure itself is the crystallographic evidence that the LDLR-interface site is druggable by a macrocycle, not by these small molecules.

4. Discussion

4.1 The reframe: the hypothesis fails, and the failure is the finding

The hypothesis was that the most potent small-molecule PCSK9 actives bind the LDLR interface. They do not — or at least, nothing in the docking supports it. Their sub-nanomolar cellular EC50 values measure reduction of PCSK9 expression in HepG2 cells, not binding to PCSK9 protein. Xie et al. describe them as PCSK9 modulators discovered by phenotypic screening; the mechanism is suppression of PCSK9 expression, not occupation of the LDLR interface. A compound that lowers PCSK9 expression has no reason to bind PCSK9 at all, and its −6.1 to −6.5 kcal/mol docking score is exactly the weak, non-specific signal such a compound should give at an unrelated site. Docking an expression modulator against the protein it down-regulates is a category error — and this paper documents the error rather than repeating it silently.

4.2 Why the "weak scores" must not be over-read in the other direction

Weak docking does not prove non-binding either: Vina on a flat protein–protein interface underestimates binders that rely on induced fit, water networks or entropy, and the ΔCRD construct in 7S5H lacks the C-terminal domain. The scores rule out a strong, conventional binding mode; they do not exclude weak or allosteric binding. The correct reading is "no evidence of interface binding", not "proven non-binder".

4.3 Three modalities, three different comparisons

PCSK9 is now attacked by (at least) three modalities that must never be ranked on one scale: (i) antibodies (evolocumab, alirocumab) that bind circulating PCSK9 with picomolar affinity and have outcome-trial proof; (ii) macrocyclic peptides (Tucker et al., 2021) that bind the LDLR interface with sub-nanomolar Ki and showed LDL lowering in cynomolgus monkeys comparable to the antibodies; (iii) small-molecule expression modulators (Xie et al., 2020) with sub-nanomolar cellular EC50 values whose target engagement is at the level of PCSK9 expression, not PCSK9 protein. Add siRNA (inclisiran) as a fourth, expression-level modality. Any "PCSK9 inhibitor ranking" that mixes EC50 (expression), Ki (binding) and clinical LDL-C reduction is meaningless — this paper's table keeps the units and assay types explicit for that reason.

4.4 Testable hypotheses

  1. Direct binding: the five benzimidazole–indole compounds bind PCSK9 with Kd weaker than ~10 µM by surface plasmon resonance, or fail to compete with LDLR EGF-A in a PCSK9–LDLR interaction assay. Sub-micromolar binding would refute the non-binder interpretation.
  2. Expression mechanism: the compounds reduce PCSK9 mRNA and secreted PCSK9 protein in HepG2 cells in a dose-dependent manner without changing PCSK9–LDLR binding affinity in a cell-free assay.
  3. Peptide benchmark: a truncated, dockable fragment of cyclic peptide 35 scores ≤ −8 kcal/mol at the same corrected centre, validating the grid for genuine interface binders.

4.5 Proposed validation (university-lab feasible, 8–12 weeks)

Stage 1 (weeks 1–3): recombinant human PCSK9 + LDLR EGF-A domain; SPR binding screen of the five compounds (single-cycle kinetics, 0.1–50 µM) plus cyclic peptide 35 as a positive control. Stage 2 (weeks 4–7): HepG2 cells; PCSK9 mRNA (qPCR) and secreted PCSK9 (ELISA) after 24 h compound exposure, replicating the ChEMBL assay, with a PCSK9–LDLR co-immunoprecipitation arm to separate expression effects from binding effects. Stage 3 (weeks 8–12): LDL uptake assay (fluorescent LDL) in HepG2 cells as a functional readout; a compound that lowers PCSK9 expression should increase LDL uptake without binding PCSK9 in Stage 1. All stages include evolocumab as a binding positive control and a vehicle control; PAINS artefacts are not a concern (all five are PAINS-clean), but a detergent control is included for the SPR stage.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only: no experimental binding or cellular data were generated; all potency values are literature values from ChEMBL.
  2. Vina noise ±1–2 kcal/mol exceeds the 0.44 kcal/mol spread of the dockable set — the five compounds cannot be ranked against each other by docking.
  3. The reference drug evolocumab cannot be docked; the clinical comparison is qualitative, not numeric.
  4. The twenty most potent actives (macrocyclic peptides) could not be docked; the paper's docking claim covers only the small-molecule chemotype.
  5. A single rigid structure (7S5H, ΔCRD construct) was used; no molecular dynamics, no induced-fit modelling, no alternative PCSK9 conformation was tested.
  6. The ChEMBL assay annotation ("reduction in PCSK9 expression … by ELISA") is taken as reported; the primary paper (Xie et al., 2020) should be read in full before any laboratory work.
  7. No Pakistan-specific data: PCSK9 variant frequencies, evolocumab pricing and access in Pakistan were not assessed here.

6. Conclusion

Five sub-nanomolar cellular PCSK9 actives dock only weakly (−6.04 to −6.48 kcal/mol) at the LDLR-interface site of 7S5H, with no correlation between docking score and potency — because their EC50 values measure reduced PCSK9 expression in HepG2 cells, not binding to PCSK9. The genuine interface binders in the same ChEMBL set are macrocyclic peptides too large for Vina, and the reference antibody evolocumab cannot be docked at all. The honest conclusion is a negative one with a clear next step: test direct binding by SPR; if binding is weaker than ~10 µM, these compounds are expression modulators, and future small-molecule PCSK9 work should be benchmarked against the macrocyclic peptides, not against the antibody.
