One Molecule, Two Bottlenecks: A Predicted Dual Aldose-Reductase / SGLT2 Inhibitor and the Case for Closing the Polyol Escape Route in Diabetes

SGLT2 inhibitors are the most successful modern therapy for diabetic kidney and cardiovascular disease, yet residual risk remains: complications still progress in many treated patients.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2 November 2026 · Paper #3 — Health track, extra (Daily Research Papers)

Keywords: dual inhibitor; aldose reductase; SGLT2; polyol pathway; diabetic complications; thymoquinone; CHEMBL5288495; molecular docking

Abstract

SGLT2 inhibitors are the most successful modern therapy for diabetic kidney and cardiovascular disease, yet residual risk remains: complications still progress in many treated patients. Aldose reductase (AR) inhibitors, the drugs that block the polyol pathway driving diabetic neuropathy, retinopathy and cataract, failed clinically — but a 2023 mechanistic review reports a fact that reframes both classes: when renal SGLT2 is inhibited, downstream SGLT1 transports glucose at a higher frequency and activates the aldose reductase gene, producing sorbitol and fructose that damage the tubule. SGLT2 inhibition may therefore open a polyol escape route even as it lowers glucose. We tested, by standardised AutoDock Vina docking, whether either of two known leads already hits both targets. The SGLT2 lead CHEMBL5288495 (measured SGLT2 IC50 0.35 nM; docked −7.03 kcal/mol on 7VSI) docked to aldose reductase (PDB 1US0) at −9.56 kcal/mol — 3.09 kcal/mol better than the AR reference drug epalrestat (−6.47), consistent across all three top poses, and PAINS-clean. Thymoquinone docked to both targets as well (AR −7.28; SGLT2 −6.98, outscoring dapagliflozin −4.79 in-run), but carries a PAINS alert. No published paper has reported dual AR/SGLT2 activity for any molecule, and no head-to-head AR-inhibitor versus SGLT2-inhibitor trial exists. We propose two falsifiable steps: (1) an in-vitro AR inhibition assay of CHEMBL5288495 and its novel analogs, and (2) a combination trial design (SGLT2 inhibitor + AR inhibitor) in patients with residual albuminuria or neuropathy despite SGLT2 therapy. The honest counterpoint is stated in full: in the ARISE-HF trial of the AR inhibitor AT-001, the benefit signal appeared in the subgroup not receiving SGLT2 inhibitors — so the combination is a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion.

1. Introduction

Type 2 diabetes now affects roughly 1 in 3 adults in Pakistan and over 500 million people worldwide, and its complications — kidney failure, heart failure, neuropathy, retinopathy, cataract — are the main source of its morbidity. Two drug classes attack two different bottlenecks. SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption and have transformed cardiorenal outcomes. Aldose reductase (AR) inhibitors block the first, rate-limiting enzyme of the polyol pathway, which converts excess glucose to sorbitol and drives osmotic and oxidative injury in nerve, retina, lens and kidney. The first class succeeded; the second largely failed in the clinic, with the most recent large trial (ARISE-HF, AT-001, 2024) missing its primary endpoint.

These two stories are usually told separately. A 2023 mechanistic review of SGLT1, SGLT2 and dual inhibitors (Azizogli et al.) contains a sentence that connects them: when renal SGLT2 is inhibited, downstream renal SGLT1 "facilitates the transport of glucose at a higher frequency and activates the aldose reductase gene, making sorbitol and fructose. Fructose gets metabolized through fructokinase and leads to uric acid synthesis, oxidative stress, and cytokine inflammation, damaging the tubule." If that mechanism operates in patients, then SGLT2 inhibition — the standard of care — may itself upregulate the very enzyme AR inhibitors are meant to block, leaving a polyol escape route open behind the drug's benefit. That is a testable claim, and it reframes the AR inhibitor not as a failed monotherapy but as the missing second half of SGLT2 therapy.

This paper asks the narrowest version of that question: does any molecule already known as an SGLT2 inhibitor also inhibit aldose reductase? We cross-docked two leads against both targets under one protocol — the SGLT2 lead CHEMBL5288495 from our own LeadForge pipeline (measured IC50 0.35 nM) and thymoquinone, the black-seed quinone that outscored epalrestat on AR in our companion paper — and report the first dual AR/SGLT2 docking evidence for either molecule.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis and novelty check

We searched for prior dual AR/SGLT2 work (web and PubMed, 2 November 2026): "dual aldose reductase SGLT2 inhibitor", "thymoquinone SGLT2", and related terms. The nearest items found were (i) a 2023 comparison review of SGLT1/SGLT2/dual inhibitors (Azizogli et al.), (ii) a 2026 technical comparison of AR inhibitors versus SGLT2 inhibitors noting that no head-to-head clinical trial of the two classes exists, and (iii) a dual PTP1B + aldose-reductase flavonoid study — a different target pair. No paper reporting a dual AR/SGLT2 inhibitor, and no AR-inhibitor + SGLT2-inhibitor combination trial, was found.

2.2 Molecular docking

Docking used AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 with the LeadForge protocol, identical for every ligand in a run (same structure, same grid, same exhaustiveness 8, box 22.5 Å). Aldose reductase: PDB 1US0 (0.66 Å), centre [21.26, −6.13, 27.39]. SGLT2: PDB 7VSI (human SGLT2–MAP17 + empagliflozin, cryo-EM 2.95 Å), centre [46.73, 36.59, 40.54] — the SGLT2 pipeline uses direct Vina calls for 7VSI because the standard UniProt lookup admits X-ray structures only and all SGLT2 structures are cryo-EM. Vina's scoring noise is approximately ±1–2 kcal/mol; differences below this are not treated as significant. Affinities are the best of three poses; all three poses are reported.

2.3 Controls and a control failure, honestly reported

An initial SGLT2 run used flat connectivity SMILES (no stereochemistry) for dapagliflozin and produced an absurd control score (−2.76 for a nanomolar drug) and dropped epalrestat entirely from the AR run. Both controls were re-run with proper isomeric SMILES from PubChem, which restored them to their known values (dapagliflozin −4.79, matching the −4.84 of the earlier diabetes run; epalrestat −6.47, matching the −6.48 of the companion paper). Only the corrected, control-verified numbers are used in this paper. Thymoquinone's SGLT2 score was replicated in both runs (−6.95, then −6.98).

2.4 Honesty limits

Docking affinity is not enzyme inhibition and not efficacy. A docking "win" is triage: it tells the laboratory which assay to run first. No wet-lab data are presented. No clinical claim is made.

3. Results

3.1 The SGLT2 lead is a predicted aldose-reductase inhibitor — stronger than the AR reference drug

Ligand Aldose reductase, 1US0 (kcal/mol) Poses Verdict
CHEMBL5288495 (SGLT2 lead) −9.56 −9.56 / −9.13 / −7.58 3.09 better than epalrestat
Thymoquinone −7.28 −7.28 / −7.24 / −7.13 Beats epalrestat (see companion paper)
Epalrestat (ref) −6.47 −6.47 / −6.35 / −6.11 Reference

CHEMBL5288495 — a fluorinated dapagliflozin analog with measured SGLT2 IC50 0.35 nM and prior SGLT2 docking −7.03 — docked to aldose reductase at −9.56 kcal/mol. The margin over epalrestat (3.09 kcal/mol) exceeds Vina's ±1–2 kcal/mol noise, and all three top poses beat epalrestat's best pose. The molecule is PAINS-clean (per the LeadForge ADMET screen) and Lipinski-compliant. A structural rationale, not yet proof: AR's natural substrate is glucose, and CHEMBL5288495 carries a C-glycoside sugar moiety that plausibly occupies the sugar-binding pocket — the same pocket epalrestat binds. Pose-level interaction analysis and molecular dynamics are the required next step, not an assumption made here.

3.2 Thymoquinone hits both targets — moderately, and with a caveat

Ligand SGLT2, 7VSI (kcal/mol) Poses Verdict
Thymoquinone −6.98 −6.98 / −6.85 / −5.87 Outscores dapagliflozin in-run
Dapagliflozin (ref) −4.79 −4.79 / −2.64 / −2.63 Reference (replicates −4.84)
CHEMBL5288495 (prior run) −7.03 — Prior SGLT2 docking

Thymoquinone docked to SGLT2 at −6.98 kcal/mol, 2.19 kcal/mol better than dapagliflozin in the same run — at the edge of Vina's noise, but consistent across poses (even its worst pose, −5.87, beats dapagliflozin's best). Combined with its AR score (−7.28), TQ is a predicted dual inhibitor of both targets, though weaker than CHEMBL5288495 on AR and carrying a PAINS alert (quinone redox cycler) that the SGLT2 lead does not. TQ's dual activity is therefore a secondary lead; CHEMBL5288495 is the primary one.

3.3 The novelty statement, precisely bounded

To our knowledge, no published paper reports dual aldose-reductase/SGLT2 activity for any molecule, and no trial has combined the two classes. The nearest precedents are dual inhibitors of other pairs (e.g. PTP1B + AR flavonoids) and a comparison review that explicitly notes the absence of head-to-head AR-versus-SGLT2 trials. This paper's claim is correspondingly narrow: a computational dual-activity signal for one specific molecule, plus a mechanistic rationale and a falsifiable assay plan — not a drug, and not a clinical recommendation.

4. Discussion

4.1 The polyol escape-route hypothesis

The mechanism reported by Azizogli et al. — SGLT2 inhibition → increased downstream SGLT1 glucose transport → aldose-reductase gene activation → sorbitol/fructose → uric acid, oxidative stress, cytokine inflammation, tubular damage — predicts a specific, measurable consequence: markers of polyol flux (erythrocyte sorbitol, urinary fructose, AR expression) should rise, not fall, in some patients after SGLT2 inhibitor initiation, and that rise should track residual renal risk. If confirmed, it explains part of the residual risk on SGLT2 therapy and identifies the patients in whom adding AR inhibition should help most. If refuted — if polyol markers fall on SGLT2 therapy — the hypothesis dies cleanly and cheaply.

4.2 The counterpoint that must not be hidden

The ARISE-HF trial (AT-001, n = 691, 15 months, JACC 2024) missed its primary endpoint (peak VO2). The only benefit signal appeared in a prespecified subgroup: patients not receiving SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 RAs at baseline (+0.62 mL/kg/min peak VO2, p = .04; interaction p = .10). Read plainly, that subgroup result cuts against the combination: AR inhibition seemed to help precisely where SGLT2 inhibition was absent. Three readings are possible — (i) the subgroup is noise (interaction not significant), (ii) SGLT2 therapy already captures the benefit AR inhibition would add, or (iii) the combination was never actually tested (no patient received both drugs by design, and the subgroup is an absence, not a comparison). Only a trial that randomises the combination can distinguish them. This paper proposes that trial; it does not assume its outcome.

4.3 Two falsifiable steps

Step 1 — enzyme confirmation (8–12 weeks, university lab). In-vitro AR inhibition (IC50) of CHEMBL5288495 and its five novel analogs (best: A:Me/CH2/Cl, docked −8.19 on SGLT2), with epalrestat as control, plus SGLT2 inhibition (IC50) of thymoquinone. Confirmation = AR IC50 in a plausible range for CHEMBL5288495 with the effect surviving redox controls; refutation = no AR inhibition at ≤10 µM, or an effect that vanishes under redox/detergent controls. Step 2 — combination trial design. A randomised trial of SGLT2 inhibitor + AR inhibitor versus SGLT2 inhibitor alone in type 2 diabetes with residual albuminuria or neuropathy despite SGLT2 therapy, with polyol-flux markers (erythrocyte sorbitol, urinary fructose) as the mechanistic readout and albuminuria/neuropathy scores as clinical endpoints. The falsifiable prediction: the combination lowers polyol markers more than SGLT2 alone; if it does not, the escape-route hypothesis is wrong.

4.4 Why this matters in Pakistan specifically

Pakistan carries ~34.5 million adults with diabetes (~30.8% prevalence), and SGLT2 inhibitors are increasingly prescribed while AR inhibitors are essentially absent from practice. If the escape-route mechanism holds, the cheapest second step is not a new patented drug but the pairing of an existing SGLT2 inhibitor with a low-cost AR inhibitor — and the dual-activity signal for CHEMBL5288495 suggests the field should also look for single molecules that do both jobs, starting with the analogs already designed in our pipeline.

5. Limitations

  1. Docking only; no experimental data. 2. The AR margin for CHEMBL5288495 exceeds Vina noise, but a large ligand can score highly from contact count alone — pose inspection and dynamics are required. 3. TQ's SGLT2 margin (2.19 kcal/mol) sits at the noise edge. 4. Dapagliflozin scored −7.23 in the analogs run versus −4.84/−4.79 in two other runs — Vina run-to-run variability is real; only within-run comparisons are used here. 5. The SGLT2→AR activation mechanism rests on a single review's report; it needs direct experimental confirmation. 6. No Pakistani-market or population-specific data are presented.

6. Conclusion

One molecule built to block SGLT2 is predicted to block aldose reductase even more strongly than the AR reference drug — and the literature supplies a mechanism (SGLT2 inhibition activating the AR gene via SGLT1) that makes that dual activity therapeutically interesting rather than merely curious. The claim is narrow, the assay that settles it is cheap, and the trial that tests the combination is the obvious next step. If the assay refutes the docking, the field learns that a −9.56 Vina score can mislead; if it confirms it, the cheapest path to closing residual diabetic risk may already be sitting in the SGLT2 pipeline.

LeadForge: An AI-Driven Computational Pipeline for Accelerated Hit Discovery and Novel Analog Design — A Multi-Target Case Study

Early-stage drug discovery remains slow and expensive, with the hit-to-lead transition representing a major bottleneck. We describe LeadForge, an open, automated computational pipeline that triages candidate compounds against a protein target in seven stages: (1) target identification from UniProtKB and ChEMBL, (2) bio…

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

Zubair Ahmed

Faculty of Pharmacy, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan

Corresponding author: za0153715@gmail.com

Draft manuscript v1 — 7 October 2026. Not yet submitted for peer review. All results are computational (in silico); no experimental validation has been performed.

Abstract

Early-stage drug discovery remains slow and expensive, with the hit-to-lead transition representing a major bottleneck. We describe LeadForge, an open, automated computational pipeline that triages candidate compounds against a protein target in seven stages: (1) target identification from UniProtKB and ChEMBL, (2) bioactivity mining, (3) query verification via PubChem, (4) RDKit Morgan-fingerprint similarity screening, (5) ADMET and safety filtering (Lipinski/Veber, PAINS, and a Tox21 kNN read-across model), (6) composite lead ranking, and (7) AutoDock Vina molecular docking against experimentally determined protein structures from the RCSB Protein Data Bank. We validate the pipeline on four targets — EGFR, DPP4, SGLT2, and Escherichia coli dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) — and in each case the pipeline independently rediscovers the reference drug from the ChEMBL bioactivity set (similarity 1.0), confirming that the workflow recovers known chemistry before proposing anything new. As a design case study, we enumerated 240 analogs of the SGLT2 lead CHEMBL5288495, filtered them through novelty (<0.85 Tanimoto vs 23 known SGLT2 actives), ADMET, and docking screens to five finalists; the best candidate docks at −8.19 kcal/mol versus an in-run dapagliflozin control at −7.23 kcal/mol. All findings are computational hypotheses: no compounds have been synthesized or tested, docking scores carry run-to-run variability, and novelty is assessed computationally only. The five SGLT2 analogs are proposed for university-laboratory synthesis and assay as the next step.

Keywords: computer-aided drug design; virtual screening; molecular docking; ADMET prediction; SGLT2 inhibitors; hit-to-lead; cheminformatics

1. Introduction

Bringing a new drug to market routinely takes over a decade and costs in excess of one billion US dollars, with the majority of attrition occurring because early candidates fail on potency, selectivity, pharmacokinetics, or safety grounds that could, in principle, have been anticipated computationally (Hughes et al., 2011). The hit-to-lead phase — selecting which of thousands of plausible compounds deserve expensive synthesis and assay — is therefore one of the highest-leverage points for computational methods.

In recent years, ligand-based virtual screening, structure-based docking, and ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity) prediction have matured into practical triage tools (Sliwoski et al., 2014). Yet most academic and small-laboratory groups still assemble these steps manually, target by target, which is slow and difficult to reproduce. An integrated, automated pipeline that runs the full sequence — from target lookup to a ranked, docked shortlist — on live public data would let a small team triage a new target in hours rather than weeks.

LeadForge is such a pipeline. It chains seven stages on live data from UniProtKB, ChEMBL, PubChem, and the RCSB Protein Data Bank, applies RDKit cheminformatics and a Tox21-based kNN toxicity read-across model, and finishes with AutoDock Vina docking. This manuscript reports the pipeline's design and a multi-target case study conducted 6–7 October 2026 on four targets spanning oncology (EGFR), metabolic disease (DPP4, SGLT2), and antibacterial research (E. coli DHFR). We further report a de novo analog-design campaign around the SGLT2 lead CHEMBL5288495 that produced five computationally novel, ADMET-clean finalists proposed for synthesis.

Our contributions are: (i) a fully automated, reproducible seven-stage triage pipeline operating on live public databases; (ii) a validation-by-rediscovery protocol showing the pipeline recovers each reference drug from its target's known bioactivity set; (iii) a worked analog-design funnel (240 → 5) with full transparency on filters and attrition; and (iv) an honest accounting of the method's limitations, which we consider as important as the results.

2. Methods

2.1 Pipeline architecture

LeadForge executes seven stages sequentially for a given target–reference-drug pair. All stages ran on live public data on 6–7 October 2026; database contents are those served at query time.

Stage Operation Data source / tool
1 Target identification UniProtKB + ChEMBL (live lookup)
2 Known-ligand retrieval ChEMBL bioactivities for the target
3 Query verification PubChem PUG REST (SMILES resolution)
4 Similarity screen RDKit Morgan fingerprints, Tanimoto coefficient
5 ADMET + safety panel RDKit (Lipinski, Veber, PAINS) + ToxGuard Tox21 kNN (12 assays)
6 Lead ranking Composite score (see §2.5)
7 Molecular docking AutoDock Vina vs RCSB PDB structure (live fetch)

2.2 Data sources

UniProtKB (The UniProt Consortium) provides the canonical protein identifier, organism, and sequence length for each target. ChEMBL (EBI; Davies et al., 2015) provides the target identifier and the set of compounds with measured bioactivities against it; bioactivity sets were used as served (pChEMBL ≥ 5 where the pipeline applied a cutoff). PubChem PUG REST (Kim et al., 2016) resolves the reference drug name to a canonical isomeric SMILES. RCSB PDB (Berman et al., 2000) supplies the experimental protein structure for docking; the pipeline preferentially selects the highest-resolution inhibitor-bound X-ray structure and records the PDB ID and resolution for every run.

2.3 Similarity screening

Compounds are fingerprinted with RDKit Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2048 bits), and pairwise Tanimoto similarity to the reference drug is computed (Rogers & Hahn, 2010). A rediscovery check is performed at this stage: the reference drug is expected to appear in the target's ChEMBL bioactivity set at similarity 1.0. Failure of this check would indicate a data or identity error and halt interpretation of the run; all four runs reported here passed.

2.4 ADMET and safety panel

Each candidate is evaluated with: (i) Lipinski's Rule of Five (Lipinski et al., 1997) — molecular weight, logP, hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors, with violation counts recorded; (ii) Veber's rules (Veber et al., 2002) — rotatable bonds and topological polar surface area; (iii) PAINS filters (Baell & Holloway, 2010) via RDKit's FilterCatalog, flagging pan-assay interference substructures; and (iv) ToxGuard, a k-nearest-neighbors read-across model (k = 15) predicting outcomes across 12 Tox21 assays (Tice et al., 2013), reporting mean and maximum predicted probabilities. These are computational flags for triage, not safety determinations.

2.5 Lead ranking

Candidates are ranked by a composite score:

Score = 40 × similarity + 20 × Lipinski-pass + 10 × Veber-pass + 10 × PAINS-clean + 20 × low-tox

where each pass/fail term is 1 or 0 (low-tox = maximum Tox21 predicted probability below threshold). The score is a triage heuristic for ordering laboratory follow-up, not a potency prediction.

2.6 Molecular docking

Docking uses AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 (Eberhardt et al., 2021) with ligand preparation by meeko. For each target, the pipeline fetches the selected PDB entry from RCSB, centers a 22.5 Å cubic search box on the co-crystallized ligand position, and runs with exhaustiveness 8, retaining 3 poses per compound. Reported affinity is the best pose in kcal/mol. Because Vina's search is stochastic, scores carry run-to-run variability (observed on the order of ±0.5 kcal/mol in our runs); only within-run rankings against an in-run control are interpreted.

2.7 Novel analog design (SGLT2 campaign)

Starting from the SGLT2 lead CHEMBL5288495 (see §3.4), 240 analog combinations were enumerated across three series: Series A — aryl substituent swaps on both phenyl rings (R ∈ {Me, Et, nPr, iPr, OMe, CF₃, OCF₃}; X ∈ {Cl, F, Br, CF₃, OCF₃, OMe, Me}; linker ∈ {CH₂, O, NH, CHMe}); Series E — sugar-moiety edits (difluoro→CH₂, CH₂OH→CH₃, OH→OMe, OH→F); Series F — scaffold hops retaining the C-glycoside pharmacophore (thiophene-for-aryl-A and meta-linkage variants; pyridine-B variants failed RDKit sanitization and were dropped). Filters were applied in sequence: valid unique structures (200) → novelty (maximum Morgan Tanimoto < 0.85 against 23 known SGLT2 actives; 199 passed) → ADMET-clean (Lipinski ≤ 1 violation, Veber pass, PAINS clean, ToxGuard mean < 0.40 and max < 0.70; 199 passed) → docking of 12 prioritized candidates vs PDB 7VSI → 5 finalists. Dapagliflozin was docked in the same run as control.

3. Results

3.1 Validation by rediscovery

In all four target runs, the pipeline independently recovered the reference drug from the target's ChEMBL bioactivity set at Tanimoto similarity 1.0 (Table 1). This confirms the workflow operates on correctly identified chemistry before any ranking or docking is interpreted.

Table 1. Rediscovery validation across the four target runs (October 2026).

Target UniProt ChEMBL target Ligands mined Reference drug Rediscovered as Measured activity
EGFR P00533 CHEMBL203 35 erlotinib CHEMBL553 (sim 1.0, score 92.0) pChEMBL 10.54
DPP4 P27487 CHEMBL284 47 sitagliptin query self-match (sim 1.0, score 99.1) —
SGLT2 P31639 CHEMBL3884 22 dapagliflozin CHEMBL429910 (sim 1.0, score 99.6) IC₅₀ 0.49 nM
E. coli DHFR P0ABQ4 CHEMBL1809 37 trimethoprim CHEMBL22 (sim 1.0, score 100.0) Kᵢ 0.22 nM

3.2 EGFR (oncology)

Thirty-five known ligands were screened against human EGFR. Erlotinib was rediscovered as CHEMBL553 (similarity 1.0, composite score 92.0, pChEMBL 10.54). Docking against PDB 8A27 (X-ray, 1.07 Å) ranked the quinazoline analog CHEMBL29197 first at −8.05 kcal/mol, ahead of the erlotinib query (−7.87) and rediscovered erlotinib (−7.77), each as the best of three poses. The margin between the top three compounds (≤0.28 kcal/mol) is within expected docking variability and is not interpreted as a potency ranking.

3.3 DPP4 versus SGLT2 (type 2 diabetes)

The diabetes targets were run comparatively. DPP4 (47 bioactivities mined) produced a saturated chemical space: the top leads are all ultra-potent measured gliptins (IC₅₀ < 0.3 nM), and docking against PDB 4A5S (X-ray, 1.62 Å) ranked sitagliptin itself first (−5.92 kcal/mol), followed by CHEMBL5951803 (−5.81). One candidate (CHEMBL1203953) was excluded at the ligand-preparation stage because its salt form presented as two fragments. Nothing in the DPP4 set meaningfully separates from the reference drug.

SGLT2 (22 bioactivities) proved more interesting. Dapagliflozin was rediscovered as CHEMBL429910 (similarity 1.0, IC₅₀ 0.49 nM). Docking against PDB 7VSI — the human SGLT2–MAP17 complex in an empagliflozin-bound conformation (cryo-EM, 2.95 Å; no X-ray structure exists for this membrane transporter, so the pipeline's X-ray preference was explicitly overridden) — ranked CHEMBL5288495 first at −7.03 kcal/mol, substantially ahead of dapagliflozin (−4.84). CHEMBL5288495 is a fluorinated dapagliflozin analog (MW 413, 0 Lipinski violations) with measured IC₅₀ 0.35 nM. Its docking margin over the reference (−2.19 kcal/mol) exceeds the observed run-to-run variability and was selected as the parent for the analog-design campaign (§3.5). SMILES: CCc1ccc(Cc2cc([C@@H]3O[C@H](CO)C(F)(F)[C@H](O)[C@H]3O)ccc2Cl)cc1.

3.4 E. coli DHFR (antibacterial)

Thirty-seven ligands were screened against E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (folA), a classic antibacterial target. Trimethoprim was rediscovered as CHEMBL22 (similarity 1.0, score 100.0, measured Kᵢ 0.22 nM). All top-ranked leads are 2,4-diaminopyrimidine trimethoprim analogs differing in phenyl-ring alkoxy/alkyl substitution — a chemical space explored for decades. Docking against PDB 9PWM (X-ray, 0.89 Å) gave CHEMBL278345 −5.66 kcal/mol versus trimethoprim −5.63 kcal/mol. A difference of 0.03 kcal/mol is within docking noise; this run is reported as a validation-grade result (the pipeline rediscovers the known drug and ranks close analogs sensibly), not a discovery.

3.5 SGLT2 novel-analog campaign

The design funnel is summarized in Table 2. Of 240 enumerated combinations, 200 were valid unique structures; 199 passed the novelty filter (<0.85 Tanimoto vs 23 known SGLT2 actives); all 199 passed ADMET filters; 12 were docked; 5 finalists were selected.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the results show

The central positive finding is methodological: across four unrelated targets, an automated pipeline running on live public data recovered each reference drug at similarity 1.0 and produced ranked, docked shortlists whose top entries are chemically sensible (e.g., 2,4-diaminopyrimidines for DHFR, gliptins for DPP4). The SGLT2 case goes one step further — a ChEMBL lead (CHEMBL5288495) out-docked the marketed reference by a margin exceeding docking noise, and systematic analog enumeration around it yielded five candidates that preserve drug-likeness while improving the docking signal. This is the intended use of the pipeline: computational triage that tells a laboratory which compounds to make or buy first.

4.2 Limitations — read before citing

All results are in silico. No compound in this manuscript has been synthesized, assayed, or tested in any biological system. Docking scores are approximate binding-energy estimates, not measurements.

Docking variability is real. The dapagliflozin control scored −4.84 kcal/mol in the diabetes run and −7.23 kcal/mol in the analog-campaign run against the same 7VSI structure. Vina's stochastic search produces run-to-run shifts; only within-run rankings are meaningful, and sub-kcal/mol differences (e.g., the DHFR −5.66 vs −5.63) carry no potency information.

The SGLT2 structure is cryo-EM, not X-ray. At 2.95 Å on a membrane transporter, pose uncertainty is higher than for the X-ray structures used elsewhere (0.89–1.62 Å).

Novelty is computational. "Novel" here means maximum Morgan Tanimoto < 0.85 against 23 known SGLT2 actives in our reference set — a similarity heuristic, not a patent determination. Most finalists remain close analogs of the parent (similarity 0.78–0.85). Patent novelty requires a professional prior-art search, which has not been performed.

Prior art exists for the leads. CHEMBL5288495 and the other ChEMBL-identified leads are published compounds; they are starting points for optimization, not proprietary discoveries.

Toxicity flags are predictions. ToxGuard outputs are kNN read-across estimates from Tox21 assay data, not experimental toxicology.

No therapeutic, curative, or clinical claims are made. SGLT2 inhibitors are glucose-lowering agents for type 2 diabetes management; nothing here implies disease modification.

5. Conclusion and future work

LeadForge demonstrates that a fully automated, live-data pipeline can reproduce known drug–target chemistry across four targets and generate a focused, ADMET-clean analog shortlist for at least one of them. The five SGLT2 analogs in Table 3 are the concrete output: computationally novel, synthetically tractable (candidates 1–4 via standard building blocks), and ranked by a consistent docking protocol.

Planned next steps: (i) present the five SMILES to the university laboratory for synthesis-feasibility review; (ii) synthesize candidates 1–4 and assay SGLT2 inhibition head-to-head against dapagliflozin and the parent CHEMBL5288495; (iii) pursue a professional novelty/prior-art search through the university's ORIC (Office of Research, Innovation and Commercialization) before any intellectual-property filing; (iv) extend the pipeline's daily target rotation to accumulate a broader validation set for a follow-up study.

Run reports and machine-readable JSON for the EGFR, DPP4/SGLT2, E. coli DHFR, and SGLT2 analog-design runs are retained by the author and available on reasonable request. The LeadForge pipeline code is the author's own implementation.

Import Failure Before Leak: The Blood–Brain Barrier as a Supply Line Whose Early Shutdown Initiates Alzheimer's Disease — a Falsifiable Model and a Re-Ranking of Brain-Delivery Strategies

For a century the blood–brain barrier (BBB) has been treated as a fortress whose failure in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a leak: tight junctions break, albumin and fibrinogen flood in, neuroinflammation follows. A study published in Cell on 11 November 2026 (Zhou et al.) overturns the order of events.

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 18 November 2026 · Paper #6 — Brain track (Daily Research Papers, 5-field rotation)

Keywords: blood–brain barrier; Alzheimer's disease; apolipoprotein A1; APOA1; SR-B1; ABCA1; SERPINA1; CASS4; microglia; astrocytes; brain delivery; 5xFAD

Abstract

For a century the blood–brain barrier (BBB) has been treated as a fortress whose failure in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a leak: tight junctions break, albumin and fibrinogen flood in, neuroinflammation follows. A study published in Cell on 11 November 2026 (Zhou et al.) overturns the order of events. Using bioorthogonal proteomics, the authors tracked 861 plasma proteins in mice and found the healthy BBB samples 191 and permits only 92 (10.7%) into the brain parenchyma — a selective import system, not a wall. The imported proteins home to specific cell types: liver-derived apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) crosses via SR-B1 and engages astrocytic ABCA1, an Alzheimer's risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity; alpha-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA1) homes to microglia. In early-stage 5xFAD mice, the barrier first remodels transport — APOA1 uptake falls, SERPINA1 uptake rises — before any leak; hepatic overexpression of APOA1 restores brain APOA1 and rescues astrocytic, synaptic and behavioural deficits. We add two new quantitative facts and a synthesis. First, from UniProt (P02647), human APOA1 is a 267-amino-acid, 30,778 Da protein — 68 times the 450 Da passive-diffusion cut-off — so its brain entry is necessarily receptor-mediated, and any drug strategy that relies on passive entry cannot reproduce it. Second, the human observational record is consistent with, but does not prove, the import-first model: in the Amsterdam Dementia Cohort (n = 429 non-demented elderly, mean follow-up 2.5 years), lower plasma APOA1 predicted clinical progression in APOE ε4 carriers with subjective cognitive decline (hazard ratio 5.0; 95% CI 1.3–18.9), while higher cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) APOA1 predicted progression overall (HR 1.3 per standard deviation; 95% CI 1.0–1.6) — a pattern compatible with a disrupted plasma-to-brain gradient, but equally compatible with leak. Falsifiable claim: in preclinical AD, BBB import of liver-derived APOA1 falls before measurable barrier leak, and the CSF:plasma APOA1 ratio predicts clinical progression earlier than amyloid-PET positivity. Falsifier: a longitudinal human cohort in which the CSF:plasma APOA1 ratio does not fall before amyloid positivity, or in which gadolinium-measured leak precedes the import fall, refutes the import-first ordering; and a liver-targeted APOA1 intervention that raises brain APOA1 without slowing tau spread refutes the disease-modifying version of the claim while leaving the biomarker version intact. Causal identification for the human claim is association only; causality is established in mice only. We re-rank brain-delivery strategies against this model: receptor-mediated import restoration (endogenous SR-B1/APOA1 route; transferrin-receptor shuttles, with a company-reported >65-fold delivery gain in preclinical studies) outranks leak-sealing and passive-diffusion strategies, and we show why the peptide drugs that failed in Parkinson's trials could never have tested their own mechanism. Policy implication: Pakistan's health research funders should add the plasma/CSF APOA1 ratio to the national dementia cohort protocol and fund a liver-targeted APOA1 pilot before funding another leak-sealing trial — under the Islamic principle of hifz al-nafs (preservation of life), one of the five objectives of the Shariah.

1. Introduction

Alzheimer's disease affects more than 55 million people worldwide, and no therapy yet prevents its onset. The dominant mechanistic story of the last decade has been amyloid-first: amyloid-β accumulates, tau spreads, neurons die. The vascular story ran in parallel and in second place: the blood–brain barrier breaks down, toxic blood proteins leak in, and neuroinflammation accelerates decline. The leak story has real human evidence — Montagne et al. (Neuron, 2015) showed BBB breakdown in the aging human hippocampus, worsening with mild cognitive impairment — and it shaped drug design: if the barrier leaks, then either seal it, or exploit the leak.

The Cell paper of 11 November 2026 changes the sequence. Zhou and colleagues, led by Andrew C. Yang at the Gladstone Institutes and UCSF, mapped for the first time which circulating proteins actually cross an intact BBB. The result is a supply line, not a fortress: of 861 tracked plasma proteins, the healthy BBB samples 191 and admits 92 into the parenchyma, most of them made in distant organs — predominantly the liver — and each routed to a specific brain cell type by a molecular "ZIP code". The headline protein is APOA1, the main protein of high-density lipoprotein, made in the liver, crossing via the scavenger receptor SR-B1 and engaging astrocytic ABCA1 to drive cholesterol efflux and maintain synaptic density. The second is SERPINA1 (alpha-1 antitrypsin), routed to microglia. In early 5xFAD mice the transport system remodels first — APOA1 import falls, SERPINA1 import rises — while the barrier is still physically intact. Only later does the anatomy collapse and leak begin. And the causal arrow was tested, not merely observed: engineering the liver to overexpress human APOA1 raised brain APOA1 and rescued astrocytic, synaptic and behavioural deficits in the Alzheimer's mice.

Two independent November 2026 findings converge on the same picture from the immune side. Walsh et al. (Journal of Experimental Medicine, 2026) showed that CASS4, an Alzheimer's risk gene, controls microglial focal-adhesion biology: when CASS4 is ablated in 5xFAD mice, microglia fail to surround and compact amyloid plaques, amyloid load rises, and neurons near plaques are damaged. The brain's two defences — the vascular supply line and the microglial containment crew — are both gene-linked, both fail early, and both are peripheral in origin (liver proteins; a risk gene acting through immune cells). A third November finding, the APOE Christchurch (R136S) variant protecting against α-synuclein accumulation in mice (Soto-Faguás et al., Cell Reports, 2026; covered in our 13 November paper), points the same way: the lipid-transport axis, not the neuron alone, gates proteinopathy.

This paper does three things the Cell paper does not. First, it quantifies why APOA1's route matters for drug design: a 30.8 kDa protein cannot diffuse across the BBB, so any therapy that mimics or restores this supply line must use a receptor, and we rank the available receptor routes. Second, it tests the import-first model against the existing human record — the Amsterdam Dementia Cohort — and shows exactly where that record is ambiguous, turning the ambiguity into a specified, falsifiable human test. Third, it states the policy consequence for a low-resource health system: a blood test (plasma APOA1) is orders of magnitude cheaper than amyloid PET, and if import failure precedes amyloid positivity, the cheapest early-detection tool in dementia may already be sitting in a routine lipid panel.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

The literature sweep for this paper was conducted on 18 November 2026. Note on sources: the daily research digest series ends at 14 November 2026 (the digest job was disabled on 14 November), so no fresh digest existed for this run; the sweep therefore used targeted checks instead — PubMed E-utilities (entry-date windows 15–18 November 2026), Crossref verification of the Cell DOI, and a news sweep of neuroscience reporting for 9–17 November 2026, which surfaced the Cell atlas, the CASS4 paper and the TXP1 shuttle announcement. Every citation below was verified against PubMed, Crossref or the publisher's record on the day of writing; no citation is taken from memory. The Islamic canon leg used the verified literature map in the programme files (Ibn Sina, Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, c. 1025; Al-Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, c. 1096–1106; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, d. 1388), consulted through that map and secondary literature — the full Arabic text of the Canon was not re-read for this paper, and this is stated as a limitation.

2.2 Protein-size computation (own analysis)

Human APOA1 was retrieved from UniProt (accession P02647, reviewed entry APOA1_HUMAN) via the UniProt REST API on 18 November 2026. Recorded: 267 amino acids, molecular weight 30,778 Da (precursor; the mature circulating form is 243 amino acids, ~28.1 kDa). The passive BBB diffusion limit used is the standard CNS-likeness cut-off of 450 Da (the same criterion applied to GLP-1 receptor agonists in our 2 November paper). Ratio computed as 30,778 / 450 = 68.4. Import fractions were computed from the Cell paper's reported counts: 92 / 861 = 10.7% admitted; 191 / 861 = 22.2% sampled.

2.3 Analysis plan (stated before results)

The plan was fixed before the Results were written: (i) verify the Cell atlas and its numbers against Crossref and the published abstract; (ii) compute APOA1's size against the passive-diffusion cut-off; (iii) retrieve the best human APOA1–AD cohort study and record its effect sizes with confidence intervals, without selecting for a favourable direction; (iv) rank brain-delivery strategies by demonstrated brain gain, labelling company announcements as such; (v) state the falsifiable claim and its falsifier. No post-hoc analysis was added after seeing the results; the comparison with the Nov 2 GLP-1 paper was pre-planned as the "strongest incumbent" test.

2.4 Honesty limits

This is a literature-synthesis and computational-descriptor study plus a proposed test design. No new patient data, no animal data and no new laboratory measurements are presented. The Cell results are mouse results (5xFAD, a familial amyloid model); the human evidence is observational. The TXP1 figure is a company announcement, not a peer-reviewed result. The paper's claim is therefore narrow: the import-first ordering is established in mice and compatible with — not proven by — the human record, and the human test is specified here, not claimed as done.

3. Results

3.1 The atlas: a selective import system, not a wall

Zhou et al. (Cell, 2026; DOI 10.1016/j.cell.2026.10.039; 30 authors) used bioorthogonal click-chemistry labelling to tag the mouse plasma proteome and trace which proteins reach the brain parenchyma. The counts are the paper's core quantitative result:

Step Proteins (of 861 tracked) Share
Sampled by the BBB 191 22.2%
Admitted into brain parenchyma 92 10.7%
Excluded 769 89.3%

The 92 are enriched for carrier and metabolic functions and are mostly synthesised outside the nervous system, predominantly in the liver. They do not diffuse randomly: each homes to a designated cell type. APOA1 → astrocytes; SERPINA1 → microglia. The routing is receptor-mediated — a "BBB–parenchyma receptor hand-off": APOA1 crosses via SR-B1 (scavenger receptor class B type 1) and engages astrocytic ABCA1 (ATP-binding cassette transporter A1), which the Cell paper identifies as a key Alzheimer's risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity.

Our computation. Human APOA1 (UniProt P02647) is 267 amino acids, 30,778 Da as a precursor (≈28.1 kDa mature). Against the 450 Da passive-diffusion cut-off, it is 68 times too large to cross passively. This is not a marginal miss: it is the same order of magnitude as the GLP-1 peptides in our 2 November paper (8–11× over the cut-off, 0 of 4 CNS criteria met). The consequence is categorical — APOA1's brain entry must be active transport — and it reframes the drug-design question. A therapy that restores the APOA1 supply line cannot be a small molecule that diffuses; it must either raise the liver's own production (as the mouse experiment did), or ride a receptor (SR-B1, transferrin receptor, or an equivalent shuttle).

3.2 The ordering: import failure first, leak second

The decisive finding is temporal. In early-stage 5xFAD mice, the BBB shows selective transport remodelling — reduced APOA1 uptake and increased SERPINA1 uptake — while tight junctions are intact and there is no nonspecific leakage (contrast with lipopolysaccharide-induced leakage, which the paper used as a control). The sequence the paper establishes is:

  1. Early import shutdown. The barrier stops importing neuroprotective proteins, notably liver-derived APOA1, before it physically degrades.
  2. Synaptic erosion. Starved of peripheral signals, astrocytes fail to maintain synaptic integrity: dendritic spine loss, circuit dysfunction, early behavioural deficits.
  3. Late barrier breakdown. Only after prolonged transport starvation does the anatomical structure collapse, permitting toxic peripheral influx (the albumin/fibrinogen leak described by Montagne et al., Neuron, 2015, in the aging human hippocampus).

The causal test in mice: hepatic overexpression of human APOA1 raised circulating APOA1, increased brain APOA1, and rescued astrocytic, synaptic and behavioural deficits in 5xFAD mice. The authors' own summary is that "Alzheimer's disease may not start entirely inside the brain; it may start when the brain's supply line from the body is severed."

3.3 The human record: compatible, ambiguous, and therefore testable

The best human study of APOA1 in pre-dementia is Slot et al. (Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, 2017; PMID 28035918; DOI 10.3233/JAD-151068), from the Amsterdam Dementia Cohort: 429 non-demented elderly (206 with subjective cognitive decline, 223 with mild cognitive impairment), mean follow-up 2.5 ± 1.6 years, 117 (27%) showing clinical progression. Adjusted Cox models (age, sex, MMSE, plasma cholesterol) found:

Measure Effect on clinical progression 95% CI
CSF APOA1, per 1 SD increase HR 1.3 1.0–1.6
Lower plasma APOA1, APOE ε4 carriers with subjective cognitive decline HR 5.0 1.3–18.9

The pattern — low plasma APOA1 predicting progression, high CSF APOA1 also predicting progression — is compatible with the import-first model (a failing import gradient: less arriving from plasma, more retained or produced intrathecally), but it is equally compatible with early leak (plasma proteins entering CSF through a degrading barrier). The study cannot distinguish the two mechanisms, because it did not measure leak (no gadolinium MRI) and did not measure import (no CSF:plasma ratio tracked against amyloid-PET timing). That ambiguity is precisely what our proposed test resolves (Section 4.3). Note also the width of the second confidence interval (1.3–18.9): the APOE ε4 subgroup estimate is imprecise, and we report it as such rather than as a precise "five-fold risk".

3.4 The second defence fails in parallel: CASS4 and microglial containment

Walsh et al. (Journal of Experimental Medicine, 2026; 223(12):e20260104; DOI 10.1084/jem.20260104; first author Adeline E. Walsh, senior author John Lukens, University of Virginia) established the function of CASS4, previously only a GWAS risk signal. CASS4 controls microglial focal-adhesion biology: when CASS4 is ablated in 5xFAD mice, microglia fail to gather around amyloid plaques and compact them, plaques grow and spread more aggressively, nearby nerve fibres are damaged, and the mice show cognitive decline. Microglia-specific deletion reproduces the effect. This matters for the import-first model in two ways. First, SERPINA1 — the protein whose import rises in early 5xFAD — homes to microglia, the very cells whose containment function CASS4 controls; the import remodelling and the containment failure are two faces of one early immune-vascular failure, not two separate stories. Second, it gives the model a second falsifiable handle: if import restoration rescues synapses but plaques still spread because microglial containment is independently broken, the therapy must fix both arms.

3.5 Re-ranking brain-delivery strategies against the import-first model

The strongest incumbent against which to judge any new delivery strategy is the current standard: anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab), which must cross the BBB from the blood, do so at roughly 0.1% of the plasma dose, and carry amyloid-related imaging abnormality (ARIA) risk. The import-first model re-ranks the alternatives:

Strategy Mechanism Demonstrated brain gain Status
Hepatic APOA1 raising Restore the endogenous supply line (liver → SR-B1 → astrocyte) Rescues astrocytic, synaptic, behavioural deficits in 5xFAD mice (Zhou et al., 2026) Mouse, interventional
Transferrin-receptor shuttle (TXP1) Receptor-mediated transcytosis via TfR1 >65-fold increase in antibody brain delivery in preclinical studies incl. non-human primates Company announcement, 17 Nov 2026 (ProMIS/Ossianix) — not peer-reviewed
Peptide GLP-1 receptor agonists Passive diffusion (intended) 0 of 4 CNS-likeness criteria; no demonstrated CNS target engagement (our 2 Nov 2026 paper) Failed in phase III (Exenatide-PD3)
Leak-sealing (pericyte/tight-junction repair) Fix the late leak Targets the third step of the sequence Conceptually late
Anti-amyloid antibodies Cross BBB, clear plaque ~0.1% brain entry; modest slowing, ARIA risk Approved, incumbent

The ranking is the paper's practical contribution: strategies that use a receptor (endogenous SR-B1 or an engineered TfR1 shuttle) align with how the brain actually receives proteins; strategies that rely on passive diffusion or on sealing a leak that appears late do not. The TXP1 figure (>65-fold) is the largest delivery gain reported in this window, but it is a company-reported preclinical number and must be treated as a claim to verify, not a fact — the paper's ranking holds even if TXP1's true gain is far smaller, because the endogenous APOA1 route is already demonstrated in mice.

4. Discussion

4.1 Mechanism: the supply-line model

The mechanism we propose, synthesising Zhou et al., Walsh et al. and the human cohort data, has four links, each with a test:

  1. Liver → blood. Hepatocytes secrete APOA1 into plasma. Test: plasma APOA1 concentration tracks liver synthetic function; liver disease should predict faster cognitive decline (an existing, testable epidemiological prediction).
  2. Blood → brain. SR-B1 mediates APOA1 transcytosis across the BBB endothelium; astrocytic ABCA1 receives it and drives cholesterol efflux that maintains synaptic density. Test: endothelial SR-B1 deletion should reproduce the synaptic phenotype without any amyloid manipulation.
  3. Import failure → synaptic erosion. In early AD, transport remodels (APOA1 down, SERPINA1 up) before leak; astrocytes starved of APOA1 fail to maintain spines. Test: the longitudinal human cohort specified in Section 4.3.
  4. Parallel immune failure. SERPINA1's microglial target and CASS4-dependent microglial containment fail together; plaques spread because the containment crew is impaired, not only because amyloid is overproduced. Test: combined APOA1 restoration + CASS4 boosting should outperform either alone in 5xFAD mice.

4.2 The Islamic canon as hypothesis ancestor

The supply-line model has a genuine ancestor in the Islamic medical tradition, and the programme's rule is to name it rather than to claim it as proof. Ibn Sina's Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (Canon of Medicine, c. 1025) organised medicine around interacting organ systems and faculties: the liver as the seat of the natural faculty, producing the blood and nourishment on which the other organs depend, and the brain as the seat of the psychic faculty — sensation, imagination and reason. In that framework a disease of the brain can originate in the failure of a distant organ's supply, and treatment can act on the supplying organ rather than the suffering one. That is the structure of the Zhou et al. experiment — treat the liver, rescue the brain — stated nine centuries earlier as a system, not as a molecule. Al-Ghazali's Ihya Ulum al-Din (c. 1096–1106) makes the same structural point in moral psychology: the heart (qalb) rules the body, but its rule depends on the soundness of its members; a failure in one member corrupts the whole. Neither work proves anything about APOA1 — proof comes from the mouse and the cohort — but both show that the "brain disease as whole-body supply failure" framing is not a modern invention, and that the classical canon is a legitimate source of hypotheses, which is exactly how this programme uses it. The policy principle that follows is hifz al-nafs, preservation of life, one of the five objectives (maqasid) of the Shariah as defined by Al-Ghazali in Al-Mustasfa and systematised by Al-Shatibi in Al-Muwafaqat (d. 1388): a health system must preserve life by the most effective available means, and where a cheap blood test can detect a lethal disease earlier than an expensive scan, choosing the scan-first pathway fails that objective. The body as a trust (amanah, under the stewardship of khilafah, Qur'an 2:30) reinforces the same point: the liver–brain supply line is a trust to maintain, not a resource to exhaust.

4.3 The human test that would settle it (pre-specified design)

Design. A prospective longitudinal cohort of cognitively unimpaired adults aged 60–75 with a first-degree family history of AD or APOE ε4 carriership (n ≈ 1,000; powered on the Slot et al. progression rate of 27% over 2.5 years). At baseline and annually for 5 years: plasma APOA1, CSF APOA1 (CSF:plasma ratio as the import index), amyloid PET, and dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI for BBB leak (Ktrans). Primary analysis: does the CSF:plasma APOA1 ratio fall before amyloid-PET positivity, and does it predict clinical progression independently of amyloid? Falsifier: if the ratio does not fall before amyloid positivity, or if Ktrans leak precedes the ratio fall, the import-first ordering is refuted in humans. Therapeutic test (phase II, contingent on the cohort result): a randomised trial of a liver-targeted APOA1-raising intervention (e.g. an APOA1 mimetic peptide or a hepatocyte-targeted therapy) versus placebo in preclinical AD, with brain APOA1 (CSF) as the target-engagement readout and tau-PET spread as the outcome. Falsifier: if brain APOA1 rises without slowing tau spread, the disease-modifying version of the claim is refuted, and APOA1 remains a biomarker only. Either outcome is publishable; the design is written before the data exist, which is the point.

4.4 What this paper does not claim

It does not claim APOA1 therapy works in humans — no human interventional data exist. It does not claim the 92-protein atlas is complete in humans — it is a mouse atlas, and the human BBB proteome may differ. It does not claim plasma APOA1 alone diagnoses AD — the Slot et al. hazard ratios are modest and, in the APOE ε4 subgroup, imprecise. And it does not claim the classical Islamic physicians anticipated APOA1 — they anticipated the structure of the explanation, which is a different and smaller claim, stated as such.

5. Limitations

  1. Mouse-to-human gap. The atlas and the rescue experiment are in 5xFAD mice, a familial amyloid model that does not reproduce sporadic human AD (no tau tangles, no human aging vasculature). The import-first ordering is established in mice; in humans it is a hypothesis with a specified test, not a finding.
  2. The human evidence is observational and ambiguous. Slot et al. (2017) is a cohort study: association only. The low-plasma/high-CSF APOA1 pattern fits import failure and leak, and the APOE ε4 subgroup estimate (HR 5.0, 95% CI 1.3–18.9) is imprecise. No human study has yet measured import and leak in the same participants over time.
  3. The TXP1 figure is unverified. The >65-fold delivery gain is a company announcement (ProMIS Neurosciences / Ossianix, 17 November 2026), not a peer-reviewed result; it is used here as a directional claim, and the paper's ranking does not depend on it.
  4. The atlas is a snapshot, not a census. 861 proteins were tracked; the plasma proteome is larger, and the 92-protein set is a lower bound on import, not a complete inventory. Human BBB transport may route the same proteins differently.
  5. Classical canon consulted second-hand. The Islamic works cited (Ibn Sina's Canon, Al-Ghazali's Ihya, Al-Shatibi's Al-Muwafaqat) were consulted through the programme's verified canon map and secondary literature, not by a fresh full-text reading of the Arabic originals. The full 23-volume Kitab al-Hawi of Al-Razi exists in English only in selections, and Ibn al-Nafis's Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun (the pulmonary-circulation commentary) survives in English only in partial translation; most classical Arabic manuscripts remain undigitised in libraries (Süleymaniye, Istanbul; Dar al-Kutub, Cairo; the British Library) with no online copy. These gaps are named, not hidden.
  6. No effect size for the mouse rescue. The Cell paper's abstract reports rescue of astrocytic, synaptic and behavioural deficits without a single headline effect size; we therefore report the rescue qualitatively and do not invent a number for it.
  7. Publication-bias risk in the November window. Both anchor papers appeared within eight days of this writing (10–11 November 2026); independent replication of the atlas has not yet had time to occur, and the history of BBB research (e.g. the Ontario checklist null replication cited in our method brief) warns that single-centre findings can shrink on replication.

6. Policy implications

Decision-makers: the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations & Coordination (Pakistan), through the National Institute of Health (NIH) Islamabad; and the Higher Education Commission (HEC) for research funding. Exact changes, in order:

  1. Add the plasma/CSF APOA1 ratio to the national dementia cohort protocol as a pre-amyloid early-detection marker, alongside — not instead of — amyloid testing, with the CSF:plasma ratio recorded as the import index. Cost: a routine immunoassay, orders of magnitude cheaper than amyloid PET, which is effectively unavailable outside a few centres in Pakistan.
  2. Fund a liver-targeted APOA1 pilot before funding another leak-sealing trial. Until the human import-first test (Section 4.3) reports, public research money should prioritise the earlier step in the causal chain. If the cohort falsifies import-first, reverse this prioritisation — the falsifier is written into the policy, not added later.
  3. Require target-engagement evidence for publicly funded CNS drug trials: any central-nervous-system drug seeking HEC/NIH funding must show a CSF:plasma ratio or equivalent brain-exposure measure, so that no trial repeats the error documented in our 2 November paper — testing a drug that never reached its target.

Islamic principle: hifz al-nafs (preservation of life), one of the five maqasid al-shariah (Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat), with maslaha (public interest) as the balancing test: the policy counts benefit to the poor and the unborn, not only to those who can reach a PET scanner. Where the modern evidence and the classical principle point the same way — detect early, treat the supplying organ, spend public money on the earliest causal step — we say so; where they diverge, the evidence governs the science and the principle governs the spending priority, and both are stated.

7. Conclusion

The blood–brain barrier is not a wall that fails by leaking. It is a supply line that fails by closing: of 861 plasma proteins, only 92 (10.7%) are admitted, and in early Alzheimer's models the admission of liver-derived APOA1 stops before any leak begins. APOA1 is 68 times too large to cross passively, so its entry — and any therapy that restores it — must use a receptor. Restoring the liver's supply rescued the mouse brain. The human record is compatible with this story but cannot yet distinguish import failure from leak, and the paper specifies the cohort that would. The memorable number is 10.7%: the brain admits one protein in ten from the blood, and Alzheimer's may begin the day that gate starts to close. If the human test confirms it, the cheapest early-detection tool in dementia is already in a routine blood sample, and the most promising therapy may be one that treats the liver to save the brain.

One variant, two proteinopathies: APOE Christchurch (R136S) as a heparan-sulfate-gated brake on tau and α-synuclein seeding — a structural hypothesis and a testable therapeutic programme
