AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 13 November 2026 · Field: Brain (neuroscience) · Paper: Brain #5

Abstract

Background. APOE is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, and a rare variant — APOE3 Christchurch (APOE3ch, R136S) — protected a PSEN1 E280A carrier from dementia for roughly 28 years despite extensive amyloid deposition. Until November 2026 the protection was understood as a tau story: R136S weakens apolipoprotein E (ApoE) binding to heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs), limiting tau spread. New evidence. Soto-Faguás and colleagues (Cell Reports, 11 November 2026) now report that the Christchurch mutation engineered into mouse ApoE also prevents the accumulation of α-synuclein — the protein of Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia — in predisposed mice, with the senior author describing it as acting "like a super-APOE-2". Hypothesis. We propose a single shared mechanism: tau and α-synuclein seeds both enter neurons through the same HSPG gateway, and R136S closes that gateway for both. We test the structural premise on the real human sequence (UniProt P02649): residues 136–150 form a cationic cluster (Arg136, Arg142, Lys143, Arg145, Lys146, Arg147, Arg150) carrying a net charge of +7; R136S removes one positive charge (+7 → +6) and shifts the N-terminal domain net charge to −4 — the same value as protective APOE2, versus −2 for risk-conferring APOE4. Falsifiable claim. If the shared-gateway model is correct, recombinant ApoE3ch will reduce α-synuclein preformed-fibril uptake into primary neurons by a comparable fraction to its reduction of tau uptake, and any Christchurch-mimetic that occupies the ApoE HSPG-binding pocket will inhibit α-synuclein seeding as well as tau seeding. We specify the experiments, effect-size expectations, and the observations that would falsify the model. Conclusion. One rare variant may define one druggable gateway for two diseases — and, because women with Parkinson's disease dementia carry a substantially higher amyloid co-pathology burden, the benefit of closing that gateway should be tested with sex-stratified analysis.

Keywords

APOE Christchurch; R136S; heparan sulfate proteoglycan; tau propagation; alpha-synuclein; Parkinson's disease; Alzheimer's disease; prion-like seeding

1. Introduction

Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease are clinically distinct and pathologically overlapping. Alzheimer's is defined by amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques and tau tangles; Parkinson's by α-synuclein Lewy pathology. Yet mixed pathology is the rule, not the exception: most brains with Lewy pathology also carry amyloid, and most Alzheimer's brains carry some Lewy pathology. Treatments aimed at one protein have repeatedly left the other untouched. A therapy that acted on a mechanism shared by both seeds would therefore be worth far more than a therapy aimed at either protein alone.

APOE is the natural place to look for such a mechanism. The APOE ε4 allele is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, and ApoE is increasingly implicated in Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia as well. The decisive clue came from a single patient: a Colombian woman carrying the fully penetrant PSEN1 E280A mutation for early-onset Alzheimer's disease, who remained cognitively intact into her seventies because she was homozygous for a rare APOE variant, APOE3 Christchurch (R136S) (Arboleda-Velasquez et al., 2019). Her brain carried extremely high Aβ pathology but minimal tau burden, minimal hippocampal atrophy and minimal neuroinflammation (Nelson et al., 2023). A single amino-acid change — arginine to serine at position 136 — had apparently uncoupled amyloid from tau.

Two mechanistic studies then pinned down the tau arm. Nelson et al. (2023) engineered R136S into the APOE4 background in knock-in mice and in human induced pluripotent stem cells from an APOE4-homozygous Alzheimer's patient, and showed protection against APOE4-driven tau pathology, neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation; a major functional effect of R136S is disruption of ApoE binding to anionic HSPGs on the cell surface. Chen et al. (2025) showed that ApoE3 R136S binds tau more strongly than wild-type ApoE3, reduces tau uptake into neurons and microglia, suppresses asparagine endopeptidase (AEP) activation and tau N368 fragmentation, and attenuates tau preformed-fibril (PFF) spreading in both 5xFAD and Tau P301S mice, with improved cognition. The tau story was, by 2025, mechanistically coherent: R136S weakens the ApoE–HSPG interaction, and HSPGs are essential co-factors for cellular uptake of tau seeds (Holmes et al., 2013).

What was missing was the second proteinopathy. On 11 November 2026, Soto-Faguás and colleagues reported in Cell Reports that the Christchurch mutation, engineered into mouse ApoE, protects against Aβ-induced tau aggregation — and, for the first time, against α-synuclein aggregation in mice predisposed to accumulate it (Soto-Faguás et al., 2026). Senior author Vivek Unni (Oregon Health & Science University) described the variant as acting "like a super-APOE-2", and raised gene therapy based on the Christchurch mutation as a route to forestall cognitive and motor impairment in Parkinson's disease and related conditions. The result is striking, but the mechanism for the α-synuclein arm is untested: reduced accumulation in vivo does not by itself show reduced seed uptake.

This paper makes the missing connection explicit and testable. We synthesise the tau and α-synuclein uptake literatures, add an original sequence-level analysis of the human ApoE HSPG-binding cluster, and derive a falsifiable shared-gateway model with a concrete experimental programme — including a prediction about who should benefit most, grounded in a second November 2026 finding: women with Parkinson's disease dementia carry a substantially higher burden of Alzheimer's amyloid co-pathology than men (Dunckley et al., 2026).

2. Methods

2.1 Literature sweep

We swept the daily research digest for 13 November 2026 (PubMed E-utilities entry-date window, arXiv q-bio, bioRxiv, 627 candidates screened) and ran targeted PubMed searches for APOE Christchurch, HSPG-mediated seed uptake, and α-synuclein internalisation. Every citation in this paper was verified against PubMed (PMID) or the publisher's DOI on 13 November 2026; no citation is invented. One cited item is a preprint (Research Square) and is labelled as such. Quantitative figures attributed to Dunckley et al. (2026) are taken from the Mayo Clinic news release of 6 November 2026 reporting that study, as the underlying article's full text was not yet accessible at the time of writing.

2.2 Sequence and charge analysis (original computation)

The human ApoE sequence was retrieved live from UniProt (accession P02649, 317-amino-acid precursor) on 13 November 2026. The mature protein (residues 19–317 of the precursor, 299 amino acids) was used, with literature numbering throughout (mature-protein numbering, so that R136S, C112R and R158C refer to the positions used in the cited papers). Net charge was computed with the rule: lysine and arginine +1, aspartate and glutamate −1, histidine 0 at neutral pH. We computed, for APOE2, APOE3, APOE4 and APOE3ch (R136S): (i) the sequence and net charge of the receptor-binding / HSPG-binding region, residues 136–150; (ii) the net charge of the wider 130–150 window; (iii) the net charge of the N-terminal domain (residues 1–191); and (iv) the net charge of the full mature protein. The script and its output are archived with this paper's working files. No structural modelling was performed: this is a sequence-level analysis, and its limits are stated in Section 6.

2.3 Hypothesis construction

The hypothesis was built by requiring that each of its three legs be independently established in the peer-reviewed literature before the synthesis was drawn: (a) R136S weakens ApoE–HSPG binding; (b) tau seed uptake is HSPG-dependent; (c) α-synuclein fibril uptake is HSPG-dependent. The synthesis — that R136S therefore gates both seeds — is the new claim, and Section 5 states how to test it and what would falsify it.

3. Results

3.1 The three legs are each established

Leg A — R136S weakens ApoE–HSPG binding. The receptor-binding region of ApoE (residues 136–150) is enriched in positively charged amino acids and binds negatively charged cell-surface receptors including HSPGs (Nelson et al., 2023). The R136S substitution disrupts that binding, and ApoE also recognises the Alzheimer's-associated 3-O-sulfation of heparan sulfate; knocking out the 3-O-sulfotransferase HS3ST1 reduces ApoE cell-surface binding and uptake (Mah et al., 2023).

Leg B — tau seed uptake is HSPG-dependent. Holmes et al. (2013) showed that HSPGs mediate the internalisation and propagation of specific proteopathic seeds, including tau. Chen et al. (2025) showed the functional consequence for the Christchurch variant: ApoE3 R136S binds tau more strongly than wild-type, reduces its uptake into neurons and microglia via the receptor LRP1, and attenuates tau PFF spreading in vivo.

Leg C — α-synuclein fibril uptake is HSPG-dependent. Ihse et al. (2017) showed that internalisation of α-synuclein amyloid fibrils in neuroblastoma cells depends on heparan sulfate, as does uptake in an oligodendrocyte-like line, while soluble non-amyloid oligomers do not depend on it and astrocyte- and microglia-like lines use other routes; soluble heparin (20 µg/ml) competitively reduced uptake. Zhang et al. (2020) identified the pathway genetically: a CRISPR screen found SLC35B2, a regulator of HSPG biosynthesis, and myosin-7B (MYO7B) to be critical for α-synuclein PFF entry, with fibrils binding HSPGs through clustered K-T-K motifs and entering by clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Vanderperre et al. (2025) confirmed the axis with new regulators: deletion of SLC39A9 or C3orf58 impaired α-synuclein PFF binding and uptake, and C3orf58-knockout human iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons and microglia showed a strong reduction in PFF internalisation.

The new result. Soto-Faguás et al. (2026) close the loop in vivo: mice predisposed to accumulate tau or α-synuclein did not accumulate either protein when the Christchurch mutation was present in ApoE. The α-synuclein arm had no established mechanism; legs A–C supply one.

3.2 Original analysis: R136S removes exactly one positive charge from the HSPG-binding cluster

Table 1 gives the sequence-level result. The 136–150 cluster of APOE3 reads RLASHLRKLRKRLLR: seven basic residues (Arg136, Arg142, Lys143, Arg145, Lys146, Arg147, Arg150) and a net charge of +7 — the cationic surface that grips anionic heparan sulfate. R136S changes the first residue to serine (SLASHLRKLRKRLLR), leaving six basic residues and a net charge of +6. The wider 130–150 window falls from +6 to +5. Notably, APOE4 and APOE2 carry a 136–150 window identical to APOE3 (+7): their isoform-defining substitutions sit elsewhere (C112R for APOE4, R158C for APOE2), so the Christchurch change is the only one of the four that alters the HSPG-binding cluster itself.

Variant Residues 136–150 Basic residues Net charge 136–150 Net charge 130–150 N-terminal domain (1–191) Full mature protein
APOE3 RLASHLRKLRKRLLR 7 +7 +6 −3 −5
APOE3ch (R136S) SLASHLRKLRKRLLR 6 +6 +5 −4 −6
APOE4 RLASHLRKLRKRLLR 7 +7 +6 −2 −4
APOE2 RLASHLRKLRKRLLR 7 +7 +6 −4 −6

A second pattern emerges from the same computation and is reported here as an observation, not a proof: the two protective variants converge on the same N-terminal-domain net charge (−4 for both APOE3ch and APOE2), while neutral APOE3 is −3 and risk-conferring APOE4 is −2. Charge alone cannot explain protection — APOE2 reaches −4 through R158C, outside the HSPG-binding motif, while APOE3ch reaches it through R136S, inside the motif — so position, not just charge, matters. But the convergence is consistent with a model in which reduced electrostatic engagement with anionic surfaces is part of the protective phenotype, and it yields a quantitative prediction: a Christchurch-mimetic need only remove or mask roughly one positive charge-equivalent from the 136–150 cluster to reproduce the variant's electrostatic profile.

3.3 Who carries the most mixed pathology: the sex difference

Dunckley et al. (2026) examined brain tissue from 230 people with Parkinson's disease (74 women, 156 men) in the Arizona Study of Aging and Neurodegenerative Disorders and Brain and Body Donation Program. Women had a higher mean amyloid plaque score than men (6.5 versus 4.9 out of 15); 56.8% of women versus 39.7% of men had an elevated amyloid plaque burden; and after accounting for age at death, APOE ε4 status and Lewy body levels, women had more than twice the odds of elevated amyloid burden. There was no significant sex difference in tau buildup, and the sexes had similar rates of clinically diagnosed dementia. The implication for a dual-proteinopathy therapy is direct: the population with the heaviest mixed amyloid-plus-Lewy burden — women with Parkinson's disease dementia — is the population in which a therapy that gates both seeds should show the largest absolute benefit, and in which it should therefore be tested first and analysed separately.

3.4 A Christchurch-mimetic already exists on paper

A structure-guided docking study (Research Square preprint) targeted the ApoE HSPG-binding pocket with benzene-1,3-disulfonic acid, a small anionic molecule resembling sulfated glycosaminoglycans, reporting a top docking score of −5.93 kcal/mol and an estimated inhibition constant (Ki) of 44.6 µM. The authors propose it as a candidate Christchurch mimetic. It is a preprint, not peer-reviewed, and its pharmacokinetics preclude systemic use as reported — but it demonstrates that the pocket is druggable in silico, and it gives the shared-gateway model an immediate, concrete test compound.

4. Discussion

The shared-gateway model. The three legs and the new in-vivo result fit one mechanism. Tau and α-synuclein are different proteins with different sequences, but as amyloid fibrils they present the same kind of surface to the cell: clustered positive charges (K-T-K motifs in α-synuclein PFFs) that bind the negatively charged sulfate groups of HSPGs. ApoE sits at that gateway twice over: it binds HSPGs through its 136–150 cationic cluster, and (for tau at least) it binds the seed itself. R136S weakens the ApoE–HSPG interaction and, per Chen et al. (2025), strengthens ApoE–tau binding while reducing seed uptake — ApoE3ch appears to sequester tau away from the uptake machinery rather than escorting it in. If the same holds for α-synuclein, one substitution gates two seeds. That is the falsifiable claim of this paper.

Why the α-synuclein arm is not yet proven. Soto-Faguás et al. (2026) show reduced α-synuclein accumulation in vivo. Accumulation is the net result of production, uptake, templating and clearance; the experiment does not isolate uptake. It is possible that the α-synuclein protection works through a different route — for example, altered microglial handling, since ApoE3ch also reduces microglial activation (Chen et al., 2025), or reduced AEP activation, which cleaves both APP and tau. The shared-gateway model predicts a specific, separable effect — reduced neuronal uptake of α-synuclein PFFs — that can be tested without any new mouse line.

Cell-type limits. Ihse et al. (2017) found that astrocyte- and microglia-like cells internalise α-synuclein fibrils by means other than heparan sulfate. The model therefore predicts neuronal and oligodendroglial protection primarily, not a blanket block of all fibril uptake. That is a feature, not a flaw: microglial clearance of seeds is desirable, and a therapy that spares it while blocking neuronal uptake would be preferable to one that blocks both. Any mimetic should be screened for this selectivity.

Therapeutic routes. Three routes follow from the model, in order of tractability: (i) small-molecule Christchurch mimetics that occupy the ApoE HSPG-binding pocket, exemplified by the benzene-1,3-disulfonic acid scaffold (−5.93 kcal/mol; Ki 44.6 µM, preprint) — intranasal delivery or ligand optimisation would be needed for brain exposure; (ii) ApoE-derived peptides spanning residues 130–150 carrying the R136S substitution, as competitive inhibitors of seed uptake; (iii) APOE Christchurch gene therapy, already envisaged by the OHSU group and conceptually supported by APOE2 gene-therapy programmes in development — the longest and most expensive route, and the one requiring the most caution given that APOE is a lipid-transport protein with systemic roles. The charge analysis in Table 1 gives medicinal chemistry a quantitative target: reproduce the +7 → +6 shift in the 136–150 cluster, or the equivalent masking of one positive charge.

Sex-stratified testing. The Dunckley et al. (2026) finding reframes trial design. If a therapy gates both amyloid-driven tau seeding and α-synuclein seeding, its measurable benefit should scale with the burden of mixed pathology. Women with Parkinson's disease dementia carry more amyloid co-pathology (plaque score 6.5 vs 4.9; 56.8% vs 39.7% elevated burden; odds ratio > 2) at similar dementia rates — so a sex-stratified analysis is not a subgroup fishing expedition here; it is a pre-specified prediction of the model. The same logic applies to APOE ε4 carriers, in whom amyloid and tau co-pathology is heavier.

What would change our mind. The model stands or falls on the uptake experiments in Section 5. A negative result on prediction P1 would not invalidate the 2026 in-vivo finding, but it would force the mechanism elsewhere (clearance, AEP, or microglial handling) and would remove the rationale for HSPG-pocket mimetics against synucleinopathy specifically.

5. Falsifiable claim and how to test it

Claim. APOE Christchurch (R136S) protects against both tau and α-synuclein aggregation by one shared mechanism: weakening ApoE binding to HSPGs at the 136–150 cationic cluster, thereby reducing HSPG-dependent neuronal uptake of both proteopathic seeds. Consequently, any Christchurch-mimetic that disrupts the ApoE–HSPG interface will inhibit α-synuclein seeding as well as tau seeding.

Prediction P1 (uptake). In primary mouse or human iPSC-derived neurons, recombinant ApoE3ch will reduce uptake of fluorescently labelled α-synuclein PFFs by a comparable fraction to its reduction of tau PFF uptake, measured in matched assays (same cells, same fibril dose, same readout, e.g. pHrodo labelling with flow cytometry after 8–24 h, as in Ihse et al., 2017). Expected direction: reduction of at least 30% relative to wild-type ApoE3, mirroring the tau effect reported by Chen et al. (2025). Falsifier: ApoE3ch reduces tau PFF uptake but leaves α-synuclein PFF uptake unchanged (±10%) in the matched assay.

Prediction P2 (mimetic). Benzene-1,3-disulfonic acid, or an optimised analogue, will inhibit α-synuclein PFF uptake into neurons dose-dependently, with an inhibitory potency in the same order of magnitude as its inhibition of tau seeding (reported Ki 44.6 µM for the ApoE pocket; preprint). Falsifier: the compound blocks tau seeding but has no effect on α-synuclein PFF uptake at concentrations up to 10× its tau-seeding IC50.

Prediction P3 (in vivo, sex-stratified). In a mouse model of mixed pathology (e.g. 5xFAD crossed with an α-synuclein transgenic line) carrying the Christchurch-equivalent Apoe mutation, the reduction in α-synuclein pathology will be larger in females, tracking their higher amyloid burden; and in any future human study of an ApoE–HSPG disruptor, the absolute benefit on mixed-pathology endpoints will be larger in women with Parkinson's disease dementia than in men. Falsifier: no sex difference in the mouse cross, or a benefit confined to males.

Controls required. (i) Wild-type ApoE3 and ApoE4 arms in every uptake assay; (ii) an HSPG-deficient control (heparinase treatment or SLC35B2 knockdown) to confirm the uptake being measured is HSPG-dependent; (iii) a non-fibrillar α-synuclein oligomer arm, which Ihse et al. (2017) showed is not HSPG-dependent — the model predicts no ApoE3ch effect there, a useful negative control; (iv) microglial uptake measured in parallel, where the model predicts little or no effect.

6. Limitations

  1. The α-synuclein mechanism is inferred, not shown. The 2026 Cell Reports result is in mice, with the mutation engineered into mouse Apoe; human translation is unproven, and the in-vivo experiment does not isolate uptake from clearance or production.
  2. Sequence charge is a proxy. The +7 → +6 computation describes electrostatics, not binding free energy. Real ApoE–HSPG affinity depends on conformation, lipidation, 3-O-sulfation patterns (Mah et al., 2023), and the oligomeric state of ApoE. No docking or molecular dynamics was performed here.
  3. One preprint is cited. The benzene-1,3-disulfonic acid result (Research Square) is not peer-reviewed; its −5.93 kcal/mol score and 44.6 µM Ki are the authors' figures and have not been independently reproduced.
  4. Sex-difference figures come from a news release. The Dunckley et al. (2026) numbers (plaque scores, percentages, odds ratio) are taken from the Mayo Clinic release of 6 November 2026; the underlying article's full text was not accessible when this draft was written.
  5. Cell-type scope. The shared-gateway model applies to neuronal and oligodendroglial uptake; astrocytes and microglia use additional routes (Ihse et al., 2017), so the model does not predict a universal block of fibril uptake.
  6. APOE biology is pleiotropic. ApoE is a lipid-transport protein; disrupting its receptor interactions systemically could have off-target metabolic effects. Any mimetic or gene therapy must demonstrate that it spares ApoE's lipid-transport function.
  7. This is an AI-assisted draft. No experiment in Section 5 has been performed by the author; the paper is a hypothesis and a programme, not a report of results.

7. Conclusion

A single amino-acid change, R136S, protected one woman from a deterministic Alzheimer's mutation for roughly 28 years. Two years of mechanistic work explained the tau arm. The November 2026 extension to α-synuclein suggests the protection was never tau-specific: it was gateway-specific. Tau and α-synuclein seeds enter neurons through the same heparan sulfate gateway, and the Christchurch variant closes it for both — removing one positive charge from a seven-charge cluster, shifting the N-terminal domain to the same net charge as protective APOE2. That makes the ApoE–HSPG interface a single druggable target for two diseases, with a concrete test compound already docked in silico and a concrete experiment — matched tau versus α-synuclein uptake assays — that can falsify the idea within months. The first patients to test it in should include the people who carry the heaviest mixed pathology: women with Parkinson's disease dementia.

The Serotonin Dimmer: A Falsifiable Dip-and-Recovery Model of Visual Attention Across the First Six Weeks of SSRI Therapy

Serotonin has been known for a century as a mood chemical; its control of attention was not. Lehnert et al. Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 10 November 2026 · Paper #10 — Brain track (Daily Research Papers; 4th Brain-track paper)

Keywords: serotonin; dorsal raphe; visual attention; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; SSRI; 5-HT1A autoreceptor; attention gain; depression; falsifiable hypothesis

Abstract

Serotonin has been known for a century as a mood chemical; its control of attention was not. Lehnert et al. (Nature Communications 2026) showed that dorsal raphe serotonin neurons act as a gain control — a "dimmer switch" — on visual attention in mice: reducing serotonin activity improved detection of a faint visual target, increasing it impaired detection. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), the most widely prescribed psychiatric drugs, raise synaptic serotonin, yet the literature on their cognitive effects is contradictory: a 2018 meta-analysis of 33 studies found modest positive effects on attention in depressed patients and no effect in non-depressed participants, a 2024 fluoxetine review found the effects inconsistent and often negative in healthy animals, and a 6-week paediatric sertraline trial found no attention harm at all. We propose that these three findings are one time-course, not three contradictions. The serotonin-dimmer model states that acute elevation of serotonergic tone transiently lowers visual-attention sensitivity, and that chronic exposure restores it to or above baseline as 5-HT1A autoreceptors desensitise — predicting a measurable dip-and-recovery in attention (d′) over the first six weeks of SSRI therapy. We specify the falsifying experiment: a prospective cohort of drug-naïve depressed adults tested on a low-contrast visual search task at baseline and on days 3, 7, 14, 28 and 42, powered at n = 32 (38 with attrition) for a medium within-subject effect. If d′ does not dip in week 1, or does not recover by week 6, the model fails. This is a hypothesis and trial-design paper, not a treatment recommendation: no human attention data under SSRI initiation are presented.

1. Introduction

Everyone has moments of sharp focus and moments of drift, but the biology that sets the moment-to-moment strength of attention has remained poorly understood. Attention is usually described through its cortical machinery — frontal-parietal networks, theta oscillations that organise frontal-cortex communication (Broschard et al., 2026), and the coordinate-like maps the ventromedial prefrontal cortex uses to organise even emotional knowledge (Ma & Kragel, 2026). What has been missing is a chemical gain control: a signal that dials attention up or down without switching it on or off.

Lehnert et al. (2026) supplied one. Working at McGill, PhD student Jonas Lehnert trained mice to find a faint hidden visual target — the rodent analogue of picking a face out of a crowd — while recording and manipulating serotonin-producing neurons of the dorsal raphe nucleus. When serotonin activity was reduced, the mice focused better; when it was increased, they focused worse. The effect was graded, not binary, leading the authors (co-led by Arjun Krishnaswamy and Erik Cook) to describe dorsal raphe serotonin as a "dimmer switch" on attention. The authors explicitly caution that their precise, circuit-level manipulation differs from how serotonergic drugs act in people — and that caution is exactly where this paper starts.

SSRIs are the natural human test of the dimmer. They raise synaptic serotonin within hours, yet their therapeutic effect takes two to six weeks, and their cognitive effects are famously inconsistent. A meta-analysis of 33 studies (1998–2017) found that antidepressants modestly improve divided attention, executive function, immediate memory, processing speed, recent memory and sustained attention in depressed participants — with SSRIs showing the greatest positive effect — but found no significant cognitive effect in non-depressed participants (Prado et al., 2018). A 2024 review of fluoxetine found the picture "inconsistent and elusive": cognitive improvements in patients with underlying disorders, but negative effects in healthy, non-diseased animals, with outcomes depending on gender, treatment duration, age, disease and the test used (Ampuero et al., 2024). And a 6-week randomised trial of sertraline (25–100 mg/day) in 28 children and adolescents with anxiety found no negative effect on attention at all — divided-attention response speed even improved (p = 0.02) — while verbal-memory interference worsened (p = 0.05) (Günther et al., 2005, as cited below).

No study has yet tested attention on the time course the mechanism predicts. If serotonin is a dimmer, then the first days of SSRI therapy — when synaptic serotonin rises but autoreceptors have not yet adapted — should transiently worsen fine visual attention, and the following weeks should restore it. The literature's inconsistency is then not noise: it is the same curve sampled at different times, in different populations, with different tests. This paper formalises that curve, states the four predictions that would confirm or refute it, and designs the study that tests it.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

The literature sweep is the 2026-11-10 daily research digest (305 candidates screened: 50 PubMed, 0 arXiv q-bio, 255 bioRxiv; 8 selected — all antimicrobial-resistance or drug-discovery, none neuroscience) plus targeted searches on serotonin and attention, SSRI cognition, and November 2026 neuroscience. Every reference below was verified against its primary source on 10 November 2026: Lehnert et al. via Crossref (Nature Communications 2026, vol. 17, article 3464, published 18 March 2026; news coverage 9 November 2026) and the publisher's summary; Broschard et al. via Crossref and Cell Reports; Ma & Kragel via Crossref (PLOS Biology 2026, vol. 24, published 2 November 2026); Baker et al. via the Nature Neuroscience record (DOI 10.1038/s41593-026-02490-y); Kim et al. via NeuroImage; and the three SSRI-cognition sources via PubMed E-utilities (esummary article-IDs and DOIs). No unpublished, anecdotal or press-release-only efficacy claim is used as evidence; secondary reporting was used only to locate primary papers. This paper presents no new human data, no animal data and no simulation. Its results are a synthesis, a formal model, and a fully specified trial design.

2.2 The model (formal statement)

Let S(t) be effective serotonergic tone at the dorsal-raphe → visual-cortex pathway at time t after SSRI initiation, and A(t) be visual-attention sensitivity (signal-detection d′) on a low-contrast visual search task. The model asserts:

  1. Gain rule: A is a decreasing function of S over the physiological range (the dimmer), i.e. dA/dS < 0, for fine-discrimination tasks.
  2. Acute phase: S rises within days of SSRI initiation (reuptake blockade), before adaptation; therefore A dips in week 1.
  3. Adaptation phase: over 2–6 weeks, somatodendritic 5-HT1A autoreceptors desensitise, raphe firing recovers, and net serotonergic signalling normalises; therefore A recovers to baseline or above by week 6.
  4. Task specificity: the dip is largest for fine visual discrimination (low-contrast targets, as in Lehnert's task) and smallest or absent for simple sustained-attention tasks.

2.3 Proposed study (design, not a result)

Population: drug-naïve adults (18–55 years) with a new diagnosis of major depressive disorder, starting SSRI monotherapy (escitalopram or sertraline, clinician's choice, standard dosing). Exclusions: other psychotropics, substance use, neurological disease, uncorrected visual impairment, shift work.

Task: a computerised low-contrast visual search task modelled on Lehnert's faint-target paradigm (target present/absent, contrast titrated to ~75% baseline accuracy), plus a standard sustained-attention control task (continuous performance test). Primary endpoint: change in d′ on the visual search task at days 3–7 versus baseline. Secondary endpoints: d′ at days 14, 28 and 42; sustained-attention d′; depression severity (PHQ-9); plasma SSRI concentration at each visit.

Schedule: baseline (day 0, before first dose), day 3, day 7, day 14, day 28, day 42. A waitlist control group (depressed adults awaiting treatment, same schedule, no drug) separates drug effects from practice effects and spontaneous mood change.

Analysis: linear mixed model of d′ over time with group × time interaction; primary contrast day 3–7 versus baseline within the SSRI arm; pre-registered one-sided prediction of a dip followed by recovery (quadratic time term).

2.4 Power analysis (our computation)

Sample sizes use the normal approximation n = (Z₁₋α/₂ + Z₁₋β)² / dz² for a paired design (7.85/dz²) and n per arm = 2 × 7.85/d² for a parallel two-arm comparison, at 80% power and two-sided α = 0.05, with 15% attrition. The assumed effect is medium (dz = 0.5) — deliberately conservative, because the mouse effect direction is clear but its human magnitude is unknown. All numbers in §3.4 are computed from these stated formulas, not from data.

3. Results

3.1 The November 2026 neuroscience landscape (synthesis)

Five verified findings from October–November 2026 frame the model. None is our data; the synthesis is ours.

Finding Source What was shown (verified)
Serotonin dims visual attention Lehnert et al., Nat Commun 2026;17:3464 Dorsal raphe serotonin neurons grade the strength of visual attention in mice; less serotonin → better faint-target detection, more → worse
Theta organises frontal cognition Broschard et al., Cell Rep 2026 Theta waves (4–10 Hz) organise information across frontal cortex during a dot-pattern categorisation task in non-human primates; theta phase couples to beta amplitude, beta phase to gamma amplitude
Emotions sit on a grid map Ma & Kragel, PLOS Biol 2026;24 Ventromedial prefrontal cortex maps emotional knowledge with sixfold (60°) grid-like symmetry, across two different stimulus types
Psilocybin remodels spines by brain state Baker et al., Nat Neurosci 2026 5-HT2A receptors in layer 5 pyramidal neurons mediate psilocybin's neuroplastic (spine growth within 24 h) but not its hallucinogenic effects; chronically stressed mice show a larger spine surge and halted synapse loss, healthy mice return to baseline over three weeks
AI separates Parkinson's brain rhythms Kim et al., NeuroImage 2026 NONOS, a deep-learning separator of rhythmic from background brain activity, predicted the stepping foot in Parkinson's patients with accuracy 0.98 versus 0.54–0.79 for conventional methods, and detected the rapid beta-band fall after deep brain stimulation in mice

Two patterns matter for this paper. First, serotonin is doing two different jobs through two different receptors in the same month's literature: 5-HT signalling dims attention via the raphe (Lehnert) while 5-HT2A signalling rebuilds synapses (Baker) — receptor and circuit, not the molecule alone, determine the effect. Second, the brain's timing systems (theta organisation, grid-like maps) are about structure, while serotonin is about gain: the dimmer sets how strongly a structured system attends. That division is what makes the model testable — gain changes should show up first and largest on fine-discrimination tasks, not on all cognition at once.

3.2 The four predictions (the paper's own contribution)

  • P1 — the dip: visual-search d′ at days 3–7 is lower than baseline in the SSRI arm (predicted direction: down; predicted size: medium, dz ≈ 0.5).
  • P2 — the recovery: visual-search d′ at day 42 is at or above baseline, and higher than at days 3–7.
  • P3 — task specificity: the dip is larger on the low-contrast visual search task than on the sustained-attention control task (interaction between task type and time).
  • P4 — dose tracking: the size of the week-1 dip correlates with plasma SSRI concentration at day 7 (higher exposure → larger dip), and the recovery tracks the 2–6-week adaptation window, not the plasma level alone.

3.3 Reconciliation: three "contradictory" literatures as one curve

Read against the model, the existing evidence stops contradicting itself:

  • Healthy animals get worse (Ampuero et al., 2024): acute serotonergic elevation in a healthy brain, no depression to treat, no adaptation window sampled — the dip, observed alone.
  • Depressed patients get better (Prado et al., 2018, 33 studies): measured after weeks of treatment, when adaptation has occurred and mood improvement itself lifts attention — the recovery, observed alone.
  • No effect at 6 weeks in children (Günther et al., 2005, n = 28): measured at the recovery plateau, on tasks that mix sustained and divided attention rather than fine visual discrimination — the flat tail of the curve, on the least sensitive task.

Each literature sampled a different segment of the same dip-and-recovery curve. The model predicts that a single study sampling all six weeks, with the fine-discrimination task, will see the whole curve — and that is precisely what no published study has done.

3.4 Power analysis (our computation)

Assumed effect (dz) Paired n (80% power, α = 0.05) +15% attrition Parallel waitlist comparison (per arm)
0.35 (small–medium) 65 77 129
0.50 (medium — primary) 32 38 63
0.65 (medium–large) 19 23 38

The primary design therefore enrols 38 drug-naïve patients (32 completers) for the within-subject primary endpoint, with a waitlist control arm of 63 per arm (149 total with attrition) if the parallel comparison is funded. A pilot of n = 12, tested at baseline and day 7 only, would detect only a large effect (dz ≥ 0.8) and is recommended solely as a feasibility check for the task, not as a test of the model.

4. Discussion

Why the dimmer matters clinically. If P1 holds, the first week of SSRI therapy carries a transient, measurable cost to fine visual attention — the kind of attention used in driving, examinations and safety-critical work. Patients are currently counselled about nausea, sleep change and agitation in week 1; a transient attention dip, if real, belongs on the same counselling list, and it is testable in a single clinic visit with a 10-minute computerised task. If P1 fails, the counselling implication vanishes — which is itself a useful clinical answer.

Why the recovery matters for trial design. Antidepressant trials that measure cognition at a single post-treatment time point are sampling one point on a moving curve. A trial that tests attention at week 2 can conclude SSRIs impair cognition; the same trial at week 6 can conclude they improve it. Both can be right about their time point and wrong about the drug. Future cognition endpoints in antidepressant trials should be time-coursed, not single-point.

Mechanistic grounding and its limits. The 2–6-week delay in SSRI therapeutic onset is conventionally attributed to desensitisation of somatodendritic 5-HT1A autoreceptors, which initially suppress raphe firing and then adapt, permitting increased serotonergic transmission. Our model borrows that established pharmacological account for the timing of the recovery, and Lehnert's circuit result for the direction of the acute effect. The link between the two is inference, not measurement: no study has yet recorded raphe activity, autoreceptor sensitivity and attention in the same human across SSRI initiation. The proposed study does not measure autoreceptors either — it tests the behavioural curve the mechanism predicts. A follow-up using PET 5-HT1A imaging would test the mechanism itself.

Relation to the wider 2026 findings. The Baker et al. psilocybin result is a useful contrast: a serotonergic drug that rebuilds synapses through cortical 5-HT2A receptors, with effects that depend on the brain's prior state (stressed versus healthy). Serotonin pharmacology is therefore not one effect but a set of receptor- and circuit-specific effects with different time courses — acute gain reduction (raphe, days), structural remodelling (cortical 5-HT2A, 24 hours to weeks), and mood recovery (weeks). Any claim of the form "serotonin improves/worsens cognition" that does not specify receptor, circuit, task and time is underspecified. The NONOS result (Kim et al., 2026) shows the measurement side is ready: modern signal separation can resolve rapid, previously invisible changes in brain rhythms — the same temporal resolution the dip-and-recovery curve needs.

ADHD and comorbidity. Lehnert et al.'s authors note the relevance to ADHD. The model adds a pharmacological prediction: in patients with comorbid depression and ADHD, SSRI initiation should transiently worsen attentional symptoms in week 1 before any mood-mediated improvement — a pattern clinicians anecdotally report and no trial has pre-registered. The proposed study's task battery could be extended to an ADHD symptom scale as a secondary endpoint.

5. Limitations

  1. Mouse to human. Lehnert's result is in mice, on a visual detection task, with precise circuit manipulation. Human SSRIs raise serotonin globally and bluntly; the dimmer may not translate, or may translate only for some tasks.
  2. Depression confounds attention. Depression itself impairs attention, and mood improves over six weeks. The within-subject dip (P1) is protected from this confound — mood does not worsen in week 1 while attention dips — but the recovery (P2) is not: recovery could reflect mood improvement rather than autoreceptor adaptation. The waitlist control and the plasma-level correlation (P4) are the design's answers, and they are partial.
  3. No data are presented. This is a hypothesis and design paper. The model is falsifiable, not confirmed.
  4. The 5-HT1A mechanism is inferred. Autoreceptor desensitisation is the standard account of SSRI onset delay, but it is not measured in the proposed study; a PET follow-up is needed to test the mechanism rather than its behavioural shadow.
  5. Publication timing. Lehnert et al. was published 18 March 2026; the November 2026 date attached to it in news coverage is the coverage date, not the publication date. The model is built on a March finding, synthesised in November — the synthesis is new, the anchor is eight months old, and any newer replication would supersede it.

6. Conclusion

Serotonin is a dimmer on attention, not a switch — and the most prescribed serotonergic drugs in medicine have never been tested against that dimmer on its own time course. The serotonin-dimmer model predicts a dip in fine visual attention in the first week of SSRI therapy and a recovery by week six, explains three apparently contradictory literatures as three segments of one curve, and fails cleanly if the dip does not appear. The experiment needs 38 drug-naïve patients, a 10-minute computerised task, and six weeks. Until it is run, no clinician should counsel a patient that SSRIs will either help or harm their attention in week 1 — because the honest answer, today, is that nobody has looked at the right time, with the right task.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 6 November 2026 · Paper #6 — Brain track (Daily Research Papers)

Keywords: glymphatic system; brain clearance; Alzheimer's disease; vasomechanic treatment; nitric oxide; Piezo1; whole-body vibration; plasma p-tau217; sleep; prevention trial

Abstract

Two human trials published in 2026 closed the two halves of the same question. Dagum et al. showed in a randomised crossover trial (n = 39) that normal sleep, versus sleep deprivation, raises morning plasma amyloid-beta and tau — the first direct human evidence that the glymphatic system clears Alzheimer's proteins from brain to blood during sleep. Three days ago, Tuunanen et al. showed that the same clearance can be switched on while awake: one session of sublingual nitroglycerin (0.5 mg) plus Piezo1-targeted whole-body vibration (22–50 Hz, 37 min) in 29 healthy adults raised serum amyloid-beta 40 by 32.2%, amyloid-beta 42 by 34.6% and glial fibrillary acidic protein by 30.5%, with larger proteins unchanged — a size-selective efflux consistent with a ~68 kDa gate. We recompute the published results: the three low-molecular-weight markers give a mean per-session efflux of +32.4%, the effect sizes are dz = 0.52–0.53, and the blood-pressure drop that drives the effect correlates with the biomarker rise (r = −0.49 to −0.63). Vibration alone produced no significant brain-fluid change and nitric oxide alone recapitulated sleep physiology, so the combination — not either arm alone — is the intervention. We propose the awake-clearance framework: a 12-week, sham-controlled trial of thrice-weekly vasomechanic sessions in amyloid-positive adults aged 55–75, powered (n = 58 per arm, 138 with attrition) from the published effect sizes, with plasma p-tau217 as the primary endpoint. The falsifiable claim: if the per-session efflux is real clearance, plasma p-tau217 must fall versus sham; if it does not fall while per-session amyloid-beta 42 efflux rises, the plasma rises are redistribution, not clearance, and the prevention rationale fails. This paper is a synthesis and a trial design, not a treatment recommendation — no brain amyloid, cognition or durability data exist yet.

1. Introduction

Alzheimer's disease (AD) begins a decade or more before symptoms, and every disease-modifying drug approved so far is given after symptoms appear. Prevention therefore needs an intervention that acts before symptoms — and, until 2026, the field had no human evidence that brain clearance of amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau could be measured, let alone enhanced. The glymphatic system — cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flowing along perivascular spaces, through brain tissue via astrocytic aquaporin-4, and out to the venous sinuses and meningeal lymphatics — was described in mice in 2012 (Iliff et al.), where sleep expanded the interstitial space by ~60% and roughly doubled Aβ clearance (Xie et al., 2013), and where ageing impaired Aβ clearance by ~40% (Kress et al., 2014). But whether this system moves Aβ and tau out of the human brain, and whether it can be deliberately enhanced, remained unproven.

2026 answered both questions in the same journal, nine months apart. First, Dagum et al. (Nature Communications, January 2026) ran a randomised crossover trial in 39 participants comparing a night of normal sleep with a night of sleep deprivation, and found higher morning plasma Aβ and tau after normal sleep — the first direct human evidence of sleep-driven glymphatic clearance of AD proteins to blood. Second, on 3 November 2026, Tuunanen et al. (Nature Communications) reported that a vasomechanic intervention — nitric-oxide (NO) vasodilation plus Piezo1-targeted whole-body vibration — raises the same brain-derived proteins in blood in awake humans. Neither paper proposes a prevention trial. This paper does three new things: (i) it recomputes the Tuunanen results into comparable, standardised quantities (per-session efflux, effect sizes, sample sizes); (ii) it combines the two trials with the 2025 mechanism work on norepinephrine-driven vasomotion into a single clearance framework; and (iii) it converts that framework into a fully specified, falsifiable prevention-trial design. The paper's own contribution is arithmetic and synthesis, not new human data — and it states, plainly, the single experiment that would refute it.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

The literature sweep is the 2026-11-06 daily research digest (651 candidates screened: 117 PubMed, 8 arXiv, 526 bioRxiv; 8 selected) plus targeted searches on the two anchor trials. Both anchor papers were read in full text: Tuunanen et al., Nature Communications 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-78894-y (open access, read 6 November 2026); Dagum et al., Nature Communications 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-68374-8, PMID 41593094 (abstract and figures via PubMed, read 6 November 2026). Mechanistic context is Hauglund et al., Cell 2025 (norepinephrine-driven slow vasomotion; zolpidem suppression), and the 2026 reviews by Zare et al. (Brain and Behavior) and the Journal of Clinical Medicine systematic review on sleep architecture and clearance (DOI 10.3390/jcm15166454). The p-tau217 endpoint is taken from the companion paper in this series (Ali, Paper #4 — Brain track, 3 November 2026), which established plasma p-tau217 strata and their absolute five-year progression risks. No unpublished, anecdotal or press-release-only efficacy claim is used as evidence; secondary reporting (University of Oulu press release, 3 November 2026) was used only to locate the primary paper, and every number in the Results is taken from the primary papers themselves.

2.2 Recomputation

All derived numbers in §3 are computed from the published group means, medians, t-statistics and correlations of Tuunanen et al., and are labelled as recomputations:

  • Percent change = (post − pre) / pre × 100, using the published pre and post (haemodilution-corrected) values.
  • Per-session efflux index (PEI) = the arithmetic mean of the percent changes of the three low-molecular-weight markers that rose (Aβ40, Aβ42, GFAP).
  • Standardised effect size for a paired design, dz = |t| / √n, from the published paired t-statistics.
  • Sample sizes for 80% power at two-sided α = 0.05: paired replication, n = (Z₁₋α/₂ + Z₁₋β)² / dz² = 7.84 / dz²; parallel two-arm trial, n per arm = 2 × 7.84 / dz²; attrition-adjusted total = 2 × (n per arm) / 0.85, rounded up.
  • The molecular-weight gate is inferred from the pattern the authors themselves report: proteins below 68 kDa rose, proteins at or above it did not.

No new human data, no animal data and no simulation are presented. The trial design in §3.5 is a proposal, not a result.

3. Results

3.1 The two 2026 anchor trials

Sleep clears AD proteins in humans (Dagum et al., n = 39). In a randomised crossover trial (a benchmarking study at The Villages, Florida, and a replication study at the University of Washington), participants spent one night with normal sleep opportunity and one night sleep-deprived. Morning plasma levels of Aβ40, Aβ42, non-phosphorylated tau-181, non-phosphorylated tau-217 and p-tau181 were higher after normal sleep than after sleep deprivation, and the pattern matched a six-compartment model in which glymphatic efflux/influx rate constants (k_glymph_out, k_glymph_in) rise by a factor of 1.5 during the 8-hour sleep window while neuronal solute release (k_cell_rel) falls by 30%. The authors' conclusion, quoted in the abstract: sleep-active physiological processes, particularly reduced brain parenchymal resistance, enhance overnight glymphatic clearance of AD biomarkers to plasma. Limitations stated in the paper: the clearance monitor was an investigational device, and the trial measured one night, not years of habit.

Awake clearance can be switched on (Tuunanen et al., n = 29). Healthy adults (15 women; mean age 44 ± 10 years, range 27–61) underwent, in randomised crossover order on separate days, Piezo1-targeted whole-body vibration (WBVp, n = 27) and the combined protocol of NO-mediated vasodilation with WBVp (NO+WBVp, n = 26), plus an exploratory NO-only session in a subset (n = 12). NO was sublingual nitroglycerin 0.5 mg; WBVp was modulated 22–50 Hz vibration for ~37 min, delivered by a commercial whole-body vibration device and aimed at Piezo1 mechanosensitive channels. Trial registration: EudraCT 2021-000625-27. During NO+WBVp, systolic blood pressure fell from 134 ± 14 to a nadir of 114 ± 9 mmHg (−14.9 ± 6.3%) and diastolic from 79 ± 8 to 67 ± 7 mmHg (−14.8 ± 9.0%).

3.2 Recomputation 1 — the per-session efflux (our analysis)

Table 1 recomputes the published serum changes. All three low-molecular-weight brain-derived proteins rose by roughly one-third; the two larger proteins did not move.

Marker Molecular weight Pre Post (haemodilution-corrected) Change n P
Aβ40 ~4.3 kDa 38.2 ± 19.0 pg/mL 50.5 ± 25.2 pg/mL +32.2% 22 0.03
Aβ42 ~4.5 kDa 2.6 ± 1.4 pg/mL 3.5 ± 1.8 pg/mL +34.6% 23 0.03
GFAP ~50 kDa 65.2 pg/mL (median) 85.1 pg/mL (median) +30.5% 25 <0.0001
Neurofilament light ~68 kDa — — no change 25 0.67
pTau-181 ~55–60 kDa* — — no change 23 0.75
S100B ~21 kDa 0.05 µg/L (median) 0.04 µg/L (median) no change 25 0.23

* pTau-181 is phosphorylated tau, which circulates largely in larger assemblies; the authors group it with the larger proteins. S100B did not rise despite its small size, so molecular weight alone does not explain every result — see §3.3 and §4.

The three rising markers give a per-session efflux index (PEI) of +32.4% — the mean of +32.2%, +34.6% and +30.5%. We propose PEI as a standardised, comparable metric for future clearance studies: any intervention that claims to enhance brain clearance should report the mean percent rise of the same three markers, measured with the same assay (Quanterix Simoa HD-X) and the same haemodilution correction, so that effect sizes can be compared across studies instead of argued about. The PEI is a proposal, not a validated biomarker: it inherits every limitation of the single-session data it is built on.

Two further published numbers support the efflux interpretation over a redistribution artefact. First, the intervention reduced whole-brain T2 dark-fluid MRI signal intensity by 4.6 ± 6.1% (P = 0.008, n = 24) — less brain water/macromolecule content — while extracerebral CSF volume rose by 6.5 ± 9.8 mL (P = 0.02): fluid and protein left the brain and entered the CSF/blood compartment, in the same session, in the same participants. Second, the magnitude of the NO-mediated blood-pressure reduction correlated with the biomarker rise (Aβ40 r = −0.63, P = 0.004; Aβ42 r = −0.57, P = 0.009; GFAP r = −0.49, P = 0.02): the more the vessels dilated, the more protein appeared in blood. A pure redistribution or assay artefact would not be expected to track the physiological driver this closely.

3.3 Recomputation 2 — the size gate, and its exception (our analysis)

The authors' own framing is that proteins below 68 kDa rose and larger ones did not: neurofilament light (~68 kDa) was unchanged (P = 0.67) and pTau-181 was unchanged (P = 0.75). That is consistent with a perivascular transport route that admits small solutes and excludes large ones — the same size-selectivity seen in mouse tracer studies, where a 40 kDa FITC-dextran tracer was cleared from CSF to blood after NO-donor infusion in the supporting mouse experiments of the same paper.

S100B (~21 kDa) is the exception that tests the rule: it did not change (P = 0.23). S100B is predominantly astrocytic and its plasma level is dominated by extracerebral sources, so its flat result does not refute the size gate — but it does warn against treating "small protein rises" as proof of brain origin for any single marker. The honest reading: the efflux claim rests on the pattern (three brain-derived markers rising together, correlated with vasodilation, corroborated by MRI fluid shifts), not on any one analyte. Any future trial that uses plasma rises as its engagement signal should pre-specify the three-marker PEI, not cherry-pick the marker that moves most.

3.4 Recomputation 3 — effect sizes and the sample sizes they imply (our analysis)

From the published paired t-statistics: Aβ42, t(22) = −2.5, n = 23, gives dz = 2.5 / √23 = 0.52; Aβ40, t(21) = −2.5, n = 22, gives dz = 2.5 / √22 = 0.53. These are medium standardised effects, and they are the numbers a replication must be powered on — not the 30–35% rises, which look large only because the baseline values are small and the standard deviations wide (Aβ40 SD 19.0 on a mean of 38.2; Aβ42 SD 1.4 on a mean of 2.6).

Applying the standard formula (80% power, two-sided α = 0.05):

Design n required
Paired replication of the single-session effect (dz = 0.52) 29 participants
Parallel two-arm RCT, same standardised effect 58 per arm
Same RCT, allowing 15% attrition 69 per arm (138 total)

The paired replication number (29) is, coincidentally, the size of the original trial — which is reassuring: the original study was approximately correctly powered for its own primary signal, and a replication of the same size is a fair test. The parallel-trial number (138 total) is the basis for the design in §3.5. Note that these sizes power the engagement signal (per-session efflux), not the clinical signal (a fall in p-tau217 over 12 weeks); the clinical endpoint is powered by assumption, and §4 states that assumption as a limitation rather than hiding it.

3.5 The awake-clearance framework and the CLEAR-AWAKE trial design (our proposal)

The two trials, plus the mechanism work, assemble into one framework:

  1. Sleep is the natural clearance state. Norepinephrine oscillations from the locus coeruleus drive slow vasomotion (~0.02 Hz) during NREM sleep, pumping CSF through the brain; zolpidem suppresses those oscillations and reduces glymphatic flow (Hauglund et al., Cell 2025). Sleep architecture — preserved slow-wave sleep and sleep oscillatory coupling — tracks with favourable clearance biomarkers across the early AD continuum (systematic review, Journal of Clinical Medicine 2026). A 2026 randomised crossover trial (Dagum et al.) confirms in humans that sleep moves Aβ and tau from brain to plasma, with glymphatic rate constants rising ~1.5-fold during sleep.
  2. Awake clearance is inducible. NO vasodilation recapitulates key elements of sleep physiology — it lowers blood pressure, amplifies ~0.1 Hz vasomotor waves and respiratory pulsations — and combined with Piezo1-targeted vibration it raises brain-protein efflux by ~32% per session (Tuunanen et al.). The combination matters: vibration alone produced no significant voxel-wise changes in brain pulsation power and no significant T2 dark-fluid voxel changes, while NO alone produced T2DF reductions (−4.8 ± 6.8% at 15 min, P = 0.04) and CSF expansion (+7.0 ± 9.7 mL, P = 0.04) of similar magnitude to the combined arm but over a 2–6 times smaller spatial extent. A sham resting cohort (n = 13) showed no significant T2DF change.
  3. The two clearance windows are additive in principle and must be tested in combination. A prevention regimen would therefore pair (a) sleep protection — slow-wave sleep preservation, and avoidance of sleep aids that suppress norepinephrine oscillations — with (b) thrice-weekly awake vasomechanic sessions, and (c) plasma p-tau217 monitoring, because p-tau217 is the blood marker with established absolute progression risks (Paper #4 in this series: five-year progression risk 12% low, 15% intermediate, 24% high, 38% very high).

CLEAR-AWAKE — proposed trial. A 12-week, double-blind, sham-controlled, parallel-group randomised trial in amyloid-positive adults aged 55–75, cognitively unimpaired or with mild cognitive impairment.

Element Specification
Population Amyloid-positive (PET or CSF), age 55–75, no PDE5-inhibitor use, no symptomatic orthostatic hypotension, no uncontrolled hypertension
Intervention Sublingual nitroglycerin 0.5 mg + Piezo1-targeted whole-body vibration 22–50 Hz, ~37 min, 3 sessions/week, 12 weeks — the Tuunanen protocol, repeated
Control Sham vibration (device on, sub-threshold stimulus) + placebo sublingual tablet, same schedule
Primary endpoint Change in plasma p-tau217 (Simoa) from baseline to week 12, between groups
Engagement biomarker Per-session efflux index (PEI) at week 1 — the mean percent rise of Aβ40, Aβ42 and GFAP after a session
Secondary endpoints Amyloid PET SUVR; plasma Aβ42/40 ratio; DTI-ALPS glymphatic index; slow-wave sleep time (actigraphy/EEG); cognition (PACC)
Sample size 69 per arm (138 total), powered on dz = 0.52 with 15% attrition (§3.4)
Safety Blood-pressure monitoring each session; headache/nausea recording (4/29 headache, 3/29 nausea, 1 discontinuation for vomiting in Tuunanen et al.); exclusion of PDE5-inhibitor users (nitroglycerin interaction)

3.6 The falsifiable claim

Claim: In amyloid-positive adults aged 55–75, 12 weeks of thrice-weekly combined NO-vasodilation + Piezo1-targeted whole-body vibration will reduce plasma p-tau217 relative to sham vibration + placebo, and the reduction will correlate with the participant's week-1 per-session efflux index — i.e. the people whose brains flush most per session will show the largest fall in the burden marker over 12 weeks.

How it is tested: the CLEAR-AWAKE trial in §3.5, with the week-1 PEI and the week-12 p-tau217 change pre-specified as co-primary, and their correlation pre-specified as the mechanistic test.

What refutes it: (a) no between-group difference in plasma p-tau217 at 12 weeks despite a reproducible per-session Aβ42 efflux rise — this would show the plasma rises are redistribution of existing protein into blood, not net removal from brain, and the prevention rationale fails; or (b) a fall in p-tau217 that does not correlate with the week-1 PEI — this would show the effect, if any, is not mediated by the clearance mechanism proposed here, and the framework as stated is wrong even if the trial is positive. Either outcome is informative, and both are pre-specified before any data are collected.

4. Discussion

What is genuinely new here. Before November 2026, "enhance brain clearance" was a mouse claim. Two human trials in one year changed that: sleep moves Aβ and tau to blood (Dagum), and a drug-plus-vibration session moves the same proteins to blood while the person is awake (Tuunanen). Our contribution is to put the two together, quantify the awake effect in comparable units (PEI +32.4%, dz = 0.52–0.53, replication n = 29), identify the dose–response (blood-pressure drop predicts efflux), and convert the whole picture into a trial that can fail cleanly. The history of this research programme matters here: our Paper #1 was refuted by its own re-analysis when a grid-centre audit moved the docking site 13 Å, and the corrected result reversed the conclusion. That experience is why this paper pre-specifies its own refutation conditions in §3.6 rather than leaving them to a reviewer.

Why the combination, not the parts. The Tuunanen data are unusually clear on this point. Vibration alone changed no brain pulsation power and no T2 dark-fluid voxel; NO alone changed fluid dynamics but over a smaller area; the combination changed fluid dynamics over 2–6 times the volume of either alone, and only the combination was tested for blood biomarkers. Mechanistically this is coherent: NO dilates vessels and amplifies the ~0.1 Hz vasomotor waves that resemble sleep, while Piezo1 activation constricts vessels and drives lymphatic drainage — a push–pull cycle rather than a single push. A trial of vibration alone, or of nitroglycerin alone, would be testing a weaker hypothesis than the data support.

Why p-tau217 is the right primary endpoint. A 12-week trial cannot measure dementia prevention. It can measure a burden marker that predicts progression. Plasma p-tau217 is the marker with the best-established absolute risks in cognitively unimpaired people (Paper #4: 38% five-year progression risk in the very-high stratum, 78% at ten years), it is measurable in blood with the same Simoa platform used for the efflux markers, and — critically — it was not moved by a single Tuunanen session (pTau-181 was unchanged, and p-tau217 was not among the measured analytes), so a 12-week fall would be a new finding rather than a re-measurement of the acute effect. Amyloid PET SUVR is the confirmatory secondary endpoint, because plasma p-tau217 can fall without brain amyloid falling, and the claim is about the brain.

The sleep-aid warning is part of the framework, not an aside. Hauglund et al. showed zolpidem suppresses the norepinephrine oscillations that drive glymphatic flow — the drug helps people fall asleep while impairing the clearance that sleep is for. Any prevention regimen built on clearance must therefore treat sleep-aid choice as an intervention variable: the CLEAR-AWAKE protocol excludes regular zolpidem use and records sleep architecture as a secondary endpoint. This is also the most immediately actionable part of the paper for a clinician reader, and it costs nothing: prefer sleep hygiene and slow-wave-sleep preservation over a sedative that suppresses the mechanism.

Safety and translation, stated plainly. Nitroglycerin is a real drug with real contraindications: it must not be combined with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil and related drugs), and it causes headache (4 of 29), nausea (3 of 29) and occasional vomiting (1 discontinuation) — all transient in the trial, but in older adults with autonomic dysfunction the ~15% blood-pressure drop is a genuine orthostatic risk. Whole-body vibration is well tolerated (no discomfort reported) but the 22–50 Hz modulated protocol is specific: ordinary commercial vibration plates are not the same intervention. Nothing in this paper supports home use, "brain detox" products, or any commercial claim — no compound has been shown to enhance glymphatic clearance in humans over weeks, and no cognitive or amyloid outcome has been measured at all. The intervention is a trial protocol, not a recommendation.

What this paper does not do. It does not claim that a 32% per-session plasma rise equals a 32% reduction in brain amyloid — plasma appearance is necessary but not sufficient evidence of net clearance, which is exactly why §3.6 makes the p-tau217 result the arbiter. It does not model the cumulative effect of repeated sessions, because no repeated-session data exist; any such model would be invented. It does not address tau tangles, which are intracellular and unlikely to be cleared by a perivascular route. And it does not propose screening asymptomatic people with p-tau217 outside research — the companion paper's position stands.

5. Limitations

  1. Single session, healthy middle-aged adults. Tuunanen et al. studied one session in 29 healthy volunteers (mean age 44, no cognitive impairment, no amyloid measurement). Nothing is known about repeated sessions, older adults, amyloid-positive people, durability, or whether the efflux habituates. The CLEAR-AWAKE design extrapolates a single-session effect to 36 sessions — the trial is the test of that extrapolation, not evidence for it.
  2. No placebo pill. The Tuunanen trial had no placebo tablet arm; the comparison was between active arms and a separate sham resting cohort (n = 13) for imaging only. Expectation and supine rest effects on blood biomarkers are therefore not fully controlled, and the PEI is built on within-session pre–post changes.
  3. Small numbers, wide variance. The Aβ42 effect (2.6 → 3.5 pg/mL) rests on 23 participants with a standard deviation of 1.4 pg/mL at baseline; the P-values (0.03) are just inside significance and would not survive a stringent correction across all measured analytes. The dz = 0.52 used for powering is computed from the same data it powers — a replication could find a smaller effect, in which case 138 participants would be underpowered.
  4. Plasma rise is not proof of net clearance. Higher plasma Aβ after a session could reflect redistribution from a peripheral pool, reduced peripheral degradation, or altered blood flow rather than brain-to-blood transport. The MRI fluid shifts and the blood-pressure correlation argue against a pure artefact, but only a brain measure (PET SUVR, CSF) can settle it — which is why PET is a secondary endpoint in CLEAR-AWAKE.
  5. The size gate has an exception. S100B (~21 kDa) did not rise, so molecular weight alone does not predict efflux; the gate is a pattern, not a law, and the mechanism of selectivity is not established.
  6. The clinical endpoint is powered by assumption. The sample size in §3.4 powers the engagement signal (per-session efflux). The 12-week p-tau217 effect has no prior estimate; if the true standardised effect on p-tau217 is smaller than 0.5, CLEAR-AWAKE will be underpowered for its primary endpoint, and a null result would be ambiguous rather than refuting. A pilot phase (n = 30, 6 weeks) measuring the p-tau217 variance under the intervention should precede the full trial.
  7. No population diversity. The anchor trials were conducted in Finland and the United States; no South Asian, African or low-resource-setting data exist, and the nitroglycerin–vibration protocol has not been tested in the population this author serves. Cost and access (MRI, Simoa assays, vibration device) are real barriers to replication in Pakistan, and a low-cost version of the engagement biomarker (plasma Aβ42/40 ratio alone, without MRI) needs validation before the framework can be tested there.
  8. This is a synthesis, not an experiment. Every number traces to the two anchor papers and the cited mechanism work; the paper's new content is recomputation, a metric proposal (PEI) and a trial design. It must not be cited as evidence that vasomechanic treatment prevents Alzheimer's disease.

6. Conclusion

Two 2026 human trials turned brain clearance from a mouse phenomenon into a measurable, inducible human physiology: sleep moves amyloid-beta and tau from brain to blood, and a single session of nitroglycerin plus Piezo1-targeted vibration does the same while awake, raising three low-molecular-weight brain proteins by ~32% per session with a dose–response tied to vasodilation. The honest next step is not a product but a trial: 12 weeks of repeated sessions in amyloid-positive older adults, judged by plasma p-tau217, with the per-session efflux as the engagement signal and pre-specified conditions under which the framework fails. If the trial is positive, prevention gains a cheap, non-invasive, drug-plus-device lever. If it is negative despite per-session efflux, the field learns that plasma rises are not clearance — a result worth knowing before anyone builds a clinic on it. Either way, the experiment is now writable, affordable, and falsifiable. That is the whole point.

8. Data availability

No new data were generated. All numbers in §3 are recomputations from the published results of Tuunanen et al. (reference 1, open access, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-78894-y, including its Source Data file) and Dagum et al. (reference 2, PMID 41593094). The recomputation steps are fully specified in §2.2 and can be reproduced from the two papers with a pocket calculator: percent changes from the published pre/post means and medians; dz = |t| / √n from the published t-statistics; sample sizes from the standard normal-approximation formula with Z₁₋α/₂ = 1.96 and Z₁₋β = 0.84. The literature sweep for this paper is the daily research digest of 6 November 2026 (~/workspace/research-team/digests/2026-11-06.md), which screened 651 candidates and selected 8 papers. The trial design in §3.5 is a proposal; no trial has been registered and no participants have been recruited.
