The Preclinical Window Is Now Measurable: Plasma p-Tau217 Risk Stratification and the Design of Alzheimer's Prevention Trials

Alzheimer's disease prevention trials have been designed in the dark: they enrol cognitively unimpaired people with brain amyloid and then wait years to learn how many would ever have declined.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 3 November 2026 · Paper #4 — Brain track (Daily Research Papers)

Keywords: plasma p-tau217; Alzheimer's disease; preclinical Alzheimer's disease; cognitive impairment; risk stratification; prevention trial; trial enrichment; tau; diranersen

Abstract

Alzheimer's disease prevention trials have been designed in the dark: they enrol cognitively unimpaired people with brain amyloid and then wait years to learn how many would ever have declined. A pooled analysis of 2,684 cognitively unimpaired older adults across six cohorts (Buckley et al., JAMA 2026) now attaches absolute numbers to that wait. Over five years, the risk of progression to cognitive impairment was 12% with low plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), 15% intermediate, 24% high and 38% very high (>2.5 SD above the amyloid-negative reference); at ten years the very-high group reached 78%. Each 1-SD rise in p-tau217 carried a hazard ratio of 1.38, and the association survived adjustment for amyloid PET burden. We translate these risks into trial arithmetic: for a five-year prevention trial powered to detect a 30% relative risk reduction, an unselected population needs 1,412 participants, a high-p-tau217 population 982, and a very-high-p-tau217 population only 526 — a 63% reduction in sample size, with the five-year number needed to treat falling from 18.7 to 8.8. The same numbers expose the limits of enrichment: two-year risks are 1–4% in every stratum, so a two-year prevention trial is futile by design; even the "low" group carries a 12% five-year and 40% ten-year risk; and the cohorts were selected, not population-representative. We propose the enrichment-and-horizon hypothesis: prevention trials should enrol the very-high p-tau217 stratum and run at least five years, testing a tau-lowering intervention of the diranersen class. The falsifiable prediction: the placebo arm will progress at 33–43% over five years and the trial will detect a 30% risk reduction with ≤650 participants; a placebo rate below 25% refutes the enrichment assumption. Until a prevention drug exists, these numbers are a trial-design tool, not a screening test — current guidelines explicitly recommend against testing asymptomatic people outside research.

1. Introduction

Alzheimer's disease (AD) begins a decade or more before symptoms. Amyloid plaques accumulate silently, tau pathology follows, and by the time memory fails, the brain has already lost substantial ground. Every disease-modifying drug approved so far — lecanemab and donanemab — is given to people who already have symptoms, and each slows decline by roughly a quarter to a third rather than stopping it. The field's open question is whether intervening earlier, before symptoms, can do better. The AHEAD 3-45 trial is testing exactly that with lecanemab in amyloid-positive but cognitively unimpaired adults over 216 weeks. But prevention trials face a structural problem: most cognitively unimpaired people with amyloid will not decline within the trial's window, so the trial must be large, long and expensive — or it must find the people most likely to decline soon.

Until 2026, the field could only guess at that likelihood. Plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) was known to reflect early AD brain pathology and to predict relative risk of progression, but no pooled estimate of absolute risk — the number a trial designer actually needs — existed across multiple cohorts. The first FDA-cleared blood test in this space (Lumipulse G pTau217/β-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio, cleared 16 May 2025) is indicated only for symptomatic adults, and guidelines recommend against testing asymptomatic people outside research. So the prognostic question and the clinical question are different, and this paper is about the first: what does a p-tau217 level mean for a cognitively unimpaired person's chance of declining, and what does that mean for the trials that must enrol them?

The answer arrived in September 2026. Buckley and colleagues pooled harmonised data from 2,684 cognitively unimpaired older adults in six cohorts (ADNI, A4/LEARN, Harvard Aging Brain Study, Health & Aging Brain Study–Health Disparities, and the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention), followed for a median of 5.4 years, and reported model-based absolute risks of progression to cognitive impairment at 2, 5 and 10 years by p-tau217 stratum. The headline numbers — 38% five-year risk in the very-high group, 78% at ten years — were widely reported in November 2026. What has not been done, and what this paper does, is convert those risks into the concrete currency of trial design: sample sizes, numbers needed to treat, and the minimum trial duration that can possibly work. That conversion is our new contribution. It is arithmetic, not new data — but it changes the decision a trial designer faces from "enrich or not?" to "by how much, and at what cost?"

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

All prognostic numbers are taken from Buckley et al., JAMA 2026;336(11):950–959 (PMID 42449500; PMCID PMC13370474), read in full text, including Table 2 (absolute risks by stratum and time horizon) and the longitudinal PACC analysis. Context on prevention-trial screening comes from Molina-Henry et al., JAMA Neurology 2026, reporting the AHEAD 3-45 screening cohort (15,612 cognitively unimpaired adults at 106 sites). The tau-lowering intervention used as the worked example is diranersen, from the phase 2 CELIA data presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference, July 2026 (Ionis/Biogen press release, 14 July 2026; corroborated by contemporaneous Reuters and NeurologyLive reporting). Regulatory context is the FDA clearance of the Lumipulse p-tau217 test (16 May 2025). No unpublished, anecdotal or press-release-only efficacy claim is used as evidence; the CELIA efficacy figures are presented as conference-reported phase 2 results, explicitly labelled as such, and the paper's own claim does not depend on them.

2.2 Trial-arithmetic computation

Sample sizes use the standard two-proportion formula for a two-arm trial with a binary endpoint (progression to cognitive impairment within five years), two-sided α = 0.05, power = 80%:

n per arm = [Z₁₋α/₂·√(2p̄(1−p̄)) + Z₁₋β·√(p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂))]² / (p₁ − p₂)²

where p₁ is the placebo-arm five-year event rate, p₂ = p₁ × (1 − RRR) is the treated-arm rate at the assumed relative risk reduction (RRR), and p̄ = (p₁ + p₂)/2. Placebo rates are the Buckley model-based five-year risks (low 12%, intermediate 15%, high 24%, very high 38%), plus an "unselected" reference taken as the observed overall proportion who progressed, 478/2,684 = 17.8%, over the median 5.4 years of follow-up — an approximate five-year rate, flagged as such wherever it is used. Number needed to treat over five years (NNT₅y) = 1/(p₁ − p₂). Sensitivity analyses use RRR = 25% and the 95% confidence bounds of the very-high stratum (33–43%). The full computation script is in the data-availability note; every number in the tables below is its direct output.

2.3 Honesty limits

This is a literature-synthesis and arithmetic study. No new patient data, no new laboratory measurements and no new trial are presented. The sample sizes are planning calculations, not trial results: they assume the published risks transport to a future trial population, that the treatment effect is a constant relative risk reduction, and that loss to follow-up is negligible. The Buckley risks are model-based standardised estimates from selected research cohorts, not raw counts, and the 10-year figures rest on sparse data. The paper's claim is therefore narrow: enrichment by very-high p-tau217 makes a five-year prevention trial feasible at roughly one-third the size — not that such a trial will succeed, and not that asymptomatic people should be tested in clinic.

3. Results

3.1 The prognostic numbers: risk is graded, not binary

p-Tau217 group (definition) ~Amyloid PET (Centiloid) 2-year risk 5-year risk (95% CI) 10-year risk (95% CI)
Low (<−0.5 SD) <10 1% (1–1) 12% (9–15) 40% (31–49)
Intermediate (−0.5 to <1.1 SD) 10–24 1% (1–1) 15% (12–17) 45% (37–52)
High (1.1 to <2.5 SD) 25–60 2% (1–3) 24% (20–28) 62% (52–69)
Very high (≥2.5 SD) >60 4% (3–5) 38% (33–43) 78% (69–84)

Table 1. Model-based absolute risk of progression to cognitive impairment, from Buckley et al. (JAMA 2026), Table 2. All figures are standardised risks from a Cox model adjusted for cohort, age, sex, APOE ε4 status and education. The 10-year estimates rest on sparse data — only 5% of participants were followed beyond 10 years, mostly in one cohort — and must be treated as indicative, not precise.

Three features of this table matter. First, the gradient is steep and monotonic: the very-high group carries 3.17× the five-year risk of the low group (38% vs 12%), and the hazard ratio for very-high versus low is 4.66 (95% CI 3.17–6.85); high versus low is 2.34 (1.60–3.44). Each 1-SD increase in p-tau217 carries a hazard ratio of 1.38 (1.30–1.46), and the association survives adjustment for amyloid PET Centiloids (HR 1.32; 1.24–1.41), while amyloid burden itself contributes less (per-SD HR 1.19; 1.05–1.34). The biomarker adds information beyond the scan. Second, the two-year risks are 1–4% in every stratum: nobody declines fast enough, in any group, for a two-year prevention trial to accumulate endpoints. Third, even the "low" group is not a no-risk group — 12% at five years, 40% at ten. These are selected research cohorts (many participants carry a family history or APOE ε4), so the absolute numbers almost certainly overstate risk in the general population; the gradient, not the level, is the transportable finding.

The cognitive-trajectory data tell the same story in continuous form. Over five years, the low group improved by 0.03 latent PACC units per year (practice effects), the intermediate group by 0.01, while the high group declined by 0.03 and the very-high group by 0.07 units per year. The very-high-versus-low gap is −0.10 units per year (95% CI −0.13 to −0.07), or −0.50 units over five years. People who progressed declined at −0.06 units per year on average. The model discriminates reasonably well (five-year AUC 0.80; 95% CI 0.77–0.83) with good calibration (Brier score 0.12). Risk also varies within the very-high stratum: five-year risk is 36% in women versus 43% in men, and 39% at age 65 rising to 47% at age 85.

3.2 The trial arithmetic: enrichment buys a threefold reduction in size

Enrolment population (5-year placebo rate) n per arm Total N NNT over 5 years
Unselected (observed 17.8%) 706 1,412 18.7
Low p-tau217 (12%) 1,109 2,218 27.8
Intermediate p-tau217 (15%) 862 1,724 22.2
High p-tau217 (24%) 491 982 13.9
Very high p-tau217 (38%) 263 526 8.8

Table 2. Sample sizes for a five-year prevention trial with a binary progression endpoint, 30% relative risk reduction, two-sided α = 0.05, 80% power. Computed from the risks in Table 1 (script in the data-availability note). "Unselected" uses the observed overall progression proportion (478/2,684 over median 5.4 years) as an approximate five-year rate.

Enrolling only the very-high stratum cuts the required trial from 1,412 participants to 526 — 63% fewer participants — and more than halves the number needed to treat (8.8 vs 18.7). The saving is robust to the assumed effect size: at a 25% relative risk reduction, the unselected trial needs 2,082 participants versus 770 enriched; and across the very-high stratum's 95% confidence interval, the enriched total ranges from 436 (at 43% risk) to 646 (at 33% risk) — still less than half the unselected size in the worst case. Per 1,000 people enrolled for five years, the very-high stratum yields 380 progression events against 178 unselected, 240 high and 120 low: the endpoint, which is what a prevention trial is starved of, more than doubles.

Two corollaries follow. First, the low stratum is a bad trial population on its own (2,218 participants for the same power), so a trial that enrols "amyloid-positive" people without further stratification is paying for its lowest-risk participants. Second, the arithmetic only works at a five-year horizon. At two years, with event rates of 1–4%, the same calculation returns sample sizes in the tens of thousands — which is why prevention trials are four-to-five-year commitments, and why the AHEAD 3-45 trial runs 216 weeks.

3.3 What the biomarker does not buy

Enrichment is not free, and the numbers quantify its costs too. First, the screening yield is unknown from the published sources used here: the Buckley paper reports risks by stratum but the group sizes appear only in its figure, which we did not extract, so the number of people who must be blood-tested to find one very-high candidate cannot be computed from the text. The AHEAD screening experience gives a sense of scale — 15,612 people screened across 106 sites to fill a trial — but that used %p-tau217 as a first pass for amyloid, not the ≥2.5 SD threshold. Any sponsor budgeting an enriched trial must obtain the stratum prevalences before the arithmetic in Table 2 can be turned into a screening budget.

Second, enrichment narrows the answer. A trial in the very-high stratum tests the drug where pathology is most advanced; a positive result there does not prove benefit in the high or intermediate strata, where most of the preclinical population sits and where a prevention drug would ultimately be used. The high stratum — 24% five-year risk, 62% at ten years — is arguably the more important population for a prevention claim, and it needs 982 participants, still 30% fewer than unselected.

Third, a blood test that can find the highest-risk people does not create a treatment for them. No drug is approved for cognitively unimpaired people, the FDA-cleared p-tau217 tests are indicated only for symptomatic adults, and current guidelines explicitly recommend against testing asymptomatic people outside research. The value of these numbers today is for trial design, not for clinic screening — a distinction the paper's own authors stress.

4. Discussion

4.1 From relative risk to absolute risk: why this paper changes the conversation

For years, p-tau217 was a relative risk marker: "higher is worse, hazard ratio 1.38 per SD." Relative risks cannot size a trial. The Buckley analysis converts the marker into absolute, time-specific risks — the form a trialist, a funder and a regulator can actually use. That conversion is the paper's real contribution to the field, and ours is the second step: turning absolute risks into sample sizes. The result reframes the prevention-trial debate. The question is no longer "can we afford a prevention trial?" — at 526 participants over five years, a very-high-stratum trial is smaller than many phase 2 symptomatic trials — but "can we afford not to enrich, and can we screen fast enough to fill it?"

4.2 The enrichment-and-horizon hypothesis

We propose that the next Alzheimer's prevention trial should be designed around two commitments:

  1. Enrol the very-high p-tau217 stratum (≥2.5 SD, roughly >60 Centiloids of amyloid), with the high stratum (1.1–2.5 SD) as a pre-specified second cohort, so that both the highest-risk and the broader preclinical populations are tested in one protocol.
  2. Run at least five years with progression to cognitive impairment as the primary endpoint, with the latent PACC slope as a co-primary continuous readout — the very-high group declines at −0.07 units per year against +0.03 in the low group, so a treatment that returns the slope toward zero is measurable within the trial's window.

The intervention to test first is a tau-lowering drug of the diranersen class. The July 2026 CELIA phase 2 data give the rationale: in 416 people with early symptomatic AD, the antisense oligonucleotide diranersen (60 mg intrathecally every six months) lowered CSF total tau by 50–65% across all doses, reduced tau PET signal in every brain region examined, and slowed decline by 26% on CDR-SB (0.54 points), 42% on ADAS-Cog13 and 50% on MMSE at 18 months — roughly the magnitude of the approved anti-amyloid antibodies — with no ARIA events. The trial missed its primary dose-response endpoint (higher doses did not do better), so the efficacy signal is provisional and Biogen's confirmatory phase 3, starting in 2027 with data expected 2030–2031, is the proper test in symptomatic disease. But the mechanistic case for testing tau-lowering before symptoms is now the strongest it has ever been: tau burden, not amyloid burden, tracks cognition, and p-tau217 is the blood read-out of that burden. A prevention trial that enriches on p-tau217 and intervenes on tau is the first trial in which the enrichment marker, the drug target and the outcome measure all point at the same biology.

4.3 The falsifiable claim

Claim: A five-year, randomised, placebo-controlled prevention trial enrolling cognitively unimpaired adults with very-high plasma p-tau217 (≥2.5 SD) and testing a tau-lowering intervention will (a) observe a placebo-arm progression rate of 33–43% (point estimate 38%), and (b) detect a 30% relative risk reduction with ≤650 total participants at 80% power.

Test: Enrol ~526 participants (263 per arm) with very-high p-tau217, randomise to a tau-lowering intervention or placebo for five years, with progression to cognitive impairment (MCI, dementia, or two consecutive global CDR scores ≥0.5 — the Buckley endpoint) as primary, and latent PACC slope as co-primary.

What counts as refutation: If the placebo-arm five-year progression rate falls below 25%, the enrichment assumption is refuted — the Buckley risks do not transport to a trial population, and the sample-size arithmetic in Table 2 is void. If the placebo rate is within 33–43% but the treated arm shows no risk reduction despite demonstrated tau lowering (CSF total tau down ≥50%, as in CELIA), the tau-lowering prevention hypothesis is refuted in this population. If the placebo rate holds and the risk reduction appears, the enrichment strategy is validated and justifies a phase 3 in the broader high stratum.

4.4 The ethics of knowing: patients-in-waiting

A test that can put a number on a healthy person's future creates a new kind of patient. A very-high p-tau217 result in a cognitively unimpaired person means a 38% chance of impairment within five years and 78% within ten — and no approved treatment to offer them. A JAMA Viewpoint in October 2026 warned that such results can turn healthy adults into "patients-in-waiting" with few legal protections, and the study authors themselves advise against clinical testing of asymptomatic people. This paper agrees, and draws the line sharply: p-tau217 enrichment belongs in research, not in routine screening, until a prevention drug exists. The ethical design of an enriched prevention trial must therefore include pre-test counselling, a right not to know one's stratum, and a plan for what participants are told when the trial ends. Enrichment that is scientifically efficient but ethically careless will destroy the trust on which prevention research depends.

4.5 Why this matters beyond wealthy health systems

For Pakistan and other low- and middle-income countries, the blood test matters more than the PET scan it replaces. Amyloid PET costs thousands of dollars per scan and exists in a handful of centres; a plasma p-tau217 assay is a blood draw. The AHEAD screening programme already uses %p-tau217 as the first pass before PET, across 106 sites on four continents, and showed the marker works across racial and ethnic groups (Molina-Henry et al., 2026). That makes p-tau217 the first AD biomarker that could plausibly be deployed at population scale in a country like Pakistan. But deployment without treatment is surveillance, not care: Pakistan has no prevention drug, no reimbursement pathway for one, and a dementia-care infrastructure that is largely family-based. The honest sequence is research participation first — Pakistani cohorts in global prevention trials, with the same counselling and protections — and clinical screening only after a prevention drug exists and is affordable. The numbers in this paper are offered as a design tool for that research, not as a reason to sell tests to healthy people.

5. Limitations

  1. The Buckley risks are model-based standardised estimates from six selected research cohorts; participants were enriched for family history and APOE ε4, so absolute risks likely overstate those in the general population. The gradient between strata is more transportable than the levels.
  2. The 10-year risks rest on sparse data (5% of participants followed beyond 10 years, mostly in one cohort) and are indicative only.
  3. The "unselected" reference rate (17.8%) is the observed proportion progressed over a median 5.4 years, not a model-based five-year risk; it is an approximation, and the unselected sample size inherits that approximation.
  4. Sample sizes assume a constant 30% relative risk reduction, no loss to follow-up, and no competing risks; real trials need inflation for attrition and for the fact that some participants will die of other causes before progressing.
  5. Stratum prevalences (the fraction of screened people who are very-high) are not extracted here, so the number needed to screen — and therefore the screening cost of enrichment — is not computed. This is the largest practical gap in the paper.
  6. The diranersen efficacy figures are conference-reported phase 2 results; the primary dose-response endpoint was missed, and the drug has not been tested in cognitively unimpaired people. It is used here as the worked example of a tau-lowering intervention, not as proven prevention therapy.
  7. No new experimental data are presented. The trial arithmetic is computation from published risks; the hypothesis is untested.

6. Conclusion

A blood test can now put a number on an asymptomatic person's five-year risk of cognitive impairment: 12% if p-tau217 is low, 38% if it is very high. That number turns Alzheimer's prevention from an un-sizeable aspiration into a designable trial. Our arithmetic shows the scale of the change: a five-year prevention trial powered to detect a 30% risk reduction needs 1,412 unselected participants, 982 in the high stratum, and only 526 in the very-high stratum — with the number needed to treat falling from 18.7 to 8.8. The same numbers set the floor: no prevention trial can work in under five years, because two-year risks are 1–4% in every stratum. The next step is a trial that takes the numbers seriously — very-high p-tau217 enrichment, a five-year horizon, a tau-lowering intervention, and a pre-specified refutation rule. If the placebo arm progresses at the predicted rate and the drug does not slow it, the tau-prevention hypothesis fails cleanly; if it does, prevention becomes real. Either outcome is worth five years. What is not worth doing is testing healthy people in clinic before any of this exists.

The Blood–Brain Barrier Gap: Why First-Generation GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Failed in Parkinson's Disease, and the Penetrance-and-Enrichment Trial That Could Settle It

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) entered Parkinson's disease (PD) trials on a strong mechanistic rationale — brain insulin resistance, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired proteostasis — and early-phase signals were encouraging.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification. Do not cite as established evidence.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto Medical University (SMBBMU), Larkana, Pakistan Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2 November 2026 · Paper #2 — Brain track (Daily Research Papers)

Keywords: GLP-1 receptor agonist; Parkinson's disease; blood–brain barrier; exenatide; lixisenatide; disease modification; insulin resistance; CNS drug design

Abstract

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) entered Parkinson's disease (PD) trials on a strong mechanistic rationale — brain insulin resistance, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired proteostasis — and early-phase signals were encouraging. The field has now turned: the phase III Exenatide-PD3 trial (n = 194, 96 weeks) found no effect on motor progression (adjusted coefficient 0.92; 95% CI −1.56 to 3.39; p = 0.47), and a 2026 meta-analysis of four randomised trials (667 patients) found no motor benefit in either the OFF-medication (mean difference −0.69; 95% CI −2.81 to 1.43; p = 0.52) or ON-medication state, with significantly increased nausea (risk ratio 2.48), vomiting (4.53) and weight loss (3.32). Yet the phase II LIXIPARK trial of lixisenatide reported a significant 3.08-point benefit (95% CI 0.86–5.30; p = 0.007), and the flagship negative trial is now under a Lancet Expression of Concern (June 2026) following a regulatory inspection that found critical and major trial-conduct concerns at one of six sites. We add a new quantitative fact to this contradiction: using PubChem structures (cross-checked with RDKit), every peptide GLP-1 RA trialled in PD sits 8–11× above the 450 Da molecular-weight cut-off and 17–23× above the 90 Å² polar-surface-area cut-off for passive blood–brain barrier (BBB) penetration, meeting 0 of 4 standard CNS-likeness criteria — and no PD trial of these agents ever demonstrated CNS target engagement. The paradox is that lixisenatide, the least BBB-permeable agent in our table, produced the only positive trial, so penetrance alone cannot explain the pattern. We therefore propose the penetrance-and-enrichment hypothesis: the class has not been fairly tested, because trials combined (i) agents with no demonstrated brain exposure, (ii) unselected patients, diluting any effect in the insulin-resistant subgroup where the mechanism should act, and (iii) no biomarker of target engagement. The falsifiable prediction: in early PD with documented insulin resistance, a brain-penetrant incretin (CSF:plasma ratio ≥ 0.05, or a measurable rise in neuronal extracellular-vesicle insulin signalling) will slow MDS-UPDRS Part III progression by ≥ 3 points versus placebo at 12 months; if engagement is demonstrated without motor benefit, the mechanism is engaged but not disease-modifying. Either outcome settles the question that the first-generation trials could not.

1. Introduction

Parkinson's disease is the world's fastest-growing neurodegenerative disorder, and no therapy has yet been shown to slow its progression. Repurposing antidiabetic drugs became one of the most credible disease-modification strategies after epidemiological and mechanistic work linked type 2 diabetes and PD through shared pathways: brain insulin resistance, chronic neuroinflammation, mitochondrial failure, defective autophagy and proteostasis, and cerebrovascular injury. GLP-1 receptors are expressed across neurons, glia and the cerebral vasculature, and in preclinical models GLP-1 receptor agonism showed anti-neuroinflammatory signalling, mitochondrial preservation, enhanced autophagy, anti-apoptotic effects, improved synaptic plasticity and better glymphatic clearance.

The clinical translation followed the classic repurposing arc: a small phase II exenatide trial (Athauda et al., 2017) reported a motor benefit of ~3.5 points on the MDS-UPDRS Part III that persisted after washout; the phase II LIXIPARK trial of lixisenatide (Meissner et al., 2024) reported a significant 3.08-point between-group difference; then the larger, longer phase III Exenatide-PD3 trial (Vijiaratnam et al., 2025) found no benefit at all. Two 2026 pooled analyses now conclude the class offers no motor benefit in the general PD population. On that reading, the story is over.

We argue the story is not over — it was never properly tested. Three facts, taken together, undermine the "class failed" verdict. First, the negative verdict leans heavily on a single phase III trial that is now under a Lancet Expression of Concern over trial-conduct findings. Second, the positive and negative trials used agents and regimens that differ in ways never controlled for — daily versus weekly dosing, immediate- versus extended-release formulations, and different molecules. Third, and the new contribution of this paper, not one agent trialled in PD was designed to enter the brain, and none demonstrated that it did: we quantify here, for the first time in one table, just how far outside BBB-permeable chemical space every trialled GLP-1 RA sits, and we show that the small-molecule incretins now in development sit far closer to that space. A drug that never reaches its target cannot test its target's hypothesis.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature basis

Trial results, effect sizes and safety data are taken from the published trials and pooled analyses cited in the References, as synthesised in a 2026 narrative review of GLP-1 RAs in PD and Alzheimer's disease (search through May 2026) and in contemporaneous reporting of the 2026 MDS Congress. The Expression of Concern is cited from The Lancet (2026). No unpublished, anecdotal or press-release-only efficacy claim is used as evidence; the KP405 phase I data are presented only as a biomarker signal from a conference abstract, explicitly labelled exploratory.

2.2 Blood–brain barrier descriptor computation

Canonical structures for seven incretin agents were retrieved from PubChem (PUG REST, 2 November 2026) by compound name, recording PubChem CID, molecular weight, topological polar surface area (TPSA), hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor counts, rotatable-bond count and XLogP. Descriptors were independently cross-checked with RDKit (version in the LeadForge environment) from the same SMILES: exenatide MW 4186.6 (PubChem 4187), TPSA 1750 (PubChem 1780); danuglipron MW 555.6, TPSA 114 (exact match); orforglipron MW 883.0, TPSA 156 (PubChem 144). Small differences reflect the TPSA/H-bond-count algorithms of the two toolkits and do not change any conclusion. Each agent was scored against four standard CNS-likeness criteria for passive BBB penetration: molecular weight ≤ 450 Da, TPSA ≤ 90 Å², hydrogen-bond donors ≤ 3, and 1 ≤ logP ≤ 3. The full computation script and outputs are in the data-availability note. NLY01, a PEGylated exenatide included in the four-trial meta-analysis, has no defined small-molecule PubChem record and is excluded from the descriptor table; its exclusion does not affect the conclusion, since PEGylation increases, not decreases, molecular weight.

2.3 Honesty limits

This is a literature-synthesis and computational-descriptor study. No new patient data, no animal data and no new laboratory measurements are presented. Descriptor cut-offs predict passive BBB diffusion only; peptides may reach the brain in small amounts via saturable transport or circumventricular organs, and peripheral mechanisms (systemic inflammation, vascular function, glymphatic clearance) could in principle mediate CNS effects without substantial brain penetration. The paper's claim is therefore narrow: CNS target engagement was never demonstrated, not that it was zero.

3. Results

3.1 The trial record, 2017–2026

Trial (agent) Phase n Duration / design Primary result (MDS-UPDRS Part III, OFF-medication unless stated)
Exenatide-PD (Athauda 2017) II 62 48 weeks, twice-daily exenatide ~3.5-point between-group benefit, persisting after washout
LIXIPARK (Meissner 2024) II 156 12 months, daily lixisenatide 20 µg 3.08-point benefit (95% CI 0.86–5.30; p = 0.007); nausea in 46% of treated patients
Exenatide-PD3 (Vijiaratnam 2025) III 194 96 weeks, weekly extended-release exenatide 2 mg No effect: scores worsened 5.7 (exenatide) vs 4.5 (placebo) points; adjusted coefficient 0.92 (95% CI −1.56 to 3.39; p = 0.47); serious adverse events 9% vs 11%
Pooled meta-analysis (Neurol Sci 2026) — 667 (4 trials) Exenatide, lixisenatide, NLY01 vs placebo OFF: MD −0.69 (95% CI −2.81 to 1.43; p = 0.52); ON: MD −0.86 (95% CI −3.53 to 1.63; p = 0.50); no benefit on non-motor symptoms, cognition or quality of life
Network meta-analysis (Ali et al. 2026) — 708 (5 trials) All GLP-1 RAs pooled Pairwise MD −2.00 (95% CI −5.46 to 1.46); I² = 80.5% — trials disagree substantially

Two features of this record matter. First, heterogeneity is extreme (I² = 80.5% in the network meta-analysis): pooling agents, formulations and regimens into one "class effect" obscures more than it reveals. Second, the single largest and longest trial — the one that dominates the negative verdict — is now formally questioned: in June 2026 The Lancet issued an Expression of Concern (2026;407(10548):2588) after a regulatory inspection at King's College Hospital, one of the six UK sites, identified department-wide concerns relating to trial conduct, oversight and governance, including findings classified by regulators as critical and major. Whether those findings affect the data or conclusions is, at the time of writing, unresolved. A negative verdict that rests substantially on a trial under such a cloud is a provisional verdict, not a closed one.

3.2 No trialled agent can passively cross the blood–brain barrier

Agent PubChem CID MW (Da) × 450 Da limit TPSA (Å²) × 90 Å² limit H-bond donors H-bond acceptors XLogP CNS criteria met (of 4)
Exenatide 45588096 4187 9.3× 1780 19.8× 58 66 −21.0 0/4
Lixisenatide 90472060 4858 10.8× 2090 23.2× 70 77 −30.8 0/4
Liraglutide 16134956 3751 8.3× 1510 16.8× 54 55 −3.4 0/4
Semaglutide 56843331 4114 9.1× 1650 18.3× 57 63 −5.8 0/4
Tirzepatide 166567236 4813 10.7× 1790 19.9× 58 70 −6.8 0/4
Orforglipron 137319706 883 2.0× 144 1.6× 1 10 6.8 1/4
Danuglipron 134611040 556 1.2× 114 1.3× 1 9 1.4 2/4

Every peptide GLP-1 RA trialled in PD — exenatide, lixisenatide, and the comparators liraglutide, semaglutide and tirzepatide — is a 3.8–4.9 kDa peptide with 54–70 hydrogen-bond donors and a polar surface area of 1510–2090 Å²: roughly an order of magnitude above the molecular-weight cut-off and 17–23× above the polar-surface-area cut-off for passive BBB penetration. All five meet 0 of 4 CNS-likeness criteria. By contrast, the small-molecule GLP-1 RAs now in clinical development are far closer to BBB-permeable space: danuglipron (556 Da, TPSA 114 Å², 1 H-bond donor) exceeds the cut-offs by only ~1.2–1.3× and meets 2 of 4 criteria; orforglipron (883 Da, TPSA 144 Å²) exceeds them by ~1.6–2.0× but is too lipophilic (XLogP 6.8). Neither small molecule has yet been trialled in PD. The same gap is now being addressed from the peptide side: KP405, a dual GLP-1/GIP agonist incorporating a short cell-penetrating peptide sequence intended to carry the molecule into the brain, showed exploratory changes in neuron-derived extracellular-vesicle biomarkers of insulin signalling, neuroprotection and neuroinflammation after 7 days in a small phase I study (8 participants per cohort; 6 on drug, 2 on placebo; MDS Congress 2026, late-breaking abstract LBA23). The investigators stress the study was not designed or powered for efficacy — but it is the first incretin PD study to even measure a brain-derived engagement signal.

3.3 The lixisenatide paradox

The descriptor table creates a problem for any simple penetrance story: lixisenatide — the largest molecule in the table (4858 Da), the highest TPSA (2090 Å²), the most hydrogen-bond donors (70) — produced the only statistically significant positive trial, while exenatide, the least impermeable of the trialled peptides, failed in phase III. If brain penetration were the whole story, the ranking should be reversed. Three explanations are compatible with the data, and the literature does not currently distinguish them:

  1. Chance and attrition. LIXIPARK was a 156-patient phase II trial with substantial gastrointestinal dropout (nausea in 46% of treated patients); differential dropout can bias a motor endpoint. The result (p = 0.007) is real but fragile.
  2. Exposure pattern, not molecule. Lixisenatide was given daily; Exenatide-PD3 used a weekly extended-release formulation, while the positive phase II exenatide trial used twice-daily immediate-release dosing. Daily peaks versus flat weekly exposure may matter for a receptor that desensitises — but no trial has tested this.
  3. Peripheral mechanisms. If the benefit is mediated outside the brain — systemic anti-inflammatory effects, cerebrovascular protection, improved glymphatic clearance — then BBB penetration is irrelevant, and the molecule ranking is meaningless. This is plausible but unproven, because no trial measured a peripheral mediator alongside the motor endpoint.

The honest conclusion is that the existing trials cannot distinguish these three explanations — because none of them measured brain exposure, a target-engagement biomarker, or a pre-specified insulin-resistant subgroup. The field ran efficacy trials before establishing pharmacology.

4. Discussion

4.1 What the first-generation trials actually tested

They tested whether systemic administration of large, non-brain-penetrant peptides improves motor scores in unselected PD. That is a legitimate question, and the answer, on current evidence, is no — with the LIXIPARK exception and the Exenatide-PD3 caveat noted above. But it is not the question the mechanistic literature posed. The mechanistic literature proposes that GLP-1 receptor signalling inside the brain — on neurons and microglia — is neuroprotective. No trial has tested that proposition, because no trial used an agent shown to reach the brain, or verified that it did. The distinction matters for what comes next: abandoning the mechanism on the basis of these trials would be like abandoning a drug because the oral formulation never reached the bloodstream.

4.2 The penetrance-and-enrichment hypothesis

We propose that the next incretin trial in PD should be designed to test the mechanism, not repeat the exposure error. Its three design commitments:

  1. A brain-penetrant agent, with exposure proven. Either a molecule engineered for CNS entry (KP405-class, with its cell-penetrating design) or a small-molecule GLP-1 RA (danuglipron-class, the closest to BBB space in our table), with a pre-specified CSF:plasma ratio threshold (≥ 0.05) measured in every participant.
  2. Biomarker enrichment. Enrol early PD with documented insulin resistance (e.g. HOMA-IR ≥ 2.5) and/or elevated neuroinflammatory markers — the subgroup in which the mechanism should act. Unselected enrolment diluted any signal in the first-generation trials; the 2026 meta-analyses explicitly note they could not perform diabetic versus non-diabetic subgroup analyses for lack of data.
  3. Target engagement as a co-primary readout. Neuronal extracellular-vesicle insulin-signalling scores (the KP405 phase I approach) or CSF markers, measured alongside MDS-UPDRS Part III. Engagement without clinical benefit and clinical benefit without engagement are both informative — the former kills the mechanism, the latter points to a peripheral one.

4.3 The falsifiable claim

Claim: In early Parkinson's disease with documented insulin resistance, a brain-penetrant incretin that achieves measurable CNS target engagement will slow MDS-UPDRS Part III progression by ≥ 3 points (the accepted minimal clinically important difference) versus placebo at 12 months.

Test: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II trial (n ≈ 120–150, powered for a 3-point difference), enrolling Hoehn & Yahr ≤ 2 patients with HOMA-IR ≥ 2.5, randomised to a brain-penetrant incretin or placebo for 12 months, with (a) CSF drug concentration and CSF:plasma ratio in all participants, (b) neuronal extracellular-vesicle insulin-signalling scores, and (c) OFF-medication MDS-UPDRS Part III as the primary clinical endpoint.

What counts as refutation: If the agent reaches the pre-specified CSF threshold and the engagement biomarker moves, but the motor difference is < 3 points (or null), the incretin-neuroprotection mechanism is refuted as a disease-modifying strategy in this population. If engagement is not achieved, the trial is inconclusive about the mechanism and the agent — not the hypothesis — has failed. If engagement is achieved and the motor benefit appears, the mechanism survives its first fair test and justifies phase III.

4.4 Cost and feasibility — why this matters beyond neurology

The proposed trial is feasible in a resource-constrained setting: the agents are repurposed or in late development, the enrichment test (HOMA-IR) costs pennies, and the engagement readouts (CSF sampling, extracellular-vesicle assays) are available at academic centres. For Pakistan, where diabetes prevalence approaches 30% and the PD population is therefore disproportionately insulin-resistant, the enrichment strategy is not a niche refinement — it is the population. A negative result under this design would be as valuable as a positive one, because it would close a decade-long question cleanly instead of leaving it to another under-powered, unmeasured trial.

5. Limitations

  1. Descriptor cut-offs predict passive diffusion; they do not rule out low-level brain entry via saturable transport, circumventricular organs or receptor-mediated uptake. Our claim is that engagement was never demonstrated, not that it was zero.
  2. LogP estimates are method-dependent (PubChem XLogP versus RDKit MolLogP differ substantially for these molecules); no conclusion here rests on logP.
  3. The Exenatide-PD3 Expression of Concern is unresolved; we do not claim the trial's data are wrong, only that a verdict resting on it is provisional.
  4. LIXIPARK's positive result may be chance; we present it as an unresolved signal, not as proof of efficacy.
  5. KP405 phase I data are conference-abstract level, exploratory, and from 6 treated participants per cohort; they are cited only as proof that engagement can be measured, not as evidence of benefit.
  6. No new experimental data are presented. The descriptor table is computational; the hypothesis is untested.

6. Conclusion

First-generation GLP-1 receptor agonists did not fail in Parkinson's disease because the incretin-neuroprotection hypothesis was tested and found wanting. They failed — with one positive exception and one trial now under a cloud — without ever demonstrating that the drug reached its target in the brain, in patients selected for the mechanism, with engagement measured. Our descriptor analysis quantifies the gap: every trialled peptide sits 8–11× above the molecular-weight limit and 17–23× above the polar-surface-area limit for passive BBB penetration. The next trial should close that gap first — brain-penetrant agent, insulin-resistant enrichment, engagement as a co-primary readout — and let the result, whichever way it falls, actually answer the question.

Pinning the Cosmic Shoreline with JWST: LTT 1445 A b and c Are Airless Above the Line, LHS 1140 b Keeps Its Helium Below It

Two results published in November 2026 test the cosmic shoreline — the I ∝ v_esc^4 boundary that separates rocky planets with atmospheres from airless worlds — from opposite sides.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan — ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-14 Field: Space (astronomy / exoplanet atmospheres)

Abstract

Two results published in November 2026 test the cosmic shoreline — the I ∝ v_esc^4 boundary that separates rocky planets with atmospheres from airless worlds — from opposite sides. The JWST Rocky Worlds programme reports MIRI/F1500W secondary eclipses of LTT 1445 A b and c (Ih et al., arXiv:2611.17300): eclipse depths of 157(+18/−17) and 154(+54/−37) ppm give 15-µm brightness temperatures of 528(+39/−29) K and 625(+109/−79) K, both consistent with dark bare rock; for b, CO2 partial pressure is <0.6 mbar and surface pressure ≲0.1 bar. LTT 1445 A b is the closest planet to the shoreline yet observed in eclipse. In the same week, ground-based spectroscopy reported metastable helium escaping from the habitable-zone super-Earth LHS 1140 b in 2024 but not in 2025 (Cherubim et al., Science 2026), while four JWST NIRISS transits rule out helium at the reported level (Radica 2026; Bennett et al. 2026). We place all three planets on the classical Mars-anchored XUV shoreline, I_XUV = (a⊕/a)^2 (L*/L⊙)^0.4, and find LTT 1445 A b 2.3× above the line, LTT 1445 A c 11.9× above it, and LHS 1140 b 8.5× below it — every planet on its predicted side. The two results bracket the shoreline zero point to log10 I_XUV = 4 log10 v_esc + D with D in [−4.10, −2.81], against the canonical −3.17. We state this as a falsifiable claim: any substantial atmosphere found on a rocky planet more than 0.36 dex above the classical line, or any bare rock more than 0.93 dex below it, falsifies the classical zero point; simultaneous ground- and space-based helium transits of LHS 1140 b will decide whether its lower bound stands.

Keywords: exoplanet atmospheres; cosmic shoreline; atmospheric escape; JWST; M dwarfs; LTT 1445; LHS 1140 b; helium

1. Introduction

Which rocky planets keep their atmospheres? The question decides where habitable worlds can exist, and for a decade the organising idea has been the "cosmic shoreline" of Zahnle & Catling (2017): when Solar System bodies are arranged by escape velocity (v_esc) against the radiation they receive, a single straight line of slope four on logarithmic axes, I ∝ v_esc^4, separates the bodies with atmospheres from those without. The line is now the target-selection metric for the largest rocky-atmosphere survey ever attempted — the JWST Rocky Worlds Director's Discretionary Time (DDT) programme, 500 hours of JWST time plus 240 Hubble orbits, which uses secondary-eclipse photometry to test, planet by planet, whether rocky worlds around M dwarfs retain atmospheres (Ji et al. 2025).

Two results published within days of each other in November 2026 test the shoreline from opposite sides, and both concern the nearest rocky systems known. First, the Rocky Worlds programme reports MIRI/F1500W (15 µm) secondary eclipses of LTT 1445 A b and c, the transiting rocky siblings in the nearest M-dwarf system (6.9 pc): both planets are consistent with dark bare rock, and planet b — the closest planet to the canonical XUV-driven shoreline yet observed in eclipse — has no substantial atmosphere (Ih et al. 2026). Second, ground-based high-resolution spectroscopy reports metastable helium escaping from LHS 1140 b, a temperate super-Earth in the habitable zone of its M dwarf, detected in 2024 but not in 2025 (Cherubim et al. 2026), while four archival JWST NIRISS transits spanning December 2023 to July 2026 find no helium absorption at the reported level (Radica 2026; Bennett et al. 2026) — a dispute covered the same week in Nature Astronomy (Maltagliati 2026).

This paper does the quantitative step neither result takes on its own: it places all three planets on the same classical shoreline, using the published cumulative-XUV scaling, and derives the numerical bracket the two results jointly impose on the shoreline's zero point. The shoreline's slope is fixed by energy-limited escape physics; its height — the zero point — was set in 2017 by a single Solar System anchor, Mars, and has never been tested by exoplanets on both sides at once. These three planets now test it from both sides.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature sweep

The daily research digest for 2026-11-14 (health-focused; no space entries) was read, and targeted searches were run on arXiv (astro-ph.EP) and in the press for exoplanet-atmosphere results dated 10–14 November 2026. Every cited result was verified against its arXiv record or publisher page: the LTT 1445 paper (arXiv:2611.17300, submitted 12 November 2026), the LHS 1140 b helium detection (arXiv:2607.14326) and its two JWST follow-ups (arXiv:2608.13470; arXiv:2608.13473), and the Nature Astronomy News & Views piece (DOI 10.1038/s41550-026-03029-8, published 13 November 2026). No citation, number, or identifier in this manuscript is invented; where a number is our own derivation, the formula and inputs are shown in full.

2.2 The shoreline calculation (own analysis)

Escape velocity. v_esc = √(2GM_p/R_p), computed from published masses and radii relative to Earth (v_esc,⊕ = 11.186 km/s).

Cumulative XUV instellation. Following Zahnle & Catling (2017, Eq. 27), as restated by Meni-Gallardo & Pallé (2026):

I_XUV = (a⊕ / a)^2 × (L* / L⊙)^0.4

in Earth units, where a is the planet's semi-major axis and L* the stellar luminosity. This is the total stellar XUV flux integrated over the planet's lifetime, not the present-day bolometric insolation — the distinction matters for M dwarfs, whose long pre-main-sequence and flare activity make their cumulative XUV far larger than their present-day brightness suggests.

Shoreline and zero point. The classical shoreline is log10 I_XUV = 4 log10 v_esc + D. The zero point D was fixed by Zahnle & Catling by assuming Mars marks the boundary between worlds with and without atmospheres. We adopt that convention exactly: the shoreline passes through Mars's (v_esc, I_XUV) point, giving D = −3.17 (Mars: v_esc = 5.03 km/s, a = 1.524 AU, L* = L⊙, I_XUV = 0.43). A planet's shoreline distance is Δ = log10(I_XUV / I_XUV,shore), positive above the line (airless side), negative below it (retaining side).

Dayside temperature scale. For reference, the maximum dayside temperature for instant reradiation with zero albedo is T_day,max = T_eq × 4^(1/4), where T_eq is the zero-albedo equilibrium temperature. The observed 15-µm brightness temperature is a band temperature, not a bolometric dayside temperature, so ratios against T_day,max are reported as a scale comparison only; the papers' own conclusion ("consistent with the dark, bare rock limit") is what we rely on.

Inputs. LTT 1445 A b/c masses, radii, semi-major axes, instellations and equilibrium temperatures are from Pass et al. (2023, HST/WFC3 joint fit): b, M = 2.73 M⊕, R = 1.34 R⊕, a = 0.03813 AU, S = 5.7 S⊕, T_eq = 431 K; c, M = 1.37 ± 0.19 M⊕, R = 1.07 R⊕, a = 0.02659 AU, S = 11.7 S⊕, T_eq = 516 K; stellar luminosity L* = 0.00805 L⊙. LHS 1140 b uses the most precise values to date (Cherubim et al. 2026): M = 5.60 ± 0.19 M⊕, R = 1.730 ± 0.025 R⊕; with system parameters from Ment et al. (2019): a = 0.0936 AU, L* = 0.00441 L⊙, S = 0.503 S⊕, T_eq = 230 K. All arithmetic was computed in Python 3 and is reproducible from the formulae above.

Robustness checks. (i) Using the earlier Winters et al. (2022) masses and radii for LTT 1445 A b/c (M = 2.87/1.54 M⊕, R = 1.305/1.147 R⊕) changes the shoreline ratios from 2.29 to 1.96 (b) and 11.91 to 10.83 (c) — no conclusion changes. (ii) Pass et al. (2025), as summarised by Ji et al. (2025), revised cumulative XUV fluxes for mid-to-late M dwarfs upward by roughly a factor of 3 (pre-main-sequence plus flares); we repeat the calculation with I_XUV × 3 as a sensitivity test.

3. Results

3.1 LTT 1445 A b and c: bare rock at the shoreline

Ih et al. (2026) present Rocky Worlds DDT MIRI/F1500W observations of LTT 1445 A b and c — two eclipses of each planet across three visits — with three independent reductions and a joint fit including all existing JWST data and 220 radial velocities, improving the precision on planetary radii, masses, and orbital parameters by factors of 1.6–2.3. They measure eclipse depths of 157(+18/−17) ppm (b) and 154(+54/−37) ppm (c), corresponding to 15-µm brightness temperatures of 528(+39/−29) K and 625(+109/−79) K, both consistent with the dark, bare-rock limit. For planet b, combining these data with the archival MIRI/LRS spectrum in a Bayesian retrieval limits the CO2 partial pressure to <0.6 mbar and the surface pressure to ≲0.1 bar, while forward models exclude thick aerosol layers that could mimic a bare surface in transmission; the authors conclude planet b has no substantial atmosphere. For planet c, a potentially grazing eclipse and overlapping events leave the depth poorly constrained, and the data rule out only thick, CO2-bearing atmospheres (≳1 bar with ≥1% CO2). The paper states explicitly that LTT 1445 A b is the planet closest to the canonical XUV-driven Cosmic Shoreline observed in eclipse so far, and that its lack of a substantial atmosphere implies the shoreline cannot lie much farther toward the airless side than nominally predicted. This agrees with the earlier MIRI/LRS spectrum (Wachiraphan et al. 2025), which found a dayside brightness temperature of 525 ± 15 K and excluded >1 bar CO2 atmospheres at >4σ, and with the climate-constrained Bayesian analysis of Wogan et al. (2026), which found the bare-rock model moderately favoured over any atmospheric model (2σ upper limits ≲1 bar for O2/N2/CO, ≲0.1 bar for CO2).

3.2 LHS 1140 b: helium detected, then not — and JWST says no

Cherubim et al. (2026) observed LHS 1140 b with the WINERED high-resolution spectrograph on the Magellan Clay Telescope. In a transit on 23 September 2024 they detected excess absorption at the 1.083 µm metastable helium triplet: 1.24(+0.22/−0.23)% depth at the blended long-wavelength peaks, with FWHM 0.86 Å (23.9 km/s), interpreted as helium escaping from the upper atmosphere — the first evidence of an atmosphere, albeit a primordial one, around a rocky world in the classical habitable zone. A repeat transit in September 2025 showed no helium absorption, with an upper limit of 0.6% on the line depth, indicating time-variable escape; no helium was detected for the smaller, more irradiated sibling LHS 1140 c. The authors interpret the result as an upper atmosphere dominated by helium and depleted in hydrogen, consistent with atmospheric fractionation models.

Two independent JWST analyses challenge the persistence of that signal. Radica (2026) analyses four archival NIRISS/SOSS transits spanning December 2023 to July 2026: each visit disfavours helium absorption against a flat continuum with odds ratios of 3.9–11.6:1, and helium at the amplitude and width reported by Cherubim et al. is strongly ruled out, with odds ratios of 300–8.6×10^4:1 — though none of the JWST transits is contemporaneous with the ground-based detection — setting an abundance upper limit of 350–500 ppm. Bennett et al. (2026) likewise detect no helium in any of the four visits, reject the best-fit ground-based model at >3σ in each visit, and find no clear trend in mass loss with time; they conclude the reported detection may be spurious, although variability cannot be excluded if detectable helium absorption occurs in ≲50% of transits. Maltagliati (2026), in Nature Astronomy, frames the episode as "helium peekaboo": the first helium-escape claim for a habitable-zone rocky planet, contradicted in every JWST epoch so far.

3.3 Our calculation: three planets, three shoreline distances, one bracket

Table 1 gives the shoreline positions computed by §2.2. All three planets fall exactly on their predicted sides: the two planets above the line are airless, and the planet below the line shows (at least in one epoch) an escaping atmosphere.

Table 1. Shoreline positions of the three newly measured rocky planets (own calculation from published inputs).

Planet v_esc (km/s) I_XUV (Earth units) I_XUV,shore Ratio Δ (dex) JWST / ground verdict
LTT 1445 A b 15.97 99.95 43.71 2.29 +0.36 Airless (CO2 < 0.6 mbar)
LTT 1445 A c 12.66 205.53 17.26 11.91 +1.08 Thick CO2 ruled out
LHS 1140 b 20.13 13.04 110.34 0.12 −0.93 He escape reported 2024; JWST rules it out in 4/4 transits

The two results jointly bracket the shoreline zero point. Planet b's airlessness requires the shoreline at v_esc = 15.97 km/s to sit at or below I_XUV = 99.95, i.e. D ≤ −2.81: the zero point cannot be more than a factor 2.29 above its canonical Mars-anchored value (D = −3.17). LHS 1140 b's reported atmosphere requires the shoreline at v_esc = 20.13 km/s to sit at or above I_XUV = 13.04, i.e. D ≥ −4.10: the zero point cannot be more than a factor 8.46 below canonical. The allowed interval is therefore D ∈ [−4.10, −2.81], a factor-of-19.4 band that contains the canonical value with room on both sides — but with a hard, new upper edge set by the closest-to-the-line airless planet ever measured in eclipse.

The Pass et al. (2025) 3× XUV revision, applied as a sensitivity test, moves all three ratios up by a factor of 3 (b: 6.86, c: 35.72, LHS 1140 b: 0.35) and flips none of the three classifications: LHS 1140 b remains below the line even under the revised fluence. The dayside-temperature scale is consistent throughout: T_b/T_day,max = 0.866 (b) and 0.856 (c), with T_b/T_eq = 1.23 and 1.21 — hot daysides with no sign of the heat redistribution a substantial atmosphere would provide (with the §2.2 caveat that 15-µm brightness temperature is a band temperature).

3.4 The falsifiable claim

Claim. The classical Mars-anchored XUV cosmic shoreline (log10 I_XUV = 4 log10 v_esc − 3.17) correctly separates airless from atmosphere-bearing rocky planets, with zero point D ∈ [−4.10, −2.81]: LTT 1445 A b (Δ = +0.36 dex) and c (Δ = +1.08 dex) are airless, and LHS 1140 b (Δ = −0.93 dex) retains an atmosphere.

How to test it. (i) The Rocky Worlds programme will eclipse roughly a dozen more rocky planets. The shoreline predicts that every planet with Δ > +0.36 dex — further above the line than LTT 1445 A b — will be airless, and every planet with Δ < −0.93 dex will show an atmosphere signature. A single substantial atmosphere found above +0.36 dex, or a single bare rock found below −0.93 dex, falsifies the classical zero point (and, if the counterexample sits far from the line, the slope as well), forcing a move toward the steeper empirical shoreline of Meni-Gallardo & Pallé (2026) or the hydrodynamic shoreline of Ji et al. (2025). (ii) The lower bound stands or falls with the reality of LHS 1140 b's helium: a simultaneous WINERED + JWST NIRISS transit campaign will decide it. If helium at the 2024 level (1.24%) reappears in both instruments at once, variability is real and the lower bound D ≥ −4.10 stands; if JWST rules it out again while ground data show it, the discrepancy is systematic, the lower bound must be re-derived from transmission data alone, and the shoreline's retaining side loses its only habitable-zone anchor.

4. Discussion

The value of this result is not that the shoreline survives — it was designed to survive these three planets — but that the shoreline is now a measured, bracketed quantity rather than a single-anchor extrapolation. Before November 2026, the zero point rested on Mars alone: one planet, with a 6-mbar remnant atmosphere, sitting essentially on the line. Now the upper edge is set by an exoplanet: LTT 1445 A b is the first airless world measured in eclipse close enough to the line to matter, and its distance from the line (+0.36 dex) is the tightest exoplanet constraint on how far the shoreline can move toward the airless side. The lower edge is set by LHS 1140 b, the only temperate rocky planet with a claimed escaping atmosphere, 0.93 dex below the line.

Three features of the bracket deserve emphasis. First, it is asymmetric: the shoreline is pinned 2.3× from above but 8.5× from below, because the airless side now has a near-line calibrator while the retaining side has only one planet, far below the line, whose atmosphere is itself disputed. The most valuable next measurement is therefore not another far-above-the-line bare rock — the Rocky Worlds programme already has several (TRAPPIST-1 b and c, GJ 3929b, GJ 367b) — but a planet just below the line, which would tighten the lower edge the way LTT 1445 A b tightened the upper one. Second, the bracket is robust to the largest known systematic: tripling the cumulative XUV fluence for M dwarfs, as Pass et al. (2025) propose, changes no classification, because the three planets sit far enough from the line in ratio space (2.3×, 11.9×, 8.5×) that a factor-3 shift cannot cross them. Third, the bracket is compatible with, but does not require, the two 2025–2026 revisions of the shoreline: the steeper empirical shoreline of Meni-Gallardo & Pallé (2026), anchored to Mars plus four exoplanets with tentative atmospheric detections, and the hydrodynamic shoreline of Ji et al. (2025), which finds that varying the initial volatile inventory (0.01%–1% of planetary mass) blurs any single line. Both revisions predict that the classical line is an approximation; our bracket quantifies how good an approximation it is, and §3.4 gives the observations that would break it.

The LHS 1140 b dispute also carries a methodological lesson. The ground-based detection and the JWST non-detections are not yet in direct conflict, because no JWST transit was contemporaneous with the ground-based detection, and Bennett et al. show variability below a ~50% duty cycle is still allowed. But the episode shows that single-epoch helium claims for rocky planets are now in the regime where a claimed atmosphere can be challenged within months by archival data — the standard of evidence for "this rocky planet has an atmosphere" has risen, and the shoreline's lower bound should be treated as provisional until a simultaneous campaign settles it.

5. Limitations

  1. No new data. This is a synthesis and analytic re-derivation from published results; the shoreline positions are calculations, not measurements.
  2. Mars anchoring. The zero point D = −3.17 assumes Mars marks the boundary, following Zahnle & Catling (2017). Mars has a 6-mbar atmosphere, so whether it sits just above or just below the line is a judgement call in the original paper; shifting the anchor by Mars's own ambiguity moves D by ≲0.1 dex, small against the bracket width.
  3. The I_XUV scaling is a proxy. The (L*/L⊙)^0.4 scaling compresses stellar XUV evolution, pre-main-sequence duration, and flare history into one exponent; the Pass et al. (2025) 3× revision is tested as a sensitivity case, but the true fluence for any individual M dwarf is uncertain by factors of a few.
  4. Slope fixed at 4. We test the classical slope; the steeper empirical slope of Meni-Gallardo & Pallé (2026) would change the bracket, and is itself falsifiable by the same test in §3.4.
  5. Band temperatures. The 15-µm brightness temperatures are not bolometric dayside temperatures; the T_b/T_day,max ratios are a scale comparison only.
  6. The lower bound is conditional. D ≥ −4.10 assumes the Cherubim et al. (2026) helium detection is genuine. If it is spurious, the lower bound weakens to whatever JWST transmission data support for LHS 1140 b (a water-world or thin-atmosphere interpretation), and the bracket's lower edge must be re-derived.
  7. Small numbers. Three planets bracket a line; the test in §3.4 is the point — the bracket will tighten or break as the Rocky Worlds programme reports its remaining targets.
  8. Research agents. The installed research agents (Co-Scientist, Denario, EvoScientist) remain blocked on authentication — they need a real API key in the Authorization header, which this run does not hold — and Mimosa's literature-synthesis run is blocked on an unresolved MCP-discovery stall; the literature sweep and analysis here were therefore done directly from the daily digest and targeted arXiv checks.

6. Conclusion

In a single week, JWST and ground-based spectroscopy bracketed the cosmic shoreline from both sides. LTT 1445 A b — the closest planet to the line yet observed in eclipse — is airless, with CO2 below 0.6 mbar and surface pressure below 0.1 bar; its sibling c is airless too. LHS 1140 b, 0.93 dex below the line, shows escaping helium in one epoch and none in four JWST transits. Our re-derivation puts numbers on what those results mean together: the shoreline's zero point lies in D ∈ [−4.10, −2.81], no more than 2.3× above and 8.5× below its canonical Mars-anchored value. The next Rocky Worlds eclipses and a simultaneous helium transit campaign for LHS 1140 b will either tighten that bracket or break the classical line — and either outcome is progress, because the shoreline is now a falsifiable, measured quantity instead of a sketch anchored on Mars alone.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan — ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 2026-11-11 Field: Space (astronomy / gravitational-wave astrophysics)

Abstract

Two results published within days of each other in November 2026 bracket the black-hole mass spectrum from opposite ends. At the stellar-mass end, the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration's black-hole spectroscopy of GW250114 — the loudest gravitational-wave signal recorded to date, network signal-to-noise ratio 76 — requires at least two quasi-normal modes in the ringdown, constrains the dominant quadrupolar mode and its first overtone to match the Kerr prediction to tens of percent, and bounds the quadrupolar frequency to within a few percent of general relativity, delivering the most stringent single-event test of general relativity to date. At the supermassive end, the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array Collaboration reports the first direct nanohertz gravitational-wave limits on supermassive black-hole binaries at cosmic dawn (Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 191401, 2 November 2026), with a best all-sky chirp-mass upper limit of 8.47 × 10^9 solar masses and sensitivity mapped to redshift ~20 after correcting for a redshift bias earlier work ignored. We combine the two results into a single quantitative test. Treating the 1.2 × 10^10 solar-mass black hole in the quasar J0100+2802 (z = 6.327) as a hypothetical equal-mass binary gives a chirp mass of 5.22 × 10^9 solar masses — a factor of 1.62 below the current best pulsar-timing limit and a factor of 1.91 below the ~10^10 solar-mass exclusion quoted for that source, matching the published statement that the limits come within a factor of ~2 of the quasar's mass. A chirp-mass sensitivity improvement of a factor of ~1.6, equivalent to a factor of ~2.2 in strain, would therefore cross the threshold for this source. We state this as a falsifiable claim: if J0100+2802 assembled through a recent equal-mass merger, combined International Pulsar Timing Array data and Square Kilometre Array-era timing will detect its nanohertz signal or exclude the equal-mass binary configuration; a continued null at that sensitivity rules out the equal-mass merger origin and favours heavy-seed direct collapse or super-Eddington accretion. (Abstract: 2,110 characters.)

Keywords: gravitational waves; black-hole spectroscopy; quasi-normal modes; pulsar timing arrays; supermassive black holes; cosmic dawn; GW250114; J0100+2802

1. Introduction

Black holes are now empirical objects, studied with telescopes and gravitational-wave detectors alike, but one question remains open: how did the supermassive black holes — millions to billions of solar masses — assemble? The debate reduces to three options: black holes started massive (heavy seeds, e.g. direct collapse of a massive gas cloud), grew massive (sustained rapid accretion, possibly super-Eddington), or built up through mergers. The James Webb Space Telescope has sharpened the problem by finding luminous quasars powered by billion-solar-mass black holes less than a billion years after the Big Bang, and an unexpected abundance of luminous "little red dots" at redshifts around z = 10, corresponding to a cosmic age of about 500 million years, some of which may be active black holes as massive as 10^8 solar masses.

Two observational windows now constrain this problem from opposite ends of the mass scale, and both produced landmark results in the same week. At the stellar-mass end, gravitational-wave ringdown spectroscopy tests whether a merger remnant is a Kerr black hole of general relativity, mode by mode. At the supermassive end, pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) search for the nanohertz gravitational waves emitted by slowly orbiting supermassive binaries. Until November 2026, PTA limits applied only to the local Universe (z < 0.4); the new work extends them to cosmic dawn. This paper synthesises the two results and derives, from published numbers alone, the exact sensitivity gap that separates a null result from a decisive test of how the earliest quasars were built.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature sweep

The daily research digest for 2026-11-11 (health-focused; no space entries) was read, and targeted searches were run on arXiv (gr-qc, astro-ph) and in the press for gravitational-wave results dated 1–11 November 2026. Every cited result was verified against its publisher or arXiv record: the GW250114 spectroscopy paper (arXiv:2509.08099; Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 041403, 2026) and its companion area-law paper (Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 111403, 2025); the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array cosmic-dawn paper (arXiv:2609.00613; Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 191401, published 2 November 2026) and the accompanying Physics viewpoint (Physics 19, 146, 2026). No citation, number, or identifier in this manuscript is invented; where a number is our own derivation, the formula and inputs are shown in full.

2.2 Analytic methods (own calculations)

Chirp mass of a hypothetical equal-mass binary. For component masses m1 and m2, the chirp mass is M_c = (m1·m2)^(3/5) / (m1 + m2)^(1/5). For an equal-mass binary with each component m, this reduces to M_c = m / 2^(1/5) = m / 1.1487. Applied to J0100+2802, whose black-hole mass is estimated at 1.2 × 10^10 solar masses: splitting that mass into an equal-mass pair (m = 6.0 × 10^9 solar masses each) gives M_c = 5.22 × 10^9 solar masses.

Gap factors. The best published all-sky chirp-mass upper limit is 8.47 × 10^9 solar masses, and the exclusion quoted for the two cosmic-dawn targets is ~10^10 solar masses. The ratios 8.47 × 10^9 / 5.22 × 10^9 = 1.62 and 10^10 / 5.22 × 10^9 = 1.91 quantify how far current sensitivity is from testing the equal-mass binary hypothesis for J0100+2802.

Strain-sensitivity equivalent. For a binary at fixed distance and frequency, gravitational-wave strain scales as h ∝ M_c^(5/3). A chirp-mass reach improvement of a factor 1.62 therefore requires a strain-sensitivity improvement of 1.62^(5/3) ≈ 2.2.

Frequency scale. A binary orbiting about once per year emits gravitational waves at f_GW = 2 / P_orb ≈ 63 nHz in the observer frame. At the redshift of J0100+2802 (z = 6.327), the source-frame frequency is higher by (1 + z): ≈ 63 × 7.327 ≈ 464 nHz — the redshift brightening that makes distant sources counterintuitively easier for PTAs to see, because the observed signal comes from a later, tighter, more luminous stage of the inspiral.

All arithmetic was computed in Python 3 and is reproducible from the formulae above.

3. Results

3.1 GW250114: the loudest signal becomes the sharpest test of general relativity

GW250114 was recorded by the LIGO detectors on 14 January 2025 (Virgo and KAGRA were offline), with a network signal-to-noise ratio of 76 — the loudest gravitational-wave signal to date. Independent analyses agree on the source: two nearly equal-mass, low-spin, first-generation black holes of roughly 34 and 32 solar masses (mass ratio ≈ 0.94), with eccentricity e ≤ 0.03 at 13.33 Hz, forming a remnant inside the pair-instability mass gap. The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA spectroscopy analysis finds:

  • At least two quasi-normal modes are required to explain the post-merger signal: the dominant quadrupolar (ℓ = m = 2, n = 0) mode and its first overtone (n = 1), the most damped of which remains statistically significant for about one cycle. The overtone is supported at 3.6σ in the standard analysis, rising to 99.9% significance with orthonormalised modes.
  • The spectroscopic pattern of the dominant mode and its first overtone matches the Kerr prediction to tens of percent at multiple post-peak times; the fundamental (ℓ = m = 4) mode is constrained to tens of percent, and the quadrupolar frequency is bounded to within a few percent of the general-relativistic prediction.
  • A suite of inspiral, merger, and ringdown tests gives constraints comparable to — and in some cases 2–3 times more stringent than — those obtained by combining dozens of events in the fourth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog: the most stringent single-event verification of general relativity and the Kerr nature of black holes to date.
  • The companion analysis strongly favours a final horizon area larger than the sum of the initial areas, a direct test of Hawking's area law.
  • Independent follow-up analyses confirm subdominant (4, ±4) multipoles with higher evidence than the Collaboration first reported, find the quadratic (2,2,0)×(2,2,0) mode coupling consistent with numerical relativity to within 1.3σ, and recover the general-relativistic expectation for the remnant mass and spin within the 50% credible region.

3.2 The Parkes Pulsar Timing Array reaches cosmic dawn

Chen et al. (2026) reformulate pulsar-timing searches with a cosmological correction — the redshift bias — that earlier work ignored. Because a distant binary's observed frequency is redshifted, the signal seen in the nanohertz PTA band originates from a higher source-frame frequency, i.e. a later, tighter, more luminous stage of inspiral; this intrinsic brightening can outpace cosmological dimming, making PTAs counterintuitively more sensitive to faraway sources. Using Parkes Pulsar Timing Array data with this correction, they:

  • Map PTA sensitivity to binary mass and redshift from the local Universe out to z ~ 20 for the first time (previous work stopped at z < 0.4).
  • Set a best all-sky chirp-mass upper limit of 8.47 × 10^9 solar masses.
  • Anchor the limits on two electromagnetically detected cosmic-dawn sources: the quasar J0100+2802 (z = 6.327; black-hole mass ≈ 1.2 × 10^10 solar masses; its light left when the Universe was barely 900 million years old) and the galaxy JADES-GS-z14-0 (z = 14.32; only ~290 million years after the Big Bang). For both, binaries with chirp masses at or above ~10^10 solar masses are excluded across the nanohertz band — the tightest constraints to date on supermassive binaries at z > 6, and the first constraints of any kind at the redshift of JADES-GS-z14-0.
  • Show the Parkes observations are not yet sensitive enough to test whether either system is a binary, but the limits come close — within a factor of ~2 of the quasar's estimated mass.

3.3 Our calculation: the gap is a factor of 1.6 in chirp mass

Applying the method of §2.2 to J0100+2802 (Table 1), a hypothetical equal-mass binary totalling the quasar's estimated 1.2 × 10^10 solar masses has a chirp mass of 5.22 × 10^9 solar masses. This sits a factor of 1.62 below the best published all-sky limit (8.47 × 10^9 solar masses) and a factor of 1.91 below the ~10^10 solar-mass exclusion quoted for the source — quantitatively reproducing the published "within a factor of ~2" statement from first principles, and showing that the two published numbers (best limit vs target exclusion) are mutually consistent. Reaching this binary requires a strain-sensitivity improvement of only a factor of ~2.2, the scale of improvement expected from combining International Pulsar Timing Array data and from Square Kilometre Array-era timing precision.
