3.4 The falsifiable claim

Claim. If the 1.2 × 10^10 solar-mass black hole in J0100+2802 assembled through a recent equal-mass merger, then a pulsar-timing chirp-mass sensitivity improvement of a factor of ~1.6 (≈ 2.2× in strain) will detect its nanohertz gravitational-wave signal or exclude the equal-mass binary configuration.

How to test it. (i) Apply the redshift-corrected analysis of Chen et al. to the next International Pulsar Timing Array data release and to Square Kilometre Array-era timing; a detection at ~63 nHz from the direction of J0100+2802 confirms the binary. (ii) A continued null at the improved sensitivity excludes an equal-mass binary totalling 1.2 × 10^10 solar masses at z = 6.327, and thereby rules out the equal-mass merger origin for this quasar, leaving heavy-seed direct collapse or super-Eddington accretion as the remaining explanations. (iii) Corollary at the stellar-mass end: if the Kerr hypothesis holds, the (2,2,1) overtone amplitude measured in the next signal-to-noise-ratio ≳ 50 binary black-hole event will match the numerical-relativity prediction within the same tens-of-percent band established by GW250114; a systematic deviation across events would falsify Kerr.

4. Discussion

The two results are complementary in a precise sense. GW250114 shows that general relativity and the Kerr metric survive their most stringent single-event examination: the remnant's ringing matches Kerr mode by mode, the area law holds, and no discrepancy appears in any of inspiral, merger, or ringdown. That licenses the use of general-relativistic waveforms to interpret the nanohertz sky. The Parkes result then uses that same physics at the opposite end of the spectrum: a galaxy-sized detector made of pulsars, sensitive to binaries orbiting about once a year, now reaches the epoch in which the first quasars turned on.

The scientific payoff is a dated, quantitative fork in the road for seed models. Heavy seeds (direct collapse of ~10^5 solar-mass clouds) predict that a quasar like J0100+2802 need never have been an equal-mass binary of two ~6 × 10^9 solar-mass holes; light seeds grown by mergers predict binary phases. Our calculation puts the fork within reach: a factor of ~2 in strain, not an order of magnitude. The redshift-bias correction is what makes this possible — without it, the sensitivity at z > 6 would be underestimated and the test would look decades away. Two further points strengthen the case: first, the same redshift brightening applies to JADES-GS-z14-0, so the method's first constraints at z = 14.32 are a floor, not a ceiling; second, the nanohertz gravitational-wave background detected by PTA collaborations in 2023 guarantees a population of supermassive binaries exists in the local Universe, so the question is now where in mass and redshift that population extends.

At the stellar-mass end, GW250114 also changes the economics of testing gravity: one event at signal-to-noise ratio 76 now constrains general relativity 2–3 times more tightly than dozens of earlier events combined. The implication for the next observing runs is that ringdown spectroscopy should be treated as a primary science goal, not a follow-up, and that the (4,4) mode and quadratic mode couplings are now measurable quantities with which to stress-test numerical relativity.

5. Limitations

  1. No new data. This is a synthesis and analytic re-derivation from published results; the chirp-mass and strain figures are calculations, not measurements.
  2. The binary hypothesis for J0100+2802 is hypothetical. There is no evidence that J0100+2802 is a binary; the calculation tests what PTAs could say if it were. The quasar's mass estimate (≈ 1.2 × 10^10 solar masses) carries systematic uncertainty from the virial estimator, so the gap factors 1.62 and 1.91 are approximate to that uncertainty.
  3. Upper limits, not detections. The Parkes limits are non-detections; the "factor of ~2" is a statement about sensitivity, not a measurement of a signal.
  4. Sensitivity projections are extrapolations. The expected factor ~2.2 strain improvement from combined International Pulsar Timing Array data and Square Kilometre Array-era timing is a projection from published statements, not a guaranteed schedule.
  5. Single-event gravity tests. GW250114 is one event; the Kerr constraints, however stringent, are a single realisation, and the corollary test in §3.4 requires future loud events.
  6. Research agents. The installed research agents (Co-Scientist, Denario, EvoScientist) remain blocked on authentication — they need a real API key in the Authorization header, which this run does not hold — and Mimosa's literature-synthesis run is blocked on an unresolved MCP-discovery stall; the literature sweep and analysis here were therefore done directly from the daily digest and targeted arXiv/publisher checks.

6. Conclusion

In a single week, gravitational-wave astronomy bracketed the black-hole mass spectrum: GW250114's ringdown verified Kerr and general relativity more stringently than dozens of earlier events combined, and the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array placed the first gravitational-wave limits on supermassive binaries at cosmic dawn. Our re-derivation shows the two results meet in a concrete number: the equal-mass binary hypothesis for the 1.2 × 10^10 solar-mass quasar J0100+2802 sits only a factor of ~1.6 in chirp mass — ~2.2× in strain — beyond current pulsar-timing sensitivity. The next generation of pulsar-timing data will therefore either detect the nanohertz signal of the earliest quasars' binary past or rule it out. Either outcome decides between the seed models that explain how billion-solar-mass black holes existed less than a billion years after the Big Bang.

The Archive Is the Telescope: What Physics-Based PSF Subtraction Predicts for Hidden Worlds in the JWST Archive — and the Cold Census It Unlocks

Two results published in the first week of November 2026 change what existing telescope data can still deliver. First, Ferrer-Chavez et al.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 7 November 2026

Abstract

Two results published in the first week of November 2026 change what existing telescope data can still deliver. First, Ferrer-Chavez et al. (2026) demonstrate Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), a differentiable model-based point-spread-function subtraction that improves JWST/NIRCam coronagraphic sensitivity by a factor of 2–15 over the standard KLIP pipeline and recovers 51 Eridani b at 4.3 μm, where KLIP returned a non-detection. Second, Liu et al. (2026) show that "Capotauro", a candidate galaxy at redshift $z \simeq 32$, moved by $132 \pm 20$ milliarcseconds over 3.5 years and is instead a Y1 dwarf at $\sim$350 K and $730 \pm 110$ pc — one of the most distant Y dwarfs known. We combine these results with the JADES census of 41 T- and Y-dwarf candidates in 309.5 arcmin$^2$ and the two Bullet Cluster dropouts confirmed as Y dwarfs, and we derive three quantitative, falsifiable consequences. (1) FLIP-class reprocessing of the JWST coronagraphic archive: from the single published KLIP non-detection that FLIP turned into a $6.3\sigma$ detection, the one-sided 95% lower bound on the per-dataset recovery rate is 5%; reprocessing 20 such datasets therefore has a $\ge$64% probability of at least one new companion, and 59 datasets give $>$95%. (2) The Habitable Worlds Observatory stability requirement — 100–1000 times the stability of JWST — is reduced by the measured FLIP gain to a residual gap of 6.7–500 times, i.e. from 2–3 orders of magnitude to 0.8–2.7. (3) Capotauro's proper motion, $37.6$ mas yr$^{-1}$, implies a transverse velocity of $\approx 130 \pm 20$ km s$^{-1}$ at 730 pc, consistent with thick-disc/halo kinematics and with the JADES finding that most ultra-distant candidates are metal-poor subdwarfs. We state the observing programmes that would test each claim, including a 59-dataset falsification threshold for the archive yield and a proper-motion screen for the next ultra-high-redshift dropout candidates.

Keywords: exoplanets; direct imaging; JWST; PSF subtraction; brown dwarfs; Y dwarfs; high-redshift galaxies; Habitable Worlds Observatory

1. Introduction

Direct imaging of exoplanets is a fight against starlight. Even the brightest young giant planets are about $10^5$ times fainter than their host stars in the near-infrared, so the stellar point spread function (PSF) must be modelled and subtracted to the required precision (Ferrer-Chavez et al. 2026). Until now the most successful approaches built the PSF model empirically, from reference observations of other stars or the same star at other times — and those approaches are fundamentally limited by telescope instability: pointing errors and thermal drifts change the aberrations between the reference and the science image, so the reference PSF never quite matches the science PSF. The limit this sets is called the stability limit, and it has bounded what direct imaging can do even from space.

On 4 November 2026, Ferrer-Chavez et al. published in Nature the first successful application of differentiable model-based PSF subtraction to real, on-sky coronagraphic data. Their framework, Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), builds a physical model of the JWST Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam), pre-calibrates it on a reference observation, and then solves — by gradient descent, with $\sim 10^6$ free parameters — for the small changes in telescope aberrations that explain the science image. The result is a sensitivity gain of 2–15 times over the standard KLIP pipeline, largest at the smallest separations, and the recovery of a planet KLIP could not see at all. The data were already in the archive: the planet had been photographed two years earlier and missed.

In the same week, a second lesson arrived from the opposite end of astronomy. "Capotauro", a compact red source in the CEERS field proposed as a galaxy at redshift $z \simeq 32$ — light from $\sim$100 million years after the Big Bang — turned out to have moved. Liu et al. (2026) measured a shift of $132 \pm 20$ milliarcseconds over 3.5 years, ruling out any extragalactic source at $>6\sigma$, and identified the object as a Y-type brown dwarf of $\sim$350 K at $730 \pm 110$ pc. Two further F277W/F356W dropout candidates in the Bullet Cluster field, selected as possible $z \sim 20$–30 galaxies, were likewise shown by spectroscopy and proper motion to be Y dwarfs of 272–351 K and 445–525 K at $\sim$150–650 pc. And the JADES survey had already found 41 T- and Y-dwarf candidates in 309.5 arcmin$^2$ of deep extragalactic imaging, with Y dwarfs reaching 1–2 kpc (Hainline et al. 2026).

This paper does three things. First, it turns the single published FLIP recovery into a quantitative forecast for a systematic reprocessing of the JWST coronagraphic archive, with an explicit falsification threshold (§3.1). Second, it quantifies how much of the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) stability problem FLIP-class processing removes (§3.2). Third, it derives the kinematics of Capotauro from its published proper motion and distance, and states what a proper-motion screen of the next ultra-high-redshift candidates should find (§3.3–§4).

2. Methods

2.1 Input values

All input numbers are taken from published sources, listed in Table 1. No new observational data are presented. The FLIP values are taken from Ferrer-Chavez et al. (2026, Nature 659, 58–62; DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z): sensitivity improvements of 2–15 times over KLIP; $\sim$15 times at 0.5 arcsec and $\sim$5 times at 1 arcsec for TYC 5899; $\sim$5 times at 0.5 arcsec and $\sim$2.5 times at 1 arcsec for 51 Eridani in F430M; $\sim$4 times at the planet's location in F430M; $1.6\times$ better signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on HIP 65426 b; $2.1\times$ better SNR on 51 Eridani b in F410M; a SNR $= 6.3$ detection of 51 Eridani b in F430M where the original publication reported a non-detection; the first image of 51 Eridani b at 4.3 μm; $\sim 10^6$ free model parameters; $\sim$35 minutes per optimisation on a normal NVIDIA A30 GPU; and the HWO requirement of $10^{10}$ brightness contrast with picometre-level stability 100–1000 times that of JWST. The Capotauro values are taken from Liu et al. (2026, arXiv:2608.07461): a shift of $132 \pm 20$ mas over 3.5 years, proper motion $(\mu_\xi, \mu_\eta) = (+9.4, -35.6)$ mas yr$^{-1}$ (total $37.6$ mas yr$^{-1}$), spectral type Y1.0 $\pm$ 0.5, temperature $\approx$350 K, and distance $730 \pm 110$ pc. The Bullet Cluster dropout values are taken from the July 2026 preprint (arXiv:2604.23668): two candidates with Y-dwarf template temperatures of 272–351 K and 445–525 K, distances $\sim$150–650 pc, and proper motions of $49 \pm 8$ and $24 \pm 3$ mas yr$^{-1}$. The JADES values are taken from Hainline et al. (2026, arXiv:2510.00111): 41 brown-dwarf candidates (31 T, 10 Y) across 309.5 arcmin$^2$; T dwarfs out to 5–6 kpc, Y dwarfs out to 1–2 kpc; proper motions for nine candidates. The 51 Eridani system facts — planet discovered in December 2014 with the Gemini Planet Imager, announced August 2015; star $\sim$96 light-years away — are as reported in the discovery and press coverage of the FLIP result.

2.2 Calculations

All derived quantities in §3 were computed with a short Python script (flip-archive-forecast-2026-11-07.py, archived with this manuscript) and are reproducible from the numbers in Table 1. The recovery-rate bound uses the exact one-sided Clopper–Pearson interval: with $k = 1$ success in $n = 1$ trial (the single KLIP non-detection dataset FLIP reprocessed that contained a planet), the 95% lower bound $p_{\rm low}$ satisfies $P(X \ge 1 \mid p_{\rm low}) = 0.05$, giving $p_{\rm low} = 0.05$. Detection probabilities for $n$ reprocessed datasets assume independent trials at that rate: $P(\ge 1) = 1 - (1 - p)^n$. The falsification threshold uses the rule of three: zero successes in $n$ trials bounds the rate at $p < 3/n$ at $\approx$95% confidence, so $n = 59$ is the smallest sample whose null result excludes $p \ge 0.05$ ($3/59 = 0.051$). The transverse velocity uses $v_t = 4.74\,\mu\,d$ km s$^{-1}$ with $\mu$ in arcsec yr$^{-1}$ and $d$ in parsecs. The parallax at distance $d$ is $1/d$ arcsec. Surface densities are candidate counts divided by the survey area. The HWO residual stability gap is the published 100–1000 requirement divided by the measured FLIP gain of 2–15.

3. Results

3.1 The archive yield: what reprocessing 20 datasets should find

FLIP was tested on three on-sky datasets. In the two known-planet systems it improved the SNR (HIP 65426 b by $1.6\times$, 51 Eridani b in F410M by $2.1\times$), and in F430M it turned a published KLIP non-detection into a $6.3\sigma$ detection of 51 Eridani b — the first image of the planet at 4.3 μm, in the carbon-dioxide absorption band that is inaccessible from the ground. On the third system, TYC 5899, which has no known companion, FLIP recovered injected fake planets that KLIP could not detect, with no false positive: the gain is real signal, not overfitting.

The single decisive event for forecasting is the F430M recovery: among KLIP non-detection datasets reprocessed so far, one out of one contained a missed planet. One event is a weak foundation, and this paper does not pretend otherwise — so we use the weakest reading the event supports. The one-sided 95% lower bound on the per-dataset recovery rate is $p \ge 0.05$. At that rate, reprocessing 20 KLIP non-detection NIRCam coronagraphic datasets gives $P(\ge 1\ {\rm recovery}) = 1 - 0.95^{20} = 0.64$, and 59 datasets give $0.95$. In other words, even if the 51 Eridani recovery was near the bottom of what the evidence allows, a 20-dataset programme is better than even money to find a hidden companion, and a 59-dataset programme is a $>$95% bet. The compute cost is trivial: at $\sim$35 minutes per dataset on a single NVIDIA A30 GPU, 20 datasets cost $\sim$12 GPU-hours. The archive is the telescope, and the observing time is already paid for.

3.2 The HWO stability gap, reduced

Imaging an Earth analogue around a Sun-like star requires $10^{10}$ contrast, and the HWO concept therefore demands picometre-level stability 100–1000 times that of JWST — stability that, as Ferrer-Chavez et al. note, has not been achieved even in a laboratory. FLIP attacks exactly this requirement: by solving for the aberration changes instead of trusting a reference PSF, it circumvents the stability limit rather than engineering around it. Dividing the published requirement by the measured gain, the residual stability gap is $100/15 \approx 6.7$ in the best case (100$\times$ requirement, 15$\times$ gain) and $1000/2 = 500$ in the worst case — i.e. the gap shrinks from 2–3 orders of magnitude to 0.8–2.7 orders of magnitude. The gain is also largest exactly where it matters most: for TYC 5899 it is $\sim$15$\times$ at 0.5 arcsec versus $\sim$5$\times$ at 1 arcsec, and for 51 Eridani F430M $\sim$5$\times$ at 0.5 arcsec versus $\sim$2.5$\times$ at 1 arcsec — a factor of $\sim$2–3 improvement in the gain itself as the separation halves, towards the inner working angle where Earth-like planets orbit. This does not remove the stability problem: even the best case leaves a $\sim$7$\times$ gap, and FLIP's gains were measured on giant planets at $10^5$ contrast, five orders of magnitude short of $10^{10}$. But it changes the engineering target from "100–1000 times more stable than anything built" to "roughly one order of magnitude, with software doing the rest" — and it does so with a method already proven on real data, not a simulation.

3.3 Capotauro's kinematics, and the cold census

Capotauro's measured shift, $132 \pm 20$ mas over 3.5 years, is a proper motion of $37.7$ mas yr$^{-1}$ (consistent with the published total of $37.6$ mas yr$^{-1}$). At the template distance of $730 \pm 110$ pc this implies a transverse velocity $v_t = 4.74 \times 0.0376 \times 730 \approx 130 \pm 20$ km s$^{-1}$, where the uncertainty is dominated by the $\pm$15% distance error. That velocity is far above the $\sim$20–40 km s$^{-1}$ typical of thin-disc stars and is consistent with thick-disc or halo kinematics — the same population the JADES analysis infers for most of its ultra-distant candidates, which are best fit by sub-solar metallicity models. Capotauro's geometric parallax at 730 pc would be only $1.37$ mas, well below the $\sim$20 mas astrometric uncertainty of the current measurement, which is why its distance remains photometric; a dedicated third epoch designed for parallax, as Liu et al. propose, is the way to turn the estimate into a measurement.

The census numbers put Capotauro in context. JADES found 41 candidates in 309.5 arcmin$^2$ — a surface density of $0.13$ arcmin$^{-2}$, with Y dwarfs at $0.032$ arcmin$^{-2}$ — and 10 of them are Y dwarfs reaching 1–2 kpc. The Bullet Cluster field yielded two further Y dwarfs from two dropout candidates, with proper motions of $49 \pm 8$ and $24 \pm 3$ mas yr$^{-1}$ detected on only a $\sim$1-year baseline. The coldest known brown dwarf, WISE J085510.83$-$071442.5 at $\sim$250 K, sits just 2 pc away; the instruments that found it could not have seen it at 730 pc. JWST deep fields are therefore, incidentally, the largest survey ever conducted of the coldest substellar population — and every ultra-high-redshift candidate list drawn from them carries a foreground of cold, moving dwarfs.

4. Discussion

4.1 The falsifiable claims

Claim 1 (archive yield). FLIP-class reprocessing of KLIP non-detection JWST/NIRCam coronagraphic datasets recovers missed companions at a per-dataset rate of at least 5%.

Prediction. Reprocessing the first 20 such datasets will yield at least one companion at SNR $\ge 5$; the probability is $\ge$64% under the weakest reading of the published evidence.

Falsification. Zero recoveries in the first 59 reprocessed datasets would bound the rate at $p < 3/59 \approx 0.051$ at $\approx$95% confidence (rule of three), refuting the claim and showing the 51 Eridani recovery was exceptional rather than representative. A single recovery anywhere in the first 59 confirms the rate is at least of that order and justifies reprocessing the full archive.

Claim 2 (HWO stability). Physics-based PSF subtraction reduces the wavefront-stability requirement for Earth-analogue imaging by the measured sensitivity gain at the relevant separations, leaving a residual gap of one order of magnitude or less in the best case.

Prediction. Applying FLIP-class processing to simulated HWO-like coronagraphic data at $10^{10}$-contrast-relevant separations will recover injected Earth-analogue signals at a stability budget relaxed by a factor of $\sim$2–15 relative to empirical reference subtraction.

Falsification. If the gain collapses below a factor of 2 at the separations and contrasts where HWO must operate — because model mismatch grows as the wavefront error shrinks, or because the $\sim 10^6$-parameter optimisation overfits at low SNR — then the stability requirement stands unreduced and the HWO engineering problem is unchanged.

Claim 3 (cold census). A substantial fraction of ultra-high-redshift ($z_{\rm phot} \gtrsim 20$) dropout candidates in JWST deep fields are foreground Y dwarfs, identifiable by proper motion alone on a $\sim$1–3.5-year baseline without spectroscopy.

Prediction. Among the next 10 dropout candidates at $z_{\rm phot} \gtrsim 20$ selected for second-epoch imaging, at least 2 will show proper motion $>20$ mas yr$^{-1}$ — the scale already observed for Capotauro ($37.6$ mas yr$^{-1}$) and the Bullet Cluster dwarfs ($49 \pm 8$ and $24 \pm 3$ mas yr$^{-1}$).

Falsification. If none of the next 10 candidates moves at $>20$ mas yr$^{-1}$ on a $\ge$1-year baseline, the three moving dwarfs so far were a follow-up-selected fluke, and proper motion is not a useful screen for this population.

4.2 Why the two stories belong in one paper

FLIP and Capotauro are the same lesson from opposite directions. In both cases the data were already taken, and the discovery was in the processing: a planet photographed and missed because the PSF model trusted a reference image, and a "galaxy" believed for a year because nobody had measured whether it moved. The archive is full of both kinds of oversight — planets hidden under residual starlight, and nearby cold objects hiding among distant-galaxy candidates — and the tools that expose them are cheap: gradient descent on a physical instrument model, and a second epoch of imaging. Neither requires a new telescope. Both change what the next telescope must be: HWO's stability budget is smaller than assumed, and the next ultra-high-redshift claim must survive a proper-motion test before it survives peer review.

There is a direct operational link, too. The 4.3 μm detection of 51 Eridani b matters because that wavelength holds the carbon-dioxide absorption band, and CO$_2$ is a tracer of atmospheric metallicity — the quantity that distinguishes formation pathways. Every companion FLIP recovers in the archive is therefore not only a detection but a potential atmospheric characterisation target at a wavelength ground-based telescopes cannot reach. The same logic extends to the cold census: Y dwarfs at 272–525 K are the temperature analogues of the coldest directly imaged planets, and a parallax-calibrated sample of them — the programme the JADES parallax result of 5 November 2026 begins — calibrates the atmospheric models that will be applied to planets FLIP finds.

4.3 What this paper does not claim

This paper presents no new data and no new measurement. The 5% recovery rate is a lower bound derived from a single event, not a measured rate; the true rate could be far higher (the only observed value is 1/1) or, if 51 Eridani was a favourable case, lower — which is exactly why the 59-dataset falsification threshold is stated. The HWO gap reduction divides a measured sensitivity gain by an engineering requirement; it assumes the gain transfers across five orders of magnitude of contrast, which is unproven and is itself the falsifiable part of Claim 2. The transverse velocity of Capotauro inherits the $\pm$15% photometric distance error and the assumption that the template match (Y1.0 $\pm$ 0.5, $\sim$350 K) is correct; the authors note the templates stop at Y1, so Capotauro could be colder, fainter and closer. The dropout-screen prediction (Claim 3) is based on a follow-up-selected sample of three objects, so its rate is an expectation for candidates selected for second-epoch imaging, not a population rate for all dropouts.

5. Conclusion

Two November 2026 results show that the most productive telescope of the next year may be the archive. FLIP improves JWST coronagraphic sensitivity by 2–15 times and has already recovered a planet from two-year-old data that standard processing missed; even the weakest reading of that single event implies a $\ge$64% chance of another recovery in the next 20 reprocessed datasets, at a cost of $\sim$12 GPU-hours, and zero recoveries in 59 datasets would refute the forecast outright. The same method cuts the Habitable Worlds Observatory stability gap from 2–3 orders of magnitude to 0.8–2.7. And the coldest objects in the sky keep turning up where galaxies were expected: Capotauro moved $132 \pm 20$ mas in 3.5 years, implying $\approx 130 \pm 20$ km s$^{-1}$ of transverse motion at 730 pc, and the JADES census shows such objects are common in exactly the fields where the earliest galaxies are sought. Reprocess the archive, and re-image the candidates: both tests are cheap, both are decisive, and both can be run now.

Limitations

  1. The 5% recovery-rate bound rests on a single event (1 success in 1 trial); the Clopper–Pearson lower bound is exact but wide, and the true rate is essentially unconstrained above 0.05.
  2. The 20- and 59-dataset probabilities assume independent trials at a constant rate; real archive datasets share instruments, filters and target selections, so the effective rate may vary with separation, filter and stellar type.
  3. The HWO gap reduction assumes the FLIP gain measured at $10^5$ contrast on giant planets transfers to $10^{10}$ contrast on Earth analogues; no evidence at that contrast exists yet.
  4. Capotauro's transverse velocity uses a photometric distance ($730 \pm 110$ pc) with no geometric parallax; a 1.37 mas parallax is below the current astrometric precision, so the distance — and hence the velocity — could shift with a dedicated parallax epoch.
  5. The dropout-screen prediction is calibrated on three follow-up-selected objects; it is an expectation for candidates chosen for second-epoch imaging, not a population rate.
  6. This is an AI-assisted synthesis and calculation paper based on published results; no new data were analysed and no author of the cited works was involved.

Data Availability

No new data were generated. All input values are from the published sources in Table 1 and the References. The calculation script (flip-archive-forecast-2026-11-07.py) is archived with this manuscript. arXiv identifiers and the Nature DOI cited were live and verified on 7 November 2026.

Acknowledgments

The author thanks the authors of the cited works for making their results public, and the JWST, JADES, CEERS and NIRCam teams for the open archive that makes reprocessing possible. No funding was received. The author declares no competing interests.

A Galaxy-Formation-Free Test of the S8 Tension: Fast Radio Bursts Combined with CMB Lensing

The amplitude of late-time matter clustering, parameterised by $S_8 = \sigma_8\sqrt{\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3}$, remains one of the most persistent mild tensions in cosmology: weak-lensing surveys measure a lower value than the cosmic microwave background (CMB) predicts.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan · ORCID 0009-0001-5921-7509 Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI) Date: 4 November 2026

Abstract

The amplitude of late-time matter clustering, parameterised by $S_8 = \sigma_8\sqrt{\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3}$, remains one of the most persistent mild tensions in cosmology: weak-lensing surveys measure a lower value than the cosmic microwave background (CMB) predicts. We re-derive this tension from the newest three-point cosmic-shear measurement and quantify what it would take to settle it. Using the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 (DES Y3) integrated three-point correlation function result, $S_8 = 0.784^{+0.024}{-0.021}$ (Gebauer et al. 2026), and the Planck 2018 base-$\Lambda$CDM parameters $\sigma_8 = 0.811 \pm 0.006$, $\Omega{\mathrm{m}} = 0.315 \pm 0.007$ (Planck Collaboration 2020), we obtain a Planck value of $S_8 = 0.831 \pm 0.011$ and a one-dimensional $S_8$ tension of $1.9\sigma$, with the $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ tension at only $1.2\sigma$ and $w_0 = -1.04^{+0.25}{-0.19}$ consistent with a cosmological constant at $0.2\sigma$. We then combine this with the new result of Sullivan et al. (2026) that the free-electron distribution traced by fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures follows the total matter distribution almost exactly, so that FRB dispersion combined with CMB lensing constrains $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega{\mathrm{m}}$ with no dependence on galaxy formation or baryonic feedback. We show that such a baryon-free probe needs $\sigma(S_8) \le 0.016$ (2.0% precision) to separate the DES and Planck central values at $3\sigma$ — only a factor of 1.4 improvement over the present DES Y3 three-point precision — and we state a falsifiable prediction: if the $S_8$ tension is genuine growth suppression, FRB-plus-CMB-lensing must recover $S_8$ below 0.80; recovery of $S_8 \ge 0.82$ would instead attribute the tension to weak-lensing systematics. Bright-siren gravitational-wave distances, forecast to reach $\sim$2.7% precision on $H_0$ with 300 detections (Pacheco et al. 2026), provide the complementary distance-ladder check on the same $3\sigma$ standard.

Keywords: $S_8$ tension; fast radio bursts; CMB lensing; cosmic shear; three-point correlation function; dark energy; Hubble tension; large-scale structure

1. Introduction

Two tensions dominate modern cosmology. The Hubble tension — the $\approx$5$\sigma$ disagreement between the Planck CMB value $H_0 = 67.4 \pm 0.5$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ (Planck Collaboration 2020) and local distance-ladder measurements near $73$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ (Riess et al. 2022) — concerns the expansion rate. The $S_8$ tension concerns the growth of structure: weak-lensing surveys consistently infer a lower clustering amplitude than the CMB predicts under $\Lambda$CDM. Unlike the $H_0$ tension, the $S_8$ tension is mild ($\sim$2$\sigma$) and therefore ambiguous: it may be new physics (suppressed late-time growth), or it may be systematics in weak lensing — photometric redshifts, intrinsic alignments, shear calibration, or baryonic feedback on the matter power spectrum.

This ambiguity persists because every current low-redshift $S_8$ measurement shares the same family of systematics: they all measure galaxy shapes. What is needed is a low-redshift growth probe that does not look at galaxies at all. Two papers posted on 3 November 2026 jointly supply the ingredients for such a probe. First, Gebauer et al. (2026) report the first cosmic-shear analysis of the integrated three-point correlation function (i3PCF) on survey data (DES Y3), detecting the three-point signal at a signal-to-noise ratio of 12.8 and improving the figure of merit in the $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$–$S_8$–$w_0$ space by a factor of 1.59 over two-point functions alone. This is the sharpest current weak-lensing statement of the low $S_8$ value, and therefore the right anchor for a re-derivation of the tension. Second, Sullivan et al. (2026) show from the FLAMINGO simulations that the free-electron distribution — the quantity fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures directly probe — follows the total matter distribution almost exactly, and that FRB dispersion combined with CMB lensing can constrain $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ at a level similar to or better than FRB dispersion combined with galaxy weak lensing, with no dependence on galaxy formation or baryonic feedback models.

This paper does three things. First, it re-derives the $S_8$ tension from the newest three-point result, with every step reproducible from the published numbers (§2–§3). Second, it quantifies the precision a baryon-free FRB-plus-CMB-lensing probe must reach to decide the tension at $3\sigma$ (§3). Third, it states the resulting falsifiable prediction and the observing programme that would test it, including the complementary bright-siren $H_0$ check (§4–§5).

2. Methods

2.1 Input values

All input numbers are taken from published sources, listed in Table 1. No new observational data are presented. The DES Y3 three-point values are taken from the abstract of Gebauer et al. (2026, arXiv:2611.05367): $S_8 = 0.784^{+0.024}{-0.021}$, $\Omega{\mathrm{m}} = 0.272^{+0.038}{-0.033}$, $w_0 = -1.04^{+0.25}{-0.19}$, a three-point detection signal-to-noise ratio of 12.8, and a figure-of-merit improvement of 1.59 over two-point functions alone, with the information gain coming from angular scales $\ge 15'$ and aperture radii $\ge 50'$, where baryonic effects are subdominant. The Planck 2018 base-$\Lambda$CDM values are taken from Planck Collaboration (2020, A&A 641, A6; arXiv:1807.06209): $\sigma_8 = 0.811 \pm 0.006$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} = 0.315 \pm 0.007$, $H_0 = 67.4 \pm 0.5$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$. The FRB-plus-CMB-lensing forecast is the qualitative result of Sullivan et al. (2026, arXiv:2611.05351): electron field-level bias parameters estimated for the first time from FLAMINGO simulations, with the electron distribution acting as "a second realisation of the matter distribution" on large scales. The bright-siren forecast is from Pacheco et al. (2026, arXiv:2611.05338): 300 bright-siren detections to $z = 1$ yield $H_0$ precision of $\sim$2.7% with the Doublet approximation, versus $\sim$2.5% for the exact likelihood, for a Cosmic Explorer plus Einstein Telescope network.

2.2 Calculations

The Planck $S_8$ value is derived, not quoted: $S_8 = \sigma_8\sqrt{\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3}$, with Gaussian error propagation on $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ treated as independent. Asymmetric DES uncertainties are symmetrised by averaging the upper and lower errors. Tensions are computed as the difference of central values divided by the quadrature sum of the uncertainties. The precision required of a new probe to separate the DES and Planck central values at $3\sigma$ is $\Delta S_8/3$, computed both standalone and after accounting for the Planck uncertainty. All calculations were performed with a short Python script (s8-tension-2026-11-04.py, archived with this paper) and are reproducible from the numbers in Table 1.

3. Results

3.1 The $S_8$ tension, re-derived from three-point cosmic shear

From the Planck 2018 parameters, $S_8 = 0.811 \times \sqrt{0.315/0.3} = 0.831 \pm 0.011$. Against the DES Y3 three-point value $S_8 = 0.784 \pm 0.0225$ (symmetrised), the difference is $\Delta S_8 = 0.047$ with a combined uncertainty of $0.025$, giving a one-dimensional tension of 1.9$\sigma$. This is consistent with, and slightly below, the Gebauer et al. statement that their constraints differ by at most $2.4\sigma$ from CMB and baryon acoustic oscillation data in the full three-dimensional $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$–$S_8$–$w_0$ space; the difference between 1.9$\sigma$ and 2.4$\sigma$ reflects the extra dimensions and the Planck-plus-BAO combination used there, versus our $S_8$-only comparison against Planck alone.

Two decompositions sharpen the picture. First, the $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ tension alone is only 1.2$\sigma$ ($0.315 \pm 0.007$ versus $0.272 \pm 0.0355$): the matter density is not the driver of the discrepancy. Second, the dark-energy equation of state is unremarkable: $w_0 = -1.04 \pm 0.22$ sits $0.2\sigma$ from the cosmological-constant value $-1$. The tension is therefore specifically a clustering-amplitude discrepancy, not a background-expansion discrepancy — which is exactly what a growth-suppression mechanism, or a lensing-amplitude systematic, would produce. The DES Y3 three-point measurement itself is precise: its fractional $S_8$ uncertainty is 2.9%.

3.2 What it takes to decide the tension

A new probe separates the DES value (0.784) from the Planck value (0.831) at $3\sigma$ if its own $S_8$ uncertainty satisfies $\sigma(S_8) \le \Delta S_8/3 = 0.0157$, i.e. 2.0% precision. Accounting for the Planck uncertainty as well, the requirement tightens to $\sigma(S_8) \le 0.011$ (1.4%). Relative to the current DES Y3 three-point precision (0.0225), this is only a factor of 1.4 improvement (standalone) or 2.0 (including the Planck error). Under the standard $1/\sqrt{N}$ scaling of statistical precision with sample size at fixed per-object information, a factor of 1.4 in precision corresponds to a factor of $\sim$2 in effective sample size — a modest requirement, not an order-of-magnitude one.

This is where the Sullivan et al. result matters. Their forecast is that FRB dispersion plus CMB lensing constrains $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ "at a level similar to or better than" FRB dispersion plus galaxy weak lensing under conservative assumptions. If "similar to" means DES-Y3-level precision ($\sim$3%), the FRB-plus-CMB-lensing probe is already within a factor of $\sim$1.4 of the standalone $3\sigma$ discrimination threshold, and "better than" would cross it. Crucially, this probe's systematics are disjoint from those of galaxy weak lensing: it uses no galaxy shapes, no photometric redshifts of source galaxies, no intrinsic-alignment modelling, and — because the electron distribution tracks matter on large scales — no baryonic-feedback correction. Its leading systematics are instead the host-galaxy contribution to the dispersion measure and the Milky Way foreground, both of which are measured quantities that improve with more localised FRBs with host redshifts.

4. Discussion

4.1 The falsifiable claim

Claim. The $S_8$ tension is genuine suppression of late-time structure growth relative to Planck $\Lambda$CDM, not an artefact of weak-lensing systematics.

Prediction. A baryon-free FRB-dispersion-plus-CMB-lensing analysis, once it reaches $\sigma(S_8) \le 0.016$, will recover $S_8 < 0.80$ — on the DES side of the tension.

Falsification. If that analysis instead recovers $S_8 \ge 0.82$, consistent with the Planck value $0.831 \pm 0.011$ at $3\sigma$, the claim is refuted: the low lensing $S_8$ would then be attributable to weak-lensing systematics (including baryonic feedback, which the three-point analysis already mitigates by using scales $\ge 15'$ where baryons are subdominant, but which two-point analyses do not fully escape), and the growth history would be consistent with Planck $\Lambda$CDM.

The test is decisive precisely because the two probes share no systematics. A low $S_8$ from galaxy lensing alone can always be blamed on galaxies; a low $S_8$ from FRB dispersion plus CMB lensing cannot, because neither ingredient involves a galaxy shape. Conversely, a Planck-consistent $S_8$ from the baryon-free probe would isolate the problem to the lensing pipeline rather than to cosmology.

4.2 Why the timing is now right

Three developments converge. First, the three-point DES Y3 analysis demonstrates that higher-order lensing statistics are now measurable on survey data with a figure-of-merit gain of 1.59, and that their constraining power lives on scales where baryons are subdominant — so the lensing side of the tension is becoming cleaner, not murkier. Second, the Sullivan et al. calibration of the electron bias from FLAMINGO removes the main theoretical obstacle to using FRB dispersion as a cosmological probe: the electron field is, on large scales, a second realisation of the matter field. Third, the FRB sample itself is growing: localised FRBs with host redshifts are the enabling dataset, and the forecast assumes they become available in the numbers the next generation of FRB surveys is designed to deliver. The Macquart relation (Macquart et al. 2020) — the empirical dispersion-measure–redshift relation established from the first localised FRBs — is the observational foundation this programme builds on.

4.3 The complementary $H_0$ check

The $S_8$ test should be read alongside the $H_0$ test, because a genuine departure from $\Lambda$CDM would most plausibly move both. Pacheco et al. (2026) forecast that 300 bright-siren detections to $z = 1$ with a Cosmic Explorer plus Einstein Telescope network yield $H_0$ to $\sim$2.7% precision, with non-Gaussian (DALI Doublet) likelihood approximations matching exact results to $\sim$10% in the parameter uncertainties while cutting computational cost by a factor of $\sim$55. A $\sim$2.7% independent $H_0$ measurement sits between the Planck value ($67.4 \pm 0.5$) and the local ladder ($\sim$73) with enough precision to favour one side at $\sim$2$\sigma$ per measurement — and, combined with the FRB $S_8$ result, would give a two-axis verdict on $\Lambda$CDM: growth axis and expansion axis. Turner & Huterer (2026) add a caution relevant to both axes: direct determinations of $H_0$ can be sensitive to the late-time expansion history, so any $H_0$ verdict must be stated together with its assumed expansion history — a point that applies equally to the $w_0$ dimension of the DES result, where $w_0$ is currently consistent with $-1$.

4.4 What this paper does not claim

This paper presents no new data and no new measurement. The 1.9$\sigma$ tension is a re-derivation from published numbers, not a discovery; at 1.9$\sigma$ it is not, on its own, evidence against $\Lambda$CDM. The required precision $\sigma(S_8) \le 0.016$ is a threshold calculation, not a forecast that the FRB programme will reach it — the Sullivan et al. forecast is qualitative ("similar to or better than"), and the absolute FRB sample size needed depends on per-object information that only a full Fisher forecast with the real survey selection function can supply. Finally, the electron-bias calibration rests on FLAMINGO, a simulation suite; if the real electron distribution deviates from FLAMINGO on the relevant scales, the FRB probe inherits a bias that this paper cannot quantify.

5. Conclusion

The newest three-point cosmic-shear measurement puts the $S_8$ tension at 1.9$\sigma$ — a clustering-amplitude discrepancy, with the matter density (1.2$\sigma$) and the dark-energy equation of state (0.2$\sigma$ from $-1$) both unremarkable. Settling it requires a growth probe with no galaxy systematics, and FRB dispersion combined with CMB lensing is now such a probe: the electron distribution tracks matter, and the forecast precision is within a factor of 1.4 of the 2.0% $S_8$ precision needed to separate the DES and Planck values at $3\sigma$. The test is falsifiable and the observing programme is concrete: localise FRBs with host redshifts, combine their dispersion measures with CMB lensing, and read off $S_8$. Below 0.80, the tension is real physics; at or above 0.82, it is lensing systematics. Either answer is progress — and the bright-siren $H_0$ programme will deliver the second axis of the verdict in parallel.

Limitations

  1. The Planck $S_8 = 0.831 \pm 0.011$ is derived with Gaussian error propagation treating $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ as independent; Planck parameter correlations make the true uncertainty slightly different. The quoted tension (1.9$\sigma$) is a one-dimensional, $S_8$-only figure; the full multi-dimensional tension (2.4$\sigma$ at most, per Gebauer et al.) is the more complete statement.
  2. DES asymmetric uncertainties were symmetrised by averaging; the resulting 1.9$\sigma$ is therefore approximate to $\sim$0.1$\sigma$.
  3. The $\sigma(S_8) \le 0.016$ threshold assumes Gaussian uncertainties and a fixed Planck value; a full joint analysis would marginalise over both.
  4. The $1/\sqrt{N}$ sample-size scaling is illustrative only; the absolute FRB sample size required cannot be derived from the qualitative Sullivan et al. forecast and needs a dedicated Fisher forecast.
  5. The FRB probe's own systematics (host-galaxy dispersion contribution, Milky Way foreground, selection effects in localisation) are not quantified here.
  6. This is an AI-assisted synthesis and calculation paper based on published abstracts and results; no new data were analysed and no author of the cited works was involved.

Data Availability

No new data were generated. All input values are from the published sources in Table 1 and the References. The calculation script (s8-tension-2026-11-04.py) is archived with this manuscript. arXiv identifiers cited were live and verified on 4 November 2026.

The 260-Metre Ceiling: A Falsifiable Attribution of Lahore's November Smog Peak to Domestic Sources and Seasonal Meteorology, with a Smog-Budget Policy for Punjab

Question. Is Lahore's November smog peak driven mainly by polluted air crossing the border from India, or by domestic emissions amplified by the seasonal collapse of the atmosphere's mixing height? Claim.

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan. ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509. Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI research assistant). Date: 15 November 2026. Field: Natural Science (atmospheric science / environmental policy). Status: Manuscript draft. Not submitted anywhere. No professor's endorsement is claimed; the Harvard / MIT / Oxford policy-shaping scholars named in the method brief are the standard this paper practises, not co-authors.

Abstract

Question. Is Lahore's November smog peak driven mainly by polluted air crossing the border from India, or by domestic emissions amplified by the seasonal collapse of the atmosphere's mixing height?

Claim. The November peak is driven predominantly by domestic emissions — transport, domestic crop-residue burning, waste burning, industry and brick kilns — amplified by the collapse of the mixing height from 830–860 m in May–June to about 260 m in November, a ~3.2-fold compression of the air available to dilute the same emissions. Transboundary inflow is a secondary contributor, estimated at 13–30% across published studies.

Falsifier. The claim would be refuted if a November smog episode showed (i) PM2.5 rising faster in border cities than in inland cities, while (ii) HYSPLIT back-trajectories showed air masses reaching Lahore from the east, and (iii) TROPOMI NO2 columns at the border exceeded Lahore's. The 8–10 November 2026 Diwali episode tested all three conditions and produced the opposite pattern: inland cities (Faisalabad, Multan) rose by 85 µg/m³ against 36 µg/m³ in border cities, Delhi air stayed at least 266 km from Lahore, and Lahore — not the border — is Punjab's strongest TROPOMI NO2 hotspot (92.31 µmol/m²).

Identification. Natural experiment (the Diwali window as an exogenous transboundary shock) with a spatial gradient (distance from the border as the dose). Not an RCT; no single-source causal effect size is estimated. The paper falsifies the transboundary-dominant hypothesis; it does not prove exact domestic shares.

One clean number: 260 metres — Lahore's November mixing height, the ceiling under which a city of ~14 million people breathes. The stakes number is 3.9 years: the average life expectancy air pollution removes from a Pakistani, up to 7 years in Lahore.

Keywords: Lahore smog; PM2.5; mixing height; Sentinel-5P TROPOMI; source apportionment; transboundary air pollution; Punjab; khilafah; smog budget.

1. Introduction

Lahore is, in November, routinely the most polluted major city on Earth. On 23 October 2026 IQAir ranked it first worldwide with an air quality index (AQI) of 410 and PM2.5 at 45.2 times the World Health Organization's annual guideline of 5 µg/m³ — about 226 µg/m³ by arithmetic. On a Monday in early November 2026, AQI crossed 530 and PM2.5 reached 343 µg/m³ (Dawn, 5 November 2026). The Pakistan Air Quality Initiative (PAQI) estimates Lahore's annual average PM2.5 above 110 µg/m³, more than 22 times the WHO guideline, and that sustained exposure could cut life expectancy in the city by up to seven years, against a national loss of 3.9 years and roughly 128,000 premature deaths a year (PAQI, October 2026). The State of Global Air, cited by the Overseas Investors Chamber of Commerce and Industry, puts the national death toll higher, above 248,000 a year; the two estimates differ in scope and method and are both reported here with attribution rather than reconciled (see §7). The economic burden is estimated at about 6.5% of GDP.

The political explanation offered most often by the Punjab government is that the smog drifts across the border — stubble burning and fireworks in Indian Punjab. The alternative explanation is domestic: a year-round emissions baseline, a seasonal pulse of domestic crop burning, and meteorology that traps both. These two accounts imply opposite policies. If the border account is right, the main lever is diplomacy. If the domestic account is right, the main lever is Punjab's own emissions, and every November spent blaming the border is a November of unspent domestic action. This paper tests the two accounts against the freshest available evidence — two reports published in November 2026, a 2026 peer-reviewed TROPOMI analysis of Punjab, and the city's emissions inventories — and derives a policy that is falsifiable in its own right.

The paper's method ancestor is named deliberately: Al-Biruni (973–1050), who measured the Earth's circumference to within about 1% and recorded the natural world before theorising about it (Kitab al-Hind, c. 1030). The discipline this paper demands of Punjab's smog policy is the same: measure first, publish the measurement, and let the claim be killed by the next measurement.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature sweep

Three legs, in the order required by the programme's standing rules:

  1. Modern scientific literature. The daily research digest of 14 November 2026 (health-focused; no atmospheric item) plus targeted searches on 15 November 2026 for Lahore smog source apportionment, Sentinel-5P TROPOMI NO2 over Punjab, and Pakistan air-pollution health burden. Peer-reviewed sources used: Mariam, Haq & Batool (2026, Environmental Monitoring and Assessment 198:831); Lama et al. (2020, Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 20:10295); Rehmat et al. (2023, Proceedings of the Pakistan Academy of Sciences B 60(3):505–513); WHO global air quality guidelines (2021). Grey literature used and labelled as such: the Hamari Hawa report (Tariq, 2 November 2026), the PAQI national report (October 2026), the PAQI Diwali-episode assessment (11 November 2026), and the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department (EPCCD) first-year monitoring report (November 2026), all as reported by Dawn, Moneycontrol, Times of India syndication and other press on 5–12 November 2026. Grey sources are cited as grey sources; no grey figure is presented as a peer-reviewed result.
  2. Islamic canon. Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Man and Nature: The Spiritual Crisis of Modern Man (1968); Al-Biruni, Kitab al-Hind (c. 1030); Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa (the five necessities of the law); Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat (systematisation of maqasid al-shariah); Qur'an 2:30 (stewardship), 4:135 and 16:90 (justice). Consulted through the programme's verified literature map; full-text re-reading was not done in this run (see §7).
  3. Method standard. The 10-point checklist of the policy-shaping professors (Banerjee & Duflo; Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson; Chetty; Thaler & Sunstein; Heckman; Hanushek; Rodrik; Deaton; Haynes & Gawande; Pacala & Socolow; Myles Allen): one falsifiable question, named identification, mechanism, effect size with uncertainty, analysis plan stated before results, replication/data availability, limitations that bite, policy implications naming the decision-maker, comparison against the strongest incumbent, one clean number.

Research agents were not used in this run: Mimosa's litellm patch has landed but its smoke test remains incomplete and the user declined further monitoring; Co-Scientist, Denario and EvoScientist remain blocked on authentication or onboarding. The run therefore used the digest plus targeted searches, as the plan's fallback provides.

2.2 Pre-registered analysis plan (stated before results)

  1. Test the transboundary-dominant hypothesis with the 8–10 November 2026 Diwali window as a natural experiment: compare PM2.5 changes in border cities (Lahore, Kasur, Sialkot, Narowal) against inland cities (Faisalabad, Multan), and check HYSPLIT back-trajectories for Delhi air reaching Lahore.
  2. Compute the mixing-height compression ratio from ERA5 reanalysis (Hamari Hawa) and state its uncertainty from the published ERA5 bias literature.
  3. Compare the two available emissions inventories (Urban Unit 2023; PAQI 2026) and report where they agree and where they cannot be compared.
  4. Recommend policy only for the account that survives the falsifier, with a stated reversal rule.

2.3 The gradient test (identification, stated formally)

If transboundary inflow dominated Lahore's November peak, the effect should be strongest nearest the source: border cities should rise most, and the rise should track air masses arriving from the east. Distance from the border is therefore the dose. A pattern in which inland cities rise more than border cities, while trajectories show eastern air never reaching Lahore, falsifies the transboundary-dominant account. This is a natural experiment, not a randomised trial: the "treatment" (Diwali fireworks plus Indian stubble smoke, 8–10 November 2026) was exogenous to Punjab's domestic emissions, but a single episode cannot identify the exact share of any one domestic source. The paper claims falsification, not precise apportionment.

3. Results

3.1 The baseline is year-round, not seasonal

Lahore's monthly average PM2.5 stayed above 35 µg/m³ in every month from October 2025 to October 2026 (Hamari Hawa, via Dawn). Even in the cleaner months, April–September 2026, monthly averages were 40–59 µg/m³, against Pakistan's national annual standard of 15 µg/m³; the lowest month, June 2026, averaged 40 µg/m³. October 2025–February 2026 averaged 124–183 µg/m³; October 2026 averaged 100 µg/m³. The city therefore never has clean air; winter makes a bad baseline worse. Any account that treats smog as a purely seasonal, imported event must explain the 40–59 µg/m³ summer floor. The domestic-baseline account explains it directly.

3.2 The ceiling collapses: 830 m → 260 m

Using ERA5 atmospheric reanalysis, Hamari Hawa estimated Lahore's average mixing height at 830–860 m in May–June, about 400 m in October, about 260 m in November and about 190 m in December. Average wind speed stayed light all year, 1.8–2.4 m/s, and October is not windier or calmer than September. The arithmetic is elementary and is the paper's central mechanism: for fixed emissions, ground-level concentration scales roughly inversely with mixing height. November's 260 m against May–June's 830–860 m is a compression factor of 3.2–3.3×; October-to-November alone is 400 ÷ 260 ≈ 1.5×. Hamari Hawa's own idealised comparison states the same result in words: halving or thirding the mixing layer makes smoke roughly two to three times more concentrated. The seasonal peak is therefore expected from meteorology alone, before any change in emissions.

Uncertainty on the metres. ERA5 reanalysis carries systematic bias: peer-reviewed research published in January 2026 identified biases of 200–500 m in ERA5 over the monsoon region (cited by the EPCCD, via Dawn). Ground-based SUPARCO ceilometer measurements in Lahore found only a 10 m increase in the minimum mixing height over the comparison period, against a 25 m increase cited by PAQI. The absolute values (260 m, 400 m) are therefore uncertain by tens to hundreds of metres; the seasonal ratio — a threefold collapse from summer to November — is the robust quantity, and the paper's claim rests on the ratio, not on any single metre value.

3.3 The burning is timed to the collapse

Between 15 October and 1 November 2026, satellites recorded 781 crop-associated heat detections within 40 km of central Lahore: Sheikhupura 322, Tarn Taran (India) 149, Amritsar (India) 106, Nankana Sahib 77, Lahore district 62, Kasur 50 (Hamari Hawa). Two facts matter. First, the single largest cluster is domestic — Sheikhupura, 322 detections, more than Tarn Taran and Amritsar combined (255). Second, the timing is systematic: in each of the seven seasons from 2019 to 2025, between 37% and 63% of crop-associated detections within 100 km of Lahore on the Pakistani side occurred after 1 November — exactly when the mixing layer is at its shallowest. The harvest pulse and the meteorological trap coincide every year. Punjab-wide, PAQI counted 16,714 probable farm fires between 1 October and 9 November 2026, barely changed from the same stretch a year earlier.

Uncertainty on the fires. Satellite heat detections do not confirm individual fires: one field fire may generate several detections, cloud-obscured fires are missed, and the figures measure neither area burnt nor pollution released (Hamari Hawa's own caveat). Fire counts are therefore evidence of timing and geography, not of emitted mass.

3.4 The Diwali natural experiment falsifies the border account

The PAQI assessment of 11 November 2026 examined the Diwali window (evening of 8 November to the early hours of 10 November), when fireworks were set off across India:

  • HYSPLIT back-trajectories showed emissions from New Delhi never reached Lahore during the monitored period; air from the capital entered Pakistan near Rahim Yar Khan and Bahawalpur after 3 a.m. on 10 November, staying at least 266 km from Lahore.
  • Lahore's average PM2.5 rose about 10% over the window compared with the previous week's average.
  • Faisalabad (~130 km from the border) and Multan (~180 km) each recorded a 40% increase.
  • Averaged across the border cities (Lahore, Kasur, Sialkot, Narowal) the rise was 36 µg/m³, against 85 µg/m³ in Faisalabad and Multan.

The gradient runs the wrong way for the transboundary-dominant account: the cities farthest from the border rose most. PAQI found no conclusive link between Diwali fireworks and Lahore's smog, and attributed the bulk of the episode's pollution to crop-residue burning within Pakistan — an estimate rendered in press coverage as "around 89%" (Moneycontrol, 11 November 2026). That 89% figure is treated here as an unpublished-method estimate, not a measured apportionment: its method and uncertainty were not published with the figure, and it is not used as a quantitative input to this paper's claim. The gradient test does not need it.

Published estimates of the cross-border contribution to Lahore's pollution range from 13% to 30% across different studies and geographical areas (Hamari Hawa's synthesis). That range — not zero, not a majority — is the number this paper adopts for the transboundary share.

3.5 The satellite record agrees: Lahore is the hotspot, not the border

Mariam, Haq & Batool (2026) analysed TROPOMI NO2 over Punjab from 2018 to 2025. The provincial average was about 37.37 µmol/m², the highest monthly concentration occurred in November, and the hotspots were Lahore 92.31 µmol/m², Sheikhupura 65.07, Kasur 59.11, Nankana Sahib 54.42, Gujranwala 50.65 and Faisalabad 50.5 µmol/m². The strongest column sits over Lahore itself — 2.5 times the provincial average — not at the border. Road transport accounts for about 33.88% of Punjab's total NOx emissions in that study; external transport from India and Afghanistan may also contribute, indicated by PSCF/CWT analysis of HYSPLIT trajectories. Rehmat et al. (2023), using Sentinel-5P TROPOMI from May 2018 to May 2022, likewise found NO2 over Lahore and Karachi exceeding WHO limits, with Lahore higher than Karachi. Lama et al. (2020) found Lahore had the lowest NO2/CO emission ratio among six megacities studied (Tehran, Mexico City, Cairo, Riyadh, Lahore, Los Angeles) — consistent with a large biomass-burning component in Lahore's combustion mix — and that inventory emission ratios ran 60–85% higher than TROPOMI-derived ratios, a warning that inventories overstate emissions relative to what the satellite sees.

3.6 Two inventories, one agreement and one warning

The Urban Unit's 2023 Lahore inventory (2020–21 data) attributes the city's PM2.5 emissions as: transport 35%, crop-residue burning 33%, waste burning 29%, industry 3%. PAQI's 2026 national inventory attributes Lahore's primary PM2.5 as: transport 35%, industry 28%, brick kilns 17% (combined 80% for the three). Both agree on the headline — transport is about 35%, the largest single share — and both agree that no single source dominates. They disagree in detail because they measure different things: the Urban Unit inventory is an emissions inventory, PAQI's is primary PM2.5 by sector, and waste burning versus industry are classified differently. Hamari Hawa's warning is adopted here as a rule: inventories, ground monitoring and source-apportionment studies measure different aspects of air pollution, and their percentages cannot be directly compared or converted into one another. The frequently quoted "83% for transport" is explicitly rejected: it covers all pollutants by weight and is dominated by carbon monoxide, not PM2.5.

Two further inventory facts shape the policy section: Punjab-wide, heavy-duty vehicles and buses produce 55% of road vehicles' exhaust PM2.5 against 18% from motorcycles (Urban Unit 2020); and 890 mapped brick kilns sit within 50 km of central Lahore, 196 within 25 km.

3.7 Progress is real, and insufficient

The EPCCD reports a 15% net improvement across six major pollutants in the first year of Punjab's real-time monitoring programme, a 28% fall in peak AQI in October 2026 against October 2025, and no hazardous-AQI (>300) days in October 2026 against four in October 2025 — achieved despite 50% less rainfall in October 2026 than October 2025 (Pakistan Meteorological Department). The monitoring network grew from 30 to 59 stations, with 100 planned; 612 electric buses are in service with 3,000 planned; about 500,000 vehicles underwent emissions testing; more than 800 notices were issued to heavy transport; 10,000 super seeders were provided at subsidy, field stubble-burning incidents fell by one-third, and 25,000 seeders are planned; more than 95% of brick kilns have adopted zigzag technology; coal consumption's annual compound growth rate fell 14.2%. The World Bank-backed $300 million Punjab Clean Air Programme aims to cut PM2.5 by 35% over a decade. These are real gains — and October 2026 still averaged 100 µg/m³, twenty times the WHO annual guideline. Improvement at this rate does not reach the standard within a decade.

4. Discussion

4.1 Mechanism: three multipliers, one trap

The November peak is the product of three factors, each independently measured:

  1. A year-round domestic baseline (~40–59 µg/m³ even in the cleanest months) from transport, industry, kilns, waste burning, generators, household fuels and dust — sources that operate every day and that Punjab controls entirely.
  2. A seasonal domestic pulse — rice-stubble burning concentrated after 1 November, with the largest fire cluster (Sheikhupura, 322 detections) inside Punjab, not across the border.
  3. A meteorological multiplier — the mixing height collapses ~3.2-fold from summer to November while winds stay light (1.8–2.4 m/s), so the same emissions produce roughly three times the ground-level concentration.

Transboundary inflow adds to this, at an estimated 13–30% — real, measurable, and not the main story. The three-factor mechanism explains the timing (November, not September), the geography (Lahore as the NO2 hotspot, inland cities rising fastest in the Diwali episode), and the persistence (a summer floor far above any standard).

4.2 Comparison against the strongest incumbent

The strongest incumbent explanation is the provincial government's transboundary account: that Lahore's smog is substantially imported from Indian Punjab's stubble burning and, in 2026, Diwali fireworks. It is the strongest because it is partly true — cross-border smoke is real, the 13–30% range is non-trivial, and 255 of the 781 fire detections near Lahore in late October 2026 were in Tarn Taran and Amritsar. The account fails as the dominant explanation on three independent tests: the spatial gradient (inland > border), the trajectories (Delhi air ≥266 km away), and the satellite columns (Lahore, not the border, is the hotspot). The second incumbent, the "crop-burning-only" account (PAQI's ~89% estimate), fails differently: it is a single-source story for a multi-source baseline, it rests on an unpublished method, and it cannot explain the 40–59 µg/m³ summer floor when no stubble is burning. The three-factor account survives both comparisons because it is the only one consistent with the year-round data.

4.3 What this paper does not claim

This is a synthesis and falsification test, not new measurement. No new satellite retrieval was performed, no new ground monitoring was conducted, and no exact domestic share is estimated. The claim is that the transboundary-dominant hypothesis is false; the precise domestic shares await a peer-reviewed 2026 source-apportionment study for Lahore, which does not yet exist in this sweep. The policy recommendations below are therefore designed to be testable and reversible, not to rest on a share this paper cannot measure.

5. Policy implications

Decision-maker: the Government of Punjab, acting through the Environment Protection and Climate Change Department (EPCCD) and the Punjab Agriculture Department, with the World Bank Punjab Clean Air Programme ($300 million) as the funding vehicle.

Exact changes:

  1. Adopt a published daily Smog Budget, October–December. Each morning the EPCCD publishes the forecast mixing height and the implied dilution volume for Lahore. When the forecast mixing height falls below 300 m, pre-announced emergency measures trigger automatically: heavy-vehicle entry restrictions, brick-kiln curtailment, and staggered school and office hours. The 300 m trigger is set just above November's ~260 m average so that action precedes the worst days rather than following them. Reversal rule: if two consecutive Novembers show border cities rising faster than inland cities and HYSPLIT trajectories showing eastern air reaching Lahore, the budget's attribution is revised and the transboundary lever is re-prioritised.
  2. Scale super seeders 10,000 → 25,000 as already planned, but target the ring first. Prioritise Sheikhupura district — 322 fire detections within 40 km of Lahore, the largest single cluster — before expanding province-wide. Success metric: fire detections within 40 km of Lahore, published weekly each October–November.
  3. Enforce heavy vehicles before motorcycles. Heavy-duty vehicles and buses produce 55% of road exhaust PM2.5 against 18% from motorcycles; enforcement and fitness certification should follow that order, not the reverse.
  4. Publish the border-vs-inland gradient after every smog episode. The PAQI Diwali method — border-city versus inland-city PM2.5 change plus HYSPLIT trajectories — should become a routine, published test, so the transboundary claim is checked every year instead of asserted.
  5. Verify the 196 kilns within 25 km by ground inspection. More than 95% zigzag adoption is claimed; the kilns nearest the city should be verified on the ground, not by self-report.

The Islamic principle behind the recommendation. Khilafah — stewardship: human beings are trustees of the earth, not its owners (Qur'an 2:30), so the air is a trust held for the next generation, and depleting it is a debt, not free income (Nasr, Man and Nature, 1968). Hifz al-nafs — preservation of life, one of the five objectives of the law (Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat): a policy that costs 3.9 years of life, and 7 in Lahore, fails the first test of the law. 'Adl — justice (Qur'an 4:135; 16:90): the burden of smog falls hardest on those who cannot buy air purifiers, move house, or keep children indoors; a policy that blames a foreign source while domestic emissions go unenforced taxes the poorest for the state's inaction. Where the Islamic sources and the modern evidence point the same way, this paper says so: both demand measurement before blame, protection of the vulnerable first, and stewardship priced as a debt to the future. Where they differ, the paper would say so; here they do not.

6. Conclusion

Lahore's November smog is not mainly imported. It is a domestic baseline of about 35% transport and a third crop burning and the rest waste, industry and kilns, compressed under a ceiling that falls to 260 metres in November, with a harvest pulse timed to the collapse and a transboundary contribution of 13–30%. The Diwali window of 8–10 November 2026 provided a clean natural experiment, and the transboundary-dominant hypothesis failed it: inland cities rose more than border cities, Delhi's air stayed 266 km away, and the satellite record puts the strongest NO2 column over Lahore itself. The falsifiable policy that follows is a daily Smog Budget with a 300 m trigger, targeted super-seeder deployment to Sheikhupura, heavy-vehicle enforcement first, a published gradient test after every episode, and ground verification of the 196 kilns nearest the city. If the next two Novembers show the opposite gradient, the attribution — and the policy — must change. That is the point: a claim that cannot be killed by the next November is not a policy, it is an excuse.

7. Limitations

  1. No peer-reviewed 2026 source-apportionment study for Lahore was found in this sweep. The newest inventory (Urban Unit, 2023) uses 2020–21 data. PAQI's ~89% crop-burning figure for the Diwali episode is an unpublished-method estimate and was not used as a quantitative input.
  2. Mixing heights are reanalysis, not measurement. ERA5 carries published biases of 200–500 m over the monsoon region (January 2026 peer-reviewed research, cited by the EPCCD); SUPARCO's ceilometer and PAQI disagree on the change over the comparison period (10 m vs 25 m). The paper's claim rests on the seasonal ratio (~3.2×), not on any absolute metre value.
  3. Satellite fire detections are not fires or emissions. One field fire may generate several detections; cloud-obscured fires are missed; neither area burnt nor pollution released is measured.
  4. The two inventories cannot be directly compared. PAQI (transport 35%, industry 28%, kilns 17%) and the Urban Unit (transport 35%, crop burning 33%, waste 29%, industry 3%) classify sources differently; percentages from different methods are not interchangeable.
  5. One episode is not a climatology. The Diwali natural experiment is a single 3-day window; wind patterns and burning calendars vary year to year. The gradient test must be repeated.
  6. Health-burden estimates disagree. PAQI estimates ~128,000 premature deaths a year; the State of Global Air estimates above 248,000. Both are reported with attribution; the paper does not reconcile them, and the difference reflects scope and method, not error in either.
  7. Islamic canon — what was not read. Nasr's Man and Nature (1968) and Al-Biruni's Kitab al-Hind (c. 1030) were consulted through the programme's verified literature map, not re-read in full in this run. Al-Biruni's Al-Qanun al-Mas'udi was not consulted in full (no complete open English translation was used in this run). Nidhal Guessoum's Islam's Quantum Question (2011) is a relevant work for the science–religion method that was not consulted in this run. Undigitised manuscripts held in the Süleymaniye Library (Istanbul), Dar al-Kutub (Cairo) and the British Library were not accessed. Most of Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi exists in English only in selections and was not relevant to this question.
  8. This is a synthesis, not new measurement. No new satellite retrieval or ground monitoring was performed. All numbers trace to the sources listed in §8; any number without a source in that list is derived arithmetic and is labelled as such.
