2026-11-16 Social Science Draft — not submitted

The Ten-Percent Ceiling: Ibn Khaldun's Fiscal Curve and Pakistan's Tax Record, 2001–2025

Question. Pakistan has raised its statutory tax rates repeatedly for a quarter of a century — general sales tax from 16% to 18%, a new super tax up to 10%, a 29% corporate rate stacked with surcharges — yet its tax-to-GDP ratio has not durably risen.

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan. ORCID: 0009-0001-5921-7509. Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI research assistant). Date: 16 November 2026. Field: Social Science (public economics / fiscal policy). Status: Manuscript draft. Not submitted anywhere. No professor's endorsement is claimed; the Harvard / MIT / Oxford policy-shaping scholars named in the method brief are the standard this paper practises, not co-authors.

Abstract

Question. Pakistan has raised its statutory tax rates repeatedly for a quarter of a century — general sales tax from 16% to 18%, a new super tax up to 10%, a 29% corporate rate stacked with surcharges — yet its tax-to-GDP ratio has not durably risen. Is the country on the wrong side of the fiscal curve Ibn Khaldun described in 1377, where higher rates shrink the base faster than they raise the yield?

Claim. Yes — on the evidence available, Pakistan sits past the peak of its Khaldunian curve. Over 2001–2024 the tax-to-GDP ratio moved only inside a 7.9–11.4% band (mean 9.7%), and the Federal Board of Revenue's own ratio stayed in single digits for 24 consecutive fiscal years (2000-01 to 2023-24), while statutory rates rose at every margin. The binding constraint is the base, not the rate: about 5.9 million returns were filed for tax year 2025 in a country of 241.5 million people, and only about 3 million taxpayers show any taxable income at all.

Falsifier. The claim is refuted if either (i) the FBR-only tax-to-GDP ratio rises above 12% and holds there for three consecutive fiscal years with no new statutory rate increase, or (ii) a legislated cut in a major rate — general sales tax back to 16%, or super-tax relief — is followed within two fiscal years by a fall, rather than a rise, in the FBR tax-to-GDP ratio. The fiscal year 2025-26 outturn (target Rs 14.131 trillion) is the first scheduled test.

Identification. Association only. This is a descriptive time-series test on published aggregates, with no control group and no randomised or quasi-experimental variation in rates. Confounders — GDP growth, inflation, IMF programme conditions, enforcement drives — are named, not controlled. The paper falsifies the claim that "rate rises raise the ratio"; it does not estimate a causal effect of any single rate. A regression-discontinuity design on the February 2023 GST rise (17% → 18%) and a randomised rate pilot are proposed as the causal tests.

One clean number: 24 years below 10% — the number of consecutive fiscal years the FBR's tax-to-GDP ratio stayed in single digits while rates rose. The stakes number is 3 million: the people in a country of 241.5 million who show any taxable income.

Keywords: Ibn Khaldun; Laffer curve; tax-to-GDP ratio; Pakistan; FBR; fiscal policy; tax base; super tax; maqasid; 'adl.

1. Introduction

Every Pakistani budget of the last decade has done the same thing: raised a rate. The general sales tax (GST) went from 16% to 17% in 2013 and to 18% in February 2023. A super tax on high earners was invented in 2022 at 1–4% and raised to 10% in 2023. The corporate rate stands at 29%, with banks at 42–43%, and the Overseas Investors Chamber of Commerce and Industry (OICCI) reports that the effective burden on large-scale industries approaches 49% once surcharges stack. And after all of it, the tax-to-GDP ratio — the single number that says whether a state can pay for itself — has barely moved. The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) itself reports that its tax-to-GDP ratio stayed in single digits for 24 consecutive fiscal years, from 2000-01 to 2023-24. The World Bank lent $400 million in 2019 to lift the ratio to 17%; the target was later cut to 10%.

This is not a new puzzle. In 1377, Ibn Khaldun wrote in the Muqaddimah — in the Rosenthal translation, the passage every economics textbook now quotes — "It should be known that at the beginning of the dynasty, taxation yields a large revenue from small assessments. At the end of the dynasty, taxation yields a small revenue from large assessments." His mechanism was dynastic: as a dynasty ages, its cohesion ('asabiyyah) decays, its spending grows, and it imposes fresh taxes and raises old rates — "but the effects on business of this rise in taxation make themselves felt," enterprises contract, and revenue falls. Six centuries later Arthur Laffer drew the same curve on a napkin; the profession calls it the Laffer curve, and Laffer himself credited Ibn Khaldun as the originator. A 2018 study of Malaysia (Annuar et al., ISRA International Journal of Islamic Finance) tested the Khaldunian curve directly with an autoregressive distributed lag model on 1996–2014 data and found the inverted U-shape, with a revenue-maximising corporate rate of 25.5156%.

This paper applies the same test to Pakistan, the country where the question matters most urgently: a state that cannot fund its schools, clinics or courts from its own revenue, that returns to the IMF every few years, and that answers each crisis by raising rates on the same narrow base. The test is deliberately simple and deliberately honest about its limits. It asks whether 24 years of published data are consistent with the Khaldunian prediction — rates up, ratio flat, base narrow — and it states in advance what evidence would kill the claim.

The method standard is the one this programme practises: Banerjee and Duflo's demand for one small testable question; Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson's use of a source of variation no one can manipulate; Rodrik's growth diagnostics — find the binding constraint before prescribing; Deaton's insistence that measurement is the argument. The binding-constraint diagnosis is the paper's central move: if the constraint is the rate, raise it; if the constraint is the base, widen it. Twenty-four years of data say the constraint is the base.

2. Methods

2.1 Literature sweep

Three legs, in the order required by the programme's standing rules:

  1. Modern scientific and policy literature. The daily research digest of 14 November 2026 is health-focused and contains no fiscal item; the sweep for this paper is therefore targeted searches conducted on 16 November 2026 for Pakistan's tax-to-GDP series, FBR annual collections, filer counts, GST and super-tax rate history, and the empirical literature on Ibn Khaldun's tax theory. Peer-reviewed sources used: Annuar, Isa, Ibrahim and Solarin (2018), "Malaysian corporate tax rate and revenue: the application of Ibn Khaldun tax theory", ISRA International Journal of Islamic Finance 10:251–262, doi:10.1108/IJIF-07-2017-0011. Policy and official sources used, each labelled as such: FBR annual collection figures as reported by The News, ProPakistani, PakBanker and Mettis Global (July–October 2025); the World Bank Pakistan Raises Revenue programme implementation report as reported by The Express Tribune (2026); the OICCI report Pakistan's Tax Paradox as reported by Dawn (22 February 2026); the Auditor General of Pakistan's audit of the FBR's Broadening of Tax Base wing as reported by TaxationPk (30 June 2025); OECD Revenue Statistics in Asia and the Pacific 2026: Pakistan; CEIC tax-revenue series (World Bank / Ministry of Finance / Pakistan Bureau of Statistics data). Press-reported figures are cited as press-reported, with the underlying official source named wherever the report names it; no press figure is presented as a peer-reviewed result.
  2. Islamic canon. Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddimah (1377), Chapter 3, the section on taxation (Rosenthal translation, Princeton University Press, 1958/1969); Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa (the five necessities of the law, including preservation of wealth, hifz al-mal); Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat (systematisation of maqasid al-shariah); Al-Mawardi, Al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyya (constitutional theory: taxation by lawful authority and consultation); Muhammad al-Tahir Ibn Ashur, Maqasid al-Shari'ah al-Islamiyyah (written 1946; expanded maqasid to freedom, justice and equality); M. Umer Chapra, Islam and the Economic Challenge (1992); Muhammad Taqi Usmani, An Introduction to Islamic Finance (2002); Qur'an 4:135 and 16:90 ('adl — justice), 42:38 (shura — consultation), 9:60 (zakat). Consulted through the programme's verified literature map; full-text re-reading was not done in this run (see §7).
  3. Method standard. The 10-point checklist of the policy-shaping professors (Banerjee & Duflo; Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson; Chetty; Thaler & Sunstein; Heckman; Hanushek; Rodrik; Deaton; Haynes & Gawande; Pacala & Socolow; Myles Allen): one falsifiable question, named identification, mechanism, effect size with uncertainty, analysis plan stated before results, replication/data availability, limitations that bite, policy implications naming the decision-maker, comparison against the strongest incumbent, one clean number.

Research agents were not used in this run: Mimosa's litellm patch has landed but its smoke test remains incomplete; Co-Scientist, Denario and EvoScientist remain blocked on authentication or onboarding. The run therefore used the digest plus targeted searches, as the plan's fallback provides.

2.2 Pre-registered analysis plan (stated before results)

  1. Assemble the rate history from primary legislation and official notifications: GST 16% → 17% → 18%; super tax 0% → 4% → 10%; corporate rate and surcharges.
  2. Assemble the revenue series on two definitions, kept strictly separate: (a) the FBR-only tax-to-GDP ratio (federal collections), and (b) the all-levels-of-government ratio (OECD/CEIC). Report both; never mix them.
  3. Test the Khaldunian prediction in its weakest falsifiable form: if rates rose and the ratio did not durably rise, the "rate rises raise the ratio" claim fails; if the base stayed narrow while rates rose, the mechanism (base contraction) is consistent with the data.
  4. Stress-test against the incumbent's best year (FY2024-25): if the strongest enforcement year on record broke the ceiling durably, say so and weaken the claim accordingly.
  5. Recommend policy only for the account that survives, with a stated reversal rule and a named causal test for the future.

2.3 Identification (stated formally)

Association only. The design is a descriptive time series on national aggregates. There is no control group, no random assignment of tax rates, and no instrument. Rate changes coincide with IMF programmes, inflation shocks, floods, and enforcement drives, any of which could move the ratio independently. The paper therefore claims a pattern (rates up, ratio flat, base narrow) and a falsification (the rate-raises-revenue claim fails on its own terms), not a causal effect size for any rate. The causal tests that could identify one are specified in §4.3: a regression discontinuity around the February 2023 GST rise, and a randomised low-rate pilot on a defined taxpayer segment.

3. Results

3.1 The rates rose at every margin

  • General sales tax. The standard rate was 16%, raised to 17% in the Finance Bill 2013-14 (a rise the Supreme Court later examined in Engineer Iqbal Zafar Jhagra v Federation of Pakistan, 2013), and raised again to 18% with effect from 14 February 2023 by SRO 179(I)/2023, confirmed in the Finance (Supplementary) Bill 2023 — a Rs 170 billion "mini-budget" and an explicit IMF programme condition. Luxury items were put at 25%.
  • Super tax. Introduced by the Finance Act 2022 (Income Tax Ordinance 2001, section 4C) at graduated rates of 1–4% on income above Rs 150 million, with 10% for fifteen specified industries above Rs 300 million. The Finance Act 2023 raised the schedule to 1–10%, with 10% on income above Rs 500 million (8% on Rs 400–500 million, 6% on Rs 350–400 million); banking companies pay 10% above Rs 300 million. The levy was litigated immediately: the Sindh High Court declared the tax-year 2022 charge ultra vires, and the Lahore and Islamabad High Courts ruled against retrospective application of the higher rates.
  • Corporate and other rates. The standard corporate rate is 29% (20% for small companies; 42% for banks in tax year 2027, down from 43%). Federal excise duty on cigarettes was raised alongside the GST rise, and FED on beverages and sugary drinks from 13% to 20%. Withholding taxes were extended year after year until they supplied 59% of all income-tax collection in FY2024-25.

3.2 The ratio did not move: 24 years below 10%

The FBR's own reporting, summarised in June 2025, is that its tax-to-GDP ratio remained in single digits in every fiscal year from 2000-01 to 2023-24 — 24 consecutive years. The anchor points: FY2021-22, 9.2%; FY2022-23, 8.5%; FY2023-24, 8.8% (Rs 9,299.1 billion collected against GDP of over Rs 105 trillion). The broader all-tax series (CEIC, from Ministry of Finance and Pakistan Bureau of Statistics data) tells the same story on a slightly higher level: 2001–2024, mean 9.7%, all-time high 11.4% in 2017, record low 7.9% in 2001, 10.3% in 2024. The OECD's all-levels-of-government measure puts Pakistan at 12.3% in 2024 (up from 10.6% in 2023 and 9.3% in 2011) — higher because it counts provincial taxes the FBR series excludes — against an Asia-Pacific average of 19.7% and an OECD average of 34.1%.

Three facts make the flatness striking rather than trivial. First, the level of collections rose enormously in nominal rupees (Rs 9.3 trillion to Rs 11.7 trillion in a single year, §3.4) — but the ratio is the test, and the ratio is what did not move. Second, the flat band survived every kind of government and every kind of reform: military and civilian, IMF programme and no programme. Third, the 2017 peak of 11.4% — the best year in the series — was followed by retreat, not by a new plateau; the ratio does not ratchet up, it reverts.

Uncertainty on the ratio. The two definitions differ by 1.5–3.5 percentage points in the same year (FBR-only 8.8–10.3% versus OECD all-levels 12.3% in 2024), because the FBR series excludes provincial taxes and the OECD series includes them. The paper's 24-year claim is anchored to the FBR-only series, which is the series the FBR itself reported as single-digit for 24 years; the OECD series is reported alongside so the reader can see the definitional gap. No conclusion in this paper depends on which definition is used: on either definition, the ratio is far below the 15% the World Bank and IMF treat as the minimum for sustainable growth, and far below regional peers (India 17%, Bangladesh 12%, per OICCI).

3.3 The base stayed narrow while the rates rose

The mechanism Ibn Khaldun named — rising rates shrink the base — is visible in the filer counts:

  • Income tax: 4,738,595 active income-tax filers in FY2023-24 (FBR report). Against a 2023 census population of 241,499,431, that is about 2.0% of the population.
  • Sales tax: only 234,193 individuals and entities filed sales-tax returns in FY2023-24 — roughly one sales-tax filer for every twenty income-tax filers, in an economy where GST supplies about a third of federal revenue.
  • The filer surge that bought nothing. The Auditor General of Pakistan found returns filed rose 76%, from 2.959 million (tax year 2023) to 5.215 million (tax year 2024) — yet the tax-to-GDP ratio fell over the comparable window, from 10.6% in 2016-17 to 8.7%. The audit's explanation: most new filers entered the system to obtain reduced withholding rates on property and vehicle transactions, not to declare income. For tax year 2025, 5.9 million returns were filed (up 17.6%), but about one-third carried zero tax, and only about 3 million of 6.53 million active taxpayers show any taxable income at all — about 1.2% of the population.
  • The missing 20 million. FBR's own estimates, cited in the Business Recorder analysis of the FBR Year Book, put the number of individuals liable to file at no more than 20 million. The gap between 20 million liable and ~5–7 million filing is the base that rate rises never reach.
  • Tax paid without filing. 120 million unique mobile-phone users pay 15% advance income tax on their usage — roughly 25 times the number of active income-tax filers. The state already taxes a quarter of the population's phones; it cannot get a fortieth of the population to file a return. Withholding taxes supplied 59% of income-tax collection in FY2024-25: the system collects at source from people it never registers, and calls the result compliance.

3.4 The incumbent's best year: FY2024-25

Fiscal year 2024-25 is the strongest possible test of the rival account — that the ratio can be raised by squeezing harder at existing rates — because it was the strongest enforcement year on record. FBR collected Rs 11,744.3 billion, up 26.3% (Rs 2,445.2 billion) on FY2023-24's Rs 9,299.1 billion, the largest annual addition ever. The composition: income tax Rs 5.784 trillion (+28%), sales tax Rs 3.9 trillion (+26%), customs Rs 0.767 trillion (+16%), federal excise Rs 1.284 trillion (+27%).

The decomposition of the increase is the paper's most informative number. Of the Rs 2,445.2 billion increase, autonomous growth — what the economy would have delivered at unchanged policy — contributed only Rs 766 billion (31%), because inflation fell to 0.3% in the last quarter, GDP grew about 2.5%, and large-scale manufacturing contracted 1.52%. Policy measures contributed Rs 805 billion (33%) and enforcement Rs 865 billion (35%). The enforcement figure is 8.2 times the previous best on record (Rs 105 billion). Without policy and enforcement, collection would have been about Rs 10.07 trillion.

Three conclusions follow. First, the ratio did rise — to 10.3%, the first time the FBR series has crossed 10% in the 24-year window, and the strongest single-year improvement in 23 years by the FBR Chairman's own account. Second, it still missed the target: the original parliamentary target was Rs 12.97 trillion (shortfall about Rs 1.23 trillion); even the twice-revised target of Rs 11.9 trillion was missed by about Rs 0.17 trillion. Third, the increase was bought by squeezing the existing base harder, not by widening it: the filer counts above are from the same period, withholding remains 59% of income tax, and the World Bank's own verdict on its $400 million Pakistan Raises Revenue programme — whose target was a 17% ratio — was to downgrade the programme and cut the target to 10%. A system that needs record enforcement to reach 10.3% has not escaped the Khaldunian trap; it has demonstrated it. The scheduled test is FY2025-26, whose target is Rs 14.131 trillion: if the ratio holds above 12% for three years with no new rate rise, the falsifier in the Abstract is triggered and this paper's claim falls.

3.5 The cross-country benchmark: where the peak sits

The only peer-reviewed ARDL test of the Khaldunian curve in a Muslim-majority economy is Annuar et al. (2018) on Malaysia, 1996–2014: an inverted-U relationship between the corporate tax rate and corporate tax revenue, with a revenue-maximising rate of 25.5156% and long-run unidirectional causality from the rate to revenue. Pakistan's headline corporate rate of 29% already sits 3.5 points above that estimated optimum; with the super tax, a large company's headline rate reaches 39% — 13.5 points above it — and OICCI reports effective burdens approaching 49% for large-scale industries once surcharges stack. The Malaysian optimum is not Pakistan's optimum — different economy, different base, different period — and this paper does not transplant it. It is used as the paper's benchmark for what "past the peak" looks like in a comparable setting, and as the prior that the proposed Pakistani ARDL replication (§4.3) would test against.

The regional comparison points the same way. OICCI's Pakistan's Tax Paradox (reported by Dawn, 22 February 2026) describes Pakistan's system as "a narrow tax base and high tax rates, with tax revenues remaining largely stagnant as a share of GDP despite growth in absolute collections," and notes the ratio stuck at 9–10% for over a decade against India at 17% and Bangladesh at 12%. OICCI's own proposal — corporate tax phased from 29% to 25% over three years, super tax eliminated, GST from 18% to 17% and then 15% — is, in substance, the Khaldunian prescription, proposed by the taxpayers themselves. Where the taxed and the theorist agree, the disagreement is not about the direction; it is about whether the state will do it.

4. Discussion

4.1 Mechanism: Khaldun's chain, in modern dress

Ibn Khaldun's mechanism has four links, and each has a modern Pakistani analogue, stated here as the hypothesis the data are consistent with — not as a proven causal chain:

  1. Cohesion decays, spending grows. Khaldun: the dynasty's 'asabiyyah weakens, rulers' "needs and exigencies grow… owing to the luxury in which they have been brought up." Modern analogue: a state that funds itself by borrowing and by IMF programmes rather than by a broad tax bargain has weak fiscal cohesion — it does not need to persuade citizens to pay, so it never builds the bargain.
  2. Fresh taxes and higher rates follow. Khaldun: rulers "impose fresh taxes on their subjects… and sharply raise the rate of old taxes to increase their yield." Modern analogue: GST 17% → 18% by SRO in February 2023; super tax 4% → 10%; withholding extended to mobile-phone top-ups, bank transactions, property and vehicle transfers.
  3. Business contracts and the base shrinks. Khaldun: "the effects on business of this rise in taxation make themselves felt… Cultural enterprises grow and increase [only] because the low taxes bring satisfaction." Modern analogue: activity migrates to untaxed or lightly taxed margins — agriculture, real estate, cash trade, the informal sector; firms litigate rather than comply (the super tax spent its first years in the Sindh, Lahore and Islamabad High Courts); individuals file nil returns for the transaction benefit rather than declaring income (Auditor General's finding, §3.3).
  4. Revenue falls — or, in the modern version, stalls. Khaldun: "taxation yields a small revenue from large assessments." Modern analogue: the ratio stays in a 7.9–11.4% band for 24 years; each rate rise is followed by a revenue bump that does not survive as a higher ratio; the World Bank cuts its target from 17% to 10%.

The alternative mechanism — that the flat ratio reflects low state capacity rather than high rates — is not excluded by this paper and is partly true: a state that cannot register 20 million liable filers has a capacity problem. But capacity and rates interact in exactly the Khaldunian direction: high rates raise the return to evasion, which raises the cost of enforcement, which the state meets with more withholding at source — taxing phones instead of incomes. The FY2024-25 decomposition (§3.4) is the evidence: 35% of the increase came from enforcement, the most expensive and least durable margin.

4.2 Comparison against the strongest incumbent

The strongest incumbent explanation is the IMF/FBR model: raise statutory rates, widen withholding, and enforce harder on the existing base. It is the strongest because it is partly right — FY2024-25 proved that enforcement can move the ratio, from 8.8% to 10.3% in one year, the best single-year improvement in 23 years. It fails as a durable explanation on three counts. First, the improvement was bought with Rs 865 billion of enforcement, 8.2 times the previous record: a margin that cannot be repeated at that multiple every year. Second, the target was still missed — by Rs 1.23 trillion against the original target — so the model under-delivered on its own terms. Third, the model's own sponsors have retreated from it: the World Bank cut the programme target from 17% to 10%, and OICCI, the chamber of the largest taxpayers, now proposes the opposite instrument (lower rates, wider base).

The second incumbent, the "capacity-only" account — that Pakistan's ratio is low only because the state cannot administer taxes — fails differently: it cannot explain why the ratio was equally flat in the years when capacity was being built (the $400 million PRR programme, the Track and Trace system, IRIS 3.0) or why a 76% surge in filers coincided with a falling ratio. Capacity matters, but capacity spent on squeezing the same base is capacity spent on the wrong margin. The Khaldunian account survives both comparisons because it is the only one consistent with all four facts: rates up, ratio flat, base narrow, enforcement exhausted.

4.3 What this paper does not claim — and the causal test it proposes

This paper does not estimate the revenue-maximising tax rate for Pakistan, does not prove that any particular rate cut would raise revenue, and does not claim that Ibn Khaldun's dynastic theory is a complete theory of a modern fiscal state. It claims a pattern and a falsification, and it proposes the test that would settle the causal question:

  1. Regression discontinuity on the GST rise. The February 2023 rise from 17% to 18% was imposed by SRO on a single date (14 February 2023) for administrative reasons tied to the IMF programme, not to the business cycle. Monthly GST collection and registered-filer counts around that date, with a discontinuity design, can estimate the causal effect of a one-point rise on revenue and on registrations.
  2. A randomised low-rate pilot. Offer a randomly selected group of non-filing traders a reduced effective rate (for example, the Tajir Dost scheme at a lower presumptive rate) against a control group at the standard rate, and measure registration, declared income and revenue per trader over two years. This is the Banerjee–Duflo template applied to taxation: shrink the grand question into one small testable question, randomise, measure.
  3. An ARDL replication of Annuar et al. (2018) on Pakistani data. The same inverted-U specification, on FBR corporate collections and the statutory corporate rate 1996–2025, would estimate Pakistan's own revenue-maximising rate — the number this paper deliberately does not invent.

5. Policy implications

Decision-makers: the Federal Minister for Finance and Revenue and the Chairman of the Federal Board of Revenue, acting through the Finance Act and FBR administration; the National Assembly's Standing Committee on Finance as the oversight body; the World Bank and IMF as the programme counterparts whose targets the policy must satisfy.

Exact changes:

  1. Freeze statutory rates for three fiscal years (FY2026-27 to FY2028-29). No increase in GST, corporate rate, super tax or withholding rates; every new revenue measure must come from the base. Success metric: the FBR-only tax-to-GDP ratio, published monthly, with the base (active filers, nil-filers, withholding share) published alongside it.
  2. Legislate the OICCI glide path, conditional on base targets. Corporate tax 29% → 25% over three years and GST 18% → 15%, each step conditional on the active-filer count rising by at least 1 million in the preceding year. The conditionality is the point: the rate cut is earned by base growth, so the policy cannot be attacked as a giveaway.
  3. Redirect the enforcement machine from squeezing to registering. The Rs 865 billion enforcement capacity demonstrated in FY2024-25 should be retargeted at the ~13–15 million liable non-filers, starting with the 120 million mobile users already paying 15% advance income tax — a population the state already reaches, whose incomes it already touches, and whom it has never registered. Success metric: registrations from this population, published quarterly.
  4. Publish a monthly "base versus rate" dashboard. Filers, nil-filers, withholding share of income tax, and the FBR-only ratio — so that the next rate rise, if anyone proposes one, must answer the dashboard first.
  5. Commission the causal tests in §4.3 now. The GST regression discontinuity can be run on data the FBR already holds; the randomised pilot can be fielded in one city in one quarter. No rate cut should be made permanent before the pilot reports — and no rate rise should be made before the discontinuity study reports.

Reversal rule. If the FBR-only ratio rises above 12% and holds for three consecutive years with no new rate increase, the "stuck below the ceiling" claim is refuted and the freeze should be lifted. If a legislated rate cut is followed within two years by a fall in the ratio, the low-rates-raise-revenue half of the claim is refuted and the cut should be reversed. If neither happens, the policy continues.

The Islamic principle behind the recommendation. 'Adl — justice: "O you who believe, stand out firmly for justice, as witnesses to God, even if it be against yourselves, your parents, and your relatives" (Qur'an 4:135); "Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct" (Qur'an 16:90). A tax system that takes 59% of its income tax by withholding at source, from people it never registers, while 15% is levied on the phone top-ups of 120 million users — many of them poor — and while large firms litigate the super tax in the High Courts, distributes its burden by convenience of collection rather than by justice. Hifz al-mal — preservation of wealth, one of the five objectives of the law (Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa; systematised by Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat; extended to freedom and justice by Ibn Ashur, Maqasid al-Shari'ah al-Islamiyyah): a rate that destroys the enterprise it taxes destroys the wealth the law exists to preserve, which is exactly Ibn Khaldun's mechanism. Maslaha — public interest: the cost–benefit test must count the 20 million unregistered citizens and the unborn, not only next year's collection. Shura — consultation (Qur'an 42:38): a rate rise imposed by SRO without parliamentary approval — the practice the Supreme Court examined in 2013 and that recurred in February 2023 — is the opposite of consultation; Al-Mawardi's Al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyya makes lawful authority, not executive convenience, the condition of taxation. And the positive model is already in the tradition: zakat is a flat 2.5% levy on wealth above a threshold, owed by every Muslim who holds it (Qur'an 9:60 names its recipients) — a low rate on a broad base, designed for compliance rather than extraction. Where the Islamic sources and the modern evidence point the same way, this paper says so: both demand low rates on a wide base, justice in who bears the burden, and consultation before the rate is set. Where they differ, the paper would say so; here they do not.

6. Conclusion

For 24 years Pakistan raised its tax rates and its tax-to-GDP ratio did not durably rise: the FBR's ratio stayed in single digits from 2000-01 to 2023-24, the broader series averaged 9.7% with a 7.9–11.4% band, and the base stayed at about 2% of the population filing and about 1.2% showing any taxable income. The strongest enforcement year on record, FY2024-25, lifted the ratio to 10.3% — and still missed its target by over a trillion rupees, with two-thirds of the increase coming from policy and enforcement rather than from the economy. That is the pattern Ibn Khaldun described in 1377: "at the beginning of the dynasty, taxation yields a large revenue from small assessments. At the end of the dynasty, taxation yields a small revenue from large assessments." The falsifiable policy that follows is a three-year rate freeze, a conditional glide path down (corporate 29% → 25%, GST 18% → 15%), enforcement retargeted at the 13–15 million liable non-filers, a public base-versus-rate dashboard, and the causal tests that would settle the question properly. If the ratio breaks 12% and holds for three years without a new rate rise, or if a rate cut is followed by a falling ratio, this paper's claim falls and the policy reverses with it. That is the point: a fiscal claim that cannot be killed by the next three budgets is not a policy, it is a habit.

7. Limitations

  1. Association only. There is no causal identification in this paper: no control group, no instrument, no discontinuity exploited. Rate changes coincide with IMF programmes, inflation, floods and enforcement drives. The claim is a pattern and a falsification, not an effect size.
  2. Two definitions of the ratio differ by 1.5–3.5 points. The FBR-only series (8.8–10.3%) and the OECD all-levels series (12.3% in 2024) measure different things; the 24-year claim is anchored to the FBR-only series as the FBR reported it. A reader who prefers the OECD definition should read the claim as "below 13% for the available series" — the substantive conclusion is unchanged, but the headline number moves.
  3. Press-reported figures. FBR collections, filer counts, the AGP audit findings and the OICCI report are used as reported in the press (June 2025–February 2026), because the underlying FBR Year Book and audit report were not directly accessed in this run. Any figure that the FBR's own publications revise should supersede the press figure; the paper's claims are stated so that they survive small revisions (the band, not any single year, carries the argument).
  4. The FY2024-25 jump is a genuine counter-signal. The ratio crossed 10% for the first time in the window, driven by record enforcement. If FY2025-26 and FY2026-27 hold above 12% without new rates, the falsifier is triggered and the claim is refuted; this paper's own test is already running.
  5. The Malaysian optimum does not transfer. Annuar et al.'s 25.5156% is Malaysia's revenue-maximising corporate rate for 1996–2014, estimated with controls this paper does not replicate. It is a benchmark and a prior, not Pakistan's number; the ARDL replication proposed in §4.3 is the work that would estimate Pakistan's.
  6. Post-window legislation. The Finance Act 2026 (June 2026) reportedly changed super-tax thresholds and rates after the analysis window closed; those changes are not in the data and are not evaluated here. They are, however, a live natural experiment on the paper's own question, and the FY2025-26 outturn should be read against them.
  7. Islamic canon — what was not read. Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah, Al-Ghazali's Al-Mustasfa, Al-Shatibi's Al-Muwafaqat, Al-Mawardi's Al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyya and Ibn Ashur's Maqasid al-Shari'ah al-Islamiyyah were consulted through the programme's verified literature map, not re-read in full in this run. Chapra's Islam and the Economic Challenge (1992) and Usmani's An Introduction to Islamic Finance (2002) were consulted the same way. No Qur'anic verse is quoted beyond the four cited (4:135, 16:90, 42:38, 9:60), and no hadith is cited. Undigitised manuscripts held in the Süleymaniye Library (Istanbul), Dar al-Kutub (Cairo) and the British Library were not accessed. Most of Al-Razi's Kitab al-Hawi exists in English only in selections and was not relevant to this question.
  8. This is a synthesis, not new measurement. No new dataset was compiled, no FBR micro-data was accessed, and no econometric estimation was performed. All numbers trace to the sources listed in §8; any number without a source in that list is derived arithmetic and is labelled as such.

9. Data availability

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan · Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI)

Week of 2026-11-09 → 2026-11-15 (7 daily targets)

STATUS: DRAFT ONLY — never submit. Journal submission is Zubair's action under his own name.

Proposed title (placeholder)

"Multi-target computational triage of known bioactive chemical space against seven disease targets: similarity screening, ADMET/toxicity read-across and AutoDock Vina docking"

Abstract

We screened the bioactive chemical space of ChEMBL against seven therapeutically relevant targets in one week of automated LeadForge runs (9–15 Nov 2026): Plasmodium falciparum dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (PfDHODH), Staphylococcus aureus enoyl-ACP reductase (FabI), tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2), cyclin-dependent kinase 7 (CDK7), myeloid cell leukemia 1 (MCL1), peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARG) and respiratory syncytial virus fusion protein F (RSV F). For each target, the reference drug was recovered from live ChEMBL data (rediscovery check), 44–58 known ligands were similarity-screened (FabI: 430 compounds via a pinned-target run; TYK2: PubChem fallback after a ChEMBL outage), leads were ranked on a composite of similarity, Lipinski/Veber drug-likeness, PAINS and kNN toxicity read-across, and the top five leads were docked with AutoDock Vina against the best available X-ray structure, with the reference drug re-docked as control. Four runs produced leads that docked better than their reference drug: PfDHODH (all five leads, best −9.72 vs −8.21 kcal/mol for DSM265), FabI (three leads, best −11.44 vs −10.15 for afabicin), CDK7 (two leads, best −9.98 vs −8.91 for samuraciclib) and MCL1 (two stereoisomer leads, best −9.33 vs −8.26 for S63845), plus PPARG (one lead, −10.26 vs −9.05 for pioglitazone). Two runs were honest negatives (TYK2: closest lead 0.19 kcal/mol behind deucravacitinib, inside noise; RSV F: no novel lead beat presatovir). The RSV F run also caught and corrected a structure-selection error: the auto-picked PDB 29QJ is an HR1 fragment with a stapled peptide, not the presatovir pocket, and the comparison was re-run at prefusion structure 6VKE. All findings are computational triage; no compound is claimed as a drug, and wet-lab validation is required.

Methods

Pipeline (LeadForge, same flow for all seven runs). (1) Target identification from UniProtKB + ChEMBL (live). (2) Known-ligand retrieval from ChEMBL bioactivities. (3) Query-compound verification via PubChem PUG REST. (4) Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen vs known actives. (5) ADMET + safety panel: RDKit descriptors (Lipinski, Veber), PAINS filter, ToxGuard kNN read-across over 12 Tox21-style assays. (6) Composite lead ranking (similarity 40 / Lipinski 20 / Veber 10 / PAINS 10 / tox 20). (7) Molecular docking: AutoDock Vina, exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses, 22.5 Å box centred on the co-crystallised ligand centroid of the best X-ray structure (resolution < 3.0 Å); grid centre verified as the largest drug-like HETATM group with cofactors, glycans, waters and ions excluded (centre-fix audit, Nov 2026), and the PDB domain checked against the reference drug's binding site (TYK2/RSV F correction, Nov 2026). Reference drug re-docked in the same pocket as control. Vina noise is taken as ~±0.5–1 kcal/mol (up to ~2 kcal/mol in the literature); margins inside noise are reported as ties.

Targets, references and structures. PfDHODH / DSM265 (PDB 7L01, 1.60 Å); FabI / afabicin (PDB 6YUR, 1.96 Å, SKTS1 complex); TYK2 / deucravacitinib (PDB 6NZH, JH2 pseudokinase domain); CDK7 / samuraciclib (PDB 8R9A, 1.71 Å); MCL1 / S63845 (PDB 6UDV, 1.35 Å; exhaustiveness lowered to 2 after Vina timeouts on ~830–1050 Da ligands); PPARG / pioglitazone (PDB 9F7W, 1.25 Å, BPA-bound); RSV F / presatovir (PDB 6VKE, 2.10 Å, prefusion F + JNJ-40012665; auto-pick 29QJ discarded as the wrong domain).

Results summary

Date Target Reference Best lead (docking) Reference (docking) Verdict
9 Nov PfDHODH DSM265 CHEMBL3289670, −9.72 −8.21 All 5 leads beat DSM265; best margin 1.51, IC50 35 nM — but all are DSM265 triazolopyrimidine analogues, one scaffold family, and the margin sits inside Vina error
10 Nov FabI afabicin CHEMBL567711, −11.44 −10.15 Three leads beat afabicin; best margin 1.29 (0.86 vs the active form AFN-1252, −10.58); IC50 20 nM — promising backup chemotypes, not proven wins
11 Nov TYK2 deucravacitinib CID 162675488, −10.15 −10.34 Honest negative — no lead beats deucravacitinib; closest is 0.19 kcal/mol behind, inside sampling noise. ChEMBL was down; run used the PubChem similarity fallback, so no measured potency is attached
12 Nov CDK7 samuraciclib CHEMBL428690, −9.98 −8.91 Two leads beat samuraciclib; best margin 1.07 kcal/mol — backup chemotypes for a CDK7 programme
13 Nov MCL1 S63845 CHEMBL5538127, −9.33 −8.26 Two stereoisomer leads beat S63845 by ~1.0 kcal/mol (Ki 0.026 nM) — one chemotype, not two independent hits; docking at exhaustiveness 2, one lead undocked (Vina timeout)
14 Nov PPARG pioglitazone CHEMBL6145236, −10.26 −9.05 Clear win — 1.21 kcal/mol margin, scaffold hop (sim 0.163), EC50 0.49 nM, clean panel; most interesting lead of the week because it is NOT a pioglitazone look-alike
15 Nov RSV F presatovir CHEMBL4779491, −5.14 −6.14 Honest negative — no novel lead beats presatovir; best novel lead 1.00 kcal/mol behind. The presatovir record itself (CHEMBL3410450, −6.64) out-scores the re-dock, a stereochemistry/sampling effect, not a new lead

Headline results. 5 of 7 runs produced a docking lead better than the reference (PfDHODH, FabI, CDK7, MCL1, PPARG); 2 were negatives (TYK2, RSV F). The strongest single result is CHEMBL6145236 against PPARG: a non-thiazolidinedione chemotype docking 1.21 kcal/mol better than pioglitazone with sub-nanomolar measured potency. The FabI series (CHEMBL567711, CHEMBL586043) is the second genuine outcome: two backup chemotypes against a validated antibacterial target, though the margins shrink against the active metabolite AFN-1252. The PfDHODH result is the weakest "win": all five leads beat DSM265, but they are all DSM265 analogues, so the screen re-ranked one scaffold family rather than finding a new one. Across the week, every reference drug was recovered by the pipeline (rediscovery check passed in all runs where the reference was in ChEMBL).

Discussion

The week's pattern is the same one the screen keeps showing: docking wins are cheap inside a reference drug's own chemotype family, and the interesting hits are the ones that leave it. PPARG's CHEMBL6145236 is the week's only scaffold hop with a docking win, which is why it leads the paper. FabI and MCL1 are solid backup-series results with honest caveats (prodrug comparator for FabI; stereoisomer duplication and a timed-out dock for MCL1). PfDHODH shows the screen's failure mode — a full house of wins that are all the same molecule family — and is reported as such rather than as five independent hits. The two negatives are reported as results, not failures: TYK2 shows the screen can say no even for a well-studied kinase, and RSV F shows it can say no for a viral target where the measured potencies (sub-3 nM EC50s) look better than the reference on paper but do not survive a head-to-head pocket comparison. The RSV F correction — discarding the auto-picked 29QJ HR1-fragment structure for the prefusion 6VKE structure — is the week's methodological point: automated structure selection must be audited against the reference drug's binding site, and the audit caught the error before the report was written.

Limitations. (i) All scores are computational; no wet-lab data were generated. (ii) Docking used rigid receptors and single pockets; covalent mechanisms (none in this week's targets) and induced fit are not modelled. (iii) Measured potencies come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays and are not head-to-head comparisons — most clearly in RSV F, where sub-nanomolar leads and a micromolar reference record come from different assays. (iv) Similarity-anchored screening limits chemical diversity by design. (v) ToxGuard is kNN read-across, not a safety verdict. (vi) Mutant targets were not modelled (PfDHODH resistance, FabI, TYK2, MCL1, PPARG selectivity vs PPAR-alpha/delta, RSV F escape mutations). (vii) MCL1 docking ran at exhaustiveness 2 with ~0.2 kcal/mol run-to-run variation; one lead was not docked at all.

  • UniProtKB accessions: PfDHODH Q08210; FabI Q2FZQ3; TYK2 P29597; CDK7 P50613; MCL1 Q07820; PPARG P37231; RSV F P03420.
  • ChEMBL (EBI) target + bioactivity records, accessed live 9–15 Nov 2026 (TYK2 via PubChem fastsimilarity_2d fallback during a ChEMBL outage).
  • PubChem PUG REST (reference-compound verification).
  • RCSB PDB: 7L01 (PfDHODH, 1.60 Å); 6YUR (FabI–SKTS1, 1.96 Å); 6NZH (TYK2 JH2, deucravacitinib site); 8R9A (CDK7, 1.71 Å); 6UDV (MCL1, 1.35 Å); 9F7W (PPARG–BPA, 1.25 Å); 6VKE (prefusion RSV F + JNJ-40012665, 2.10 Å); 29QJ (RSV F HR1 fragment, discarded as the wrong domain).
  • LeadForge pipeline: run_pipeline + dock (centre-fix audit + domain check, Nov 2026). Individual daily reports: leadforge-daily-{DHODH,FabI,TYK2,CDK7,MCL1,PPARG,RSV-F}-2026-11-{09..15}.md.

STATUS: DRAFT ONLY — never submit. Journal submission is Zubair's action under his own name.

Proposed title (placeholder)

"Multi-target computational triage of known bioactive chemical space against seven disease targets: similarity screening, ADMET/toxicity read-across and AutoDock Vina docking"

Abstract

We screened the bioactive chemical space of ChEMBL against seven therapeutically relevant targets in one week of automated LeadForge runs (2–8 Nov 2026): FLT3, Plasmodium falciparum ATP4, Pseudomonas aeruginosa LpxC, acetylcholinesterase (AChE), isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1), Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) and menin (MEN1). For each target, the reference drug was recovered from live ChEMBL data (rediscovery check), 19–53 known ligands were similarity-screened, leads were ranked on a composite of similarity, Lipinski/Veber drug-likeness, PAINS and kNN toxicity read-across, and the top five leads were docked with AutoDock Vina against the best available X-ray structure, with the reference drug re-docked as control. Two runs produced leads that docked clearly better than their reference drug: CHEMBL5816906 against menin (−10.10 vs −8.37 kcal/mol for revumenib) and three scaffold-distinct leads against LpxC (best −10.85 vs −9.34 for ACHN-975). Three runs were effective ties (FLT3, AChE, IDH1) and one was an honest negative (BTK: no lead beat ibrutinib). One run (PfATP4) had no structure for docking but identified CHEMBL5591927, the strongest measured PfATP4 active in ChEMBL (EC50 4.6 nM), as a scaffold-distinct backup to cipargamin. All findings are computational triage; no compound is claimed as a drug, and wet-lab validation is required.

Methods

Pipeline (LeadForge, same flow for all seven runs). (1) Target identification from UniProtKB + ChEMBL (live). (2) Known-ligand retrieval from ChEMBL bioactivities. (3) Query-compound verification via PubChem PUG REST. (4) Morgan-fingerprint similarity screen vs known actives. (5) ADMET + safety panel: RDKit descriptors (Lipinski, Veber), PAINS filter, ToxGuard kNN read-across over 12 Tox21-style assays. (6) Composite lead ranking (similarity 40 / Lipinski 20 / Veber 10 / PAINS 10 / tox 20). (7) Molecular docking: AutoDock Vina, exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses, 22.5 Å box centred on the co-crystallised ligand centroid of the best X-ray structure (resolution < 3.0 Å); grid centre verified as the largest drug-like HETATM group with cofactors, glycans, waters and ions excluded (centre-fix audit, Nov 2026). Reference drug re-docked in the same pocket as control. Vina noise is taken as ~±0.5–1 kcal/mol (up to ~2 kcal/mol in the literature); margins inside noise are reported as ties.

Targets, references and structures. FLT3 / gilteritinib; PfATP4 / cipargamin (no structure — docking not possible); LpxC / ACHN-975; AChE / donepezil; IDH1 / ivosidenib; BTK / ibrutinib (PDB 5P9J, 1.08 Å); menin / revumenib (PDB 6O5I, 1.24 Å).

Results summary

Date Target Reference Best lead (docking) Reference (docking) Verdict
2 Nov FLT3 gilteritinib CID 66642725, −8.21 −7.60 Nominal win, inside noise; no measured FLT3 potency in screen — re-run pending ChEMBL recovery
3 Nov PfATP4 cipargamin (no structure) — No docking possible; CHEMBL5591927, EC50 4.6 nM, strongest measured PfATP4 active, scaffold-distinct — test vs G358S mutant
4 Nov LpxC ACHN-975 CHEMBL4437188, −10.85 −9.34 Three leads dock better; best is sub-nanomolar Kd 0.065 nM, PAINS-clean — backup series for a stalled clinical lead
5 Nov AChE donepezil CHEMBL3585775, −9.74 −10.02 Tie by docking; leads carry picomolar measured Ki/IC50 (0.0105–0.0269 nM) — sulfamoyl-carbamate backup chemotype
6 Nov IDH1 ivosidenib CHEMBL4282663, −8.24 −8.29 Tie by docking (0.05 gap); IC50 1.0 nM leads in the set — ivosidenib-analog backup family; pocket is wild-type, not R132H mutant
7 Nov BTK ibrutinib CHEMBL5749648, −10.13 −10.83 Honest negative — no lead beats ibrutinib; does not address the C481S resistance gap
8 Nov Menin (MEN1) revumenib CHEMBL5816906, −10.10 −8.37 Clear win — 1.73 kcal/mol margin, scaffold hop (sim 0.211), IC50 3.0 nM, clean panel; test vs resistance mutants (M327I/G331R)

Headline results. 2 of 7 runs produced a docking lead clearly better than the reference (menin, LpxC); 3 were ties (FLT3, AChE, IDH1); 1 was a negative (BTK); 1 had no structure but a measured-potency lead (PfATP4). Across the week, every reference drug was recovered by the pipeline (rediscovery check passed in all runs where the reference was in ChEMBL).

Discussion

The week's strongest single result is CHEMBL5816906 against menin: a scaffold-distinct binder docking 1.73 kcal/mol better than the FDA-approved revumenib, with nanomolar measured activity and a clean safety panel. Its value is conditional on the resistance question — menin inhibitors fail clinically via interface mutations, and no mutant structure was tested. The LpxC series (CHEMBL4437188 and two siblings) is the second genuine outcome: a sub-nanomolar, scaffold-distinct backup family for a target whose lead inhibitor stalled in the clinic. The three ties (FLT3, AChE, IDH1) are not failures: each carries measured potency at least as strong as the reference, which keeps them as backup chemotypes, but docking alone cannot rank them above the reference. The BTK negative is reported as a result, not a failure: it shows the screen can say no. The PfATP4 run exposes a structural-data gap — a high-value antimalarial target with no usable structure for docking — and points to the mutant-resistance assay as the decisive experiment.

Limitations. (i) All scores are computational; no wet-lab data were generated. (ii) Docking used rigid receptors and single pockets; covalent mechanisms (BTK Cys481) are not modelled. (iii) Measured potencies come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays and are not head-to-head comparisons. (iv) Similarity-anchored screening limits chemical diversity by design. (v) ToxGuard is kNN read-across, not a safety verdict. (vi) Mutant targets (IDH1 R132H, BTK C481S, menin M327I/G331R, PfATP4 G358S) were not modelled.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan · Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI)

Week of 2026-10-26 → 2026-11-01 (7 daily targets)

STATUS: DRAFT ONLY — never submit. Journal submission is Zubair's action under his own name.

Proposed title (placeholder)

"Computational small-molecule triage against seven high-burden disease targets using live public chemical data (LeadForge AI pipeline): a seven-day screening campaign"

Abstract

We describe a reproducible, fully automated computational triage pipeline that runs daily against one high-burden disease target, using only live public data sources (UniProtKB, ChEMBL, PubChem, the RCSB Protein Data Bank). Each daily run executes seven steps: (1) target identification from UniProtKB, (2) known-ligand retrieval from ChEMBL, (3) query-drug verification from PubChem, (4) Morgan-fingerprint / Tanimoto similarity screening with RDKit, (5) ADMET screening (Lipinski, Veber, PAINS, ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across), (6) composite-score lead ranking, and (7) AutoDock Vina docking (meeko ligand preparation) against the best available experimental structure. Across the week of 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-01 we screened seven targets spanning antifungal (Candida CYP51), antiviral (SARS-CoV-2 Mpro, influenza neuraminidase, HIV-1 integrase — attempted), antimicrobial resistance (MRSA PBP2a) and tuberculosis (MmpL3) and Alzheimer's disease (BACE1). Each run included a rediscovery control (verifying the pipeline recovers the reference drug or its scaffold from ChEMBL) and a head-to-head docking comparison between ranked leads and the reference therapy. Honest interpretation is enforced at every step: docking margins within ±1 kcal/mol are reported as noise-equivalent, failed or wrong-target runs are reported as failures rather than re-labelled, and all candidates are presented as computational starting points requiring wet-lab validation. No efficacy or therapeutic claims are made. Two runs this week produced above-noise docking margins (CYP51, PBP2a); two runs were invalid or corrected mid-run (HIV-1 integrase, MmpL3) and are reported as such.

Keywords: virtual screening; AutoDock Vina; ChEMBL; target triage; CYP51; Mpro; PBP2a; MmpL3; BACE1; neuraminidase; HIV-1 integrase

Introduction (draft)

Drug discovery for high-burden diseases in resource-limited settings needs a cheap, reproducible first filter: a computational triage step that converts open chemical data into a short wet-lab shortlist. This draft reports one week of daily automated screening from the LeadForge AI pipeline. The scope is deliberately narrow — computational candidate triage only — and the methods are designed so any other group can re-run them against the same live databases. This week is notable for its failures as much as its hits: two of the seven runs exposed target-mapping traps (polyprotein accessions, missing ChEMBL components) that the pipeline caught and reported rather than silently passing.

Target selection rationale

Targets were chosen for disease burden and the presence of a marketed or clinical-stage reference small molecule for head-to-head comparison: - Antifungal: Candida albicans CYP51/ERG11 (fluconazole) - Antiviral: SARS-CoV-2 Mpro (nirmatrelvir), influenza A neuraminidase (oseltamivir), HIV-1 integrase (dolutegravir — attempted, invalid run) - Antimicrobial resistance: MRSA PBP2a (ceftaroline) - Tuberculosis: M. tuberculosis MmpL3 (SQ109) - Alzheimer's disease: BACE1 (verubecestat)

Methods (draft)

7.1 Daily pipeline (identical all 7 days)

  1. Target identification: UniProtKB live search → human/pathogen protein, accession recorded.
  2. Known-ligand retrieval: ChEMBL target (accession-mapped), top bioactivities by pChEMBL.
  3. Query-drug verification: reference small-molecule drug confirmed live via PubChem PUG REST.
  4. Similarity screen: RDKit Morgan fingerprints, Tanimoto vs known actives, top 25 kept.
  5. ADMET screen: Lipinski / Veber rules, PAINS filters, ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays).
  6. Lead ranking: composite score (similarity 40 + Lipinski 20 + Veber 10 + PAINS 10 + tox 20).
  7. Docking: AutoDock Vina, meeko ligand prep, best available experimental structure (X-ray preferred), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses; reference drug docked head-to-head in the same grid.

7.2 Rediscovery control

Each run includes a rediscovery check: whether the pipeline recovers the reference drug's scaffold from the ChEMBL ligand set (positive controls validate the screen; negatives bound its recall).

7.3 Honest-interpretation rules (applied in every run)

  • Docking differences < ~1 kcal/mol = method noise, never "wins".
  • Measured Ki/IC50 values come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays — directional, not rankings.
  • When docking and measured potency disagree, the disagreement is reported, not averaged away.
  • ToxGuard outputs are kNN read-across: "no red flag found", not "proven safe".
  • All leads are existing ChEMBL compounds; patent paths need university/teacher review.
  • A run whose docking structure or ChEMBL target is wrong is reported as invalid, with the corrected re-run (if any) replacing it — never silently re-labelled.

Per-target result notes (from daily reports)

  • HIV-1 integrase (10-26): INVALID RUN, no verdict. UniProt P04585 is the whole Gag-Pol polyprotein (protease + RT + integrase), and the PDB auto-pick returned 6DV4 — an HIV-1 protease structure. Dolutegravir's −9.88 and CHEMBL3683705's −9.91 are cross-docking at a protease site, meaningless for integrase. Lesson recorded for the rotation: an integrase re-run needs an integrase-specific UniProt entry / ChEMBL integrase target, never the polyprotein.
  • CYP51 (10-27): strongest docking margin of the week. CHEMBL5566404 −10.70 (+3.57 vs fluconazole −7.13), CHEMBL5094280 −9.88 (+2.75), and CHEMBL638 = voriconazole −7.69 (+0.56) — an approved antifungal recovered by the screen. Fluconazole's own ChEMBL record (CHEMBL106, Kd 45 nM) docked −6.91. All three beating leads carry prior reported ChEMBL activity (IC50/Kd 45–323 nM) — known chemotypes, not novel molecules. Structure 5TZ1, X-ray 2.0 Å. Human CYP51A1 was explicitly excluded; this is the fungal ERG11 target.
  • Mpro (10-28): CHEMBL5574604 −9.21 vs nirmatrelvir −8.26 (+0.95, just under the ±1 kcal/mol floor) with measured Ki 0.04 nM — more potent than nirmatrelvir's reported Ki 0.26 nM — but similarity 0.913, a close analog, not a new scaffold. Docking used 7VH8 (1.59 Å), the reference drug's own co-crystal, after two failed attempts: the stock run picked maltase-glucoamylase (CHEMBL2074) and the auto-picked PDB 7TX0 was the NSP3 macrodomain, not Mpro. Polyprotein accessions defeat PDB auto-pick — verify the structure title before docking.
  • PBP2a (10-29): the week's most careful run. Two independent structures (1MWS, 2.00 Å; 3ZG0, 2.60 Å, ceftaroline's own co-crystal) both agree: CHEMBL4862632 beats active ceftaroline by +1.68/+1.20 kcal/mol, and CHEMBL4847813 beats it in both too. But the docking winner is NOT the wet-lab pick: CHEMBL4847813 has the strongest measured MecA binding (Kd 129 nM) and clean ADMET, while CHEMBL4862632 has the weakest Kd (264 nM), a Veber fail and a higher tox flag. Docking ≠ potency, stated in the report. Data is thin — only 4 ChEMBL MecA ligands exist (CHEMBL3512 PBP2a has zero bioactivities) — and the first attempt (wrong MecA adapter protein P60185 → maltase-glucoamylase) was discarded. Ceftaroline itself was not recovered in the mined set (no pChEMBL record).
  • MmpL3 (10-30): CHEMBL5436935 −9.02 vs SQ109 −7.88 (+1.14) and CHEMBL5428840 −8.78 (+0.90) — above/near noise — but all measured activities are against M. smegmatis MmpL3, the laboratory homologue: ChEMBL holds no M. tuberculosis MmpL3 target, so the ranking is homologue-guided triage and Mtb activity is unconfirmed. Rediscovery positive (CHEMBL561057 = SQ109 chemotype, sim 1.000). Stock run picked maltase-glucoamylase and was discarded. Structure 7NVH, 3.02 Å (cryo-EM-era resolution, noted honestly).
  • Neuraminidase (10-31): validation, not discovery. Rediscovery positive (oseltamivir CHEMBL1229, sim 1.000, IC50 0.06 nM, score 100). Top docking hits are oseltamivir itself, its active metabolite (carboxylate, −6.97) and a close analog (−6.98) vs reference −6.59 — all within noise, and docking was against the H274Y resistant mutant (3CKZ, 1.9 Å), not wild-type. Stock run picked human ABL1 kinase (CHEMBL1862) via the "NA"-in-"kiNAse" substring trap and was discarded. Same bug class as MmpL3: viral / non-human targets need an explicit ChEMBL target check, never the stock fallback.
  • BACE1 (11-01): no meaningful win. CHEMBL4861687 −10.11 (+0.16) and CHEMBL5092328 −10.00 (+0.05) vs verubecestat −9.95 — inside noise. The strongest measured binder, CHEMBL3982593 (IC50 0.011 nM, pChEMBL 10.96), docks worse than the reference (−9.50) — another docking-vs-measured disconnect. All top leads are amidine/thiazine analogs of verubecestat — low novelty. Target-level context: verubecestat failed Phase III (EPOCH stopped Feb 2017 for futility; APECS Feb 2018; NEJM 2018 no benefit, worsened cognition), so BACE1 carries clinical target risk beyond any binding score. Structure 7MYI, X-ray 1.25 Å (LY3202626 series co-crystal). Rediscovery negative — verubecestat absent from the 54 screened ligands. SR-MMP ToxGuard read-across 0.42–0.81 flagged for follow-up.

Weekly tallies (final)

  • 7/7 runs completed with docking numbers; 1 (HIV-1 integrase) with NO valid verdict — docking ran against the wrong protein and is reported as invalid, not as a result.
  • Rediscovery positives: 3 of 7 (MmpL3 SQ109 chemotype, neuraminidase oseltamivir, CYP51 fluconazole record CHEMBL106); negatives: BACE1, PBP2a (reference absent from the mined ChEMBL set); Mpro/PBP2a notes per daily reports — verify against daily JSONs before citing.
  • Above-noise docking margins: 2 runs (CYP51 +3.57/+2.75; PBP2a +1.68/+1.20 in two structures) plus MmpL3 +1.14 (homologue-guided only) — all still assay-gated, never declared wins.
  • Within-noise "better than reference" candidates: 3 runs (Mpro +0.95, neuraminidase +0.39, BACE1 +0.16) — priority candidates only, or validation-only in the neuraminidase case.
  • Stock-pipeline target bugs caught and discarded: 5 incidents across 4 runs (HIV-1 integrase auto-pick, Mpro attempt 1 target + auto-pick, MmpL3, neuraminidase, PBP2a attempt 1) — the week's dominant method lesson is that polyprotein accessions and non-human targets defeat the stock fallback; accession/organism verification before any run is trusted is now a standing rule.
  • Novelty: low across the week — analog series in 5 runs (CYP51, Mpro, PBP2a's DBO-adjacent set, neuraminidase metabolite family, BACE1 amidine family); MmpL3's adenosine-derived sulfonamides are the most structurally distinct output; PBP2a's non-beta-lactam leads (sim 0.09–0.30 to ceftaroline) are the most novel chemotypes.

Discussion (draft)

  1. The week's real product is the failure catalogue. Three stock runs picked unrelated human targets (maltase-glucoamylase twice, ABL1 kinase once) and one auto-picked PDB was the wrong domain of a polyprotein (NSP3 macrodomain for Mpro; protease for integrase). Every one was caught by accession/organism/structure-title verification and discarded with its evidence kept — the pipeline's honesty rules worked as designed.
  2. Rediscovery is the screen's calibration — and its limits are visible. Where the reference drug was in the ChEMBL set (neuraminidase, MmpL3, CYP51), the screen found it at the top; where it was absent (BACE1, PBP2a), the run says so rather than faking a positive. A negative rediscovery bounds recall, it does not invalidate the run.
  3. Noise discipline kept every head-to-head honest. Only CYP51 and PBP2a cleared the ±1 kcal/mol floor, and even those are reported as assay-gated candidates, not discoveries. Mpro's +0.95 sits just under the floor and is reported as such.
  4. Docking and measured potency disagree — and the disagreement is data. PBP2a (docking winner has the weakest Kd) and BACE1 (strongest measured binder docks worse than the reference) both show Vina ranking diverging from assay history; the paper's claim must be that docking is a triage filter, not a potency predictor. In both cases the report picks the wet-lab candidate on measured potency, not on docking.
  5. Thin data is the week's second theme. PBP2a (4 ligands) and MmpL3 (3 ligands, homologue only) show how little measured data exists for some high-burden targets — the screen can only rank what ChEMBL holds, and the report says so.
  6. Target risk outranks binding scores. BACE1's Phase III history (verubecestat: EPOCH futility 2017, APECS 2018, NEJM 2018) means a better binder would still face the same clinical question — a point the daily report states, and the paper must keep.
  7. Limitations. Computational only; no synthesis, no assays, no wet-lab validation in this draft. ChEMBL assay heterogeneity, ToxGuard read-across weakness, ±1 kcal/mol docking noise, single-gene runs, one invalid run (integrase) with no re-run yet. Weekly cadence means one target per method replicate — no cross-day replicates of the same target.

What this paper is NOT (for the author)

  • Not a discovery claim for any molecule.
  • Not a therapeutic, efficacy, or cure claim for any disease.
  • Not submission-ready: needs Zubair's authorship decisions, target-method narrative, figure set (workflow diagram, docking pose overlays, score distributions), and a chosen venue.
  • The HIV-1 integrase run must NOT be cited as an integrase result — it is a documented method failure, and a correct integrase re-run is still owed.

2026-10-25 Drug Discovery Draft — not submitted

Computational small-molecule triage against seven high-burden disease targets (week of 19-25 Oct 2026)

We describe a reproducible, fully automated computational triage pipeline that runs daily against one high-burden disease target, using only live public data sources (UniProtKB, ChEMBL, PubChem, the RCSB Protein Data Bank).

PDF · Markdown

Read full paper

AI-assisted draft — NOT peer-reviewed, NOT published. All claims require independent laboratory verification.

Author: Zubair Ali, Pharm-D student, SMBBMU Larkana, Pakistan · Drafting assistant: Lapis (AI)

Week of 2026-10-19 → 2026-10-25 (7 daily targets)

STATUS: DRAFT ONLY — never submit. Journal submission is Zubair's action under his own name.

Proposed title (placeholder)

"Computational small-molecule triage against seven high-burden disease targets using live public chemical data (LeadForge AI pipeline): a seven-day screening campaign"

Abstract

We describe a reproducible, fully automated computational triage pipeline that runs daily against one high-burden disease target, using only live public data sources (UniProtKB, ChEMBL, PubChem, the RCSB Protein Data Bank). Each daily run executes seven steps: (1) target identification from UniProtKB, (2) known-ligand retrieval from ChEMBL, (3) query-drug verification from PubChem, (4) Morgan-fingerprint / Tanimoto similarity screening with RDKit, (5) ADMET screening (Lipinski, Veber, PAINS, ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across), (6) composite-score lead ranking, and (7) AutoDock Vina docking (meeko ligand preparation) against the best available experimental structure. Across the week of 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-25 we screened seven targets spanning oncology (KRAS G12C, VEGFR2, ALK, JAK2), tuberculosis (DprE1) and antimicrobial resistance (NDM-1, KPC-2). Each run included a rediscovery control (verifying the pipeline recovers the reference drug or its scaffold from ChEMBL) and a head-to-head docking comparison between ranked leads and the reference therapy. Honest interpretation is enforced at every step: docking margins within ±1 kcal/mol are reported as noise-equivalent, boron-containing references that Vina cannot dock are reported as non-comparable rather than as losses, and all candidates are presented as computational starting points requiring wet-lab validation. No efficacy or therapeutic claims are made.

Keywords: virtual screening; AutoDock Vina; ChEMBL; target triage; KRAS; VEGFR2; DprE1; NDM-1; KPC; ALK; JAK2

Introduction (draft)

Drug discovery for high-burden diseases in resource-limited settings needs a cheap, reproducible first filter: a computational triage step that converts open chemical data into a short wet-lab shortlist. This draft reports one week of daily automated screening from the LeadForge AI pipeline. The scope is deliberately narrow — computational candidate triage only — and the methods are designed so any other group can re-run them against the same live databases.

Target selection rationale

Targets were chosen for disease burden and the presence of a marketed or clinical-stage reference small molecule for head-to-head comparison: - Oncology: KRAS G12C (sotorasib), VEGFR2 (sunitinib), ALK (alectinib), JAK2 (ruxolitinib) - Tuberculosis: DprE1 (macozinone, clinical-stage) - Antimicrobial resistance: NDM-1 (taniborbactam), KPC-2 (relebactam)

Methods (draft)

7.1 Daily pipeline (identical all 7 days)

  1. Target identification: UniProtKB live search → human/pathogen protein, accession recorded.
  2. Known-ligand retrieval: ChEMBL target (accession-mapped), top bioactivities by pChEMBL.
  3. Query-drug verification: reference small-molecule drug confirmed live via PubChem PUG REST.
  4. Similarity screen: RDKit Morgan fingerprints, Tanimoto vs known actives, top 25 kept.
  5. ADMET screen: Lipinski / Veber rules, PAINS filters, ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays).
  6. Lead ranking: composite score (similarity 40 + Lipinski 20 + Veber 10 + PAINS 10 + tox 20).
  7. Docking: AutoDock Vina, meeko ligand prep, best available experimental structure (X-ray preferred), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses; reference drug docked head-to-head in the same grid.

7.2 Rediscovery control

Each run includes a rediscovery check: whether the pipeline recovers the reference drug's scaffold from the ChEMBL ligand set (positive controls validate the screen; negatives bound its recall).

7.3 Honest-interpretation rules (applied in every run)

  • Docking differences < ~1 kcal/mol = method noise, never "wins".
  • Boron-containing ligands (taniborbactam) cannot be prepared by Vina/PDBQT — reported as non-comparable, never as a loss or a win.
  • Measured Ki/IC50 values come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays — directional, not rankings.
  • When docking and measured potency disagree (JAK2, DprE1), the disagreement is reported, not averaged away.
  • ToxGuard outputs are kNN read-across: "no red flag found", not "proven safe".
  • All leads are existing ChEMBL compounds; patent paths need university/teacher review.

Results — weekly summary table

Thu 10-22 NDM-1 (C7C422) taniborbactam 26 CHEMBL3809719 (IC50 160 nM) N/A — reference undockable (boron), no head-to-head possible
Fri 10-23 KPC-2 (Q9F663) relebactam 4 CHEMBL5483057 (IC50 44 nM) +0.14 kcal/mol — noise; measured potency is the stronger signal

Per-target result notes (from daily reports)

  • KRAS G12C (10-19): strongest docking margin of the week. Rediscovery positive (sotorasib rank #1, score 95.9, sim 1.000). All four novel leads beat sotorasib on docking; best CHEMBL5892737 (−10.97) is also the strongest measured binder of the four (Kd 0.3 nM, pChEMBL 9.52) — the week's cleanest docking-plus-measured agreement. Structure PDB 9IAY, X-ray 0.95 Å.
  • VEGFR2 (10-20): three leads beat sunitinib by more than the noise floor: CHEMBL3954818 (−11.83, +1.88), CHEMBL3967940 (−11.75, +1.80), CHEMBL3930485 (−11.10, +1.15) vs sunitinib −9.95. Structure 2XIR, X-ray 1.50 Å, DFG-out conformation — pocket-bias caveat applies (a DFG-out pocket favours type-II-like chemotypes).
  • DprE1 (10-21): three benzothiazinone-family analogs beat macozinone on docking (CHEMBL4752208 −11.16 / +0.84, CHEMBL4763381 −10.69 / +0.37, CHEMBL4868912 −10.48 / +0.16 vs −10.32) — all within noise, and all three carry weaker measured IC50 values (50–200 nM) than macozinone (10 nM). Direct evidence that Vina ranking ≠ measured potency; reported as such. Structure 4P8N, 1.79 Å.
  • NDM-1 (10-22): two method lessons. First, the initial query resolved to the wrong protein (human MBLAC2, Q68D91) and was caught and re-run against the true bacterial enzyme (C7C422) — non-human targets need accession/organism verification before any run is trusted. Second, the reference taniborbactam contains boron, which Vina/PDBQT cannot type, so no head-to-head docking comparison exists; best combined candidate CHEMBL3809719 (IC50 160 nM, docking −7.44, non-boron scaffold, 0 Lipinski violations, PAINS-clean) is a starting point, not a winner. Structure 5XP6, X-ray 0.95 Å. Taniborbactam was also not recovered as a ChEMBL ligand (clinical boronate absent from NDM-1 bioactivity records).
  • KPC-2 (10-23): only 4 known KPC ligands retrieved — the thinnest ligand set of the week, all diazabicyclooctane (DBO) analogs of relebactam, so chemical novelty is low. CHEMBL3989959 docked best (−7.66 vs relebactam −7.34, +0.32, noise) but has the weakest measured IC50 (869 nM); CHEMBL5483057 (−7.48, +0.14) carries the strongest measured activity (44 nM) and is the shortlist pick on measured potency, not docking. Structure 6TD0, X-ray 0.99 Å.
  • ALK (10-24): two leads beat alectinib within noise: CHEMBL3946496 (−10.14, +0.65) and CHEMBL3929615 (−10.12, +0.63) vs −9.49. Both are close alectinib analogs with reported sub-nM IC50 values (0.32 / 0.30 nM) — analog series, not scaffold hops. Rediscovery positive (alectinib rank #1, sim 1.0, score 98.3). Structure 4Z55.
  • JAK2 (10-25): CHEMBL3652404 docked −6.82 vs ruxolitinib −6.57 (+0.25, noise) with measured IC50 0.0165 nM, Lipinski/Veber pass, PAINS-clean. The week's clearest docking-vs-measured disconnect: all top leads are sub-nM actives yet dock weakly (−4.6 to −6.8), so measured IC50 is the stronger signal here and docking is secondary. All top leads share the pyrrolo-pyrimidine core — analog family, low Tanimoto (0.21–0.25) but shared core. Structure 8BXH, X-ray 1.3 Å. Rediscovery positive (ruxolitinib rank #1, sim 1.0, score 98.6).

Weekly tallies (final)

  • 7/7 runs completed with docking numbers; 1 (NDM-1) with no reference head-to-head (boron limit, documented honestly).
  • Rediscovery positives: 5 of 7 (KRAS, ALK, JAK2 confirmed; VEGFR2/DprE1/KPC reports imply query recovery — verify against daily JSONs before citing); NDM-1 negative (reference absent from ChEMBL).
  • Above-noise docking margins: 2 runs (KRAS +2.46, VEGFR2 +1.88/+1.80/+1.15) — still assay-gated, never declared wins.
  • Within-noise "better than reference" candidates: 4 runs (DprE1, KPC, ALK, JAK2) — priority candidates only.
  • Novelty: analog series in 5 runs (DprE1, KPC, ALK, JAK2, plus VEGFR2 chemotype family); scaffold hops modest (KRAS leads at Tanimoto 0.16); NDM-1's non-boron chemotype is the most structurally distinct output of the week.

Discussion (draft)

  1. Rediscovery is the screen's calibration. Three runs independently re-found the reference scaffold at Tanimoto 1.00 (KRAS, ALK, JAK2) — evidence the similarity screen recovers genuine actives.
  2. Noise discipline kept every head-to-head honest. Only KRAS and VEGFR2 cleared the ±1 kcal/mol floor, and even those are reported as assay-gated candidates, not discoveries.
  3. Docking and measured potency disagree — and the disagreement is data. DprE1 (beaters weaker on IC50) and JAK2 (sub-nM actives docking weakly) both show Vina ranking diverging from assay history; the paper's claim must be that docking is a triage filter, not a potency predictor.
  4. Structure and tooling limits shape the answer. The NDM-1 boron failure and the VEGFR2 DFG-out pocket show how the experimental structure and the docking engine constrain what the screen can say — documented per-run, not averaged away.
  5. Novelty is uneven. KPC's 4-ligand DBO set and ALK's close analogs are weak patent footing; KRAS's low-similarity leads and NDM-1's non-boron chemotype are the stronger starting points for analog design.
  6. Limitations. Computational only; no synthesis, no assays, no wet-lab validation in this draft. ChEMBL assay heterogeneity, ToxGuard read-across weakness, ±1 kcal/mol docking noise, single-gene runs. Weekly cadence means one target per method replicate — no cross-day replicates of the same target.

What this paper is NOT (for the author)

  • Not a discovery claim for any molecule.
  • Not a therapeutic, efficacy, or cure claim for any disease.
  • Not submission-ready: needs Zubair's authorship decisions, target-method narrative, figure set (workflow diagram, docking pose overlays, score distributions), and a chosen venue.

Proposed title (placeholder)

"Computational small-molecule triage against seven high-burden disease targets using live public chemical data (LeadForge AI pipeline): a seven-day screening campaign"

Abstract

We describe a reproducible, fully automated computational triage pipeline that runs daily against one high-burden disease target, using only live public data sources (UniProtKB, ChEMBL, PubChem, the RCSB Protein Data Bank). Each daily run executes seven steps: (1) target identification from UniProtKB, (2) known-ligand retrieval from ChEMBL, (3) query-drug verification from PubChem, (4) Morgan-fingerprint / Tanimoto similarity screening with RDKit, (5) ADMET screening (Lipinski, Veber, PAINS, ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across), (6) composite-score lead ranking, and (7) AutoDock Vina docking (meeko ligand preparation) against the best available experimental structure. Across the week of 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-18 we screened seven targets spanning antimicrobial resistance (S. aureus DHFR, P. falciparum DHFR-TS), oncology (CDK4, PARP1), and cardiometabolic disease (HMGCR, GLP1R, PCSK9). Each run included a rediscovery control (verifying the pipeline recovers the reference drug or its scaffold from ChEMBL) and a head-to-head docking comparison between ranked leads and the reference therapy. [TODO: add final tallies once PCSK9 completes.] Honest interpretation is enforced at every step: docking margins within ±1 kcal/mol are reported as noise-equivalent, resistant-allele strain effects are flagged, and all candidates are presented as computational starting points requiring wet-lab validation. No efficacy or therapeutic claims are made.

Keywords: virtual screening; AutoDock Vina; ChEMBL; target triage; DHFR; CDK4; PARP1; HMGCR; GLP1R; PCSK9

Introduction (draft)

Drug discovery for high-burden diseases in resource-limited settings needs a cheap, reproducible first filter: a computational triage step that converts open chemical data into a short wet-lab shortlist. This draft reports one week of daily automated screening from the LeadForge AI pipeline. The scope is deliberately narrow — computational candidate triage only — and the methods are designed so any other group can re-run them against the same live databases.

Target selection rationale

Targets were chosen for disease burden and the presence of a marketed reference small molecule for head-to-head comparison: - Antimicrobial: S. aureus DHFR (dfrA, trimethoprim resistance), P. falciparum DHFR-TS (pyrimethamine resistance) - Oncology: CDK4 (palbociclib), PARP1 (olaparib) - Cardiometabolic: HMGCR (atorvastatin), GLP1R (orforglipron), PCSK9 (enlicitide)

Methods (draft)

7.1 Daily pipeline (identical all 7 days)

  1. Target identification: UniProtKB live search → human/pathogen protein, accession recorded.
  2. Known-ligand retrieval: ChEMBL target (accession-mapped), top ~50 bioactivities by pChEMBL.
  3. Query-drug verification: reference small-molecule drug confirmed live via PubChem PUG REST.
  4. Similarity screen: RDKit Morgan fingerprints, Tanimoto vs known actives, top 25 kept.
  5. ADMET screen: Lipinski / Veber rules, PAINS filters, ToxGuard Tox21 kNN read-across (12 assays).
  6. Lead ranking: composite score (similarity 40 + Lipinski 20 + Veber 10 + PAINS 10 + tox 20).
  7. Docking: AutoDock Vina, meeko ligand prep, best available experimental structure (X-ray preferred, cryo-EM where no X-ray exists), box 22.5 Å, exhaustiveness 8, 3 poses; reference drug docked head-to-head in the same grid.

7.2 Rediscovery control

Each run includes a rediscovery check: whether the pipeline recovers the reference drug's scaffold from the ChEMBL ligand set (positive controls validate the screen; negatives bound its recall).

7.3 Honest-interpretation rules (applied in every run)

  • Docking differences < ~1 kcal/mol = method noise, never "wins".
  • Resistant-allele structures (K1 P. falciparum, Tn4003 S. aureus) are flagged; head-to-head results against them are interpreted accordingly.
  • Measured Ki/IC50 values come from heterogeneous ChEMBL assays — directional, not rankings.
  • ToxGuard outputs are kNN read-across: "no red flag found", not "proven safe".
  • All leads are existing ChEMBL compounds; patent paths need university/teacher review.
